0.title: Ezekiel: The LORD Is There
0.overview:
The message. Ezekiel tells people who have lost everything that God has not lost them. The exiles in Babylon were sure that Jerusalem could never fall and that they would soon go home. God sent Ezekiel to tell them that the city would fall, and why: their idols had driven his glory out of his own temple. But the same God who judged them would gather them, wash them, give them “a new heart” and put his own Spirit within them (36:26–27), raise a dead people to life and come to live among them for ever. He would do it not because they deserved it, but “for the sake of my holy name” (36:22), so that all the world would “know that I am the LORD”. The book opens with the glory of God beside a foreign canal and ends with a city named “The LORD Is There” (48:35).

Background: the writer. Ezekiel was “the priest, the son of Buzi” (1:3), brought up to serve in the temple at Jerusalem. In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon took the city and carried King Jehoiachin into exile with 10,000 captives (2 Kings 24:14), Ezekiel among them. He lived at Tel-abib by the Chebar canal (3:15), an irrigation channel probably near Nippur, where the elders came to his house to consult him (8:1). In 593 BC, in “the thirtieth year” (1:1), probably his own age, when priests began to serve (Numbers 4:3), “the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God”. The man who would never serve in the temple was made a prophet. Jews and Christians have always received the book, written mostly in the first person, as Ezekiel’s. Some scholars of the last century broke it up and dated much of it centuries later, but most now agree that it comes substantially from Ezekiel himself; its single style, its dates and its careful design support that, and this commentary takes it as his own work.

When and where. His dated prophecies run from 593 BC to about 571 BC (1:2; 29:17). These were the last years of Judah’s kings. Babylon had set Zedekiah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, on the throne; he broke his oath and turned to Egypt (17:11–21), and Babylon came back. After a long siege the city fell in 587 or 586 BC and the temple was burned. Ezekiel in Babylon and his older contemporary Jeremiah in Jerusalem preached the same message, while Daniel served at Nebuchadnezzar’s court; Ezekiel most likely names him among the righteous (14:14). He probably did not live to see the exiles go home under Cyrus in 538 BC, but he saw much further than that.

The first hearers. The exiles clung to two false hopes: that they would soon be home, and that Jerusalem, with God’s house in it, was safe. Their prophets were “saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace” (13:10), and they blamed their fathers for their troubles (18:2). Ezekiel’s task was to break those hopes, to make each of them own his sin, and then, once the worst had happened, to give them a true hope. Many listened as to “one who sings lustful songs with a beautiful voice” (33:32), enjoying it and changing nothing.

The kind of writing. Ezekiel is prophecy of an unusual kind: visions that carry him to Jerusalem and back; sign-acts, messages acted out instead of spoken, such as lying on his side for 390 days (4:4–5); riddles, allegories and funeral songs. Several visions lean toward the apocalyptic writing of Daniel and Revelation, with pictures such as wheels full of eyes: ask what each picture means, not how it would look. Some have called Ezekiel mentally ill, but his strange acts were deliberate and explained: God’s way of making a deaf people see. Two allegories picture Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife in words meant to shock (chapters 16 and 23); they are about idolatry, and never excuse violence against any woman.

How the book makes its case. The glory of God frames the book. In the opening chapters (1–3) Ezekiel sees “the likeness of the glory of the LORD” (1:28) in Babylon and is made “a watchman for the house of Israel” (3:17). Then comes judgment on Jerusalem (4–24): sign-acts of siege and exile, idols in the temple and the glory leaving it (10:18; 11:23), and Israel’s history retold as unfaithfulness from the start. Yet the door stays open: “I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live” (18:32). Judgment turns on the nations that gloated over Judah’s fall, above all proud Tyre and Egypt, the broken reed Judah leaned on (25–32). Chapter 33 is the hinge: the news comes, “The city has been struck down” (33:21), and the prophet’s mouth is opened. Now the promises pour out (34–37): God will shepherd his flock, give a new heart and his Spirit, and raise dry bones. Gog’s last assault is crushed (38–39). Finally, in a vision of a new temple and land (40–48), “the glory of the LORD filled the temple” (43:5), a river flows out to heal the Dead Sea, and the city is named for God’s presence.

Gog and the temple: future events or pictures? Christians read the last chapters differently. Many dispensationalists expect Gog to be a literal invasion of the land of Israel still to come, and the temple of chapters 40–48 to be built in a future millennium, with memorial sacrifices. They want to honour every detail of God’s promises, and are our brothers and sisters in Christ. Others read these chapters as prophetic pictures: Gog as the last gathering of the nations against God’s people, and the measured temple, river and city as God dwelling in holiness with a cleansed people. This commentary’s view is the second, because the New Testament reads them that way. Revelation uses “Gog and Magog” for the nations gathered against “the camp of the saints” (Revelation 20:8–9), not a modern state such as Russia, and in the new Jerusalem John “saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). After Christ’s sacrifice “there is no longer any offering for sin” (Hebrews 10:18).

Where it leads: to Christ. Ezekiel leads to Christ by the need it lays bare, by promise and by pattern. The need is a heart of stone that no law could soften. The promise is a shepherd: “I, I myself will search for my sheep” (34:11), and “one shepherd, my servant David” (34:23). Jesus is both: the Lord who came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10) and David’s son, “the good shepherd” who “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He told Nicodemus that one must be “born of water and the Spirit” (John 3:5), the washing and new heart of 36:25–27. The pattern is the temple and the glory. The glory that left Jerusalem came back in a man: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). He called his body the temple (John 2:19–21), and he is the Lamb from whose throne flows “the river of the water of life” (Revelation 22:1). Ezekiel was “son of man”, only a man before the glory; Jesus, taking the title from Daniel 7, is the Son of Man who is the glory.

For us. Ezekiel is for anyone who has felt far from God, watched something precious fall, or wondered whether a dead heart can live. It strips away false comfort, such as a religion that entertains but never changes us, and puts us where Ezekiel stood: face down before a holy God. Then it shows that God saves sinners for his own name’s sake, which is why his salvation cannot fail. In Christ he has washed us, given us his Spirit and made us his dwelling. “Son of man, can these bones live?” (37:3). By his word and Spirit, they can. And the last words of the book are the hope of every believer: “The LORD Is There”.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I was among the exiles by the Chebar canal, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.<sup>2</sup>On the fifth day of the month (it was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin),<sup>3</sup>the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the Chebar canal, and the hand of the LORD was upon him there.<sup>4</sup>As I looked, behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually, and in the midst of the fire, as it were gleaming metal.<sup>5</sup>And from the midst of it came the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance: they had a human likeness,<sup>6</sup>but each had four faces, and each of them had four wings.<sup>7</sup>Their legs were straight, and the soles of their feet were like the sole of a calf's foot. And they sparkled like burnished bronze.<sup>8</sup>Under their wings on their four sides they had human hands. And the four had their faces and their wings thus:<sup>9</sup>their wings touched one another. Each one of them went straight forward, without turning as they went.<sup>10</sup>As for the likeness of their faces, each had a human face. The four had the face of a lion on the right side, the four had the face of an ox on the left side, and the four had the face of an eagle.<sup>11</sup>Such were their faces. And their wings were spread out above. Each creature had two wings, each of which touched the wing of another, while two covered their bodies.<sup>12</sup>And each went straight forward. Wherever the spirit would go, they went, without turning as they went.<sup>13</sup>As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of torches moving to and fro among the living creatures. And the fire was bright, and out of the fire went forth lightning.<sup>14</sup>And the living creatures darted to and fro, like the appearance of a flash of lightning.<sup>15</sup>Now as I looked at the living creatures, I saw a wheel on the earth beside the living creatures, one for each of the four of them.<sup>16</sup>As for the appearance of the wheels and their construction: their appearance was like the gleaming of beryl. And the four had the same likeness, their appearance and construction being as it were a wheel within a wheel.<sup>17</sup>When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went.<sup>18</sup>And their rims were tall and awesome, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.<sup>19</sup>And when the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them; and when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose.<sup>20</sup>Wherever the spirit wanted to go, they went, and the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.<sup>21</sup>When those went, these went; and when those stood, these stood; and when those rose from the earth, the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.<sup>22</sup>Over the heads of the living creatures there was the likeness of an expanse, shining like awe-inspiring crystal, spread out above their heads.<sup>23</sup>And under the expanse their wings were stretched out straight, one toward another. And each creature had two wings covering its body.<sup>24</sup>And when they went, I heard the sound of their wings like the sound of many waters, like the sound of the Almighty, a sound of tumult like the sound of an army. When they stood still, they let down their wings.<sup>25</sup>And there came a voice from above the expanse over their heads. When they stood still, they let down their wings.<sup>26</sup>And above the expanse over their heads there was the likeness of a throne, in appearance like sapphire; and seated above the likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance.<sup>27</sup>And upward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were gleaming metal, like the appearance of fire enclosed all around. And downward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and there was brightness around him.<sup>28</sup>Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God meets his people where they are, even in exile. The opening is precise because it is real: a date, a canal and a man. Ezekiel, a priest who should have been starting his work at the temple, is a deportee by the Chebar canal in Babylon, five years after King Jehoiachin was taken (vv. 1–2). There, far from the holy city, the heavens are opened and he sees visions of God. Three things come to him together: the visions, the word of the LORD and the hand of the LORD upon him (v. 3). The God whose house stood in Jerusalem has come to the exiles.
verseByVerse.theology: The God of Israel is not confined to Jerusalem; he opens heaven over his people in exile.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I was among the exiles by the Chebar canal, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God. On the fifth day of the month (it was the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin), the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the Chebar canal, and the hand of the LORD was upon him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far from the temple, a priest who could not serve sees the heavens open: God has come to his people in exile.

By the Chebar canal. Ezekiel is not in the temple courts but hundreds of miles away in Babylon, beside an irrigation canal with a settlement of deported Judeans. Five years earlier the Babylonians had emptied Jerusalem of its king, its officials, its soldiers and its skilled workers (2 Kings 24:14–15), and Ezekiel was among them.

In the thirtieth year. Probably Ezekiel’s own age (see the box below), which would make it a painful birthday: thirty was the age at which a priest began “to do the work in the tent of meeting” (Numbers 4:3). The year he should have started serving at the altar, he was a refugee with no temple within reach.

The heavens were opened. Exactly there. God did not wait for Ezekiel to get back to the holy city; he came to the place of exile. “Visions of God” are both from God and of God.

The fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin. The exiles counted time from the day their king was taken. It is about 593 BC; Jerusalem still stands, and many expect to go home soon.

The hand of the LORD was upon him. Visions to see, a word to hear, and the LORD’s hand gripping him. Ezekiel is a priest by birth but will work as a prophet, and his book is full of what a priest cares about: holiness, glory, the temple, and how a holy God can live among an unclean people.

Heaven opened. At the Jordan “the heavens were opened” over Jesus (Matthew 3:16), and he promised, “you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51). What Ezekiel was given for a moment, Christ has made lasting: in him heaven stands open to exiles.

For anyone far from home. This is the book’s first word to anyone who feels far from where God is supposed to be: in a hospital, a prison, a foreign country, a season of spiritual dryness. “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Psalm 139:7).

Uncertain wording. No one knows for certain what “the thirtieth year” counts from. Ezekiel’s age is likeliest, since verse 2 gives the official date and thirty was when priests began to serve. Others suggest thirty years from the finding of the Book of the Law under Josiah (about 622 BC), but no such reckoning is used elsewhere. Nothing in the passage depends on it.
verseByVerse.note: Ezekiel was taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC; his call came five years later, in 593 BC.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who has come to Babylon is holy fire, attended by mighty servants. A storm sweeps in from the north with cloud, fire and something gleaming at its heart, the signs that went with God’s coming at Sinai (v. 4). Out of it come four living creatures, later named as cherubim: human in form, each with four faces, four wings and gleaming feet (vv. 5–9). Their faces of man, lion, ox and eagle gather the strength of creation around God’s throne (v. 10). They go straight ahead wherever the spirit goes, never turning (vv. 11–12), and they burn and flash like coals, torches and lightning (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The living creatures show a God of overwhelming majesty, whose servants move only at his Spirit's direction.

verseByVerse.quote: As I looked, behold, a stormy wind came out of the north, and a great cloud, with brightness around it, and fire flashing forth continually, and in the midst of the fire, as it were gleaming metal. And from the midst of it came the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance: they had a human likeness, but each had four faces, and each of them had four wings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of a storm like the one at Sinai come four living creatures, the cherubim who bear God’s throne.

A stormy wind came out of the north. Storm, cloud, fire and brightness went with God’s appearing at Sinai, where “there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain” and “the LORD had descended on it in fire” (Exodus 19:16, 18). The storm comes out of the north, the direction from which Jeremiah had said disaster would break upon Judah (Jeremiah 1:14), because armies from Mesopotamia reached the land by the northern route round the desert. The vision begins from the quarter where Judah’s danger lay.

As it were. Ezekiel keeps saying “as it were”, “likeness”, “appearance”. What he saw was real but beyond ordinary language, so he can only say what it was like.

Four living creatures. Later Ezekiel sees the same beings again and says, “I knew that they were cherubim” (10:20). Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24), and their golden images spread their wings over the ark in the Most Holy Place, where God said, “There I will meet with you” (Exodus 25:22). Israel praised God as “enthroned upon the cherubim” (Psalm 80:1). So the throne that belonged in the Most Holy Place has come to Babylon. God’s presence has not been captured in a building.

Is talk of God only poetry? Many suspect so: if believers must fall back on “likeness” and “appearance”, perhaps religious language is moving but about nothing. Yet words strain wherever people meet something larger than themselves. Physicists say light behaves in some ways like a wave and in others like a particle, without being simply either, and no one concludes that light is imaginary. Lovers and mourners reach for pictures because plain words are too small, not because nothing is there. And Ezekiel’s caution is itself evidence: a man inventing a god would describe him confidently; this man is struggling to report what overwhelmed him. We cannot know God fully, but we can know him truly, because he is a person who chooses to speak. The chapter ends not with a better description but with a voice (v. 28), and the God who spoke by the prophets “at many times and in many ways” has “in these last days … spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “gleaming metal” (ḥashmal, also in v. 27 and 8:2) occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament, and its exact meaning is not known. The ESV margin offers “amber”, following the ancient Greek translation, whose word can mean amber or electrum, an alloy of gold and silver; others suggest polished bronze. Whatever the substance, Ezekiel means something glowing at the heart of the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: Their legs were straight, and the soles of their feet were like the sole of a calf's foot. And they sparkled like burnished bronze. Under their wings on their four sides they had human hands. And the four had their faces and their wings thus: their wings touched one another. Each one of them went straight forward, without turning as they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The creatures picture perfect service: strong, ready, moving as one, and never turning aside.

They sparkled like burnished bronze. Every detail speaks of strength and readiness: feet that shine like polished bronze, hands ready for work under the wings, and wings touching so that the four move as a single square.

Without turning as they went. This detail keeps returning (vv. 9, 12, 17). Facing every direction at once, the creatures never need to turn round, and they do not waver, hesitate or turn aside. Here is what God’s service looks like: single-minded, whole-hearted, going where he sends without looking back. “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God”, Jesus said (Luke 9:62).

verseByVerse.quote: As for the likeness of their faces, each had a human face. The four had the face of a lion on the right side, the four had the face of an ox on the left side, and the four had the face of an eagle. Such were their faces. And their wings were spread out above. Each creature had two wings, each of which touched the wing of another, while two covered their bodies. And each went straight forward. Wherever the spirit would go, they went, without turning as they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The four faces gather the noblest of creation around God’s throne, and the creatures go only where the spirit goes.

The likeness of their faces. A man, a lion, an ox, an eagle. Many readers have seen in each the chief of its kind: man, the lion among wild beasts, the ox among farm animals, the eagle among birds. Together they suggest all the strength, wisdom and swiftness of creation gathered to serve God.

Two covered their bodies. Even these mighty beings cover themselves before God, as the seraphim covered their faces and feet in Isaiah’s vision (Isaiah 6:2).

Wherever the spirit would go, they went. The ESV notes that “spirit” may be rendered “Spirit”. The creatures have no plans of their own; they want only what God wants, so perfect obedience is their perfect freedom.

Around the throne in heaven. John saw the same four around the throne: “the first living creature like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature with the face of a man, and the fourth living creature like an eagle in flight”, and “day and night they never cease to say, ‘Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty’” (Revelation 4:7–8). The creatures in the storm are worshippers: what is greatest in creation exists to adore God.

Led by the Spirit. This is the pattern for every believer. Jesus said, “The wind blows where it wishes … So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8). A life led by God’s Spirit is not aimless; it goes straight, wherever he leads.

What it does not mean. From early times Christians matched the four faces with the four Gospels. It is a pleasing picture for a church window, but neither Ezekiel nor John decodes the faces one by one; together they show the whole of living creation gathered in worship around the throne.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like the appearance of torches moving to and fro among the living creatures. And the fire was bright, and out of the fire went forth lightning. And the living creatures darted to and fro, like the appearance of a flash of lightning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God these creatures serve is holy fire, not a tame helper.

Like burning coals of fire. With coals, torches and lightning, the whole vision is alive with fire and speed. Fire in Scripture speaks of God’s holiness, his purity that burns up what is unclean: “our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). Ezekiel is about to be sent to a people who have treated God lightly, and before he says a word to them he must see that the God they have despised is fire. Holy fire is good news only for those sheltered from it, which is why this throne will turn out to be ringed with a rainbow (v. 28).

Why this matters. The church in every age is tempted to think of God as a comfortable helper who fits into our plans. The God of Ezekiel 1 is utterly beyond our control, and he comes in the storm.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s throne is not fixed in one place: it sees everything and can go anywhere. Beside each creature stands a gleaming wheel, built as a wheel within a wheel, so that it can roll in any of four directions without turning (vv. 15–17). The rims are tall, awesome and full of eyes all around (v. 18). The wheels go, stand and rise with the creatures, because the spirit of the creatures is in them (vv. 19–21), and Ezekiel repeats himself to drive the point home: one will moves the whole throne, and nothing in it pulls against anything else. Jerusalem could not keep God in, and Babylon could not keep him out.
verseByVerse.theology: God's throne is not fixed to one place; it goes anywhere, and it sees everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as I looked at the living creatures, I saw a wheel on the earth beside the living creatures, one for each of the four of them. As for the appearance of the wheels and their construction: their appearance was like the gleaming of beryl. And the four had the same likeness, their appearance and construction being as it were a wheel within a wheel. When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went. And their rims were tall and awesome, and the rims of all four were full of eyes all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s throne goes anywhere and sees everything: a warning to those who thought him shut in their temple, a comfort to exiles who feared he had lost sight of them.

A wheel within a wheel. Wheels mean movement. “A wheel within a wheel” is perhaps two wheels set crosswise, so that they can roll in any direction (v. 17).

A throne on the move. Jerusalem believed God would never leave his temple; the exiles feared he had been left behind there. The wheels answer both errors. God’s throne can go anywhere: to judge a city that trusts in its temple, and to meet exiles by a canal. Solomon had said it at the temple’s dedication: “heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27).

Full of eyes all around. Nothing escapes this God: “The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good” (Proverbs 15:3). That is a warning to the people in Jerusalem who thought no one saw what they did in secret (8:12), and a comfort to exiles who feared they had dropped out of God’s sight: “the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him” (2 Chronicles 16:9). The same eyes that expose sin watch over the faithful.

Are the wheels a UFO? No. Ezekiel calls the whole sight “the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD” (v. 28): the wheels are the throne of God in motion. Nor should each rim, spoke and eye be given its own hidden meaning. Ezekiel gives one key to the whole, the glory of the LORD, and the details pile up into one overwhelming impression: a living throne that sees everything and can go anywhere.

Uncertain wording. How “a wheel within a wheel” was built is not said; verse 17 gives the point: it could go any way without turning. The Hebrew of verse 18 is compressed, literally something like their rims, and height to them, and dread to them, which the ESV renders “tall and awesome”. The stone called “beryl” (v. 16) cannot be identified for certain.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them; and when the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels rose. Wherever the spirit wanted to go, they went, and the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels. When those went, these went; and when those stood, these stood; and when those rose from the earth, the wheels rose along with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creatures, wheels and spirit move as one: nothing in God’s rule of history pulls against anything else.

When those went, these went. Ezekiel repeats himself as if the sight is too big to take in. Everything moves together because one spirit drives it all. The ESV notes that “the spirit of the living creatures” may also be read “the spirit of life”.

One will, done at once. What God wills is done, completely. Paul speaks of the God “who works all things according to the counsel of his will” and who has seated Christ at his right hand, “far above all rule and authority” (Ephesians 1:11, 20–21).

When history seems out of control. To the exiles history seemed to be spinning out of control, with Babylon rising and Judah collapsing. But over the storm is a throne, and the wheels of history go only where the Spirit of God sends them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–28 — The Likeness of the Glory of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the summit of the vision is a throne, and on it a figure like a man, blazing with glory and ringed with covenant mercy. Ezekiel’s eyes climb. Above the creatures is an expanse shining like crystal, and their wings roar like many waters until a voice comes from above and they fall still (vv. 22–25). Above the expanse is a throne like sapphire, and on it a likeness with a human appearance, fire from the waist upward and downward, with brightness all around (vv. 26–27). The brightness is like a rainbow in the clouds. This, says Ezekiel, was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD; he fell on his face and heard a voice (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Ezekiel's ministry begins where all true ministry begins: face down before the glory of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Over the heads of the living creatures there was the likeness of an expanse, shining like awe-inspiring crystal, spread out above their heads. And under the expanse their wings were stretched out straight, one toward another. And each creature had two wings covering its body. And when they went, I heard the sound of their wings like the sound of many waters, like the sound of the Almighty, a sound of tumult like the sound of an army. When they stood still, they let down their wings. And there came a voice from above the expanse over their heads. When they stood still, they let down their wings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above the creatures is the crystal floor of heaven, and the roar of their wings falls silent so that a voice from above can speak.

The likeness of an expanse. Ezekiel’s eyes move upward to a platform shining like crystal. The word is the one used for the “expanse” of the sky in Genesis 1:6–8; Ezekiel sees, as it were, the floor of heaven. When Moses and the elders saw God at Sinai, “There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness” (Exodus 24:10).

Like the sound of many waters. Now sound joins sight. The wings roar like a waterfall or the ocean, “like the sound of the Almighty”, like an army on the move. When John saw the risen Christ, “his voice was like the roar of many waters” (Revelation 1:15): the sound that rose from the wings of the throne’s bearers, John heard from the mouth of Jesus.

A voice from above the expanse. Then everything stops. The wings drop, and the whole spectacle falls silent so that God can speak; all Ezekiel has seen prepares him to hear. It is the same in our worship: all the glory of God is meant to bring us to silence before his word.

verseByVerse.quote: And above the expanse over their heads there was the likeness of a throne, in appearance like sapphire; and seated above the likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance. And upward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were gleaming metal, like the appearance of fire enclosed all around. And downward from what had the appearance of his waist I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and there was brightness around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the throne at the top of the vision is a likeness with a human appearance, blazing with divine fire: the glory of God in human form, which the New Testament shows us in Jesus.

A likeness with a human appearance. Above everything is a throne like sapphire (the ESV notes it may be “lapis lazuli”). Ezekiel does not say he saw God’s face, for “man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20); he saw a likeness. Yet it is astonishing that the form on the throne of the universe looked like a man.

Fire above and fire below. Gleaming metal (see the box on vv. 4–6) and fire above, fire below, brightness all around. John’s vision of the risen Jesus is strikingly similar: “his eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze, refined in a furnace”, and “his face was like the sun shining in full strength” (Revelation 1:14–16). The man on the throne is not less than God.

The glory of God has a human face. The New Testament explains why. “No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). John says that Isaiah, who saw the Lord on his throne, “saw his glory and spoke of him”, that is, of Jesus (John 12:41). The glory of God has a human face because the eternal Son took our nature: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). Ezekiel saw a likeness. We know the name.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud on the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The throne of judgment is ringed with the rainbow of covenant mercy, and the sight of the glory puts Ezekiel on his face to hear God’s voice.

The bow that is in the cloud. Around the throne is a rainbow. After the flood God told Noah, “I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant”, and “When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant” (Genesis 9:13, 16). John saw it too: “around the throne was a rainbow” (Revelation 4:3).

Judgment ringed with mercy. Ezekiel is about to be sent to announce judgment on Jerusalem, yet the throne of that judgment is ringed with the sign of God’s covenant mercy. Judgment is real, but it comes from a God who remembers his promises. The storm does not have the last word; the rainbow does.

The likeness of the glory of the LORD. The layers of caution are deliberate: the appearance, of the likeness, of the glory. Ezekiel has not seen God as he is in himself, only his glory, and that only in likeness. Yet it is enough to put him flat on the ground.

I fell on my face. That is the only right response. Isaiah said, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). John “fell at his feet as though dead” (Revelation 1:17). Saul of Tarsus, blinded by “a light from heaven”, fell to the ground (Acts 9:3–4).

The thread through the book. This glory runs through the whole book. Ezekiel will watch it leave the temple and stand on the mountain east of Jerusalem (11:22–23), and he will watch it come back: “the glory of the LORD filled the temple” (43:5). The book ends with a city named “The LORD Is There” (48:35). Christians know where that glory came to live: “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Has it put us on our faces? A God who never humbles us is not the God of Ezekiel 1. But what follows matters as much: “I heard the voice of one speaking”. God did not show Ezekiel his glory to crush him but to speak to him, and his next words will be “stand on your feet” (2:1). The glory that throws us down is the glory that raises us up and sends us out.

1.title: Visions of God by the Chebar Canal
1.overview:
Where we are. The book opens with a date, a place and a vision. Ezekiel, a priest who has never served in the temple, has lived five years among the deportees in Babylon (see the introduction). This chapter and the next two tell of his call.

The message. God has not been left behind in Jerusalem, and he cannot be shut up in it. His throne is alive, sees everything and goes wherever his Spirit wills, even to refugees beside a foreign canal. He is holy fire, about to judge his own people; yet his throne is ringed with the rainbow of his covenant mercy, and the glory that throws a man on his face is a glory that speaks.

Why it was said. The exiles tied God’s presence to his temple: some were sure he would never let Jerusalem fall, others feared they were beyond his reach (see the introduction). Before hearing that the city would fall, they needed to see a God far greater than the city.

How the chapter makes its case. Heaven opens over an exile in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity (vv. 1–3). Out of a storm from the north come four living creatures with four faces and four wings, burning like coals and moving wherever the spirit goes (vv. 4–14). Beside them are wheels full of eyes that can roll in any direction, because the creatures’ spirit is in them (vv. 15–21). Then Ezekiel’s eyes climb: above the creatures a crystal expanse, from which a voice silences their roaring wings (vv. 22–25); above that a throne, and on it a likeness with a human appearance, blazing with fire and ringed by a rainbow (vv. 26–28). He falls on his face and hears a voice.

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ, as the New Testament shows. The glory on the throne had “a human appearance” (v. 26), and John says of Jesus, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The risen Christ appears to John with eyes like fire and a voice like many waters (Revelation 1:14–15), and around the throne in heaven are the same four creatures and the same rainbow (Revelation 4:3, 6–7). The glory Ezekiel saw only in likeness is now “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

For us. No place is too far for God’s glory to reach: not a hospital ward, a prison cell or a long season of dryness. A faith that has never put us on our faces has not yet met the God of Ezekiel 1; but the God who throws us down speaks next, and his word is “stand on your feet” (2:1).
1.theology:
God is not confined to a place. He opens heaven over his people in exile, and his throne moves wherever his Spirit wills (vv. 1, 15-21; 1 Kgs 8:27; Ps 139:7-10).

God is holy fire and overwhelming majesty; the mightiest creatures cover themselves before him and exist to worship him (vv. 4, 11, 13-14; Rev 4:6-8; Heb 12:29).

God sees everything, to expose the wicked and to support the faithful (v. 18; Prov 15:3; 2 Chr 16:9).

Nothing in history pulls against God's rule: everything moves where his Spirit sends it (vv. 12, 19-21).

The throne of judgment is surrounded by the sign of covenant mercy (v. 28; Gen 9:13-16; Rev 4:3).

The glory on the throne appeared in human likeness, pointing to the incarnate Son, in whom the glory of God is fully seen (vv. 26-28; John 1:14, 18; 12:41; 2 Cor 4:6; Heb 1:3; Rev 1:13-17).

Truly knowing God humbles a person before it sends him out: the prophet falls on his face and hears the voice (v. 28; Isa 6:5).
1.examples:
A priest, perhaps on his thirtieth birthday, sits by a canal in Babylon, and the heavens open over a refugee settlement. He sees a throne on wheels, creatures whose faces turn every way so that they never have to turn back, and eyes on every rim.

Wings roar like a waterfall and fall silent for a voice. On the throne of the universe is a man, and around the storm a rainbow. Ezekiel ends face down, and the next word he hears is stand on your feet.

keyVerse.quote: Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking.
keyVerse.note: This sentence names everything Ezekiel has tried to describe: not God as he is in himself, but the appearance of the likeness of his glory, and even that is enough to throw him to the ground. It also sets the pattern of the whole book and of every true meeting with God: first humbled before the glory, then addressed by the voice. The glory seen here will leave Jerusalem and return (11:23; 43:5), and the New Testament shows it at last in the face of Jesus Christ.

1.reflection:
The heavens opened over Ezekiel not in the temple but among refugees by a canal in Babylon (vv. 1–3). Where have you felt furthest from God? What does this chapter say to that place?

Ezekiel keeps saying “likeness” and “appearance”, struggling to describe what he saw. How does his care with words help us speak about God both truly and humbly? Why does the chapter end with a voice rather than a clearer picture?

The wheels go anywhere and are full of eyes (vv. 15–21). Which comforts you more, and which unsettles you more: that God sees everything, or that he cannot be confined to the places where we expect him?

The throne of judgment is ringed with a rainbow, and the figure on it has a human appearance (vv. 26–28). How does knowing that this glory is seen in Jesus change the way you approach a holy God?

2.text: <sup>1</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you."<sup>2</sup>And as he spoke to me, the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me.<sup>3</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, I send you to the people of Israel, to nations of rebels, who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me to this very day.<sup>4</sup>The descendants also are impudent and stubborn: I send you to them, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.'<sup>5</sup>And whether they hear or refuse to hear (for they are a rebellious house) they will know that a prophet has been among them.<sup>6</sup>And you, son of man, be not afraid of them, nor be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with you and you sit on scorpions. Be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house.<sup>7</sup>And you shall speak my words to them, whether they hear or refuse to hear, for they are a rebellious house.<sup>8</sup>"But you, son of man, hear what I say to you. Be not rebellious like that rebellious house; open your mouth and eat what I give you."<sup>9</sup>And when I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me, and behold, a scroll of a book was in it.<sup>10</sup>And he spread it before me. And it had writing on the front and on the back, and there were written on it words of lamentation and mourning and woe.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God raises a mere man by his Spirit and sends him with God’s own words to people who have long refused them. The voice from the throne calls Ezekiel “son of man” and tells him to stand, and the Spirit enters him and sets him on his feet (vv. 1–2). He is sent to the people of Israel, a nation of rebels like their fathers before them, with the message “Thus says the Lord GOD”; whether they hear or refuse, they will know that a prophet has been among them (vv. 3–5). Though living among them will be like sitting on thorns and scorpions, he must not fear their words or their looks, but speak (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's success is measured by faithfulness to God's word, not by the response of his hearers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, stand on your feet, and I will speak with you." And as he spoke to me, the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls the prophet a mere “son of man”, commands him to stand, and by his Spirit does what he commands.

Son of man. Face down before the glory (1:28), Ezekiel hears a name and a command. The ESV notes that “son of man” may be rendered “son of Adam”. It means simply a human being, a mortal made of dust: “what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:4). Beside the blazing figure on the throne, Ezekiel is reminded what he is: a creature.

Why a man is sent. This is not an insult but the reason he is sent. God does not send angels to rebels; he sends a man, one of their own, weak and mortal, to carry his word.

Stand on your feet. God commands it, and then does it for him: “the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet”. What God requires, God supplies.

The Son of Man who came to die. Jesus often called himself “the Son of Man”. He drew chiefly on Daniel’s vision of “one like a son of man” who comes with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14), but he also took up all the lowliness of the name: “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20), and “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Ezekiel was a son of man sent to rebels. Jesus is the Son of Man who came to die for them.

In everyday life. We are commanded to stand, speak and obey, and cannot do it in our own strength: “our sufficiency is from God, who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:5–6).
verseByVerse.note: “Son of man” stresses Ezekiel’s humanity before God’s glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, I send you to the people of Israel, to nations of rebels, who have rebelled against me. They and their fathers have transgressed against me to this very day. The descendants also are impudent and stubborn: I send you to them, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.' And whether they hear or refuse to hear (for they are a rebellious house) they will know that a prophet has been among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends his prophet to generations of rebels with God’s own word, and measures success by faithfulness, not results.

Nations of rebels. God’s own people are called “nations of rebels”, as if no different from the pagans, and their rebellion runs back through their fathers. Their children are “impudent and stubborn”, literally hard of face and strong of heart, a phrase that returns when God hardens Ezekiel’s own face to match (3:7–9). And yet: “I send you to them.” God keeps sending messengers to people who have rejected every one before: patience beyond anything human.

Thus says the Lord GOD. The preacher’s authority is borrowed from God, which is both humbling and freeing: he does not have to be clever; he has to be faithful.

Whether they hear or refuse to hear. Success is not whether they hear, but that “they will know that a prophet has been among them”. The result is in God’s hands; the task is in Ezekiel’s. When his words come true, God says, “then they will know that a prophet has been among them” (33:33).

His own people did not receive him. Jesus lived this. “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). He was not a failure. He was faithful.

For those who see no response. This frees every pastor, missionary, parent or friend who has spoken the truth and seen nothing change. You are responsible for the speaking, not the hearing, and the Spirit who set Ezekiel on his feet gives the courage for that too.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, son of man, be not afraid of them, nor be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns are with you and you sit on scorpions. Be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house. And you shall speak my words to them, whether they hear or refuse to hear, for they are a rebellious house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life among hostile people will hurt, but the prophet must not be ruled by fear; he must speak God’s words whatever the response.

Be not afraid of them. Again and again: be not afraid, be not dismayed. God knows his servant will be tempted to fear what people say and how they look at him. He does not promise that it will not hurt; he commands him not to be ruled by fear.

The cure for fear. The fear of people is broken by the fear of God, and Ezekiel has just been on his face before the throne. Once you have seen that glory, the frowns of rebels shrink. Jesus gave his disciples the same cure: “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28).

You shall speak my words to them. This is the refrain of Ezekiel’s commission: my words, whether they hear or refuse. Paul charged Timothy in the same way: “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew words for “briers” and “thorns” are rare, the first found only here, so the exact plants are uncertain, and the ESV notes that “on scorpions” may be “on scorpion plants”. Either way the picture is plain: life among these people will scratch and sting.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — A Scroll of Lamentation and Mourning and Woe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The messenger must first receive and obey the message himself. Before he speaks to a rebellious house, Ezekiel is warned not to be rebellious like them, but to open his mouth and eat what God gives him (v. 8). A hand reaches out to him holding a scroll (v. 9). It is spread out before him, written on the front and on the back, full to the edges, with words of lamentation and mourning and woe (v. 10). That is the message he must carry, and the next chapter tells how he takes it in.
verseByVerse.theology: The messenger must first receive and submit to the word he is sent to deliver.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you, son of man, hear what I say to you. Be not rebellious like that rebellious house; open your mouth and eat what I give you." And when I looked, behold, a hand was stretched out to me, and behold, a scroll of a book was in it. And he spread it before me. And it had writing on the front and on the back, and there were written on it words of lamentation and mourning and woe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet must not rebel himself: he must take in God’s word, a scroll full of woe, before he gives it out.

Be not rebellious like that rebellious house. Now the warning turns on Ezekiel. The greatest danger to a preacher of repentance is not the hardness of his hearers but his own. Before he speaks the word, he must obey it, and his first test is to eat what God gives (see 3:1–3). “We who teach will be judged with greater strictness” (James 3:1).

Writing on the front and on the back. Scrolls were normally written on one side only. This one is full on both sides, with no room to add anything: the message is complete, and it is God’s, not Ezekiel’s. John saw a scroll like it in the right hand of the one on the throne, “written within and on the back” (Revelation 5:1), and no one was worthy to open it but the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:9).

Lamentation and mourning and woe. Ezekiel’s first years of ministry will be almost entirely bad news. But the book that begins with woe ends with a new heart, dry bones living, a river of life and a city called “The LORD Is There” (48:35). The woe is not the last word, but it has to be spoken first.

2.title: Son of Man, I Send You
2.overview:
Where we are. Ezekiel lies face down before the glory of the LORD by the Chebar canal (1:28). Chapters 2 and 3 record what the voice from the throne said to him there: his commission as a prophet.

The message. God sends a mere man, raised to his feet by God’s Spirit, to speak God’s own words to a people who have rebelled against him for generations. His success will not be measured by how many listen but by his faithfulness: whether they hear or refuse, they will know that a prophet has been among them. And before he speaks the word, he must take it in and obey it himself, even when it is a scroll full of woe.

Why it was said. The exiles were a hard audience: proud of their descent, sure of a quick return home, and listening to prophets who told them what they wanted to hear (see the introduction). Ezekiel needed to know before he began that he would be resisted, and that resistance would not mean he had failed.

How the chapter makes its case. The voice calls him “son of man” and tells him to stand, and the Spirit enters him and sets him on his feet (vv. 1–2). He is sent to a rebellious house with one message, “Thus says the Lord GOD”, and told that the outcome is not his to decide (vv. 3–5). Again and again he is told not to fear their words or their looks, though living among them will be like sitting among thorns and scorpions (vv. 6–7). Then the warning turns on him: he must not rebel like them, but open his mouth and eat what God gives; a hand holds out a scroll written on both sides with lamentation, mourning and woe (vv. 8–10).

Where it leads. The link is a pattern. Ezekiel is a son of man, a mortal sent to rebels with words that are not his own, enabled by the Spirit and refused by his own people. Jesus took the title “Son of Man”, drawing chiefly on Daniel 7 but embracing its lowliness too. He also was sent to his own, and “his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11); he spoke only what the Father gave him to say (John 12:49), and endured the hostility of sinners to the end (Hebrews 12:3). But Ezekiel could only announce the woe written on the scroll. Jesus came to bear it.

For us. Everyone who speaks for God, from the pulpit to the kitchen table, is a son or daughter of man: weak, dependent and sent. We are answerable for speaking faithfully, not for whether others listen, and we must not refuse the word ourselves before we pass it on. What God commands, his Spirit supplies.
2.theology:
God's messenger is a mortal, a son of man, enabled by the Spirit to stand and speak (vv. 1-2; Ps 8:4; 2 Cor 3:5-6). Jesus took the title in both its lowliness and its glory (Mark 10:45; Dan 7:13-14).

God keeps sending his word to a rebellious people; the preacher has no authority of his own, only Thus says the Lord GOD (vv. 3-4).

Faithfulness, not response, is the measure of a messenger (vv. 5, 7; 33:33; John 1:11).

The fear of people is overcome by the fear of God (v. 6).

The messenger must receive and obey the word before he delivers it (vv. 8-10; Jas 3:1).
2.examples: Ezekiel is given a name that means he is made of dust, and a command to stand, with the Spirit who stands him up. His success will not be measured by how many listen, though speaking will feel like sitting in a thorn bush on a nest of scorpions. And he is handed a scroll with no room left to write his own opinions.

keyVerse.quote: And you shall speak my words to them, whether they hear or refuse to hear, for they are a rebellious house.
keyVerse.note: This is Ezekiel’s commission in a single sentence, and it returns as a refrain (2:5; 3:11, 27). The words are God’s, the hearers are hard, and the outcome is not the prophet’s to decide; his task is to speak faithfully. That frees every servant of God from measuring obedience by results.

2.reflection:
God calls Ezekiel “son of man”, a reminder that he is a mortal creature, and then sends him precisely as one (vv. 1–3). Why does God so often choose weak human messengers rather than overwhelming ones? How does that encourage you?

God commanded Ezekiel to stand and then his Spirit set him on his feet (v. 2). Where are you facing a command you feel unable to obey? What would it look like to depend on the Spirit there?

Ezekiel was to speak “whether they hear or refuse to hear” (vv. 5, 7). How would it change your witness to family, friends or colleagues if faithfulness rather than visible results were the measure? What fears most often keep you quiet?

Before speaking to rebels, Ezekiel was warned not to be rebellious himself (v. 8). Which parts of God’s word are you most tempted to pass on to others while not taking them in yourself?

3.text: <sup>1</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, eat whatever you find here. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel."<sup>2</sup>So I opened my mouth, and he gave me this scroll to eat.<sup>3</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, feed your belly with this scroll that I give you and fill your stomach with it." Then I ate it, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey.<sup>4</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, go to the house of Israel and speak with my words to them.<sup>5</sup>For you are not sent to a people of foreign speech and a hard language, but to the house of Israel—<sup>6</sup>not to many peoples of foreign speech and a hard language, whose words you cannot understand. Surely, if I sent you to such, they would listen to you.<sup>7</sup>But the house of Israel will not be willing to listen to you, for they are not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart.<sup>8</sup>Behold, I have made your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads.<sup>9</sup>Like emery harder than flint have I made your forehead. Fear them not, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house."<sup>10</sup>Moreover, he said to me, "Son of man, all my words that I shall speak to you receive in your heart, and hear with your ears.<sup>11</sup>And go to the exiles, to your people, and speak to them and say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD,' whether they hear or refuse to hear."<sup>12</sup>Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great earthquake: "Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place!"<sup>13</sup>It was the sound of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another, and the sound of the wheels beside them, and the sound of a great earthquake.<sup>14</sup>The Spirit lifted me up and took me away, and I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the LORD being strong upon me.<sup>15</sup>And I came to the exiles at Tel-abib, who were dwelling by the Chebar canal, and I sat where they were dwelling. And I sat there overwhelmed among them seven days.<sup>16</sup>And at the end of seven days, the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>17</sup>"Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me.<sup>18</sup>If I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, in order to save his life, that wicked person shall die for his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand.<sup>19</sup>But if you warn the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness, or from his wicked way, he shall die for his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul.<sup>20</sup>Again, if a righteous person turns from his righteousness and commits injustice, and I lay a stumbling block before him, he shall die. Because you have not warned him, he shall die for his sin, and his righteous deeds that he has done shall not be remembered, but his blood I will require at your hand.<sup>21</sup>But if you warn the righteous person not to sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because he took warning, and you will have delivered your soul."<sup>22</sup>And the hand of the LORD was upon me there. And he said to me, "Arise, go out into the valley, and there I will speak with you."<sup>23</sup>So I arose and went out into the valley, and behold, the glory of the LORD stood there, like the glory that I had seen by the Chebar canal, and I fell on my face.<sup>24</sup>But the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and he spoke with me and said to me, "Go, shut yourself within your house.<sup>25</sup>And you, O son of man, behold, cords will be placed upon you, and you shall be bound with them, so that you cannot go out among the people.<sup>26</sup>And I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, so that you shall be mute and unable to reprove them, for they are a rebellious house.<sup>27</sup>But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.' He who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s messenger takes the word into himself and then holds his ground against a hard people. Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it is as sweet as honey in his mouth (vv. 1–3). He is sent not to foreigners whose language he cannot understand, who would have listened, but to Israel, who will not listen to him because they will not listen to God (vv. 4–7). So God makes his forehead like emery, harder than flint, a match for their hard foreheads (vv. 8–9). He must receive all God’s words in his heart and go to the exiles, his own people, with “Thus says the Lord GOD”, whether they hear or refuse to hear (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: God's word is sweet to the one who receives it, and God makes his servant firm enough to stand against hard-hearted hearers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, eat whatever you find here. Eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel." So I opened my mouth, and he gave me this scroll to eat. And he said to me, "Son of man, feed your belly with this scroll that I give you and fill your stomach with it." Then I ate it, and it was in my mouth as sweet as honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet takes God’s word right into himself before he speaks it, and finds it sweet, though it is full of woe.

Eat this scroll, and go, speak. The order matters: eat, then go, then speak. The word must become part of him before it comes out of him. And it is God who does the feeding: “he gave me this scroll to eat”. Ezekiel opens his mouth; God puts the word in it. The preacher is first of all a receiver.

Fill your stomach with it. Not a taste but a meal. Man lives “by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

As sweet as honey. The surprise is that a scroll full of “lamentation and mourning and woe” (2:10) tastes as sweet as honey. How can woe be sweet? Because it is God’s word, and whatever God says is good to the one who loves him. “How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm 119:103). Jeremiah said the same: “Your words were found, and I ate them” (Jeremiah 15:16).

Sweet and bitter. John too was given a scroll to eat: “It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter” (Revelation 10:10). Both are true of every faithful messenger. The word is sweet because it is God’s; it turns bitter as he carries it to people who will not hear. Ezekiel will feel the bitterness by verse 14.

In everyday life. Here is a question for our own Bible reading: do we find God’s word sweet only when it comforts us? The prophet found it sweet when it was full of woe.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, go to the house of Israel and speak with my words to them. For you are not sent to a people of foreign speech and a hard language, but to the house of Israel— not to many peoples of foreign speech and a hard language, whose words you cannot understand. Surely, if I sent you to such, they would listen to you. But the house of Israel will not be willing to listen to you, for they are not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel is sent to his own people, not to foreigners, and they will refuse him because they refuse God.

Not sent to a people of foreign speech. Ezekiel shares his hearers’ language, history, Scriptures and exile, and God says that is exactly the problem. If he were sent to foreigners, “they would listen to you”.

Outsiders who listened. It came true again and again. Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching. Jesus said, “if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago” (Matthew 11:21), and Paul told the Jews of Rome, “this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen” (Acts 28:28).

The danger of familiarity. People who have grown up with God’s word are always in danger of having heard it all, so that it no longer surprises them. Outsiders sometimes hear with fresher ears than insiders.

They are not willing to listen to me. Ezekiel must not take their rejection personally. It is not about his eloquence; they are rejecting God. Jesus said the same to his disciples: “the one who rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have made your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads. Like emery harder than flint have I made your forehead. Fear them not, nor be dismayed at their looks, for they are a rebellious house." Moreover, he said to me, "Son of man, all my words that I shall speak to you receive in your heart, and hear with your ears. And go to the exiles, to your people, and speak to them and say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD,' whether they hear or refuse to hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes his prophet’s face harder than his hearers’, and sends him to his own people with all of God’s word.

Like emery harder than flint. They have hard foreheads; God gives Ezekiel a harder one. It is stubbornness turned to good use: a holy determination that will not be worn down by their resistance.

A set face, not a hard heart. This is not harshness of heart, for Ezekiel will sit overwhelmed among these people (v. 15). It is a set face: he will not be pushed off God’s word by pressure. The Servant of the LORD says, “I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah 50:7), and Jesus, knowing what waited for him, “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51).

Receive in your heart. Receiving in the heart comes before hearing with the ears. And then: “to your people”. They are rebels, but they are his people, and God does not let his prophet speak of them as outsiders. A preacher who does not love the people he warns will not warn them well.

All my words. Ezekiel is not free to choose the parts of the message that will go down well and leave out the rest. God had told Israel long before, “You shall not add to the word that I command you, nor take from it” (Deuteronomy 4:2). A preacher who edits God’s word to suit his hearers has stopped being God’s messenger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–15 — Overwhelmed Among Them Seven Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before he says a word, the prophet sits with his people in their grief. The Spirit lifts Ezekiel up, and behind him he hears the roar of the living creatures and the wheels and a cry, “Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place!” (vv. 12–13). He is carried away and goes in bitterness, in the heat of his spirit, with the hand of the LORD strong upon him (v. 14). He comes to the exiles at Tel-abib by the Chebar canal, sits where they live, and remains there overwhelmed among them for seven days (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The messenger must first sit where his hearers sit and feel the weight of the word he carries.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Spirit lifted me up, and I heard behind me the voice of a great earthquake: "Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place!" It was the sound of the wings of the living creatures as they touched one another, and the sound of the wheels beside them, and the sound of a great earthquake. The Spirit lifted me up and took me away, and I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the LORD being strong upon me. And I came to the exiles at Tel-abib, who were dwelling by the Chebar canal, and I sat where they were dwelling. And I sat there overwhelmed among them seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet goes in bitterness under God’s strong hand, and sits silent among the exiles for a week before he speaks.

Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place! As Ezekiel is carried away, he hears the vision rumbling behind him and a cry of praise (the ESV notes that “Spirit” may be “wind”, and “voice” may be “sound”). The glory is leaving the place of vision, but it is blessed wherever it goes.

In bitterness in the heat of my spirit. The honey has turned bitter. He is walking toward a hard people with a hard message, and he does not feel good about it. That is honest.

The hand of the LORD being strong upon me. Faithful ministry is often done not because the servant feels like it but because God’s hand will not let him go. “For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” (1 Corinthians 9:16).

I sat where they were dwelling. Ezekiel does not arrive and start preaching. For seven days he says nothing, overwhelmed. Job’s friends did the same, and it was the best thing they did: “they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him” (Job 2:13). Seven days was the time of mourning for the dead (Genesis 50:10) and also of a priest’s ordination (Leviticus 8:33), so this priest’s silent week may carry something of both. Tel-abib itself was probably named from a Babylonian word for an old ruin-mound, one of the abandoned sites where the deportees were settled to farm.

Christ sat where we sit. Ezekiel’s silent week was a sign; Christ’s hidden years were the thing itself. He did more than sit where we sit; he became one of us, and before he preached a single public sermon, he spent some thirty years in an ordinary town, working, eating and grieving among ordinary people (Luke 3:23).

The hot take and the seven days. Within an hour of any tragedy, statements are issued and explanations offered, and silence is read as not caring. Ezekiel had more reason than anyone to speak at once: he had God’s own words in his stomach. Yet he sat for a week, not because the word could wait, but because a true word thrown at suffering people from a distance lands like a stone, while the same word from someone who has sat in the dust with them can land like bread. Our culture is rich in commentary and poor in presence, and Christians can be quick to explain a loss they have not yet wept over. Sit where they sit first.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 12 reads “Blessed be the glory of the LORD”, and the ESV keeps it. But the word “blessed” differs by a single similar-looking letter from “when … rose”, and some modern translations read as the glory of the LORD rose from its place, which fits the sound of the departing wings in verse 13. Either way, Ezekiel hears the glory going on its way behind him.
verseByVerse.note: Tel-abib (probably “mound of the flood”, an old ruin mound) was a settlement of exiles; seven days was the customary time of mourning (Job 2:13), and also the length of a priest's ordination (Lev 8:33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Watchman for the House of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes his prophet a watchman, answerable for warning people of God’s own judgment. After seven days the word comes: Ezekiel is a watchman for the house of Israel, and must warn from God whenever God speaks (vv. 16–17). If he does not warn the wicked, the wicked man dies in his iniquity, but his blood is required at Ezekiel’s hand; if he warns and is ignored, he has delivered his soul (vv. 18–19). The same is true of a righteous man who turns to sin: unwarned, he dies, and the watchman is answerable; warned, he may turn and live (vv. 20–21). The whole purpose is rescue.
verseByVerse.theology: Those entrusted with God's word are accountable for warning others, while each hearer is accountable for his response.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of seven days, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me. If I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you give him no warning, nor speak to warn the wicked from his wicked way, in order to save his life, that wicked person shall die for his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness, or from his wicked way, he shall die for his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel must warn the wicked of God’s own coming judgment; if he is silent he is answerable for their blood, and if he warns he is clear.

A watchman for the house of Israel. A watchman on the city wall blew the trumpet when he saw an enemy coming. His job was not to fight the enemy or to save the city by himself, but to warn.

Warning from me. The danger Ezekiel watches for is not Babylon. It is God himself, coming in judgment, and the warning is “from me”. God warns people about God. That is mercy: the Judge sends a herald before the judgment, so that people can turn.

In order to save his life. The purpose is rescue, not accusation. Christian preaching warns because it loves: “Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone” (Colossians 1:28).

His blood I will require at your hand. God sets out two cases. In both, the wicked person who does not turn dies “for his iniquity” (the ESV notes it may be “in his iniquity”): he is responsible for his own sin. But the watchman is responsible too. If he stays silent, “his blood I will require at your hand”. In Ezekiel “live” and “die” have first in view surviving or perishing in the judgment about to fall, but they reach beyond it to life with God or death without him (18:23, 32).

You will have delivered your soul. That is, you will have saved your own life: the watchman who warns is not guilty of the death of the one who ignores him. Paul told a young pastor, “Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:16). The one who warns others must keep watch over his own soul first.

Silence is not neutral. This sobers everyone entrusted with God’s truth: pastors most of all, but also parents, teachers and every Christian. Paul could say to the Ephesian elders, “I am innocent of the blood of all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26–27). None of us has been so faithful. But Christ, the true watchman who warned and wept over his city, was faithful where we have been silent, and his blood “cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7), the guilt of our silence included. Forgiven, we speak not by willpower but by the Spirit: “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Acts 1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, if a righteous person turns from his righteousness and commits injustice, and I lay a stumbling block before him, he shall die. Because you have not warned him, he shall die for his sin, and his righteous deeds that he has done shall not be remembered, but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the righteous person not to sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because he took warning, and you will have delivered your soul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A righteous person who turns to sin needs warning too: past righteousness is no insurance, and a warning heeded saves a life.

If a righteous person turns from his righteousness. The second case is the person who has been living rightly and turns away. God will “lay a stumbling block before him”, letting him fall under the consequences of his choice. And past righteousness is no insurance: “his righteous deeds that he has done shall not be remembered”. Ezekiel develops this at length in chapter 18.

He shall surely live, because he took warning. Here is the happy case: a warning given, taken, and a life saved. Believers need warning too, not only unbelievers, and a loving church tells its members the truth before they fall. Its leaders “are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account” (Hebrews 13:17).

Where Christians differ. Can a truly righteous person fall away and be lost? Arminian Christians, who take these warnings with great seriousness, read them as showing that a true believer can lose salvation, and faithful Christians have differed here.

This commentary’s view. Ezekiel is speaking first of outward covenant life in Israel: of the righteous man who turns from his righteousness and persists in evil. Scripture shows that such a person was never truly made new, since those God has given a new heart (36:26) are kept by him (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and “if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which God keeps his own from falling: “Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart … exhort one another every day” (Hebrews 3:12–13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet’s mouth now belongs entirely to God. The hand of the LORD sends Ezekiel out into the valley, where the glory he saw by the canal stands before him, and he falls on his face again; again the Spirit sets him on his feet (vv. 22–24). He is told to shut himself in his house, where he will be bound with cords so that he cannot go out among the people (vv. 24–25). God will make his tongue cling to the roof of his mouth, so that he cannot reprove them (v. 26). Only when God speaks will his mouth be opened, to say, “Thus says the Lord GOD” (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet speaks only when God speaks; his silence and his words alike belong to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And the hand of the LORD was upon me there. And he said to me, "Arise, go out into the valley, and there I will speak with you." So I arose and went out into the valley, and behold, the glory of the LORD stood there, like the glory that I had seen by the Chebar canal, and I fell on my face. But the Spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and he spoke with me and said to me, "Go, shut yourself within your house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel meets the glory again and is raised by the Spirit, only to be told to shut himself in his house.

Arise, go out into the valley. The ESV notes that “valley” may be “plain”. Ezekiel goes out alone, and the glory is waiting for him; again he falls on his face. He will need to see it again and again. No servant of God can live on a single past sight of his glory.

Shut yourself within your house. Again the Spirit sets him on his feet (2:2). But this time the command is unexpected: not “go and preach” but “shut yourself within your house”.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, O son of man, behold, cords will be placed upon you, and you shall be bound with them, so that you cannot go out among the people. And I will make your tongue cling to the roof of your mouth, so that you shall be mute and unable to reprove them, for they are a rebellious house. But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you shall say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD.' He who will hear, let him hear; and he who will refuse to hear, let him refuse, for they are a rebellious house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bound and silent, Ezekiel becomes a sign that God’s word is being withdrawn from a people who would not hear it; he will speak only when God opens his mouth.

Bound and mute. Ezekiel’s ordinary speech is taken from him, so that he cannot even argue with them.

Who places the cords? The verse does not say. It may be the exiles themselves, hostile to a prophet they do not want to hear, or it may be a restraint God puts on him as part of the sign. Either way, nothing done to Ezekiel, even by his opponents, escapes the hand of the LORD that is on him.

Until Jerusalem fell. This muteness lasts a long time. It ends only on the day the news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen: “my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute” (33:22; 24:27).
