I will open your mouth. How then does Ezekiel prophesy all through chapters 4–32? Because “when I speak with you, I will open your mouth”. He is silent except when God gives him a word, and everything that comes out of his mouth in those years is “Thus says the Lord GOD”.

He who will hear, let him hear. Jesus ended his parables the same way: “He who has ears, let him hear” (Matthew 13:9). The word is spoken; the responsibility now rests with the hearer.

In everyday life. That is a searching standard. How much of what we say about God is really his word, and how much is our own talk? Ezekiel’s mouth was shut to everything but the message.

Uncertain wording. “Unable to reprove them” is literally you shall not be to them a man who reproves. The same Hebrew word is used of an “arbiter” between two parties (Job 9:33), so some take it that Ezekiel may no longer plead the people’s case as a go-between; others, with the ESV, take it simply of rebuking them. Either way, only God’s words are heard. Job’s longing for an arbiter “who might lay his hand on us both” is answered in the “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

3.title: A Watchman for the House of Israel
3.overview:
Where we are. The commission begun in chapter 2 is completed here. Ezekiel has been shown a scroll full of woe (2:8–10); now he must eat it and go.

The message. God’s messenger must first take God’s word into himself and find it sweet, even when it is hard, and then speak all of it to people who will resist, with a face as set as theirs. He is a watchman, answerable to God for giving warning, because God warns in order to save. And his mouth belongs to God: it stays shut except when God opens it.

Why it was said. The exiles were not foreigners hearing God’s word for the first time but insiders who had heard it all and would not listen (see the introduction). They needed a prophet who could not be worn down, and who loved them enough to warn them.

How the chapter makes its case. Ezekiel eats the scroll and finds it as sweet as honey (vv. 1–3). He is sent to his own people, who will refuse him because they refuse God, when foreigners would have listened (vv. 4–7); so God makes his forehead harder than flint and tells him to receive all God’s words in his heart (vv. 8–11). He goes in bitterness and sits stunned among the exiles at Tel-abib for seven days (vv. 12–15). Then God makes him a watchman: if he fails to warn the wicked or the righteous man turning aside, their blood is required at his hand; if he warns, he is clear (vv. 16–21). Finally the glory appears again, and he is shut in his house, bound and silent except when God opens his mouth (vv. 22–27).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. A watchman can warn but cannot save, and cannot even guarantee his own faithfulness. Jesus is the faithful watchman who wept over Jerusalem because it did not know the day of its visitation (Luke 19:41–44), and then bore the judgment he warned of. Ezekiel’s face was made like flint against a hard people; Jesus “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51) to die for them. Ezekiel spoke only when God opened his mouth; Jesus spoke just as the Father had taught him (John 8:28).

For us. Do we find God’s word sweet only when it comforts us? Every Christian is in some measure a watchman for those God has set near them, and silence is not neutral. Christ’s blood covers the guilt of our silences, and his Spirit gives us words, so we can warn in love, having first sat where others sit.
3.theology:
God's word must be received inwardly before it is spoken outwardly, and it is sweet even when its content is woe (vv. 1-3, 10; Ps 119:103; Rev 10:9-10).

Rejection of God's messenger is rejection of God; people who have long known God’s word can be harder to reach than strangers to it (vv. 5-7; Matt 11:21; Acts 28:28).

God strengthens his servants with holy firmness against hard hearts (vv. 8-9; Isa 50:7; Luke 9:51).

The messenger must sit where his hearers sit (v. 15; Job 2:13).

Those entrusted with God's word are accountable to warn; each hearer is accountable for his response (vv. 17-21; Acts 20:26-27; Heb 13:17). Warnings to the righteous are one of the means by which God keeps his people (v. 21; Heb 3:12-14; John 10:28; 1 John 2:19).

The prophet speaks only when God speaks (vv. 26-27).
3.examples:
A scroll full of woe tastes like honey, and a people who share the prophet's language still cannot hear him. God gives him a forehead harder than flint, yet his heart sits overwhelmed for seven days of silence before he says a word.

He becomes a watchman who would be guilty of blood if he kept silent, and his mouth is shut to everything except Thus says the Lord GOD.

keyVerse.quote: Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me.
keyVerse.note: This verse defines Ezekiel’s task for the rest of the book, and it is repeated when the news of Jerusalem’s fall arrives (33:7). The watchman’s message is not his own: he warns “from me”, so God himself sends the herald before the judgment, which is mercy. The verse also lays a solemn trust on everyone who knows the truth: to speak it so that others may live.

3.reflection:
Ezekiel found a scroll full of woe “as sweet as honey” (v. 3). Do you find God’s word sweet only when it comforts you? What would help you love its hard parts too?

God says foreigners would have listened, but Israel would not, because they would not listen to him (vv. 5–7). In what ways can familiarity with the Bible dull our hearing? How can a church guard against that?

Ezekiel sat silent among the exiles for seven days before he spoke (v. 15). When someone you know is suffering, how can you sit where they sit before you speak? Why is it often so hard to wait?

God made Ezekiel a watchman, answerable for warning others (vv. 16–21). Who has God placed near you who needs a loving warning or the good news of Christ? How does knowing that Christ’s blood covers our past silence free us to speak?

So long shall you bear the punishment of the house of Israel.<sup>6</sup>And when you have completed these, you shall lie down a second time, but on your right side, and bear the punishment of the house of Judah. During the number of days that you lie on your side, 390 days, you shall eat it.<sup>10</sup>And your food that you eat shall be by weight, twenty shekels a day; from day to day you shall eat it.<sup>11</sup>And water you shall drink by measure, the sixth part of a hin; from day to day you shall drink.<sup>12</sup>And you shall eat it as a barley cake, baking it in their sight on human dung."<sup>13</sup>And the LORD said, "Thus shall the people of Israel eat their bread unclean, among the nations where I will drive them."<sup>14</sup>Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I have never defiled myself. From my youth up till now I have never eaten what died of itself or was torn by beasts, nor has tainted meat come into my mouth."<sup>15</sup>Then he said to me, "See, I assign to you cow's dung instead of human dung, on which you may prepare your bread."<sup>16</sup>Moreover, he said to me, "Son of man, behold, I will break the supply of bread in Jerusalem. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself will besiege Jerusalem, and his people will bear the full count of their punishment. Ezekiel’s first message is a performance. He scratches Jerusalem on a clay brick, surrounds it with model siege walls, ramps, camps and battering rams, and sets an iron griddle as a wall between himself and the city, his face against it (vv. 1–3). Then he lies on his left side for 390 days, bearing the punishment of Israel, and on his right side for 40 days for Judah, a day for each year (vv. 4–6). With arm bared he prophesies against the city, bound with cords so that he cannot turn until the days of the siege are done (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgment on his own people is certain and measured, and in the end it is borne by another, Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, take a brick and lay it before you, and engrave on it a city, even Jerusalem. And put siegeworks against it, and build a siege wall against it, and cast up a mound against it. Set camps also against it, and plant battering rams against it all around. And you, take an iron griddle, and place it as an iron wall between you and the city; and set your face toward it, and let it be in a state of siege, and press the siege against it. This is a sign for the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With a model siege and an iron wall, Ezekiel shows the exiles that Jerusalem will be besieged, and that God himself is pressing the siege.

Take a brick. Ezekiel is bound in his house and cannot speak except when God opens his mouth (3:25–27), so his first sermon is silent. He takes a soft clay brick and scratches a map of Jerusalem on it.

Put siegeworks against it. Imagine the exiles watching a grown man, a priest, playing war on the ground, with tiny ramps, tiny camps and tiny battering rams around a clay city. Some would laugh, but everyone would ask what it meant.

This is a sign for the house of Israel. The exiles were hoping Jerusalem would hold out and they would go home. Ezekiel’s model said the opposite. God chose a picture because it gets past defences that words cannot.

An iron wall between you and the city. An ordinary kitchen griddle becomes an iron wall between the prophet and the city. Ezekiel, playing God’s part, sets his face against Jerusalem, and nothing from the city can reach him through it. This is the fearful part of the sign. The siege is not only Babylon’s: God himself is pressing it, and a barrier stands between the city and him. Prayers will not get through. “Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God” (Isaiah 59:2). The only thing that has ever broken that wall is the cross, where “the curtain of the temple was torn in two” (Matthew 27:51).
verseByVerse.note: This is the first of Ezekiel's many acted-out signs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then lie on your left side, and place the punishment of the house of Israel upon it. For the number of the days that you lie on it, you shall bear their punishment. For I assign to you a number of days, 390 days, equal to the number of the years of their punishment. So long shall you bear the punishment of the house of Israel. And when you have completed these, you shall lie down a second time, but on your right side, and bear the punishment of the house of Judah. Forty days I assign you, a day for each year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lying bound on his side, a day for each year, Ezekiel acts out the punishment God has counted out for his people.

Lie on your left side. For more than a year Ezekiel lies on his side in public, most likely for some hours each day (see the question below). The ESV notes that “punishment” may also be rendered “iniquity”: he bears the iniquity of Israel and Judah. The two sides fit the map. A Hebrew facing east had the north on his left and the south on his right, so the left side stands for the northern kingdom, Israel, and the right for Judah in the south.

A day for each year. The pattern goes back to the wilderness, when Israel refused to enter the land: “forty days, a year for each day, you shall bear your iniquity forty years” (Numbers 14:34). Whatever the numbers count exactly (see the box below), the main point is plain: the punishment has been counted out by God. It is long, it is real, and it has an end.

You shall bear their punishment. Look at what the prophet is made to act out: a man lying bound, bearing the iniquity of his people, day after day. Ezekiel could not take their sin away; he could only show it. But his sign points forward to one who did: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6), and “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). What Ezekiel acted out, Christ accomplished.

Did Ezekiel really lie on his side for 390 days? Some take it as a vision; others suggest he lay for part of each day. The text presents it as a public sign the people saw, and the likeliest reading is that he lay bound for some hours each day for that period, eating his rationed bread (vv. 9–12).

Uncertain wording. What the 390 and 40 years count exactly is not explained, and careful readers have reckoned them in different ways. Perhaps the long number looks back over the centuries of sin since the kingdom divided, and the forty echo the wilderness again. (The Greek Old Testament reads 190 days instead of 390 in verses 5 and 9; the Hebrew 390 is followed by the ESV and most translations.)
verseByVerse.note: 390 days for Israel and 40 for Judah: a day for each year of punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall set your face toward the siege of Jerusalem, with your arm bared, and you shall prophesy against the city. And behold, I will place cords upon you, so that you cannot turn from one side to the other, till you have completed the days of your siege.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has bared his arm against Jerusalem, and the siege will run its full course.

With your arm bared. A bared arm is ready for action, sleeve pulled back. It is how Scripture pictures God getting to work: “The LORD has bared his holy arm before the eyes of all the nations” (Isaiah 52:10). There that arm is bared to save. Here it is bared against a city that refused to be saved.

I will place cords upon you. He cannot roll over, cannot get comfortable, cannot escape. Neither will Jerusalem: the siege, once it begins, will run its full course.

What obedience cost. This cost Ezekiel months of discomfort, ridicule and restriction for the sake of a message. God’s servants are sometimes asked to live the message out, not merely to say it, and it hurts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The coming siege will mean starvation, and exile will mean defilement. During his days on his side Ezekiel eats bread made from whatever grains and beans can be mixed together, weighed out at a starvation ration, with water measured by the cup (vv. 9–11). He is to bake it over human dung in the people’s sight, because Israel will eat unclean bread among the nations (vv. 12–13). He protests that he has never defiled himself, and God allows cow’s dung instead (vv. 14–15). Then God explains: he will break Jerusalem’s supply of bread, so that its people eat and drink in fear and dismay and waste away in their iniquity (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: When God removes his provision, people learn how completely they depended on it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, take wheat and barley, beans and lentils, millet and emmer, and put them into a single vessel and make your bread from them. During the number of days that you lie on your side, 390 days, you shall eat it. And your food that you eat shall be by weight, twenty shekels a day; from day to day you shall eat it. And water you shall drink by measure, the sixth part of a hin; from day to day you shall drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A daily ration of mixed-grain bread and a cup of water show the starvation that is coming to Jerusalem.

Wheat and barley, beans and lentils. Six kinds of grain and pulse go into one jar. This is the bread of scarcity: you throw in whatever is left at the bottom of every sack.

Twenty shekels a day. Using the ESV’s notes, twenty shekels is about eight ounces of bread a day, and a sixth of a hin is well under a quart of water. It is a starvation ration, measured out carefully so that it lasts. That is what siege life is: every mouthful weighed, every cup counted.

Hunger as a weapon. Hunger was the weapon Babylon would use, and it worked. When the city finally fell, “the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land” (2 Kings 25:3).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “millet” occurs only here, and “emmer” (an ancient wheat) is not certain either. The point does not change: a little of everything, because there is not enough of anything.
verseByVerse.note: Twenty shekels was about 8 ounces of bread a day, and a sixth of a hin about two-thirds of a quart of water.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall eat it as a barley cake, baking it in their sight on human dung." And the LORD said, "Thus shall the people of Israel eat their bread unclean, among the nations where I will drive them." Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I have never defiled myself. From my youth up till now I have never eaten what died of itself or was torn by beasts, nor has tainted meat come into my mouth." Then he said to me, "See, I assign to you cow's dung instead of human dung, on which you may prepare your bread."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In exile God’s people will have no way to stay clean, yet God hears his servant’s honest protest.

Baking it in their sight on human dung. Dried dung was a common fuel where wood was scarce, but human dung was unclean under the law. The point is spelled out: in exile God’s people will have no way to keep themselves clean. Hosea had warned, “they shall eat unclean food in Assyria” (Hosea 9:3). Losing the land meant losing the whole ordered life of holiness that went with it.

Ah, Lord GOD! For the first time, Ezekiel objects. He has lain on his side without complaint, but this touches his conscience as a priest. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says his “soul (or throat)” has never been made unclean: he has kept the food laws his whole life.

I assign to you cow’s dung instead. God listens and changes the instruction. The message stays the same, but God respects his servant’s tender conscience. The God who sets his face against a rebellious city bends down to hear the honest protest of a faithful man. You may bring your conscience to God; he does not despise it.

Peter’s objection. Centuries later another devout man said almost the same thing to God: “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean” (Acts 10:14). Peter was being taught that in Christ the old food laws were fulfilled; Jesus “declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). Ezekiel lived before that day, and his conscience was right to object.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, he said to me, "Son of man, behold, I will break the supply of bread in Jerusalem. They shall eat bread by weight and with anxiety, and they shall drink water by measure and in dismay. I will do this that they may lack bread and water, and look at one another in dismay, and rot away because of their punishment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As his covenant had warned, God will break Jerusalem’s bread supply, and its people will waste away in fear.

I will break the supply of bread. The ESV notes that “supply” is literally “staff”: bread was the staff a person leaned on, and God will break it. This too was written long before in the covenant warnings: “When I break your supply of bread … and shall dole out your bread again by weight, and you shall eat and not be satisfied” (Leviticus 26:26).

By weight and with anxiety. The worst part of famine is not only the hunger but the fear: will there be anything tomorrow? Picture neighbours staring at each other across empty tables, each hoping the other has something left. People who had forgotten that every meal came from God’s hand learn it by losing the meal.

In everyday life. Every harvest and every loaf is a gift, and it is right to thank God for daily bread while it is on the table. And there is a bread no siege can cut off: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35).

4.title: The Siege Acted Out
4.overview:
Where we are. Ezekiel has been commissioned and then shut in his house, silent except when God opens his mouth (3:24–27). So his first message is acted rather than spoken: the first of the book’s sign-acts (see the introduction), which run on into chapter 5.

The message. Jerusalem, the city the exiles trusted to stand, will be besieged, and God himself is pressing the siege. Its people will bear the punishment of long years of sin, starve on rationed bread and eat unclean food among the nations. Yet the God who sets his face against the city still bends to hear the honest protest of his servant.

Why it was said. In 593 BC the exiles were sure that Jerusalem would hold and that they would soon go home, and their prophets said so (see the introduction). Words had not moved them, so God gave them something to watch.

How the chapter makes its case. First the siege (vv. 1–3): Ezekiel draws Jerusalem on a brick, surrounds it with model siegeworks and sets an iron griddle between himself and the city, his face against it as God’s is. Then the punishment (vv. 4–8): he lies on his left side 390 days for Israel and on his right side 40 days for Judah, a day for each year, with his arm bared toward the city and cords holding him so that he cannot turn. Then the famine (vv. 9–17): bread of mixed grains weighed out by the day, water by the measure, baked over dung, the food of the siege and of exile. Ezekiel protests, God allows cow’s dung instead, and explains the sign: he will break Jerusalem’s supply of bread until its people waste away in their iniquity.

Where it leads. By pattern and by the need it exposes. A man lies bound, bearing the iniquity of his people for an appointed time, yet he cannot take it away; he can only show it. The sign waits for the one of whom Isaiah wrote, “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6), who “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). The iron wall between God and the city points the same way: only the cross broke it, when “the curtain of the temple was torn in two” (Matthew 27:51). And to a world that eats its bread “by weight and with anxiety”, Jesus says, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

For us. God’s warnings are not empty, and sin is costly: it separates, it starves and it defiles. But what Ezekiel could only act out, God has borne in his Son, and the God who hears an honest conscience welcomes anyone who comes to him for bread.
4.theology:
God uses visible signs to break through the defences of people who will not listen to words (vv. 1-3).

The siege of Jerusalem is God's own act, and a barrier of iniquity stands between the city and him (v. 3; Isa 59:2).

God's judgment is measured and has an end (vv. 4-6; Num 14:34).

The prophet who lies bound bearing his people's iniquity points to Christ, who truly bore it (vv. 4-6; Isa 53:6; 1 Pet 2:24).

Losing the land meant losing the ordered life of holiness; the covenant warning of a broken bread supply came true (vv. 13, 16; Lev 26:26; Hos 9:3).

God hears the honest conscience of his servant (vv. 14-15).
4.examples:
A priest plays war with a clay brick, and a frying pan becomes an iron wall. For more than a year he lies bound on his side, living on eight ounces of bread a day mixed from the bottom of every sack.

When the servant protests, God changes the fuel. And the sign ends with neighbours staring at each other over empty tables.

keyVerse.quote: Then lie on your left side, and place the punishment of the house of Israel upon it. For the number of the days that you lie on it, you shall bear their punishment.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the chapter’s signs: a man lying bound in public, bearing the punishment, or iniquity, of his people day after day. It tells the exiles that their sin has been counted and will be paid for. It also leaves a question the whole Old Testament leaves open, which Isaiah 53 and the cross answer: who can bear iniquity in a way that takes it away?

4.reflection:
God gave the exiles a model siege to watch because they would not hear his words (vv. 1–3). Why are pictures and actions sometimes able to get past our defences when words cannot? How does God still speak to us in visible ways, for example in baptism and the Lord’s Supper?

The iron griddle stood as a wall between God and the besieged city (v. 3). What does it mean that sin separates us from God? How has Christ broken that wall?

Ezekiel lay bound, bearing the punishment of his people (vv. 4–8). How does this sign help you understand what Jesus did on the cross? What did Christ do that Ezekiel could not?

Ezekiel protested honestly, and God listened and changed the instruction (vv. 14–15). What does this teach you about bringing your conscience and your objections to God in prayer?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — A Sword for a Razor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s judgment on Jerusalem will be exact, complete and inescapable, and even among the survivors only those God truly keeps are safe. Ezekiel, a priest forbidden to shave his beard, takes a sword as a razor to his head and beard, and weighs the hair on scales (v. 1). A third is burned in the model city when the siege is over, a third struck with the sword around it, and a third scattered to the wind with a sword drawn after it (v. 2). A few hairs are bound in the fold of his robe, but even some of these are thrown into the fire, and from that fire judgment spreads to all Israel (vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment will fall on all, and even the few who are spared are not safe apart from God's mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, O son of man, take a sharp sword. Use it as a barber's razor and pass it over your head and your beard. Then take balances for weighing and divide the hair. A third part you shall burn in the fire in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are completed. And a third part you shall take and strike with the sword all around the city. And a third part you shall scatter to the wind, and I will unsheathe the sword after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon’s sword will shave Jerusalem bare, and God has weighed out exactly what will happen to her people: a third burned, a third cut down, a third scattered and pursued.

Use it as a barber’s razor. The razor is a sword, the instrument of war put to a barber’s job. For a priest this was shocking: priests “shall not make bald patches on their heads, nor shave off the edges of their beards” (Leviticus 21:5). A shaved beard was also public disgrace: an enemy king humiliated David’s envoys when he “shaved off half the beard of each” (2 Samuel 10:4). Isaiah had warned that the Lord would shave Judah “with a razor that is hired beyond the River” (Isaiah 7:20). Then the razor was the king of Assyria; now it is Babylon, and the sword in Ezekiel’s hand says so.

Balances for weighing. The hair is weighed out on scales: judgment is exact, not random. Even the scattered third is chased by a drawn sword. Verse 12 explains the thirds: pestilence and famine inside, the sword outside, exile and pursuit beyond.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall take from these a small number and bind them in the skirts of your robe. And of these again you shall take some and cast them into the midst of the fire and burn them in the fire. From there a fire will come out into all the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A small remnant is kept in the fold of the prophet’s robe, yet even some of these perish: being among the survivors is no guarantee of safety.

A small number … some cast into the fire. The hairs tucked into his robe are the remnant God keeps. Yet even some of these go into the fire, and from that fire judgment spreads to “all the house of Israel”. Some who escaped the siege would still perish, and even in exile judgment would go on falling on those who did not turn.

Membership is not enough. Outward membership in God’s people does not save; only a living relationship with God does. And the remnant that is truly kept is kept by God’s hand, not by its own strength. Christ says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–17 — I, Even I, Am Against You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God explains the sign: Jerusalem has sinned against greater light than anyone, so God himself is against her. “This is Jerusalem”, set at the centre of the nations, yet more rebellious than they, not even keeping the standards of the pagans (vv. 5–7). So God will execute judgments in her midst before those same nations, a judgment like no other, in which families devour one another (vv. 8–10). Because she defiled his sanctuary, he will withdraw and not spare, and the thirds of hair are explained (vv. 11–12). His anger will spend itself and they will know that he is the LORD (v. 13); Jerusalem will become a warning to the world, under famine, wild beasts, pestilence and sword, all guaranteed by “I am the LORD; I have spoken” (vv. 14–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The greater the privilege of God's people, the greater the judgment when they despise it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: This is Jerusalem. I have set her in the center of the nations, with countries all around her. And she has rebelled against my rules by doing wickedness more than the nations, and against my statutes more than the countries all around her; for they have rejected my rules and have not walked in my statutes. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you are more turbulent than the nations that are all around you, and have not walked in my statutes or obeyed my rules, and have not even acted according to the rules of the nations that are all around you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem was set at the centre of the nations to show them what life under God looks like, and she became worse than they were. The greater the privilege, the greater the guilt.

This is Jerusalem. Three words interpret everything: the hair, the brick and the siege are all about the holy city.

In the center of the nations. Jerusalem was placed where the world could see her. Moses had said that the nations, seeing Israel’s laws, would say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people” (Deuteronomy 4:6), and God’s people were always meant to be “a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6). Instead she became darker than the darkness around her: the city with the law behaved worse than the cities without it, and did not even keep the standards of the pagans (v. 7).

A warning for the church. Paul makes the same charge against those who have God’s law and break it: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2:24). When the church lives worse than the world, the world thinks less of God. The way back is the one Ezekiel will preach: “so turn, and live” (18:32).

Uncertain wording. “More turbulent” translates a rare Hebrew form whose meaning is not certain. The ESV links it to a word for tumult; older translations such as the King James Version took it as “multiplied”. Either way, Jerusalem has outdone the nations in rebellion. In verse 7 the ESV notes that some manuscripts lack “not”, which would make the charge: you have acted just like the nations. Either reading condemns her.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I, even I, am against you. And I will execute judgments in your midst in the sight of the nations. And because of all your abominations I will do with you what I have never yet done, and the like of which I will never do again. Therefore fathers shall eat their sons in your midst, and sons shall eat their fathers. And I will execute judgments on you, and any of you who survive I will scatter to all the winds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself is now Jerusalem’s enemy, and the rules she would not keep become the judgments she cannot escape, carried out in full view of the nations.

I, even I, am against you. Not Babylon against you, but God. The ESV notes explain a play on words: the same Hebrew expression can mean “obey rules” or “execute judgments”. Jerusalem would not obey God’s rules (v. 7), so God will execute judgments, “in the sight of the nations” who were meant to see her obedience.

What I have never yet done. God says this judgment will have no equal (v. 9). Jesus used similar language of the city’s later destruction: “great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now” (Matthew 24:21). How can two disasters both be beyond compare? This is Scripture’s way of saying that something has no equal of its kind, as when two different kings are each said to have had no equal (2 Kings 18:5; 23:25): not a ranking of every event in history, but a judgment terrible beyond words.

Fathers shall eat their sons. Verse 10 names the worst horror of siege, foretold in the covenant curses (Leviticus 26:29) and mourned with tears in Lamentations (Lamentations 4:10). Sin tears apart even the family, and those who suffer it are to be wept over, not despised.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things and with all your abominations, therefore I will withdraw. My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity. A third part of you shall die of pestilence and be consumed with famine in your midst; a third part shall fall by the sword all around you; and a third part I will scatter to all the winds and will unsheathe the sword after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jerusalem has filled God’s sanctuary with idols, God will withdraw his protecting presence and no longer spare her.

You have defiled my sanctuary … I will withdraw. Here is the heart of the charge: the holiest place on earth has been filled with “detestable things”, as chapter 8 will show. So God pulls back his protecting presence; chapters 10–11 will show the glory actually leaving.

My eye will not spare. God is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (Psalm 103:8). But his patience is not endless for those who treat his holiness with contempt: “Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4).

The sign explained. Now the hair of verses 1–2 is explained, third by third. The sign was not theatre but a map of what was coming.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “I will cut you down” instead of “I will withdraw”. The verb in the main text means to take away or cut short, and is used of shorn beards (compare “every beard is shorn”, Isaiah 15:2), so it may echo the shaving of verse 1. Either way, God is removing his protection from the city.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus shall my anger spend itself, and I will vent my fury upon them and satisfy myself. And they shall know that I am the LORD—that I have spoken in my jealousy— when I spend my fury upon them. Moreover, I will make you a desolation and an object of reproach among the nations all around you and in the sight of all who pass by. You shall be a reproach and a taunt, a warning and a horror, to the nations all around you, when I execute judgments on you in anger and fury, and with furious rebukes—I am the LORD; I have spoken—
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s anger will run its full course until justice is done, and through it the nations will learn what it means to despise him.

Thus shall my anger spend itself. God’s wrath is not endless rage; it is a just response that ends when justice is done. “Satisfy myself” does not mean that God enjoys inflicting pain, for he says, “I have no pleasure in the death of anyone” (18:32). It means that justice is done in full, and then it is finished.

Spent on the Son. That is why the gospel speaks of Christ as “a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25). God’s just anger against sin was fully spent on his Son, so that nothing is left over for those who trust him.

In my jealousy. God’s jealousy is not petty envy but the burning love of a husband whose wife has gone after other lovers. He will not share his people with idols, because idols destroy them.

They shall know that I am the LORD. This sentence, in one form or another, comes some seventy times in Ezekiel: it is the goal of everything God does in the book, in judgment and restoration alike. Those who would not know God through his kindness will know him through his judgments. Far better to know him the other way.

A warning and a horror. Jerusalem was meant to be a showcase; now people will point at her ruins and learn what it means to despise God. Her story warns us still: “these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

verseByVerse.quote: when I send against you the deadly arrows of famine, arrows for destruction, which I will send to destroy you, and when I bring more and more famine upon you and break your supply of bread. I will send famine and wild beasts against you, and they will rob you of your children. Pestilence and blood shall pass through you, and I will bring the sword upon you. I am the LORD; I have spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Famine, wild beasts, pestilence and sword, the curses Moses had warned of, will come exactly as God has said, because the God who speaks also acts.

The deadly arrows of famine. These are the covenant curses listed long before. Moses had heard God say, “I will spend my arrows on them; they shall be wasted with hunger, and devoured by plague” (Deuteronomy 32:23–24). “Supply” is literally “staff” (the ESV notes), as in 4:16: bread was the staff that kept life standing.

I am the LORD; I have spoken. The chapter ends with this signature, on which every warning and every promise in the Bible stands. The same God who says “I have spoken” about the siege will say it about the new heart and the new spirit (36:36). What he says, he does.

5.title: This Is Jerusalem
5.overview:
Where we are. In chapter 4 Ezekiel acted out the siege of Jerusalem with a model city and siege rations; now comes the last and most shocking sign of the series, and then God himself explains what all of it means.

The message. Jerusalem, the city God set at the centre of the nations to show the world what life under him looks like, has become worse than the nations, and has filled his sanctuary with idols. So God himself is now against her, and his judgment will be exact, complete and public. The privileged are judged most strictly, and the God who has spoken will do what he says.

Why it was said. The exiles believed Jerusalem could not fall, because God’s house was there (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that the temple is not a shield against God; it is the very thing they have defiled.

How the chapter makes its case. First the sign (vv. 1–4): Ezekiel shaves his head and beard with a sword, weighs the hair on scales and divides it into thirds, to be burned, struck and scattered; a few hairs are saved in his robe, and even some of those go into the fire. Then the word (vv. 5–17). “This is Jerusalem”: set among the nations, she has rebelled more than they (vv. 5–7). So “I, even I, am against you” (vv. 8–10), with a judgment like no other. Because she defiled the sanctuary, God will withdraw and not spare, and the thirds are explained as pestilence and famine, sword and scattering (vv. 11–12). His anger will spend itself, and under the covenant curses she will become a warning to the nations (vv. 13–17). Three times God signs it: “I am the LORD; I have spoken” (vv. 13, 15, 17).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God it reveals. God’s holy anger against sin is real and must be spent; the gospel tells us where it was spent. On the cross the Son bore the curse of the broken covenant (Galatians 3:13), so that those who trust him hear not “I am against you” but “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). The few hairs bound in the prophet’s robe point to a remnant kept by God’s own hand, and Christ says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

For us. The church, like Jerusalem, is set where the world can see it, and privilege brings responsibility, not immunity. Belonging to the right group does not save; only the God who keeps his people does. Take his warnings as seriously as his promises, because he has spoken both, and flee to the one in whom his anger has already been spent.
5.theology:
God's judgment is exact and complete, and even among survivors only those God truly keeps are safe (vv. 1-4).

The more God gives, the more he requires: Jerusalem, set before the nations to display God's ways, was judged for being worse than they (vv. 5-7; Deut 4:6-8; Rom 2:24).

The rules God's people will not keep become the judgments they cannot escape (vv. 7-8).

When his people defile what is holy, God withdraws (v. 11; Rom 2:4).

God's wrath is just and comes to an end when it is satisfied; in Christ it has been fully spent (v. 13; Rom 3:25).

The goal of God's acts is that people know he is the LORD (v. 13), and his spoken word guarantees both judgment and promise (v. 17; 36:36).
5.examples: A priest shaves his beard with a sword and weighs the hair on scales; a few hairs are tucked into his robe, and some of them are still burned. A city set in the shop window of the world finds that the rules it would not keep have become the judgments it cannot escape, and over it all stands the signature: I am the LORD; I have spoken.

keyVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: This is Jerusalem. I have set her in the center of the nations, with countries all around her.
keyVerse.note: These words turn the sign into a verdict: the shaved hair is the holy city. They also explain why the judgment is so severe. Jerusalem was placed where the nations could see what life under God looks like, and the greater the privilege, the greater the guilt when it is betrayed.

5.reflection:
Ezekiel’s hair was weighed on scales before it was burned, struck and scattered (vv. 1–2). What does this teach about the exactness of God’s judgment? Why might that be a comfort as well as a warning?

Even some of the hairs saved in the prophet’s robe went into the fire (vv. 3–4). Why is belonging to God’s people outwardly not the same as being kept by God? How does that shape the way we think about our churches and our families?

Jerusalem was set “in the center of the nations” to display God’s ways, but lived worse than they did (vv. 5–7). Where does the world watch the church today? What does it see?

God says his anger will “spend itself” (v. 13). How does the cross show where that anger was spent for those who trust Christ? How should this make us both serious about sin and confident in him?

6.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them,<sup>3</sup>and say, You mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! Thus says the Lord GOD to the mountains and the hills, to the ravines and the valleys: Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places.<sup>4</sup>Your altars shall become desolate, and your incense altars shall be broken, and I will cast down your slain before your idols.<sup>5</sup>And I will lay the dead bodies of the people of Israel before their idols, and I will scatter your bones around your altars.<sup>6</sup>Wherever you dwell, the cities shall be waste and the high places ruined, so that your altars will be waste and ruined, your idols broken and destroyed, your incense altars cut down, and your works wiped out.<sup>7</sup>And the slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the LORD.<sup>8</sup>"Yet I will leave some of you alive. When you have among the nations some who escape the sword, and when you are scattered through the countries,<sup>9</sup>then those of you who escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me and over their eyes that go whoring after their idols. And they will be loathsome in their own sight for the evils that they have committed, for all their abominations.<sup>10</sup>And they shall know that I am the LORD. I have not said in vain that I would do this evil to them."<sup>11</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas, because of all the evil abominations of the house of Israel, for they shall fall by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence.<sup>12</sup>He who is far off shall die of pestilence, and he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and is preserved shall die of famine. Thus I will spend my fury upon them.<sup>13</sup>And you shall know that I am the LORD, when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, under every green tree, and under every leafy oak, wherever they offered pleasing aroma to all their idols.<sup>14</sup>And I will stretch out my hand against them and make the land desolate and waste, in all their dwelling places, from the wilderness to Riblah. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hilltop shrines where Israel gave her heart to other gods will become the places where she dies, and her idols will be shown to be helpless. Ezekiel, far away in Babylon, sets his face toward the mountains of Israel and speaks to the land itself: God will bring a sword against the high places (vv. 1–3). Altars will be smashed and the people laid dead in front of their idols, with their bones scattered round the altars they thought holy (vv. 4–5). Every city will be waste, every idol broken and every work of their hands wiped out, and through it they will know that he is the LORD (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The false gods people trust will lie broken beside those who trusted them.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy against them, and say, You mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! Thus says the Lord GOD to the mountains and the hills, to the ravines and the valleys: Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks to the mountains of Israel themselves, because that is where his people betrayed him, and announces a sword against their hilltop shrines.

Set your face toward the mountains of Israel. Ezekiel is in Babylon, but he is told to turn and face the hills of home, speaking to mountains hundreds of miles away. The word of God is not limited by distance.

I will destroy your high places. Why speak to mountains? Because that is where the idolatry happened. The high places were hilltop shrines where Israel worshipped other gods, or worshipped the LORD in pagan ways. God had commanded them at the beginning to destroy “all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, on the high mountains and on the hills and under every green tree” (Deuteronomy 12:2). Instead Israel took them over. And God speaks to the ravines and valleys too, as both witness and accused: the land had seen everything.

The promise to the same mountains. The promise will come to these same mountains. In chapter 36 God will say, “But you, O mountains of Israel, shall shoot forth your branches and yield your fruit to my people Israel” (36:8). The hills cursed here will be blessed there.
verseByVerse.note: “High places” were local hilltop shrines.

verseByVerse.quote: Your altars shall become desolate, and your incense altars shall be broken, and I will cast down your slain before your idols. And I will lay the dead bodies of the people of Israel before their idols, and I will scatter your bones around your altars. Wherever you dwell, the cities shall be waste and the high places ruined, so that your altars will be waste and ruined, your idols broken and destroyed, your incense altars cut down, and your works wiped out. And the slain shall fall in your midst, and you shall know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worshippers will lie dead before their idols, and the gods they trusted will do nothing, because they can do nothing. Through it Israel will know who the LORD is.

Your slain before your idols. It is a grim picture, and a deliberate one. The idols look on and do nothing: “They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see … Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:5, 8).

I will scatter your bones around your altars. Dead bodies and bones made a place unclean. The altars they thought holy will be defiled with the corpses of the people who served there.

Your works wiped out. The words pile up the ruin: waste, ruined (the ESV notes it may be “punished”), broken, destroyed, cut down, wiped out. “Your works” means everything they made with their own hands to replace God.

The end of idolatry. This is always the end of idolatry, ancient or modern. Whatever we build to trust instead of God, whether a career, a reputation, a relationship or a comfort, cannot hold our weight in the day of trouble, and will be broken. Yet the God who breaks idols also turns hearts from them by his Spirit, as he did in Thessalonica, where people “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

You shall know that I am the LORD. They would not know God as the LORD when he gave them the land and every good gift; they will know him when their idols lie in pieces. In the Bible, to know someone is to meet him and acknowledge him for who he is, the way you know a friend, not the way you know a fact. “The LORD”, in capitals, stands for Yahweh, the name God gave Moses at the bush: “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14), the God who simply is and keeps his word. Israel had kept the name and lost the person. A god you can carry is easier to manage than a holy God you must meet, and we feel the same pull: we want a God we can use.

Known in the one who was struck. Yet God will give a heart that can know him: “a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). Jesus said, “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3), and he took the name on his own lips: “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). The God whom Jerusalem would know as “the LORD, who strikes” (7:9) has made himself known in the one who was struck for us. This week, before you ask him for anything, spend a minute telling him who he is. See Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — Broken over Their Whoring Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment is not God’s last word: he will keep a remnant, and in exile their hearts will be broken as his has been. “Yet I will leave some of you alive” (v. 8). Scattered among the nations, the survivors will remember God and how he was broken over their unfaithful heart and their eyes that went after idols (v. 9). Seeing their sin from his side, they will loathe themselves for their evils, the beginning of true repentance. And they will learn that God did not threaten in vain (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: God grieves over his people's unfaithfulness, and true repentance begins when they see their sin as he sees it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet I will leave some of you alive. When you have among the nations some who escape the sword, and when you are scattered through the countries, then those of you who escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me and over their eyes that go whoring after their idols. And they will be loathsome in their own sight for the evils that they have committed, for all their abominations. And they shall know that I am the LORD. I have not said in vain that I would do this evil to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will keep a remnant alive, and in exile they will remember him and see that their unfaithfulness broke his heart; then they will hate their sin.

Yet I will leave some of you alive. After seven verses of destruction, one word changes the tone: “Yet”. Judgment is never God’s final word to his people.

I have been broken over their whoring heart. Read slowly. The Lord of the storm and fire of chapter 1, who is sending sword and famine, speaks like a betrayed husband whose heart has been crushed. It stands with “it grieved him to his heart” (Genesis 6:6), and with Jesus over Jerusalem: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). Sin is not only law-breaking; it wounds a love: “do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30). This is real love put in human terms. It does not mean God is overthrown by feeling as we are, but it does mean his judgments never come from indifference.

Can the universe love you? Many who have left organised religion still speak of something out there: the universe, energy, a higher power. It feels more modest than the God of the Bible, and far less demanding. But a force can be tapped and harnessed; it cannot be grieved, because it does not love. That is why such spirituality is so comfortable and, in the end, so lonely: it keeps us safe from being judged, and leaves us unable to be loved. Ezekiel’s God is infinitely beyond us, and yet he says his people’s unfaithfulness has broken him. Only a person can be betrayed, and only a person can forgive. And the God who grieved over Israel’s whoring heart took a human heart in his Son, and let it be broken for the very people who had broken faith with him: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Their eyes that go whoring. The language is deliberate. Idolatry is adultery: the love promised to God is given to another. And it begins in the heart and the eyes before it ever reaches a hilltop altar.

Loathsome in their own sight. When the exiles finally see what their sin did to God, they will hate it. Ezekiel will say it again: “you will remember your evil ways … and you will loathe yourselves” (36:31). This is not self-hatred for its own sake but the beginning of true repentance, seeing sin from God’s side: “godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

I have not said in vain. The people had heard God’s warnings so long that they had stopped believing them. But God keeps his word, in warning and in promise.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of “I have been broken” is unusual, and some translations take it as God breaking their unfaithful heart instead. The ESV’s reading, followed here, fits the grief of the whole verse; either way, God will deal with the heart that left him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet must grieve as he announces judgment, because there will be no escape anywhere in the land. Ezekiel claps his hands, stamps his foot and cries “Alas” over the abominations of Israel (v. 11). Far or near, fleeing or holding out, pestilence, sword and famine will reach everyone (v. 12). The slain will lie among their idols on every hill and under every green tree, the very places where they offered “pleasing aroma” to false gods (v. 13), and God’s outstretched hand will make the whole land desolate (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Where people worshipped their idols, there their ruin will be seen.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: "Clap your hands and stamp your foot and say, Alas, because of all the evil abominations of the house of Israel, for they shall fall by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence. He who is far off shall die of pestilence, and he who is near shall fall by the sword, and he who is left and is preserved shall die of famine. Thus I will spend my fury upon them. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, under every green tree, and under every leafy oak, wherever they offered pleasing aroma to all their idols. And I will stretch out my hand against them and make the land desolate and waste, in all their dwelling places, from the wilderness to Riblah. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel must announce the judgment with anguish, because it will reach every corner of the land and every place where idols were worshipped.

Clap your hands and stamp your foot. Ezekiel must act out his grief and cry “Alas”. The message is not delivered calmly from a distance; the prophet feels it in his body. Anyone who speaks about God’s judgment should speak like this: not with satisfaction, but with anguish.

He who is far off and he who is near. Far or near, fleeing or staying, there is no hiding place: those far away die of disease, those close by by the sword, those who hold out inside of hunger.

Wherever they offered pleasing aroma. “Pleasing aroma” was the language of sacrifices God accepted. Israel offered it to idols instead, so the places of their false worship become the places of their death.

I will stretch out my hand against them. The hand that once stretched out to bring Israel out of Egypt is stretched out against them, from the southern wilderness to the far north. But the book will not end there. The same God says, a few chapters on, “I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them” (11:19).

Textual note. The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read “Diblah”, a place otherwise unknown, rather than Riblah. If Riblah is right, it is a town in the far north, and it would become a name of horror: there the king of Babylon killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, and then put out his eyes (Jeremiah 39:6–7).

6.title: Against the Mountains of Israel
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 4–5 acted out and explained the fall of Jerusalem. Now the prophet’s face turns from the city to the whole land: chapters 6 and 7 are a pair of sermons that carry the judgment out to every hill and valley of Israel.

The message. The places where Israel gave her heart to idols will become the places where she dies, and the idols will be shown up as helpless. Yet God will keep a remnant alive, and in exile they will at last remember him and see what their unfaithfulness did: it broke his heart. Through judgment and through that broken-hearted remembering, they will know that he is the LORD.

Why it was said. For centuries Israel had worshipped at hilltop shrines, mixing the LORD with the gods of Canaan (see the introduction). The exiles needed to see that this was not a harmless local custom but adultery against their God, and the reason their land was being lost.

How the chapter makes its case. Ezekiel faces the mountains of Israel and pronounces a sword on the high places (vv. 1–3): altars smashed, worshippers lying dead before their idols, bones scattered round the altars, every work of their hands wiped out (vv. 4–7). Then the tone turns on one word, “Yet”: survivors among the nations will remember how God was broken over their whoring heart, and will loathe their evil (vv. 8–10). Finally the prophet claps, stamps and cries “Alas” as pestilence, sword and famine reach far and near, and the land lies desolate from the wilderness to Riblah (vv. 11–14). Four times the refrain sounds: they will know that I am the LORD (vv. 7, 10, 13, 14).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God it reveals and by the need it exposes. The God who was “broken” over his people’s unfaithfulness came in his Son and wept over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37), and then let his own heart be broken on the cross for the people who had broken faith with him. The chapter also shows the need: smashed shrines do not change a whoring heart, and only the new heart and spirit God promises (36:26) can. Jesus ended the age of holy mountains: “neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father” (John 4:21), for the true worshippers worship in spirit and truth, through him.

For us. Our idols are rarely carved, but whatever we trust and love in God’s place will fail us in the day of trouble. Sin is not only a broken rule but a wound to a loving God, and true repentance begins when we see it from his side and hate it, then run to the Saviour whose heart was broken for us.
6.theology:
God's word reaches wherever he sends it, even to distant mountains (vv. 1-3).

Idols cannot save; their worshippers will lie dead before them (vv. 4-6; Ps 115:4-8).

Judgment is not God's final word: he leaves a remnant (v. 8).

Idolatry is spiritual adultery that begins in the heart and eyes, and it breaks God's heart (v. 9; Gen 6:6; Matt 23:37; Eph 4:30).

True repentance sees sin from God's side and loathes it (v. 9; 36:31; 2 Cor 7:10).

God's warnings are not in vain; he does what he says (v. 10).
6.examples:
A prophet in Babylon preaches to the hills of home, where worshippers will lie dead in front of gods that cannot see them. Their eyes were unfaithful before their feet ever climbed the hill.

In the middle of it the God of the storm says, I have been broken, and his prophet claps, stamps and cries Alas.

keyVerse.quote: then those of you who escape will remember me among the nations where they are carried captive, how I have been broken over their whoring heart that has departed from me and over their eyes that go whoring after their idols.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of sword and ruin, this verse opens God’s heart. Israel’s idolatry was not just rule-breaking but adultery that broke the heart of the God who loved her. When the survivors finally see their sin from his side, they will loathe it, and that is where true repentance begins.

6.reflection:
God told Ezekiel to speak to the mountains of Israel, because the high places on them were where Israel’s heart had gone astray (vv. 1–3). What are the “high places” in our culture, the places or things people turn to instead of God? Which pull hardest on you?

The worshippers lay dead before idols that could do nothing (vv. 4–7). Think of something you have trusted that let you down when it mattered. What did it teach you about where to put your weight?

God says, “I have been broken over their whoring heart” (v. 9). How does it change the way you see sin to know that it grieves God, not only breaks his law? How does the cross show the depth of that love?

Ezekiel was told to clap, stamp and cry “Alas” as he announced judgment (v. 11). How can Christians speak about sin and judgment today with that kind of grief rather than coldness or satisfaction?

The end has come upon the four corners of the land.<sup>3</sup>Now the end is upon you, and I will send my anger upon you; I will judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations.<sup>4</sup>And my eye will not spare you, nor will I have pity, but I will punish you for your ways, while your abominations are in your midst. He who is in the field dies by the sword, and him who is in the city famine and pestilence devour.<sup>16</sup>And if any survivors escape, they will be on the mountains, like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, each one over his iniquity.<sup>17</sup>All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water.<sup>18</sup>They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces, and baldness on all their heads.<sup>19</sup>They cast their silver into the streets, and their gold is like an unclean thing. Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD. They cannot satisfy their hunger or fill their stomachs with it. For it was the stumbling block of their iniquity.<sup>20</sup>His beautiful ornament they used for pride, and they made their abominable images and their detestable things of it. Therefore I make it an unclean thing to them.<sup>21</sup>And I will give it into the hands of foreigners for prey, and to the wicked of the earth for spoil, and they shall profane it.<sup>22</sup>I will turn my face from them, and they shall profane my treasured place. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — An End! The End Has Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s long patience has run out: the end has come, and he will judge Judah exactly according to its ways. The sentence falls like a bell: “An end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land” (v. 2). God will send his anger and repay their ways and their abominations, without pity, and they will know that he is the LORD (vv. 3–4). Then the same message again, with rising urgency: disaster after disaster, an end that has “awakened”, a day of tumult rather than festival shouting on the mountains (vv. 5–7). Verses 8–9 repeat verses 3–4 and add a new name: “the LORD, who strikes”.
verseByVerse.theology: There is a real end to God's patience, and it comes on the day he has set.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "And you, O son of man, thus says the Lord GOD to the land of Israel: An end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land. Now the end is upon you, and I will send my anger upon you; I will judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations. And my eye will not spare you, nor will I have pity, but I will punish you for your ways, while your abominations are in your midst. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The warnings are over: God’s judgment has arrived on the whole land, and it will match exactly what the people have done.

An end! The end has come. Chapter 7 reads like a bell tolling, the word “end” striking again and again. For centuries Israel had heard warnings; now they are over. More than a century and a half earlier the LORD had said the same to the northern kingdom through Amos: “The end has come upon my people Israel” (Amos 8:2). The north did not listen, and it fell. Now Judah hears the same sentence.

The four corners of the land. The whole of it, with nowhere excluded. The ESV notes that “land” may be “earth”, as if Judah’s end were a picture of a greater end still to come for all the world.

According to your ways. Judgment is not random; it fits what was done. God does not punish people for sins they did not commit, and he does not overlook the ones they did.

While your abominations are in your midst. They are still clinging to their idols as the end comes. God’s patience has been long, but it has not been answered with repentance: “Do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience?” (Romans 2:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: Disaster after disaster! Behold, it comes. An end has come; the end has come; it has awakened against you. Behold, it comes. Your doom has come to you, O inhabitant of the land. The time has come; the day is near, a day of tumult, and not of joyful shouting on the mountains. Now I will soon pour out my wrath upon you, and spend my anger against you, and judge you according to your ways, and I will punish you for all your abominations. And my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity. I will punish you according to your ways, while your abominations are in your midst. Then you will know that I am the LORD, who strikes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment people thought was asleep has woken up, and they will meet a side of God they had forgotten: the LORD who strikes.

It has awakened against you. In Hebrew “the end” and “it has awakened” sound almost the same, a deliberate play on words. For years people said the judgment was asleep and nothing would happen. Peter describes the same attitude in the last days, scoffers asking, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (2 Peter 3:4). But “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you”, and “the day of the Lord will come like a thief” (2 Peter 3:9–10). What looks like sleep is patience.

Not of joyful shouting on the mountains. The mountains, where people shouted at harvest festivals and idol feasts, will hear a different noise: the tumult of an invading army.

The LORD, who strikes. Verses 8–9 repeat verses 3–4 almost word for word, hammering the message home, and add a new name: “the LORD, who strikes”. They had known him as the LORD who delivers, provides and blesses, and had forgotten that he also strikes. A God who never judges is not the God of the Bible.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read “Disaster! A unique disaster!” rather than “Disaster after disaster!”: either one disaster after another, or one disaster like no other. The meaning of the word behind “doom” (vv. 7, 10) is also uncertain, as the ESV notes; the King James Version took it as “morning”, and others as “your turn”. The picture is clear either way: the day has come.
verseByVerse.note: A sound-play: “end” (qets) and “awakened” (heqits) sound alike.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–22 — Silver and Gold Cannot Deliver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the end comes, everything Judah trusted will fail her. Pride has come into flower as the rod that will beat her, and none of her wealth or rank will remain (vv. 10–11). Buying and selling lose their meaning, because the exile will outlast the sellers (vv. 12–13). The trumpet sounds but no one marches; sword outside, famine and pestilence within; survivors moan on the hills, each over his own sin, and every face is covered with shame (vv. 14–18). Silver is thrown into the streets, because it cannot deliver on the day of wrath and was the very thing that tripped them (v. 19). The gold they made into idols will be plundered, and when God turns his face away, robbers will profane his treasured place (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The wealth people trust becomes worthless on the day of God's wrath, and the thing they made into an idol becomes their stumbling block.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the day! Behold, it comes! Your doom has come; the rod has blossomed; pride has budded. Violence has grown up into a rod of wickedness. None of them shall remain, nor their abundance, nor their wealth; neither shall there be preeminence among them. The time has come; the day has arrived. Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn, for wrath is upon all their multitude. For the seller shall not return to what he has sold, while they live. For the vision concerns all their multitude; it shall not turn back; and because of his iniquity, none can maintain his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s pride has come into full flower as the rod that will beat her, and when the end comes, ordinary buying and selling will lose all meaning.

The rod has blossomed. Like a plant growing quietly, Judah’s pride has come into flower, and so has the rod of punishment. Perhaps there is an echo of Aaron’s staff, which “had sprouted and put forth buds and produced blossoms” as a sign of God’s choosing (Numbers 17:8); if so, what once blossomed as a sign of God’s favour now blossoms as a sign of his judgment. Sin grows quietly for a season, and then its full result appears.

Violence has grown up into a rod of wickedness. The violence Judah practised has grown into the rod that will beat it. None of their wealth, none of their rank, will survive.

Let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn. Normally the buyer is glad of a good deal and the seller sorry to part with land. When the end comes, neither matters: the buyer will not keep what he bought, and the seller has lost nothing worth grieving. Under the law, land that was sold returned to its family in the year of jubilee (Leviticus 25:13), but “the seller shall not return”: the exile will last longer than the sellers will live.

In everyday life. Paul tells Christians to live as “those who buy as though they had no goods”, because “the present form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:30–31). Knowing that this world will end puts property in its place. Hold what you own loosely, because what God keeps for his people in Christ cannot pass away.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the last sentence of verse 11 is uncertain, and that “multitude” (vv. 12–14) may be “abundance”. The thrust is plain: the violence and wealth they trusted will come to nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: "They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but none goes to battle, for my wrath is upon all their multitude. The sword is without; pestilence and famine are within. He who is in the field dies by the sword, and him who is in the city famine and pestilence devour. And if any survivors escape, they will be on the mountains, like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, each one over his iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one fights and no one escapes, and the few who survive are at last driven to grieve over their own sin.

But none goes to battle. The trumpet sounds, the weapons are ready, and no one marches out. Courage has drained away, because God’s wrath is on them. An army without God’s blessing is paralysed.

The sword is without. Field or city, there is nowhere safe: in the country the sword finds you; behind the walls hunger and disease find you. Amos pictured the same inescapable day: “as if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him, or went into the house and leaned his hand against the wall, and a serpent bit him” (Amos 5:19). There is no hiding place from God except in God himself.

Each one over his iniquity. The few who get away hide in the hills, moaning like mourning doves. And at last they are moaning over the right thing: their own iniquity. Suffering has finally driven them to face their sin. It is a terrible way to come to repentance, but better than never coming at all.

verseByVerse.quote: All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water. They put on sackcloth, and horror covers them. Shame is on all faces, and baldness on all their heads. They cast their silver into the streets, and their gold is like an unclean thing. Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD. They cannot satisfy their hunger or fill their stomachs with it. For it was the stumbling block of their iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proud are reduced to shame, and the wealth they trusted proves worthless on the day of God’s wrath, because it was the very thing that led them into sin.

All hands are feeble. Limp hands, knees that give way, sackcloth, shaved heads, faces burning with shame. The proud city of verse 10 is reduced to mourners. Pride always ends in shame when God acts.

They cast their silver into the streets. People throw silver into the gutter because it is useless: you cannot eat gold in a siege, and you cannot buy your way out of God’s judgment. Zephaniah said it in almost the same words: “Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the LORD” (Zephaniah 1:18). “Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death” (Proverbs 11:4).

The stumbling block of their iniquity. It was worse than useless. Their wealth was what tripped them up: money had fed their pride, paid for their idols and bought their comfort while the poor suffered.

In a wealthy culture. What we trust for security may be exactly what keeps us from God. “For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?” (Matthew 16:26). There is only one ransom that works on the day of wrath, and it was not paid “with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

verseByVerse.quote: His beautiful ornament they used for pride, and they made their abominable images and their detestable things of it. Therefore I make it an unclean thing to them. And I will give it into the hands of foreigners for prey, and to the wicked of the earth for spoil, and they shall profane it. I will turn my face from them, and they shall profane my treasured place. Robbers shall enter and profane it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gold God gave them they turned into idols, so he will hand it to plunderers; and when he turns his face away, even his temple has no protection.

His beautiful ornament they used for pride. The gold God had given them as a beautiful ornament they turned into a source of pride and then melted down into idols. It is the golden calf all over again: the people took “the rings of gold that were in their ears”, and Aaron “made a golden calf” (Exodus 32:3–4). God’s gifts, turned against the Giver.

My treasured place. This is the temple, and above all its inner sanctuary (the ESV notes it may be “secret” place). Robbers will walk into it, and the reason is given first: “I will turn my face from them”. The temple’s protection was never its walls. It was God’s face turned toward his people, his favour and care. When he turns away, anyone can walk in.

Into the hands of foreigners. God uses foreigners, “the wicked of the earth”. That troubled the prophet Habakkuk deeply when God told him, “I am raising up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation”, and he asked why God would “remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he” (Habakkuk 1:6, 13). Scripture’s answer is that God can use wicked people to carry out his just purposes, and then hold them accountable for their own wickedness, as he did with Babylon.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A violent land will be taken captive, and when the people finally seek peace and a word from God, they will find neither. Ezekiel is to forge a chain, because the land is full of bloodshed and the city full of violence (v. 23). The worst of the nations will take their houses and humble the proud (v. 24). They will seek peace and there will be none (v. 25); disaster and rumour will pile up, and the prophet, priest and elders will have nothing to give (v. 26). From king to people all will be paralysed, and God will judge them by their own standards, so that they know that he is the LORD (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: When the end comes, every source of guidance people once ignored is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: "Forge a chain! For the land is full of bloody crimes and the city is full of violence. I will bring the worst of the nations to take possession of their houses. I will put an end to the pride of the strong, and their holy places shall be profaned. When anguish comes, they will seek peace, but there shall be none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A land full of violence will be led away in chains, and when the people finally seek peace, there will be none.

Forge a chain! Make the chains ready; the captives are coming. And the reason is not idolatry alone but “bloody crimes” and “violence”. Sin against God always shows itself as sin against neighbour.

The worst of the nations … the pride of the strong. Ruthless Babylon will move into Judah’s homes. Judah’s leaders had trusted their strength, their alliances and their fortress city, but God’s way through history is always the same: “he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52). (Where the ESV reads “their holy places”, it notes the Hebrew as “those who sanctify them”.)

They will seek peace, but there shall be none. For years the false prophets had been “saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace” (Jeremiah 6:14). Now the people seek it and find nothing. There is a time when peace with God can be found, and a time when it is too late: “Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).
verseByVerse.note: “Chain” probably refers to an instrument of captivity (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Disaster comes upon disaster; rumor follows rumor. They seek a vision from the prophet, while the law perishes from the priest and counsel from the elders. The king mourns, the prince is wrapped in despair, and the hands of the people of the land are paralyzed by terror. According to their way I will do to them, and according to their judgments I will judge them, and they shall know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
