Too late, the people look for a word from God and find none, and God judges them by the same measure they used on others.

They seek a vision from the prophet. Now, too late, they want to hear from God. But the priest has no instruction (the ESV notes “law” may be “instruction”) and the elders have no counsel. The sources of guidance they had ignored for years are gone. Lamentations mourned it: “the law is no more, and her prophets find no vision from the LORD” (Lamentations 2:9). Do not assume God’s word will always be there when you finally want it; while he still speaks, listen.

According to their judgments. From the king down to the ordinary people, everyone is paralysed. And the last sentence is exact justice: they were harsh and unjust to others, and God will measure them with their own measure. Jesus warned, “with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged” (Matthew 7:2).

The end has already come. Yet for those in Christ, the end has already come in another sense. Christ “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26). The final judgment on sin fell on him at the cross. Those joined to him do not face the end as doom; they are the ones “on whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Corinthians 10:11) as salvation.

7.title: The End Has Come
7.overview:
Where we are. This chapter closes the first group of messages against Jerusalem (chapters 4–7). Chapter 6 spoke to the mountains of Israel; now God speaks to the whole land with a sentence that tolls like a bell: the end has come.

The message. God’s long patience with Judah is over, and the day of reckoning has arrived. Everything the people trusted will fail them: their wealth cannot buy deliverance, their army will not march, their temple will be entered by robbers, and their prophets, priests and elders will have no word. God will judge them exactly according to their ways, and they will know that he is the LORD.

Why it was said. The exiles, and the people still in Jerusalem, believed that disaster could be put off indefinitely: God had been patient so long that judgment seemed asleep (see the introduction). Ezekiel tells them that the warnings have run out and the day is here.

How the chapter makes its case. First the announcement (vv. 1–9): “An end! The end has come”, twice over, with judgment according to their ways and without pity, until they know “the LORD, who strikes”. Then what the end will do (vv. 10–22): pride has bloomed into the rod that strikes; buying and selling lose their meaning; no one marches to battle; survivors moan on the hills over their sin; silver is thrown into the streets because it cannot deliver; the gold they made into idols is given to plunderers, and robbers profane God’s treasured place. Finally the chains (vv. 23–27): a land full of violence will be taken by the worst of the nations, people will seek peace and a word from God and find neither, and God will judge them by their own standards.

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by covenant. When the day of wrath comes, “their silver and gold are not able to deliver them” (v. 19). The New Testament answers exactly that need: we were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). The end that fell on Jerusalem fell on Christ at the cross, when he “appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26). For those joined to him, the end has already come, and it was salvation.

For us. God’s patience is real, but it is patience, not indifference, and a day is coming when it will be too late to seek him. Hold possessions loosely: they cannot save you and can trip you. Listen to God’s word while he is still speaking, and trust the only ransom that works on the day of wrath.
7.theology:
God's patience has an end, and judgment fits the ways of those judged (vv. 2-4, 27; Amos 8:2; Rom 2:4-5).

The LORD who delivers is also the LORD who strikes (v. 9).

Wealth cannot deliver in the day of wrath and often becomes the very stumbling block of sin (v. 19; Zeph 1:18; Prov 11:4; Matt 16:26).

God's gifts turned into idols become unclean to their owners (vv. 20-22; Exod 32:2-4).

The protection of God's house is God's face, not its walls (v. 22).

Guidance ignored may be withdrawn when it is finally sought (vv. 25-26; Lam 2:9).

At the end of the ages the judgment on sin fell on Christ, so that for those in him the end is salvation, not doom (Heb 9:26; 1 Cor 10:11).
7.examples:
The chapter tolls like a bell: the end, the end, the end. Pride comes into flower, buyer and seller both lose, and a trumpet blasts with nobody marching.

Silver is thrown into the gutter, jewellery that was melted into idols is carried off, and people run to the prophet when there are no more visions.

keyVerse.quote: Their silver and gold are not able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: When the end comes, everything Judah trusted fails, and this verse names the hardest lesson: money cannot buy deliverance from God’s judgment, and it was the very thing that tripped them. It points us to the one ransom that does avail on the day of wrath, paid not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19).

7.reflection:
God says “the end has come” after centuries of patience (vv. 2–6), and Peter says his patience is meant to lead us to repentance (2 Peter 3:9). Why do people, including Christians, so easily mistake God’s patience for indifference?

In the day of wrath, people threw their silver into the streets because it could not save them (v. 19). What do people around you trust for security? What would it look like for you to hold money and possessions more loosely?

The trumpet sounded but no one went to battle, and the survivors moaned over their sin (vv. 14–16). Why does it so often take suffering to make us face our sin? How can we learn to repent before things come to that?

Too late, the people sought a vision from the prophet (v. 26). How do you treat God’s word while it is freely available? How does knowing that judgment fell on Christ at “the end of the ages” change the way you face the coming day?

8.text: <sup>1</sup>In the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I sat in my house, with the elders of Judah sitting before me, the hand of the Lord GOD fell upon me there.<sup>2</sup>Then I looked, and behold, a form that had the appearance of a man. Below what appeared to be his waist was fire, and above his waist was something like the appearance of brightness, like gleaming metal.<sup>3</sup>He put out the form of a hand and took me by a lock of my head, and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and brought me in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the gateway of the inner court that faces north, where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy.<sup>4</sup>And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, like the vision that I saw in the valley.<sup>5</sup>Then he said to me, "Son of man, lift up your eyes now toward the north." So I lifted up my eyes toward the north, and behold, north of the altar gate, in the entrance, was this image of jealousy.<sup>6</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, do you see what they are doing, the great abominations that the house of Israel are committing here, to drive me far from my sanctuary? But you will see still greater abominations."<sup>7</sup>And he brought me to the entrance of the court, and when I looked, behold, there was a hole in the wall.<sup>8</sup>Then he said to me, "Son of man, dig in the wall." So I dug in the wall, and behold, there was an entrance.<sup>9</sup>And he said to me, "Go in, and see the vile abominations that they are committing here."<sup>10</sup>So I went in and saw. And there, engraved on the wall all around, was every form of creeping things and loathsome beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And before them stood seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, with Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan standing among them. Each had his censer in his hand, and the smoke of the cloud of incense went up.<sup>12</sup>Then he said to me, "Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the dark, each in his room of pictures? For they say, 'The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land.'"<sup>13</sup>He said also to me, "You will see still greater abominations that they commit."<sup>14</sup>Then he brought me to the entrance of the north gate of the house of the LORD, and behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz.<sup>15</sup>Then he said to me, "Have you seen this, O son of man? You will see still greater abominations than these."<sup>16</sup>And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the LORD. And behold, at the entrance of the temple of the LORD, between the porch and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs to the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun toward the east.<sup>17</sup>Then he said to me, "Have you seen this, O son of man? Is it too light a thing for the house of Judah to commit the abominations that they commit here, that they should fill the land with violence and provoke me still further to anger? Behold, they put the branch to their nose.<sup>18</sup>Therefore I will act in wrath. My eye will not spare, nor will I have pity. And though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows his prophet that idolatry has invaded his own house, beside the very place where his glory stands. Fourteen months after his call, as the elders of Judah sit before him in exile, a figure of fire and brightness lifts Ezekiel by his hair and brings him “in visions of God to Jerusalem” (vv. 1–3). At the north gate of the inner court stands the “image of jealousy”, so called because it provokes the LORD to jealousy, and there too is the glory of God, as he had seen it before (vv. 3–5). God asks whether Ezekiel sees what they are doing “to drive me far from my sanctuary”, and promises that there is worse (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry in God's house provokes his jealousy and drives his presence away.

verseByVerse.quote: In the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I sat in my house, with the elders of Judah sitting before me, the hand of the Lord GOD fell upon me there. Then I looked, and behold, a form that had the appearance of a man. Below what appeared to be his waist was fire, and above his waist was something like the appearance of brightness, like gleaming metal. He put out the form of a hand and took me by a lock of my head, and the Spirit lifted me up between earth and heaven and brought me in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the gateway of the inner court that faces north, where was the seat of the image of jealousy, which provokes to jealousy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the exiled elders wait for a word, God carries Ezekiel in a vision to Jerusalem and sets him before an idol at the gate of the temple.

As I sat in my house. About fourteen months have passed since the first vision, in late summer 592 BC. The leaders of the exiles, the elders of Judah, have come to Ezekiel’s house and sit before him, presumably to hear a word from God. They get God’s answer to every exile who thought Jerusalem was innocent and would be spared.

A form that had the appearance of a man. This is the figure Ezekiel saw on the throne (1:27): fire below, brightness above. Most readers take the guide who shows him the temple to be the Lord himself, though some think of an angel sent from his presence.

In visions of God to Jerusalem. Ezekiel does not travel in body, but what he sees is real. He is set down at the gate of the inner court, and the first thing in front of him is an idol.

The image of jealousy. It is so called because it provokes the LORD to jealousy. God had said at Sinai, “You shall not make for yourself a carved image … for I the LORD your God am a jealous God” (Exodus 20:4–5). An idol in his house is like a lover’s photograph on a married couple’s bedside table: “They stirred him to jealousy with strange gods” (Deuteronomy 32:16). King Manasseh had once set “the carved image of Asherah” inside the temple (2 Kings 21:7). The reforms since then had not lasted.

Uncertain wording. We do not know exactly what the image of jealousy was. Many think it was an image of the goddess Asherah, like the one Manasseh had set up, but the text does not name it; it is described only by its effect on God.

Textual note. For “a man” in verse 2 the ESV follows the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation; the Hebrew reads “fire”. The ESV also notes that “gleaming metal” may be “amber”.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth year of King Jehoiachin's exile (1:2) was about 592 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was there, like the vision that I saw in the valley. Then he said to me, "Son of man, lift up your eyes now toward the north." So I lifted up my eyes toward the north, and behold, north of the altar gate, in the entrance, was this image of jealousy. And he said to me, "Son of man, do you see what they are doing, the great abominations that the house of Israel are committing here, to drive me far from my sanctuary? But you will see still greater abominations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s glory and an idol stand in the same courtyard, and God says plainly that his people are driving him out of his own house.

The glory of the God of Israel was there. Both are in the courtyard at once: the glory of God and the image of jealousy. How long can the holy God stay in a house where an idol stands at the gate?

North of the altar gate. People going to the altar to worship the LORD walked past the idol: his worship had been mixed with idol worship.

To drive me far from my sanctuary. Here is the reason the glory will leave in chapters 10–11. God does not simply abandon his house; his people drive him out. Sin pushes God away.

For Christians. “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). The Spirit does not leave a true believer, but believers can grieve him and lose the felt sense of his nearness when they make room for idols in the heart.

Still greater abominations. The refrain begins: “you will see still greater abominations”. Each room Ezekiel enters is worse than the last.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The leaders of Israel are worshipping idols in secret, telling themselves that God does not see. Ezekiel is shown a hole in the wall, digs through, and enters a hidden room whose walls are carved with creeping things, unclean beasts and idols (vv. 7–10). Seventy elders of Israel, Jaazaniah son of Shaphan among them, stand there with censers, wrapped in a cloud of incense (v. 11). Each has his own room of pictures, and their excuse is a lie about God: “The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land” (v. 12). And there is still worse to see (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Secret sin is never hidden from God, and it is often most at home among the leaders.

verseByVerse.quote: And he brought me to the entrance of the court, and when I looked, behold, there was a hole in the wall. Then he said to me, "Son of man, dig in the wall." So I dug in the wall, and behold, there was an entrance. And he said to me, "Go in, and see the vile abominations that they are committing here." So I went in and saw. And there, engraved on the wall all around, was every form of creeping things and loathsome beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind a wall, in a hidden room, Israel’s worship has sunk to bowing before carvings of creeping things and unclean animals.

Dig in the wall. This worship happens out of sight, in a secret room: the religion of people who know that what they are doing is wrong.

Every form of creeping things. The walls are covered with carvings of reptiles, insects and unclean animals, exactly what the law forbade: “the likeness of any animal that is on the earth … the likeness of anything that creeps on the ground” (Deuteronomy 4:17–18). Paul describes the same exchange in every culture: people “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things” (Romans 1:23). The glory of God is in the court, and in the dark room they bow to beetles and snakes. That is the tragic foolishness of all idolatry: trading the Creator for creeping things.

verseByVerse.quote: And before them stood seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, with Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan standing among them. Each had his censer in his hand, and the smoke of the cloud of incense went up. Then he said to me, "Son of man, have you seen what the elders of the house of Israel are doing in the dark, each in his room of pictures? For they say, 'The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land.'" He said also to me, "You will see still greater abominations that they commit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders who should lead Israel in true worship burn incense to idols in secret, comforting themselves that God does not see; but he sees everything.

Seventy men of the elders. The number is deliberate. At Sinai “seventy of the elders of Israel” went up the mountain, “and they saw the God of Israel” (Exodus 24:9–10). Their successors now burn incense to carved animals in a dark room.

Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan. One man is named. If this is the Shaphan who served King Josiah during the great reform (2 Kings 22:12), whose son Ahikam protected Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24), then he comes from a faithful family. Godly parents do not guarantee godly children; every generation must turn to God for itself.

Each in his room of pictures. Each had his own private shrine. And their excuse is a claim about God: “The LORD does not see us, the LORD has forsaken the land”. Since the exile of Jehoiachin God seemed absent, so they looked for other help.

The LORD does see. But Ezekiel has seen the wheels “full of eyes all around” (1:18). “He who formed the eye, does he not see?” (Psalm 94:9). “No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13).

In everyday life. Many people keep a room of pictures (a hidden screen, a secret habit, a private idol) behind a wall while they appear devout in public. God sees into that room, and he sees it so that it can be brought into the light and forgiven before it is exposed in judgment. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9), and the Spirit who lives in believers gives strength to tear the pictures down.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the very centre of God’s house, his people have turned their backs on him, and he will no longer hear them. At the north gate women weep for Tammuz, a dying god of the seasons (vv. 14–15). In the inner court, between the porch and the altar where priests prayed for the people, about twenty-five men stand with their backs to the temple of the LORD, bowing to the rising sun (v. 16). Their false worship goes with violence that fills the land and provokes God further, so he will act in wrath, and though they cry loudly, he will not hear (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: To turn your back on God while standing in his house is the height of rebellion, and it invites his judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me to the entrance of the north gate of the house of the LORD, and behold, there sat women weeping for Tammuz. Then he said to me, "Have you seen this, O son of man? You will see still greater abominations than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the gate of the living God’s house, women mourn a dead god of the seasons who could save no one.

Women weeping for Tammuz. Tammuz was a Mesopotamian god whose death was mourned every year, tied to the dying of vegetation in the dry season.

Grieving the wrong death. The irony is sharp. They have the living God, and they weep for a god of the seasons who could save no one. The death to weep over and to trust in is the death of Jesus, who rose again.
verseByVerse.note: The name lived on: the fourth month of the later Jewish calendar is still called Tammuz.

verseByVerse.quote: And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the LORD. And behold, at the entrance of the temple of the LORD, between the porch and the altar, were about twenty-five men, with their backs to the temple of the LORD, and their faces toward the east, worshiping the sun toward the east. Then he said to me, "Have you seen this, O son of man? Is it too light a thing for the house of Judah to commit the abominations that they commit here, that they should fill the land with violence and provoke me still further to anger? Behold, they put the branch to their nose. Therefore I will act in wrath. My eye will not spare, nor will I have pity. And though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the holiest court of all, men turn their backs on God to worship the sun, and because their false worship has filled the land with violence, God will not hear their cries.

Between the porch and the altar. Now the innermost court, the place where the priests stood to pray for the people. About twenty-five men stand there with their backs to God’s house and bow to the rising sun.

Worshiping the sun toward the east. Moses had warned, “beware lest you raise your eyes to heaven, and when you see the sun and the moon and the stars … you be drawn away and bow down to them” (Deuteronomy 4:19). Josiah had removed “the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun, at the entrance to the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 23:11). Now sun worship is back, at the very centre of the temple.

With their backs to the temple of the LORD. The posture says everything. God had said through Jeremiah, “they have turned their back to me, and not their face” (Jeremiah 2:27). You can stand in the right building and have your back to God.

They should fill the land with violence. False worship and violence go together. When people turn their backs on God, they soon turn their fists on each other.

I will not hear them. The final words are terrible: “though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them”. Wisdom had warned long ago, “they will call upon me, but I will not answer” (Proverbs 1:28). There is a time when calling on God is too late.

Zeal for your house will consume me. But this vision is being told to elders sitting in a house in Babylon, while there is still time, and the warning is itself mercy. Jesus, finding his Father’s house full of traders, drove them out, and “His disciples remembered that it was written, ‘Zeal for your house will consume me’” (John 2:17). His zeal did consume him: he died so that a people could become a temple where God is worshipped “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23).

Uncertain wording. “They put the branch to their nose” is an obscure gesture, and no one is sure what it meant. The ESV notes that “their” may be “my”, which would make it an insult pushed into God’s own face.

8.title: Abominations in the Temple
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 4–7 announced that Jerusalem would fall. Chapter 8 begins a single great vision (chapters 8–11), dated about fourteen months after Ezekiel’s call, that shows why: the prophet is carried in spirit to the temple and taken through it room by room, and by the end of the vision the glory of God has left.

The message. The house that was supposed to protect Jerusalem has been filled with idols, from the gate to the innermost court. The leaders who should have guarded true worship are worshipping other gods in secret, telling themselves that God does not see. God sees everything, and his people are driving him out of his own house.

Why it was said. The elders in Ezekiel’s house still believed Jerusalem was innocent and safe (see the introduction). This vision answers them: the city’s religion is rotten at its centre, and God’s judgment is not arbitrary.

How the chapter makes its case. A figure of fire and brightness lifts Ezekiel by his hair and brings him “in visions of God to Jerusalem”, where the glory of God stands near an idol called the image of jealousy at the north gate (vv. 1–6). Each scene is deeper and worse: through a hole in the wall, seventy elders burn incense before carvings of unclean animals in the dark, saying, “The LORD does not see us” (vv. 7–13); women at the north gate weep for the dying god Tammuz (vv. 14–15); and in the inner court, between the porch and the altar, about twenty-five men turn their backs on the LORD’s house to bow to the rising sun (v. 16). Religion like this goes with violence, so God will act in wrath and not hear their cries (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The temple was meant to be the place where God lived among his people, and they defiled it. When Jesus came to his Father’s house and found it corrupted, he drove out the traders, “His disciples remembered that it was written, ‘Zeal for your house will consume me’” (John 2:17), and he spoke of the temple of his own body. His zeal did consume him on the cross, so that sinners could become a temple where God is worshipped “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23). The God who sees into every dark room sent “the light of the world” (John 8:12) to bring hidden sin into the open and forgive it.

For us. Believers are now God’s temple. It is possible to stand in the right building with your back to God, and to keep a private room of pictures behind a wall. God sees it, not to shame us but so that it can be brought into the light, confessed and forgiven while there is still time.
8.theology:
God is jealous for his people's exclusive worship, and idolatry in his house drives his presence away (vv. 3, 5-6; Exod 20:4-5; Deut 32:16).

Idolatry exchanges the glory of God for images of creatures (v. 10; Deut 4:16-18; Rom 1:22-23).

Secret sin is seen by God; the claim that he does not see is folly (v. 12; Ps 94:7-9; Heb 4:13).

Leaders bear special guilt in false worship, and false worship breeds violence (vv. 11, 16-17). There comes a time when cries for help are too late (v. 18), so the warning given beforehand is mercy.

Christ's zeal for his Father's house led him to the cross, to make a people who worship in spirit and truth and are themselves God's temple (John 2:17; 4:23-24; 1 Cor 3:16-17).
8.examples: The chapter is a gallery of pictures that stay in the mind: an idol on the path to the altar; seventy elders, one of them the son of a faithful family, burning incense to beetles in the dark; women weeping for a god who cannot save; and men standing in God's own house with their backs to him.

keyVerse.quote: Son of man, do you see what they are doing, the great abominations that the house of Israel are committing here, to drive me far from my sanctuary? But you will see still greater abominations.
keyVerse.note: This question opens the tour of the temple and explains the whole vision. God does not leave his house on a whim: his people are driving him out with their idols. The refrain “still greater abominations” then leads Ezekiel deeper, scene by scene, until the glory departs in chapters 10–11.

8.reflection:
The glory of God and the “image of jealousy” stood in the same courtyard (vv. 3–5). Where are we tempted to mix the worship of God with trust in something else? Why does God call that jealousy-provoking rather than merely a mistake?

The elders worshipped in secret, telling themselves, “The LORD does not see us” (v. 12). What “rooms of pictures” do people keep hidden today? How does the promise of 1 John 1:9 make it safe to bring them into the light?

Jaazaniah was probably the son of a godly man who served Josiah (v. 11). What does this teach about faith passing from one generation to the next? How can we pray for and encourage the young people around us?

The men in the inner court stood with their backs to the temple (v. 16). How is it possible to be in church and yet have our backs to God? How does Jesus’ zeal for his Father’s house, and his death for us, give hope to people who have done that?

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying, "Bring near the executioners of the city, each with his destroying weapon in his hand."<sup>2</sup>And behold, six men came from the direction of the upper gate, which faces north, each with his weapon for slaughter in his hand, and with them was a man clothed in linen, with a writing case at his waist. And they went in and stood beside the bronze altar.<sup>3</sup>Now the glory of the God of Israel had gone up from the cherub on which it rested to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed in linen, who had the writing case at his waist.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to him, "Pass through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it."<sup>5</sup>And to the others he said in my hearing, "Pass through the city after him, and strike. Your eye shall not spare, and you shall show no pity.<sup>6</sup>Kill old men outright, young men and maidens, little children and women, but touch no one on whom is the mark. And begin at my sanctuary." So they began with the elders who were before the house.<sup>7</sup>Then he said to them, "Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain. Go out." So they went out and struck in the city.<sup>8</sup>And while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, "Ah, Lord GOD! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel in the outpouring of your wrath on Jerusalem?"<sup>9</sup>Then he said to me, "The guilt of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of blood, and the city full of injustice. For they say, 'The LORD has forsaken the land, and the LORD does not see.'<sup>10</sup>As for me, my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity; I will bring their deeds upon their heads."<sup>11</sup>And behold, the man clothed in linen, with the writing case at his waist, brought back word, saying, "I have done as you commanded me."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — A Man Clothed in Linen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God protects his own before a single blow falls. A loud voice summons six executioners, each with a weapon, and with them a seventh figure, dressed in priestly linen with a scribe’s writing case at his waist; together they take their stand beside the bronze altar (vv. 1–2). The glory of God has already risen from the cherub to the threshold of the temple, the first step of its departure (v. 3). Then the LORD sends the man in linen through Jerusalem ahead of the others, to mark the foreheads of everyone who sighs and groans over the abominations done in it (v. 4). Grief over sin, not religious performance, is the sign of those God keeps.
verseByVerse.theology: Before judgment falls, God marks and protects those who grieve over sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he cried in my ears with a loud voice, saying, "Bring near the executioners of the city, each with his destroying weapon in his hand." And behold, six men came from the direction of the upper gate, which faces north, each with his weapon for slaughter in his hand, and with them was a man clothed in linen, with a writing case at his waist. And they went in and stood beside the bronze altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God summons his agents of judgment, and among them stands a priest with a pen instead of a sword.

Then he cried in my ears with a loud voice. Chapter 8 ended with God saying that though the people “cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them” (8:18). Now God cries in Ezekiel’s ears with a loud voice, calling for the executioners. The people’s cry comes too late; God’s comes on time.

A man clothed in linen, with a writing case at his waist. This is a vision, so these are heavenly agents of judgment, though on earth God would use Babylon’s army. Six carry weapons. The seventh is different: he wears linen, the fabric of priests (Leviticus 16:4), and carries a scribe’s writing case instead of a sword. Daniel too saw “a man clothed in linen” (Daniel 10:5). They come from the north, where the idol of jealousy stood (8:5) and from where Babylon would come.

Beside the bronze altar. They take their stand at the altar of sacrifice. Judgment starts where sin was supposed to be dealt with by sacrifice. The people had kept up the sacrifices and ignored the God they were offered to.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the glory of the God of Israel had gone up from the cherub on which it rested to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed in linen, who had the writing case at his waist. And the LORD said to him, "Pass through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before anyone is struck, God marks and keeps those who grieve over the sin around them.

To the threshold of the house. The glory has moved from its place above the cherubim in the Most Holy Place to the doorway. The departure has begun. God leaves his house step by step, as if reluctant to go (see the note on 10:18–19).

Put a mark on the foreheads. The man in linen goes first and marks “the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations”. The mark goes not to those who performed the right rituals, but to those who grieve over sin. The psalmist was one of them: “My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law” (Psalm 119:136).

An echo of Passover. It is the Passover again: “The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). It also looks forward to the last judgment, when God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads and the plagues harm “only those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads” (Revelation 7:3; 9:4). “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). For Christians, God’s mark of ownership is the Holy Spirit, given through Christ: “when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13).

A question for us. When you see sin in the church, in the culture and in your own heart, do you shrug, or sneer, or grieve? The people God marks are the grieving ones. That grief is not a merit that earns the mark; it is the work of the Spirit in those God has already made his own, and it drives them to the mercy he promised.

A hint of the cross? Because of the shape of the letter behind “mark” (see the note), many Christians have seen here a hint of the cross. It is a lovely echo, but in the text the mark simply means ownership: these belong to the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word for "mark" is taw, also the name of the last Hebrew letter, which in the older script was written like an X or a cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment begins at God’s own house, and it is just. The executioners follow the man in linen through the city, sparing no one except those with the mark, beginning with the elders at the sanctuary and filling the courts with the slain (vv. 5–7). Ezekiel, left alone, falls on his face and pleads, “Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel?” (v. 8). God answers that the guilt is exceedingly great: the land is full of blood, the city full of injustice, and the people say the LORD does not see, so their deeds will come back on their heads (vv. 9–10). The chapter closes with the man in linen reporting that his work of marking is done (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment begins with those closest to God's house, and God's servants plead for mercy even as it falls.

verseByVerse.quote: And to the others he said in my hearing, "Pass through the city after him, and strike. Your eye shall not spare, and you shall show no pity. Kill old men outright, young men and maidens, little children and women, but touch no one on whom is the mark. And begin at my sanctuary." So they began with the elders who were before the house. Then he said to them, "Defile the house, and fill the courts with the slain. Go out." So they went out and struck in the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment falls without pity and begins at God’s house, yet no one with the mark is touched.

Your eye shall not spare. These are hard words, and they should not be softened. When Jerusalem fell, all ages suffered. Children die when cities are destroyed, and the Bible does not pretend otherwise.

Begin at my sanctuary. Judgment starts with the people nearest to God’s house, and with its leaders, “the elders who were before the house”, perhaps the very men Ezekiel had seen with their backs to the temple (8:16). Peter says the same principle holds for the church: “it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God” (1 Peter 4:17). Those given most must answer for most. For those who are in Christ, what begins at God’s household is a Father’s discipline, not condemnation, because the condemnation fell on him (Romans 8:1).

Defile the house. God himself commands the defiling of his temple. The people had already defiled it with idols; now corpses will make that defilement visible. A holy God will not protect a building that has become a shrine to other gods.

What do we do with this? First, remember whose judgment it is. Abraham, pleading for Sodom, held on to one certainty: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). We do not see as God sees, and we do not know every heart. Second, notice the exception, stated in the same breath: “touch no one on whom is the mark”. God’s judgment is not indiscriminate; he knows his own. Third, this is a vision of what sin brings on a whole community, meant to terrify people into repentance while there is time. Fourth, God takes no pleasure in such death (33:11), and believers can entrust the little ones who die in such disasters to the Judge who is both just and merciful.

verseByVerse.quote: And while they were striking, and I was left alone, I fell upon my face, and cried, "Ah, Lord GOD! Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel in the outpouring of your wrath on Jerusalem?" Then he said to me, "The guilt of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of blood, and the city full of injustice. For they say, 'The LORD has forsaken the land, and the LORD does not see.' As for me, my eye will not spare, nor will I have pity; I will bring their deeds upon their heads." And behold, the man clothed in linen, with the writing case at his waist, brought back word, saying, "I have done as you commanded me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel pleads for the remnant; God answers that the guilt is past bearing, yet every marked person is safe.

I fell upon my face. Ezekiel is left alone in courts full of bodies, and he does what the faithful have always done: he falls down and pleads. Abraham drew near and asked, “Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?” (Genesis 18:23). Amos cried, “O Lord GOD, please forgive! How can Jacob stand?” (Amos 7:2). The prophet who announces judgment is not hard-hearted. God will later look for someone to “stand in the breach before me for the land” (22:30), and every believer is called to stand there for others in prayer. The greatest intercessor does more than plead: Christ “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

Exceedingly great. God answers honestly. The guilt is exceedingly great: blood, injustice, and the proud lie that “the LORD does not see”, which the elders had already spoken in their dark room (8:12). The judgment is simply their own deeds coming back on their heads.

A question God answers. God does not rebuke Ezekiel for asking. The question “Will you destroy all the remnant of Israel?” will be answered, gloriously, later in the book: there will be a remnant, a new heart, dry bones living. Such pleading is never wasted.

I have done as you commanded me. The chapter ends not with the executioners’ report but with that of the man who marked the faithful. None was missed. Many Christians have seen in this figure a picture of our great High Priest, Jesus, who could say to his Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). The one who marks God’s people does not fail to finish his work.

9.title: The Mark on the Foreheads
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 continues the vision of 8:1, in which Ezekiel was carried in the Spirit from his house in Babylon to Jerusalem. He has seen four scenes of idolatry in the temple, each worse than the last, ending with men worshipping the sun with their backs to the house of God (8:16), and God has said, “My eye will not spare” (8:18). Now the sentence is carried out in vision.

The message. God’s judgment on his sinning people is real, and it begins at his own house. Yet before a single blow falls, he marks and keeps those who grieve over sin. His judgment is neither blind nor careless: the Lord knows those who are his, and he hears the prophet who pleads, even as he answers that the guilt is past bearing.

Why it was said. The exiles were sure that Jerusalem was safe because the temple stood in it (see the introduction). This vision tells them that the temple is where judgment starts, and that the only safety is the mark God himself gives.

How the chapter makes its case. Six executioners and a man in linen with a scribe’s writing case stand beside the bronze altar, while the glory moves to the threshold, the first step of its departure (vv. 1–3). The man in linen goes first, marking the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over the city’s abominations (v. 4). Then the others strike, beginning at the sanctuary with the elders and sparing only the marked (vv. 5–7). Ezekiel, left alone among the dead, falls on his face and pleads for the remnant (v. 8). God answers that the guilt is exceedingly great (vv. 9–10). The chapter ends with the man in linen reporting, “I have done as you commanded me” (v. 11).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. The mark recalls the Passover blood that kept Israel’s houses from the destroyer (Exodus 12:13), and it looks ahead to the seal of God on the foreheads of his servants (Revelation 7:3). The need is plain: if judgment begins at the house of God, who can stand? Only those God marks as his own. In Christ believers are “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13), and the priestly figure who finishes his work of marking is a fitting picture of the High Priest who said to his Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4).

For us. Ask whether the sin in the church, in the culture and in your own heart makes you shrug, sneer or grieve: the people God marked were the grieving ones. Shelter not in religious belonging but in Christ, who bore the judgment, and then, like Ezekiel, plead for others.
9.theology:
Before judgment falls, God marks and protects his own, those who grieve over sin (v. 4; Exod 12:13; Rev 7:3; 2 Tim 2:19).

Judgment begins at God's house and with its leaders (v. 6; 1 Pet 4:17).

God's judgment is just, even when we cannot see all its reasons (vv. 6, 9-10; Gen 18:25).

God's servants plead for others even as judgment falls, and God does not despise their pleading (v. 8; Gen 18:23; Amos 7:2; Ezek 22:30).

Many Christians have seen in the priestly figure who marks the faithful and completes his task a picture of Christ, who seals his people by the Spirit and finished the work the Father gave him (vv. 2, 11; Eph 1:13; John 17:4).
9.examples: Before a single sword moves, a scribe's pen goes ahead of the six, marking everyone who grieves over sin. Judgment starts at the altar, and the prophet is left alone among the dead, still praying. The last word belongs not to the swords but to the man in linen: I have done as you commanded me.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD said to him, “Pass through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations that are committed in it.”
keyVerse.note: Before a single executioner moves, God marks his own. This verse holds the comfort inside the chapter’s terror: judgment is real and begins at God’s house, but it is not blind, and those who grieve over sin bear the mark of the God who keeps them, as believers today are sealed with his Spirit.

9.reflection:
The people God marked were those who “sigh and groan” over the abominations in the city (v. 4). What is the difference between grieving over sin and merely disapproving of it? When you see sin around you, or in yourself, are you more likely to shrug, sneer or grieve?

Judgment began “at my sanctuary”, with the elders (v. 6; compare 1 Peter 4:17). Why does God hold those nearest to him most responsible? What does that mean for church leaders, and for every member?

Left alone among the dead, Ezekiel fell on his face and pleaded for the remnant (v. 8). For whom are you standing in the breach in prayer? How does Christ’s own intercession for his people encourage you to keep praying?

The people said, “The LORD does not see” (v. 9). In what ways do we live as if that were true? How does knowing that God has marked his people as his own, sealing them with his Spirit (Ephesians 1:13), change the way we live?

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then I looked, and behold, on the expanse that was over the heads of the cherubim there appeared above them something like a sapphire, in appearance like a throne.<sup>2</sup>And he said to the man clothed in linen, "Go in among the whirling wheels underneath the cherubim. Fill your hands with burning coals from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city." And he went in before my eyes.<sup>3</sup>Now the cherubim were standing on the south side of the house, when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court.<sup>4</sup>And the glory of the LORD went up from the cherub to the threshold of the house, and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks.<sup>6</sup>And when he commanded the man clothed in linen, "Take fire from between the whirling wheels, from between the cherubim," he went in and stood beside a wheel.<sup>7</sup>And a cherub stretched out his hand from between the cherubim to the fire that was between the cherubim, and took some of it and put it into the hands of the man clothed in linen, who took it and went out.<sup>8</sup>The cherubim appeared to have the form of a human hand under their wings.<sup>9</sup>And I looked, and behold, there were four wheels beside the cherubim, one beside each cherub, and the appearance of the wheels was like sparkling beryl.<sup>10</sup>And as for their appearance, the four had the same likeness, as if a wheel were within a wheel.<sup>11</sup>When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went, but in whatever direction the front wheel faced, the others followed without turning as they went.<sup>12</sup>And their whole body, their rims, and their spokes, their wings, and the wheels were full of eyes all around—the wheels that the four of them had.<sup>13</sup>As for the wheels, they were called in my hearing "the whirling wheels."<sup>14</sup>And every one had four faces: the first face was the face of the cherub, and the second face was a human face, and the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle.<sup>15</sup>And the cherubim mounted up. These were the living creatures that I saw by the Chebar canal.<sup>16</sup>And when the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them. And when the cherubim lifted up their wings to mount up from the earth, the wheels did not turn from beside them.<sup>17</sup>When they stood still, these stood still, and when they mounted up, these mounted up with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in them.<sup>18</sup>Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim.<sup>19</sup>And the cherubim lifted up their wings and mounted up from the earth before my eyes as they went out, with the wheels beside them. And they stood at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them.<sup>20</sup>These were the living creatures that I saw underneath the God of Israel by the Chebar canal; and I knew that they were cherubim.<sup>21</sup>Each had four faces, and each four wings, and underneath their wings the likeness of human hands.<sup>22</sup>And as for the likeness of their faces, they were the same faces whose appearance I had seen by the Chebar canal. Each one of them went straight forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Coals of Fire over the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fire of God’s holiness, which should have cleansed Jerusalem, is now sent to burn it. A throne like sapphire appears above the cherubim, the throne of chapter 1, and the man clothed in linen, who has just marked the faithful, is told to fill his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city (vv. 1–2). As he goes in, the cloud fills the house, the glory rises to the threshold, and the sound of the cherubim’s wings carries to the outer court “like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks” (vv. 3–5). A cherub puts the fire into his hands, deliberately and under God’s command (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The fire of God's holy presence, which should have purified his people, now falls on them in judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I looked, and behold, on the expanse that was over the heads of the cherubim there appeared above them something like a sapphire, in appearance like a throne. And he said to the man clothed in linen, "Go in among the whirling wheels underneath the cherubim. Fill your hands with burning coals from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city." And he went in before my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the throne Ezekiel met in Babylon, the man who marked the faithful takes holy fire to burn the city.

In appearance like a throne. The vision of chapter 1 is here, in the temple courts: the expanse, the throne like sapphire (the ESV notes, “lapis lazuli”). Now Ezekiel calls the creatures cherubim. The throne that met him in Babylon is the throne of the Most Holy Place.

Fill your hands with burning coals. The same man who marked the faithful in chapter 9 is now sent with fire. He fills his hands with burning coals from between the cherubim, fire from the very presence of God, and scatters them over Jerusalem. In history the fire came through Babylon’s army: in 586 BC Nebuchadnezzar’s commander “burned the house of the LORD and the king’s house and all the houses of Jerusalem” (2 Kings 25:9).

The same holy fire. Remember Isaiah’s vision. A seraph took “a burning coal” from the altar and touched his lips: “your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for” (Isaiah 6:6–7). The same holy fire now burns Jerusalem. God’s holiness is always fire: it will either purify you or consume you. The difference is whether you come to it confessing, as Isaiah did, “Woe is me! For I am lost”, or with your back turned, as Jerusalem did.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the cherubim were standing on the south side of the house, when the man went in, and a cloud filled the inner court. And the glory of the LORD went up from the cherub to the threshold of the house, and the house was filled with the cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the LORD. And the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty when he speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory blazes out one last time as it rises to the doorway: this is not a dedication but a farewell.

The house was filled with the cloud. The cloud fills the house, and the courtyard shines with the glory. It is like the day Solomon dedicated the temple, when “a cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud” (1 Kings 8:10–11). But the brightest moment in the courts is the moment of leaving.

Like the voice of God Almighty. “God Almighty” is the name by which God bound himself to Abraham in covenant (Genesis 17:1). Now the sound of that covenant God carries into the outer court where ordinary worshippers stood. Did anyone hear? The people who said “The LORD does not see” (9:9) went on with their business while the voice of God Almighty rumbled over their heads.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he commanded the man clothed in linen, "Take fire from between the whirling wheels, from between the cherubim," he went in and stood beside a wheel. And a cherub stretched out his hand from between the cherubim to the fire that was between the cherubim, and took some of it and put it into the hands of the man clothed in linen, who took it and went out. The cherubim appeared to have the form of a human hand under their wings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s judgment is never hasty: the fire is handed over with care, to the one who marked the faithful.

He went in and stood beside a wheel. The details slow down. A cherub reaches out with the human hand under its wings (v. 8), takes fire and places it in the man’s hands. Every coal is handed over under God’s command.

The fire and the pen. The one who carries the fire is the one who carried the pen. The priestly figure who marks for salvation also brings judgment. Christians may well think here of Christ: the Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), and the Saviour who seals his people is the Judge who will come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The throne leaving Jerusalem is the very throne that came to the exiles: it sees everything, and it can go anywhere. Ezekiel describes again the four wheels gleaming like beryl, each like a wheel within a wheel, moving in any direction without turning (vv. 9–11). Bodies, wings and wheels are full of eyes, and the wheels are named “the whirling wheels” (vv. 12–13). Each creature has four faces (v. 14), and Ezekiel recognises them: “These were the living creatures that I saw by the Chebar canal” (v. 15). Creatures and wheels rise and stop as one, because one spirit moves them (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The same throne that met the exiles in Babylon now moves out of Jerusalem's temple.

verseByVerse.quote: And I looked, and behold, there were four wheels beside the cherubim, one beside each cherub, and the appearance of the wheels was like sparkling beryl. And as for their appearance, the four had the same likeness, as if a wheel were within a wheel. When they went, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went, but in whatever direction the front wheel faced, the others followed without turning as they went. And their whole body, their rims, and their spokes, their wings, and the wheels were full of eyes all around—the wheels that the four of them had. As for the wheels, they were called in my hearing "the whirling wheels."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the very throne Ezekiel saw in Babylon: it sees everything, and it can go anywhere.

Four wheels beside the cherubim. Ezekiel describes the wheels almost word for word as in chapter 1, so that we know this is the same throne. The God who came to the exiles is the God now leaving Jerusalem.

Full of eyes all around. Now it is not only the rims but the whole body that is covered with eyes. Everything around the throne sees. The elders in the dark room said God does not see (8:12). The throne leaving their temple is covered with eyes.

The whirling wheels. The very name suggests motion. The throne of God is not a fixed monument; it is on the move.

Uncertain wording. The list in verse 12 is hard to pin down. The ESV reads “their whole body, their rims, and their spokes, their wings”, but notes another possible rendering: “their whole body, their backs, their hands, and their wings”. On that reading the eyes cover the creatures themselves as well as the wheels. Either way the point is clear: nothing escapes the sight of this throne.

verseByVerse.quote: And every one had four faces: the first face was the face of the cherub, and the second face was a human face, and the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle. And the cherubim mounted up. These were the living creatures that I saw by the Chebar canal. And when the cherubim went, the wheels went beside them. And when the cherubim lifted up their wings to mount up from the earth, the wheels did not turn from beside them. When they stood still, these stood still, and when they mounted up, these mounted up with them, for the spirit of the living creatures was in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creatures and wheels rise as one, moved by one spirit: heaven’s departure is orderly, deliberate and final.

Every one had four faces. In chapter 1 the four faces were man, lion, ox and eagle (1:10). Here “the face of the cherub” stands where the ox was. The text does not explain the difference, and Ezekiel insists they are “the same faces” he saw before (v. 22). What matters is that he recognises them, not every detail.

And the cherubim mounted up. They are rising, ready to leave, and creatures and wheels move as one, because one spirit drives them (the ESV notes, “spirit of life”).

The same throne in Revelation. John saw around God’s throne “four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind”, with faces like a lion, an ox, a man and an eagle (Revelation 4:6–7), and at the centre of the throne “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). The all-seeing throne that left Jerusalem in judgment is the throne from which the slain Lamb now reigns.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The glory of the LORD leaves his house, yet the God who goes is the God who has already come to his scattered people. The glory goes out from the threshold and takes its place above the cherubim (v. 18). They rise and pause at the entrance of the east gate, with the glory over them (v. 19), the gate through which it will one day return (43:2). Ezekiel now understands what he saw by the Chebar canal: “I knew that they were cherubim” (v. 20). The guardians of the Most Holy Place, with the same faces, wings and hands, had met him in exile (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: God's presence does not leave his people in one abrupt moment, but step by step, giving time to repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim. And the cherubim lifted up their wings and mounted up from the earth before my eyes as they went out, with the wheels beside them. And they stood at the entrance of the east gate of the house of the LORD, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of the LORD leaves his temple by stages and pauses at the east gate, while the city carries on as if nothing has happened.

The glory of the LORD went out. This is a sentence of heartbreak. Trace the steps: from the cherub to the threshold (9:3; 10:4), now from the threshold to the cherubim, and in 11:23 out of the city altogether. God does not slam the door. He leaves step by step, pausing at each stage, as if waiting for someone to call him back.

Why God withdraws. Hosea heard God say, “I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face” (Hosea 5:15). God withdraws not to abandon his people but to call them to repent.

At the entrance of the east gate. They pause again at the east gate, facing the Mount of Olives and the rising sun. It is the gate through which the glory will one day return: “the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east” (43:2).

Ichabod again. Centuries before, when the Philistines captured the ark, a dying mother named her son Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel!” (1 Samuel 4:21). Now it is happening again, not because an enemy took the glory, but because God’s own people drove it out. Six centuries later Jesus stood in the rebuilt temple and said, “See, your house is left to you desolate”, and “Jesus left the temple and was going away” (Matthew 23:38; 24:1).

The departure nobody noticed. The most unsettling thing about this vision is what happened next in Jerusalem: nothing. The glory left by stages, and the city went on trading, scheming and sacrificing as before. That is usually how a people loses God: not by a great argument, but by a slow drift in which his absence stops registering as a loss and starts to feel like ordinary life. The sociologist Max Weber described himself as religiously unmusical: not hostile, simply unable to hear the tune, and many today would say the same without bitterness. But Ezekiel will not let this be a story only about secular people. The glory left a temple full of worshippers: religious people can lose God with the services still running. Yet God does not leave in order to be rid of us. The same glory went into exile with the captives, and came back at last in a man who looked at the city that had not noticed, and wept over it (Luke 19:41–44).
verseByVerse.note: The departure is reversed in 43:1-5, and in the vision of the new temple the east gate, once the glory has come back through it, is to stay shut (44:1-2).

verseByVerse.quote: These were the living creatures that I saw underneath the God of Israel by the Chebar canal; and I knew that they were cherubim. Each had four faces, and each four wings, and underneath their wings the likeness of human hands. And as for the likeness of their faces, they were the same faces whose appearance I had seen by the Chebar canal. Each one of them went straight forward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beings who met Ezekiel in Babylon were the cherubim of God’s own throne: the glory leaving Jerusalem had already gone to the exiles.

I knew that they were cherubim. Ezekiel says it with the force of a discovery. The beings he met by the canal were the guardians of God’s own throne in the Most Holy Place.

What the exiles learned. For the exiles this was both devastating and wonderful: devastating, because the glory was leaving Jerusalem; wonderful, because it had already come to them. God had not abandoned his people; he had gone with them into exile.

The glory that returned. That is still true. God is not tied to a building. The glory that left this temple would come back in a way no one expected, in the flesh of Jesus, who “is the radiance of the glory of God” (Hebrews 1:3). Through him God now builds his people, Jew and Gentile together, into “a holy temple in the Lord”, “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:21–22).

10.title: The Glory at the Threshold
10.overview:
Where we are. The vision of chapters 8 to 11 continues. In chapter 9 the man clothed in linen marked the faithful and the executioners struck the city, while the glory of God moved to the threshold of the temple (9:3). Now the same man is sent with fire, and the throne Ezekiel first saw by the Chebar canal appears in the temple courts, ready to leave.

The message. The holy God who lived among his people is leaving his house, and his leaving is itself the judgment. The fire that should have purified Jerusalem will now burn it. Yet the throne that departs is a throne on wheels, the same one that came to the exiles in Babylon: God is not tied to a building, and he has not abandoned those he scattered.

Why it was said. The exiles trusted that the LORD would never leave his temple, and so would never let Jerusalem fall (see the introduction). Ezekiel shows them the unthinkable: the glory going out of the door, while the city carries on as if nothing has happened.

How the chapter makes its case. A throne like sapphire appears above the cherubim, and the man in linen is told to fill his hands with burning coals from between them and scatter them over the city (vv. 1–2). The glory rises to the threshold, filling the house with cloud and the court with brightness, while the cherubim’s wings sound like the voice of God Almighty (vv. 3–5). A cherub puts the fire into the man’s hands (vv. 6–8). The whirling wheels and four faces are described again (vv. 9–17). Then the glory leaves the threshold, mounts the cherubim and pauses at the east gate (vv. 18–19). Ezekiel knows at last what he saw by the canal: these are the cherubim of God’s own throne (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by promise. The glory that left this temple step by step came back in a way no one expected: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). Jesus in his turn left the temple, saying, “See, your house is left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38), and through him God now builds his people into “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). The east gate where the glory pauses is the gate through which it will return (43:2).

For us. A church can lose God with its services still running, and hardly notice. Ask whether his absence would register with you as a loss, and come to his holy fire as Isaiah did, confessing, to be cleansed rather than consumed. Wherever you have been scattered, the God whose throne has wheels can meet you there in Christ.
10.theology:
God's holy fire either cleanses those who come confessing or consumes those who refuse him (vv. 2, 7; Isa 6:6-7).

God's presence can depart from a place of worship that has been given over to idols (vv. 4, 18-19; 1 Sam 4:21-22; Matt 23:38).

God's withdrawal is gradual and deliberate, a call to repent rather than a sudden abandonment (vv. 4, 18-19; Hos 5:15).

God sees everything, and his throne is not bound to any building (vv. 12, 16-17, 20-22).

The God who leaves Jerusalem has already come to his people in exile; he goes with them (vv. 15, 20-22; Eph 2:21-22).

The priestly figure who marks for salvation also carries the fire of judgment, a picture that brings to mind Christ, to whom all judgment is given (vv. 2, 7; John 5:22).
10.examples:
The fire that cleansed Isaiah's lips is scattered over a city, and the brightest moment the courts have seen since Solomon is the moment of leaving. The voice of God Almighty rumbles over people who never look up, while the throne they think is blind is covered in eyes.

Yet the glory pauses at every doorway, and the throne leaving the temple is the same throne that met the exiles by the canal.

keyVerse.quote: Then the glory of the LORD went out from the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubim.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the vision of chapters 8 to 11, and one of the saddest sentences in the Old Testament: the LORD leaves the house that bore his name. Everything else in the chapter, the fire, the wheels and the recognition by the canal, explains what it means that God can leave his temple, and where he goes when he does.

10.reflection:
The same holy fire that cleansed Isaiah’s lips (Isaiah 6:6–7) is scattered over Jerusalem in judgment (v. 2). What made the difference? What does it mean to come to a holy God confessing, rather than with our backs turned?

The glory left the temple by stages, and the city seems not to have noticed (vv. 4, 18–19). How can a church, or a Christian, lose the sense of God’s presence while everything carries on as usual? What are the warning signs?

Ezekiel recognises that the throne leaving Jerusalem is the same throne that met him in exile (vv. 15, 20). What comfort does that give to people who feel far from God, or far from the church they once knew?

The glory that left the temple came back in Jesus (John 1:14), and God now makes his people “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). How should that shape the way we think about the church, and about our own lives?
