verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Cauldron and the Meat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The men who feel safest are in the greatest danger. At the east gate twenty-five of Jerusalem’s leaders, among them Jaazaniah and Pelatiah, give wicked counsel and boast that the city is a cauldron and they are the meat, safe inside its walls (vv. 1–3). God, who knows what comes into their minds, turns the proverb against them: the only meat left in the pot will be the people they have murdered, while they are dragged out and judged at the border of Israel, because they lived by the rules of the nations (vv. 4–12). As Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah falls dead, and Ezekiel cries, “Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?” (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who feel safe in their privileged position while oppressing others will find no shelter in it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit lifted me up and brought me to the east gate of the house of the LORD, which faces east. And behold, at the entrance of the gateway there were twenty-five men. And I saw among them Jaazaniah the son of Azzur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people. And he said to me, "Son of man, these are the men who devise iniquity and who give wicked counsel in this city; who say, 'The time is not near to build houses. This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat.' Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, O son of man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s leaders steer the city with confident, wicked counsel, sure that its walls keep them safe and that they, not the exiles, are the ones who matter.

There were twenty-five men. The glory has paused at the east gate (10:19), and that is where Ezekiel is taken. There he sees twenty-five of Jerusalem’s leaders, “princes of the people”, two of them named. (This Jaazaniah is the son of Azzur, a different man from the Jaazaniah of 8:11.)

Who devise iniquity and who give wicked counsel. Their sin is not only what they do but what they advise. Leaders shape a whole city by the counsel they give, and these men were steering Jerusalem toward disaster with confident talk. The first psalm begins by blessing the man “who walks not in the counsel of the wicked” (Psalm 1:1). Be careful whose counsel you take, and more careful still about the counsel you give.

This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat. Here is their slogan. A cooking pot protects the meat inside from the fire. The walls of Jerusalem are the pot; they, the ruling class who stayed behind, are the choice cuts, and the exiles are the scraps thrown away. In other words: we are the ones who matter, and we are safe.

Good figs and rotten figs. God had already said the opposite through Jeremiah. In the vision of two baskets of figs, “Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah”, and those who stayed in Jerusalem were the rotten figs (Jeremiah 24:5). The people who felt most secure were the ones in the most danger.

Uncertain wording. The first half of the slogan, “The time is not near to build houses”, is obscure. The ESV notes that it may be a question: “Is not the time near…?” As a statement it may mean there is no hurry to build, because the city is safe as it is; as a question, that now is the time to build, perhaps on the property of the exiles (v. 15). Either way it breathes confidence, and the second half is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD fell upon me, and he said to me, "Say, Thus says the LORD: So you think, O house of Israel. For I know the things that come into your mind. You have multiplied your slain in this city and have filled its streets with the slain. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Your slain whom you have laid in the midst of it, they are the meat, and this city is the cauldron, but you shall be brought out of the midst of it. You have feared the sword, and I will bring the sword upon you, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God knows their private thoughts and turns their proverb against them: the only meat safe in the pot will be the people they killed, and the sword they feared will find them.

I know the things that come into your mind. They had not said all this in public. God answers what they thought. “Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether” (Psalm 139:4).

They are the meat, and this city is the cauldron. God turns their proverb inside out. Yes, the city is a cauldron, but the meat in it is the people you murdered. Their corrupt leadership had filled the streets with victims of injustice, and those victims are the only ones who will stay in the pot. You will not be kept safe inside; you will be dragged out.

You have feared the sword. They trusted the walls because they feared Babylon’s sword. The thing they feared is the thing that will come. Security built on injustice always fails.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will bring you out of the midst of it, and give you into the hands of foreigners, and execute judgments upon you. You shall fall by the sword. I will judge you at the border of Israel, and you shall know that I am the LORD. This city shall not be your cauldron, nor shall you be the meat in the midst of it. I will judge you at the border of Israel, and you shall know that I am the LORD. For you have not walked in my statutes, nor obeyed my rules, but have acted according to the rules of the nations that are around you." And it came to pass, while I was prophesying, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. Then I fell down on my face and cried out with a loud voice and said, "Ah, Lord GOD! Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proud leaders will die as captives at the edge of the land, and when Pelatiah falls dead, Ezekiel does not gloat but cries for mercy.

Into the hands of foreigners. These were the men who looked down on the exiles as people cast far from the LORD (v. 15). They will end as captives in foreign hands themselves. God has a way of bringing the proud down to the very place they despised.

At the border of Israel. This came true. When Jerusalem fell, the captain of the guard took leading men of the city “to the king of Babylon at Riblah”, and the king “put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath” (2 Kings 25:20–21), at the northern border. They were not killed in the city they thought would protect them; they were led out and executed at the edge of the land.

The rules of the nations. And the charge: they had lived by “the rules of the nations”. God’s people had adopted the values of the world around them, power, wealth and violence, while keeping the name of God’s city.

Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. In the middle of the sermon, one of the named leaders drops dead: proof that the word is not empty. His name means something like “the LORD rescues”, which makes his death, and Ezekiel’s cry about the remnant, all the sharper. Ezekiel’s reaction is not triumph. He falls on his face and cries out, as he did in 9:8. If even the leaders are dying, will anyone be left?

The right heart. That is the right heart for anyone who sees God’s judgment fall on others: not satisfaction, but a cry for mercy. And God’s answer to Ezekiel’s question is the rest of this chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — A Sanctuary for a While, and a New Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s answer to Ezekiel’s cry is a remnant he had not been thinking about: the despised exiles. The people left in Jerusalem sneer that the exiles have gone far from the LORD and that the land now belongs to those who stayed (vv. 14–15). But God himself has been a sanctuary to his scattered people, even without a temple (v. 16). He will gather them and give them the land, and they will clear it of its idols (vv. 17–18). Above all he will change them from within: one heart, a new spirit, a heart of flesh in place of a heart of stone, so that they walk in his ways and are his people, and he is their God (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: God is present with his scattered people, and he promises the inward renewal that alone makes obedience possible.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, your brothers, even your brothers, your kinsmen, the whole house of Israel, all of them, are those of whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem have said, 'Go far from the LORD; to us this land is given for a possession.' Therefore say, 'Thus says the Lord GOD: Though I removed them far off among the nations, and though I scattered them among the countries, yet I have been a sanctuary to them for a while in the countries where they have gone.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem wrote the exiles off as far from God, but God himself has been their sanctuary in a foreign land.

Your brothers, even your brothers. Ezekiel has asked whether the remnant will perish. God points him to a remnant he had not been thinking about: his fellow exiles. The ESV notes that “kinsmen” is literally “the men of your redemption”: the relatives who had the family duty to buy one another back out of debt or slavery.

Go far from the LORD. The people in Jerusalem looked down on them: the exiles, they said, had been thrown out of God’s presence, and the land and God belonged to those who stayed. It is an old temptation for religious people to decide who is near to God by who is in the right place, the right building, the right group. God sees otherwise.

I have been a sanctuary to them. This is a sweet verse for exiles. They had no temple. They were far from Jerusalem. And God says: “I have been a sanctuary to them”. Not a building: God himself was their sanctuary.

Not a place but a person. This is the heart of the New Testament hope. God’s dwelling is not a place but a person: Christ among his people. “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20). And in the new creation, “I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). If you are far from where you think you should be, cut off from the church you knew or the home you loved, God himself can be your sanctuary there.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “for a while” may instead mean “in small measure”. Either way, even a small measure of God’s presence was more than the whole temple once the glory had left it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore say, 'Thus says the Lord GOD: I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you out of the countries where you have been scattered, and I will give you the land of Israel.' And when they come there, they will remove from it all its detestable things and all its abominations. And I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, that they may walk in my statutes and keep my rules and obey them. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises not only to bring his scattered people home but to change them from within, removing the heart of stone and giving a heart of flesh, so that at last they walk in his ways as his own people.

I will gather you. The people in Jerusalem claimed the land; God gives it back to the exiles. And when they come, they themselves will clear out the idols of chapter 8. Restoration is not simply going home. It is going home changed.

The heart of stone. Here is the answer to everything chapters 1 to 11 have exposed. The problem was never only the idols in the temple. It was the idols in the heart (14:3), a heart of stone, hard, cold and unmoved by God’s word no matter how many prophets he sent.

A heart of flesh. God does not promise to soften it a little. He promises surgery: “I will remove the heart of stone” and “give them a heart of flesh”, a heart that is alive, that feels, that responds to him. And “one heart”, undivided, no longer split between God and idols. And “a new spirit”: chapter 36 will say more, “I will put my Spirit within you” (36:27).

The same promise elsewhere. This is the new birth: God makes a dead heart alive. Jeremiah promised the same: “I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever” (Jeremiah 32:39). Paul says the Spirit writes God’s word “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3). God “saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).

That they may walk in my statutes. The order matters: new heart first, then obedience. God does not say, “Obey me and I will give you a new heart.” He gives the new heart so that they can obey. That is grace. And the goal is the oldest promise in the covenant: “they shall be my people, and I will be their God”.

If your heart is hard. If you find your heart hard toward God, do not wait until you have softened it yourself. Ask him to do what he promised.

Where Christians differ. The return from Babylon was the first fulfilment of this promise of return, but how is the rest fulfilled? Some Christians (often called dispensationalists, after their scheme of distinct ages in God’s dealings) look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. Faithful Christians differ on whether Scripture also promises a future return of the Jewish people to the land itself.

This commentary’s view. The promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. This commentary reads the land promise as widening in Christ to the whole renewed earth (Romans 4:13; Matthew 5:5), while honouring brothers and sisters who expect more.

Textual note. Some ancient copies, including the Greek Old Testament, read “another” or “a new” heart here, as in 36:26; either way the promise is the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — The Glory Leaves the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise does not cancel the warning, and the glory completes its departure. Those whose hearts still go after their idols will have their deeds brought on their own heads (v. 21). Then the cherubim lift their wings, and the glory of the LORD rises from the midst of the city and stands on the mountain to the east, the Mount of Olives (vv. 22–23). The vision ends: the Spirit carries Ezekiel back to the exiles in Chaldea, and he tells them everything the LORD has shown him, the judgment and the hope together (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's presence leaves a city, it is the end of its protection, but not the end of his purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for those whose heart goes after their detestable things and their abominations, I will bring their deeds upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD." Then the cherubim lifted up their wings, with the wheels beside them, and the glory of the God of Israel was over them. And the glory of the LORD went up from the midst of the city and stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who cling to their idols cannot shelter behind the promise, and the glory now leaves the city itself, pausing on the Mount of Olives to look back.

I will bring their deeds upon their own heads. The promise does not cancel the warning. Those whose hearts keep chasing their idols will receive what their deeds deserve. The promise of a new heart is no shelter for anyone who loves the old one and keeps it.

The glory of the LORD went up. The last stage. The glory leaves not just the temple but the city, and stops on the mountain to the east, almost certainly the Mount of Olives, “that lies before Jerusalem on the east” (Zechariah 14:4). It pauses there, looking back over the city one last time.

The glory walked its streets. Hold that picture beside the Gospels. After Jesus told the leaders of Jerusalem “your house is left to you desolate”, he “left the temple” and sat “on the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 23:38; 24:1, 3). Coming down that same mountain a few days earlier, he “saw the city” and “wept over it” (Luke 19:41). And from that mountain he ascended, with the promise that he “will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11–12). The glory that left Jerusalem in Ezekiel’s vision walked its streets in the flesh, and it will return. John puts it in one sentence: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The word for “dwelt” means to pitch a tent, like the tabernacle where the glory first came to live among Israel.
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives rises across the Kidron valley, higher than the temple hill, so the glory stops where it can still look down on the city.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit lifted me up and brought me in the vision by the Spirit of God into Chaldea, to the exiles. Then the vision that I had seen went up from me. And I told the exiles all the things that the LORD had shown me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel tells the exiles everything the LORD has shown him, the hard parts and the hopeful parts: that is the task of every faithful messenger.

I told the exiles. The vision ends, and Ezekiel is back in his house in Babylon, with the elders still sitting in front of him (8:1). And he tells them “all the things that the LORD had shown me”: the idols, the executioners, the departing glory, and the promise of a new heart.

Telling all of it. That is the task of every faithful messenger: to tell all of it. The glory leaving, and the God who is a sanctuary in exile. The heart of stone, and the heart of flesh. Paul could say the same to the elders of Ephesus: “I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:27).

11.title: A New Heart and a Departing Glory
11.overview:
Where we are. The vision that began in 8:1 reaches its end. The glory of God has left the threshold of the temple and paused at the east gate (10:19), and there Ezekiel is shown the men who are running the city. Then the vision lifts.

The message. Those who feel safest are in the greatest danger, and those who have been written off are the ones God is keeping. Jerusalem’s leaders thought themselves the choice meat, safe in the pot, and the exiles mere scraps; God turns both judgments upside down. To the despised exiles he has been a sanctuary himself, and he promises what neither exile nor temple could produce: one heart, a new spirit, a heart of flesh in place of a heart of stone, so that they will be his people and he will be their God.

Why it was said. The people left in Jerusalem claimed the land and God’s favour for themselves, and looked on the exiles as cast off (see the introduction). This chapter tells the exiles that God’s presence and God’s future are with them, and that the city’s proud rulers are doomed.

How the chapter makes its case. At the east gate twenty-five leaders give wicked counsel, saying the city is the cauldron and they are the meat (vv. 1–3). God turns the proverb inside out: they will be dragged out and judged at the border of Israel (vv. 4–12). Pelatiah drops dead, and Ezekiel cries out for the remnant (v. 13). God answers by pointing to the exiles whom Jerusalem despised: he has been their sanctuary, and he will gather them, cleanse the land and give them a new heart and spirit (vv. 14–20), though those who cling to their idols will be judged (v. 21). Then the glory leaves the city for the mountain to the east, and Ezekiel tells the exiles all he has seen (vv. 22–25).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The promise of a heart of flesh and a new spirit is the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; 36:26–27), sealed in Christ’s blood (Luke 22:20) and given by his Spirit in the new birth (John 3:5; Titus 3:5). The pattern is the departing glory. It stops on the Mount of Olives; centuries later Jesus left the temple, wept over the city from that hill and ascended from it, promising to return (Luke 19:41; Acts 1:11–12).

For us. Being in the right place, the right church or the right family is no safety; only the new heart God gives is. If your heart is hard, do not wait until you have softened it yourself: ask him to do what he promised. And if you are far from where you feel you belong, God himself can be your sanctuary there.
11.theology:
Privilege and position are no protection for those who oppress others; God judges by the heart and the deeds (vv. 2-12; 2 Kgs 25:20-21).

God knows every thought (v. 5; Ps 139:4).

It is not where they live that makes people God's people; he himself is the sanctuary of his scattered people (v. 16; Matt 18:20; Rev 21:22).

The root problem is the heart, and God promises to replace the heart of stone with a heart of flesh and to give a new spirit; obedience follows the gift (vv. 19-20; 36:25-27; Jer 32:39; 2 Cor 3:3; Titus 3:5).

The promise of renewal does not cancel judgment on those who cling to idols (v. 21).

The glory that left Jerusalem for the mountain east of the city came back in Jesus, who wept over the city from that mountain, ascended from it, and will return (vv. 22-23; Luke 19:41; Acts 1:11-12).
11.examples:
Jerusalem's leaders think they are the prime cuts in a safe pot, until God turns the proverb inside out: the only meat left in it will be their victims. One of them drops dead in the middle of the sermon.

Against that dark background the chapter's comfort shines: God himself as a sanctuary in a foreign country, a heart of stone taken out and a heart of flesh put in, and the glory pausing on the Mount of Olives to look back.

keyVerse.quote: And I will give them one heart, and a new spirit I will put within them. I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, that they may walk in my statutes and keep my rules and obey them. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of doomed leaders and departing glory, this is God’s answer to Ezekiel’s cry, “Will you make a full end of the remnant of Israel?” (v. 13). The remnant will live because God himself will change their hearts, and the order is the gospel’s order: the new heart comes first, and obedience flows from it. The promise is repeated in 36:26–27 and fulfilled in the new birth by Christ’s Spirit.

11.reflection:
Jerusalem’s leaders said, “This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat” (v. 3), sure that their position kept them safe. What false securities do people, and churches, rely on today? Why are those who feel safest often in the most danger?

When Pelatiah died, Ezekiel did not gloat but fell on his face and cried for mercy (v. 13). How should we respond when we see God’s judgment fall on others, even on people who have opposed us?

To exiles without a temple God says, “I have been a sanctuary to them” (v. 16). When have you known God’s presence in a place you never wanted to be? How does Christ make this promise real for believers today?

God gives the new heart first, “that they may walk in my statutes” (vv. 19–20). How does this order, grace first and then obedience, change the way you pray about a heart that feels hard or cold, your own or someone else’s?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes his message visible to people who will not see: the king and people of Jerusalem are going into exile, and no one outruns his word. The exiles have eyes but do not see, so Ezekiel acts out an escape in their sight, packing a refugee’s bundle by day, digging through the wall at dusk and carrying it out with his face covered (vv. 1–7). Next morning, when they ask what he is doing, he explains: “I am a sign for you” (vv. 8–11). The prince in Jerusalem will flee the same way and be caught in God’s net, brought to Babylon yet never seeing it; his troops will scatter, and a few will survive to confess Judah’s sins among the nations (vv. 12–16).
verseByVerse.theology: God's word was fulfilled to the smallest detail in the fall of Jerusalem's king.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, you dwell in the midst of a rebellious house, who have eyes to see, but see not, who have ears to hear, but hear not, for they are a rebellious house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exiles’ problem is not that they cannot see but that they will not: a rebellious heart keeps its eyes shut.

Who have eyes to see, but see not. The problem is not lack of information. The exiles had eyes and ears. They had watched Ezekiel’s brick and his hair and heard his warnings for more than a year. They see not because they will not.

The same blindness later. Isaiah had been told his hearers would be like this (Isaiah 6:9–10), and Jesus said the same about the crowds of his day: “seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand” (Matthew 13:13). He even said it to his own disciples: “Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear?” (Mark 8:18). Spiritual blindness is a condition of the heart, not the eyes, and only God can cure it.

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, son of man, prepare for yourself an exile's baggage, and go into exile by day in their sight. You shall go like an exile from your place to another place in their sight. Perhaps they will understand, though they are a rebellious house. You shall bring out your baggage by day in their sight, as baggage for exile, and you shall go out yourself at evening in their sight, as those do who must go into exile. In their sight dig through the wall, and bring your baggage out through it. In their sight you shall lift the baggage upon your shoulder and carry it out at dusk. You shall cover your face that you may not see the land, for I have made you a sign for the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel acts out a fugitive’s escape so that people who will not listen might at least see: a second exile is coming.

Go into exile by day in their sight. Picture a refugee’s bundle: a blanket, a water skin, a little food, whatever can be carried on one shoulder. Ezekiel packs one in broad daylight, where everyone can watch.

Perhaps they will understand. Listen to God’s heart: “Perhaps they will understand”. (The ESV notes this may be read “will see that”.) Even with a rebellious house, God keeps trying. He does not give up on people easily.

In their sight. Six times in these verses: “in their sight”. The whole performance is for them. Digging through a mud-brick wall at dusk is what someone does who cannot leave by the gate, a fugitive sneaking out. And the covered face says: you will never see this land again. The exiles hoped for a quick return; Ezekiel shows them a second exile still to come, from Jerusalem itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And I did as I was commanded. I brought out my baggage by day, as baggage for exile, and in the evening I dug through the wall with my own hands. I brought out my baggage at dusk, carrying it on my shoulder in their sight. In the morning the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, has not the house of Israel, the rebellious house, said to you, 'What are you doing?' Say to them, 'Thus says the Lord GOD: This oracle concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel who are in it.' Say, 'I am a sign for you: as I have done, so shall it be done to them. They shall go into exile, into captivity.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel obeys before he understands, and he himself becomes the sign: what he has done will be done to Jerusalem.

I did as I was commanded. Simple, complete obedience, however strange the instruction. Ezekiel dug through his own house with his bare hands.

Obey first, understand later. The explanation came only “In the morning” (v. 8). He obeyed first and understood afterward. That is often how God leads his people. Jesus said to Peter, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand” (John 13:7).

What are you doing? The sign did at least this: it made people ask. That question is an opening. Faithful witness often looks strange enough to make people curious.

I am a sign for you. The prophet’s own body has become the message. Ezekiel’s life was not his own; it was a sermon God preached through him. In a far greater way the Son is God’s message in a human life: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “This oracle concerns” may be rendered “This burden is”. The Hebrew here is very compressed, and the word can mean either a prophetic oracle or a load carried, so there may be a play on the bundle Ezekiel has just carried on his shoulder. The exact wording is uncertain, but the sense is plain: the sign is about the prince and the people in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And the prince who is among them shall lift his baggage upon his shoulder at dusk, and shall go out. They shall dig through the wall to bring him out through it. He shall cover his face, that he may not see the land with his eyes. And I will spread my net over him, and he shall be taken in my snare. And I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans, yet he shall not see it, and he shall die there. And I will scatter toward every wind all who are around him, his helpers and all his troops, and I will unsheathe the sword after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sign is decoded with astonishing precision: Zedekiah will flee by night, be caught in God’s net, and die blind in Babylon.

The prince who is among them. “The prince” is Zedekiah, king in Jerusalem. Ezekiel usually calls him prince rather than king, probably because many exiles still counted Jehoiachin, the king taken to Babylon in 597 BC, as the rightful king; Ezekiel even dates his oracles by Jehoiachin’s exile (1:2). About six years later, when the Babylonians broke into the city, “all the men of war fled by night by the way of the gate between the two walls” (2 Kings 25:4). The king ran in the dark.

I will spread my net over him. It is God who catches him. Babylon’s soldiers did the chasing, but it was God’s net. No one outruns the word of God.

Yet he shall not see it. Then the riddle: “I will bring him to Babylon… yet he shall not see it, and he shall die there”. How could a man be taken to Babylon and not see it? The king of Babylon “put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him in chains, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon, and put him in prison till the day of his death” (Jeremiah 52:11). He went to Babylon blind, and died there.

His helpers and all his troops. And so it happened: “all his army was scattered from him” (2 Kings 25:5). The men who were supposed to protect the king ran for their lives.

Does this contradict Jeremiah? Jeremiah told Zedekiah that his eyes would see the king of Babylon (Jeremiah 34:3). Both came true. Zedekiah was brought before Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah and saw him face to face; then he watched his sons killed, and his eyes were put out (Jeremiah 39:5–7). He saw the king of Babylon, but he never saw Babylon.
verseByVerse.note: The sign was given about 592 BC; Jerusalem fell, and Zedekiah fled, in 586 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: And they shall know that I am the LORD, when I disperse them among the nations and scatter them among the countries. But I will let a few of them escape from the sword, from famine and pestilence, that they may declare all their abominations among the nations where they go, and may know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spares a few, not because they deserve it, but so that they will confess among the nations why Jerusalem fell.

Why spare a few? So that they may “declare all their abominations among the nations”. Wherever they go, they will have to explain why Jerusalem fell: not because Babylon’s gods were stronger, but because Judah sinned and the LORD judged.

A strange kind of witness. That is a strange but real kind of witness: confessing sin. The nations would learn about the holiness of Israel’s God from the lips of people who had broken his law. God’s glory is displayed even in the honest confession of those he disciplines.

Our own exile. Christians too are called “sojourners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11), with no lasting city here (Hebrews 13:14). Part of our witness in the world is being honest about our sin and pointing to the grace that forgives it. The same chapter tells why that grace is there. Zedekiah went out through the wall of the city under God’s judgment for his own sins; Jesus “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12), bearing a judgment that was not his, so that exiles might have “the city that is to come” (Hebrews 13:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Violence brings fear on those who practise it, and the judgment reaches even the dinner table. Ezekiel must eat his bread with quaking and drink his water with trembling and anxiety (v. 18), as a sign that the people of Jerusalem will eat and drink in dread while their land is stripped bare, because of the violence of all who live in it (v. 19). Their inhabited cities will be laid waste and the land made a desolation, and through it they will know that he is the LORD (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who make others live in fear will lose their own safety.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, eat your bread with quaking, and drink water with trembling and with anxiety. And say to the people of the land, Thus says the Lord GOD concerning the inhabitants of Jerusalem in the land of Israel: They shall eat their bread with anxiety, and drink water in dismay. In this way her land will be stripped of all it contains, on account of the violence of all those who dwell in it. And the inhabited cities shall be laid waste, and the land shall become a desolation; and you shall know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A city that made others live in fear will itself eat in dread.

Eat your bread with quaking. Another sign, this time at the table. Ezekiel eats with shaking hands, as if every meal might be the last, like someone eating during an air raid.

On account of the violence. The reason is stated plainly: “on account of the violence of all those who dwell in it”. Jerusalem’s people had made others live in fear through oppression and bloodshed. Now they will live in fear themselves. What we do to others has a way of coming back to us.

In everyday life. A table where people eat in peace is one of God’s quiet gifts. Many believers across the world today eat their bread with anxiety because of persecution or war. Pray for them. And give thanks when you can eat without fear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — None of My Words Will Be Delayed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word cannot be waited out. The people have a proverb: “The days grow long, and every vision comes to nothing” (v. 22). God will put an end to it and give them a new one: the days are near, and the fulfilment of every vision; false visions and flattering divination will cease, for what he speaks he performs (vv. 23–25). Others grant that Ezekiel’s visions may be true but say they are “for many days from now” (vv. 26–27). The answer is the same: “None of my words will be delayed any longer” (v. 28). Scoffing and postponing are two forms of the same unbelief.
verseByVerse.theology: That God's word has not yet happened does not mean it never will; it will be done in his time, and that time is closer than scoffers think.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, what is this proverb that you have about the land of Israel, saying, 'The days grow long, and every vision comes to nothing'? Tell them therefore, 'Thus says the Lord GOD: I will put an end to this proverb, and they shall no more use it as a proverb in Israel.' But say to them, The days are near, and the fulfillment of every vision. For there shall be no more any false vision or flattering divination within the house of Israel. For I am the LORD; I will speak the word that I will speak, and it will be performed. It will no longer be delayed, but in your days, O rebellious house, I will speak the word and perform it, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people waved the prophets away with a proverb; God replaces it with his own: the days are near, and what he speaks he performs.

Every vision comes to nothing. The people had a saying, and the ESV notes that the “you” is plural: everyone was saying it. The prophets have been warning for years, and nothing has happened: it is all talk.

An old unbelief. This is an old and dangerous form of unbelief. It does not argue against God’s word; it just waits it out. Peter heard the same in his day: “Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were” (2 Peter 3:4).

The days are near. God rewrites the proverb. Not “every vision comes to nothing”, but “The days are near, and the fulfillment of every vision”. (The ESV notes that “fulfillment” is literally “word”: every vision’s word is about to come true.)

Flattering divination. This is prophecy that tells people pleasant things about themselves. Events will expose and silence the flatterers. Flattery always feels kind and always does harm: “a flattering mouth works ruin” (Proverbs 26:28). Be wary of any voice, in the pulpit or in your own head, that only ever tells you how well you are doing.

I will speak the word that I will speak, and it will be performed. That is the difference between God’s word and every other voice. “It shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose” (Isaiah 55:11). The delay was patience, not weakness. “If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come” (Habakkuk 2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, behold, they of the house of Israel say, 'The vision that he sees is for many days from now, and he prophesies of times far off.' Therefore say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: None of my words will be delayed any longer, but the word that I speak will be performed, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Others push the visions into the distant future, but God’s word will not be delayed: live ready now.

For many days from now. This is a subtler unbelief. These people do not say the visions are false, only that they are about the distant future: not us, not now. That is exactly how many people treat God’s warnings today. Judgment, death, the return of Christ: yes, perhaps, some day, but far off, not something to act on this week.

None of my words will be delayed any longer. Within a few years, Jerusalem fell. The “far-off” vision arrived in their own lifetime.

Living ready. The lesson is not to calculate dates but to live ready. “Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). The word God has spoken about the end will be performed, and “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9). Do not mistake his patience for a postponement you can use to put off repentance.

12.title: Baggage for Exile
12.overview:
Where we are. The great temple vision of chapters 8 to 11 is over, and Ezekiel is back among the exiles in Babylon. Now, as in chapters 4 and 5, he acts out the message, and God answers the sayings the people used to shrug off every warning.

The message. God’s word will come true, and soon. The exiles still hoped for a quick return; instead their king in Jerusalem would creep out through a hole in the wall, be caught in God’s net and die blind in Babylon. People who have eyes but will not see may call every vision empty, or put it off to a distant future, but the LORD says, “I will speak the word and perform it” (v. 25).

Why it was said. The exiles expected Jerusalem to stand and themselves to go home soon, and false prophets fed that hope (see the introduction). This chapter shows them a second exile still to come, and takes away their two favourite excuses for not listening.

How the chapter makes its case. Among a rebellious house that will not see, Ezekiel packs an exile’s bundle by day, digs through the wall at dusk and carries it out with his face covered (vv. 1–7). Next morning he explains: the prince in Jerusalem will flee the same way, be caught in God’s net and brought to Babylon, yet he will not see it; his troops will be scattered, and a few survivors will confess Judah’s sins among the nations (vv. 8–16). Then he eats and drinks trembling, a sign of the fear and ruin coming on the land because of its violence (vv. 17–20). Finally God silences two sayings: that every vision comes to nothing (vv. 21–25), and that the visions are for times far off (vv. 26–28). Both meet the same reply: none of his words will be delayed.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. Zedekiah went out through the wall of his city under God’s judgment for his own sins; Jesus “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12), bearing a judgment that was not his, so that exiles might have a lasting city. And the God who performs every word he speaks has kept his greatest promises in Christ: “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. Unbelief rarely argues; it waits, or it says “some day, but not yet”. God’s patience is not a postponement we can use to put off repentance: now is the day of salvation. Live ready for the word he has spoken about Christ’s return, and let honest confession of sin, and of the grace that forgives it, be part of your witness to a watching world.
12.theology:
Spiritual blindness is a matter of the will and the heart, and God graciously keeps offering signs (vv. 2-3; Isa 6:9-10; Matt 13:13).

God's word is fulfilled in precise detail: the blinded king taken to Babylon who never saw it (vv. 12-13; 2 Kgs 25:4-7; Jer 52:11).

God can make even the confession of disciplined sinners a witness to the nations (v. 16).

Violence against others brings its own fear and loss (v. 19).

The delay of judgment is patience, not weakness, and God's word will not return empty (vv. 22-28; Isa 55:11; Hab 2:3; 2 Pet 3:4, 9).

Treating God's warnings as far off is a dangerous form of unbelief; now is the day of salvation (vv. 27-28; 2 Cor 6:2).
12.examples:
A priest packs a refugee's bundle in broad daylight and digs through his own wall with his hands, and the riddle he acts out comes true to the letter: a king taken to Babylon who never saw Babylon. At the table the same prophet eats with shaking hands.

The chapter ends with two kinds of unbelief that are still common: the shrug that says it is all talk, and the polite delay that says it is true, but not for us, not now.

keyVerse.quote: For I am the LORD; I will speak the word that I will speak, and it will be performed. It will no longer be delayed, but in your days, O rebellious house, I will speak the word and perform it, declares the Lord GOD.
keyVerse.note: This verse stands behind everything in the chapter. The exile’s bundle and the trembling meal are guaranteed by it, and both of the people’s excuses, “it will never happen” and “not yet”, are silenced by it. The God who speaks is the God who acts: a warning to the careless, and a deep comfort to all who trust his promises in Christ.

12.reflection:
The exiles had “eyes to see, but see not” (v. 2). What is the difference between being unable to see and refusing to see? Where might we be refusing to see what God is plainly showing us?

Ezekiel packed, dug and carried his bundle before he was told what it meant (vv. 7–8). When have you had to obey God before you understood why? What helped you trust him?

The survivors were spared so that they might “declare all their abominations among the nations” (v. 16). How can honest confession of our sin, and of the grace that forgives it, be part of our witness to Christ today?

Two sayings dismissed God’s word: “every vision comes to nothing” and “he prophesies of times far off” (vv. 22, 27). Which is more tempting for you? How does God’s answer in verse 28 call you to live ready for Christ’s return?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophets who promise peace without repentance are building nothing and will fall with what they have painted. Ezekiel addresses those who “prophesy from their own hearts” and have “seen nothing” (vv. 1–3). Like jackals in ruins they profit from the nation’s collapse, never going up into the breach (the gap broken in a city wall) to call the people back to God, and they say “Declares the LORD” when he has not spoken (vv. 4–7). So they will be cut off from God’s people (vv. 8–9). Their message of “Peace” is whitewash smeared on a flimsy wall, and God’s storm of rain, hail and wind will bring wall and prophets down together (vv. 10–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Preachers who cover sin with comforting words instead of exposing it will fall with the wall they whitewashed.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel, who are prophesying, and say to those who prophesy from their own hearts: 'Hear the word of the LORD!' Thus says the Lord GOD, Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit, and have seen nothing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God condemns prophets whose message comes from their own hearts: they speak with confidence, but they have seen nothing. Ezekiel was not the only prophet among the exiles, nor the most popular.

Who prophesy from their own hearts. Their messages came from their own imagination, hopes and ambitions. In Jerusalem Jeremiah was fighting the same men: “They speak visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:16). Peter describes the opposite: “no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

Who follow their own spirit, and have seen nothing. Confident, eloquent and empty. “Foolish” in the Old Testament means not a lack of intelligence but a life that leaves God out.

The prophet who spoke only his Father’s words. Set beside these men the true Prophet: “I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me” (John 8:28). The test of any preacher is not how moving he is, but whether his message comes from God’s word or from his own heart; and the listener must apply it too, since we trust most easily the voice that says what we wanted to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Your prophets have been like jackals among ruins, O Israel. You have not gone up into the breaches, or built up a wall for the house of Israel, that it might stand in battle in the day of the LORD. They have seen false visions and lying divinations. They say, 'Declares the LORD,' when the LORD has not sent them, and yet they expect him to fulfill their word. Have you not seen a false vision and uttered a lying divination, whenever you have said, 'Declares the LORD,' although I have not spoken?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false prophets fed on the nation’s ruin instead of standing in the gap to save it, and they put God’s name on words he never spoke.

Like jackals among ruins. Jackals rebuild nothing; they feed on the wreckage. So these prophets gained followers, influence and income while the nation fell apart.

You have not gone up into the breaches. When an enemy breaks a gap in a city wall, someone must stand in it. A true prophet stands in that gap by calling the people to repent and pleading with God for them, the only defence on “the day of the LORD”, the day he comes to judge. Moses did it when Israel made the golden calf (Psalm 106:23). God will later say he searched for such a man “but I found none” (22:30). The false prophets stayed where it was comfortable.

Yet they expect him to fulfill their word. They believed their own borrowed words, and those who have first deceived themselves deceive others most easily.

Although I have not spoken. Moses had given the test: “when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken” (Deuteronomy 18:22). It is a grave thing to put “God told me” in front of your own ideas.

The one who stood in the breach. Finding no one, God came himself: “He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation” (Isaiah 59:16). Jesus not only stood in the breach but broken in it, taking the judgment breaking in on his people, and now “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

What it does not mean. Not that every preacher who gets something wrong is a false prophet. These men claimed visions they never had; a pastor who honestly misreads a passage needs correcting from Scripture, not condemning as a fraud.

Where Christians differ: does God still speak through prophets today? Many continuationists hold that a fallible gift of prophecy continues, always tested by Scripture. This commentary’s view: prophecy as new revelation belonged to the church’s foundation, and claims to new words from God would add to Scripture. All agree with Ezekiel that no one may say “Declares the LORD” over his own impressions.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "Because you have uttered falsehood and seen lying visions, therefore behold, I am against you, declares the Lord GOD. My hand will be against the prophets who see false visions and who give lying divinations. They shall not be in the council of my people, nor be enrolled in the register of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who falsely claim to speak for God will be shut out of the people of God.

They shall not be in the council of my people. Three exclusions, each worse than the last. They will lose their seat in the council, the circle of trusted counsel among God’s people. Their names will not be written in the register of Israel, the list of those who belong. Such lists mattered: after the return from exile, men whose names could not be found in the family records “were excluded from the priesthood as unclean” (Ezra 2:62). And they will never return to the land.

Enrolled in the register. Jesus told his disciples not to rejoice in spiritual power, “but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). It is possible to speak in God’s name, draw crowds and still not be written in God’s book (Matthew 7:22–23). What matters is whether God knows us as his own, and every name in “the Lamb’s book of life” (Revelation 21:27) is there by grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Precisely because they have misled my people, saying, 'Peace,' when there is no peace, and because, when the people build a wall, these prophets smear it with whitewash, say to those who smear it with whitewash that it shall fall! There will be a deluge of rain, and you, O great hailstones, will fall, and a stormy wind break out. And when the wall falls, will it not be said to you, 'Where is the coating with which you smeared it?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false prophets told a doomed people “Peace” and painted over their crumbling plans, but no coat of whitewash can hold a wall up in God’s storm.

When there is no peace. This is the heart of their error. Jeremiah had used almost the same words (Jeremiah 6:14). The nation was under God’s judgment, and the prophets said everything was fine. In these very years Hananiah was promising in Jerusalem that within two years God would bring the exiles and the temple vessels back (Jeremiah 28:2–4), and prophets among the exiles in Babylon were saying the same, until Jeremiah wrote to warn them (Jeremiah 29:8–9, 15).

Smear it with whitewash. The people build a flimsy wall (the Hebrew word suggests a thin partition rather than a city wall): their own plans for security, their alliances, their hopes. It will not stand. The prophets come along and “smear it with whitewash” (the ESV notes, “plaster”). The cracks are covered, but nothing is fixed. So false comfort paints over sin instead of dealing with it. Jesus called religious leaders “whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones” (Matthew 23:27), and Paul, struck on the high priest’s orders, called him “you whitewashed wall!” (Acts 23:3).

You, O great hailstones, will fall. God even speaks to the weather. The storm is not blind nature: wind and hail are his servants, “fire and hail, snow and mist, stormy wind fulfilling his word!” (Psalm 148:8). The creation the false prophets ignored will carry out God’s verdict on their work.

Where is the coating with which you smeared it? Whitewash cannot stop a storm. When the wall falls, people will ask the prophets where their reassurances are now.

The house on the rock. Jesus told the same story about two houses: “the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it” (Matthew 7:27). Only what is built on the rock of his word, heard and obeyed, stands in the storm. And the peace the false prophets offered for nothing is real in him, because he paid for it: “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: I will make a stormy wind break out in my wrath, and there shall be a deluge of rain in my anger, and great hailstones in wrath to make a full end. And I will break down the wall that you have smeared with whitewash, and bring it down to the ground, so that its foundation will be laid bare. When it falls, you shall perish in the midst of it, and you shall know that I am the LORD. Thus will I spend my wrath upon the wall and upon those who have smeared it with whitewash, and I will say to you, The wall is no more, nor those who smeared it, the prophets of Israel who prophesied concerning Jerusalem and saw visions of peace for her, when there was no peace, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will bring the wall down to its foundations, and the false prophets will perish with the false security they painted.

I will make a stormy wind break out in my wrath. The storm is God’s own: “in my wrath … in my anger”. When the wall comes down, even “its foundation will be laid bare”: everything false will be exposed to the bottom, and the prophets who whitewashed it will be crushed under it. In 586 BC the storm came as Babylon’s army, and the city these men had called safe fell.

The wall is no more, nor those who smeared it. The false security and the false preachers disappear together.

A word for preachers. This is a searching word for every pastor, and for every church that wants to hear only good news. The most loving thing a preacher can do is tell the truth about sin, so that people can find real peace, the peace that comes not from whitewash but from the cross. Soothing words that leave people unrepentant are not kindness. They are cruelty dressed as compassion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Spiritual power sold for gain is a hunt for souls, and God will set its prey free. Ezekiel turns to women who, like the men, prophesy out of their own hearts, binding magic bands on wrists and veils on heads to trap people as a fowler traps birds (vv. 17–18). For handfuls of barley they pronounce false verdicts of life and death, profaning God’s name among his people (v. 19). God will tear the bands and veils away and let the souls go free (vv. 20–21), because they have disheartened the righteous and encouraged the wicked not to turn (v. 22). The chapter ends with his promise: “I will deliver my people out of your hand” (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: False spirituality preys on people for gain, discourages the righteous and comforts the wicked; God rescues his people from it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people, who prophesy out of their own hearts. Prophesy against them and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the women who sew magic bands upon all wrists, and make veils for the heads of persons of every stature, in the hunt for souls! Will you hunt down souls belonging to my people and keep your own souls alive? You have profaned me among my people for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread, putting to death souls who should not die and keeping alive souls who should not live, by your lying to my people, who listen to lies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women who sold charms and false verdicts in God’s name were hunting people’s souls, feeding themselves on those they claimed to help.

The daughters of your people. A second group also “prophesy out of their own hearts”. The problem is not that they are women, for Scripture honours true prophetesses such as Deborah and Huldah (Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14), but that their message, like the men’s, is their own invention.

Who sew magic bands upon all wrists. These are occult practices: bands tied on wrists, veils put over heads, rituals sold as spiritual power. God calls it “the hunt for souls”: they trap people as a fowler traps birds.

Keep your own souls alive? They fed themselves by feeding on others, “for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread”. That is the mark of every false shepherd: the flock exists for them, not they for the flock. False spirituality has always been a business: people pay to hear what they want, or to buy protection from what they fear.

You have profaned me among my people. The deepest wrong: they used God’s holy name to make a living. Paul warned against those “imagining that godliness is a means of gain” (1 Timothy 6:5). When religion becomes a business, God himself is dishonoured.

Putting to death souls who should not die. Worse, they pronounced life and death falsely, terrifying the innocent and reassuring the guilty. The people went along because they “listen to lies”. There is always a market for spiritual falsehood where people prefer comfort to truth.

For us. The charms have changed, not the trade: horoscopes, fortune-tellers, lucky objects, preachers who promise health and wealth for a gift. The gospel offers what no charm can: life freely given by the one who holds “the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18).

Uncertain wording. The words translated “magic bands” and “veils” occur only in this passage, and no one knows exactly what the objects were. Babylonian magic used knotted cords and bindings, and many scholars think the bands were something of that kind, tied on the wrists of clients or of the women themselves (v. 20 speaks of tearing them “from your arms”). “Persons of every stature” may mean veils made to fit people of every size, that is, for anyone who would pay. The point is clear even where the details are not: these were tools of sorcery used to trap people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against your magic bands with which you hunt the souls like birds, and I will tear them from your arms, and I will let the souls whom you hunt go free, the souls like birds. Your veils also I will tear off and deliver my people out of your hand, and they shall be no more in your hand as prey, and you shall know that I am the LORD. Because you have disheartened the righteous falsely, although I have not grieved him, and you have encouraged the wicked, that he should not turn from his evil way to save his life, therefore you shall no more see false visions nor practice divination. I will deliver my people out of your hand. And you shall know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will tear the snares away and set his people free, because the soul-hunters crushed the righteous and comforted the wicked.

Let the souls whom you hunt go free. Good news in the middle of judgment: “We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped!” (Psalm 124:7).

Disheartened the righteous … encouraged the wicked. Verse 22 sums up false teaching in every age. It loads guilt and fear on people whom God himself has not grieved, and it tells people living in sin that they have nothing to fear, “that he should not turn from his evil way to save his life”. True preaching comforts the broken-hearted and warns the complacent. “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20); the false prophets of Jerusalem “strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns from his evil” (Jeremiah 23:14). Ask of any teaching you listen to: does it lead the guilty to repentance and the repentant to peace?

The good shepherd lays down his life. Jesus set himself against every such hunter: “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:10–11). The hunters fed on the flock to keep their own souls alive; he laid down his own life so that the souls they trapped might live.

If you have been trapped. Some believers have been controlled for years by a leader or group that used God’s name to rule through fear, guilt or threats. God takes the side of the trapped. Talk to mature believers or faithful elders outside that circle, test what you were told by Scripture, and know you are free to leave a group that rules by fear; where there has been abuse, seek safety and report it. And if you were taught that God is never pleased with you, hear “although I have not grieved him”: he is not the author of that heaviness.

I will deliver my people out of your hand. The chapter ends with God’s promise. He exposes false teachers and rescues those they have trapped.

13.title: Whitewash on a Crumbling Wall
13.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 12 ended by silencing the exiles’ favourite sayings: “The days grow long, and every vision comes to nothing” (12:22), and “The vision that he sees is for many days from now” (12:27). Chapter 13 turns from the sayings to the people who fed them, the prophets who had promised that all would soon be well.

The message. Words spoken in God’s name are not God’s word just because they are spoken in his name. The prophets of Israel invented their own visions, told a doomed people “Peace” and painted over their sin instead of calling them to repent, and God will bring down their comfort and them with it. But he will not leave his people in the hands of those who prey on them: he will tear the snares open and set them free.

Why it was said. The exiles in Babylon, like the people left in Jerusalem, were hearing confident voices that promised a quick return and a safe city (see the introduction; Jeremiah 28:2–4; 29:8–9). Ezekiel’s hearers had to choose whom to believe, and their whole future hung on the choice.

How the chapter makes its case. First the male prophets. Their message comes “from their own hearts”, and they have seen nothing (vv. 1–3). Like jackals in the ruins they feed on a falling nation instead of standing in the breach, and they put “Declares the LORD” over words he never spoke (vv. 4–7), so they will lose their place among God’s people (vv. 8–9). Their “Peace” is whitewash on a flimsy wall, and God’s storm will bring the wall down on them (vv. 10–16). Then the women who sell charms and false verdicts for handfuls of barley, hunting souls like birds (vv. 17–19). God will tear their snares away, set his people free and stop them from disheartening the righteous and encouraging the wicked (vv. 20–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by contrast. Israel needed a prophet who spoke only what God gave him, and a man who would stand in the breach; God searched and “found none” (22:30). Jesus is both. He said, “I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me” (John 8:28), and he did not merely stand in the gap but was broken in it, so that the peace false prophets promised cheaply is now real: “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). Where the hunters fed on the flock, the good shepherd “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).

For us. We are always tempted to prefer the voice that tells us all is well. Test what you hear by God’s word, not by how it makes you feel, and look for the teaching that leads the guilty to repentance and the repentant to peace. And if you have been trapped by fear or manipulation in God’s name, hear verse 23: “I will deliver my people out of your hand.”
13.theology:
A true message comes from God, not from the preacher's own heart; claiming God's authority for one's own words is grave sin (vv. 2-3, 6-7; Jer 23:16; 2 Pet 1:20-21; Deut 18:20-22).

Faithful ministry stands in the breach and calls people to repentance before the day of the LORD (v. 5; 22:30).

Speaking about God is not the same as being known by God (v. 9; Luke 10:20).

False peace whitewashes sin instead of dealing with it, and it will not survive God's storm (vv. 10-16; Jer 6:14; Matt 7:24-27; 23:27).

False spirituality preys on people for gain, discourages the righteous and encourages the wicked (vv. 18-22; Isa 5:20; Jer 23:14).

God rescues his people from false teachers; Christ the good shepherd gives life where the thief takes it (vv. 20-23; Ps 124:7; John 10:10-11).
13.examples:
The false prophets are jackals growing fat in the ruins, while nobody stands in the gap in the wall. Their comfort is a fresh coat of whitewash on a wall that is already cracking, and when the storm brings it down the people ask where the plaster is now.

The soul-hunters sell spiritual advice for a handful of barley. But the chapter ends with the snare torn open and the birds flying free.

keyVerse.quote: Precisely because they have misled my people, saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace, and because, when the people build a wall, these prophets smear it with whitewash,
keyVerse.note: This verse names the false prophets’ sin and gives the chapter its picture. Their crime was not a lack of comfort but a false one: they covered the cracks in a doomed people’s hopes instead of calling them to repent. Everything else in the chapter, the storm, the fallen wall and the snares, shows what such comfort costs those who trust it.

13.reflection:
The false prophets spoke “from their own hearts” and told people what they wanted to hear (vv. 2, 10). Why are we so drawn to voices like that? How can we test what we hear by God’s word rather than by how it makes us feel?

God looked for someone to “stand in the breach” (v. 5; 22:30). What does it look like for a Christian today to stand in the gap for family, church or neighbours, and how does Jesus’ own standing in the breach shape and encourage us?

Verse 22 says false teaching disheartens the righteous and encourages the wicked. Where do you see each of these today, inside the church as well as outside it?

The chapter ends with God setting trapped people free (vv. 20–23). Who might need to hear that promise, and how can a church become a safe place for people who have been manipulated in God’s name?

They would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness.<sup>21</sup>"For thus says the Lord GOD: How much more when I send upon Jerusalem my four disastrous acts of judgment, sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast!<sup>22</sup>But behold, some survivors will be left in it, sons and daughters who will be brought out; behold, when they come out to you, and you see their ways and their deeds, you will be consoled for the disaster that I have brought upon Jerusalem, for all that I have brought upon it.<sup>23</sup>They will console you, when you see their ways and their deeds, and you shall know that I have not done without cause all that I have done in it, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not let himself be used by people who keep their idols, but he confronts them in order to win them back. Elders come to Ezekiel for a word from God, but God sees the idols they have taken into their hearts and the stumbling block they keep before their faces (vv. 1–3). He will answer such inquirers himself, to lay hold of hearts estranged from him (vv. 4–5). So he calls them to repent and turn, and warns that he will set his face against anyone, Israelite or foreigner, who will not (vv. 6–8). The prophet who flatters them shares their guilt, and the goal of it all is the covenant: “that they may be my people and I may be their God” (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be used by people who keep their idols; he confronts them in order to win back their hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Then certain of the elders of Israel came to me and sat before me. And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, these men have taken their idols into their hearts, and set the stumbling block of their iniquity before their faces. Should I indeed let myself be consulted by them?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders come to ask God for guidance, but God sees idols in their hearts and asks whether he should answer such men at all.

Certain of the elders of Israel came to me. The elders come again to Ezekiel’s house (as in 8:1). Outwardly it looks good: leaders seeking a word from God.

These men have taken their idols into their hearts. God sees what Ezekiel cannot. There may have been no statues in their homes in Babylon; the idols had moved inside. This is a deep insight into sin. Idolatry is not first about carved images but about what the heart loves, trusts and serves in God’s place. The New Testament calls greed “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5), and its last word to believers is “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21). Anything we look to for the security, meaning or joy only God can give is an idol: money, approval, success, a relationship, comfort, control.

The stumbling block of their iniquity. They keep it right in front of their faces, where it trips them every day, and still come, as it were, to church to ask God for guidance. “Should I indeed let myself be consulted by them?” God will not be a consultant to people who have no intention of giving up their idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore speak to them and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: Any one of the house of Israel who takes his idols into his heart and sets the stumbling block of his iniquity before his face, and yet comes to the prophet, I the LORD will answer him as he comes with the multitude of his idols, that I may lay hold of the hearts of the house of Israel, who are all estranged from me through their idols.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will answer the idolater himself, not with the answer he wants, but in order to lay hold of his heart and bring it back.

I the LORD will answer him as he comes with the multitude of his idols. The answer fits what he is carrying, not what he is asking. God deals with the heart that comes, not the words it says.

That I may lay hold of the hearts. Here is the purpose, full of grace. God confronts them not to push them away but to take hold of them. Their hearts had drifted, “estranged from me”, and he wants them back. That is why God sometimes refuses the easy answer we pray for: he is after our hearts, not just our requests. It is the same seeking love that sent the Son “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Repent and turn away from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your abominations. For any one of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn in Israel, who separates himself from me, taking his idols into his heart and putting the stumbling block of his iniquity before his face, and yet comes to a prophet to consult me through him, I the LORD will answer him myself. And I will set my face against that man; I will make him a sign and a byword and cut him off from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way back is to turn from the idols, and anyone who will not turn will find God himself set against him.

Repent and turn away. The call is simple and total. Not merely feel sorry, but turn: first from the idols, then the face from the abominations. Repentance is a change of direction, a change of what you are looking at. The God who calls them to turn has just said he wants their hearts back, and he promises the new heart and Spirit that make the turning possible (11:19; 36:26–27).

Who separates himself from me. The same rule applies to Israelites and to foreigners living among them; God has no double standard. And idolatry is not a small addition to faith; it is a separation from God.

I the LORD will answer him myself. The answer is “I will set my face against that man”. It is a fearful thing to come to God with a divided heart and find that God himself answers. Jesus quoted Isaiah about such worship: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me” (Matthew 15:8–9). Religious activity without a heart turned from idols is not neutral. It is in vain.

verseByVerse.quote: And if the prophet is deceived and speaks a word, I, the LORD, have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand against him and will destroy him from the midst of my people Israel. And they shall bear their punishment —the punishment of the prophet and the punishment of the inquirer shall be alike— that the house of Israel may no more go astray from me, nor defile themselves anymore with all their transgressions, but that they may be my people and I may be their God, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hands those who love lies over to the lying prophets they seek, and both fall together, so that his people may come back to him.

I, the LORD, have deceived that prophet. A hard verse, to be read carefully. It does not mean God lies or tempts anyone to lie: God “never lies” (Titus 1:2). It means that when people insist on hearing falsehood, God may hand them over to it. A prophet willing to tell idol-worshippers what they want to hear will be allowed to do so, and both will fall together. God rules even over the lies people choose, without being their author.

The same pattern elsewhere. When King Ahab wanted only prophets who agreed with him, Micaiah told him, “the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets” (1 Kings 22:23). Paul says of those who “refused to love the truth and so be saved”: “Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false” (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11). This is God’s judgment on people who have already chosen lies. The best protection is to love the truth, even when it hurts.

Equal guilt. The ESV notes that “punishment”, three times in verse 10, may be “iniquity”. The false prophet and the one who seeks him out share the same guilt: the one who asks for a lie is as responsible as the one who tells it.

That they may be my people. Again the purpose is restoration. The goal of all this severity is the covenant promise, “that they may be my people and I may be their God”, the promise God keeps in the new covenant sealed by Christ’s blood (Hebrews 8:10). His discipline always aims at bringing his people home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one can be saved by someone else’s goodness, and God never judges without cause. Ezekiel imagines a land under judgment by famine, wild beasts, sword and pestilence, and four times God swears that even Noah, Daniel and Job, three men famous for righteousness, would deliver only their own lives, not their sons or daughters (vv. 12–20). How much more when all four judgments fall together on Jerusalem (v. 21)! Yet some survivors will be brought out to Babylon, and when the exiles see their ways and deeds, they will understand that all God did in the city was just (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology: No human righteousness can rescue another person; only the righteousness of Christ counts for others.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, when a land sins against me by acting faithlessly, and I stretch out my hand against it and break its supply of bread and send famine upon it, and cut off from it man and beast, even if these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God judges a land, even the most righteous people who ever lived could save only themselves.

When a land sins against me. A new message answers a quiet hope: surely God will spare Jerusalem for the sake of the righteous people still living there. Abraham had once pleaded for Sodom for the sake of ten righteous (Genesis 18:32). (The ESV notes that “supply” in v. 13 is literally “staff”, the bread that held life up.)

Noah, Daniel, and Job. God names three men famous for righteousness. Noah “was a righteous man, blameless in his generation” (Genesis 6:9); Job “was blameless and upright” (Job 1:1); and Daniel, most naturally the young man taken to Babylon years before (Daniel 1:6), stood faithful in a pagan court. Noah saved his family through the flood, and Job prayed for his children and his friends (Job 1:5; 42:8). Yet even they, God says, would deliver “but their own lives”.

No one rides on another’s faith. That shatters a comfortable idea: that we can ride into God’s favour on someone else’s righteousness, a godly parent, a faithful church, a praying grandmother. “Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life” (Psalm 49:7). Each person must stand before God for himself.

Uncertain wording. Which Daniel? Some think of Danel, a righteous king in ancient Canaanite legend, because he is listed between Noah and Job, two figures from long ago, and because the Hebrew spells the name a little differently here (Dan’el). But Ezekiel would hardly hold up a pagan hero as an example to Israel, and Daniel of Babylon was already renowned for righteousness and wisdom (28:3; Daniel 1:20). The likeliest reading is Ezekiel’s contemporary.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel had been taken to Babylon in 605 BC, some thirteen years before this oracle.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I cause wild beasts to pass through the land, and they ravage it, and it be made desolate, so that no one may pass through because of the beasts, even if these three men were in it, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, they would deliver neither sons nor daughters. They alone would be delivered, but the land would be desolate. "Or if I bring a sword upon that land and say, Let a sword pass through the land, and I cut off from it man and beast, though these three men were in it, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, they would deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone would be delivered. "Or if I send a pestilence into that land and pour out my wrath upon it with blood, to cut off from it man and beast, even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in it, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, they would deliver neither son nor daughter. They would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four times God swears it: in a land ripe for judgment, the righteous could not save even their own sons and daughters.
