Neither sons nor daughters. Three more times the same pattern, each sealed with an oath, “as I live”: wild beasts, sword, pestilence, and the same verdict. This is striking because Noah’s righteousness did save his family (Hebrews 11:7). But not here, not in a land ripe for judgment.

A word for parents. That is a sobering word for parents, and a painful one for those whose children have wandered. We long for our children to be saved, and we should pray and teach and live for that. But our faith cannot be counted as theirs; each child must come to God personally. Yet the God of this chapter is the one who lays hold of estranged hearts (v. 5), so a parent’s prayers are never wasted, even though the parent cannot do the saving.

One righteousness that can be credited. There is one righteousness that can be credited to others, and only one. “For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). Noah, Daniel and Job could not save a single son or daughter; Jesus Christ saves everyone who trusts him: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). The gospel gives exactly what this chapter says no human being could ever provide.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: How much more when I send upon Jerusalem my four disastrous acts of judgment, sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast! But behold, some survivors will be left in it, sons and daughters who will be brought out; behold, when they come out to you, and you see their ways and their deeds, you will be consoled for the disaster that I have brought upon Jerusalem, for all that I have brought upon it. They will console you, when you see their ways and their deeds, and you shall know that I have not done without cause all that I have done in it, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If one judgment was beyond the righteous to avert, all four on Jerusalem are certain, and the survivors will show the exiles that God was just.

Sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence. These four are the covenant curses Moses listed (Leviticus 26:22–26), and they appear again at the end of the Bible, when the fourth horseman is given authority “to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by wild beasts of the earth” (Revelation 6:8). Jerusalem’s fall previews the judgment that will come on the whole world, and Ezekiel 14 presses the question of the last day: whose righteousness will you stand in?

Some survivors will be left in it. A surprising kind of consolation. Survivors will arrive in Babylon, not because they were righteous, but so that the exiles may see what they are like. When the exiles see “their ways and their deeds”, they will understand: the destruction was not cruelty.

I have not done without cause all that I have done. There is real comfort in knowing that God’s judgments are just. When we face disasters we cannot explain, we may not see the reasons, but we can rest on this: the Judge of all the earth does nothing without cause (Genesis 18:25), and one day every act of his will be seen to be right.

What it does not mean. Not that every disaster in our lives is God’s punishment for a particular sin. Jerusalem’s fall was explained by God’s own prophets as judgment; our own hard providences are not. Jesus refused to read tragedy as a verdict on its victims (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:3). What we may always know is that God is just and good, and that in Christ there is no condemnation for those who are his (Romans 8:1).

14.title: Idols in the Heart
14.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 exposed the prophets who told the exiles what they wanted to hear. Now the elders of the exiles come to Ezekiel’s house to hear a word from God (as in 8:1), and God shows the prophet what lies behind their visit.

The message. God cannot be consulted like an adviser by people who keep their idols in their hearts; he answers the heart, not the question, and he answers in order to win that heart back. And no one can shelter behind another person’s goodness: when God judges, even Noah, Daniel and Job could save only themselves. Each must turn to God for himself, and God’s judgments, when they come, are never without cause.

Why it was said. The exiles were religious enough to seek out a prophet, yet still clung to the gods and hopes that had ruined them, and some hoped Jerusalem would be spared for the sake of the righteous still in it (see the introduction). Ezekiel takes both comforts away.

How the chapter makes its case. God sees that the elders have taken their idols into their hearts and asks whether he should let himself be consulted by them (vv. 1–3). He will answer such people himself, to lay hold of hearts estranged from him (vv. 4–5). So he calls them to repent and warns that he will set his face against anyone who will not (vv. 6–8). A prophet who flatters them will fall with them, so that Israel may again be his people (vv. 9–11). Then four times over, with famine, wild beasts, sword and plague, God declares that Noah, Daniel and Job would deliver only their own lives (vv. 12–20). How much more when all four fall on Jerusalem; yet the survivors who reach Babylon will show the exiles that God did nothing without cause (vv. 21–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes. If the three most righteous men of history could not save a son or daughter, no human goodness can be borrowed for another. That is exactly what makes the gospel astonishing: there is one righteousness that can be counted for others, “so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). And the heart God set out to lay hold of (v. 5) he finally wins through his Son and gives a new heart by his Spirit (36:26).

For us. It is possible to pray, read and attend church while some idol stays in the heart, and God loves us too much to answer only our requests. Ask what you are looking to for the security or joy only he can give. Do not lean on a godly parent or a faithful church for your standing with God; stand in Christ’s righteousness, and pray for those you love in hope, for the God of this chapter lays hold of wandering hearts.
14.theology:
Idolatry is first a matter of the heart; anything loved and trusted in God's place is an idol (vv. 3-4; Col 3:5; 1 John 5:21).

God will not be consulted by people who keep their idols, yet his confrontation aims to win back their hearts (vv. 3-5, 11).

Repentance means turning from idols and turning the face away from sin (v. 6); worship without it is in vain (Matt 15:8-9).

As a judgment, God may hand those who love lies over to the lies they want, though he himself never lies (vv. 9-10; 1 Kgs 22:20-23; 2 Thess 2:10-12; Titus 1:2).

No human righteousness can save another person, not even one's own children (vv. 14-20; Ps 49:7-8).

Only the righteousness of Christ is credited to others (Rom 5:19; 2 Cor 5:21).

God's judgments are never without cause (v. 23).
14.examples:
Elders ask God for guidance with idols tucked inside, keeping their stumbling block right in front of their faces, and God answers what they are carrying, not what they are saying.

Noah, Daniel and Job, for all their righteousness, could not save a single child. That makes the one righteousness that can be credited to someone else, the righteousness of Christ, all the more wonderful.

keyVerse.quote: even if these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness, declares the Lord GOD.
keyVerse.note: This verse takes away the hope of sheltering behind someone else’s goodness, and it is repeated four times in the chapter so that no one misses it. Even the most righteous people in history could save only themselves. It leaves us looking for the one man whose righteousness can be counted for others, and the gospel names him.

14.reflection:
The elders had “taken their idols into their hearts” though there may have been no statues in sight (v. 3). What are some of the idols of the heart in our culture, and how can we recognise our own?

God answers the idolater “that I may lay hold of the hearts” of his people (v. 5). Have you known times when God refused the easy answer you prayed for in order to win your heart? What did that look like?

Noah, Daniel and Job could not save their own children (vv. 14–20). How does this chapter both sober and encourage parents and grandparents praying for those they love?

The only righteousness that can be credited to another is Christ’s (Romans 5:19). How does that truth change the way we think about our standing before God, and the way we speak to others about theirs?

15.text: <sup>1</sup>And the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, how does the wood of the vine surpass any wood, the vine branch that is among the trees of the forest?<sup>3</sup>Is wood taken from it to make anything? Do people take a peg from it to hang any vessel on it?<sup>4</sup>Behold, it is given to the fire for fuel. When the fire has consumed both ends of it, and the middle of it is charred, is it useful for anything?<sup>5</sup>Behold, when it was whole, it was used for nothing. How much less, when the fire has consumed it and it is charred, can it ever be used for anything!<sup>6</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Like the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so have I given up the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<sup>7</sup>And I will set my face against them. Though they escape from the fire, the fire shall yet consume them, and you will know that I am the LORD, when I set my face against them.<sup>8</sup>And I will make the land desolate, because they have acted faithlessly, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Good for Nothing but Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A vine is worth nothing except for its fruit, and a burnt one is worth even less. God asks what makes vine wood better than any other wood among the trees of the forest (v. 2). The answer is nothing: no one can make anything from it, not even a peg to hang a pot on (v. 3). Throw it on the fire, let both ends burn and the middle char, and it is useful for less still (vv. 4–5). The picture prepares the verdict that follows: Israel’s whole worth lay in the fruit she was planted to bear.
verseByVerse.theology: A vine exists for fruit; without fruit it has no other use.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, how does the wood of the vine surpass any wood, the vine branch that is among the trees of the forest? Is wood taken from it to make anything? Do people take a peg from it to hang any vessel on it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vine wood is useless for anything but fruit, and that is the whole point: Israel’s worth lay in the fruit God planted her to bear.

God’s vine. Israel was proud to be God’s vine. The psalm sang, “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Psalm 80:8). The exiles might have thought: surely God would never burn his own vine.

The wood of the vine. So God asks a question a child could answer. Compared with the timber of the forest, oak, cedar, cypress, what is so special about vine wood?

Do people take a peg from it to hang any vessel on it? The honest answer is: nothing. Vine wood is thin, twisted and weak. You cannot build a house with it, carve a tool from it, or even make a peg strong enough to hang a cooking pot. A vine has one purpose, to bear grapes; its glory is entirely in its fruit.

Israel’s calling. God did not choose Israel because they were strong timber (Deuteronomy 7:7). He planted them to bear the fruit of justice, faithfulness and worship. Isaiah said, “he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!” (Isaiah 5:7), and Jeremiah, “I planted you a choice vine … How then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine?” (Jeremiah 2:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, it is given to the fire for fuel. When the fire has consumed both ends of it, and the middle of it is charred, is it useful for anything? Behold, when it was whole, it was used for nothing. How much less, when the fire has consumed it and it is charred, can it ever be used for anything!
verseByVerse.commentary:
If vine wood is useless when whole, a half-burned vine is useless twice over: Jerusalem has already been through the fire and is fit for nothing.

It is given to the fire for fuel. Now picture a vine branch already thrown on the fire. Both ends are burned away; the middle is blackened. If it was useless before, what is it now?

When the fire has consumed both ends of it. One way to read the picture: both ends had already burned. The northern kingdom had been destroyed by Assyria, and the first deportation in 597 BC had taken King Jehoiachin and the leaders of Jerusalem to Babylon. What remained in the middle was charred.

How much less. The logic is merciless. A fruitless vine is worthless whole; a fruitless, half-burned vine is worth even less. The people in Jerusalem thought that, having survived the first deportation, they were the precious remnant (11:3). God says they are the charred middle of a stick.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem is the fruitless vine, and God has given her to the fire because she has been faithless. Like vine wood thrown on the fire, the inhabitants of Jerusalem have been handed over to judgment (v. 6). God has set his face against them: those who escaped the first fire, the deportation of 597 BC, will be consumed by the next (v. 7). The land will be made desolate, and the reason is given in the chapter’s last words: “because they have acted faithlessly” (v. 8). Fruitlessness grows out of unfaithfulness.
verseByVerse.theology: God's people who bear no fruit have lost the only reason for their privileged place.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Like the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so have I given up the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And I will set my face against them. Though they escape from the fire, the fire shall yet consume them, and you will know that I am the LORD, when I set my face against them. And I will make the land desolate, because they have acted faithlessly, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem is the vine wood and God’s judgment is the fire; the city that bore no fruit because it kept no faith will burn, and its only hope lies beyond the chapter, in the true Vine.

So have I given up the inhabitants of Jerusalem. The picture is explained in one sentence. Being God’s people outwardly was no shield from judgment; being God’s vine meant being expected to bear fruit. Jesus told of a fig tree that bore nothing for three years: “Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?” (Luke 13:7). And he warned the leaders of his day, “the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits” (Matthew 21:43).

Though they escape from the fire, the fire shall yet consume them. Those who survived 597 BC thought they had escaped. The burning of the city in 586 BC (some date it 587) was still to come.

Because they have acted faithlessly. The last words give the root. They were fruitless because they were unfaithful: the fruit failed because the relationship had broken. Chapter 16 will tell that story of unfaithfulness in full.

The true vine. That is exactly where Jesus takes this picture. Israel was the vine that failed, so he says, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser” (John 15:1). Christ is everything Israel was meant to be and was not. Then he speaks of us: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch bears fruit only by staying joined to him.

Abiding in the vine. He uses Ezekiel’s warning too: “If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned” (John 15:6). The fire of Ezekiel 15 is real. But the answer is not to try harder to be good timber. It is to abide in the true Vine, whose life flows into the branches by his Spirit and produces the fruit God is looking for (Galatians 5:22–23).

Where Christians differ: does John 15:6 mean a true Christian can be cast off? Many in the Arminian tradition read it as a warning that a true believer who stops abiding can be lost for ever. This commentary’s view: the warning is real, and God uses it to keep his people abiding, but those truly joined to Christ will not finally be cut off (John 10:28). The branches burned bear no fruit: like Jerusalem, they were attached outwardly but never shared the vine’s life. True branches are pruned, not burned (John 15:2).

15.title: The Wood of the Vine
15.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 ended with God’s insistence that he does nothing without cause. Before the long story of Jerusalem’s unfaithfulness in chapter 16, this short chapter gives the verdict in a single picture: a vine.

The message. Israel’s worth was never in her own strength but in the fruit God planted her to bear. A vine that bears no fruit is good for nothing, not even a peg, and a vine already half burned is good for even less. Jerusalem, fruitless because faithless, will be given to the fire, and those who think they have escaped one fire will meet the next.

Why it was said. The exiles and the people left in Jerusalem took comfort in being God’s chosen vine, the nation he had brought out of Egypt and planted (Psalm 80:8). Surely God would not burn his own vine. Those who had survived the deportation of 597 BC thought they were the precious remnant (11:3; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God asks a question a child could answer: what is vine wood good for, compared with the timber of the forest? Not even a peg to hang a pot on (vv. 1–3). Throw it on the fire, burn both ends and char the middle, and it is useful for even less (vv. 4–5). So God has given Jerusalem to the fire; those who escape one burning will be consumed by the next, and the land will be desolate “because they have acted faithlessly” (vv. 6–8).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. Israel was the vine that failed. Jesus took up the picture and said, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1): he is the faithful Israel who bore all the fruit God looked for. And he made Ezekiel’s point about us: branches bear fruit only by abiding in him, and apart from him can do nothing (John 15:5). The answer to the fire is not better timber but union with the true Vine.

For us. Church membership, a Christian upbringing and religious privilege are no shield if there is no living union with Christ. Do not try to make yourself strong timber; stay joined to him in faith, through his word and prayer, and his life will produce in you the fruit God is looking for.
15.theology:
God's people were planted to bear fruit, and their value lies there, not in any strength of their own (vv. 2-5; Ps 80:8-9; Isa 5:7; Jer 2:21).

Religious privilege without fruit is no protection from judgment (vv. 6-7; Luke 13:6-9; Matt 21:43).

Fruitlessness grows out of unfaithfulness (v. 8).

Christ is the true vine where Israel failed, and those who abide in him bear fruit; those who do not are gathered for the fire (John 15:1-6).
15.examples:
The chapter turns on a stick too weak to hang a cooking pot on, then on a branch burned at both ends and charred in the middle, whose survivors think that escaping one fire means they are safe.

Its answer lies beyond it, in the true Vine, whose branches cannot bear fruit on their own but bear much fruit in him.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Like the wood of the vine among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so have I given up the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
keyVerse.note: This verse turns the picture into its verdict. Everything in verses 1–5 about useless, charred wood is said in order to be applied here to the city that trusted in being God’s vine. It prepares for Jesus’ words, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1), where the only hope for fruitless branches is to be joined to him.

15.reflection:
Vine wood is good for nothing except fruit (vv. 2–5). What does that say about where the value of God’s people lies? Why are we tempted to rely instead on our own strength, history or reputation?

The people in Jerusalem thought that surviving one disaster proved they were safe (v. 7). In what ways can we mistake God’s patience or our own escapes for his approval?

The chapter ends, “because they have acted faithlessly” (v. 8). How is fruitfulness connected with faithfulness? What does it look like in ordinary life to “abide” in Christ, the true Vine (John 15:4–5)?

Jesus says that apart from him we can do nothing (John 15:5). Where do you most need to stop trying to be strong timber and depend on him instead?

16.text: <sup>1</sup>Again the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations,<sup>3</sup>and say, Thus says the Lord GOD to Jerusalem: Your origin and your birth are of the land of the Canaanites; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite.<sup>4</sup>And as for your birth, on the day you were born your cord was not cut, nor were you washed with water to cleanse you, nor rubbed with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling cloths.<sup>5</sup>No eye pitied you, to do any of these things to you out of compassion for you, but you were cast out on the open field, for you were abhorred, on the day that you were born.<sup>6</sup>"And when I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood, I said to you in your blood, 'Live!' I said to you in your blood, 'Live!'<sup>7</sup>I made you flourish like a plant of the field. And you grew up and became tall and arrived at full adornment. Your breasts were formed, and your hair had grown; yet you were naked and bare.<sup>8</sup>"When I passed by you again and saw you, behold, you were at the age for love, and I spread the corner of my garment over you and covered your nakedness; I made my vow to you and entered into a covenant with you, declares the Lord GOD, and you became mine.<sup>9</sup>Then I bathed you with water and washed off your blood from you and anointed you with oil.<sup>10</sup>I clothed you also with embroidered cloth and shod you with fine leather. I wrapped you in fine linen and covered you with silk.<sup>11</sup>And I adorned you with ornaments and put bracelets on your wrists and a chain on your neck.<sup>12</sup>And I put a ring on your nose and earrings in your ears and a beautiful crown on your head.<sup>13</sup>Thus you were adorned with gold and silver, and your clothing was of fine linen and silk and embroidered cloth. You ate fine flour and honey and oil. You grew exceedingly beautiful and advanced to royalty.<sup>14</sup>And your renown went forth among the nations because of your beauty, for it was perfect through the splendor that I had bestowed on you, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>15</sup>"But you trusted in your beauty and played the whore because of your renown and lavished your whorings on any passerby; your beauty became his.<sup>16</sup>You took some of your garments and made for yourself colorful shrines, and on them played the whore. The like has never been, nor ever shall be.<sup>17</sup>You also took your beautiful jewels of my gold and of my silver, which I had given you, and made for yourself images of men, and with them played the whore.<sup>18</sup>And you took your embroidered garments to cover them, and set my oil and my incense before them.<sup>19</sup>Also my bread that I gave you— I fed you with fine flour and oil and honey—you set before them for a pleasing aroma; and so it was, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>20</sup>And you took your sons and your daughters, whom you had borne to me, and these you sacrificed to them to be devoured. Were your whorings so small a matter<sup>21</sup>that you slaughtered my children and delivered them up as an offering by fire to them?<sup>22</sup>And in all your abominations and your whorings you did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and bare, wallowing in your blood.<sup>23</sup>"And after all your wickedness (woe, woe to you! declares the Lord GOD),<sup>24</sup>you built yourself a vaulted chamber and made yourself a lofty place in every square.<sup>25</sup>At the head of every street you built your lofty place and made your beauty an abomination, offering yourself to any passerby and multiplying your whoring.<sup>26</sup>You also played the whore with the Egyptians, your lustful neighbors, multiplying your whoring, to provoke me to anger.<sup>27</sup>Behold, therefore, I stretched out my hand against you and diminished your allotted portion and delivered you to the greed of your enemies, the daughters of the Philistines, who were ashamed of your lewd behavior.<sup>28</sup>You played the whore also with the Assyrians, because you were not satisfied; yes, you played the whore with them, and still you were not satisfied.<sup>29</sup>You multiplied your whoring also with the trading land of Chaldea, and even with this you were not satisfied.<sup>30</sup>"How sick is your heart, declares the Lord GOD, because you did all these things, the deeds of a brazen prostitute,<sup>31</sup>building your vaulted chamber at the head of every street, and making your lofty place in every square. Yet you were not like a prostitute, because you scorned payment.<sup>32</sup>Adulterous wife, who receives strangers instead of her husband!<sup>33</sup>Men give gifts to all prostitutes, but you gave your gifts to all your lovers, bribing them to come to you from every side with your whorings.<sup>34</sup>So you were different from other women in your whorings. No one solicited you to play the whore, and you gave payment, while no payment was given to you; therefore you were different.<sup>35</sup>"Therefore, O prostitute, hear the word of the LORD:<sup>36</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD, Because your lust was poured out and your nakedness uncovered in your whorings with your lovers, and with all your abominable idols, and because of the blood of your children that you gave to them,<sup>37</sup>therefore, behold, I will gather all your lovers with whom you took pleasure, all those you loved and all those you hated. I will gather them against you from every side and will uncover your nakedness to them, that they may see all your nakedness.<sup>38</sup>And I will judge you as women who commit adultery and shed blood are judged, and bring upon you the blood of wrath and jealousy.<sup>39</sup>And I will give you into their hands, and they shall throw down your vaulted chamber and break down your lofty places. They shall strip you of your clothes and take your beautiful jewels and leave you naked and bare.<sup>40</sup>They shall bring up a crowd against you, and they shall stone you and cut you to pieces with their swords.<sup>41</sup>And they shall burn your houses and execute judgments upon you in the sight of many women. I will make you stop playing the whore, and you shall also give payment no more.<sup>42</sup>So will I satisfy my wrath on you, and my jealousy shall depart from you. I will be calm and will no more be angry.<sup>43</sup>Because you have not remembered the days of your youth, but have enraged me with all these things, therefore, behold, I have returned your deeds upon your head, declares the Lord GOD. Have you not committed lewdness in addition to all your abominations?<sup>44</sup>"Behold, everyone who uses proverbs will use this proverb about you: 'Like mother, like daughter.'<sup>45</sup>You are the daughter of your mother, who loathed her husband and her children; and you are the sister of your sisters, who loathed their husbands and their children. Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite.<sup>46</sup>And your elder sister is Samaria, who lived with her daughters to the north of you; and your younger sister, who lived to the south of you, is Sodom with her daughters.<sup>47</sup>Not only did you walk in their ways and do according to their abominations; within a very little time you were more corrupt than they in all your ways.<sup>48</sup>As I live, declares the Lord GOD, your sister Sodom and her daughters have not done as you and your daughters have done.<sup>49</sup>Behold, this was the guilt of your sister Sodom: she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy.<sup>50</sup>They were haughty and did an abomination before me. So I removed them, when I saw it.<sup>51</sup>Samaria has not committed half your sins. You have committed more abominations than they, and have made your sisters appear righteous by all the abominations that you have committed.<sup>52</sup>Bear your disgrace, you also, for you have intervened on behalf of your sisters. Because of your sins in which you acted more abominably than they, they are more in the right than you. So be ashamed, you also, and bear your disgrace, for you have made your sisters appear righteous.<sup>53</sup>"I will restore their fortunes, both the fortunes of Sodom and her daughters, and the fortunes of Samaria and her daughters, and I will restore your own fortunes in their midst,<sup>54</sup>that you may bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all that you have done, becoming a consolation to them.<sup>55</sup>As for your sisters, Sodom and her daughters shall return to their former state, and Samaria and her daughters shall return to their former state, and you and your daughters shall return to your former state.<sup>56</sup>Was not your sister Sodom a byword in your mouth in the day of your pride,<sup>57</sup>before your wickedness was uncovered? Now you have become an object of reproach for the daughters of Syria and all those around her, and for the daughters of the Philistines, those all around who despise you.<sup>58</sup>You bear the penalty of your lewdness and your abominations, declares the LORD.<sup>59</sup>"For thus says the Lord GOD: I will deal with you as you have done, you who have despised the oath in breaking the covenant,<sup>60</sup>yet I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish for you an everlasting covenant.<sup>61</sup>Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed when you take your sisters, both your elder and your younger, and I give them to you as daughters, but not on account of the covenant with you.<sup>62</sup>I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall know that I am the LORD,<sup>63</sup>that you may remember and be confounded, and never open your mouth again because of your shame, when I atone for you for all that you have done, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Live! The Foundling Made a Queen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem’s whole existence was a gift of undeserved love. Her origins were pagan, “of the land of the Canaanites” (vv. 1–3). On the day she was born she was left uncared for and thrown into an open field to die, pitied by no one (vv. 4–5). God passed by, saw her in her blood and said, “Live!”, and she grew to womanhood under his care (vv. 6–7). Passing by again, he spread his garment over her and entered into covenant with her: “you became mine” (v. 8). Then he washed, clothed and crowned her until her beauty was famous among the nations, “perfect through the splendor that I had bestowed on you” (vv. 9–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything God's people have — life, beauty, honour — is his undeserved gift to the helpless.

verseByVerse.quote: Again the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD to Jerusalem: Your origin and your birth are of the land of the Canaanites; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Jerusalem’s story as a marriage, and begins by stripping away her pride: there was nothing in her origins to make him choose her.

How to read the picture. This chapter is meant to shock. God tells the story of Jerusalem as a baby girl abandoned at birth, rescued, raised, married and made a queen, who then betrays her husband with every passing stranger. The husband is the LORD. The wife is not any real woman but the city of Jerusalem and its people. Her lovers are the idols and foreign powers Judah trusted instead of God, her adultery is idolatry and those alliances, and her stripping and stoning are the siege and fall of the city to Babylon’s army. It is a parable about a nation’s worship, told in the language of marriage because the covenant was a marriage and idolatry betrayed it. God wants his people to feel what their idolatry is like from his side.

Your origin and your birth are of the land of the Canaanites. The first blow is to Jerusalem’s pride in her holy history: your roots are pagan. Jerusalem had been a Canaanite city, held by the Jebusites until David “took the stronghold of Zion” (2 Samuel 5:7). Amorites and Hittites were among the old peoples of the land (Genesis 15:19–21), so the point is simply that she had no Israelite pedigree at all.

Your father was an Amorite. God is not sneering at her ancestry. His point is that there was nothing in her to make him choose her. Moses had told Israel the same: “It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you … but it is because the LORD loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). God’s love does not find something lovely and choose it. It chooses, and then makes it lovely.
verseByVerse.note: With 63 verses, this is the longest chapter in Ezekiel.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for your birth, on the day you were born your cord was not cut, nor were you washed with water to cleanse you, nor rubbed with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling cloths. No eye pitied you, to do any of these things to you out of compassion for you, but you were cast out on the open field, for you were abhorred, on the day that you were born.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem began as a newborn left uncared for and thrown out to die, and that is where grace finds every one of us.

Your cord was not cut. Picture a newborn left exactly as she came into the world. No one has cut the cord, washed her, rubbed her skin with salt as midwives did, or wrapped her in cloths to keep her warm. Every ordinary act of care has been refused.

You were cast out on the open field. Then she is thrown into an open field to die. “No eye pitied you”; “you were abhorred”. In the ancient world unwanted babies, often girls, were sometimes left out in exactly this way.

Our story too. This is not only Jerusalem’s story. The Bible describes every human being by nature in the same terms: “dead in the trespasses and sins”, “by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:1, 3), helpless and unable to do a single thing to save ourselves. That is where grace finds us: “while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).

verseByVerse.quote: "And when I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood, I said to you in your blood, 'Live!' I said to you in your blood, 'Live!' I made you flourish like a plant of the field. And you grew up and became tall and arrived at full adornment. Your breasts were formed, and your hair had grown; yet you were naked and bare.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When everyone else had passed by, God stopped, and his word “Live!” gave the dying child life.

When I passed by you and saw you. Everyone else had passed by and looked away; God stops. He does not wait until she is cleaned up. He speaks to her “in your blood”, and twice: “Live!”

Live! That word does what it says. A baby cannot decide to live; God’s command gives the life it commands. So it is with every believer: “God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:4–5). Jesus said, “the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25). If you are a Christian, this is your story. You did not find God. He passed by, saw you in your blood, and said, “Live!”

Yet you were naked and bare. The rescued baby grows into a young woman under God’s care, alive but not yet clothed, not yet his bride. Life is only the beginning of what God intends.

verseByVerse.quote: "When I passed by you again and saw you, behold, you were at the age for love, and I spread the corner of my garment over you and covered your nakedness; I made my vow to you and entered into a covenant with you, declares the Lord GOD, and you became mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God took the grown girl as his bride in a solemn covenant, and the best words in the verse are the last: “you became mine”.

When I passed by you again. The second passing is not rescue but romance: “you were at the age for love”.

I spread the corner of my garment over you. This was a gesture of marriage. Ruth asked Boaz to do exactly this: “Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer” (Ruth 3:9). It meant protection, provision and belonging (see Weddings and Betrothal).

I made my vow to you and entered into a covenant with you. This is Sinai, where God bound himself to Israel: “you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples” (Exodus 19:5). And then: “and you became mine”.

The Bible’s great marriage. God does not just rescue people and leave them; he takes them as his own. The whole Bible is the story of a marriage, from God’s covenant with Israel to “the marriage of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:7). Paul says of the church, “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word for corner of a garment here is the word translated wings in Ruth 3:9.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I bathed you with water and washed off your blood from you and anointed you with oil. I clothed you also with embroidered cloth and shod you with fine leather. I wrapped you in fine linen and covered you with silk. And I adorned you with ornaments and put bracelets on your wrists and a chain on your neck. And I put a ring on your nose and earrings in your ears and a beautiful crown on your head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The husband washed, anointed and dressed his bride as a queen, and every piece she wore was his gift.

I bathed you with water. He does what no one did at her birth: he washes her, cleans off the blood and anoints her with oil. Everything that was neglected, he supplies. This is what Christ does for his bride: he “gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:25–27).

I clothed you also with embroidered cloth. Embroidered cloth (the ESV notes, “rich fabric”), fine leather sandals, linen, silk, bracelets, a necklace, a nose ring, earrings, a crown: everything a queen would wear. The girl from the field is dressed as royalty.

Every piece a gift. She bought none of it. That is how the gospel describes salvation: “he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). Like the returning prodigal, given “the best robe” and “a ring on his hand” (Luke 15:22), the bride wears what her husband gave.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “fine leather” is the one used for the outer covering of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:14), and its exact meaning is unknown; suggestions include fine goatskin and the hide of a sea creature. Several of her garments, embroidered cloth and fine linen among them, are also tabernacle materials, which may hint that the bride is dressed like God’s own dwelling.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus you were adorned with gold and silver, and your clothing was of fine linen and silk and embroidered cloth. You ate fine flour and honey and oil. You grew exceedingly beautiful and advanced to royalty. And your renown went forth among the nations because of your beauty, for it was perfect through the splendor that I had bestowed on you, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem rose to royal splendour and international fame, but her beauty was borrowed: it was perfect only through the splendour God had put on her.

You ate fine flour and honey and oil. The best food, and then, “you … advanced to royalty”: this is the kingdom of David and Solomon, when Jerusalem became a royal city with a temple of gold.

Your renown went forth among the nations. The nations talked about Jerusalem, and the queen of Sheba came to see (1 Kings 10:1). But the last phrase is the key: “perfect through the splendor that I had bestowed on you”. Her beauty was real, and it was borrowed.

The question the chapter turns on. “What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The moment we forget that our gifts are gifts, we are ready to use them against the Giver.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–34 — You Trusted in Your Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem trusted in the gifts instead of the Giver, and so turned his love into adultery. She “trusted in your beauty” and gave it to every passer-by, making shrines from the clothes he gave her (vv. 15–16). His gold, silver, oil, incense and bread became offerings to idols (vv. 17–19). She even sacrificed her children, his children, because she did not remember the days when she lay in her blood (vv. 20–22). Her shrines rose at every street corner (vv. 23–25). She ran after Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, never satisfied (vv. 26–29), and, unlike any prostitute, paid her lovers to come (vv. 30–34).
verseByVerse.theology: Unfaithfulness to God begins when his gifts are trusted instead of the Giver, and it never satisfies.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you trusted in your beauty and played the whore because of your renown and lavished your whorings on any passerby; your beauty became his. You took some of your garments and made for yourself colorful shrines, and on them played the whore. The like has never been, nor ever shall be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s fall began not with an obvious sin but with trusting her beauty instead of the one who gave it, and then giving that beauty to strangers.

But you trusted in your beauty. After all that grace, one word, “But”, turns the story. This is where it began: trusting the gift instead of the Giver.

Played the whore. The ESV notes that “played the whore” may also be rendered “were unfaithful”, and “whorings” “unfaithfulness”. The language is shocking on purpose. Idolatry is not a harmless religious preference; it is adultery against a husband who rescued you from death. James uses the same picture for Christians who love the world: “You adulterous people!” (James 4:4).

Your beauty became his. The beauty God gave her she gave away to strangers. Every idol Israel worshipped was paid for with God’s gifts.

You took some of your garments. The clothes her husband gave her she cut up to decorate pagan shrines: the very gifts of grace turned into the furnishings of idolatry.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the last sentence of verse 16, “The like has never been, nor ever shall be”, is uncertain; the Hebrew is very compressed. It most likely means that her unfaithfulness was without parallel.

verseByVerse.quote: You also took your beautiful jewels of my gold and of my silver, which I had given you, and made for yourself images of men, and with them played the whore. And you took your embroidered garments to cover them, and set my oil and my incense before them. Also my bread that I gave you— I fed you with fine flour and oil and honey—you set before them for a pleasing aroma; and so it was, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem took the gold, silver, oil, incense and bread God had given her and offered them to idols.

Of my gold and of my silver. Listen to the repeated word “my”: my gold, my silver, my oil, my incense, my bread. God keeps pointing out whose gifts they were. Hosea said the same: “she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil, and who lavished on her silver and gold, which they used for Baal” (Hosea 2:8).

The picture in plain terms. Imagine a wife melting down the jewellery her husband gave her to make statues of other men, dressing them in the clothes he bought, and feeding them meals from his table. That is idolatry.

Our own idols. It is not only ancient. Every gift God gives can be turned into an idol: money, sexuality, intelligence, beauty, family, even ministry. The test is simple: am I using this to love and serve God, or to love and serve something in his place?

verseByVerse.quote: And you took your sons and your daughters, whom you had borne to me, and these you sacrificed to them to be devoured. Were your whorings so small a matter that you slaughtered my children and delivered them up as an offering by fire to them? And in all your abominations and your whorings you did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and bare, wallowing in your blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idolatry ended in the sacrifice of children, God’s own children, and it all grew from forgetting the grace that first rescued her.

You took your sons and your daughters. Now the worst. Judah’s kings had actually burned their children as offerings. Ahaz “even burned his son as an offering” (2 Kings 16:3), and so did Manasseh (2 Kings 21:6). In the Valley of Hinnom they built altars “to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind” (Jeremiah 7:31).

You slaughtered my children. God says “my children”: they had been “borne to me”. Idolatry always ends up sacrificing the next generation. Cultures that worship pleasure, success or self still sacrifice children on those altars, sometimes literally, often in quieter ways.

You did not remember the days of your youth. Here is the root of it all. She forgot where she came from: the field, the blood, the voice that said “Live!” Moses had warned: “lest, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them … then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 8:12, 14).

Remembering grace. The cure for unfaithfulness is remembering grace. Christians gather around the Lord’s Table for exactly this reason: to remember. And the Spirit, who pours God’s love into believers’ hearts (Romans 5:5), keeps that memory alive and turns it into love for the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after all your wickedness (woe, woe to you! declares the Lord GOD), you built yourself a vaulted chamber and made yourself a lofty place in every square. At the head of every street you built your lofty place and made your beauty an abomination, offering yourself to any passerby and multiplying your whoring.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What once was hidden is now flaunted: Jerusalem builds her shrines on every street corner.

A lofty place in every square. The idolatry is no longer hidden. Shrines stand “in every square” and “at the head of every street”. What once would have been done in secret is now done in public, without shame. That is how sin progresses: first it is hidden (8:12), then tolerated, then celebrated on every street corner.

Woe, woe to you! God’s cry in the middle of the charge is a cry of grief as well as judgment.

Uncertain wording. The words translated “vaulted chamber” and “lofty place” are uncertain. They seem to mean a raised mound or platform, perhaps a shrine for idol worship or a place of prostitution, built where everyone passed. Either way the point is that her unfaithfulness was public and everywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: You also played the whore with the Egyptians, your lustful neighbors, multiplying your whoring, to provoke me to anger. Behold, therefore, I stretched out my hand against you and diminished your allotted portion and delivered you to the greed of your enemies, the daughters of the Philistines, who were ashamed of your lewd behavior. You played the whore also with the Assyrians, because you were not satisfied; yes, you played the whore with them, and still you were not satisfied. You multiplied your whoring also with the trading land of Chaldea, and even with this you were not satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s alliances with Egypt, Assyria and Babylon were adultery too, and like every idol, none of them could satisfy her.

You also played the whore with the Egyptians. Now the unfaithfulness turns political. Each time, instead of trusting God, Judah ran to a superpower for protection, and took on its gods as part of the deal.

Who were ashamed of your lewd behavior. Even the pagan Philistines were ashamed. When God’s people behave worse than the world, the world notices.

You were not satisfied. Three times: “not satisfied”. That is the nature of every idol: it promises fulfilment and leaves you hungrier. Each new lover is a little more exciting and a little less satisfying.

Only the true Husband satisfies. Jesus said at a well to a woman who had had five husbands, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (John 4:13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: "How sick is your heart, declares the Lord GOD, because you did all these things, the deeds of a brazen prostitute, building your vaulted chamber at the head of every street, and making your lofty place in every square. Yet you were not like a prostitute, because you scorned payment. Adulterous wife, who receives strangers instead of her husband! Men give gifts to all prostitutes, but you gave your gifts to all your lovers, bribing them to come to you from every side with your whorings. So you were different from other women in your whorings. No one solicited you to play the whore, and you gave payment, while no payment was given to you; therefore you were different.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem was worse than a prostitute: she paid her lovers, and so paid for her own ruin, while God would one day pay for his bride.

How sick is your heart. The diagnosis goes to the heart; the outward deeds come from within.

You gave payment. A humiliating twist. A prostitute at least gets paid; Jerusalem paid her lovers. She sent tribute to Egypt and Assyria, bribing them to come. “Ephraim has hired lovers”, Hosea said (Hosea 8:9). That is what idolatry does: it makes us pay for our own ruin, spending money, time, health and relationships on things that give us nothing back.

God paid for his bride. Set it against the gospel. God’s people paid their lovers; God paid for his bride. Hosea was told to buy back his unfaithful wife: “So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver” (Hosea 3:2). Christ bought his church at an infinitely higher price, “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that another way of reading the Hebrew vowels in verse 30 gives “How I am filled with anger against you” instead of “How sick is your heart”. Either reading fits the passage: the one names her disease, the other God’s response to it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lovers Jerusalem courted will become the instruments of her judgment, and God’s wrath will run its course. Because of her idols and the blood of her children, God will gather all her lovers against her and judge her as an adulteress and a murderer is judged (vv. 35–38). They will tear down her shrines, strip her of all he gave her, and burn her houses: the picture of an adulteress’s punishment becomes the reality of a city besieged and burned (vv. 39–41). Then God’s jealous anger will be satisfied and end, for she did not remember the days of her youth (vv. 42–43).
verseByVerse.theology: God's jealous love will not overlook covenant betrayal; the very powers she courted become the instruments of her judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, O prostitute, hear the word of the LORD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Because your lust was poured out and your nakedness uncovered in your whorings with your lovers, and with all your abominable idols, and because of the blood of your children that you gave to them, therefore, behold, I will gather all your lovers with whom you took pleasure, all those you loved and all those you hated. I will gather them against you from every side and will uncover your nakedness to them, that they may see all your nakedness. And I will judge you as women who commit adultery and shed blood are judged, and bring upon you the blood of wrath and jealousy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment fits the sin: the lovers Jerusalem courted will be gathered against her, and she will be judged as an adulteress and a murderer.

Because of the blood of your children. The charges are summed up: unfaithfulness, idols, and the blood of her children.

I will gather all your lovers. The nations she courted will be gathered against her. Babylon, whom she invited in, will be the army at her walls, and the shame she displayed to them will be exposed by them. The things we run to instead of God often become the very things that turn on us.

The blood of wrath and jealousy. Under the law, adultery and murder were capital crimes (Leviticus 20:10; Numbers 35:31), and Jerusalem was guilty of both. The judgment comes with jealousy, the burning anger of a wronged husband. God’s wrath is not cold; it is the wrath of betrayed love.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “lust” in verse 36 is unusual. Some take it to mean “copper”, that is, money poured out, which would fit the payments to her lovers in verses 31–34. Either way, she poured herself out on her lovers.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give you into their hands, and they shall throw down your vaulted chamber and break down your lofty places. They shall strip you of your clothes and take your beautiful jewels and leave you naked and bare. They shall bring up a crowd against you, and they shall stone you and cut you to pieces with their swords. And they shall burn your houses and execute judgments upon you in the sight of many women. I will make you stop playing the whore, and you shall also give payment no more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God gave is taken back, and the city that played the adulteress is besieged, broken and burned; these verses picture God’s judgment on a city, never a pattern for any husband.

Leave you naked and bare. The clothes and jewels are gone, and she is left “naked and bare”, the very words used of her as a girl before God covered her (v. 7). When grace is despised, a person ends up back where grace first found them.

In the sight of many women. The picture of an adulteress stoned becomes the reality of a city besieged, broken and burned, “in the sight of many women”, in front of all the nations. And the idolatry will stop, because the city that practised it will be gone.

Does this chapter excuse a man who shames or hurts his wife? Never. These verses describe God’s just judgment on a city for centuries of idolatry and bloodshed, carried out by an invading army; they are not a pattern for any marriage. The only pattern Scripture gives husbands is Christ, who “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), and it forbids harshness (Colossians 3:19). This commentary holds that abuse is never to be tolerated. Anyone being abused should seek safety at once and tell someone who can help; abuse must be reported, and the church must stand with the one harmed. Leaving to escape abuse is not the separation Scripture forbids. Women who have been hurt may find these verses painful to read; the God of this chapter is the one who stopped for the abandoned girl and said, “Live!”

verseByVerse.quote: So will I satisfy my wrath on you, and my jealousy shall depart from you. I will be calm and will no more be angry. Because you have not remembered the days of your youth, but have enraged me with all these things, therefore, behold, I have returned your deeds upon your head, declares the Lord GOD. Have you not committed lewdness in addition to all your abominations?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s anger is real, and it has an end: when justice is done it is satisfied, and for his people it was satisfied in Christ.

I will be calm and will no more be angry. God’s wrath does not simmer for ever. When justice has been done, it is satisfied.

Wrath satisfied in Christ. That is the heart of the gospel. God’s wrath against the sin of his people did not simply fade away. It was satisfied, but it fell on Christ and not on them: “whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25). A propitiation is a sacrifice that bears God’s anger and so turns it away. So God can say to his people, as he said through Isaiah, “I have sworn that I will not be angry with you, and will not rebuke you” (Isaiah 54:9).

You have not remembered the days of your youth. Forgetfulness is named as the root of it all a second time (v. 22). The best defence against drifting from God is a daily, grateful memory of what he has done.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem, who looked down on her sisters, has become worse than both, and will receive mercy only alongside them. “Like mother, like daughter”: she has gone back to her pagan roots, and her sisters are Samaria to the north and Sodom to the south (vv. 44–47). Sodom’s guilt was pride, plenty and ease without help for the poor, and an abomination before God, yet Jerusalem has done worse (vv. 48–50) and made her sisters look righteous by comparison (vv. 51–52). God will restore the fortunes of all three together, so that Jerusalem bears her shame (vv. 53–55); the city that once used Sodom as a byword is now a byword herself (vv. 56–58).
verseByVerse.theology: The self-righteous who despise notorious sinners may be more guilty than they, and God's mercy reaches farther than they imagine.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, everyone who uses proverbs will use this proverb about you: 'Like mother, like daughter.' You are the daughter of your mother, who loathed her husband and her children; and you are the sister of your sisters, who loathed their husbands and their children. Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite. And your elder sister is Samaria, who lived with her daughters to the north of you; and your younger sister, who lived to the south of you, is Sodom with her daughters. Not only did you walk in their ways and do according to their abominations; within a very little time you were more corrupt than they in all your ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem has gone back to her pagan roots, and is now worse than the sisters she despised.

Like mother, like daughter. A new picture. Jerusalem has become exactly like the pagan family she came from, a mother who loathed her husband and children. For all God’s grace, she went back to her roots.

Your elder sister is Samaria. Two sisters: Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom, destroyed by Assyria for its idolatry; and Sodom, the byword for wickedness, destroyed by fire. The people of Jerusalem looked down on both. “Elder” and “younger” probably mean larger and smaller, as the Hebrew can.

More corrupt than they. God says: you are worse than both, and it did not take you long.

verseByVerse.quote: As I live, declares the Lord GOD, your sister Sodom and her daughters have not done as you and your daughters have done. Behold, this was the guilt of your sister Sodom: she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy. They were haughty and did an abomination before me. So I removed them, when I saw it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sodom’s sin was pride, plenty and ease that ignored the poor, together with an abomination before God, and Jerusalem, with far more light, has done worse.

Your sister Sodom. With an oath God declares that Sodom was not as bad as Jerusalem. That would have stunned every hearer. Jerusalem had the law, the temple, the prophets and the covenant, and sinned anyway. The more light God has given you, the more serious it is to sin against it (Matthew 11:23–24).

This was the guilt of your sister Sodom. Many people have never noticed this description: “pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy”. Alongside it stands “They were haughty and did an abomination before me”. Genesis records the men of Sodom surrounding Lot’s house to abuse his guests (Genesis 19:4–5), and Jude says they “indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire” (Jude 7). Scripture holds both together: the sexual abomination and the proud, comfortable neglect of the poor. We must not point to one in order to play down the other.

A word for prosperous churches. Amos pictured the same people: “Woe to those who lie on beds of ivory … but are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph!” (Amos 6:4, 6). Paul told Timothy to charge the rich “not to be haughty” but “to be generous and ready to share” (1 Timothy 6:17–18). Before we condemn Sodom, we should ask whether its description fits us.

Where Christians differ: some read verse 49 as showing that Sodom’s sin was only injustice and pride, not sexual sin, and so set Genesis 19 aside in the debate over same-sex relationships. This commentary’s view: the historic view, held with compassion. Verse 50 adds “did an abomination”, the word Leviticus uses for sexual sin (Leviticus 18:22), and Jude 7 names sexual immorality plainly; the sexual ethic itself rests on creation, not on these verses alone. Both sins are real, and both are forgiven to all who come to Christ (1 Corinthians 6:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Samaria has not committed half your sins. You have committed more abominations than they, and have made your sisters appear righteous by all the abominations that you have committed. Bear your disgrace, you also, for you have intervened on behalf of your sisters. Because of your sins in which you acted more abominably than they, they are more in the right than you. So be ashamed, you also, and bear your disgrace, for you have made your sisters appear righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Next to Jerusalem, Samaria and Sodom look righteous, so she must bear her own disgrace instead of pointing at others.

You have made your sisters appear righteous. A devastating reversal for a people who defined themselves by being better than others.

Bear your disgrace. Twice: “bear your disgrace”. Jerusalem must accept her shame instead of pointing at others.

Measuring ourselves by others. Religious people are always tempted to measure themselves against the worst sinners they can find. The Pharisee prayed, “God, I thank you that I am not like other men” (Luke 18:11). Paul says, “in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things” (Romans 2:1). The measure is not other people. It is God.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will restore their fortunes, both the fortunes of Sodom and her daughters, and the fortunes of Samaria and her daughters, and I will restore your own fortunes in their midst, that you may bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all that you have done, becoming a consolation to them. As for your sisters, Sodom and her daughters shall return to their former state, and Samaria and her daughters shall return to their former state, and you and your daughters shall return to your former state.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Astonishingly, God will restore Sodom and Samaria as well as Jerusalem, and Jerusalem will be restored among them, not above them.

I will restore their fortunes. No one could have expected this. God will restore not only Jerusalem, but Sodom and Samaria too: the destroyed city and the fallen northern kingdom are included in the promise of mercy.

In their midst. Jerusalem is placed among them, not above them. When God restores her, it will not be as the superior sister but as one sinner among others, humbled and receiving the same mercy.

Mercy farther than pride imagined. How this will be fulfilled is not spelled out, but the direction is clear: God’s mercy reaches farther than Jerusalem’s pride could imagine, to the despised and the destroyed. The New Testament gives a foretaste when “Samaria had received the word of God” (Acts 8:14), and when the gospel went out to the nations.

Will Sodom be saved? Sodom suffered “a punishment of eternal fire” (Jude 7), and this verse does not reverse that. It is said to shame Jerusalem: if God would restore even Sodom, how great is the mercy shown to Judah. Some see its fulfilment in the nations, once like Sodom, brought into God’s people through the gospel; it does not teach universal salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: Was not your sister Sodom a byword in your mouth in the day of your pride, before your wickedness was uncovered? Now you have become an object of reproach for the daughters of Syria and all those around her, and for the daughters of the Philistines, those all around who despise you. You bear the penalty of your lewdness and your abominations, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city that once used Sodom as a byword in her pride has become a byword herself.

In the day of your pride. Jerusalem used to say “Sodom” as a byword, a joke, an insult. Now her own wickedness has been uncovered, and the neighbours mock her.

Humility is safer. The people we sneer at in our pride may one day watch our own sins exposed. Humility is always safer than contempt.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “of Edom” for “of Syria”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bride broke the covenant, but the husband will keep it, and he will pay for her sin himself. God will deal with Jerusalem as she has done, yet he will remember his covenant made in the days of her youth and establish an everlasting covenant (vv. 59–60). Then at last she will remember her ways and be ashamed, receiving the sisters she despised as daughters (v. 61). God will establish his covenant, and she will never again open her mouth to boast or excuse herself, “when I atone for you for all that you have done” (vv. 62–63). The darkest chapter in Ezekiel ends in pure grace.
verseByVerse.theology: Where the bride failed completely, the Husband keeps the covenant and makes atonement himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: I will deal with you as you have done, you who have despised the oath in breaking the covenant, yet I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish for you an everlasting covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem forgot and broke the covenant, but God will remember it and establish an everlasting covenant that does not depend on her.

I will deal with you as you have done. Justice first. She despised the oath and broke the covenant, and God will deal with her accordingly.

Yet I will remember my covenant with you. Here is the turn of the whole chapter. Twice Jerusalem did not remember the days of her youth (vv. 22, 43). Now God says he will remember. She forgot; he remembers. Her faithfulness failed; his does not.

I will establish for you an everlasting covenant. He will do more than restore the old covenant. He will make one that cannot be broken because it does not depend on her. Jeremiah heard the same promise: “I will make with them an everlasting covenant, that I will not turn away from doing good to them. And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me” (Jeremiah 32:40).

The new covenant in my blood. That covenant was sealed on the night Jesus said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20), and “the God of peace … brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus … by the blood of the eternal covenant” (Hebrews 13:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed when you take your sisters, both your elder and your younger, and I give them to you as daughters, but not on account of the covenant with you. I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall know that I am the LORD, that you may remember and be confounded, and never open your mouth again because of your shame, when I atone for you for all that you have done, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God atones for his bride, she will at last remember, be ashamed and fall silent before such grace.

Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed. When grace comes, memory finally works. This is not the shame of being caught, but the healthy shame of seeing clearly what you were and what God has done.

I give them to you as daughters. The sisters she despised will be given to her as daughters, brought into the family of God through her.

When I atone for you. The last line of this long, dark chapter is pure gospel: “when I atone for you for all that you have done”. Not when you atone. When I atone. The husband pays for the adultery of the bride.

Never open your mouth again. The result is silence, not of despair but of wonder: no excuses, no boasting, no comparing yourself with others. So “every mouth may be stopped” before God (Romans 3:19), and every sinner who is saved is saved “by grace … not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Where the chapter leaves us. A foundling picked up out of her blood, a queen who betrayed her rescuer, and a husband who, instead of divorcing her, makes atonement for her himself. The story ends where the Bible ends: “the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “but not on account of the covenant with you” (v. 61) may be read “not apart from the covenant with you”. On the first reading the sisters are given by sheer grace, not because of anything in the old covenant; on the second they come in through the covenant God makes with her. Either way, the gift is God’s.

16.title: The Foundling Bride
16.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 15 pictured Jerusalem as a useless vine fit only for the fire, “because they have acted faithlessly” (15:8). Chapter 16, the longest in the book, tells the story behind that verdict: the whole history of Jerusalem, from birth to judgment and beyond, as the story of a marriage.

The message. Everything Jerusalem had was grace: she was an abandoned baby whom God brought to life, married and made a queen. Her idolatry was not a harmless religious choice but the betrayal of that love by a bride who forgot where she came from, and it will bring the judgment she has earned. Yet the last word belongs to the husband. He will remember his covenant, make an everlasting one and atone for her himself, so that she is silenced, not by shame alone, but by grace.

Why it was said. Jerusalem was proud of her holy history and looked down on Samaria and Sodom, and the exiles still trusted that God would never give up his city (see the introduction). Ezekiel must make them see their idolatry from God’s side. The language is deliberately shocking, and it is about a city’s worship, never a licence for violence against any woman (see the note on vv. 39–41).

How the chapter makes its case. Grace: a Canaanite baby is thrown into a field at birth, and God passes by and says “Live!” (vv. 1–7); he takes her in covenant, “and you became mine”, then washes, clothes and crowns her until her beauty is famous, all of it his gift (vv. 8–14). Betrayal: she trusts in her beauty, turns his gifts into idols, sacrifices her children and even pays her foreign lovers, because she does not remember the days of her youth (vv. 15–34). Judgment: the lovers she courted will strip and destroy her, until God’s wrath is satisfied (vv. 35–43). Comparison: she has become worse than her sisters Samaria and Sodom, yet God will restore all three, to her shame (vv. 44–58). Covenant: he will remember his covenant, establish an everlasting covenant and atone for all she has done (vv. 59–63).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The promise of an everlasting covenant and of God himself making atonement is fulfilled on the night Jesus said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The pattern is the marriage: Christ is the husband who “loved the church and gave himself up for her”, washing her and presenting her “in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:25–27). The story ends where the Bible ends, with “the holy city, new Jerusalem … prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2).

For us. Every Christian is that foundling, found “in your blood” and told to live. Remember it daily, for forgetting grace is where unfaithfulness begins; hold every gift as his, not as a rival to him; and never look down on others as Jerusalem looked down on Sodom. When you see your sin, run to the husband who has already atoned for it.
16.theology:
God's love is sovereign and undeserved: he chooses and gives life to the helpless and unlovely (vv. 3-8; Deut 7:7-8; Eph 2:1-5).

Everything God's people have is his gift; beauty and honour are bestowed, not earned (vv. 9-14; 1 Cor 4:7).

Idolatry is spiritual adultery, unfaithfulness to the God who has bound himself to his people; it begins with trusting the gifts instead of the Giver, uses God's gifts for other gods, and never satisfies (vv. 15-34; Hos 2:8; Jas 4:4; John 4:13-14).

Forgetting grace is the root of unfaithfulness (vv. 22, 43; Deut 8:11-14).

Greater privilege brings greater guilt; the proud who despise notorious sinners may be worse than they (vv. 47-52; Luke 18:11; Rom 2:1).

Sodom's sin included both sexual abomination and proud, comfortable neglect of the poor (vv. 49-50; Gen 19:4-5; Jude 7).

God’s wrath is real, and it ends when justice has been done; for his people, justice was done when Christ bore that wrath (v. 42; Rom 3:25).

Where the bride failed, the husband remembers his covenant, establishes an everlasting covenant and makes atonement himself, silencing all boasting (vv. 60-63; Jer 32:40; Luke 22:20; Heb 13:20; Rom 3:19; Eph 2:8-9).

Christ is the Bridegroom who cleanses, clothes and presents his bride (Eph 5:25-27; Rev 19:7-8; 21:2).
16.examples:
The chapter's pictures move from grace to betrayal and back to grace. A newborn is left in a field with the cord still uncut, until a voice says Live! to the baby in her blood. Later a cloak is spread over the grown young woman, and God says, you became mine.

Then the queen melts down her wedding jewellery to make statues of other men, and even pays the lovers who ruin her. Her sister Sodom's sins (pride, full stomachs, easy lives and closed hands) look mild beside her own.

Yet the last picture is the husband who, instead of divorcing her, atones for her himself, and a mouth that never opens again except in wonder.

keyVerse.quote: yet I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish for you an everlasting covenant.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the longest chapter in Ezekiel. Twice Jerusalem “did not remember” the grace that saved her (vv. 22, 43); now God says he will remember. After sixty verses of unfaithfulness, the future rests not on the bride’s faithfulness but on the husband’s, and the everlasting covenant he promises is the new covenant sealed in Christ’s blood.

16.reflection:
God found Jerusalem “in your blood” and said, “Live!” (v. 6). How does this picture describe what God has done for every Christian (Ephesians 2:1–5)? What difference does it make to remember it?

Jerusalem’s fall began when she “trusted in your beauty” (v. 15) and used God’s gifts for other gods (vv. 17–19). Which of God’s good gifts to you are most easily turned into idols, and how can you tell when it is happening?

God says Sodom’s guilt included “pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease” without help for the poor (v. 49), and that Jerusalem was worse. How does this chapter challenge the way we look at people we consider worse sinners than ourselves?

The chapter ends with God saying, “I atone for you for all that you have done” (v. 63). How does Christ fulfil this, and why does grace like this silence our boasting and excuses?
