verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — A Riddle of Two Eagles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A vine that has everything it needs and still reaches for more will be torn up. Ezekiel is told to put a riddle to the exiles (vv. 1–2). A great eagle snaps off the top of a cedar in Lebanon and carries it to a city of merchants, then plants a native seed by abundant waters, where it grows into a low spreading vine turned toward him (vv. 3–6). When a second great eagle appears, the vine bends its roots toward him, though it was already planted in good soil (vv. 7–8). Twice God asks, “Will it thrive?” The answer is no: it will be pulled up with little effort and will wither when the east wind strikes (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: A vine planted in safety that turns away from its keeper to seek other help will wither.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, propound a riddle, and speak a parable to the house of Israel; say, Thus says the Lord GOD: A great eagle with great wings and long pinions, rich in plumage of many colors, came to Lebanon and took the top of the cedar. He broke off the topmost of its young twigs and carried it to a land of trade and set it in a city of merchants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God puts the fall of Jerusalem’s king into a riddle: a great empire swoops down and carries off the top of David’s royal tree to a foreign city.

Propound a riddle, and speak a parable. A story makes people work, and a truth you work out for yourself sticks. Jesus often taught the same way (Mark 4:33–34).

A great eagle with great wings. Picture a magnificent eagle swooping on the forests of Lebanon, snapping off the highest shoot of a cedar and carrying it away to a trading city.

Took the top of the cedar. The cedar was a royal tree: Solomon’s palace was built of it (1 Kings 7:2). The top shoot is the king, the eagle is a great empire, and the city of merchants is Babylon, as God will say plainly in v. 12. Ezekiel’s hearers were themselves part of the shoot that had been carried away.
verseByVerse.note: The eagle was a familiar picture of a conquering king; Jeremiah too says an invader will fly swiftly like an eagle (Jer 48:40).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he took of the seed of the land and planted it in fertile soil. He placed it beside abundant waters. He set it like a willow twig, and it sprouted and became a low spreading vine, and its branches turned toward him, and its roots remained where it stood. So it became a vine and produced branches and put out boughs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Babylon set up a smaller, dependent kingdom in Judah under Zedekiah: not glorious, but alive and rooted, God’s way for the nation to survive.

He took of the seed of the land. The eagle does not destroy the land. He plants a native seed (the ESV notes, “in a field of seed”) in fertile soil beside abundant waters.

A low spreading vine. Not a towering cedar but a low vine, its branches turned toward the eagle who planted it. This is Judah under Zedekiah: smaller and dependent on Babylon, but alive, rooted and fruitful. It was a gift. God had provided a way for the nation to survive through humble submission, and Jeremiah urged exactly that (Jeremiah 27:12).

A lower place. A low vine that stays rooted is better than a tall tree torn up. For anyone living in a reduced situation after a loss, a lower place accepted from God’s hand is still a place where life can grow.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “willow twig” occurs only here in the Old Testament. Most take it as a kind of willow, a tree that roots easily by water, but the exact plant is not known. The sense is plain either way: the shoot was set where it could hardly fail to grow.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there was another great eagle with great wings and much plumage, and behold, this vine bent its roots toward him and shot forth its branches toward him from the bed where it was planted, that he might water it. It had been planted on good soil by abundant waters, that it might produce branches and bear fruit and become a noble vine. "Say, Thus says the Lord GOD: Will it thrive? Will he not pull up its roots and cut off its fruit, so that it withers, so that all its fresh sprouting leaves wither? It will not take a strong arm or many people to pull it from its roots. Behold, it is planted; will it thrive? Will it not utterly wither when the east wind strikes it—wither away on the bed where it sprouted?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vine that had all it needed bent its roots toward a second eagle, and so it will be torn up and wither where it stands.

There was another great eagle. The vine does something unnatural: it bends its roots toward him. Plants do not move their roots. The picture is of a king twisting away from where he was planted, looking for something better. The second eagle is Egypt (v. 15).

Planted on good soil by abundant waters. It needed nothing more. It was restless not because it lacked anything but because it was ungrateful, which is often how sin works: planted by God with all we need, we still bend our roots toward something that promises more.

Will it thrive? Asked twice, and the answer is no. A vine that has loosened its own roots is easy to pull out (“It will not take a strong arm”), and the hot east wind from the desert will dry it up in the very bed where it grew. For Judah, that wind blew from Babylon.

Where to put down roots. Jesus, “the true vine”, says the reverse of Zedekiah’s restlessness: “Abide in me” (John 15:1, 4). The branch that stays joined to him bears fruit; the one that reaches elsewhere withers (John 15:5–6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Breaking an oath sworn in God’s name is breaking faith with God, and no ally can rescue the one who does it. God explains the riddle: the king of Babylon took Jerusalem’s king and princes and made one of the royal family swear a covenant, so that the kingdom would stay humble and survive (vv. 11–14). But that king sent to Egypt for horses and an army; he will die in Babylon, and Pharaoh will not help him (vv. 15–18). Then the deepest reason: “it is my oath that he despised, and my covenant that he broke” (v. 19). God himself will net him, bring him to Babylon and judge him there, and his best troops will fall (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Breaking a promise made in God's name is breaking faith with God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me: "Say now to the rebellious house, Do you not know what these things mean? Tell them, behold, the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, and took her king and her princes and brought them to him to Babylon. And he took one of the royal offspring and made a covenant with him, putting him under oath (the chief men of the land he had taken away), that the kingdom might be humble and not lift itself up, and keep his covenant that it might stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God explains the riddle: Nebuchadnezzar took King Jehoiachin to Babylon and set up Zedekiah under oath, so that a humbled Judah could survive.

Do you not know what these things mean? The first eagle is Nebuchadnezzar. The cedar top is King Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon with his officials in 597 BC (see the introduction).

One of the royal offspring. Literally “seed”, as the ESV notes: this is Zedekiah. “And the king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, king in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah” (2 Kings 24:17). And he put him under oath. A covenant here is a treaty between a great king and a lesser one, sealed with an oath.

That the kingdom might be humble. Humility was the path to survival. Had Zedekiah kept his word, Judah would have stood; only pride could bring it down.

verseByVerse.quote: But he rebelled against him by sending his ambassadors to Egypt, that they might give him horses and a large army. Will he thrive? Can one escape who does such things? Can he break the covenant and yet escape? "As I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely in the place where the king dwells who made him king, whose oath he despised, and whose covenant with him he broke, in Babylon he shall die. Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company will not help him in war, when mounds are cast up and siege walls built to cut off many lives. He despised the oath in breaking the covenant, and behold, he gave his hand and did all these things; he shall not escape.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zedekiah broke his sworn word and turned to Egypt for horses and an army, but Egypt will fail him and he will die in Babylon.

But he rebelled against him. The second eagle is Egypt. “And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon” (2 Kings 24:20), trusting Egyptian horses and chariots. Isaiah had warned long before: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses” (Isaiah 31:1).

Pharaoh with his mighty army. Egypt did fail him, as v. 17 foretold. Pharaoh’s army marched out, and then went home (Jeremiah 37:7). Zedekiah was captured and blinded, taken to Babylon in chains and kept in prison till he died there (Jeremiah 52:11), so he died in a land he never saw (12:13).

He gave his hand. He shook on it, a solemn pledge, and broke it. God counts that a serious sin, though the promise was made to a pagan king.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: As I live, surely it is my oath that he despised, and my covenant that he broke. I will return it upon his head. I will spread my net over him, and he shall be taken in my snare, and I will bring him to Babylon and enter into judgment with him there for the treachery he has committed against me. And all the pick of his troops shall fall by the sword, and the survivors shall be scattered to every wind, and you shall know that I am the LORD; I have spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Zedekiah swore in the LORD’s name, his broken treaty was treachery against God himself, and God will catch him in his own net.

It is my oath that he despised. The surprising turn: “my oath… my covenant”. The promise was made to Nebuchadnezzar; how is it God’s? Because Nebuchadnezzar “had made him swear by God” (2 Chronicles 36:13). Zedekiah took an oath in the LORD’s name, so breaking it was breaking faith with the LORD. And God himself had given Judah into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand for a time and told Zedekiah through Jeremiah to bow to it (Jeremiah 27:6–8, 12), so the rebellion defied God’s word as well as a treaty.

I will spread my net over him. The same picture as in 12:13. The king who broke faith with God is caught by God, for the treachery was ultimately “against me”.

The King who kept his word. Zedekiah, the last of David’s line to reign in Jerusalem, despised his oath to save himself. David’s greater Son kept faith with his Father though it cost him everything, “becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8). All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Keeping our word. Christians keep their word, in business, marriage and contracts, even with people who do not share their faith. The godly person “swears to his own hurt and does not change” (Psalm 15:4). Jesus said, “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). A broken promise wrongs more than a person, because God’s name is attached to our word. We keep faith because we belong to the God who has never broken his own (v. 24), and where we have failed, the way back is not excuses but confession to the one who is “faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

What it does not mean. A promise to do what God forbids, such as to keep abuse secret, does not bind; it is undone by repenting of it, not by keeping it. Zedekiah’s oath was lawful, which is why breaking it was treachery.

Textual note. In v. 21 the ESV notes that most manuscripts read “all the fugitives” for “all the pick of his troops”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–24 — A Tender Sprig on a High Mountain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where human kings fail, God himself will plant a King. Taking up the riddle’s own picture, God says that he himself will take a tender sprig from the top of the cedar and plant it on the high mountain of Israel (v. 22). There it will grow into a noble cedar, and birds of every sort will nest in the shade of its branches (v. 23). Then all the trees of the field will learn the lesson of the whole chapter: the LORD brings low the high tree and makes high the low tree, and what he has said, he will do (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Where human kings fail, God himself will plant a lowly King whose kingdom shelters the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: "I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of the cedar and will set it out. I will break off from the topmost of its young twigs a tender one, and I myself will plant it on a high and lofty mountain. On the mountain height of Israel will I plant it, that it may bear branches and produce fruit and become a noble cedar. And under it will dwell every kind of bird; in the shade of its branches birds of every sort will nest. And all the trees of the field shall know that I am the LORD; I bring low the high tree, and make high the low tree, dry up the green tree, and make the dry tree flourish. I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where every king has failed, God himself will plant a tender shoot from David’s line on his holy mountain, and it will grow into a great tree that shelters the nations.

I myself will take a sprig. Now it is not an eagle but God, and twice he says “I myself”. The kings of Babylon and Egypt planted and uprooted; now God will plant.

A tender one. A tender twig from the top of David’s cedar, small and fragile, planted on a high mountain: this is a promise of a future King from David’s line. Isaiah used the same picture: “There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1); and of the Servant, “he grew up before him like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground” (Isaiah 53:2). The New Testament does not quote these verses, but it applies the same family of promises, the shoot and root of Jesse and the righteous Branch, to Jesus (Romans 15:12, quoting Isaiah 11:10; compare Jeremiah 23:5). The “high and lofty mountain” is most likely Zion, where God sets his King (Psalm 2:6).

Every kind of bird. The twig becomes “a noble cedar”, and birds of every sort shelter in it: a picture of the nations. Jesus described the kingdom of God in almost the same words: a tiny mustard seed that “grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade” (Mark 4:32).

Christ is that sprig. Laid in a manger (Luke 2:7), from a family of no importance, he was a tender shoot from the cut-down stump of David’s line, and his kingdom has become a tree where people of every nation find rest.

I bring low the high tree, and make high the low tree. This is the pattern of God’s kingdom throughout Scripture. Hannah sang, “he brings low and he exalts” (1 Samuel 2:7). Mary sang, “he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52). Proud kings are cut down; a humble twig becomes a cedar.

Make the dry tree flourish. That is good news for the low, the dry and the overlooked, and a warning to the high and green. And the chapter ends with God’s signature: “I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it.”
verseByVerse.note: Ancient Jewish readers also took the sprig as the Messiah: the Targum, the old Aramaic paraphrase, speaks here of a child from the house of David.

17.title: Two Eagles and a Tender Sprig
17.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 12 to 24 press home one hard truth: Jerusalem will fall. Now Ezekiel turns to a riddle of eagles, a cedar and a vine, aimed at the hope many exiles still clung to, King Zedekiah in Jerusalem and his secret dealings with Egypt.

The message. God holds kings and empires in his hand, and a king who breaks an oath sworn in God’s name will not escape. Zedekiah could have lived as a humble vine under Babylon, but he reached for Egypt, and he will die in Babylon. Yet God has not finished with David’s line: he himself will plant a tender shoot from it on the mountain of Israel, and it will become a great cedar where every kind of bird finds shelter. The LORD brings low the high and lifts up the low.

Why it was said. The exiles hoped that Zedekiah’s rebellion, backed by Pharaoh, would break Babylon’s grip and bring them home soon (see the introduction). Ezekiel tells them the plan is doomed, and why: not only bad politics, but broken faith with God. Then he gives them a hope that does not hang on any scheming king.

How the chapter makes its case. First the riddle (vv. 1–10): a great eagle carries off the top of a cedar and plants a low vine that does well, until it bends its roots toward a second eagle. Then the explanation (vv. 11–21): Nebuchadnezzar set Zedekiah on the throne under oath, Zedekiah sent to Egypt for horses, and because the oath was sworn by the LORD, it is God’s covenant he broke and God’s net that will catch him. Finally the riddle becomes a promise (vv. 22–24): God himself will plant a tender sprig on a high mountain, and all the trees will know that he brings low the high tree and makes high the low.

Where it leads. To Christ by promise. The tender sprig from the top of David’s cedar belongs with Isaiah’s shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1) and Jeremiah’s righteous Branch (Jeremiah 23:5), promises the New Testament applies to Jesus. Born to a family of no importance, he is the low tree God made high, and his kingdom has grown like his mustard seed, with birds nesting in its shade (Mark 4:32). And where Zedekiah despised his oath to save himself, David’s greater Son kept faith with his Father to the cross.

For us. God hears the promises we make, and sees the “Egypts” we turn to when we are restless with the place he has planted us. The way home is not a better scheme but humble trust in the King God has planted, under whose shade the weary of every nation find rest.
17.theology:
God rules the rise and fall of empires and kings (vv. 3-4, 12).

Humble submission to God's appointed circumstances can be the path to life; pride and restless seeking of other help lead to ruin (vv. 5-10, 14-15).

A promise sworn in God's name binds before God, even when made to unbelievers (vv. 16-19; 2 Chr 36:13; Ps 15:4; Matt 5:37).

God will himself raise up a humble King from David's line, whose kingdom shelters the nations (vv. 22-23; Isa 11:1; 53:2; Mark 4:30-32).

God brings low the proud and exalts the lowly (v. 24; 1 Sam 2:7-8; Luke 1:52).
17.examples:
An eagle snaps off the top of a cedar, and a low vine that was alive and safe is not content, but tries to bend its roots toward a different eagle. A handshake with a pagan king turns out to be what God calls my oath.

Then the riddle ends in hope: a tender twig planted by God himself on a mountain, with birds of every sort nesting in its shade.

keyVerse.quote: And all the trees of the field shall know that I am the LORD; I bring low the high tree, and make high the low tree, dry up the green tree, and make the dry tree flourish. I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers up the whole chapter. Zedekiah, the high tree that reached for Egypt, is brought low; the tender sprig God plants is made high. It is the pattern of God’s kingdom from Hannah’s song to Mary’s, and it finds its fullest form in Christ, the shoot from a cut-down stump whom God has highly exalted.

17.reflection:
The vine in vv. 5–8 was “planted on good soil by abundant waters”, yet it bent its roots toward another eagle. Where are you tempted to be restless with the place God has planted you, and what “Egypt” promises you more?

God calls Zedekiah’s treaty with a pagan king “my oath” and “my covenant” (v. 19). What does this teach about the promises Christians make at work, in marriage and in church? How do we put things right when we have broken our word?

Verse 24 says the LORD brings low the high tree and makes high the low tree. Where have you seen this pattern in Scripture, in history or in your own life? Why is it both a comfort and a warning?

The tender sprig becomes a cedar where every kind of bird finds shelter (vv. 22–23). How does Jesus fulfil this picture, and what does it mean for the kind of welcome your church gives to people of every background?

18.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"What do you mean by repeating this proverb concerning the land of Israel, 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge'?<sup>3</sup>As I live, declares the Lord GOD, this proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel.<sup>4</sup>Behold, all souls are mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine: the soul who sins shall die.<sup>5</sup>"If a man is righteous and does what is just and right—<sup>6</sup>if he does not eat upon the mountains or lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, does not defile his neighbor's wife or approach a woman in her time of menstrual impurity,<sup>7</sup>does not oppress anyone, but restores to the debtor his pledge, commits no robbery, gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment,<sup>8</sup>does not lend at interest or take any profit, withholds his hand from injustice, executes true justice between man and man,<sup>9</sup>walks in my statutes, and keeps my rules by acting faithfully—he is righteous; he shall surely live, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>10</sup>"If he fathers a son who is violent, a shedder of blood, who does any of these things<sup>11</sup>(though he himself did none of these things), who even eats upon the mountains, defiles his neighbor's wife,<sup>12</sup>oppresses the poor and needy, commits robbery, does not restore the pledge, lifts up his eyes to the idols, commits abomination,<sup>13</sup>lends at interest, and takes profit; shall he then live? He shall not live. He has done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon himself.<sup>14</sup>"Now suppose this man fathers a son who sees all the sins that his father has done; he sees, and does not do likewise:<sup>15</sup>he does not eat upon the mountains or lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, does not defile his neighbor's wife,<sup>16</sup>does not oppress anyone, exacts no pledge, commits no robbery, but gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment,<sup>17</sup>withholds his hand from iniquity, takes no interest or profit, obeys my rules, and walks in my statutes; he shall not die for his father's iniquity; he shall surely live.<sup>18</sup>As for his father, because he practiced extortion, robbed his brother, and did what is not good among his people, behold, he shall die for his iniquity.<sup>19</sup>"Yet you say, 'Why should not the son suffer for the iniquity of the father?' When the son has done what is just and right, and has been careful to observe all my statutes, he shall surely live.<sup>20</sup>The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself.<sup>21</sup>"But if a wicked person turns away from all his sins that he has committed and keeps all my statutes and does what is just and right, he shall surely live; he shall not die.<sup>22</sup>None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him; for the righteousness that he has done he shall live.<sup>23</sup>Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?<sup>24</sup>But when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice and does the same abominations that the wicked person does, shall he live? None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered; for the treachery of which he is guilty and the sin he has committed, for them he shall die.<sup>25</sup>"Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' Hear now, O house of Israel: Is my way not just? Is it not your ways that are not just?<sup>26</sup>When a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice, he shall die for it; for the injustice that he has done he shall die.<sup>27</sup>Again, when a wicked person turns away from the wickedness he has committed and does what is just and right, he shall save his life.<sup>28</sup>Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die.<sup>29</sup>Yet the house of Israel says, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' O house of Israel, are my ways not just? Is it not your ways that are not just?<sup>30</sup>"Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, declares the Lord GOD. Repent and turn from all your transgressions, lest iniquity be your ruin.<sup>31</sup>Cast away from you all the transgressions that you have committed, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?<sup>32</sup>For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Soul Who Sins Shall Die
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one is punished for another’s sin, and no one is trapped by it, because every person belongs to God. The exiles have a proverb that blames their fathers for their troubles: the fathers ate the sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge (vv. 1–2). God bans it with an oath (v. 3) and lays down the foundation of the whole chapter: “all souls are mine”, father and son alike, and “the soul who sins shall die” (v. 4). Each person stands before God for himself, which is both sobering and freeing.
verseByVerse.theology: Every person belongs to God and answers to him for his own life; no one can hide behind the sins of others.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "What do you mean by repeating this proverb concerning the land of Israel, 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exiles blamed their parents for their troubles with a popular proverb, using a half-truth to excuse themselves and accuse God.

The fathers have eaten sour grapes. Imagine biting into an unripe grape so sour that it sets your teeth on edge; now imagine your father ate it and your teeth are the ones aching. The exiles were saying: we are in Babylon because of what our parents and grandparents did, and it is not our fault.

What do you mean by repeating this proverb? The ESV notes that “you” is plural. This was not one bitter man’s complaint but a popular saying, repeated everywhere; Jeremiah heard it in Jerusalem too (Jeremiah 31:29).

A half-truth misused. There was truth in it. The sins of Manasseh’s generation had brought judgment on Judah (2 Kings 24:3–4), and children do suffer from their parents’ sins. But the proverb used that truth to excuse the present generation from its own guilt and to accuse God of unfairness, and that is what God refuses.

The proverb today. We still say it: “It’s my upbringing. It’s my genes. It’s the system. It’s what was done to me.” Some of that may be real, and deserves compassion. But none of it removes a person’s own responsibility before God.

verseByVerse.quote: As I live, declares the Lord GOD, this proverb shall no more be used by you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is mine: the soul who sins shall die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God bans the proverb: every person belongs to him directly, and each will answer for his own sin.

This proverb shall no more be used. God does not argue with the proverb; he bans it, with an oath: “As I live”.

All souls are mine. Here is the foundation of the whole chapter. A “soul” here is a whole living person, not only the inner part. Every human being belongs directly to God, so a son’s standing with God is not fixed by his father’s record; God deals with each one personally. That is sobering, because no one can shelter behind anyone else, and freeing, because no one is doomed by anyone else. You are not trapped by your family’s history.

Neither the tribe nor the self. Our culture offers two answers to the question of whom we belong to. One says: to myself; I am answerable to no one, and my story is mine to write. The other says: to my group; I am my nation, class, race or family, and its honour, grievance or guilt is mine whatever I have done. The first leaves people lonely and the second leaves them trapped, and many of us manage to believe both on different days. The exiles had chosen the second, because it let them blame their fathers. God’s answer cuts through both: “all souls are mine”. You do not belong to yourself, so you cannot simply invent who you are. You do not belong to your tribe’s ledger, so you are not doomed by it. You belong to God, who deals with you face to face.

Bought with a price. The gospel goes further. The one person who never needed to answer for anyone chose to answer for us, so that Paul can tell every believer, “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20), and find in that not the loss of a self but the only safe place to have one.

The soul who sins shall die. The verdict is short, and Paul says the same: “the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). Death here means more than physical death; it is being cut off from the life of God, the real disaster behind every other one.

Does this contradict Exodus 20:5? The commandment speaks of God “visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me”: children who continue in their parents’ sin. And the law itself says, “Each one shall be put to death for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16). Sin’s consequences can run through families; guilt before God belongs to the one who sins.

Does this deny original sin? No. Ezekiel answers the exiles’ complaint that they were being punished for their fathers’ sins (v. 2): each is judged for his own guilt. Scripture also teaches that in Adam all sinned and died (Romans 5:12), and that we are born with a sinful nature (Psalm 51:5). Both are true: Adam’s guilt and corruption are ours, and every person also answers for his own sins.

What about so-called generational curses? Some teach that Christians must break curses inherited from their ancestors before they can be free. This chapter says the opposite for anyone who turns to God: the son who turns “shall not die for his father’s iniquity” (v. 17). Family patterns and wounds are real and may need patient help, prayer and counsel, but a believer is not under a hidden ancestral sentence. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), and “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Each generation stands or falls before God on its own life, not on its father’s or its son’s. Ezekiel paints three portraits. A righteous man, faithful in worship, in marriage and with money, and generous to the hungry, “shall surely live” (vv. 5–9). His violent son, who does all that his father refused, cannot shelter behind his father’s goodness: “he shall surely die” (vv. 10–13). The grandson sees his father’s sins and does not copy them, and “he shall not die for his father’s iniquity” (vv. 14–18). When the people object, God repeats the principle both ways: neither father nor son bears the other’s guilt (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Neither a godly family nor a wicked one decides a person's standing before God.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man is righteous and does what is just and right— if he does not eat upon the mountains or lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, does not defile his neighbor's wife or approach a woman in her time of menstrual impurity,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first portrait is of a righteous man, whose righteousness begins with undivided worship of the LORD and shows in faithfulness in marriage.

If a man is righteous. Three case studies across three generations. The first man’s righteousness is specific, not vague spirituality.

He does not eat upon the mountains. First, worship. He does not join the sacrificial feasts at the pagan high places, the hilltop shrines, and does not even “lift up his eyes to the idols”. His heart and eyes are fixed on the LORD, and everything else in a righteous life flows from there.

Does not defile his neighbor’s wife. Second, sexual purity. He is faithful in marriage, and keeps the law’s boundaries of purity within his own marriage too (Leviticus 18:19). Faithfulness to God shows itself in the most intimate area of life.

verseByVerse.quote: does not oppress anyone, but restores to the debtor his pledge, commits no robbery, gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment, does not lend at interest or take any profit, withholds his hand from injustice, executes true justice between man and man, walks in my statutes, and keeps my rules by acting faithfully—he is righteous; he shall surely live, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous man treats the poor with justice and generosity, refuses to profit from their need and walks with God, and he shall surely live.

Does not oppress anyone. Third, justice and mercy. When a poor man leaves his cloak as security for a loan, he gives it back, as the law required: “that is his only covering… in what else shall he sleep?” (Exodus 22:27). He does not rob.

Gives his bread to the hungry. He goes beyond not harming. Isaiah described true religion the same way: “to share your bread with the hungry… when you see the naked, to cover him” (Isaiah 58:7). And Jesus will say on the last day, “I was hungry and you gave me food… I was naked and you clothed me” (Matthew 25:35–36).

Does not lend at interest. Fourth, money. The ESV notes that “profit” here means profit that comes from charging interest to the poor. The law said of a brother in need, “Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God, that your brother may live beside you” (Leviticus 25:36). The righteous man does not make money out of other people’s desperation, and he deals honestly “between man and man”.

He is righteous; he shall surely live. The summary of it all: he “walks in my statutes, and keeps my rules by acting faithfully”.

Only one man fits. Read this list honestly and it exposes all of us: “None is righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10). Only one man fits vv. 5–9 completely: Jesus. He alone could say that he should surely live. And yet he died, “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). The soul who sins shall die; the Righteous One died in the place of sinners.

Is Ezekiel teaching that people earn life by good works? No. This is the life of a person who belongs to God by faith. “The righteous shall live by his faith” (Habakkuk 2:4), and true faith shows itself in a changed life: “I will show you my faith by my works” (James 2:18). The righteous man here is not sinless; his life is turned toward God.

Does this forbid charging interest? The law forbade profiting from a poor neighbour’s need (Exodus 22:25) and allowed interest in trade with foreigners (Deuteronomy 23:20). Ordinary lending is not sin; exploiting the desperate, as predatory lenders do, is.
verseByVerse.note: The list is like the entrance psalms (Ps 15; 24:3-6), which ask who may stand in God's presence; Psalm 15 also names the man who does not put out his money at interest.

verseByVerse.quote: "If he fathers a son who is violent, a shedder of blood, who does any of these things (though he himself did none of these things), who even eats upon the mountains, defiles his neighbor's wife, oppresses the poor and needy, commits robbery, does not restore the pledge, lifts up his eyes to the idols, commits abomination, lends at interest, and takes profit; shall he then live? He shall not live. He has done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A righteous father’s goodness cannot save a violent son: the son will die for his own sins.

If he fathers a son who is violent. The second generation. The righteous man has a violent son who does everything his father avoided. Can he live on his father’s goodness? “He shall not live… his blood shall be upon himself.”

A word for grieving parents. This is the point of chapter 14 again (14:14–20): a godly parent cannot save an ungodly child. Faithful parents who grieve over children who have turned away should keep praying and loving, but they are not guilty for their child’s choices: “whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). And if you were raised in a Christian home, your parents’ faith will not count for you; you must come to God yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now suppose this man fathers a son who sees all the sins that his father has done; he sees, and does not do likewise: he does not eat upon the mountains or lift up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, does not defile his neighbor's wife, does not oppress anyone, exacts no pledge, commits no robbery, but gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with a garment, withholds his hand from iniquity, takes no interest or profit, obeys my rules, and walks in my statutes; he shall not die for his father's iniquity; he shall surely live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grandson who looks honestly at his father’s sins and refuses to copy them will live: the cycle can be broken.

He sees, and does not do likewise. The word comes twice: “sees… he sees”. He looks honestly at what his father did. He does not excuse it, and he does not copy it, and “he shall not die for his father’s iniquity”.

Breaking the cycle. This is a deeply hopeful passage for anyone who grew up in a broken, abusive, addicted or ungodly family. The cycle can be broken; you are not doomed to repeat it. By God’s grace you can see what was done, refuse to do likewise, and live. That usually takes help as well as resolve: a church that walks with you and, where the wounds are deep, a wise biblical counsellor. Your past explains much, but it does not determine your destiny before God.

Textual note. For “withholds his hand from iniquity” (v. 17) the ESV follows the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation; it notes that the Hebrew reads “from the poor”.

verseByVerse.quote: As for his father, because he practiced extortion, robbed his brother, and did what is not good among his people, behold, he shall die for his iniquity. "Yet you say, 'Why should not the son suffer for the iniquity of the father?' When the son has done what is just and right, and has been careful to observe all my statutes, he shall surely live. The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people want the old proverb to be true, because it would excuse them, but God insists that neither father nor son carries the other’s guilt.

Why should not the son suffer for the iniquity of the father? A strange objection: they seem to want the proverb to be true. If they are only suffering for their parents’ sins, they do not have to repent of their own. It is comfortable to believe that others have fixed your fate, because it takes away your responsibility.

The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father. God repeats the principle and makes it run both ways: “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself.”

The free, willing exchange of grace. There is one great exception, and it is the heart of the gospel. The righteousness of one man has been placed on others, and the sin of others has been placed on him: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). This is not the unfairness of the sour grapes proverb, forced on unwilling children. It is the free, willing exchange of grace, which the Son chose for himself (John 10:18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — Is My Way Not Just?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What counts before God is not only the family you come from but the way you are facing now. A wicked person who turns will live, and not one of his past sins will be remembered against him (vv. 21–22), for God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked and wants him to turn and live (v. 23). A righteous person who turns to evil cannot lean on his past (v. 24). The people call this unjust, but twice God turns the charge back: “Is it not your ways that are not just?” (vv. 25–29). Mercy to the repentant is not unfairness; refusing to repent is.
verseByVerse.theology: God judges each person by the direction of his life, and he delights not in death but in repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if a wicked person turns away from all his sins that he has committed and keeps all my statutes and does what is just and right, he shall surely live; he shall not die. None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him; for the righteousness that he has done he shall live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wicked person who turns from his sins will live, and God will not hold one of his past sins against him.

But if a wicked person turns away. The chapter moves from generations to individual lives. What matters is not only which family you come from but which way you are facing now. A wicked person can turn, and if he does, “he shall surely live; he shall not die.”

None of the transgressions that he has committed. Here is astonishing grace. Not some, but none, “shall be remembered against him”. God does not keep a file open in case the repentant sinner slips. “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins” (Isaiah 43:25); “I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12).

A thief who turned. Zacchaeus was a thief and a traitor. When he turned, Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). No past is so dark that God will not forget it when a sinner turns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked; what he wants is for sinners to turn and live.

Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? This verse is the heart of the chapter, and it shows the heart of God. The question expects the answer no. What he wants is “that he should turn from his way and live”.

Not eager to condemn. Many people imagine God eager to condemn. Ezekiel, the prophet of judgment, says the opposite: God judges because he is just, but he delights in mercy. Paul says God “desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4); Peter, that he is “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). Jesus said “there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” (Luke 15:7), and he wept over the city that would not come to him (Luke 19:41–42).

If you are far from God. This is his heart toward you. He is not waiting to crush you. He is waiting for you to turn.

Where Christians differ: if God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, how can he choose some and not others? Arminian Christians answer that God gives all the same grace and leaves the choice to them. Reformed Christians distinguish what God commands and delights in from what he decrees: he sincerely calls all to turn and live, and the death of the wicked is no pleasure to him, yet he has not chosen to give the new heart (36:26) to all, for reasons he has not revealed (Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 9:18–23). This commentary’s view: the Reformed view does justice to both truths that Scripture states. The call to repent is sincere, and no one who comes to Christ is turned away (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: But when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice and does the same abominations that the wicked person does, shall he live? None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered; for the treachery of which he is guilty and the sin he has committed, for them he shall die. "Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' Hear now, O house of Israel: Is my way not just? Is it not your ways that are not just? When a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice, he shall die for it; for the injustice that he has done he shall die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A person who turns from a righteous life to wickedness cannot lean on his past, and it is the people’s way, not God’s, that is unjust.

When a righteous person turns away from his righteousness. The same principle works the other way. One who has lived rightly and then turns to wickedness cannot lean on his past: “None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered”. God judges the direction of a life, not a stored record of old good deeds.

A real warning. As in 3:20, this is a real warning, and God uses it to keep his people: “the one who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13). No one can rest on a past spiritual experience while living in present rebellion.

Is my way not just? The people complain that it is unfair for a wicked man to turn and be forgiven, or for a righteous man to turn and be lost. God throws the charge back: “Is it not your ways that are not just?” What would be unjust is to punish a son for his father, or to refuse mercy to the repentant. The problem is not God’s justice but their unwillingness to face their own guilt. “Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!” (Romans 9:14).

If you have stumbled. If you are a believer who has stumbled badly and fears these verses describe you, they do not describe a Christian who falls, grieves and comes back, but a settled turning from God that does not return. The word to the stumbling is in this same chapter, turn and live, and “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

Where Christians differ: can a truly righteous person fall away and be lost? Arminian Christians read warnings like this as showing that a true believer can lose salvation. This commentary’s view: Ezekiel speaks of one who turns from his righteousness and persists in evil, and Scripture shows that such a person was never truly made new. Those to whom God has given a new heart (36:26) are kept by him (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and “if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which God keeps his own from falling.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, when a wicked person turns away from the wickedness he has committed and does what is just and right, he shall save his life. Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die. Yet the house of Israel says, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' O house of Israel, are my ways not just? Is it not your ways that are not just?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repentance begins when a person stops to consider his life and then turns from his sins; that is the way to life, and God’s way is just.

He considered and turned away. Two steps. Repentance begins with thinking: stopping, looking honestly at your life, weighing where it is going. Then it acts: he “turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed”. The prodigal son “came to himself”, then arose and went to his father (Luke 15:17–20).

Stop and consider. Many people never repent because they never stop to consider. Sit still long enough to ask where your life is going and what God says about it. When people keep accusing God of unfairness (v. 29), it is usually because they would rather argue than repent.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends not with a verdict but with a plea. God will judge each person by his ways, so he calls the whole house of Israel to repent and throw away its sins (v. 30), and commands what only he can give: “make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit!” Then comes the cry of his heart: “Why will you die, O house of Israel?” (v. 31). He has no pleasure in the death of anyone, so the last word is an open door: “so turn, and live” (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who commands a new heart pleads with sinners to turn and live, and in Christ he gives what he commands.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, declares the Lord GOD. Repent and turn from all your transgressions, lest iniquity be your ruin. Cast away from you all the transgressions that you have committed, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God will judge each person by his ways, he pleads with his people to throw away their sins and receive a new heart, for he does not want them to die.

I will judge you, O house of Israel. Now the chapter becomes an appeal. God will judge “every one according to his ways”, and “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). So: “Repent and turn”. (The ESV notes that the last phrase may be rendered “lest iniquity be your stumbling block”.)

Cast away from you all the transgressions. Like throwing off filthy clothes. Then comes a command that seems impossible: “make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit!”

How can anyone make himself a new heart? In 11:19 and again in 36:26 God promises, “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.” So which is it? Both. God commands what he alone can give, so that we will stop trusting ourselves and ask him for it: the command shows us our duty and our inability, the promise shows us his grace. Paul holds both together: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). The new spirit is in the end God’s own Spirit, “I will put my Spirit within you” (36:27), the Spirit by whom Jesus said we must be born again (John 3:5–7), who now lives in every believer and makes the turning real.

Why will you die, O house of Israel? God is not describing an inevitable fate; he is pleading. You do not have to die. Why would you choose it?

verseByVerse.quote: For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has no pleasure in the death of anyone, so his last word is an open invitation: turn, and live.

I have no pleasure in the death of anyone. Not anyone. God’s heart toward sinners is not hostile but pleading, and the door is open. The chapter ends with four words that sum up the whole gospel invitation: “so turn, and live”.

Why people are lost. Jesus said to religious people who knew the Scriptures well, “you refuse to come to me that you may have life” (John 5:40). The tragedy of the lost is not that God refused them, but that they refused him. And the Bible’s last invitation echoes this one: “let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (Revelation 22:17).

God’s word to you today. Whatever your family, whatever your past, whatever you have done, God’s word to you today is the same: turn, and live.

18.title: Turn, and Live
18.overview:
Where we are. We are still in the long run of warnings before Jerusalem falls (chapters 12 to 24). Chapter 17 exposed a king who would not own his broken oath; chapter 18 turns to the whole people and the excuse on everyone’s lips.

The message. You are not being punished for your parents’ sins, and you are not trapped by them. Every person belongs to God and answers to him for his own life, and the God who judges takes no pleasure in anyone’s death. So the door stands open: turn, and live.

Why it was said. The exiles had a proverb: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (v. 2). It explained their disaster as their fathers’ fault, accused God of unfairness and excused them from repentance (see the introduction). Beneath it lay despair as well: if others have fixed our fate, why try?

How the chapter makes its case. God bans the proverb with an oath and lays the foundation: all souls are his, and the soul who sins shall die (vv. 1–4). Three generations prove it: a righteous man lives, his violent son dies for his own sins, and the grandson who sees his father’s ways and refuses them lives (vv. 5–20). Then from families to the turns of a single life: the wicked who turns will live, his sins remembered no more, for God has no pleasure in his death, while the righteous who turns to evil cannot lean on his past; and when the people call this unjust, God turns the charge back on them (vv. 21–29). The chapter ends as a plea: cast away your sins, make yourselves a new heart, why will you die? Turn, and live (vv. 30–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God it reveals. Measured against the righteous man of vv. 5–9, no one but Jesus lives; and the command to make a new heart shows that we cannot, and sends us to the promise that God will give one (36:26). The one great exception to “the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father” is the gospel itself: the Righteous One freely bore the sins of others (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 3:18). And the God who says “I have no pleasure in the death of anyone” wept over Jerusalem in Jesus (Luke 19:41) and gave his Son so that sinners need not die.

For us. Stop blaming and stop despairing: your family’s past does not seal your future, and your own sins are yours to confess. Whatever you have done, God’s word to you today is the same: turn, and live.
18.theology:
Every soul belongs to God and is personally accountable to him; no one may hide behind the sins of parents or society (vv. 2-4, 20; Deut 24:16; Jer 31:29-30).

True righteousness is specific: pure worship, sexual faithfulness, justice, mercy to the poor and honesty with money (vv. 5-9; Isa 58:7; Matt 25:35-36).

The righteous live by faith, and faith shows itself in a changed life; yet no one but Christ fully meets this standard, and he died for the unrighteous (v. 9; Hab 2:4; Jas 2:18; Rom 3:10; 1 Pet 3:18).

A godly family cannot save an ungodly child, and an ungodly family cannot doom a child who turns to God (vv. 10-18).

Righteousness and guilt pass from one person to another only at the cross, where Christ freely took his people’s sin and gave them his righteousness (2 Cor 5:21).

God forgets the sins of the repentant and does not count past righteousness in favour of those who turn away from him for good (vv. 21-26; Isa 43:25; 1 John 2:19; Matt 24:13).

God takes no pleasure in the death of anyone; he pleads with sinners to turn and live (vv. 23, 32; 1 Tim 2:4; 2 Pet 3:9; Luke 15:7).

God commands a new heart and promises to give it, so that repentance is both our duty and his gift (v. 31; 11:19; 36:26; Phil 2:12-13).
18.examples:
The chapter begins with a bitter joke about sour grapes and aching teeth, and answers it with ordinary pictures of a righteous life, like a poor man's cloak given back before the sun goes down. Its most hopeful figure is the son who saw everything his father did, and did not do likewise.

For anyone afraid of their past, it offers a God who keeps no file on the sins of those who turn, and who asks, as a plea rather than a threat, Why will you die, O house of Israel? Its last four words are the whole invitation: so turn, and live.

keyVerse.quote: For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter has been building to this. God has answered the excuse that blames the fathers and the complaint that his ways are unjust, and what is left is his heart: he does not want anyone to die. It is the Old Testament form of the gospel invitation, which Jesus himself made when he wept over those who would not come to him.

18.reflection:
The exiles’ proverb blamed their troubles on their parents (v. 2). What versions of “the fathers have eaten sour grapes” do people use today? Where is the line between understanding how our past has shaped us and using it as an excuse?

God says “all souls are mine” (v. 4). How does belonging to God free us both from the loneliness of belonging only to ourselves and from the trap of being defined by our family or group?

Verses 21–23 say that none of a repentant sinner’s transgressions will be remembered, and that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. How does this picture of God’s heart compare with the way you or people you know tend to picture him?

God commands, “make yourselves a new heart” (v. 31), yet promises, “I will give you a new heart” (36:26). How do the command and the promise work together? How might this shape the way you pray for yourself and for someone far from God?

19.text: <sup>1</sup>And you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel,<sup>2</sup>and say: What was your mother? A lioness! Among lions she crouched; in the midst of young lions she reared her cubs.<sup>3</sup>And she brought up one of her cubs; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men.<sup>4</sup>The nations heard about him; he was caught in their pit, and they brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>When she saw that she waited in vain, that her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion.<sup>6</sup>He prowled among the lions; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men,<sup>7</sup>and seized their widows. He laid waste their cities, and the land was appalled and all who were in it at the sound of his roaring.<sup>8</sup>Then the nations set against him from provinces on every side; they spread their net over him; he was taken in their pit.<sup>9</sup>With hooks they put him in a cage and brought him to the king of Babylon; they brought him into custody, that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel.<sup>10</sup>Your mother was like a vine in a vineyard planted by the water, fruitful and full of branches by reason of abundant water.<sup>11</sup>Its strong stems became rulers' scepters; it towered aloft among the thick boughs; it was seen in its height with the mass of its branches.<sup>12</sup>But the vine was plucked up in fury, cast down to the ground; the east wind dried up its fruit; they were stripped off and withered. As for its strong stem, fire consumed it.<sup>13</sup>Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land.<sup>14</sup>And fire has gone out from the stem of its shoots, has consumed its fruit, so that there remains in it no strong stem, no scepter for ruling. This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Lioness and Her Cubs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s kings, meant to be lions that protected their people, became predators and were caught. Ezekiel is told to sing a funeral song for the princes of Israel (v. 1). Their mother, Judah, was a lioness who raised a cub; he learned to devour men, and the nations caught him in a pit and dragged him with hooks to Egypt (vv. 2–4). She raised another, fiercer still, who laid waste the land with his roaring, until he too was netted, caged and brought to the king of Babylon, “that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel” (vv. 5–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Kings who rule like predators end as captives, and the royal house that bred them mourns.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel, and say: What was your mother? A lioness! Among lions she crouched; in the midst of young lions she reared her cubs. And she brought up one of her cubs; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men. The nations heard about him; he was caught in their pit, and they brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel sings a funeral song for David’s royal house: Judah the lioness raised a king who learned to devour his own people, and he was dragged away to Egypt.

Take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel. A lamentation was a funeral song. Ezekiel is told to sing a dirge for Judah’s kings while Zedekiah was still on the throne. It is like playing a funeral march for a man who has not yet died: the royal house is already as good as dead.

What was your mother? A lioness! The mother is Judah and its royal house, and the lion was Judah’s own emblem. On his deathbed Jacob had said, “Judah is a lion’s cub… he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him?” and “The scepter shall not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:9–10). Judah was the tribe of kings, and its kings were meant to be lions: strong, courageous protectors. But she raised her cubs among the lions of the nations, and they learned the ways of the nations.

He learned to catch prey; he devoured men. A king was supposed to be a shepherd who protected his people. These kings became predators who fed on them (compare 34:2–3). Power used to devour instead of to serve always ends in a pit.

They brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt. The first cub is taken to Egypt, which identifies him as Jehoahaz, son of Josiah. He “reigned three months in Jerusalem” (2 Kings 23:31) before Pharaoh Neco put him in bonds, and “he came to Egypt and died there” (2 Kings 23:34).
verseByVerse.note: Hebrew laments often used a limping rhythm, a longer line answered by a shorter one, like a broken sob, and much of this chapter follows it.

verseByVerse.quote: When she saw that she waited in vain, that her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion. He prowled among the lions; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men, and seized their widows. He laid waste their cities, and the land was appalled and all who were in it at the sound of his roaring. Then the nations set against him from provinces on every side; they spread their net over him; he was taken in their pit. With hooks they put him in a cage and brought him to the king of Babylon; they brought him into custody, that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second king, fiercer still, terrorised the land until he too was caught, caged and taken to Babylon, and his roar was silenced.

Her hope was lost. Her first cub will not come back, so she pins her hopes on another. That is the story of Judah’s last years: one king after another, each expected to save the nation, each failing.

He devoured men, and seized their widows. The second cub is even more violent, laying waste cities and terrifying the land with his roar, and he is carried off to Babylon. Most likely this is Jehoiachin, whom Nebuchadnezzar took prisoner and carried away to Babylon (2 Kings 24:12, 15); some think it points to Zedekiah, whose capture was still to come. Either way, the pattern is the same.

With hooks they put him in a cage. A caged lion, and the sad line: “that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel”. The roar that once terrified the land falls silent.

The true Lion of Judah. John wept because no one could open the scroll, and an elder said, “Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered”. But when John turned to look, he saw “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:5–6). Judah’s lions devoured men; the true Lion of Judah was slain for them. His power is the power of self-giving love, and his voice will never be silenced.

Power that serves. Everyone with power over others, a parent, an employer, a pastor, faces these kings’ temptation: to feed on those we are meant to protect. Jesus named it and reversed it: “whoever would be great among you must be your servant” (Mark 10:43).

Uncertain wording. In v. 7 “seized their widows” is literally “knew their widows”, as the ESV notes, an odd expression for a lion; some translations change one letter of the Hebrew and read “strongholds” or “palaces” instead of widows. In v. 9 “in a cage” may be “in a wooden collar” (ESV note). However the details are read, the picture is clear: a savage king, caught and silenced.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The royal house that God had planted and blessed has been uprooted, and the fire came from within. Judah is pictured again, now as a vine by abundant water, so fruitful that its strong stems became royal sceptres and it towered above the rest (vv. 10–11). But it was plucked up in fury, dried by the east wind and burned (v. 12), and now it is planted in a dry and thirsty wilderness, the exile (v. 13). Fire from its own stem has left it with “no strong stem, no scepter for ruling”, and the song meant for the future has already come true (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The line of David's kings seemed to end in fire and exile, but God's promise of a coming King did not die.

verseByVerse.quote: Your mother was like a vine in a vineyard planted by the water, fruitful and full of branches by reason of abundant water. Its strong stems became rulers' scepters; it towered aloft among the thick boughs; it was seen in its height with the mass of its branches. But the vine was plucked up in fury, cast down to the ground; the east wind dried up its fruit; they were stripped off and withered. As for its strong stem, fire consumed it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah was once a vine richly planted and blessed, growing kings like strong branches, but God plucked it up in anger and it withered.

Your mother was like a vine. A second picture of the same mother, now a vine “planted by the water”, lush and fruitful: Judah in its days of blessing, with every advantage God could give (compare Isaiah 5:1–4).

It towered aloft among the thick boughs. Its strong branches became royal sceptres: kings grew from this vine. It towered high, impressive and admired, as the house of David was at its height under Solomon.

The vine was plucked up in fury. Then, all at once, it was thrown to the ground, dried by the east wind from Babylon, its fruit stripped and its strongest stem burned. Height is no protection when God uproots.

Uncertain wording. In v. 10 the ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read “in your blood” instead of “in a vineyard”; the Hebrew is difficult, and the ESV, like most translations, follows a slightly different reading. In v. 11 “among the thick boughs” may be “among the clouds” (ESV note). Neither changes the picture of a vine once rich and towering.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land. And fire has gone out from the stem of its shoots, has consumed its fruit, so that there remains in it no strong stem, no scepter for ruling. This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The royal vine now lies in the desert of exile, burned by a fire from its own stem, with no king left to rule; yet the lament leaves room for the King God has promised.

Now it is planted in the wilderness. The vine that grew beside abundant water is now in “a dry and thirsty land”: exile in Babylon. It is not quite dead, but it is far from its source.

Fire has gone out from the stem of its shoots. The fire did not only come from outside; it came from within the royal line itself. Zedekiah’s rebellion lit the fire that burned Jerusalem; the kings destroyed the kingdom.

No strong stem, no scepter for ruling. It looks like the end of David’s dynasty. Jacob had said, “The scepter shall not depart from Judah… until tribute comes to him” (Genesis 49:10). Has the sceptre departed?

A sceptre still to come. Not for ever. Soon Ezekiel will hear God say of the crown, “This also shall not be, until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs, and I will give it to him” (21:27), and he has already heard the promise of a tender sprig planted by God himself (17:22). The sceptre was laid down in the dust so that it could be taken up by the true King.

This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation. What began as a song about the future became history: Ezekiel’s dirge came true. But the story of David’s line did not end with a lament. It led to Jesus, the Son of David, and to his empty tomb.

When God feels far. Many believers know what it is to be transplanted from a well-watered place to a desert: a loss, an illness, a move, a season when God feels far. Even there God can make things grow. The book of Ezekiel will end with a river flowing into the desert and making it live (47:8–9).

19.title: A Lament for the Princes
19.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 17 and 18 have spoken to Judah’s king and to its people; now Ezekiel is told to sing. Chapter 19 is a funeral song for the royal house of David, composed while Zedekiah was still on the throne, and it rounds off the section that began with the riddle of the eagles.

The message. The house of David, called to be a lion that protects and a vine that bears fruit, has destroyed itself. Its kings learned to devour their own people, and one by one they were dragged away; the fire that burned the vine came from its own stem. The dynasty the exiles were pinning their hopes on is as good as dead, and it is time to mourn it.

Why it was said. The exiles hoped that a king of David’s line, Jehoiachin in captivity or Zedekiah in Jerusalem, would restore their fortunes (see the introduction). A lament sung before the funeral told them the truth: no king of that line would save them.

How the chapter makes its case. First the lioness (vv. 1–9): Judah, the lion tribe, raised a cub who learned to devour men and was dragged with hooks to Egypt, then another, fiercer still, who was caged and taken to Babylon so that his roar was heard no more. Then the vine (vv. 10–14): planted by abundant water, it grew strong stems fit for sceptres and towered high, but it was plucked up in fury, dried by the east wind and replanted in the desert, and fire from its own stem left it “no strong stem, no scepter for ruling”. The last line says the lament has already become history.

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by contrast. Jacob had promised that the sceptre would not depart from Judah “until tribute comes to him” (Genesis 49:10), and Ezekiel will soon hear that the crown waits “until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs” (21:27). Judah’s lion cubs devoured men; the true Lion of the tribe of Judah is a Lamb who was slain for them (Revelation 5:5–6). David’s line went down into the dust, and rose again in the Son of David, whose voice will never be silenced.

For us. Those who use their power to feed on the people they should protect are brought down in the end, and that warns everyone who holds any power, in a home, a church or a nation. And when what you trusted has failed and you find yourself planted in a dry land, look to the King who grew up “like a root out of dry ground” (Isaiah 53:2).
19.theology:
Rulers are meant to be protectors; power used to devour others ends in captivity and silence (vv. 3-9).

Height is no protection when God uproots a proud house, and the royal line lit the fire that consumed it (vv. 10-14).

God's promise of a King from Judah did not die with Judah's kings; the true Lion of Judah conquers as the slain Lamb (Gen 49:9-10; Ezek 21:27; Rev 5:5-6).
19.examples: A funeral song is sung for a king still on his throne: lion cubs who hunt their own people end with their roar silenced in a cage, and a vine by the river is burned by a fire from its own royal branch. Yet behind the lament stands the Lion of Judah who turns out to be a slain Lamb.

keyVerse.quote: And fire has gone out from the stem of its shoots, has consumed its fruit, so that there remains in it no strong stem, no scepter for ruling. This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation.
keyVerse.note: The lament ends where Judah’s kings had brought it: the fire came from within the royal line, and no sceptre is left. Yet the verse leaves an empty place that God himself will fill, for the crown is kept “until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs” (21:27). The silence of David’s throne is the waiting room for Christ.

19.reflection:
Ezekiel was told to sing a funeral song while the king was still on his throne (v. 1). Why do you think God sometimes tells his people to grieve over something before it has visibly collapsed? Is there anything you have been trusting that you need to grieve and let go?

Judah’s kings were meant to be lions that protected, but they “learned to catch prey” and devoured men (vv. 3, 6). Where are you tempted to use whatever power you have, at home, at work or in church, for yourself rather than for those in your care?

Revelation 5:5–6 shows the Lion of the tribe of Judah as a Lamb that was slain. How does Jesus’ way of ruling differ from the kings of this chapter, and what does that mean for the way we follow him?

The vine once planted by abundant water is now “in a dry and thirsty land” (v. 13). How have you experienced seasons like that? What hope does the promise of a coming King (17:22; 21:27) give in them?
