As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you.<sup>4</sup>Will you judge them, son of man, will you judge them? Let them know the abominations of their fathers,<sup>5</sup>and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day when I chose Israel, I swore to the offspring of the house of Jacob, making myself known to them in the land of Egypt; I swore to them, saying, I am the LORD your God.<sup>6</sup>On that day I swore to them that I would bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land that I had searched out for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands.<sup>7</sup>And I said to them, 'Cast away the detestable things your eyes feast on, every one of you, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt; I am the LORD your God.'<sup>8</sup>But they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me. None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on, nor did they forsake the idols of Egypt. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations among whom they lived, in whose sight I made myself known to them in bringing them out of the land of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>So I led them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness.<sup>11</sup>I gave them my statutes and made known to them my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live.<sup>12</sup>Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, as a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them.<sup>13</sup>But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They did not walk in my statutes but rejected my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; and my Sabbaths they greatly profaned. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them in the wilderness, to make a full end of them.<sup>14</sup>But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out.<sup>15</sup>Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would not bring them into the land that I had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands,<sup>16</sup>because they rejected my rules and did not walk in my statutes, and profaned my Sabbaths; for their heart went after their idols.<sup>17</sup>Nevertheless, my eye spared them, and I did not destroy them or make a full end of them in the wilderness.<sup>18</sup>"And I said to their children in the wilderness, 'Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, nor keep their rules, nor defile yourselves with their idols.<sup>19</sup>I am the LORD your God; walk in my statutes, and be careful to obey my rules,<sup>20</sup>and keep my Sabbaths holy that they may be a sign between me and you, that you may know that I am the LORD your God.'<sup>21</sup>But the children rebelled against me. They did not walk in my statutes and were not careful to obey my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; they profaned my Sabbaths. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the wilderness.<sup>22</sup>But I withheld my hand and acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out.<sup>23</sup>Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the countries,<sup>24</sup>because they had not obeyed my rules, but had rejected my statutes and profaned my Sabbaths, and their eyes were set on their fathers' idols.<sup>25</sup>Moreover, I gave them statutes that were not good and rules by which they could not have life,<sup>26</sup>and I defiled them through their very gifts in their offering up all their firstborn, that I might devastate them. I did it that they might know that I am the LORD.<sup>27</sup>"Therefore, son of man, speak to the house of Israel and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: In this also your fathers blasphemed me, by dealing treacherously with me.<sup>28</sup>For when I had brought them into the land that I swore to give them, then wherever they saw any high hill or any leafy tree, there they offered their sacrifices and there they presented the provocation of their offering; there they sent up their pleasing aromas, and there they poured out their drink offerings.<sup>29</sup>(I said to them, 'What is the high place to which you go?' So its name is called Bamah to this day.)<sup>30</sup>"Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Will you defile yourselves after the manner of your fathers and go whoring after their detestable things?<sup>31</sup>When you present your gifts and offer up your children in fire, you defile yourselves with all your idols to this day. And shall I be inquired of by you, O house of Israel? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you.<sup>32</sup>"What is in your mind shall never happen—the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.'<sup>33</sup>"As I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you.<sup>34</sup>I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you are scattered, with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out.<sup>35</sup>And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face.<sup>36</sup>As I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>37</sup>I will make you pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant.<sup>38</sup>I will purge out the rebels from among you, and those who transgress against me. The blazing flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from south to north shall be scorched by it.<sup>48</sup>All flesh shall see that I the LORD have kindled it; it shall not be quenched."<sup>49</sup>Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! They are saying of me, 'Is he not a maker of parables?'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Will Not Be Inquired Of
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not be consulted by people who want his guidance while keeping their idols. In August 591 BC some of the elders of Israel come and sit before Ezekiel to inquire of the LORD (v. 1). God refuses with an oath: “I will not be inquired of by you” (vv. 2–3). Instead of the answer they want, Ezekiel is to give them the truth they need, putting them on trial by setting before them “the abominations of their fathers” (v. 4), the history they are repeating.
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be consulted like a fortune teller by people who have not dealt with their idols.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, certain of the elders of Israel came to inquire of the LORD, and sat before me. And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD, Is it to inquire of me that you come? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you. Will you judge them, son of man, will you judge them? Let them know the abominations of their fathers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders come to consult God while keeping their idols, and he refuses to answer them; instead he confronts them with their history.

Came to inquire of the LORD. The date is about August 591 BC, eleven months after the temple vision (8:1), and the elders are back at Ezekiel’s door. They are not asking to repent. They want information, perhaps about when they will go home.

I will not be inquired of by you. God refuses, with an oath. As in 14:3, they come with idols still in their hearts. God is not a fortune teller to be consulted by people who have no intention of obeying the answer.

Let them know the abominations of their fathers. Instead of an answer, a history lesson. “Will you judge them?” means: put them on trial and set out the charge (compare 22:2; 23:36). The elders want to talk about the future; God makes them face the past, because they are repeating it.

Why we ask for guidance. That is a searching thought for anyone who prays for guidance. Do we want God’s direction so that we can obey it, or only so that we can plan around it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–26 — Rebellion, and the Sake of His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s history is one long rebellion, and Israel survived only because God acted for the sake of his name. In Egypt God chose Israel and swore to bring them to a glorious land, but they clung to Egypt’s idols (vv. 5–8). For his name’s sake he brought them out and gave them his life-giving law and his Sabbaths, but they rebelled in the wilderness, and that generation never entered the land (vv. 9–17). Their children were called to break with their fathers’ ways, and rebelled too (vv. 18–22). So God swore to scatter them, and handed them over to statutes that were not good, the customs they preferred (vv. 23–26).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's whole history is a record of rebellion met by a patience grounded in God's concern for his own name.

verseByVerse.quote: and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day when I chose Israel, I swore to the offspring of the house of Jacob, making myself known to them in the land of Egypt; I swore to them, saying, I am the LORD your God. On that day I swore to them that I would bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land that I had searched out for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands. And I said to them, 'Cast away the detestable things your eyes feast on, every one of you, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt; I am the LORD your God.' But they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me. None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on, nor did they forsake the idols of Egypt. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s story began with God’s free choice and sworn promise, but from the start, even in Egypt, they would not give up their idols.

On the day when I chose Israel. The story begins with grace: “I chose… I swore… I am the LORD your God”. Before Israel did anything, God chose them and bound himself to them. “I swore” is literally “I lifted my hand” (ESV note), the gesture of an oath, here and through the chapter.

A land that I had searched out for them. God himself had scouted out the best place for his people, “the most glorious of all lands”. Every gift was prepared before they asked.

Do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt. The command is not in Exodus in so many words, but Joshua confirms it: “Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt” (Joshua 24:14). Israel carried Egypt’s idols in their hearts even while God was bringing them out. The golden calf was not a sudden lapse; it was an old love.

The detestable things your eyes feast on. The phrase is telling. Idolatry begins with the eyes, with what we keep looking at and longing for.

Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them. Exodus says little about Israel’s sin in Egypt; Ezekiel shows that they deserved destruction even there. The rescue was mercy from the first day.

verseByVerse.quote: But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations among whom they lived, in whose sight I made myself known to them in bringing them out of the land of Egypt. So I led them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness. I gave them my statutes and made known to them my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live. Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, as a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God spared and rescued Israel for the sake of his own name, and gave them his life-giving law and his Sabbaths as signs that he is the one who makes them holy.

I acted for the sake of my name. Here is the key phrase of the chapter, sounded four times in all (vv. 9, 14, 22, 44). Why did God not destroy Israel in Egypt? Not because they deserved mercy, but because his own name, his reputation and glory among the nations, was at stake.

Why God guards his name. This is not vanity. God’s name is his revealed character: faithful, gracious, true to his promises. Had he abandoned Israel, the nations would have concluded that he was weak or false, as Moses argued on the mountain (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:15–16). And it is the firmest ground of hope there is. Our salvation does not rest on our faithfulness, which fails, but on God’s commitment to his own glory, which never does. “For my name’s sake I defer my anger… My glory I will not give to another” (Isaiah 48:9, 11). “Your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake” (1 John 2:12).

Brought them into the wilderness. Freedom from Egypt did not lead straight into comfort; it led into a school. Moses told the next generation why: God led them “that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart”, and to teach them “that man does not live by bread alone” (Deuteronomy 8:2–3). Many believers find that God brings them out of one bondage and then into a hard season. It is not abandonment; it is training.

If a person does them, he shall live. At Sinai God gave his law as a gift of life (Leviticus 18:5). It showed the way of life, and it also showed that no one walks that way perfectly. Paul quotes this very sentence to show that the law cannot save sinners: “The one who does them shall live by them”, but “all who rely on works of the law are under a curse”, and “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:10, 12–13). Christ is the one man who did them and deserved to live, and he died for those who did not.

I gave them my Sabbaths. The Sabbath was a weekly sign that Israel belonged to God and that he, not they, made them holy: “that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them” (compare Exodus 31:13). Resting from work was a confession of dependence, not a way of earning holiness by resting correctly. And it pointed forward: “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God”, entered by those who rest from their own works (Hebrews 4:9–10). When Christians rest and gather on the Lord’s Day, they confess that their standing with God rests on what Christ has finished.

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath command still bind Christians? Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment continues as a Christian Sabbath on the Lord’s Day; Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ himself, who gives the rest it pictured (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10), for the New Testament calls it a shadow whose substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). The Lord’s Day is a gift: believers gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5). Faithful believers differ here in love.

verseByVerse.quote: But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They did not walk in my statutes but rejected my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; and my Sabbaths they greatly profaned. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them in the wilderness, to make a full end of them. But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out. Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would not bring them into the land that I had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands, because they rejected my rules and did not walk in my statutes, and profaned my Sabbaths; for their heart went after their idols. Nevertheless, my eye spared them, and I did not destroy them or make a full end of them in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The generation that received the law rebelled in the wilderness and died there, yet God did not wipe out the nation.

Rebelled against me in the wilderness. The second round. The same people who received the law at Sinai rejected it in the wilderness, despising the very rules that would have given them life.

For their heart went after their idols. That generation did not enter the land; they died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:28–35). And the root is named again: disobedience is always a matter of the heart’s loves.

Nevertheless, my eye spared them. The judgment was real, but it was not total. God spared the nation, even as he disciplined a generation. “Yet he saved them for his name’s sake, that he might make known his mighty power” (Psalm 106:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "And I said to their children in the wilderness, 'Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, nor keep their rules, nor defile yourselves with their idols. I am the LORD your God; walk in my statutes, and be careful to obey my rules, and keep my Sabbaths holy that they may be a sign between me and you, that you may know that I am the LORD your God.' But the children rebelled against me. They did not walk in my statutes and were not careful to obey my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; they profaned my Sabbaths. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the wilderness. But I withheld my hand and acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next generation was called to break with their fathers’ ways, but they rebelled too, and again God held back for his name’s sake.

Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers. The third round: the next generation. God calls them to break with their parents, exactly the message of chapter 18. A new generation always has a chance to choose differently.

Traditions as a rival law. God calls the fathers’ way of life “the statutes of your fathers” and “their rules”. Human traditions can harden into a rival law. Jesus said to the religious leaders of his day, “You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men” (Mark 7:8). Every generation must test the customs it inherits against God’s word.

But the children rebelled against me. That generation did not break with their parents. At Baal of Peor, on the edge of the promised land, “the people ate and bowed down to their gods” (Numbers 25:2).

I withheld my hand. A third time, “for the sake of my name”. The pattern is relentless: rebellion, deserved wrath, mercy for his name’s sake. If God’s patience depended on Israel’s goodness, there would have been no Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the countries, because they had not obeyed my rules, but had rejected my statutes and profaned my Sabbaths, and their eyes were set on their fathers' idols. Moreover, I gave them statutes that were not good and rules by which they could not have life, and I defiled them through their very gifts in their offering up all their firstborn, that I might devastate them. I did it that they might know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because they kept choosing their idols, God swore to scatter them and gave them over to the evil customs they preferred, even the horror of child sacrifice.

I would scatter them among the nations. Already in the wilderness, God warned that persistent rebellion would end in scattering (Leviticus 26:33). The exile Ezekiel’s hearers were living in had been announced centuries before.

I gave them statutes that were not good. These are hard verses, and they must be read with care. God is not saying that he commanded child sacrifice. Through Jeremiah he said of it, “which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind” (Jeremiah 7:31). He is saying that when his people rejected his good statutes, he handed them over to the evil customs they preferred. Some add that the law giving every firstborn to the LORD (Exodus 13:2, 12) was twisted into offering firstborn children to idols; either way the guilt is theirs.

Judgment by letting go. This is God’s giving people over: as a judgment, he lets them have the sin they insist on. “So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels” (Psalm 81:12). “God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven” (Acts 7:42). “God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts” (Romans 1:24). It is a terrible judgment. The statutes they chose instead of his were “not good” and could not give life. They led to the horror of offering their own firstborn, and that horror itself became part of the judgment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The present generation is repeating its fathers’ sins, and its secret wish to blend into the world will never be granted. Once in the land, the fathers worshipped on every high hill and under every leafy tree (vv. 27–29). Now God asks the elders whether they will do the same, for they still offer their children in fire, and so he will not be inquired of by them (vv. 30–31). He exposes the thought in their minds, “Let us be like the nations… and worship wood and stone”, and declares that it shall never happen (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: God will not let his people dissolve into the world, even when they want to.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, son of man, speak to the house of Israel and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: In this also your fathers blasphemed me, by dealing treacherously with me. For when I had brought them into the land that I swore to give them, then wherever they saw any high hill or any leafy tree, there they offered their sacrifices and there they presented the provocation of their offering; there they sent up their pleasing aromas, and there they poured out their drink offerings. (I said to them, 'What is the high place to which you go?' So its name is called Bamah to this day.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once in the land God had sworn to give them, the fathers turned every hill and leafy tree into a shrine for other gods.

Any high hill or any leafy tree. The fourth round is life in the land. God kept his oath and brought them in, and wherever they saw a high hill or a leafy tree, they worshipped there. Every beautiful place became a shrine to something other than God.

Worshippers by nature. That is a picture of the human heart. We are worshippers by nature. If we do not worship the Creator, we will turn every good thing he made, beauty, pleasure, nature, success, into a god (Romans 1:25).

What is the high place to which you go? God asks a question that sounds almost weary. A high place was a hilltop shrine, and the name Bamah stuck as a reminder of their unfaithfulness.

Uncertain wording. Verse 29 is a play on words that English cannot carry. The Hebrew for “high place” is bamah, and God’s question sounds like it, using the words for “what” (mah) and “go” (ba). It seems to be a scornful pun, something like “What is this bamah you keep going to?”, but exactly what the aside about the name means is not certain.
verseByVerse.note: “Bamah” means “high place” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Will you defile yourselves after the manner of your fathers and go whoring after their detestable things? When you present your gifts and offer up your children in fire, you defile yourselves with all your idols to this day. And shall I be inquired of by you, O house of Israel? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you. "What is in your mind shall never happen—the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The present generation is doing just what its fathers did, and its secret wish to blend into the nations will never be granted.

After the manner of your fathers. Now the history lesson lands on the elders in the room. You have heard what your fathers did. Will you do the same?

Offer up your children in fire. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is “make your children pass through the fire”. The same sins continue, and so the answer to their request is the same: “I will not be inquired of by you.”

Let us be like the nations. Here is what was really in their hearts: not repentance, but a wish to disappear into the nations around them. In exile, the easiest path was to blend in, adopt Babylon’s gods, customs and values, and stop being different. It is the same wish Israel had when they demanded a king, “that we also may be like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:20).

What is in your mind shall never happen. God will not let his people dissolve into the world. That is both a rebuke and a mercy. Christians face the same pull: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). That renewal is not willpower; it is the work of the Spirit God has given to the people he has already claimed as his own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–44 — The Wilderness of the Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not let his people go: he will be their king, judge them in a new exodus and bring them home for his name’s sake. With a mighty hand and wrath poured out he will gather them from the nations and meet them face to face in “the wilderness of the peoples”, as he met their fathers (vv. 33–36). Each will pass under the shepherd’s rod, and the rebels will be purged (vv. 37–38). Then, with idols renounced, all Israel will serve him on his holy mountain, accepted as a pleasing aroma (vv. 39–42), and they will loathe their sins when they see that he has dealt with them “not according to your evil ways” (vv. 43–44).
verseByVerse.theology: God's kingship will not let his people go; he purifies them and restores them by grace, not by their deserving.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you. I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you are scattered, with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out. And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. As I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will not let his people go: he will be their king, bring them out in a new exodus and meet them face to face in the wilderness.

I will be king over you. They wanted to be like the nations. God says: you are mine, and I will rule you, whether you like it or not.

With a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. This is the language of the exodus: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment” (Exodus 6:6). But now there is something added: “with wrath poured out”. God’s kingship over his rebellious people will mean both rescue and discipline.

I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples. A new exodus. God will bring them out of the nations as he brought their fathers out of Egypt, and lead them into a new wilderness, where he will meet them “face to face”, as at Sinai. The wilderness is a place of testing and sifting: before the promised land, a reckoning.

Face to face. At Sinai “The LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire” (Deuteronomy 5:4). Meeting God face to face is terrifying for rebels and glorious for the redeemed. For those in Christ, the promise is the glorious one: “now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

If you are drifting. There is deep comfort here for anyone who belongs to God and is drifting. He will not let you go. His love is not a passive feeling; it is a King’s determined claim.

verseByVerse.quote: I will make you pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant. I will purge out the rebels from among you, and those who transgress against me. I will bring them out of the land where they sojourn, but they shall not enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a shepherd counting his flock, God will examine each of his people one by one, bind the faithful to himself and purge out the rebels.

I will make you pass under the rod. A shepherd counted his sheep by making them pass one by one under his staff (Leviticus 27:32; Jeremiah 33:13). God will do that with his people. Each one will be examined, and not one will be missed.

The bond of the covenant. That is a picture of personal care as well as judgment. Jesus the Good Shepherd “calls his own sheep by name and leads them out” (John 10:3), and those who pass under his rod are brought into the bond of the covenant, bound to him again as his own people.

I will purge out the rebels from among you. The rebels will leave Babylon but will not enter the land, just as the rebellious generation left Egypt and died in the wilderness. Being among God’s people outwardly is not the same as belonging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, O house of Israel, thus says the Lord GOD: Go serve every one of you his idols, now and hereafter, if you will not listen to me; but my holy name you shall no more profane with your gifts and your idols. "For on my holy mountain, the mountain height of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, there all the house of Israel, all of them, shall serve me in the land. There I will accept them, and there I will require your contributions and the choicest of your gifts, with all your sacred offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells the half-hearted to stop mixing his worship with idols, and promises that one day all his people will serve him with undivided hearts on his holy mountain.

Go serve every one of you his idols. A startling, ironic command. If you insist, go ahead, but stop pretending to worship me at the same time. What God hates most is a mixture, idols on Monday and the LORD’s name on the Sabbath: “my holy name you shall no more profane”.

Elijah’s choice. Elijah put the same choice to Israel on Mount Carmel: “How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him” (1 Kings 18:21). God would rather have honest rejection than a divided heart that uses his name as decoration. The worst place to stand is in between.

On my holy mountain. Then the promise: “all the house of Israel, all of them, shall serve me”. Not a divided worship, but whole-hearted service. “There I will accept them.” The God who refused to be inquired of at the start of the chapter will accept his people’s worship at the end.

All the house of Israel, all of them. The divided kingdoms of north and south will worship together again. Ezekiel will hear it more fully later: “they shall be no longer two nations, and no longer divided into two kingdoms” (37:22). God’s restoration heals divisions among his people as well as their relationship with him.

verseByVerse.quote: As a pleasing aroma I will accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you have been scattered. And I will manifest my holiness among you in the sight of the nations. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I bring you into the land of Israel, the country that I swore to give to your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will accept his gathered people themselves as a pleasing sacrifice and show his holiness through them before the nations, keeping the oath he swore to their fathers.

As a pleasing aroma I will accept you. Not only their offerings, but the people themselves, will be a fragrance to God. That is the language of acceptable sacrifice.

How can sinners become a pleasing aroma to God? Only through another. “Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). In him believers become “the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15), and offer “spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5).

I will manifest my holiness among you in the sight of the nations. The nations saw God’s name profaned when Israel sinned and was scattered; they will see his holiness when he restores and purifies his people. The church’s life is meant to do the same: “let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

The country that I swore to give to your fathers. The oath of v. 5 is kept. God’s promises outlast every generation’s rebellion.

Where Christians differ: how is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Some Christians (often called dispensationalists, after their scheme of distinct ages in God’s dealings) look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. This commentary’s view: the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation. Christians who love Scripture differ on how much of this still awaits a fulfilment in the land, and should hold their views with charity.

verseByVerse.quote: And there you shall remember your ways and all your deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you shall loathe yourselves for all the evils that you have committed. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways, nor according to your corrupt deeds, O house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Restored by grace, God’s people will at last see their sin for what it was, and know that he saved them for his name’s sake, not as they deserved.

There you shall remember your ways. The order matters. First God restores them; then they remember and loathe their sin. Repentance deepens after grace, not only before it. The more clearly a believer sees God’s kindness, the more deeply he hates the sin that grace forgave.

Not according to your evil ways. The chapter’s refrain comes home: “for my name’s sake, not according to your evil ways”. This is the gospel in one line. “He does not deal with us according to our sins” (Psalm 103:10). “For your name’s sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great” (Psalm 25:11). God saves sinners not because of anything in them but because of who he is, and at the cross he did it in a way that is just as well as merciful (Romans 3:26).

Mercy based on his name. If you are tempted to think your record is too bad for God, remember that his mercy has never been based on the record. It is based on his name.

What it does not mean. “You shall loathe yourselves” is not the despair that says I am worthless. It is the clear-eyed shame of people who see what their sin was in the light of a love that has already received them (compare 16:63). If thoughts of self-loathing ever turn into hopelessness or thoughts of harming yourself, tell someone the same day: a pastor, a doctor or a trusted friend.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–49 — Fire in the Forest of the South
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment is coming on the whole land, whether people take it seriously or not. Ezekiel is told to face the south and prophesy against its forest: God will kindle a fire that devours every green tree and every dry tree, and no one will quench it (vv. 45–48). Ezekiel cries out that the people brush him aside: “Is he not a maker of parables?” (v. 49). The next chapter explains the parable without a picture, but the fire is no less real for coming in a story.
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgment spares neither the green nor the dry, and dismissing the messenger as a storyteller does not stop the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward the southland; preach against the south, and prophesy against the forest land in the Negeb. Say to the forest of the Negeb, Hear the word of the LORD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour every green tree in you and every dry tree. The blazing flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from south to north shall be scorched by it. All flesh shall see that I the LORD have kindled it; it shall not be quenched." Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! They are saying of me, 'Is he not a maker of parables?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A parable of a forest fire warns that God’s judgment will sweep through the whole land, and the people dismiss it as just another story.

Set your face toward the southland. In the Hebrew Bible this begins chapter 21 (ESV note): a short parable that leads into the prophecy of the sword that follows. The ESV notes that “toward the southland” may be “toward Teman”. The south here is Judah, which lay south of the road by which Babylon’s armies entered the land from the north; the next oracle names the target plainly as Jerusalem and its sanctuaries (21:2).

I will kindle a fire in you. A forest fire that devours “every green tree in you and every dry tree”. Judgment will reach everyone, the flourishing as well as the withered, and sweep through the whole land, “from south to north”.

When the wood is green. Perhaps Jesus had this picture in mind when, carrying his cross, he told the weeping women of Jerusalem, “if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?” (Luke 23:31). If the fire of God’s judgment fell on him, the green and innocent tree, how much more will it fall on the dry and guilty, unless they shelter in him.

Is he not a maker of parables? Ezekiel’s frustrated complaint. The people have found a way to dismiss him: he just tells stories, entertaining and clever, but not serious. God will tell him something similar later: “you are to them like one who sings lustful songs with a beautiful voice” (33:32).

Enjoyed but not obeyed. That is still a way people avoid God’s word. They enjoy the preacher, admire the illustrations and go home unchanged. Jesus spoke in parables too (Matthew 13:34), and many heard the stories and missed the King. The fire in the parable is no less real because it comes in a story.

20.title: For the Sake of My Name
20.overview:
Where we are. Eleven months after the temple vision (8:1), elders come to Ezekiel again (v. 1). This is the last dated message before the siege begins (24:1), and God answers their request with one of the hardest refusals in the book and one of its greatest promises.

The message. God will not be used. People who keep their idols and come to him for information will get no answer but the truth about themselves. Israel’s history from Egypt onward has been one long rebellion, and the only reason Israel still exists is that God has acted again and again “for the sake of my name”. That same name is their hope: he will not let them melt into the nations, but will be king over them, sift them in a new exodus and bring them home to serve him with whole hearts, dealing with them “not according to your evil ways”.

Why it was said. The exiles wanted a word about going home while still clinging to their idols, and some were ready to stop being different and become like the nations around them (v. 32; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God refuses to be consulted and turns the elders’ question into a history lesson (vv. 1–4). In Egypt, in the wilderness and with the next generation the story runs the same way: God gives, Israel rebels, and God holds back for his name’s sake, until he hands them over to the statutes they preferred (vv. 5–26). In the land and in exile it is no different, and their plan to be like the nations will never happen (vv. 27–32). Instead God will be king over them: a new exodus, the rebels purged, and all Israel serving him on his holy mountain, accepted and ashamed at last of their sin (vv. 33–44). A short parable of a forest fire closes the chapter, and the people dismiss Ezekiel as a teller of stories (vv. 45–49).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and by promise. The God who saves for his name’s sake sent the Son who prayed, “Father, glorify your name” (John 12:28). Israel failed in the wilderness; Jesus went into the wilderness and did not (Matthew 4:1–11). The law said, “if a person does them, he shall live”, and he alone did them, then bore the curse for those who had not (Galatians 3:10–13). In him sinners become a pleasing aroma to God (2 Corinthians 2:15), and the Good Shepherd counts each of his sheep by name (John 10:3).

For us. Ask why you come to God: to obey him, or only to plan around him? Your hope does not rest on your record, which is no better than Israel’s, but on his name, which he will never let fall. And he will not let his own people slip quietly into the world.
20.theology:
God will not be consulted like a fortune teller by people unwilling to give up their idols (vv. 3, 31).

Israel's history shows persistent rebellion from Egypt onward, rooted in hearts and eyes set on idols (vv. 7-8, 16, 24).

God's patience and mercy rest on the glory of his own name, which is the firmest ground of hope for sinners (vv. 9, 14, 22, 44; Isa 48:9-11; Ps 106:8; 1 John 2:12).

God's law is good and life-giving, but sinners cannot gain life by it; Christ bore its curse (vv. 11, 13, 21; Lev 18:5; Gal 3:10-13).

When people persistently reject God's ways, he may give them over to the destructive ways they prefer (vv. 25-26; Ps 81:11-12; Acts 7:42; Rom 1:24).

God will not let his people dissolve into the world; as King he sifts, purifies and restores them (vv. 32-38; Rom 12:2; John 10:3).

God accepts his people as a pleasing aroma through the sacrifice of Christ, and deals with them by grace, not by their deeds (vv. 41, 44; Eph 5:2; 2 Cor 2:15; Ps 103:10).

Repentance deepens after grace (v. 43).
20.examples:
The elders wanted a forecast and got a history lesson: a land God scouted out in advance for his people, Egypt's idols packed in the luggage of the exodus, and mercy four times over for the sake of his name.

When the people whisper, Let us be like the nations, God says never, and counts his sheep one by one under the shepherd's staff. The chapter ends with a preacher dismissed as a teller of stories, though the fire in his story is real.

keyVerse.quote: And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I deal with you for my name’s sake, not according to your evil ways, nor according to your corrupt deeds, O house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter has shown that Israel’s record could earn nothing but wrath, and that God kept acting “for the sake of my name”. Here that refrain becomes the ground of their final hope: God will save them because of who he is, not because of what they are. It is the gospel in Old Testament words, fulfilled when God justified sinners through Christ for his name’s sake.

20.reflection:
The elders came to inquire of the LORD while their idols stayed in their hearts (vv. 1–3; compare 14:3). What is the difference between seeking God’s guidance in order to obey it and seeking it in order to plan around it? How can we tell which we are doing?

Four times God says he acted “for the sake of my name” (vv. 9, 14, 22, 44). Why is it good news that our salvation rests on God’s concern for his own name rather than on our record?

The exiles thought, “Let us be like the nations” (v. 32). In what ways are Christians today tempted to blend in and stop being different? Why is God’s refusal to let that happen a mercy?

Verse 43 says God’s people will loathe their sins after he has restored them. How does seeing God’s kindness deepen repentance? Has that been true in your own experience?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s sword is drawn against Jerusalem, and his prophet must feel it before he announces it. The fire of the forest parable is now named plainly: the LORD is against the land, and his own sword will cut off righteous and wicked alike, from south to north, so that all flesh will know that he is the LORD (vv. 1–4). Once drawn, “it shall not be sheathed again” (v. 5). Ezekiel must groan before the people with a breaking heart, and when they ask why, tell them that news is coming which will make every heart melt and every knee turn to water (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's judgment falls on a nation, it touches everyone in it, and the messenger feels it first.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries. Prophesy against the land of Israel and say to the land of Israel, Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am against you and will draw my sword from its sheath and will cut off from you both righteous and wicked. Because I will cut off from you both righteous and wicked, therefore my sword shall be drawn from its sheath against all flesh from south to north. And all flesh shall know that I am the LORD. I have drawn my sword from its sheath; it shall not be sheathed again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fire of chapter 20 is God’s own sword, drawn against Jerusalem, and it will not go back into its sheath until its work is done.

Set your face toward Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries. The people had complained that Ezekiel spoke in riddles (20:49), so God now explains the parable of the fire. The forest is Jerusalem and the land; the fire is a sword; and the sword is God’s own: “my sword”. It strikes first at “the sanctuaries” the people trusted to protect them.

Both righteous and wicked. Does this contradict chapter 18, where the righteous man “shall surely live” (18:9)? No. Chapter 18 speaks of each person’s final standing before God; chapter 21 speaks of a historical catastrophe that will sweep over the whole land. When Jerusalem fell, faithful people suffered too: Jeremiah was dragged to Egypt, and Daniel and Ezekiel were already exiles.

The world believers live in. God “sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45), and disasters fall on both. Christians are not exempt from war, disease or collapse. But the same suffering has a different meaning for those who belong to God: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress … or sword? … No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:35, 37).

It shall not be sheathed again. For years the sword stayed in its sheath while God warned. Now the warnings are over.

A note on the numbering. The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this verse is 21:6; the parable of the forest fire (20:45–49) opens the chapter there.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, groan; with breaking heart and bitter grief, groan before their eyes. And when they say to you, 'Why do you groan?' you shall say, 'Because of the news that it is coming. Every heart will melt, and all hands will be feeble; every spirit will faint, and all knees will be weak as water. Behold, it is coming, and it will be fulfilled,'" declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel must announce the sword with a breaking heart, because the messenger’s grief is part of the message.

With breaking heart and bitter grief. He is not allowed to announce this calmly. He must groan publicly, “before their eyes”.

Why do you groan? When the people ask, his answer is: because I know what is coming. When the news of Jerusalem’s fall arrives, “every heart will melt” and “all knees will be weak as water”.

A preacher who groans. That is the posture of a faithful preacher of judgment. He does not stand at a distance, pointing; he feels the weight of what he announces. Jesus wept over Jerusalem before he foretold its fall (Luke 19:41–44). Anyone who can speak of God’s judgment without a breaking heart has not yet understood it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — A Sword Sharpened and Polished
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song of the sword says that judgment is now certain, because God’s people despised every lighter discipline. In harsh, repeated cries the sword is sharpened and polished to flash like lightning, ready for the hand of the slayer (vv. 9–11). It is aimed at God’s own people and their princes, who have despised the rod, so Ezekiel must wail and strike his thigh (vv. 10, 12–13). He claps his hands and the sword falls again and again, glittering at every gate and cutting right and left (vv. 14–16), until God himself claps his hands and satisfies his fury (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who despise God's gentler discipline will meet his sword.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, prophesy and say, Thus says the Lord, say: "A sword, a sword is sharpened and also polished, sharpened for slaughter, polished to flash like lightning! (Or shall we rejoice? You have despised the rod, my son, with everything of wood.) So the sword is given to be polished, that it may be grasped in the hand. It is sharpened and polished to be given into the hand of the slayer. Cry out and wail, son of man, for it is against my people. It is against all the princes of Israel. They are delivered over to the sword with my people. Strike therefore upon your thigh. For it will not be a testing—what could it do if you despise the rod?" declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s sword is sharpened and polished for slaughter, because his people despised the lighter rod of his discipline.

A sword, a sword is sharpened. This is a song of the sword: harsh, rhythmic, repetitive. Sharpened to cut, polished “to flash like lightning”; you can almost hear the blade on the whetstone. Babylon will wield it, but God has sharpened it.

You have despised the rod, my son. The rod was the instrument of a father’s discipline. “My son, do not despise the LORD’s discipline … for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:11–12). Israel had been disciplined with the rod again and again, and had despised it. Now comes the sword.

The Father’s rod. God’s lighter discipline is a Father’s mercy to children he loves, meant to spare them heavier judgment. To ignore the rod is to invite the sword; to bow under it and confess is to find him ready to forgive (Psalm 32:5).

For it is against my people. That is what makes Ezekiel wail: the sword falls on “all the princes of Israel” as well as on the people. Striking the thigh was a gesture of grief and horror (compare Jeremiah 31:19).

It will not be a testing. Whatever the exact wording, the thrust is plain: this sword is not another round of testing. It is the end of testing.

Uncertain wording. Verses 10 and 13 are among the hardest lines in Ezekiel; even “Or shall we rejoice?” may be the careless people speaking or a question meaning, is this a time to rejoice? The next words are literally “The rod of my son despises everything of wood”, and the ESV’s “You have despised the rod, my son, with everything of wood” is, as its note says, a probable reading. For verse 13 the ESV notes another possible reading: “For it is a testing; and what if even the rod despises? It shall not be!” What is clear is the contrast: Israel scorned the rod of discipline, so now comes a sword that is no mere test.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, prophesy. Clap your hands and let the sword come down twice, yes, three times, the sword for those to be slain. It is the sword for the great slaughter, which surrounds them, that their hearts may melt, and many stumble. At all their gates I have given the glittering sword. Ah, it is made like lightning; it is taken up for slaughter. Cut sharply to the right; set yourself to the left, wherever your face is directed. I also will clap my hands, and I will satisfy my fury; I the LORD have spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sword falls again and again with no way of escape, and God himself gives the signal that his sentence will be carried out.

Let the sword come down twice, yes, three times. Ezekiel claps his hands as the sword swings, and the strokes keep coming. It is “the sword for the great slaughter, which surrounds them”: there is no way out.

At all their gates I have given the glittering sword. At every entrance to the city the flashing sword stands guard, so “that their hearts may melt, and many stumble”.

Cut sharply to the right. The sword is spoken to directly, like a living thing: strike right, strike left, wherever you turn.

I also will clap my hands. Then God himself claps his hands. This is not glee; it is the signal that the verdict is given and the sentence will be carried out.

The sword fell on the Shepherd. For those who shelter in Christ, God’s fury has already been satisfied, on the cross. The sword drawn against sinners fell on the Shepherd instead, as Zechariah foresaw: “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd” (Zechariah 13:7), words Jesus applied to himself (Matthew 26:31). “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).

Uncertain wording. Several words here are hard. The ESV notes that “three times” is literally “its third”, that “many stumble” is literally “many stumbling blocks”, and that the meaning of the word rendered “taken up” is uncertain. The picture is not in doubt.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The King of Babylon at the Crossroads
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD, not the omens of Babylon, decides where the sword goes, and he leaves David’s crown waiting for its true King. Ezekiel draws a road that forks, one way to Rabbah of the Ammonites, the other to Jerusalem (vv. 18–20). At the fork Nebuchadnezzar shakes arrows, consults household idols and inspects a liver, and the lot for Jerusalem falls into his right hand (vv. 21–22). The city dismisses it as pagan nonsense, but God is bringing its guilt to remembrance (vv. 23–24). The profane prince must take off his crown, and the kingdom will lie in ruins “until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs” (vv. 25–27).
verseByVerse.theology: God directs even pagan divination to accomplish his judgment, and he removes the crown until the rightful King comes.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me again: "As for you, son of man, mark two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon to come. Both of them shall come from the same land. And make a signpost; make it at the head of the way to a city. Mark a way for the sword to come to Rabbah of the Ammonites and to Judah, into Jerusalem the fortified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel draws a road with a fork in it, to show that when Babylon’s army chooses its target, the road will lead to Jerusalem.

Mark two ways. Another sign-act. Ezekiel draws a road map, perhaps in the dust, with a fork and a signpost. The Babylonian army is marching west, and at some point the road divides. One branch leads to Rabbah, capital of Ammon across the Jordan, the other to “Jerusalem the fortified”.

Rabbah or Jerusalem? Both nations had plotted against Babylon (Ammon had sent envoys to Zedekiah, Jeremiah 27:3). Which will Nebuchadnezzar attack first? The exiles might have hoped for Rabbah. Ezekiel’s map says: watch the signpost.

verseByVerse.quote: For the king of Babylon stands at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination. He shakes the arrows; he consults the teraphim; he looks at the liver. Into his right hand comes the divination for Jerusalem, to set battering rams, to open the mouth with murder, to lift up the voice with shouting, to set battering rams against the gates, to cast up mounds, to build siege towers. But to them it will seem like a false divination. They have sworn solemn oaths, but he brings their guilt to remembrance, that they may be taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Babylon chooses his road by pagan omens, but the LORD is directing the choice, and Jerusalem’s guilt decides it.

At the parting of the way. Picture the most powerful king in the world standing at a road junction, turning to his religious specialists. He “shakes the arrows”, drawing marked arrows from a quiver like lots. He “consults the teraphim” (the ESV notes, “household idols”). He “looks at the liver” of a sacrificed animal for omens.

Superstition under God’s hand. It is superstition, and yet God controls the outcome. “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (Proverbs 21:1). Nebuchadnezzar thought his gods were guiding him. The LORD was. There is comfort here: no decision by any king, government or court is outside his hand.

What it does not mean. Not that divination works or is approved: God forbade it (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). He rules even over what he condemns.

Into his right hand comes the divination for Jerusalem. The lot falls for Jerusalem, and the verse fills with the sights and sounds of a siege: battering rams, war cries, earth ramps, siege towers.

To them it will seem like a false divination. The people of Jerusalem will dismiss it as pagan fortune-telling, and trust their “solemn oaths”. But behind the pagan omen is God, who “brings their guilt to remembrance”. They laugh at the method and miss the God who is using it.

Uncertain wording. “They have sworn solemn oaths” is compressed in the Hebrew, and whose oaths are meant is uncertain. Most likely they are Zedekiah’s broken oaths of loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar (17:13–19), which now witness against Jerusalem; others think of sworn alliances that made the city feel safe.
verseByVerse.note: Babylon’s king seeks omens: shaking arrows, consulting idols, and reading a sheep’s liver.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have made your guilt to be remembered, in that your transgressions are uncovered, so that in all your deeds your sins appear—because you have come to remembrance, you shall be taken in hand. And you, O profane wicked one, prince of Israel, whose day has come, the time of your final punishment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s own deeds keep its guilt before God, and its profane king has reached the day of his punishment.

Because you have made your guilt to be remembered. Four times in verse 24 God speaks of their guilt remembered or laid bare: it appears “in all your deeds”, and Jerusalem’s own behaviour keeps it in God’s memory.

The new covenant’s contrast. Contrast the promise of the new covenant: “I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). The difference is not that some people sin less. It is whether sin is covered by God’s atonement or left uncovered to be remembered.

O profane wicked one, prince of Israel. Now God turns to the king himself, Zedekiah (see Kings of Israel and Judah). He sat on David’s throne and swore by God’s name, then profaned both by breaking his oath (17:16–19). Now his “day has come, the time of your final punishment”. (The ESV notes that “wicked one” may be read “slain”.)

verseByVerse.quote: thus says the Lord GOD: Remove the turban and take off the crown. Things shall not remain as they are. Exalt that which is low, and bring low that which is exalted. A ruin, ruin, ruin I will make it. This also shall not be, until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs, and I will give it to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s crown is taken from the faithless king and left in the ruins, waiting for the one to whom it truly belongs.

Remove the turban and take off the crown. The ESV uses the same word, “turban”, for the high priest’s headdress (Exodus 28:37). Whatever the exact headdress, the symbols of authority are coming off. “Things shall not remain as they are”: the old order is ending.

Exalt that which is low. The principle of 17:24. The proud king will be humbled, and, as the next verse shows, one who comes low will be exalted.

A ruin, ruin, ruin I will make it. Three times: the strongest way Hebrew can say it. Kingdom, throne and crown will all be overturned.

Until he comes. In the middle of the ruin, a doorway of hope: the crown will lie vacant until one comes to whom it rightly belongs.

Jacob’s ancient promise. This echoes Jacob’s blessing of Judah: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah … until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples” (Genesis 49:10). Where the ESV reads “until tribute comes to him”, the KJV has “until Shiloh come”. The Hebrew is hard; many read it as until he comes to whom it belongs, which is just what Ezekiel seems to echo. For nearly six centuries after Zedekiah no descendant of David reigned as king in Jerusalem. Then an angel said to a young woman of David’s line, Mary: “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Luke 1:32–33).

The one to whom judgment belongs. Jesus is that King. The Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). He wore a crown of thorns before he wore the crown of glory, and on his robe is written “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16). The turban and crown were removed from the profane prince so that they could be given to the holy King, and the one to whom judgment belongs is the one who bore it for his people.

Where Christians differ. Some take “he” in verse 27 to be Nebuchadnezzar, to whom God hands the task of judging Jerusalem (compare 23:24, “I will commit the judgment to them”). Most Christian interpreters hear Genesis 49:10 and see the Messiah.

This commentary’s view. The messianic reading is best: “until” sets a limit to the ruin, the wording echoes Jacob’s promise, and Ezekiel elsewhere promises a king of David’s line (17:22–23; 34:23–24). The Hebrew word for “judgment” (mishpat) can also mean “right”, and both fit Christ: the crown is his by right, and the judgment is his to give.
verseByVerse.note: “Until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs” echoes Jacob’s blessing on Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–32 — A Sword for the Ammonites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Escaping one danger is not escaping God: Ammon, passed over at the crossroads, will still meet the sword, and with no promise beyond it. The sword song begins again, this time against the Ammonites, who mocked Judah and listened to their own diviners’ lies (vv. 28–29). God will judge them in the land where they were born, pour out his indignation and hand them to brutal men, skilled in destruction (vv. 30–31). Judah’s ruin came with an “until he comes”; Ammon’s comes only with this: “You shall be no more remembered” (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: Escaping one judgment does not mean escaping God.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD concerning the Ammonites and concerning their reproach; say, A sword, a sword is drawn for the slaughter. It is polished to consume and to flash like lightning— while they see for you false visions, while they divine lies for you—to place you on the necks of the profane wicked, whose day has come, the time of their final punishment. Return it to its sheath. In the place where you were created, in the land of your origin, I will judge you. And I will pour out my indignation upon you; I will blow upon you with the fire of my wrath, and I will deliver you into the hands of brutish men, skillful to destroy. You shall be fuel for the fire. Your blood shall be in the midst of the land. You shall be no more remembered, for I the LORD have spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ammon, which seemed to escape the sword, will meet it too, and unlike Judah it has no future beyond the ruin.

Concerning the Ammonites and concerning their reproach. The Ammonites might have thought they had escaped: the omen at the crossroads pointed to Jerusalem, not Rabbah. Their “reproach” is their scorn for Judah, which they would show openly when the temple fell (25:3, 6). But the sword song begins again for them: “A sword, a sword is drawn for the slaughter.”

While they divine lies for you. Ammon had its own diviners telling it comforting lies, and will share the fate of Judah’s “profane wicked”.

You shall be no more remembered. Judah had a future beyond the ruin: “until he comes”. Ammon is told the opposite. God will judge it at home, “in the land of your origin”, and Ammon did not endure as a nation.

Discipline and judgment. For Judah, judgment was severe but not final; a King was coming. For those who remain God’s enemies there is no such doorway. Escaping one crisis is not the same as escaping God. The only safe place is under the rule of the King to whom judgment belongs.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain who is told “Return it to its sheath” in verse 30. Most take it as spoken to Ammon: resistance is useless, and I will judge you at home. Others think Babylon’s sword is addressed, and that verses 30–32 turn to judge Babylon itself once its work is done (Jeremiah 25:12). The flow from verse 28 favours the first.

21.title: The Sword of the LORD
21.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 20 (August 591 BC) retold Israel’s whole history of rebellion and ended with a forest fire in the south and the people grumbling that Ezekiel spoke in parables (20:49). Chapter 21 drops the parable and names the fire plainly: it is the sword of the LORD, and it is coming to Jerusalem.

The message. God’s patience has an end. The sword Judah feared from Babylon is really the LORD’s own sword, drawn at last because his people despised the rod of his discipline, and no omen, oath or alliance can turn it aside. Yet in the middle of the ruin God leaves a door open: David’s crown will lie in the dust “until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs” (v. 27). For his people judgment is not the end of his purpose; for Ammon, which mocked them, it is.

Why it was said. The exiles still believed that God would never strike his own city (see the introduction). King Zedekiah had broken his oath to Babylon and was looking to Egypt (17:15), and some may have hoped that Babylon’s army would turn on Ammon instead. Ezekiel must kill those hopes, and do it with a breaking heart.

How the chapter makes its case. First the fire is named as God’s own sword, never to be sheathed, and Ezekiel must groan in public at the news (vv. 1–7). Then comes a song of the sword, sharpened and polished, falling again and again on a people who despised the rod, until God claps his hands and satisfies his fury (vv. 8–17). Next, at a fork in the road, the king of Babylon consults his omens, but the LORD turns him to Jerusalem; the profane prince loses his crown, which waits for its rightful owner (vv. 18–27). Last, Ammon, which seemed to escape, meets the same sword with no such hope (vv. 28–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The promise is verse 27, which echoes Jacob’s blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:10): David’s empty throne waits for the King to whom it belongs, and the angel told Mary that God would give her son “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). The pattern is the sword. God said through Zechariah, “Awake, O sword, against my shepherd” (Zechariah 13:7), and Jesus applied those words to himself on the night of his arrest (Matthew 26:31). The sword drawn against a guilty city fell on the innocent Shepherd, so that all who shelter in him are spared.

For us. God’s rod of discipline is a Father’s mercy, given to spare us the sword, so do not despise it. No ruler’s decision lies outside his hand, even one made by reading a sheep’s liver. And the one to whom judgment belongs is the one who bore it for us: shelter in him now, while the door stands open.
21.theology:
Disasters in history, such as war and siege, fall on righteous and wicked alike, but they cannot separate believers from the love of Christ (vv. 3-4; 18:20; Matt 5:45; Rom 8:35-37). The messenger of judgment must feel its weight (vv. 6-7, 12), and those who despise God's gentler discipline invite his severer judgment (vv. 10, 13; Prov 3:11-12).

God directs even pagan divination and the decisions of kings (vv. 21-22; Prov 16:33; 21:1). Sin not covered by God's atonement remains remembered (vv. 23-24).

God removed the crown from David's faithless heir until the coming of the one to whom judgment belongs, Jesus the Son of David (vv. 26-27; Gen 49:10; Luke 1:32-33; John 5:22; Rev 19:16). Escaping one judgment is not escaping God: for his enemies there is no doorway of hope apart from his King (vv. 28-32).
21.examples:
Picture a sword on the whetstone, polished until it flashes like lightning, and a prophet groaning in the street until people stop and ask him why. A father's rod has been despised, so a sword comes instead.

Then picture the most powerful king on earth at a road junction, peering at a sheep's liver, never guessing that the LORD is choosing his road for him. And picture a crown taken off and left waiting on an empty throne: ruin, ruin, ruin, until he comes.

keyVerse.quote: A ruin, ruin, ruin I will make it. This also shall not be, until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs, and I will give it to him.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter full of the flashing sword, this is the one ray of light. God overturns the throne of David’s faithless heir, but only “until he comes”: the crown is kept for its rightful owner. It points to Jesus, born of David’s line, to whom the Father has given the throne and all judgment.

21.reflection:
Ezekiel had to announce judgment “with breaking heart and bitter grief” (v. 6). How should this shape the way we speak to others about sin and God’s judgment?

Israel “despised the rod” before the sword came (vv. 10, 13). What does it look like to despise God’s lighter discipline, and what does it look like to receive it well (Hebrews 12:5–11)?

Nebuchadnezzar chose his road by reading a liver, yet the LORD directed his choice (vv. 21–22). Where do you need to trust that God rules over the decisions of powerful people today?

The crown waits “until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs” (v. 27). How does it change the way you think of Jesus to know that the one who will judge is the one who was judged for us?
