I have consumed them with the fire of my wrath. I have returned their way upon their heads, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s indictment of Jerusalem traces every one of her sins to a single root: she has forgotten him. Ezekiel is to confront “the bloody city” with her abominations, for bloodshed and idols have brought her day near and made her a mockery among the nations (vv. 1–5). The charge sheet follows: princes who shed blood, parents despised, strangers, orphans and widows oppressed, holy things and Sabbaths profaned (vv. 6–8); slander, idol feasts, sexual corruption, bribery and extortion, “but me you have forgotten” (vv. 9–12). God strikes his hand at their dishonest gain; their courage will fail, and he will scatter them to burn out their uncleanness (vv. 13–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Forgetting God shows itself in every kind of cruelty and corruption toward neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "And you, son of man, will you judge, will you judge the bloody city? Then declare to her all her abominations. You shall say, Thus says the Lord GOD: A city that sheds blood in her midst, so that her time may come, and that makes idols to defile herself! You have become guilty by the blood that you have shed, and defiled by the idols that you have made, and you have brought your days near, the appointed time of your years has come. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations, and a mockery to all the countries. Those who are near and those who are far from you will mock you; your name is defiled; you are full of tumult.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem, the city of God’s name, has become a “bloody city” like Nineveh, and by her bloodshed and idols she is hastening her own end.

Will you judge the bloody city? Nahum used the same words of Nineveh, the brutal capital of Assyria: “Woe to the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder” (Nahum 3:1). Now God says them of Jerusalem. The city of his name has become like the empire that destroyed Samaria.

Declare to her all her abominations. Ezekiel is made the prosecutor, and what follows reads like a charge sheet.

Blood and idols. Two sins sum up the rest: violence against neighbours and unfaithfulness to God. They always go together. With them Jerusalem has “brought your days near”: she is hastening her own end.

Your name is defiled. The city that bore God’s name has made that name a joke among the nations, mocked by “those who are near and those who are far”.

Uncertain wording. In verse 3 the ESV notes that most manuscripts read “until” for part of the line. The sense is the same either way: Jerusalem’s own bloodshed brings her appointed time upon her.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, the princes of Israel in you, every one according to his power, have been bent on shedding blood. Father and mother are treated with contempt in you; the sojourner suffers extortion in your midst; the fatherless and the widow are wronged in you. You have despised my holy things and profaned my Sabbaths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s leaders use their power to harm, and the city despises the people God most protects and the things he calls holy.

Every one according to his power. Each leader used as much power as he had to harm others. Power itself is not evil, but in corrupt hands it becomes a weapon: the more power, the more damage.

Father and mother are treated with contempt. The list moves into the home and the street. Parents are despised, against the command “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12). The most vulnerable are exploited: the sojourner (immigrant), the fatherless and the widow. God had told Israel, “You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child” (Exodus 22:21–22).

A measure of a society. How a society treats its elderly, its foreigners and its fatherless is one of God’s measures of its health. James says the same of the church: “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27).

You have despised my holy things and profaned my Sabbaths. Toward God, contempt for what is holy, including the weekly Sabbath that marked Israel as his. Sin against neighbours and sin against God are never far apart.

verseByVerse.quote: There are men in you who slander to shed blood, and people in you who eat on the mountains; they commit lewdness in your midst. In you men uncover their fathers' nakedness; in you they violate women who are unclean in their menstrual impurity. One commits abomination with his neighbor's wife; another lewdly defiles his daughter-in-law; another in you violates his sister, his father's daughter. In you they take bribes to shed blood; you take interest and profit and make gain of your neighbors by extortion; but me you have forgotten, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Slander, sexual abuse, bribery and extortion fill the city, and all of it flows from one root: “me you have forgotten”.

There are men in you who slander to shed blood. They make false accusations that get people killed. The law said, “You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people, and you shall not stand up against the life of your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:16). Words can kill.

They commit lewdness in your midst. “Eat on the mountains” means feasting at idol shrines (18:6). The list of sexual sins follows the forbidden relationships of Leviticus 18: incest, adultery, abuse. The family, which God designed as a place of safety, has become a place of violation. These are not private matters; God names them as sins that defile a whole city.

In you they take bribes to shed blood. Bribes buy death sentences. Interest exploits the poor (the ESV notes, “profit that comes from charging interest to the poor”); as in 18:8, the sin is profiting from the needy, not ordinary lending. Extortion completes the list.

But me you have forgotten. Then the line that explains everything. When God is forgotten, parents are despised, the weak are crushed, bodies are abused and money becomes a god. A society falls apart when it forgets God.

Can goodness outlive God? Many thoughtful people today hope so. They have set the faith aside, often for serious reasons, and kept its best convictions: that the weak deserve protection, that every person has dignity, that the poor must not be crushed. Friedrich Nietzsche, no friend of Christianity, thought that hope naive. He mocked the English moralists, George Eliot among them, who gave up the Christian God and imagined they could keep Christian morality, and argued that when the faith goes, the right to its morality goes with it. Ezekiel would not quite agree, since people made in God’s image never wholly lose their conscience (Romans 2:14–15). But he does trace the drift, from a forgotten God to despised parents, exploited strangers and judges for sale.

Forgetting God with a prayer book in your hand. Here is the surprise: Jerusalem had not given up religion. The temple was still open. So the cure is not a firmer grip on moral principles but a remembered God, and he is the one who promised to write his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33) and came himself to stand in the breach (v. 30).
verseByVerse.note: “Profit” means interest charged to the poor (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I strike my hand at the dishonest gain that you have made, and at the blood that has been in your midst. Can your courage endure, or can your hands be strong, in the days that I shall deal with you? I the LORD have spoken, and I will do it. I will scatter you among the nations and disperse you through the countries, and I will consume your uncleanness out of you. And you shall be profaned by your own doing in the sight of the nations, and you shall know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sees both the profit and the victims, and no one’s courage will hold when he acts; yet his aim in the exile is a clean people.

I strike my hand at the dishonest gain. Striking the hand is a gesture of anger and disgust, aimed at the money they made by cheating and the blood they shed. He sees the profit, and he sees the victims.

Can your courage endure? A question for everyone who feels strong now. “Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the heat of his anger?” (Nahum 1:6). People who seem bold in sin are not bold before God.

I will consume your uncleanness out of you. The exile will not only punish; it will purify. God’s goal is a clean people.

Profaned by your own doing. All of it is self-inflicted. Jerusalem’s shame before the nations is the harvest of her own choices, and through it she “shall know that I am the LORD”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will put his people into the furnace, because what should have been silver has become worthless dross. Israel is bronze, tin, iron and lead, cheap metals with no silver among them (v. 18). So God will gather them into Jerusalem, as a smelter gathers metal into a furnace, and blow on them with the fire of his wrath until they melt (vv. 19–21). The city they trust as a refuge becomes the crucible: “As silver is melted in a furnace, so you shall be melted in the midst of it”, and they will know that he is the LORD (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: God's fire exposes what is worthless; a people who should have been silver are found to be dross.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, the house of Israel has become dross to me; all of them are bronze and tin and iron and lead in the furnace; they are dross of silver. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have all become dross, therefore, behold, I will gather you into the midst of Jerusalem. As one gathers silver and bronze and iron and lead and tin into a furnace, to blow the fire on it in order to melt it, so I will gather you in my anger and in my wrath, and I will put you in and melt you. I will gather you and blow on you with the fire of my wrath, and you shall be melted in the midst of it. As silver is melted in a furnace, so you shall be melted in the midst of it, and you shall know that I am the LORD; I have poured out my wrath upon you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel, meant to be silver, has become dross, and Jerusalem, the refuge they run to, will be the furnace that melts them.

The house of Israel has become dross to me. A picture from the metalworker’s shop. When silver ore is melted, the pure silver separates from the worthless impurities, the dross, which is skimmed off and thrown away. Israel was meant to be silver. God says “all of them” are dross: bronze, tin, iron and lead, with no silver among them at all.

Isaiah said it first. “Your silver has become dross”, and “I will turn my hand against you and will smelt away your dross” (Isaiah 1:22, 25).

I will gather you into the midst of Jerusalem. A grim irony. People from the countryside fled into Jerusalem when the Babylonians came, thinking its walls would protect them; the Rechabites did exactly that (Jeremiah 35:11). God says: I am gathering you into the furnace. The city they ran to for safety becomes the melting pot.

The refiner’s fire. For believers, God’s fire has a different purpose. “The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and the LORD tests hearts” (Proverbs 17:3). The Lord who comes to his temple, whom the New Testament shows to be Christ (Malachi 3:1; Mark 1:2), “will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver” (Malachi 3:3). Trials that come to God’s children are refining fire, burning away dross so that what is precious remains. The question every trial asks is: what is left when the fire has done its work?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — I Sought for a Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole land is corrupt from top to bottom, and there is no one to stand between it and God’s wrath. It is a land unwashed and unwatered in the day of his anger (v. 24). Its prophets devour like a roaring lion (v. 25); its priests do violence to his law and blur the holy and the common (v. 26); its princes tear like wolves (v. 27); its prophets whitewash it all with lies (v. 28); and ordinary people rob the poor and the stranger (v. 29). God sought for a man to “stand in the breach before me for the land”, “but I found none” (v. 30). So his wrath has fallen (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: When every level of a society is corrupt and no intercessor stands in the gap, judgment comes; God himself provided the Man who stands in the breach.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, say to her, You are a land that is not cleansed or rained upon in the day of indignation. The conspiracy of her prophets in her midst is like a roaring lion tearing the prey; they have devoured human lives; they have taken treasure and precious things; they have made many widows in her midst. Her priests have done violence to my law and have profaned my holy things. They have made no distinction between the holy and the common, neither have they taught the difference between the unclean and the clean, and they have disregarded my Sabbaths, so that I am profaned among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land lies under a curse because its religious leaders have betrayed it: prophets prey on the people and priests blur every line God drew.

A land that is not cleansed or rained upon. A land with no rain is a land under a curse: no cleansing, no refreshing. Now God walks through the whole society, level by level, to show why.

The conspiracy of her prophets. First, the prophets. They are not shepherds but predators, “like a roaring lion tearing the prey”, the same picture Peter uses for the devil: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). False religious leaders do the devil’s work. They seized people’s wealth, and their violence left many women widows.

Her priests have done violence to my law. Second, the priests. Their job was to teach the difference: “You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean” (Leviticus 10:10). They blurred every line, and when teachers stop teaching the difference between holy and common, right and wrong, the people soon cannot tell.

A charge for teachers. This applies to every pastor and Bible teacher. Our calling is to teach God’s distinctions clearly, “rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15), not to blur them to make people comfortable.

verseByVerse.quote: Her princes in her midst are like wolves tearing the prey, shedding blood, destroying lives to get dishonest gain. And her prophets have smeared whitewash for them, seeing false visions and divining lies for them, saying, 'Thus says the Lord GOD,' when the LORD has not spoken. The people of the land have practiced extortion and committed robbery. They have oppressed the poor and needy, and have extorted from the sojourner without justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Officials prey like wolves, preachers whitewash their crimes, and ordinary people rob the poor: the rot runs through the whole society.

Like wolves tearing the prey. Third, the princes and officials. Zephaniah said the same: “Her officials within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves” (Zephaniah 3:3). Jesus warned of “ravenous wolves” in sheep’s clothing (Matthew 7:15), and Paul of “fierce wolves” that would come into the church (Acts 20:29).

Her prophets have smeared whitewash for them. The prophets cover for the princes, smearing whitewash over their crimes (13:10) and saying “Thus says the Lord GOD” when the LORD has not spoken. Religion is used to make corruption look respectable.

The people of the land. Fourth, the ordinary citizens are no better. They too extort, rob and oppress the poor and the sojourner. The rot is not only at the top. Micah had described the same city: “Its heads give judgment for a bribe; its priests teach for a price; its prophets practice divination for money” (Micah 3:11).

verseByVerse.quote: And I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none. Therefore I have poured out my indignation upon them. I have consumed them with the fire of my wrath. I have returned their way upon their heads, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God looked for one person to stand in the gap and plead for the land, and found none; the gospel is that he then sent his Son to stand there.

I sought for a man among them. A heart-searching verse: God himself searches. He wants one person who would “build up the wall and stand in the breach”, standing in the gap where the wall is broken, between the people and the judgment, to plead for them.

Moses in the breach. Moses had done it once. When God was about to destroy Israel after the golden calf, “Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath” (Psalm 106:23). Now God looks for another Moses among the prophets, priests, princes and people, “but I found none”.

So he became the Man. Isaiah described the same search: “He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede; then his own arm brought him salvation” (Isaiah 59:16). When no human being could stand in the breach, God sent his own Son. “There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). He stood in the breach at the cross, taking the judgment on himself, and “he always lives to make intercession” for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). God sought for a man and found none, so he became the Man.

Standing in the gap today. God still looks for people to stand in the gap in prayer for families, churches and nations. We pray weakly, but the Spirit helps us in our weakness and intercedes for us (Romans 8:26).

I have returned their way upon their heads. With no one in the breach, the wall fell and the judgment came. For Jerusalem, it was too late. For us, the Man in the breach has already come.

22.title: I Sought for a Man
22.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 21 drew God’s sword against Jerusalem and took the crown from its faithless king. Chapter 22, a few years before the siege began, explains why the sword is just. Ezekiel is made the prosecutor, and he reads the city its charge sheet.

The message. Jerusalem’s violence, greed and sexual corruption all grow from one root: “me you have forgotten” (v. 12). A people who forget God soon despise parents, crush the weak and sell justice, and the rot runs through every level, from prophets and priests to princes and ordinary citizens. So God will put the whole city in his furnace. Worst of all, when he looked for one person to stand in the breach and plead for the land, he found none.

Why it was said. The exiles thought of Jerusalem as the holy city, still under God’s protection (see the introduction). Ezekiel shows them what God sees there: a “bloody city”, like Nineveh, with a temple still open and its people’s hearts far from him. The judgment is not God abandoning his city; it is his city having abandoned him.

How the chapter makes its case. First the charge sheet: blood and idols, then sin after sin against parents, strangers, widows, God’s holy things, the family and the poor, all traced to a forgotten God; he will scatter them and burn out their uncleanness (vv. 1–16). Then a picture: Israel has become dross, cheap metal with no silver in it, and God will gather it into Jerusalem as into a furnace and melt it (vv. 17–22). Last, a survey of the whole land: predatory prophets, careless priests, wolfish princes, whitewashing preachers and an oppressive people; and God sought for a man to stand in the breach, “but I found none” (vv. 23–31).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes. The chapter ends with an empty gap in the wall: no prophet, priest, prince or citizen could stand between the people and God’s wrath, as Moses once had (Psalm 106:23). Isaiah saw the same search end with God acting himself: “then his own arm brought him salvation” (Isaiah 59:16). God sought for a man and found none, so he sent the Man, Christ Jesus, the “one mediator between God and men” (1 Timothy 2:5), who stood in the breach at the cross and “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). He is also the refiner of Malachi 3, whose fire purifies rather than destroys.

For us. It is possible to forget God with a prayer book in your hand, and the chapter shows where that forgetting leads. Remember him, and you will not easily despise the weak. Thank God that the gap is filled, and then stand in it yourself in prayer, for your family, your church and your nation.
22.theology:
Violence against people and idolatry against God belong together; both flow from forgetting God (vv. 3-4, 12). So God measures a society by how it treats parents, foreigners, orphans and widows (v. 7; Exod 22:21-22; Jas 1:27), and no one's courage can endure when he deals with sin (v. 14; Nah 1:6).

God's fire exposes worthless dross in judgment and refines his people in discipline (vv. 18-22; Isa 1:22-25; Prov 17:3; Mal 3:3). Religious leaders who blur his distinctions and cover for corruption bear heavy guilt (vv. 25-28; Lev 10:10; Matt 7:15; Acts 20:29).

God looks for intercessors, people who plead with him for others, to stand in the breach, the gap in the wall (v. 30; Ps 106:23). Where no one could, he sent his Son, the one mediator who intercedes forever (Isa 59:16; 1 Tim 2:5; Heb 7:25).
22.examples:
Imagine hearing the holy city called by the name of Nineveh, the byword for cruelty. Imagine leaders using every ounce of their power to harm, slander that ends in a death sentence, and priests who no longer teach the difference between holy and common.

Then imagine walls people ran to for refuge turning into a smelting furnace, and God searching the streets for one intercessor. Finding none, he became the Man himself.

keyVerse.quote: And I sought for a man among them who should build up the wall and stand in the breach before me for the land, that I should not destroy it, but I found none.
keyVerse.note: After a long charge sheet against every level of Jerusalem’s society, this verse lays bare the deepest problem: there was no one to stand between the people and God’s wrath. It shows our need of a mediator, and it is answered in Christ, the one man who stood in the breach and still intercedes for his people.

22.reflection:
Every sin in verses 6–12 is traced to one root: “me you have forgotten” (v. 12). How can a person, or a church, forget God while still being religious? What helps us remember him?

God measures Jerusalem by how it treats parents, immigrants, orphans and widows (v. 7). Who are the vulnerable people around you and your church, and how might you serve them?

The priests failed to teach “the difference between the unclean and the clean” (v. 26). Where are Christians tempted to blur God’s distinctions today, and why does it matter for the people we teach?

God “sought for a man among them” to “stand in the breach”, but “found none” (v. 30). How does Jesus fulfil this, and what would it look like for you to stand in the gap in prayer for others this week?

23.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother.<sup>3</sup>They played the whore in Egypt; they played the whore in their youth; there their breasts were pressed and their virgin bosoms handled.<sup>4</sup>Oholah was the name of the elder and Oholibah the name of her sister. They became mine, and they bore sons and daughters. As for their names, Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>"Oholah played the whore while she was mine, and she lusted after her lovers the Assyrians, warriors<sup>6</sup>clothed in purple, governors and commanders, all of them desirable young men, horsemen riding on horses.<sup>7</sup>She bestowed her whoring upon them, the choicest men of Assyria all of them, and she defiled herself with all the idols of everyone after whom she lusted.<sup>8</sup>She did not give up her whoring that she had begun in Egypt; for in her youth men had lain with her and handled her virgin bosom and poured out their whoring lust upon her.<sup>9</sup>Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, into the hands of the Assyrians, after whom she lusted.<sup>10</sup>These uncovered her nakedness; they seized her sons and her daughters; and as for her, they killed her with the sword; and she became a byword among women, when judgment had been executed on her.<sup>11</sup>"Her sister Oholibah saw this, and she became more corrupt than her sister in her lust and in her whoring, which was worse than that of her sister.<sup>12</sup>She lusted after the Assyrians, governors and commanders, warriors clothed in full armor, horsemen riding on horses, all of them desirable young men.<sup>13</sup>And I saw that she was defiled; they both took the same way.<sup>14</sup>But she carried her whoring further. She saw men portrayed on the wall, the images of the Chaldeans portrayed in vermilion,<sup>15</sup>wearing belts on their waists, with flowing turbans on their heads, all of them having the appearance of officers, a likeness of Babylonians whose native land was Chaldea.<sup>16</sup>When she saw them, she lusted after them and sent messengers to them in Chaldea.<sup>17</sup>And the Babylonians came to her into the bed of love, and they defiled her with their whoring lust. And after she was defiled by them, she turned from them in disgust.<sup>18</sup>When she carried on her whoring so openly and flaunted her nakedness, I turned in disgust from her, as I had turned in disgust from her sister.<sup>19</sup>Yet she increased her whoring, remembering the days of her youth, when she played the whore in the land of Egypt<sup>20</sup>and lusted after her lovers there, whose members were like those of donkeys, and whose issue was like that of horses.<sup>21</sup>Thus you longed for the lewdness of your youth, when the Egyptians handled your bosom and pressed your young breasts."<sup>22</sup>Therefore, O Oholibah, thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I will stir up against you your lovers from whom you turned in disgust, and I will bring them against you from every side:<sup>23</sup>the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans, Pekod and Shoa and Koa, and all the Assyrians with them, desirable young men, governors and commanders all of them, officers and men of renown, all of them riding on horses.<sup>24</sup>And they shall come against you from the north with chariots and wagons and a host of peoples. And behold, this is what they did in my house.<sup>40</sup>They even sent for men to come from afar, to whom a messenger was sent; and behold, they came. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells the story of his two unfaithful peoples as the story of two sisters, so that they will see their idolatry as betrayal of love. The sisters, daughters of one mother, were already unfaithful in their youth in Egypt (vv. 2–3). Yet God took them as his own: “They became mine, and they bore sons and daughters.” Then he names them: “Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem” (v. 4). Grace came first, and everything that follows in the chapter is the betrayal of that grace.
verseByVerse.theology: God's people were unfaithful from the beginning, yet he still made them his own.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, there were two women, the daughters of one mother. They played the whore in Egypt; they played the whore in their youth; there their breasts were pressed and their virgin bosoms handled. Oholah was the name of the elder and Oholibah the name of her sister. They became mine, and they bore sons and daughters. As for their names, Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God pictures Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters he made his own despite their past, so that their later unfaithfulness is seen for what it is: the betrayal of grace.

There were two women. Chapter 23 returns to the picture of chapter 16, but now there are two sisters instead of one. The language is again blunt and disturbing, and deliberately so. God wants his people to be shocked by what their spiritual unfaithfulness looks like.

Before reading on. The two women are cities, and the husband is God: this is an allegory about nations and their idols, not a pattern for any marriage. The cruelty described later in the chapter is what invading armies did, and God names it as the bitter harvest of trusting them, not as a way any man may treat a woman. Scripture never licenses abuse; a husband is to love his wife “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Anyone suffering abuse should seek safety at once. Readers who have been wounded in this way may find these verses painful, and may take comfort that the God who speaks here also judges the brutal (Jeremiah 50–51 is his sentence on Babylon), and in Christ bears shame himself.

They played the whore in Egypt. Both sisters were unfaithful even as girls in Egypt. The point is historical and spiritual: Israel’s idolatry did not begin in Canaan but in Egypt, before the exodus, as 20:7–8 has already said.

Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem. Oholah is Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel; Oholibah is Jerusalem, capital of Judah. The two kingdoms came from one people. The names are wordplay: Oholah sounds like “her tent” and Oholibah like “my tent is in her”, perhaps recalling the tabernacle, God’s tent, which was rightly at Jerusalem.

They became mine. These are the most striking words. Despite their unfaithfulness in Egypt, God took them as his own, and they bore children to him. Grace came first; everything that follows betrays that grace.

Jeremiah’s two sisters. Jeremiah had used the same picture: Israel was unfaithful and sent away, “Yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but she too went and played the whore” (Jeremiah 3:8).

Uncertain wording. The meaning of the names is not certain. Both are built on the Hebrew word for “tent” (ohel), and the explanation above is the most common one. Some take “tent” to refer instead to the tent shrines of pagan worship. Either way, the names tie both sisters to worship, the heart of the chapter’s charge.
verseByVerse.note: Oholah (Samaria) probably means “her tent” and Oholibah (Jerusalem) “my tent is in her”: perhaps contrasting Samaria’s own shrines with God’s temple in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samaria trusted the power of Assyria instead of God, and was destroyed by the power she trusted. While she belonged to God, Oholah lusted after the Assyrians, dazzled by their purple-clad officers and horsemen, and took on their idols with their friendship (vv. 5–7). She never gave up the unfaithfulness she had begun in Egypt (v. 8). So God handed her over to the lovers she desired: they stripped her, took her children and killed her, and she became a byword among the nations (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: The powers we court instead of God become the instruments of our ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: "Oholah played the whore while she was mine, and she lusted after her lovers the Assyrians, warriors clothed in purple, governors and commanders, all of them desirable young men, horsemen riding on horses. She bestowed her whoring upon them, the choicest men of Assyria all of them, and she defiled herself with all the idols of everyone after whom she lusted. She did not give up her whoring that she had begun in Egypt; for in her youth men had lain with her and handled her virgin bosom and poured out their whoring lust upon her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samaria was dazzled by Assyria’s power and glamour, and in courting it she took on its gods.

She lusted after her lovers the Assyrians. Look at what attracted her: purple uniforms, governors, commanders and cavalry, the power and glamour of empire, “all of them desirable young men”. Assyria was the superpower of the day, and Samaria wanted to be close to it.

What actually happened. This was real history. King Menahem of Israel paid the king of Assyria “a thousand talents of silver, that he might help him to confirm his hold on the royal power” (2 Kings 15:19; see Talent). Political alliance came with religious compromise.

She defiled herself with all the idols. When you give your heart to a power, you take on its gods. Admiring the world’s strength and style often ends in adopting its values.

She did not give up her whoring. She never gave up the unfaithfulness she had begun in Egypt. Sin that is not dealt with early does not fade; it grows.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, into the hands of the Assyrians, after whom she lusted. These uncovered her nakedness; they seized her sons and her daughters; and as for her, they killed her with the sword; and she became a byword among women, when judgment had been executed on her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God handed Samaria over to the lovers she chose, and the power she admired became her destroyer.

I delivered her into the hands of her lovers. This is the terrible justice of God. The Assyrians she admired destroyed her: “the king of Assyria captured Samaria, and he carried the Israelites away to Assyria” (2 Kings 17:6), in 722 BC.

When idols turn on us. The things we love in place of God have a way of turning on us. The career that was worshipped consumes the family. The pleasure that was pursued enslaves. The power that was courted crushes. “Do not love the world or the things in the world. … And the world is passing away along with its desires” (1 John 2:15, 17).

She became a byword among women. Samaria’s fall became a warning everyone talked about. And that is the point of the next verse: her sister saw it all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem saw where unfaithfulness led and went further, moving from one idol to the next and back again. Oholibah watched her sister fall and became more corrupt (v. 11). She too courted Assyria (vv. 12–13), then fell in love with painted images of Babylonian officers and sent for them (vv. 14–16). When the Babylonians had defiled her, she turned from them in disgust, and God turned in disgust from her (vv. 17–18). Yet instead of turning to him, she went back to her oldest lover, Egypt, longing for the lusts of her youth (vv. 19–21).
verseByVerse.theology: A people who have seen God's judgment on others and still follow the same path are more guilty, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: "Her sister Oholibah saw this, and she became more corrupt than her sister in her lust and in her whoring, which was worse than that of her sister. She lusted after the Assyrians, governors and commanders, warriors clothed in full armor, horsemen riding on horses, all of them desirable young men. And I saw that she was defiled; they both took the same way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem watched Samaria destroyed for her unfaithfulness, and instead of learning, did the same and worse.

Her sister Oholibah saw this. Jerusalem saw exactly where unfaithfulness led, and “became more corrupt than her sister”.

Seeing and doing it anyway. That is a dangerous position: to have seen clearly the consequences of sin in someone else’s life, and to do it anyway. Knowledge increases responsibility. The child who watched a parent destroyed by addiction, the church that watched another church collapse through compromise: seeing is meant to warn.

They both took the same way. Jerusalem too went after Assyria. King Ahaz sent word to the Assyrian king, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me”, and paid him with silver and gold “found in the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 16:7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: But she carried her whoring further. She saw men portrayed on the wall, the images of the Chaldeans portrayed in vermilion, wearing belts on their waists, with flowing turbans on their heads, all of them having the appearance of officers, a likeness of Babylonians whose native land was Chaldea. When she saw them, she lusted after them and sent messengers to them in Chaldea. And the Babylonians came to her into the bed of love, and they defiled her with their whoring lust. And after she was defiled by them, she turned from them in disgust. When she carried on her whoring so openly and flaunted her nakedness, I turned in disgust from her, as I had turned in disgust from her sister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem fell in love with Babylon through pictures, tired of what she had chosen, and found that God had turned from her in disgust.

She saw men portrayed on the wall. Now Jerusalem falls in love with pictures: painted images of Babylonian officers in bright red, with fine belts and flowing turbans. She had not even met them. She was seduced by images.

What we look at. That is strikingly modern. People are drawn into desires, lifestyles and loyalties through images long before they meet the reality, and what we look at shapes what we want. “The desires of the eyes” are part of what John calls “the world” (1 John 2:16).

Sent messengers to them in Chaldea. Judah’s flirtation with Babylon went back to Hezekiah, who welcomed Babylonian envoys and showed them everything in his treasure house. Isaiah told him that “all that is in your house … shall be carried to Babylon” (2 Kings 20:17).

She turned from them in disgust. Then disillusionment. Judah became a subject state of Babylon and then rebelled. The idol that once dazzled her now disgusted her. That is the life cycle of every idol: attraction, indulgence, disgust.

I turned in disgust from her. The disgust runs both ways. She turned from Babylon, and God turned from her. Her restless, flaunted unfaithfulness had become repellent to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet she increased her whoring, remembering the days of her youth, when she played the whore in the land of Egypt and lusted after her lovers there, whose members were like those of donkeys, and whose issue was like that of horses. Thus you longed for the lewdness of your youth, when the Egyptians handled your bosom and pressed your young breasts."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Babylon failed her, Jerusalem did not turn to God but back to her oldest idol, Egypt.

Yet she increased her whoring. Having tired of Babylon, Jerusalem went back to her oldest love. Verses 20–21 describe it in crude language, meant to disgust. Zedekiah’s hope in Egyptian horses and chariots (17:15) was, in God’s eyes, not smart politics but a return to the lusts of Israel’s youth.

Isaiah’s woe. Isaiah had pronounced woe on those “who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh” (Isaiah 30:2).

Remembering the days of her youth. This is how sin works in a life. When one idol fails, the heart does not turn to God; it goes looking for an older idol, one it thought it had outgrown. She remembers her youth not with repentance but with longing. Only the new heart and the Spirit God promises in 36:26–27 break that cycle.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem will be judged by the very powers she courted, and must drink the same cup as her sister, because she has forgotten God. The lovers she discarded, Babylonians, Chaldeans and Assyrians, will be stirred up against her from every side, and God will hand the judgment to them (vv. 22–24). In his jealousy they will mutilate her, take her children and strip her, and so end the unfaithfulness begun in Egypt (vv. 25–27). She will fall into the hands of those she hates (vv. 28–30). “You have gone the way of your sister; therefore I will give her cup into your hand”, a cup of horror she must drain (vv. 31–34), for “you have forgotten me and cast me behind your back” (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who walk their sister's road must drink their sister's cup, unless another drinks it for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, O Oholibah, thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I will stir up against you your lovers from whom you turned in disgust, and I will bring them against you from every side: the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans, Pekod and Shoa and Koa, and all the Assyrians with them, desirable young men, governors and commanders all of them, officers and men of renown, all of them riding on horses. And they shall come against you from the north with chariots and wagons and a host of peoples. They shall set themselves against you on every side with buckler, shield, and helmet; and I will commit the judgment to them, and they shall judge you according to their judgments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lovers Jerusalem courted and then rejected will come back as her judges, stirred up by God himself.

I will stir up against you your lovers. The lovers she rejected will return as enemies, and God himself will stir them up. The same glamorous officers and horsemen she admired now ride against her; the picture on the wall has become a real army at the gate.

Pekod and Shoa and Koa. Peoples in league with Babylon. Pekod is known from Babylonian records as an Aramean tribe east of the Tigris, and Jeremiah names it too (Jeremiah 50:21).

They shall judge you according to their judgments. Jerusalem chose to live by the standards of the nations. Now the nations will judge her by those standards, and they are brutal.

Uncertain wording. Shoa and Koa are not certainly identified; they may be peoples east of the Tigris known from Assyrian records. Pekod also sounds like the Hebrew for “punishment”, which may be part of the point. The ESV notes too that the meaning of one Hebrew word in verse 24 is uncertain. The sense is clear: a vast army from every side.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will direct my jealousy against you, that they may deal with you in fury. They shall cut off your nose and your ears, and your survivors shall fall by the sword. They shall seize your sons and your daughters, and your survivors shall be devoured by fire. They shall also strip you of your clothes and take away your beautiful jewels. Thus I will put an end to your lewdness and your whoring begun in the land of Egypt, so that you shall not lift up your eyes to them or remember Egypt anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind Babylon’s brutality stands God’s jealous love, and his purpose in the judgment is to end his people’s idolatry for good.

I will direct my jealousy against you. Behind Babylon’s fury is God’s jealousy, the burning love of a husband betrayed. Cutting off the nose and ears was a known punishment in the ancient world, and the beauty she used to attract lovers will be destroyed. This is the brutality of Babylon’s armies, which God allowed as judgment and later judged in turn; the verse describes what happened, it does not approve it.

I will put an end to your lewdness. Here is God’s purpose: the exile would cure Israel of the idolatry that had run from Egypt onward, “so that you shall not lift up your eyes to them or remember Egypt anymore”. In large measure it did: the Jews who came back from Babylon never again fell into the old idolatry of their fathers. Even God’s severest discipline aims to rescue and restore.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will deliver you into the hands of those whom you hate, into the hands of those from whom you turned in disgust, and they shall deal with you in hatred and take away all the fruit of your labor and leave you naked and bare, and the nakedness of your whoring shall be uncovered. Your lewdness and your whoring have brought this upon you, because you played the whore with the nations and defiled yourself with their idols.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem will be handed to the people she has come to hate, and her own unfaithfulness, not God’s harshness, is the cause.

Into the hands of those whom you hate. Once she loved them; now she hates them; and she will be handed to them. Everything she worked for, “all the fruit of your labor”, will be taken.

Your lewdness and your whoring have brought this upon you. The verdict leaves no room for excuses. Babylon was the instrument, but her own choices were the cause. God does not punish arbitrarily; he gives people over to the harvest of what they sowed.

verseByVerse.quote: You have gone the way of your sister; therefore I will give her cup into your hand. Thus says the Lord GOD: "You shall drink your sister's cup that is deep and large; you shall be laughed at and held in derision, for it contains much; you will be filled with drunkenness and sorrow. A cup of horror and desolation, the cup of your sister Samaria; you shall drink it and drain it out, and gnaw its shards, and tear your breasts; for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have forgotten me and cast me behind your back, you yourself must bear the consequences of your lewdness and whoring."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jerusalem followed her sister’s way, she must drink her sister’s cup of God’s wrath to the dregs; and Christ is the one who drank that cup for his people.

I will give her cup into your hand. A new image. Samaria drank a cup of judgment; Jerusalem walked the same road, so she will drink the same cup.

The cup of wrath. A common picture in the prophets. Jeremiah was told, “Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath” (Jeremiah 25:15), and Isaiah spoke of Jerusalem having “drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath” (Isaiah 51:17). Here it is “deep and large”, full of “horror and desolation”, drained until she gnaws the broken pieces.

You shall drink no more. One person took that cup into his own hands. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36). He drank the cup of horror and desolation to the bottom, so that God could say to his people, “Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more” (Isaiah 51:22).

You have forgotten me and cast me behind your back. God treated like something tossed over the shoulder and forgotten. God said the same of King Jeroboam (1 Kings 14:9), and the Levites confessed that Israel “cast your law behind their back” (Nehemiah 9:26). At the root of all the unfaithfulness is this: “you have forgotten me”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final indictment shows how far the sisters had gone: idolatry, child sacrifice and temple worship side by side. Ezekiel is to declare their abominations: adultery with idols, blood on their hands, even the children they had borne to God offered up to idols (vv. 36–37). On the very day they sacrificed their children they walked into God’s sanctuary to worship (vv. 38–39). They dressed up for envoys from afar and set God’s incense and oil on their table (vv. 40–42). Righteous men will sentence them as adulteresses and murderers (vv. 43–45), and an army will carry out the sentence, “that all women may take warning” and all may know that he is the Lord GOD (vv. 46–49).
verseByVerse.theology: Worship that goes on alongside idolatry and cruelty is not worship but profanation, and God makes its judgment a warning to all.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to me: "Son of man, will you judge Oholah and Oholibah? Declare to them their abominations. For they have committed adultery, and blood is on their hands. With their idols they have committed adultery, and they have even offered up to them for food the children whom they had borne to me. Moreover, this they have done to me: they have defiled my sanctuary on the same day and profaned my Sabbaths. For when they had slaughtered their children in sacrifice to their idols, on the same day they came into my sanctuary to profane it. And behold, this is what they did in my house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sisters sacrificed their children to idols and then walked into God’s house on the same day, as if worship could sit comfortably beside murder.

They have committed adultery, and blood is on their hands. Two charges. The adultery is idolatry. The blood includes the most horrifying crime of all: “the children whom they had borne to me”, offered to idols (the ESV notes, “made pass through the fire”). Children who belonged to God were given to false gods.

On the same day. That is the chilling detail. They sacrificed their children to idols, and then, the same day, walked into the LORD’s temple for worship, as if nothing had happened.

Jeremiah saw it too. “Will you steal, murder, commit adultery … and then come and stand before me in this house … and say, ‘We are delivered!’” (Jeremiah 7:9–10). It is the ultimate hypocrisy: a religion that makes room for anything, even murder, as long as you turn up to worship. God calls it profaning his sanctuary.

Worship and life. We must ask whether our worship on Sunday is disconnected from how we live on Saturday. God does not accept worship that coexists peacefully with cherished sin; but he receives the worshipper who comes confessing it: “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

verseByVerse.quote: They even sent for men to come from afar, to whom a messenger was sent; and behold, they came. For them you bathed yourself, painted your eyes, and adorned yourself with ornaments. You sat on a stately couch, with a table spread before it on which you had placed my incense and my oil. The sound of a carefree multitude was with her; and with men of the common sort, drunkards were brought from the wilderness; and they put bracelets on the hands of the women, and beautiful crowns on their heads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah made herself beautiful for foreign powers and used God’s own gifts to entertain them, partying with the world while judgment gathered.

For them you bathed yourself. The sisters prepare for foreign guests: bathing, painting their eyes, putting on jewellery. This is diplomacy pictured as seduction: Judah making herself attractive to foreign powers.

My incense and my oil. The gifts God gave for his worship were set out on the table to entertain her lovers, the same charge as 16:18: God’s gifts used to serve his rivals.

The sound of a carefree multitude. The scene is a careless party. Drunkards are brought in from the desert, and bracelets and crowns are handed out. It is a picture of a people partying with the world while judgment gathers at the gates.

Uncertain wording. Verse 42 is hard to translate. The ESV notes that “drunkards” may be “Sabeans”, people from distant Sheba, and the Hebrew words are very similar. Either way, these are guests from far off, welcomed to the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then I said of her who was worn out by adultery, 'Now they will continue to use her for a whore, even her!' For they have gone in to her, as men go in to a prostitute. Thus they went in to Oholah and to Oholibah, lewd women! But righteous men shall pass judgment on them with the sentence of adulteresses, and with the sentence of women who shed blood, because they are adulteresses, and blood is on their hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations used Israel and Judah up and went on using them, and any honest court would condemn the sisters for adultery and bloodshed.

Her who was worn out by adultery. The picture is of a woman used up, still being used. That is how the nations treated Israel and Judah: not as valued partners, but as something to exploit and discard.

How the world treats its friends. The world never loves those who sell themselves to it. It uses them. Only God loves faithfully. “Friendship with the world is enmity with God” (James 4:4), and in the end the world despises you for it too.

Righteous men shall pass judgment on them. Even by ordinary standards of justice, the verdict is obvious: adultery and bloodshed. The sisters are condemned not only by God’s holiness but by any honest court.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew of verse 43 is uncertain. The general picture, a worn-out woman still being used, is clear; the exact words are not.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the Lord GOD: "Bring up a vast host against them, and make them an object of terror and a plunder. And the host shall stone them and cut them down with their swords. They shall kill their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses. Thus will I put an end to lewdness in the land, that all women may take warning and not commit lewdness as you have done. And they shall return your lewdness upon you, and you shall bear the penalty for your sinful idolatry, and you shall know that I am the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence is carried out by armies, and the sisters’ story stands as a warning to every people, and to the church, about unfaithfulness to God.

Bring up a vast host against them. The sentence for adultery and murder under the law was death. The allegory becomes history: armies, swords, burning houses.

That all women may take warning. In the allegory the women are nations and cities, and the warning is to peoples about idolatry; it gives no one licence to shame or harm a woman. Samaria and Jerusalem are a warning to every people, and the New Testament says their story was written “for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11). The church, the bride of Christ, must learn from the sisters. John saw the final form of unfaithfulness in “the great prostitute … with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality” (Revelation 17:1–2).

You shall know that I am the Lord GOD. The chapter ends where the prophets always end: with God known for who he is.

Why this chapter matters. Ezekiel 23 is a hard chapter to read aloud. But it shows how seriously God takes faithfulness. His people are a bride, and he is a faithful husband. And the gospel shows how far that husband went: “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her … so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:25–27). The unfaithful sisters drank their cup. The faithful Bridegroom drank it for his bride.

23.title: Two Sisters
23.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 22 read Jerusalem its charge sheet and ended with no one to stand in the breach. Chapter 23, in the last years before the siege, returns to the picture of chapter 16, an unfaithful wife, but now there are two sisters: Oholah, who is Samaria, and Oholibah, who is Jerusalem.

The message. God’s people betrayed him by trusting the great powers of the world instead of him, and by taking on their gods along with their protection. Samaria did it and was destroyed by the very lovers she courted. Jerusalem watched, learned nothing and did worse, so she must drink the same cup. The language is blunt on purpose: God wants his people to feel what their betrayal looks like from his side, and to know that it was their own choices that brought the judgment.

Why it was said. Judah’s kings had spent a century looking for safety in alliances, with Assyria, then Babylon, and now, under Zedekiah, Egypt (17:15). The exiles hoped Egypt would save Jerusalem (see the introduction). Ezekiel calls it adultery. The allegory is about cities and their idols; it never excuses violence against any woman (see the note on vv. 1–4).

How the chapter makes its case. Two sisters, unfaithful since their youth in Egypt, became God’s own (vv. 1–4). Samaria lusted after Assyria’s glamour and gods, and God handed her over to the Assyrians she desired (vv. 5–10). Jerusalem saw it and did worse, courting Assyria, then Babylon, then Egypt again (vv. 11–21). So the lovers she discarded will come against her, and she must drain her sister’s cup of horror, because “you have forgotten me” (vv. 22–35). A final indictment sets idolatry beside child sacrifice and worship in God’s house on the same day, and ends in judgment “that all women may take warning” (vv. 36–49).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need exposed. The pattern is the marriage: God is the faithful husband of an unfaithful people, and in Christ that husband “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), to make her clean. The need is the cup. Jerusalem had to drink “your sister’s cup”, full of horror and desolation (vv. 32–33). In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36), and drank it, so that God can say to his people, “the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more” (Isaiah 51:22).

For us. The church is Christ’s bride, and she can still be seduced by the world’s power, glamour and images. Watch what you look at and where you look for security; learn from others’ falls instead of repeating them; and never let Sunday worship sit comfortably beside cherished sin. When you have been unfaithful, run to the Bridegroom who drank your cup.
23.theology:
God's people were unfaithful from the beginning, yet he made them his own; their idolatry is a betrayal of grace (vv. 3-4; 20:7-8). Seeing his judgment on others only increases their responsibility (v. 11; Jer 3:6-8).

Political alliances and admiration for worldly power led to adopting the gods of the nations (vv. 5-7, 12-16; 2 Kgs 15:19; 16:7-8; 20:12-17), and the powers courted instead of God became the instruments of judgment (vv. 9, 22-24, 28). Idols follow a cycle of attraction, indulgence and disgust, and the heart that will not turn to God goes back to older idols (vv. 17-21; 1 John 2:15-17).

Worship offered alongside idolatry and cruelty treats God’s holy things with contempt (vv. 38-39; Jer 7:9-10). The cup of God's wrath passes from sister to sister, and Christ drank it for his bride (vv. 31-34; Isa 51:17, 22; Mark 14:36; Eph 5:25-27).
23.examples:
The chapter's pictures are meant to stay with us: two sisters who both became his; a nation dazzled by purple uniforms and fine horses; a woman falling for a painting on a wall before she has met the men in it.

Darker still is the sister who watched her sister fall and walked the same road, and the parents who gave a child to an idol and went to the temple the same day, with God's own incense set out for foreign guests. At the end stands a cup drained to its broken pieces, and the One who would drink it for his bride.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have forgotten me and cast me behind your back, you yourself must bear the consequences of your lewdness and whoring.
keyVerse.note: Under all the chapter’s shocking pictures lies one charge: Jerusalem forgot God and tossed him over her shoulder. Her alliances and idols were the fruit of that root, and the judgment is the harvest of her own choices. Only the Bridegroom who bore the consequences in her place can rescue a people like this.

23.reflection:
Samaria was attracted to Assyria’s power and glamour (vv. 5–7), and Jerusalem fell in love with pictures on a wall (vv. 14–16). What images and powers most easily draw your heart away from trusting God?

Jerusalem saw what happened to Samaria and “became more corrupt than her sister” (v. 11). Why do we so often fail to learn from the falls of others, and how can we learn better?

The sisters sacrificed their children and came into God’s sanctuary “on the same day” (v. 39). Where might our worship be disconnected from the way we live, and what does God offer those who come to him confessing it?

Jerusalem had to drink “your sister’s cup” (v. 32). How does Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36) change the way you read this chapter?
