verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Pot on the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the day the siege begins, God tells his people that the time for cleansing is past: Jerusalem will be put in the fire. Ezekiel is to write down the date, because the king of Babylon has begun his siege “this very day” (vv. 1–2). Then he tells a parable of a pot filled with choice meat and boiled hard (vv. 3–5). The pot is the “bloody city”, corroded through, its meat thrown out without choosing, its blood left uncovered on bare rock to cry for justice (vv. 6–8). God will heap on the logs until even the bones burn, then set the empty pot on the coals to burn out its corrosion (vv. 9–12). “I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed”; now he will not relent (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: When people refuse God's cleansing, his fire must do what his mercy was not allowed to do.

verseByVerse.quote: In the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, write down the name of this day, this very day. The king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Ezekiel, hundreds of miles away in Babylon, the very day the siege of Jerusalem begins, so that no one can doubt that he had foretold it.

Write down the name of this day. An extraordinary moment. Ezekiel is in Babylon, hundreds of miles from Jerusalem, with no way of hearing the news. And God tells him: write down today’s date, because “the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day”.

Confirmed by history. The record matches it exactly: “in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem and laid siege to it” (2 Kings 25:1; Jeremiah 52:4). The date falls in January 588 BC; the Jews later kept it as a fast day (compare Zechariah 8:19).

Why write it down? So that when the news finally arrived, the exiles would know that Ezekiel had known it on the day, and that his words came from God. For years they had doubted him. Now the siege he had acted out with a brick (4:1–3) had begun.

Nothing surprises God. He knows what is happening in every place at every moment, and he can reveal it when he chooses.
verseByVerse.note: The day Babylon’s siege of Jerusalem began, about January 588 BC (some date it a year later).

verseByVerse.quote: And utter a parable to the rebellious house and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Set on the pot, set it on; pour in water also; put in it the pieces of meat, all the good pieces, the thigh and the shoulder; fill it with choice bones. Take the choicest one of the flock; pile the logs under it; boil it well; seethe also its bones in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns Jerusalem’s proud boast against it: the city is indeed a cooking pot, and the fire is now lit beneath it.

Set on the pot. It sounds like a cooking song: set on the pot, add water, put in the best cuts, pile on the logs, boil it well.

Their own slogan reversed. Remember the proud slogan of Jerusalem’s leaders: “This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat” (11:3). They thought the pot protected them, the choice cuts safe inside its walls. God takes their own picture and turns it against them. Yes, you are in the pot, and now the fire is lit.

Uncertain wording. In verse 5 the ESV notes that “the logs” follows verse 10; the Hebrew reads “the bones”. Either way, the fire is being built up under the pot.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose corrosion is in it, and whose corrosion has not gone out of it! Take out of it piece after piece, without making any choice. For the blood she has shed is in her midst; she put it on the bare rock; she did not pour it out on the ground to cover it with dust. To rouse my wrath, to take vengeance, I have set on the bare rock the blood she has shed, that it may not be covered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem is a pot corroded through by bloodshed, and because she flaunted her guilt, God leaves her blood uncovered to cry out for justice.

Woe to the bloody city. The parable darkens. The pot is corroded, rusted through, and the rust has never been cleaned out. Jerusalem is “the bloody city” (22:2), and its corruption is baked in.

Take out of it piece after piece, without making any choice. No one is selected to be spared. The meat is pulled out piece by piece, without distinction, and the choice cuts who thought they were safe are dumped out with the rest.

She put it on the bare rock. The law required that the blood of an animal killed for food be poured out and covered with earth (Leviticus 17:13). Blood left in the open cried out: “The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground”, God said to Cain (Genesis 4:10). Jerusalem did not even try to hide her bloodshed. She left it on bare rock, in plain view.

That it may not be covered. So God says: then I will leave it there. Job cried, “O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place” (Job 16:18). Innocent blood that is not covered keeps crying for justice.

Blood that speaks a better word. Only one blood can cover sin, and it cries out for something else. We have come “to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel’s blood cried for vengeance; Christ’s blood cries for mercy.

Uncertain wording. For “without making any choice” the ESV notes that the Hebrew is literally “no lot has fallen upon it”. It probably means that no lot is cast to decide who is spared: everyone goes.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the bloody city! I also will make the pile great. Heap on the logs, kindle the fire, boil the meat well, mix in the spices, and let the bones be burned up. Then set it empty upon the coals, that it may become hot, and its copper may burn, that its uncleanness may be melted in it, its corrosion consumed. She has wearied herself with toil; its abundant corrosion does not go out of it. Into the fire with its corrosion!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself stokes the fire until the meat is gone and the empty pot glows, because only fire can remove corrosion this deep.

I also will make the pile great. God himself stokes the fire. The meat is boiled until even the bones burn.

Then set it empty upon the coals. Then the empty pot itself is set on the coals until the metal glows and the rust burns away. The city will be emptied of its people, and then the empty city will be burned to purge its corruption.

She has wearied herself with toil. Perhaps all the effort to scrub the pot has failed; the corrosion is too deep. Reforms had come and gone. Josiah had cleansed the temple, and it had not lasted. Only fire could remove the rust.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “mix in the spices” in verse 10 may be read “empty out the broth”, and that the meaning of the opening of verse 12 is uncertain. The likely sense of verse 12 is that every attempt to clean the pot has worn itself out, and the corrosion remains.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of your unclean lewdness, because I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed from your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed anymore till I have satisfied my fury upon you. I am the LORD. I have spoken; it shall come to pass; I will do it. I will not go back; I will not spare; I will not relent; according to your ways and your deeds you will be judged, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God wanted to cleanse his people and they refused, so the time for cleansing is over and judgment will come without relenting.

I would have cleansed you. Here is the heartbreaking sentence at the centre of the chapter: “I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed.” God wanted to clean them. Through prophet after prophet he offered cleansing. They refused.

Jesus’ lament. Jesus said the same over the same city: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). The tragedy of judgment is not that God was unwilling to save, but that people were unwilling to be saved.

I will not relent. Six short sentences, like hammer blows: “I have spoken; it shall come to pass; I will do it. I will not go back; I will not spare; I will not relent.” There comes a point when the time for turning is over. Today, while God still offers to cleanse, is the time to let him: “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–27 — The Delight of Your Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel’s private grief becomes God’s public sign: the people will lose the temple they love so suddenly that they will be too stunned to mourn. God tells Ezekiel that he will take “the delight of your eyes” at a stroke, and that he must not mourn in public (vv. 15–17). “So I spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening my wife died. And on the next morning I did as I was commanded” (v. 18). When the people ask what it means, he explains: God will profane his sanctuary, the delight of their eyes, their children in Jerusalem will fall, and they too will be unable to mourn (vv. 19–24). On that day a fugitive will bring the news, and Ezekiel’s mouth will be opened (vv. 25–27).
verseByVerse.theology: Ezekiel's personal grief became a sign of the nation's loss, and his costly obedience points to the God who gave up the delight of his heart.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, behold, I am about to take the delight of your eyes away from you at a stroke; yet you shall not mourn or weep, nor shall your tears run down. Sigh, but not aloud; make no mourning for the dead. Bind on your turban, and put your shoes on your feet; do not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Ezekiel that his beloved wife will die suddenly, and that he must grieve in silence, without the customs of mourning.

The delight of your eyes. Deeply personal words. “The delight of your eyes” is Ezekiel’s wife. We learn almost nothing else about her, but this phrase tells us what matters most: he loved her; she was the joy of his life. And God tells him she will die “at a stroke”, suddenly. And he must not mourn: no weeping, no tears.

Sigh, but not aloud. The mourning customs of the day, taking off the turban, going barefoot, covering the lips, eating the meal that neighbours brought, are all forbidden. He must grieve silently, inwardly, and go about as normal.

Why would God take Ezekiel’s wife as a sign? It is a hard question, and the text does not soften it. Every life is God’s to give and to take, and nothing here says she died for any fault of hers or of her husband’s. God chose to make the prophet’s grief, which was real, a sign of the far greater loss coming on Jerusalem. Ezekiel was not told not to grieve, but not to mourn publicly (v. 17), so that the people would ask why. It cost him dearly, as the cross would cost the Father.

What it does not mean. This does not teach that Christians must not grieve. “Jesus wept” at the grave of his friend (John 11:35). Paul does not tell believers not to grieve, but not to “grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

verseByVerse.quote: So I spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening my wife died. And on the next morning I did as I was commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel’s wife died that evening, and the next morning, heartbroken, he obeyed God.

At evening my wife died. The verse is deeply moving, and told with almost no emotion at all: a sermon in the morning, a death at evening, obedience the next day.

I did as I was commanded. He did not argue or walk away from his calling. With his heart broken, he got up the next morning, put on his turban and his shoes, and obeyed. This is what it cost to be God’s messenger to a rebellious people.

The Father knows this loss. His loss points beyond himself. There was a Father who gave up the delight of his eyes: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). The Father knows what it is to give up the Son he loves.

For the bereaved. If you have lost a husband or wife, this verse does not ask you to hide your tears. Ezekiel’s silence was a one-time sign for a stubborn nation, not a rule for the bereaved. What the passage does give you is this: God himself calls a beloved wife “the delight of your eyes”, and he did not think that love small. The grief of the evening, and the hard work of getting up the next morning, are seen by him. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18), and Christ, who wept at a grave, will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in him (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

Loving Christ more. Few of us will ever be asked for anything like this. But every servant of Christ is called to love him more than even the dearest things in life: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). Ezekiel’s obedience was not coldness; it was love for God that held firm when everything in him was breaking. None of us loves him so perfectly. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19), and the Son who loved the Father perfectly, even in Gethsemane, did it in our place.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people said to me, "Will you not tell us what these things mean for us, that you are acting thus?" Then I said to them, "The word of the LORD came to me: 'Say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul, and your sons and your daughters whom you left behind shall fall by the sword. And you shall do as I have done; you shall not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men. Your turbans shall be on your heads and your shoes on your feet; you shall not mourn or weep, but you shall rot away in your iniquities and groan to one another. Thus shall Ezekiel be to you a sign; according to all that he has done you shall do. When this comes, then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Ezekiel lost his wife, the people will lose the temple and their children, and the blow will be so heavy that they cannot even mourn.

What these things mean for us. The people are puzzled: his wife has died, and he is not mourning. They sense that his strange behaviour is a message, and they ask what it means.

I will profane my sanctuary. The temple is “the delight of your eyes”, the very phrase used of Ezekiel’s wife. What his wife was to him, the temple was to them. God will take it, and their children left behind in Jerusalem will die. Ezekiel’s hearers had been deported with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, and many had left sons and daughters in the city, so this word struck at their own families.

The pride of your power. There is a warning here too. The people loved the temple, “the pride of your power”, more than the God of the temple. It had become their security and their idol. A psalmist could say, “One thing have I asked of the LORD … that I may dwell in the house of the LORD … to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD” (Psalm 27:4). It was the LORD’s beauty he sought, not the building’s. When a sacred place becomes the delight of our eyes instead of God himself, he may take it away.

Why will they not mourn? Because the disaster will be so overwhelming that ordinary mourning will be impossible. They will be too numb and stunned for any customs, and will simply “rot away in your iniquities and groan to one another”.

Thus shall Ezekiel be to you a sign. His marriage, his loss and his silence all became the message. The prophet’s life and the prophet’s word were one.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, surely on the day when I take from them their stronghold, their joy and glory, the delight of their eyes and their soul's desire, and also their sons and daughters, on that day a fugitive will come to you to report to you the news. On that day your mouth will be opened to the fugitive, and you shall speak and be no longer mute. So you will be a sign to them, and they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the news of Jerusalem’s fall reaches Babylon, Ezekiel’s long silence will end, and the prophet of judgment will become the prophet of hope.

Their stronghold, their joy and glory. Their stronghold, joy, glory, delight and desire, and their children too: all will go. And when the news reaches Babylon, Ezekiel’s long muteness (3:26) will end.

Your mouth will be opened. It happened just as God said: “a fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and said, ‘The city has been struck down’”, and “my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute” (33:21–22).

Where the book goes next. This chapter is a turning point. Chapters 1–24 have been almost entirely judgment on Jerusalem. The next chapters turn to the nations, and then, once the city has fallen, Ezekiel’s opened mouth will speak words of astonishing hope: a new shepherd, a new heart, dry bones living, a new temple. The silence of grief gives way to the voice of restoration.

24.title: The Delight of Your Eyes
24.overview:
Where we are. For four and a half years Ezekiel has warned that Jerusalem would fall. Now, in January 588 BC, God tells him that the siege has begun that very day. This chapter closes the first half of the book, the long message of judgment on Jerusalem (chapters 4–24).

The message. The time for warning is over. God offered again and again to cleanse his people, and they refused, so now the city will be put in the fire like a corroded pot until its rust burns away. And the loss will be so great that no one will be able to mourn it: Ezekiel’s silent grief at his wife’s death becomes the sign of the stunned grief coming when God takes the temple, “the delight of your eyes”. Yet the chapter ends with a promise that Ezekiel’s silence will end.

Why it was said. The exiles still trusted the temple and the city to stand (see the introduction). God wanted them to know, when the news came, that it was no accident: he had said it, dated it and acted it out in his prophet’s own home.

How the chapter makes its case. First the date: write down this day (vv. 1–2). Then the parable of the pot: Jerusalem’s leaders once boasted that the city was a pot protecting its meat (11:3); now it is set on the fire, its meat thrown out, its blood left uncovered on bare rock, and the empty pot heated until its corrosion burns, because “I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed” (vv. 3–14). Then the sign: God takes Ezekiel’s wife, and he must not mourn publicly; so the people will be too stunned to mourn when God takes their temple and their children (vv. 15–24). Last, the promise: when a fugitive brings the news, Ezekiel’s mouth will be opened (vv. 25–27).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God it reveals. The need is cleansing. The pot could not be scrubbed clean, and Jerusalem’s uncovered blood cried out for judgment; but we have come “to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24), and “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). God’s heart, “I would have cleansed you”, is the heart Jesus showed over the same city (Matthew 23:37). And Ezekiel’s costly loss gives a glimpse of the Father who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

For us. Today, while God still offers to cleanse, is the day to let him. Hold even the best gifts, the people and places you love most, as his, and love him more. And if you are grieving, this chapter does not ask you to hide it: God calls a beloved wife “the delight of your eyes”, and he sees the hard morning after.
24.theology:
God knows and can reveal events far away at the moment they happen; his word is proven by its fulfilment (vv. 1-2; 2 Kgs 25:1). False security in a privileged place gives no protection when he judges (vv. 3-6; 11:3).

Blood shed unjustly cries out to God, and only the blood of Christ speaks a better word (vv. 7-8; Gen 4:10; Heb 12:24). God offers cleansing, and judgment falls when it is refused (v. 13; Matt 23:37).

God may call his servants to costly obedience, and their lives can become a message (vv. 15-18, 24; Matt 10:37). Grief is not condemned, but believers do not grieve without hope (John 11:35; 1 Thess 4:13). Sacred places can become idols, and God may take away what we love more than him (vv. 21, 25; Ps 27:4). The prophet's loss points to the Father who gave up his beloved Son (Matt 3:17; Rom 8:32).
24.examples:
A date is written down in Babylon on the very day the siege begins. A rusty pot will not come clean however it is scrubbed, and blood left on bare rock goes on crying. Behind it all is God's own lament: he would have cleansed them.

Then a sermon in the morning, a death at evening, and obedience the next day: a man tying on his turban over a broken heart, and waiting for the news that will open his mouth.

keyVerse.quote: On account of your unclean lewdness, because I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed from your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed anymore till I have satisfied my fury upon you.
keyVerse.note: On the day the siege began, this verse explains why it had to come. The fault was never in God’s willingness: “I would have cleansed you.” Jerusalem refused, and a refused cleansing leaves only the fire. It is the same grief Jesus voiced over the same city, and the same urgent call to accept the cleansing his blood now offers.

24.reflection:
God told Ezekiel the very day the siege began (vv. 1–2). How does it help you, in confusing times, to know that God knows exactly what is happening everywhere?

“I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed” (v. 13). How can people resist God’s offer of cleansing while still being religious? What does it look like to accept it today (1 John 1:7–9)?

The people loved the temple, “the delight of your eyes” (v. 21), more than the God of the temple. What good things in your life, even in your church life, could become a substitute for God himself?

Ezekiel lost “the delight of your eyes” and obeyed God the next morning (vv. 16–18). How should Christians grieve, and how can we care for those who are grieving in our church?

Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay my vengeance upon them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God takes the mockery of his people in their ruin as mockery of himself. Ammon greeted the profaning of his sanctuary, the desolation of the land and the exile of Judah with one word, “Aha!” (vv. 1–3), so the people of the East will camp in Ammon’s land and eat its harvest, and its capital Rabbah will become a pasture for camels (vv. 4–5). Ammon went further, clapping its hands and stamping its feet “with all the malice within your soul” (v. 6), so God will hand it over as plunder and cut it off from the peoples (v. 7). Twice the oracle ends with its purpose: “Then you will know that I am the LORD.”
verseByVerse.theology: To gloat over the judgment of God's people is to invite God's judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward the Ammonites and prophesy against them. Say to the Ammonites, Hear the word of the Lord GOD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Because you said, 'Aha!' over my sanctuary when it was profaned, and over the land of Israel when it was made desolate, and over the house of Judah when they went into exile, therefore behold, I am handing you over to the people of the East for a possession, and they shall set their encampments among you and make their dwellings in your midst. They shall eat your fruit, and they shall drink your milk. I will make Rabbah a pasture for camels and Ammon a fold for flocks. Then you will know that I am the LORD. For thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have clapped your hands and stamped your feet and rejoiced with all the malice within your soul against the land of Israel, therefore, behold, I have stretched out my hand against you, and will hand you over as plunder to the nations. And I will cut you off from the peoples and will make you perish out of the countries; I will destroy you. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes the gloating over his people’s ruin as gloating over himself, and Ammon, which said “Aha!” when his sanctuary fell, will itself be overrun and cut off.

Set your face toward the Ammonites. With the siege begun (24:1–2) and the prophet silent toward his own people until the city falls (24:27), God speaks about the nations around Israel, beginning with Ammon, east of the Jordan.

Aha! Ammon’s sin was one word, a sneer of satisfaction at another’s ruin, spoken over the sanctuary profaned, the land made desolate and the people exiled.

Over my sanctuary. God calls the temple “my sanctuary”. He had judged it himself, but that gave no one else the right to rejoice. “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the LORD see it and be displeased” (Proverbs 24:17–18). Those who enjoy God’s discipline of his people will answer to him.

A pasture for camels. Rabbah, the capital (modern Amman), will become a camel pasture, and the mocker will be mocked. “The people of the East” were the desert tribes (Judges 6:3), and in later centuries Arab peoples did spread into the old lands of Ammon and Moab.

Clapped your hands and stamped your feet. The same gestures Ezekiel had made in grief (6:11), Ammon made in glee. And God names the root: “all the malice within your soul”.

The “Aha!” at the cross. The word was heard again at Calvary: “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, ‘Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days’” (Mark 15:29). Ammon gloated over a ruined building; they gloated over the true temple, his body, as it was destroyed (John 2:19–21). And he did not call down vengeance. He prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). The God who judges gloating bore the mockery himself and prayed for the mockers.

A warning for us. Beware of enjoying a rival’s scandal, an opponent’s failure or the collapse of a church we disagreed with. God promised Abraham, “him who dishonors you I will curse” (Genesis 12:3). Christians, shown mercy when we had brought ruin on ourselves, are called to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15), even when those who weep brought it on themselves.

Why does a book for exiles contain oracles against nations they would never meet? Because the LORD is no local god: he rules Ammon, Tyre and Egypt as surely as Jerusalem. The oracles brought comfort, for those who mocked Judah would not have the last word (28:24), and warning, for Tyre’s wealth and Egypt’s armies were what Judah trusted instead of God, and these chapters strip them of their glamour. They are God’s verdicts on real cruelty, not a licence to hate any people today; and the gospel later reached people from these same lands (Acts 2:9–11).
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 25–32 are oracles, messages of judgment, against the nations: Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon and Egypt.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Moab: Like All the Other Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To call God’s people ordinary is to call their God ordinary, and he will not let that stand. Moab, with Seir, said that the house of Judah was “like all the other nations” (v. 8): its fall proved that its God was no different from anyone else’s. So God will lay open Moab’s exposed flank, the proud frontier towns that were “the glory of the country” (v. 9), and give Moab, with Ammon, to the people of the East (v. 10). Moab will learn by judgment the very thing it denied: “they will know that I am the LORD” (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who deny that God's people are his will learn that he is the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: Because Moab and Seir said, 'Behold, the house of Judah is like all the other nations,' therefore I will lay open the flank of Moab from the cities, from its cities on its frontier, the glory of the country, Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim. I will give it along with the Ammonites to the people of the East as a possession, that the Ammonites may be remembered no more among the nations, and I will execute judgments upon Moab. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moab despised Judah as just another nation, and so despised Judah’s God; Moab will learn by judgment that he is the LORD.

Like all the other nations. Moab’s sin was different from Ammon’s. It said Judah was nothing special, and its fall proved that its God was no different from Moab’s gods. That attacked God’s name, not only Judah. Israel’s whole identity was that the LORD had chosen them (Deuteronomy 7:6), so to call them ordinary was to call him ordinary. (Seir is Edom’s hill country.)

The glory of the country. Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon and Kiriathaim were proud towns on the tableland north of the Arnon, once allotted to Reuben (Joshua 13:15–20) and long held by Moab. God will open them like a wound in the flank, and Moab will learn the very thing it denied: “that I am the LORD”.

Mercy for Moab. Yet God’s dealings with Moab are not only judgment. A Moabite widow named Ruth had said, “your God my God” (Ruth 1:16). She became David’s great-grandmother and is named in the family line of Jesus: “Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth” (Matthew 1:5). Moab said Israel’s God was like all the others; one Moabite woman found that he was not. No nation under judgment is beyond his mercy for those who turn to him.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 9 says literally I will open the shoulder of Moab. Most take it as the exposed flank of the Moabite plateau, and the repeated “from the cities” is awkward. The sense is clear: the frontier towns that guarded Moab become the breach.

Textual note. The ESV notes that the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, lacks “and Seir”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Vengeance belongs to God, and those who seize it will meet his. Edom, Israel’s brother nation, “acted revengefully against the house of Judah” in her disaster (v. 12), so God will stretch out his hand and make Edom desolate from Teman to Dedan (v. 13), laying his own vengeance on it by the hand of his people (v. 14). The Philistines took vengeance “with malice of soul to destroy in never-ending enmity” (v. 15), so God will cut off the Cherethites and the rest of the coast (v. 16). The chapter ends where every oracle has ended: when he acts, “they will know that I am the LORD” (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Vengeance belongs to God, and those who take it into their own hands against his people will meet his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: Because Edom acted revengefully against the house of Judah and has grievously offended in taking vengeance on them, therefore thus says the Lord GOD, I will stretch out my hand against Edom and cut off from it man and beast. And I will make it desolate; from Teman even to Dedan they shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Edom according to my anger and according to my wrath, and they shall know my vengeance, declares the Lord GOD. "Thus says the Lord GOD: Because the Philistines acted revengefully and took vengeance with malice of soul to destroy in never-ending enmity, therefore thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I will stretch out my hand against the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the rest of the seacoast. I will execute great vengeance on them with wrathful rebukes. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay my vengeance upon them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom and the Philistines took revenge on Judah in her fall; God, to whom vengeance belongs, will take his own vengeance on them.

Because Edom acted revengefully. Edom, descended from Esau, was Israel’s brother nation (Genesis 25:23), and it nursed an ancient grudge. When Jerusalem fell, Edom took its revenge. A psalm remembers it: “Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!’” (Psalm 137:7). Obadiah pleaded, “do not gloat over the day of your brother” (Obadiah 12). From Teman to Dedan means the whole land, end to end.

They shall know my vengeance. Edom took vengeance into its own hands; God says the vengeance is his. Personal revenge is not only wrong: it takes God’s place. Paul gives Christians the same principle: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

Never-ending enmity. The Philistines had fought Israel since the days of the judges, a hatred generations old. Many conflicts today are driven by exactly this, hatred handed from parents to children, and only the gospel, which makes enemies into brothers (Ephesians 2:14–16), can break it.

I will cut off the Cherethites. The Cherethites were a coastal people linked with the Philistines (1 Samuel 30:14), probably from Crete. The Hebrew plays on their name: God will “cut off” (hikratti) the Kerethim. Every oracle in the chapter ends the same way: “Then they will know that I am the LORD.” Mockery, contempt, revenge and hatred all end face to face with the God they despised.

Esau’s enmity and the true King. The story has a strange sequel. Herod the Great, king of Judea when Jesus was born, came from an Idumean family, descended from Edom, and he tried to kill the newborn king (Matthew 2:16). The old enmity reached for the true Son of David, and failed. That child grew up to bear God’s judgment against sin himself, so that enemies of every nation could be reconciled to God (Romans 5:10).

Does vengeance through Israel contradict Romans 12:19? No. The vengeance in verse 14 is God’s, not Israel’s, carried out by whom he chooses, as Romans 13:4 says he also uses the ruling authorities. Edom was later conquered by the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus, about 125 BC. Christians, as private persons, never take vengeance.

25.title: Against the Neighbours
25.overview:
Where we are. For twenty-four chapters Ezekiel has spoken against Jerusalem. Chapter 24 ended on the day the siege began (24:1–2), with the prophet bereaved and told that he would be silent until a survivor brought news of the city’s fall (24:25–27). In that silence, before the news arrives (33:21), God turns to the nations: chapter 25 opens eight chapters of oracles against Judah’s neighbours, Tyre and Egypt.

The message. The LORD is not the beaten god of a small nation. He judged Jerusalem himself, and he will not let those who gloated, sneered and took revenge over her fall have the last word. The way a people treat God’s people in their disgrace is the way they treat God, and every one of these nations will end where Judah’s ruin should have led them: knowing that he is the LORD.

Why it was said. The exiles could easily conclude that Babylon’s gods had beaten theirs, and their neighbours said as much (v. 8). Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia were old rivals, several of them Israel’s own relatives, and they enjoyed Judah’s collapse (see the introduction). These oracles told the exiles that their God still ruled the whole map, and that their fall was his discipline, not his defeat.

How the chapter makes its case. Four short oracles, each built the same way: because you did this, therefore I will do that, and then you will know that I am the LORD. Ammon cried “Aha!” and clapped at the temple’s ruin, so Ammon will be overrun and cut off (vv. 1–7). Moab said Judah was “like all the other nations”, so Moab’s proud frontier towns will be laid open (vv. 8–11). Edom took revenge on its brother, so God will lay his own vengeance on Edom (vv. 12–14). The Philistines nursed a “never-ending enmity”, so they will be cut off (vv. 15–17). The sins darken as the chapter goes: a gloating word, then contempt, then revenge, then inherited hatred.

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the character of God revealed in him, and by a striking pattern. God takes the mockery of his people as mockery of himself, and keeps vengeance in his own hands. At the cross the passers-by said “Aha!” over the true temple as it was destroyed (Mark 15:29), and Jesus answered not with vengeance but with prayer: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). God’s just anger against sin fell on him in the place of all who trust him, and his mercy reached even these nations: Moab gave Ruth to the family line of David and of Christ (Matthew 1:5).

For us. It is easy to enjoy the fall of a rival, a critic or a church we disagreed with, and to call it justice. This chapter says God sees that pleasure and takes it personally. Leave vengeance with him, weep with those who weep, and remember that we too were enemies, reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10).
25.theology:
The God who judges his own people also judges the nations, and judgment on Israel's enemies is also a promise to Israel. Gloating over the fall of God's people provokes him (vv. 3, 6; Prov 24:17-18; Obad 12), and to call his people ordinary is to call him ordinary (v. 8).

Vengeance belongs to God alone (vv. 12-17; Rom 12:19). Yet his mercy reaches even into nations under judgment, as Ruth the Moabite shows (Matt 1:5).
25.examples:
One word of scorn, Aha!, brings a capital city down to a camel pasture. A nation that said God's people were nothing special learns that their God is the LORD.

A brother nation settles an old score, and a people hand their hatred down to their children like an inheritance. Each of them ends face to face with the God they despised.

keyVerse.quote: Because you said, ‘Aha!’ over my sanctuary when it was profaned, and over the land of Israel when it was made desolate, and over the house of Judah when they went into exile
keyVerse.note: One word, “Aha!”, sums up the sin of all four nations in this chapter: delight in the ruin of God’s people. God calls the temple “my sanctuary”, showing that he takes the gloating personally, even over a judgment he sent himself. The same word was spoken at the foot of the cross (Mark 15:29), where the one mocked prayed for his mockers.

25.reflection:
Ammon said “Aha!” and clapped its hands at Judah’s ruin (vv. 3, 6). Why is it so tempting to enjoy the downfall of a rival, an opponent or a church we disagree with, and why does God take it so seriously?

Moab said Judah was “like all the other nations” (v. 8). If not its record, what makes the church different from any other community? How should we answer people who point to the church’s failures as proof that its God is not real?

Edom took vengeance into its own hands (v. 12), but God says the vengeance is his (v. 14; Romans 12:19). Where are you tempted to settle scores yourself, and what would it look like to leave it with God?

At the cross the mockers said “Aha!” (Mark 15:29), and Jesus prayed for them (Luke 23:34). How does his response change the way we treat those who have mocked or wronged us?

26.text: <sup>1</sup>In the eleventh year, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, because Tyre said concerning Jerusalem, 'Aha, the gate of the peoples is broken; it has swung open to me. I shall be replenished, now that she is laid waste,'<sup>3</sup>therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and will bring up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves.<sup>4</sup>They shall destroy the walls of Tyre and break down her towers, and I will scrape her soil from her and make her a bare rock.<sup>5</sup>She shall be in the midst of the sea a place for the spreading of nets, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. And she shall become plunder for the nations,<sup>6</sup>and her daughters on the mainland shall be killed by the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.<sup>7</sup>"For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, with horses and chariots, and with horsemen and a host of many soldiers.<sup>8</sup>He will kill with the sword your daughters on the mainland. He will set up a siege wall against you and throw up a mound against you, and raise a roof of shields against you.<sup>9</sup>He will direct the shock of his battering rams against your walls, and with his axes he will break down your towers.<sup>10</sup>His horses will be so many that their dust will cover you. Your walls will shake at the noise of the horsemen and wagons and chariots, when he enters your gates as men enter a city that has been breached.<sup>11</sup>With the hoofs of his horses he will trample all your streets. He will kill your people with the sword, and your mighty pillars will fall to the ground.<sup>12</sup>They will plunder your riches and loot your merchandise. They will break down your walls and destroy your pleasant houses. Your stones and timber and soil they will cast into the midst of the waters.<sup>13</sup>And I will stop the music of your songs, and the sound of your lyres shall be heard no more.<sup>14</sup>I will make you a bare rock. You shall be a place for the spreading of nets. You shall never be rebuilt, for I am the LORD; I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>15</sup>"Thus says the Lord GOD to Tyre: Will not the coastlands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan, when slaughter is made in your midst?<sup>16</sup>Then all the princes of the sea will step down from their thrones and remove their robes and strip off their embroidered garments. They will clothe themselves with trembling; they will sit on the ground and tremble every moment and be appalled at you.<sup>17</sup>And they will raise a lamentation over you and say to you, "'How you have perished, you who were inhabited from the seas, O city renowned, who was mighty on the sea; she and her inhabitants imposed their terror on all her inhabitants!<sup>18</sup>Now the coastlands tremble on the day of your fall, and the coastlands that are on the sea are dismayed at your passing.'<sup>19</sup>"For thus says the Lord GOD: When I make you a city laid waste, like the cities that are not inhabited, when I bring up the deep over you, and the great waters cover you,<sup>20</sup>then I will make you go down with those who go down to the pit, to the people of old, and I will make you to dwell in the world below, among ruins from of old, with those who go down to the pit, so that you will not be inhabited; but I will set beauty in the land of the living.<sup>21</sup>I will bring you to a dreadful end, and you shall be no more. Though you be sought for, you will never be found again, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Aha, the Gate of the Peoples Is Broken
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets himself against those who profit from the ruin of others. In the year Jerusalem fell, Tyre greeted the news as a business opportunity: “Aha, the gate of the peoples is broken… I shall be replenished, now that she is laid waste” (v. 2). So God declares, “I am against you, O Tyre”, and promises to bring many nations against her “as the sea brings up its waves” (v. 3). They will tear down her walls and towers, and God will scrape her down to “a bare rock”, a place for fishermen to spread their nets (vv. 4–5). Her mainland towns will fall, and all will know that he is the LORD (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who see another's ruin as their business opportunity will find God against them.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eleventh year, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, because Tyre said concerning Jerusalem, 'Aha, the gate of the peoples is broken; it has swung open to me. I shall be replenished, now that she is laid waste,' therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and will bring up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves. They shall destroy the walls of Tyre and break down her towers, and I will scrape her soil from her and make her a bare rock. She shall be in the midst of the sea a place for the spreading of nets, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. And she shall become plunder for the nations, and her daughters on the mainland shall be killed by the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tyre greeted Jerusalem’s fall as a business opportunity, so God sets himself against Tyre and will bring nation after nation upon it, like waves, until it is a bare rock.

The setting. Tyre was the great Phoenician port on the Mediterranean coast north of Israel, a trading empire built on ships and money, with its main city on an island just off the shore: rich, beautiful and apparently untouchable. Its “daughters on the mainland” (v. 6) were the towns along the shore that belonged to it.

Aha, the gate of the peoples is broken. Tyre’s reaction was pure business. Jerusalem had stood astride the inland trade routes; now that gate “has swung open to me. I shall be replenished”. Another city’s ruin was Tyre’s chance for profit.

As the sea brings up its waves. Tyre lived by the sea, and God turns its own world into the picture of its ruin: not one attack, but wave after wave of nations.

A place for the spreading of nets. The glittering city will become a place where fishermen dry their nets in the sun. Isaiah had said the same of Tyre: “The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory” (Isaiah 23:9).

Profiting from disaster. The attitude is not only ancient. Markets can profit from disaster, and people can treat a neighbour’s collapse as their chance to get ahead. God sees it and names it. Set beside it the Lord Jesus, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Tyre grew rich on another’s ruin; Christ became poor to make others rich.

Uncertain wording. Verse 1 gives the year and the day but no month, and a word may have dropped out of the Hebrew. Jerusalem’s wall was breached in the fourth month of that eleventh year (Jeremiah 39:2), and Tyre’s gloating shows that the word came after the news had travelled along the coast.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port, partly on an island just off the coast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first wave has a name, and behind it stands God. “I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings” (v. 7), with the full machinery of siege: mainland towns taken, siege wall and mound, battering rams and axes, cavalry whose dust covers the city (vv. 8–11). Then the subject turns from “he” to “they”: the nations plunder Tyre’s riches and throw her stones, timber and soil into the sea (v. 12). Her music will fall silent (v. 13), and she will be left a bare rock, never rebuilt, “for I am the LORD; I have spoken” (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: No wealth or fortification can stand when God sends judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, with horses and chariots, and with horsemen and a host of many soldiers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first wave has a name: Nebuchadnezzar, the greatest king on earth, comes against Tyre because God brings him.

Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings. Nebuchadnezzar (the ESV notes that the Hebrew spells it “Nebuchadrezzar” throughout Ezekiel) is called “king of kings”, the greatest ruler of his day. Daniel addressed him the same way and added the crucial point: “the God of heaven has given the kingdom” to him (Daniel 2:37). Even the king of kings is a servant of the LORD, and the one who says “I will bring” is God.

From the north. Babylon lay to the east, but its armies marched up the Euphrates and came down on Syria and Canaan from the north, so the north became the direction from which the prophets saw judgment coming (Jeremiah 1:14).

The true King of kings. Scripture gives the title at last to the Lamb, who “is Lord of lords and King of kings” (Revelation 17:14). Nebuchadnezzar served God’s purpose for a few decades and was gone; the Lamb reigns for ever, and he won his victory with his own blood.

verseByVerse.quote: He will kill with the sword your daughters on the mainland. He will set up a siege wall against you and throw up a mound against you, and raise a roof of shields against you. He will direct the shock of his battering rams against your walls, and with his axes he will break down your towers. His horses will be so many that their dust will cover you. Your walls will shake at the noise of the horsemen and wagons and chariots, when he enters your gates as men enter a city that has been breached. With the hoofs of his horses he will trample all your streets. He will kill your people with the sword, and your mighty pillars will fall to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The siege is described in full, from the fall of the mainland towns to the pillars of Tyre’s temples crashing down.

Your daughters on the mainland. Tyre itself stood on a rocky island about half a mile off the coast. Its “daughters”, the mainland towns that belonged to it (v. 6), fall first; then the siege works are raised against the city.

He will set up a siege wall. This is a full siege, and Nebuchadnezzar did besiege Tyre, for many years. Ezekiel later records that his army laboured hard, “yet neither he nor his army got anything from Tyre to pay for the labor that he had performed against her” (29:18). God’s word was not finished with Tyre (see the note on vv. 13–14).

Your mighty pillars will fall to the ground. These are probably the sacred standing pillars of Tyre’s temples. The Greek historian Herodotus saw two famous pillars in the temple of Melqart, Tyre’s god, one of gold and one of emerald. Nothing Tyre trusted is left standing, not even its gods.

verseByVerse.quote: They will plunder your riches and loot your merchandise. They will break down your walls and destroy your pleasant houses. Your stones and timber and soil they will cast into the midst of the waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The waves keep coming: not only Nebuchadnezzar but “they”, the nations after him, will plunder Tyre and throw its very stones into the sea.

They will plunder your riches. The subject changes from “he” to “they”. The waves of nations keep coming, and centuries later Tyre’s “stones and timber and soil” were literally thrown into the sea (see the note on vv. 13–14).

False security. Tyre trusted in its island walls and its wealth. “Tyre has built herself a rampart and heaped up silver like dust… But behold, the Lord will strip her of her possessions” (Zechariah 9:3–4). Security built on money and walls will one day be stripped as bare as Tyre’s rock.
verseByVerse.note: Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for many years (Josephus says thirteen); Alexander the Great finally took the island city in 332 BC by building a causeway with the rubble of the mainland city.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will stop the music of your songs, and the sound of your lyres shall be heard no more. I will make you a bare rock. You shall be a place for the spreading of nets. You shall never be rebuilt, for I am the LORD; I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proud city will be silenced and stripped back to bare rock, and the guarantee is God’s own word.

I will stop the music of your songs. Silenced music is the sign of a dead city. John uses the same picture for the final Babylon: “the sound of harpists and musicians… will be heard in you no more” (Revelation 18:22).

I will make you a bare rock. The name Tyre (Tsor) means “rock”. The proud city on its rock will be stripped back to bare rock, fit only for fishermen to spread their nets, as verse 5 had already said. The last words give the guarantee: “for I am the LORD; I have spoken”.

Did the prophecy fail, since a city called Tyre exists today? It foretold that “many nations” would come against Tyre “as the sea brings up its waves” (v. 3): Nebuchadnezzar first, then others. Alexander the Great destroyed the island city in 332 BC, scraping the ruins of the mainland town into the sea to build his causeway. Honesty adds that a town was rebuilt there: Tyre was a port in Roman times (Acts 21:3), and modern Sur stands on the old island, now joined to the shore by the silt of Alexander’s causeway. What never rose again was the Phoenician sea-power the oracle addressed. Some read “never be rebuilt” of that power, others of the island fortress as it was; either way, prophecy here speaks in the strong language of total ruin, and the ruin came.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God brings down the proud, all who leaned on them tremble. The coastlands shake at the sound of Tyre’s fall (v. 15); the princes of the sea step down from their thrones, strip off their robes and sit on the ground, appalled (v. 16). They lament the city “renowned” and “mighty on the sea” that once spread terror (vv. 17–18). Then God speaks the last word: he will bring the deep over Tyre and send her down to the pit, to the people of old, while he sets beauty in the land of the living (vv. 19–20). “Though you be sought for, you will never be found again” (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The fall of a great commercial power shakes all who trusted in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD to Tyre: Will not the coastlands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan, when slaughter is made in your midst? Then all the princes of the sea will step down from their thrones and remove their robes and strip off their embroidered garments. They will clothe themselves with trembling; they will sit on the ground and tremble every moment and be appalled at you. And they will raise a lamentation over you and say to you, "'How you have perished, you who were inhabited from the seas, O city renowned, who was mighty on the sea; she and her inhabitants imposed their terror on all her inhabitants! Now the coastlands tremble on the day of your fall, and the coastlands that are on the sea are dismayed at your passing.' "For thus says the Lord GOD: When I make you a city laid waste, like the cities that are not inhabited, when I bring up the deep over you, and the great waters cover you, then I will make you go down with those who go down to the pit, to the people of old, and I will make you to dwell in the world below, among ruins from of old, with those who go down to the pit, so that you will not be inhabited; but I will set beauty in the land of the living. I will bring you to a dreadful end, and you shall be no more. Though you be sought for, you will never be found again, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tyre’s fall shakes every port that depended on it, and God sends the city that ruled the sea down into the deep, never to be found again.

They will sit on the ground. The rulers of the coastlands sit on the ground in mourning, out of fear as much as sympathy. If Tyre can fall, who is safe?

How you have perished. The lament begins “How”, like the book of Lamentations: “O city renowned, who was mighty on the sea”. John saw the same scene at the fall of the final Babylon: “the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore” (Revelation 18:11).

Those who go down to the pit. Tyre, which ruled the sea, will be swallowed by “the deep” and go down to “the pit”, the place of the dead, to join “the people of old”, the vanished cities of the past. Set against that: “I will set beauty in the land of the living”. While proud Tyre sinks, God will give glory to his own land and people.

Though you be sought for, you will never be found. The old island city that was the wonder of the seas has vanished. The lesson is not only about Tyre: “the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17).

Jesus in Tyre and Sidon. Yet Tyre was not beyond grace. Jesus said that if his mighty works had been done there, “they would have repented long ago” (Luke 10:13); and to those who had seen them, “it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you” (Luke 10:14). He went to “the region of Tyre and Sidon”, where a Gentile mother begged for her daughter and received his mercy (Mark 7:24–30), and when Paul later landed at Tyre, he found disciples there (Acts 21:3–4). The city of merchants fell; the kingdom of Christ reached its people.

Uncertain wording. The last line of verse 20 is abrupt in Hebrew, and translations differ. The ESV has God setting beauty in his own land of the living, in contrast to Tyre; others, by a slight change, read that Tyre will have no place in the land of the living. Either way Tyre is shut out from the land of the living.

26.title: Tyre, the Bare Rock
26.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 25 dealt briefly with four of Judah’s neighbours. Now three whole chapters (26–28) go to Tyre, the rich Phoenician port on the coast north of Israel. The date is the year Jerusalem fell (v. 1), and news of the breach has already reached the coast.

The message. Tyre saw Jerusalem’s ruin as a business opportunity, and God sets himself against it. The city that seemed untouchable on its island rock will be battered by nation after nation, like waves of the sea, until it is scraped bare and sent down to the pit. No wealth, wall or market can stand when God says, “I am against you”.

Why it was said. Judah’s world admired Tyre: its money, its ships, its island fortress that armies could not easily reach (see the introduction). Judah traded with it and envied it. If even Tyre could fall, then security bought with wealth was an illusion, and the God of the exiles, not the markets, ruled the nations.

How the chapter makes its case. Four oracles, each opening “Thus says the Lord GOD”. First the charge and the verdict: because Tyre said “Aha” and hoped to be “replenished”, many nations will come against it like waves and leave it a bare rock for drying nets (vv. 1–6). Then the first wave: Nebuchadnezzar, “king of kings”, with siege works, battering rams and cavalry, followed by others who plunder the city, throw its stones into the sea and silence its music (vv. 7–14). Then the shock: the princes of the sea step down from their thrones to lament the city that once terrified them (vv. 15–18). Last, the end: God covers Tyre with the deep and sends it down to the pit, never to be found again (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and by pattern. Jesus measured his own hearers by Tyre: had it seen his mighty works, it “would have repented long ago” (Luke 10:13), and he went to its region and showed mercy to a Gentile mother (Mark 7:24–30). Tyre grew rich on another’s ruin; Christ “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). And Tyre’s fall previews the fall of every proud system of wealth (Revelation 18), while those who belong to him receive “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28).

For us. Ask where your security is anchored. Wealth, skill and strong walls are gifts, but they make a poor rock to stand on. And watch for the instinct that sees a neighbour’s disaster as an opening; the gospel turns it round, because we live by the riches of one who made himself poor for us.
26.theology:
God judges those who profit from the ruin of others (v. 2). Wealth, commerce and fortifications cannot protect a proud city (vv. 4-14; Isa 23:8-9; Zech 9:3-4), and the greatest rulers are servants of his purposes (v. 7; Dan 2:37).

God's word is fulfilled over time, wave upon wave (vv. 3, 12; 29:18). The fall of worldly powers shakes all who trusted in them, as the final Babylon will (vv. 15-18; Rev 18:9-19, 22). Yet Christ's mercy reached the region of Tyre, and a church grew there (Mark 7:24-30; Acts 21:3-4).
26.examples:
Tyre saw a neighbour's ruin as a business opportunity. What came instead was wave after wave of armies, until the city's rubble was thrown into the sea and fishermen dried their nets on the bare rock.

Kings step off their thrones to sit on the ground, and the music of the harbour stops. Everything Tyre trusted proved to be passing away.

keyVerse.quote: therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and will bring up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves.
keyVerse.note: These words turn Tyre’s own world against it: the sea that made it rich will be the picture of its ruin. “Many nations” explains how the prophecy was fulfilled, not in a single blow but wave after wave, from Nebuchadnezzar to Alexander. Behind every wave stands the God who says, “I am against you”.

26.reflection:
Tyre saw Jerusalem’s ruin as a chance to be “replenished” (v. 2). Where do people, or we ourselves, quietly profit from someone else’s misfortune? How does Christ, who “became poor” to make others rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), change that instinct?

God calls Nebuchadnezzar “king of kings” (v. 7), yet he is only God’s instrument. How does it help you to know that the powerful people of our day are under God’s rule?

The princes of the sea mourn Tyre because their own wealth depended on it (vv. 15–18). What do you rely on for security that would leave you shaken if it fell, and what would it mean to anchor yourself in “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28)?

Jesus said Tyre would have repented if it had seen his works (Luke 10:13–14), and he showed mercy in its region (Mark 7:24–30). What does that teach us about God’s judgment and mercy, and about the privilege of having heard the gospel?
