verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — I Am Perfect in Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything that made Tyre beautiful was borrowed. Ezekiel is told to sing a funeral song for Tyre, the merchant of the coastlands, who boasts, “I am perfect in beauty” (vv. 1–3). The city becomes a great ship: planks from Senir, a cedar mast from Lebanon, oars of Bashan oak, a deck inlaid with ivory, a sail of Egyptian linen and awnings of blue and purple (vv. 4–7). Her rowers come from Sidon and Arvad and her caulkers from Gebal (vv. 8–9); hired soldiers from Persia, Lud and Put hang their shields on her walls (vv. 10–11). Twice the refrain sounds: “they made perfect your beauty” (vv. 4, 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Beauty and splendour gathered by human effort breed a pride that says, I am perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Now you, son of man, raise a lamentation over Tyre, and say to Tyre, who dwells at the entrances to the sea, merchant of the peoples to many coastlands, thus says the Lord GOD: "O Tyre, you have said, 'I am perfect in beauty.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Ezekiel to sing Tyre’s funeral song while she is at the height of her glory, and her own boast, “I am perfect in beauty”, shows why she will fall.

Raise a lamentation over Tyre. A lament is a song for the dead, yet Ezekiel sings it while Tyre is at her height: in God’s sight her end is already certain. The song pictures Tyre as a great merchant ship, magnificently built, loaded with the world’s wealth, then wrecked in the open sea.

Who dwells at the entrances to the sea. Tyre’s island had harbours facing north and south, gateways for the shipping of the eastern Mediterranean. As “merchant of the peoples to many coastlands” it planted trading colonies across the sea, Carthage in North Africa among them, and its ships reached as far as Spain.

I am perfect in beauty. Here is Tyre’s heart in five words. Not “God has blessed me”, but “I am perfect”: the pride that goes before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). Scripture gives that title to one place only, Zion, where God himself is the source of the beauty: “Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shines forth” (Psalm 50:2). Beauty that comes from God is a gift to be thankful for; beauty claimed as one’s own is already on its way down.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre pictured as a magnificent merchant ship.

verseByVerse.quote: Your borders are in the heart of the seas; your builders made perfect your beauty. They made all your planks of fir trees from Senir; they took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you. Of oaks of Bashan they made your oars; they made your deck of pines from the coasts of Cyprus, inlaid with ivory. Of fine embroidered linen from Egypt was your sail, serving as your banner; blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah was your awning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ship of Tyre is built from the finest materials of the whole known world.

Your borders are in the heart of the seas. The island city and the ship are one picture: Tyre rides on the sea like a vessel built for trade.

Your builders made perfect your beauty. Every part comes from the best source: planks from Senir (Mount Hermon), a mast of Lebanon cedar, oars of oak from Bashan, east of the Jordan, famous for its great trees (Isaiah 2:13), and a deck of pine from Cyprus inlaid with ivory. The sail of “fine embroidered linen from Egypt”, “serving as your banner”, was the ship’s flag, its display to all who saw it pass.

Blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah. Tyre was itself famous for purple dye, made from the murex shellfish of its own coast, yet even its awning is imported.

Uncertain wording. Some of the woods and places cannot be identified with certainty. The wood of the deck (ESV “pines”) may be cypress or boxwood, and Elishah was probably part of Cyprus or a coast further west. The picture is clear even where the details are not: the best of every land went into Tyre.

verseByVerse.quote: The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad were your rowers; your skilled men, O Tyre, were in you; they were your pilots. The elders of Gebal and her skilled men were in you, caulking your seams; all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in you to barter for your wares. "Persia and Lud and Put were in your army as your men of war. They hung the shield and helmet in you; they gave you splendor. Men of Arvad and Helech were on your walls all around, and men of Gamad were in your towers. They hung their shields on your walls all around; they made perfect your beauty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ship’s crew and guard are drawn from the best of every nation, and the whole display is borrowed.

They were your pilots. The rowers come from Sidon and Arvad, neighbouring Phoenician cities; Tyre’s own skilled men are the pilots; and the caulkers who seal the seams come from Gebal (the Greeks’ Byblos), an old shipbuilding city (vv. 8–9). Every ship of the sea comes alongside to trade.

Persia and Lud and Put. The soldiers are hired men from the edges of the known world: Persia far to the east, Lud (probably Lydia in Asia Minor) and Put (Libya) to the west. Shields hung on the walls were a display of strength and honour (compare Song of Songs 4:4). The section ends as it began, “they made perfect your beauty” (vv. 4, 11): the whole picture is framed by the word Tyre loved.

All of it borrowed. Wood from Senir and Lebanon, linen from Egypt, sailors from Sidon, soldiers from Persia: Tyre’s “perfect” beauty was assembled from the whole world, and nothing was hers. It is a picture of every human glory, impressive and entirely on loan. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

A glory not borrowed. Only one person’s glory has never been on loan. Jesus prayed, “glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). And unlike Tyre, he does not gather the world’s beauty to adorn himself; he shares his own with those he redeems.

Uncertain wording. Helech and Gamad (v. 11) cannot be identified with certainty; Helech may be Cilicia in south-east Asia Minor.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A great market can hide a great wrong. Ezekiel lists Tyre’s trading partners like a ledger, sweeping from Tarshish in the far west through the Greek world, Asia Minor, Syria, Israel and Arabia to Mesopotamia (vv. 12–23). Metals, horses, ivory, jewels, grain, wine, wool, spices and fine cloth all pour into her market, and so, in the middle of the list, do “human beings” (v. 13). Even Judah and Israel sell their wheat and oil there (v. 17). The section ends with the ship loaded to the waterline: “So you were filled and heavily laden in the heart of the seas” (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: A global economy can be dazzling and still be built partly on the trade in human lives.

verseByVerse.quote: "Tarshish did business with you because of your great wealth of every kind; silver, iron, tin, and lead they exchanged for your wares. Javan, Tubal, and Meshech traded with you; they exchanged human beings and vessels of bronze for your merchandise. From Beth-togarmah they exchanged horses, war horses, and mules for your wares. The men of Dedan traded with you. Many coastlands were your own special markets; they brought you in payment ivory tusks and ebony. Syria did business with you because of your abundant goods; they exchanged for your wares emeralds, purple, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, and ruby. Judah and the land of Israel traded with you; they exchanged for your merchandise wheat of Minnith, meal, honey, oil, and balm. Damascus did business with you for your abundant goods, because of your great wealth of every kind; wine of Helbon and wool of Sahar and casks of wine from Uzal they exchanged for your wares; wrought iron, cassia, and calamus were bartered for your merchandise. Dedan traded with you in saddlecloths for riding. Arabia and all the princes of Kedar were your favored dealers in lambs, rams, and goats; in these they did business with you. The traders of Sheba and Raamah traded with you; they exchanged for your wares the best of all kinds of spices and all precious stones and gold. Haran, Canneh, Eden, traders of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad traded with you. In your market these traded with you in choice garments, in clothes of blue and embroidered work, and in carpets of colored material, bound with cords and made secure. The ships of Tarshish traveled for you with your merchandise. So you were filled and heavily laden in the heart of the seas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole known world traded at Tyre, and among all its wealth were human beings bought and sold.

Tarshish did business with you. Now comes a long, crowded trade list. From the far west (Tarshish) to Arabia, from Syria to the lands of the north, goods poured into Tyre: metals (v. 12), horses and mules (v. 14), ivory and ebony (v. 15), emeralds, purple, fine linen, coral and ruby (v. 16), wine and wool (v. 18), spices, precious stones and gold (v. 22), fine garments and carpets (v. 24).

Judah and the land of Israel traded with you. Even God’s own people were part of Tyre’s market (v. 17), selling their grain and oil. Nobody stands outside the world economy.

They exchanged human beings. And there, casually, in the middle of the list: “human beings” (literally “souls of men”), traded alongside bronze pots. (Javan is the Greek world; Tubal and Meshech lay in what is now Turkey.) The glittering economy of Tyre included slaves. John’s description of the final Babylon’s cargo ends the same way: “horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls” (Revelation 18:13). God reads the whole list, including the line everyone else skims past.

Bought to be set free. Set that line beside the gospel. Tyre bought and sold people for silver and bronze. Christ bought people too, but to set them free: “you were ransomed… not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19), and heaven sings that by his blood he “ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). The merchant city priced human beings with bronze pots. The Lamb paid for them with his life.

The supply chain we do not see. It is easy to shudder at the ancient world and move on. But the International Labour Organization estimated in 2022 that around fifty million people were living in modern slavery, in forced labour or forced marriage, and some of what they are made to produce ends up in ordinary shops. A phone, a shirt or a bag of prawns can reach us with no trace of the hands that made it. Tyre’s sin was not only greed but a chosen blindness, and every consumer is tempted to the same: as long as it is cheap and far away, it is not my concern. Scripture will not let us shrug, but neither does it lay on us the impossible burden of policing the whole world’s economy. People who know they were bought by the Lamb cannot stay indifferent to people who are sold. They start asking where things come from and buying differently, not to earn a clear conscience but because they have been ransomed themselves.

So you were filled and heavily laden. The ship is loaded to the waterline with wealth. It looks like success. It is also how ships sink.

Uncertain wording. Many places and goods in this list cannot now be identified with certainty, among them Minnith, Sahar, Uzal, Canneh and Chilmad; the word translated “meal” in verse 17 occurs only here, and verse 19 is especially hard in Hebrew. In verse 16 some Hebrew manuscripts read “Edom” for “Syria” (Aram); the two names look very alike in Hebrew. None of this changes the picture: the whole known world traded at Tyre.
verseByVerse.note: A catalogue of the ancient world’s trade, from Tarshish to Arabia.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–36 — Wrecked in the Heart of the Seas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What the world admires can be lost in a single storm. Tyre’s own rowers take her out into the high seas, and “the east wind has wrecked you in the heart of the seas” (v. 26). Riches, cargo, crew and soldiers all sink together (v. 27). The cry of the drowning pilots carries to the shore, where the sailors of every ship come down to land and mourn with dust, ashes, shaved heads and sackcloth (vv. 28–31). Their lament asks, “Who is like Tyre?”, remembers how she enriched the kings of the earth, and ends in horror and scorn: “you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever” (vv. 32–36).
verseByVerse.theology: Wealth that fills a ship to the waterline can sink it in a single storm.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your rowers have brought you out into the high seas. The east wind has wrecked you in the heart of the seas. Your riches, your wares, your merchandise, your mariners and your pilots, your caulkers, your dealers in merchandise, and all your men of war who are in you, with all your crew that is in your midst, sink into the heart of the seas on the day of your fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one line the storm God sends wrecks the ship, and everything that made Tyre great goes down with her.

Your rowers have brought you out into the high seas. The crew that made Tyre great (vv. 8–9) row her out into the deep water where the storm finds her. The skill and trade that made her rich carried her into danger.

The east wind has wrecked you. The east wind is the storm God sends. A psalm had sung, “By the east wind you shattered the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 48:7). All that beauty and skill, all those expert pilots, could not steer through God’s storm.

Sink into the heart of the seas. The list of verse 27 reverses the list of verses 5–11. Everything that made the ship great goes down with it: the riches and the people. That is the rich fool’s story on a national scale. He said, “Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years”, but God said, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: At the sound of the cry of your pilots the countryside shakes, and down from their ships come all who handle the oar. The mariners and all the pilots of the sea stand on the land and shout aloud over you and cry out bitterly. They cast dust on their heads and wallow in ashes; they make themselves bald for you and put sackcloth on their waist, and they weep over you in bitterness of soul, with bitter mourning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sailors of every nation mourn Tyre as if for the dead, but they grieve for their losses, not for her sin.

At the sound of the cry of your pilots. The cry of the drowning crew carries to the shore, and the whole coast shakes. The sailors of every other ship come ashore to watch.

They cast dust on their heads. Dust, ashes, shaved heads and sackcloth were the full rites of mourning for the dead (compare Isaiah 15:2–3): they mourn Tyre as a corpse, for their own livelihood sank with her.

Regret without repentance. They mourn for what they lost, not for what Tyre did. There is no repentance in their grief, only regret. The world can weep bitterly over a collapse without ever asking what God was saying through it.

verseByVerse.quote: In their wailing they raise a lamentation for you and lament over you: 'Who is like Tyre, like one destroyed in the midst of the sea? When your wares came from the seas, you satisfied many peoples; with your abundant wealth and merchandise you enriched the kings of the earth. Now you are wrecked by the seas, in the depths of the waters; your merchandise and all your crew in your midst have sunk with you. All the inhabitants of the coastlands are appalled at you, and the hair of their kings bristles with horror; their faces are convulsed. The merchants among the peoples hiss at you; you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world that once admired Tyre now looks on in horror and scorn, because its loyalty was always to her success, never to her.

Who is like Tyre? That question was once asked in admiration. Now it is asked in horror. Israel had sung the same question of the only one who deserves it: “Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods?” (Exodus 15:11). Ask it of any city, any market or any person, and the answer will one day be a lament.

You enriched the kings of the earth. The mourners say what Tyre did for them: “you satisfied many peoples; with your abundant wealth and merchandise you enriched the kings of the earth”. Whole nations had built their prosperity on Tyre. When she sank, their fortunes sank with her, and “the hair of their kings bristles with horror”. It is the panic of a financial collapse spreading from one centre to every market that depended on it.

Now you are wrecked by the seas. The song turns on one word: once (v. 33), “now” (v. 34). The sea that brought Tyre her wealth swallows it. The last line, “shall be no more forever”, is the refrain that closes each of Ezekiel’s laments over Tyre (26:21; 28:19).

The merchants hiss at you. Hissing was the sound passers-by made over a ruin, in shock and in scorn (1 Kings 9:8). Not long before, the nations had hissed over Jerusalem: “Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty?” (Lamentations 2:15). Tyre, which gloated over Jerusalem (26:2) and called itself “perfect in beauty” (v. 3), now hears the same sound. The world is loyal to success, not to people.

The same scene in Revelation. John saw this scene again at the end of history, when the great city Babylon falls: “all shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, ‘What city was like the great city?’ And they threw dust on their heads” (Revelation 18:17–19). Ezekiel 27 previews the collapse of every proud, godless system of wealth and power.

Riches that rot. The question for us is where our security is anchored. “Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted” (James 5:1–2). “For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?” (Matthew 16:26). The only treasure that does not sink is treasure in heaven.

27.title: The Wreck of the Great Ship
27.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 26 announced Tyre’s fall. Chapter 27 sings its funeral song before the funeral: Tyre is still at the height of her glory when Ezekiel is told to “raise a lamentation” over her.

The message. Tyre said, “I am perfect in beauty”, and the whole world had indeed gone into her making. But every glory she had was borrowed, her wealth was built partly on trading human lives, and the cargo that made her great is what sinks her. When God’s storm comes, all that the world admired goes down in a moment, and those who grew rich by her can only stand on the shore and wail.

Why it was said. The exiles’ world measured greatness by Tyre’s standard: trade, luxury and a market reaching every coast (see the introduction). Judah itself sold its grain and oil there (v. 17). God lets them hear the end of that story before it happens, so that they will neither envy nor trust what he is about to sink.

How the chapter makes its case. Tyre is pictured as a magnificent merchant ship. First she is built from the best of every land, timber, linen, crews and soldiers: “they made perfect your beauty” (vv. 1–11). Then she is loaded with the trade of the known world, from Tarshish in the west to Sheba and Asshur in the east, with human beings listed among the bronze pots (vv. 12–25). Then, in a single line, “The east wind has wrecked you in the heart of the seas” (v. 26): ship, cargo and crew go down together, and the sailors of every nation mourn on the shore, crying, “Who is like Tyre?” (vv. 26–36).

Where it leads. To Christ by contrast, and by the need it exposes. Tyre bought and sold people with silver and bronze; Christ ransomed people “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Tyre’s beauty was borrowed and sank; his glory is his own, the glory he had with the Father “before the world existed” (John 17:5). And the chapter is the pattern for John’s vision of the fall of Babylon (Revelation 18), where the merchants weep over the collapse of the world’s trade and heaven moves on to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9).

For us. Ask what your life is loaded with, and whether it will float when God’s storm comes. Thank God for every good gift, but do not mistake borrowed beauty for your own, and do not forget the people behind the goods we buy. The only treasure that does not sink is the treasure kept in heaven (Matthew 6:19–20).
27.theology:
Pride says, I am perfect in beauty, though every glory is borrowed (v. 3; 1 Cor 4:7). Global prosperity can include the trade in human lives, and God sees it (v. 13; Rev 18:13).

Wealth that fills a life to the brim cannot survive the storm God sends (vv. 25-27; Luke 12:19-20; Jas 5:1-3), and the world's admiration turns to horror and contempt when success collapses (vv. 32-36). Tyre's wreck previews the fall of the final Babylon and every godless system of wealth and power (Rev 18:9-19).
27.examples:
Picture a ship built from the best wood of every mountain, with a sail of embroidered linen from Egypt, and a cargo list where human beings appear between the bronze pots.

She is loaded to the waterline, and one east wind is enough. Who is like Tyre? was asked first in envy, and then in horror.

keyVerse.quote: O Tyre, you have said, ‘I am perfect in beauty.’
keyVerse.note: Tyre’s boast is the heart of the chapter. The rest of the song shows that every part of her beauty came from somewhere else, and that her proud cargo is what sank her. The only beauty that is truly perfect belongs to God (Psalm 50:2), and he gives it as a gift, never as a possession to boast in.

27.reflection:
Tyre said, “I am perfect in beauty” (v. 3), yet every part of her came from somewhere else (vv. 4–11). Which of your gifts are you tempted to treat as your own achievement? How does Paul’s question, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7), help?

“Human beings” appear in the middle of a list of trade goods (v. 13). Where might ordinary prosperity today rest on people being treated as merchandise, and what difference should it make that we were ransomed “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19)?

The ship sank because it was “heavily laden” when the storm came (vv. 25–27). What would it look like for you to hold wealth and success loosely, so that they cannot sink you?

The sailors mourned what they had lost but never asked why Tyre fell (vv. 28–36). When something we relied on collapses, how can we respond with repentance and faith rather than mere regret?

On the day that you were created they were prepared.<sup>14</sup>You were an anointed guardian cherub. I placed you; you were on the holy mountain of God; in the midst of the stones of fire you walked.<sup>15</sup>You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you.<sup>16</sup>In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence in your midst, and you sinned; so I cast you as a profane thing from the mountain of God, and I destroyed you, O guardian cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire.<sup>17</sup>Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor. I cast you to the ground; I exposed you before kings, to feast their eyes on you.<sup>18</sup>By the multitude of your iniquities, in the unrighteousness of your trade you profaned your sanctuaries; so I brought fire out from your midst; it consumed you, and I turned you to ashes on the earth in the sight of all who saw you.<sup>19</sup>All who know you among the peoples are appalled at you; you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever."<sup>20</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>21</sup>"Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against her<sup>22</sup>and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I am against you, O Sidon, and I will manifest my glory in your midst. And they shall know that I am the LORD when I execute judgments in her and manifest my holiness in her;<sup>23</sup>for I will send pestilence into her, and blood into her streets; and the slain shall fall in her midst, by the sword that is against her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD.<sup>24</sup>"And for the house of Israel there shall be no more a brier to prick or a thorn to hurt them among all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.<sup>25</sup>"Thus says the Lord GOD: When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered, and manifest my holiness in them in the sight of the nations, then they shall dwell in their own land that I gave to my servant Jacob.<sup>26</sup>And they shall dwell securely in it, and they shall build houses and plant vineyards. They shall dwell securely, when I execute judgments upon all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every human who claims to be a god is only a man, and death will prove it. The prince of Tyre says in his proud heart, “I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods, in the heart of the seas”, but God answers, “yet you are but a man, and no god” (v. 2). His wisdom is real: he is wiser than Daniel, and by it he has gathered gold and silver, but his heart has grown proud in his wealth (vv. 3–5). So God will bring “the most ruthless of the nations” against the beauty of his wisdom (vv. 6–7). He will die the shameful death of the slain, and God asks, “Will you still say, ‘I am a god,’ in the presence of those who kill you?” (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology: The proud person who makes himself a god will be shown to be only a mortal man.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Because your heart is proud, and you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods, in the heart of the seas,' yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruler of Tyre has come to think himself a god, and God answers that he is only a man. After two chapters on the city, God addresses its ruler and goes straight to the heart: “Because your heart is proud”.

I am a god. The boast is breathtaking: “I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods”. From his island fortress “in the heart of the seas”, untouched by armies and rich beyond measure, he began to think himself divine. The king at this time was probably Ethbaal (Ittobaal), under whom, according to Phoenician records quoted by Josephus, the island city held out against Nebuchadnezzar for thirteen years.

Yet you are but a man. That is the answer to every human being who puts himself in God’s place. It is the oldest temptation in the world: “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5). It led the crowd to shout of Herod, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”, and “an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory” (Acts 12:22–23). Paul warns of “the man of lawlessness” who will take his seat “in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4).

God made himself a man. Set it against Christ. The prince of Tyre was a man who made himself a god. Jesus was God who made himself a man: “though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). Tyre’s king climbed up and was thrown down. Christ came down and was lifted up.

The exhausting work of being a god. Few people say “I am a god” out loud. But the heart says it in quieter ways: “I am the master of my life. I decide what is right. I need no one.” Our culture hands each of us something like the prince’s job description: decide who you are, make your own meaning, justify your existence by what you achieve, secure your own future. It sounds like freedom, and in part it is. But a god has no one to lean on, no one to forgive him and no day off, and the strain shows in a generation more anxious and more tired than its comforts can explain. Then comes Ezekiel’s question: “Will you still say, ‘I am a god,’ in the presence of those who kill you?” (v. 9). Death is where the job description runs out. The gospel does not tell us to try harder at being divine. It tells us we may stop. “He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14), and the one who really was God became a man and carried the weight we were never built to bear. There is deep rest in being only a creature, when the Creator is that kind of Father.

verseByVerse.quote: you are indeed wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you; by your wisdom and your understanding you have made wealth for yourself, and have gathered gold and silver into your treasuries; by your great wisdom in your trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart has become proud in your wealth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s wisdom was real and made him rich, but wealth he credited to himself turned his heart proud.

You are indeed wiser than Daniel. God may be speaking with irony, or he may mean it; either way it is striking. Daniel, taken to Babylon as a young man, was famous for wisdom: Nebuchadnezzar found him and his friends “ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters” (Daniel 1:20). The king of Tyre may have been brilliant too. But wisdom without the fear of God is exactly what makes a person proud.

Your heart has become proud in your wealth. Watch the sequence: wisdom, trade, wealth, pride. Each step looks good. Skill is good; business is good; wealth can be good. But success tempts us to credit ourselves: “you have made wealth for yourself”, not God.

The cure is memory. Moses warned Israel never to say, “My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17). The cure he gave was memory: “You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:18).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew spelling of the name here (as in 14:14) differs slightly from the usual spelling of Daniel. Most take it as the Daniel of the book of Daniel, Ezekiel’s contemporary, already famous at the Babylonian court; some think instead of Danel, a wise and just king of old Canaanite stories. Either way, the name stood for wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you make your heart like the heart of a god, therefore, behold, I will bring foreigners upon you, the most ruthless of the nations; and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and defile your splendor. They shall thrust you down into the pit, and you shall die the death of the slain in the heart of the seas. Will you still say, 'I am a god,' in the presence of those who kill you, though you are but a man, and no god, in the hands of those who slay you? You shall die the death of the uncircumcised by the hand of foreigners; for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who made himself a god will die like any other man, at the hands of foreigners and in shame.

The beauty of your wisdom. Swords against “the beauty of your wisdom”: all the brilliance and splendour he was proud of will be hacked down. Wisdom cannot argue with a sword. “The most ruthless of the nations” are the Babylonians (30:10–11).

In the presence of those who kill you. Here is a searching question: “Will you still say, ‘I am a god,’ in the presence of those who kill you?” Death exposes every false claim. The man who made himself a god dies like any other man. A psalm says the same of rulers who thought themselves gods: “nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince” (Psalm 82:7).

The death of the uncircumcised. A shameful death, outside God’s people, without honour. The one who claimed to sit with the gods dies among the despised. “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — Lament for the King of Tyre
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride ruins even the most gifted creature, turning God’s gifts into the cause of its fall. Ezekiel sings a lament over the king of Tyre in the language of Eden: “You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in Eden, the garden of God”, covered with precious stones (vv. 12–13). He was “an anointed guardian cherub” on the holy mountain of God, “blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you” (vv. 14–15). Trade filled him with violence, and God cast him out (v. 16). “Your heart was proud because of your beauty” (v. 17), so God brought fire out from within him and turned him to ashes (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Whether in the heavenly realm, in Eden or in a king's palace, pride corrupts the glory God gave and brings it down.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre, and say to him, Thus says the Lord GOD: "You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering, sardius, topaz, and diamond, beryl, onyx, and jasper, sapphire, emerald, and carbuncle; and crafted in gold were your settings and your engravings. On the day that you were created they were prepared.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel laments the king of Tyre as if he had lived in Eden itself, clothed in jewels and perfect in beauty, so that his fall is a fall from paradise.

Raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre. A funeral lament again, but now the language soars far beyond any ordinary king.

You were in Eden, the garden of God. The king is described as if he had lived in paradise, covered with jewels. All nine stones named here appear, in the ESV, among the twelve stones on the breastpiece of Israel’s high priest (Exodus 28:17–20). The picture is of someone clothed in priestly and royal glory, in the very presence of God. And all of it was “prepared” on the day he was created: his glory was a gift from the start, not an achievement.

The story of every proud heart. However the details are read, the pattern is the point: a creature given magnificent gifts turned them into grounds for pride, and fell. That is the story of the devil, of Adam, of Tyre’s king and of every proud heart.

Where Christians differ. Is this Satan’s fall or the king of Tyre’s? The passage names the king of Tyre (v. 12) and speaks of his trade and violence (vv. 16, 18). Yet many, including many early Christian writers, have seen Satan behind him, because of Eden, the guardian cherub and a creature blameless from the day of his creation, and have read it alongside Isaiah’s “How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star” (Isaiah 14:12). Some draw a line between the “prince” of verses 1–10, the man, and the “king” of verses 11–19, the power behind him. Many later interpreters have been more cautious, as the Reformers were with the similar words in Isaiah 14.

This commentary’s view. The lament describes the human king in the language of Eden and the first rebellion, showing that his pride is the same pride that ruined Adam and the devil, the one who was “puffed up with conceit” (1 Timothy 3:6). It shows what Satan’s fall was like, without being a direct account of it, and the change from “prince” to “king” does not mark a change of subject, since both are ordinary titles of human rulers. The Bible’s teaching that the devil is a creature who fell does not rest on this passage (John 8:44; 1 John 3:8; Jude 6), so nothing essential is lost whichever reading is right.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of “the signet of perfection” (v. 12) is uncertain; it may picture a seal of perfect workmanship. Some of the stones cannot be identified with certainty (the ESV notes that “sapphire” may be lapis lazuli), and the meaning of the words translated “settings” and “engravings” is uncertain.
verseByVerse.note: The king of Tyre is described in language of Eden and of a fallen guardian cherub; many have seen behind him the fall of Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: You were an anointed guardian cherub. I placed you; you were on the holy mountain of God; in the midst of the stones of fire you walked. You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was given the highest honour and was made good; the evil that ruined him arose within him.

An anointed guardian cherub. Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life in Eden (Genesis 3:24) and covered the ark in God’s sanctuary. This figure had the highest place of honour: “on the holy mountain of God”, walking “in the midst of the stones of fire”. And note: “I placed you”. Everything he had, God gave.

Till unrighteousness was found in you. God did not create him evil. He was made good, and the evil arose within him. That is how Scripture always describes the origin of sin: not a flaw in God’s work, but a creature’s own turning away from the Creator. The word “found” is striking, as if God searched and discovered it: nothing escapes his eyes.

The one in whom nothing was found. Set beside this the one man in whom nothing was found. Pilate said of Jesus, “I find no guilt in him” (John 18:38), and Peter wrote, “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). The king of Tyre was blameless only until pride took hold; Christ was blameless to the end, and so could die not for his own unrighteousness but for ours.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of “guardian” is uncertain. The ancient Greek translation, followed by some modern versions, reads verse 14 as with an anointed guardian cherub I placed you, and verse 16 as the cherub driving the king out; the Hebrew consonants allow either reading. On that reading the king is not the cherub but a man in Eden beside it, like Adam, which fits the view taken in the note on verses 11–13.

verseByVerse.quote: In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence in your midst, and you sinned; so I cast you as a profane thing from the mountain of God, and I destroyed you, O guardian cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire. Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor. I cast you to the ground; I exposed you before kings, to feast their eyes on you. By the multitude of your iniquities, in the unrighteousness of your trade you profaned your sanctuaries; so I brought fire out from your midst; it consumed you, and I turned you to ashes on the earth in the sight of all who saw you. All who know you among the peoples are appalled at you; you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Violence in his trade and pride in his beauty brought him down: God cast him out, exposed him before kings and burned him from within.

In the abundance of your trade. Now the language comes back to Tyre’s business: “In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence”. Commerce pursued with a proud heart turned into exploitation and cruelty. So God “cast” him out (the ESV notes, perhaps “banished”) “as a profane thing”, thrown out of the holy place like something unclean.

Your heart was proud because of your beauty. Here is the root, stated plainly. And pride did something to his wisdom: “you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor”. Pride does not only lead to sin; it corrupts the mind. Brilliant people make foolish choices when their image matters more than truth.

I cast you to the ground. “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). He is thrown to the ground and put on display before other kings. “I brought fire out from your midst”: the destruction came from within, for pride is a fire that burns its owner from the inside. The lament ends like the lament for the city (27:36): “a dreadful end… no more forever”.

Paradise lost and given. There is a beautiful reversal in the Bible’s last pages. The precious stones that covered the proud king (jasper, sapphire, emerald, onyx, beryl, topaz) reappear as the foundations of the new Jerusalem: “The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire” (Revelation 21:19). The king was cast out of the garden of God; Christ, who said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), promised a dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). The glory the proud lost, God gives by grace to the humble.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God shows his glory and his holiness in his judgments. Sidon, Tyre’s older neighbour up the coast, is the last of Israel’s near neighbours to be addressed. God declares, “Behold, I am against you, O Sidon, and I will manifest my glory in your midst” (v. 22). Pestilence will fill her streets, and the sword will come against her on every side (v. 23). Twice the oracle gives the purpose of it all: when God acts, “they shall know that I am the LORD” (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology: God shows his holiness among the nations in judgment as well as in mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against her and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I am against you, O Sidon, and I will manifest my glory in your midst. And they shall know that I am the LORD when I execute judgments in her and manifest my holiness in her; for I will send pestilence into her, and blood into her streets; and the slain shall fall in her midst, by the sword that is against her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sidon too will be judged, and in that judgment God will show the world his glory and his holiness.

I am against you, O Sidon. Sidon was Tyre’s older sister city along the coast, also a centre of trade, and the home of Jezebel, daughter of “Ethbaal king of the Sidonians”, who brought Baal worship into Israel (1 Kings 16:31).

I will manifest my glory. God’s glory is shown not only in blessing but in judgment. When God judges evil, his holiness is displayed. The world may not like that, but a God who never judged would not be holy.

Mercy reaches Sidon. Yet Sidon also saw God’s mercy. In Jezebel’s own homeland, Elijah was sent “to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow” (Luke 4:26), and Jesus used her story to show that God’s grace was never for Israel alone. Crowds from “the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon” came to hear him and be healed (Luke 6:17). The glory that judges Sidon here was shown to its people in Christ, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracles against the nations are, in the end, good news for God’s people. The neighbours who treated Israel with contempt will no longer be briers and thorns to wound them (v. 24). God will gather his scattered people and manifest his holiness in them before the nations, and they will live in the land he gave to his servant Jacob (v. 25). They will build houses, plant vineyards and dwell securely, while those who despised them are judged, and they will know that he is “the LORD their God” (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgments on the nations serve his purpose to gather and settle his people in safety.

verseByVerse.quote: "And for the house of Israel there shall be no more a brier to prick or a thorn to hurt them among all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD. "Thus says the Lord GOD: When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered, and manifest my holiness in them in the sight of the nations, then they shall dwell in their own land that I gave to my servant Jacob. And they shall dwell securely in it, and they shall build houses and plant vineyards. They shall dwell securely, when I execute judgments upon all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these judgments turn out to be good news for God’s people: he will remove those who tormented them, gather them home and let them live safely as his own.

No more a brier to prick. The neighbours who treated God’s people with contempt, like thorns in their side, will trouble them no more. The picture goes back to Moses’ warning that the peoples Israel failed to drive out would be “barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides” (Numbers 33:55); now God himself removes them.

Manifest my holiness in them. In verse 22 God manifested his holiness in Sidon through judgment. Here he manifests it in Israel through restoration. The same holiness has two outcomes: fire for the proud, gathering for his people.

They shall build houses and plant vineyards. This is ordinary life, lived in peace. Isaiah described God’s new creation in the same homely terms: “They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit” (Isaiah 65:21).

They shall dwell securely. Twice the chapter says it. That is what the proud king of Tyre thought he had in his island fortress, and lost; God gives it to his people as a gift. And the chapter’s last words are tender: “the LORD their God”. The security Tyre sought in wealth and walls, God’s people find in belonging to him.

Where Christians differ. How is this promise of a safe home fulfilled? It was fulfilled in part when exiles came back from Babylon to build and plant again. Dispensationalist Christians (who see God’s purposes for Israel and for the church as running on separate tracks) expect a further regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see its beginning in the modern state of Israel. Christians who love Scripture differ here and should hold their views with charity.

This commentary’s view. The promise reaches beyond territory, as the rest of Ezekiel does: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. Christ gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26), and the security of verse 26 will be complete in the new creation, where no thorn will hurt them again. The modern state of Israel is not the fulfilment of these promises, though Christians should love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation.

28.title: I Am a God
28.overview:
Where we are. This is the last of the three chapters on Tyre. Chapter 26 announced the city’s fall and chapter 27 sang its funeral song; now God speaks to the man at the top, the ruler of Tyre. A short word against neighbouring Sidon then closes the oracles against Israel’s near neighbours, before Egypt fills chapters 29–32.

The message. The root of Tyre’s sin was a heart that said, “I am a god.” Wisdom, trade and wealth had led its ruler step by step to think himself divine, and God answers that he is only a man who will die like one. His fall is told in the language of Eden: a creature given every gift, placed in glory, who grew proud of his beauty and was cast out. Then the purpose of all these oracles is revealed: God will gather his scattered people, show his holiness in them and let them live in safety.

Why it was said. The exiles lived among nations whose kings were hailed as sons or servants of the gods, and Tyre’s ruler sat in an island fortress that seemed beyond the reach of any army (see the introduction). Judah’s own kings had been tempted by the same pride. The exiles needed to hear that no human greatness can stand before God, and that their own future rested on his promise.

How the chapter makes its case. First an oracle: the prince of Tyre says, “I am a god”, and God answers, “yet you are but a man” (vv. 1–10). Then a lament: the king of Tyre was once in Eden, adorned with precious stones, an anointed guardian cherub, “blameless in your ways” until unrighteousness was found in him; pride in his beauty corrupted his wisdom, and God cast him to the ground and turned him to ashes (vv. 11–19). Then Sidon is judged, and God shows his glory there (vv. 20–23). Last, a promise: no more briers for Israel, but a gathered people dwelling securely, building houses and planting vineyards (vv. 24–26).

Where it leads. To Christ by sharp contrast and by promise. The prince of Tyre was a man who made himself a god; Jesus is God who made himself a man, who “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). Unrighteousness was found in the king of Tyre, but of Jesus even Pilate said, “I find no guilt in him” (John 18:38). The king was cast out of the garden of God; Christ opened paradise to a dying thief (Luke 23:43). And the closing promise of a gathered, secure people is kept in him, who gathers into one “the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52).

For us. Few people say “I am a god” aloud, but the heart says it whenever it credits itself with what God gave, or tries to run its life without him. The way out is not to try harder at being divine but to rest in being a creature, loved by a Father, and to trust the one who came down for us.
28.theology:
The root of sin is the proud desire to be like God; every human who claims divinity is only a man (vv. 2, 9; Gen 3:5; Acts 12:21-23; 2 Thess 2:3-4; Ps 82:6-7). Wisdom and success tempt the heart to pride by crediting ourselves with what God gave (vv. 3-5), and pride corrupts wisdom and destroys from within (vv. 17-18).

Created beings were made good; sin arose within them through pride (v. 15). This commentary reads the lament of vv. 11-19 as the king of Tyre described in the language of Eden and the first rebellion, so that his pride is shown to be the pride that ruined Adam and the devil (Isa 14:12-15; 1 Tim 3:6; Prov 16:18).

God displays his holiness both in judging the proud and in restoring his people (vv. 22, 25), and the security the proud seek in wealth he gives to his people as a gift (vv. 25-26; Isa 65:21-22). Christ, who was God, humbled himself as a man, and the glory pride lost adorns the city of God's humble people (Phil 2:5-8; Rev 21:19-20).
28.examples:
A man on an island fortress says, "I am a god", and climbs there step by step, each step looking good: wisdom, trade, wealth, pride. God asks whether he will still say it to the men who kill him.

He was blameless until unrighteousness was found in him, and the fire that consumed him started inside. Yet the jewels the proud king lost are set at last in the foundations of the city of God, where his humble people build houses and plant vineyards in safety.

keyVerse.quote: Because your heart is proud, and you have said, ‘I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods, in the heart of the seas,’ yet you are but a man, and no god
keyVerse.note: This verse exposes the root beneath all of Tyre’s wealth and violence: a proud heart that claims God’s place. It is the oldest temptation, “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5), and God’s answer is simple: “you are but a man”. The gospel shows the opposite movement in Christ, who was God and made himself a man.

28.reflection:
The prince of Tyre’s path to “I am a god” ran through wisdom, trade and wealth (vv. 2–5), each good in itself. Where do your gifts or successes tempt you to credit yourself, and what cure does Moses give in Deuteronomy 8:17–18?

“Will you still say, ‘I am a god,’ in the presence of those who kill you?” (v. 9). In what quieter ways do people today try to be their own god, and why is it a relief to be only a creature in the hands of a loving Father?

The king was “blameless” until “unrighteousness was found” in him (v. 15), while of Jesus it was said, “I find no guilt in him” (John 18:38). How does Christ’s sinlessness give you hope when you find pride and sin in yourself?

The chapter ends with God’s people living securely because he has gathered them (vv. 25–26). Where do you look for security, and how does belonging to Christ give a safety that Tyre’s walls and wealth never could?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — My Nile Is My Own
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharaoh’s sin is to think he made the Nile; Israel’s is to lean on him. In January 587 BC, with Jerusalem under siege, God sets his face against Pharaoh, “the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams”, who says, “My Nile is my own; I made it for myself” (vv. 1–3). The monster that seemed untouchable will be hooked like a crocodile, dragged out with the fish of his streams clinging to his scales, and left in the open country for birds and beasts (vv. 4–5). The reason touches Israel directly: Egypt has been “a staff of reed” that snapped and wounded everyone who leaned on it (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Whoever claims to have made what God made, and whoever leans on such a power, will be broken.

verseByVerse.quote: In the tenth year, in the tenth month, on the twelfth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and prophesy against him and against all Egypt; speak, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams, that says, 'My Nile is my own; I made it for myself.' I will put hooks in your jaws, and make the fish of your streams stick to your scales; and I will draw you up out of the midst of your streams, with all the fish of your streams that stick to your scales. And I will cast you out into the wilderness, you and all the fish of your streams; you shall fall on the open field, and not be brought together or gathered. To the beasts of the earth and to the birds of the heavens I give you as food. Then all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the LORD. "Because you have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel, when they grasped you with the hand, you broke and tore all their shoulders; and when they leaned on you, you broke and made all their loins to shake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets himself against the king who claimed to have made the Nile, and against the false hope Judah placed in him. This is the first of seven oracles against Egypt in chapters 29–32, dated about January 587 BC, during the siege of Jerusalem (v. 1).

The great dragon. Pharaoh is pictured as a great dragon sprawled in the channels of the Nile. The word is used of serpents and great sea creatures (Genesis 1:21; Exodus 7:9); here it most likely means the Nile crocodile, drawn larger than life as a monster of chaos. His boast is the heart of the matter: “My Nile is my own; I made it for myself.” Egypt’s whole life depended on the Nile, and Pharaoh took the credit for it, the same pride as the prince of Tyre’s (28:2). An earlier Pharaoh had asked, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?” (Exodus 5:2). This one has the same heart.

I will put hooks in your jaws. The monster that thought itself untouchable is dragged out like a crocodile on a line, the fish of his streams, probably his people and allies, clinging to his scales, and all are left to rot in the open country. God asked Job, “Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook” (Job 41:1)? No man can. God can. Scripture often pictures God’s victory over proud powers as the defeat of the sea monster: “Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon?” (Isaiah 51:9).

A staff of reed. A reed looks like a walking stick, but lean your weight on it and it snaps, and the splintered end tears into your hand and shoulder. More than a century earlier the Assyrian commander had mocked Judah with the same picture: “you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it” (Isaiah 36:6).

What we lean on. Everyone leans on something: money, a career, a relationship, a government, our own strength. They can look like walking sticks, but everything except God is a reed, and only he can hold the full weight of a life. And he is gentle with people who are themselves bent and weak. Of his Servant God said, “a bruised reed he will not break” (Isaiah 42:3), and Matthew saw those words fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 12:20).
verseByVerse.note: Pharaoh pictured as the great crocodile of the Nile.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will strip Egypt of its greatness so that his people will never again lean on it. The picture is now put plainly: a sword, man and beast cut off, and the whole land laid waste “from Migdol to Syene”, because Pharaoh claimed the Nile as his own (vv. 8–10). For forty years Egypt will lie desolate and its people be scattered, as Judah was (vv. 11–12). Then, surprisingly, God will gather them back to Pathros, where the kingdom began, but as “the most lowly of the kingdoms” (vv. 13–15). The purpose is Israel’s good: Egypt will never again be “the reliance of the house of Israel”, a standing reminder of its unbelief (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: God humbles proud powers so that his people will stop trusting them.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and will cut off from you man and beast, and the land of Egypt shall be a desolation and a waste. Then they will know that I am the LORD. "Because you said, 'The Nile is mine, and I made it,' therefore, behold, I am against you and against your streams, and I will make the land of Egypt an utter waste and desolation, from Migdol to Syene, as far as the border of Cush.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The picture of the dragon is put in plain words: a sword will sweep the whole land, because Pharaoh claimed the river God made.

I will bring a sword upon you. The river monster of verses 3–7 becomes an invading army, with “man and beast” cut off. “Then they will know that I am the LORD”, Ezekiel’s great refrain, is now heard over Egypt: the nation that thought it owned the river will learn who rules it.

From Migdol to Syene. From Migdol, a fortress in the north-east, to Syene (modern Aswan) on the southern frontier, “as far as the border of Cush”, means the whole length of Egypt. And the charge is repeated: “Because you said, ‘The Nile is mine, and I made it’” (v. 9). God judges pride at the very thing it boasted of. The river Pharaoh claimed will not save him.

verseByVerse.quote: No foot of man shall pass through it, and no foot of beast shall pass through it; it shall be uninhabited forty years. And I will make the land of Egypt a desolation in the midst of desolated countries, and her cities shall be a desolation forty years among cities that are laid waste. I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them through the countries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt will taste what Judah was suffering: an emptied land and a scattered people.

Uninhabited forty years. Forty years is the Bible’s familiar period of discipline, the length of Israel’s wandering in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33–34), a whole generation.

I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations. This is the very judgment Judah was suffering (12:15; 22:15). The nation Judah ran to for help would share Judah’s fate: its people scattered, its cities waste.

Did Egypt lie desolate forty years? A Babylonian inscription records Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign against Egypt in about 568 BC (compare Jeremiah 43:10–13), and Egypt never again became a great empire (v. 15): within fifty years it fell to Persia, and foreign rulers held it for most of the centuries that followed. Forty years is probably a round number for a generation of humiliation; history does not record the details.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the peoples among whom they were scattered, and I will restore the fortunes of Egypt and bring them back to the land of Pathros, the land of their origin, and there they shall be a lowly kingdom. It shall be the most lowly of the kingdoms, and never again exalt itself above the nations. And I will make them so small that they will never again rule over the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment is not God’s last word to Egypt: he will bring the Egyptians home, but as a small kingdom that will never again rule others.

I will gather the Egyptians. Remarkably, God, who scatters, also gathers: he will “restore the fortunes” of a pagan nation (v. 14). But the superpower will come back small: “the most lowly of the kingdoms”, never again exalting itself above the nations or ruling over them.

The land of Pathros, the land of their origin. Pathros is Upper (southern) Egypt, where by Egyptian tradition the kingdom first began. God brings them back to where they started, and leaves them there. Jeremiah, after foretelling the same invasion, adds the same mercy: “Afterward Egypt shall be inhabited as in the days of old” (Jeremiah 46:26).

verseByVerse.quote: And it shall never again be the reliance of the house of Israel, recalling their iniquity, when they turn to them for aid. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God humbles Egypt for his people’s sake, so that they stop leaning on a power that only reminded them of their unbelief.

Recalling their iniquity. Every time Israel turned to Egypt for aid, it was “recalling their iniquity”: the alliance itself was a standing reminder of its failure to trust God.

Freed from false trust. Sometimes God breaks the things we trust, not to punish us, but to free us from them.

Egypt’s future blessing. There is more grace for Egypt than this chapter says. Isaiah foresaw a day when “the Egyptians will know the LORD”, and God would say, “Blessed be Egypt my people” (Isaiah 19:21, 25). The land Israel wrongly leaned on became, in God’s providence, a shelter for the infant Jesus, so that God called his Son “out of Egypt” (Matthew 2:15). And at Pentecost visitors from Egypt heard the gospel in their own language (Acts 2:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rules even the wages of pagan armies, and he has not forgotten his promise to Israel. In 571 BC, the latest date in the book, God observes that Nebuchadnezzar’s army has worn itself bald and raw in its long siege of Tyre and gained nothing by it (vv. 17–18). So God gives him Egypt as his pay, “because they worked for me” (vv. 19–20). On that day God will make a horn, the sign of strength, spring up for Israel, and will open his prophet’s mouth among the exiles, his word proved true (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Even pagan kings work for God and receive their wages from him; and he raises up strength for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-seventh year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army labor hard against Tyre. Every head was made bald, and every shoulder was rubbed bare, yet neither he nor his army got anything from Tyre to pay for the labor that he had performed against her. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and he shall carry off its wealth and despoil it and plunder it; and it shall be the wages for his army. I have given him the land of Egypt as his payment for which he labored, because they worked for me, declares the Lord GOD. "On that day I will cause a horn to spring up for the house of Israel, and I will open your lips among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who rules every army, pays Nebuchadnezzar for his unrewarded labour against Tyre with the land of Egypt, and promises that strength will spring up again for Israel.

In the twenty-seventh year. This is April 571 BC, the latest date anywhere in Ezekiel, some sixteen years after the prophecy against Tyre in chapter 26. It is placed here because it concerns Egypt, and shows God’s word still unfolding long after it was first spoken.

Every head was made bald. Soldiers’ heads rubbed bald by helmets, shoulders rubbed raw from carrying earth and timber for the siege works, and after years of labour against Tyre, no plunder to pay the army.

Because they worked for me. Nebuchadnezzar did not know it, but he was God’s labourer; his campaigns carried out God’s judgments, and God, who leaves no work done for him unpaid, paid his wages with Egypt. Kings, armies and empires, even pagan ones, serve in God’s hand. They receive what he gives them and nothing more.

I will cause a horn to spring up. In the middle of judgment on the nations comes a promise to Israel. A horn, like the horn of a wild ox, is a symbol of strength: God will make strength spring up for his people. The psalm promised, “There I will make a horn to sprout for David” (Psalm 132:17), and Zechariah, filled with the Spirit at the birth of John the Baptist, sang that God “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69). The promise to the exiles was a first sprouting of that hope; its full answer is Christ.

I will open your lips among them. Ezekiel’s long silence had already ended years before, when the news of Jerusalem’s fall arrived (33:22). Now God promises that when this word too comes true, his prophet will speak among the exiles with his message proved, and it will be a message of restoration.

Was Nebuchadnezzar’s siege of Tyre a failure? He besieged it for thirteen years and took the mainland city, but the island held out, probably shipping its treasures away by sea, so his army got no plunder. God gave him Egypt instead as his wages. The prophecy of chapter 26 did not fail: it foretold “many nations” against Tyre (26:3), and it was completed under Alexander the Great, who took the island city in 332 BC.
verseByVerse.note: The latest dated prophecy in the book, about 571 BC: Egypt given to Babylon as Nebuchadnezzar’s wages for Tyre.

29.title: Egypt, the Broken Reed
29.overview:
Where we are. Judgment on Jerusalem is complete (chapters 4–24), and Ezekiel has turned to the nations around Judah (chapters 25–28). Now come four chapters and seven oracles against Egypt, more than against any other nation in the book. This first chapter holds two of them, given sixteen years apart.

The message. God made the Nile, and only God can bear the weight of his people’s trust. Pharaoh claims the Nile as his own, and Judah leans on him; but God will haul the dragon out with hooks, and the staff Judah grasped will snap and tear its hand. God humbles Egypt so that his people will stop leaning on it. And he will make strength spring up again for Israel.

Why it was said. In January 587 BC Jerusalem was under siege, and many in Judah and among the exiles still hoped that Pharaoh’s army would rescue the city, the hope that had led Zedekiah to break faith with Babylon (17:15; see the introduction). The second oracle came in 571 BC, long after the city fell, to exiles wondering whether God’s words against the nations would come true.

How the chapter makes its case. Pharaoh, a river monster claiming the Nile as his own creation (vv. 1–3), will be hooked out and flung into the desert (vv. 4–5), because Egypt has been a reed that broke under Israel’s hand (vv. 6–7). In plain words: a sword, forty years of desolation and scattering (vv. 8–12), then a return, but as a lowly kingdom Israel will never again rely on (vv. 13–16). Sixteen years later God gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as wages for his unpaid labour against Tyre, and promises a horn for Israel and an open mouth for his prophet (vv. 17–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by promise. Every human staff gives way; we need one who can bear the whole weight of a life and will not crush us when we are bruised. That is Jesus, of whom Matthew writes, “a bruised reed he will not break” (Matthew 12:20). The promise is the horn God will cause to spring up for Israel (v. 21), which Zechariah saw fulfilled in the “horn of salvation” raised up “in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69). And Egypt itself is not written off: the infant Son of God would one day shelter there, and God would call him “out of Egypt” (Matthew 2:15).

For us. Everyone leans on something. This chapter asks what you lean on when the pressure comes: money, a person, a government, your own competence. Sometimes God breaks our reeds in mercy, so that we put our whole weight on Christ, who was broken for us and never breaks under us.
29.theology:
Pride claims to have made what God made, and God humbles it at the very point of its boast (vv. 3, 9; Exod 5:2). He triumphs over every proud power, which Scripture pictures as a monster of the waters (vv. 3-5; Job 41:1-2; Isa 51:9; Ps 74:13-14).

Everything but God is a broken reed that wounds those who lean on it (vv. 6-7; Isa 36:6), and God sometimes breaks what his people trust in order to free them from it (v. 16). Pagan rulers are unknowing servants of God and receive their wages from him (vv. 18-20).

God raises up a horn of strength for his people, fulfilled in Christ (v. 21; Ps 132:17; Luke 1:69), and his mercy reaches Egypt too (Isa 19:21-25; Acts 2:10).
29.examples:
A crocodile king basks in his river and boasts that he made the Nile himself, until hooks drag him out onto the sand. The superpower Judah leaned on turns out to be a walking stick that snaps and cuts the hand.

Meanwhile Babylon's soldiers, bald from their helmets and raw from their loads, labour for years at Tyre for no pay, and God says of them, "They worked for me."

keyVerse.quote: And it shall never again be the reliance of the house of Israel, recalling their iniquity, when they turn to them for aid. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the purpose behind the whole oracle: God humbles Egypt so that his people will stop leaning on it. Every appeal to Pharaoh had been a reminder of Israel’s unbelief. God breaks the reed so that his people will lean on him, and on him alone.

29.reflection:
Pharaoh said, “My Nile is my own; I made it for myself” (v. 3). In what ways do we take credit for gifts God has given us, such as health, abilities or income? What would it look like to receive them with thanks instead?

Egypt was “a staff of reed” that broke and tore the hand of anyone who leaned on it (vv. 6–7). What “reeds” are you most tempted to lean on when you are under pressure? Have you ever felt one break?

God called Nebuchadnezzar’s army his workers (v. 20). How does it change the way you read the news to know that God rules over rulers and armies who do not know him?

God humbled Egypt so that Israel would stop relying on it (v. 16). Has God ever taken something away from you that turned out to free you to trust him more? How does Jesus, who does not break a bruised reed (Matthew 12:20), make him safe to lean on?
