verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day of the LORD that fell on Jerusalem is coming for Egypt and for everyone who leans on it. Ezekiel is to wail, “Alas for the day!”, for the day of the LORD is near, a day of clouds and doom for the nations (vv. 1–3). A sword will fall on Egypt, its wealth carried off and its foundations torn down, and its allies, Cush, Put, Lud, Arabia, Libya and “the land that is in league”, will fall with it (vv. 4–5). All who support Egypt will fall from one end of the land to the other when God sets it on fire (vv. 6–8), and messengers in ships will carry terror to careless Cush (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The day of the LORD comes on the proud and on all who stand with them.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Wail, 'Alas for the day!' For the day is near, the day of the LORD is near; it will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations. A sword shall come upon Egypt, and anguish shall be in Cush, when the slain fall in Egypt, and her wealth is carried away, and her foundations are torn down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of the LORD, which has fallen on Jerusalem, is about to fall on Egypt and the nations.

Wail, ‘Alas for the day!’ “The day of the LORD” is the prophets’ phrase for the day when God steps into history to judge. It had come upon Israel (7:7, 10); now it comes for Egypt. Zephaniah described it: “A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish… a day of clouds and thick darkness” (Zephaniah 1:15).

A sword shall come upon Egypt. The slain fall, “her wealth is carried away, and her foundations are torn down”: everything that held Egypt up gives way. “Anguish shall be in Cush”, the kingdom on the upper Nile (roughly modern Sudan) whose kings had once ruled Egypt and which was still bound to it.

Uncertain wording. In verse 3 the Hebrew lacks “doom for” (ESV note), reading literally “a time of the nations”: most likely the appointed time of their judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Cush, and Put, and Lud, and all Arabia, and Libya, and the people of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword. "Thus says the LORD: Those who support Egypt shall fall, and her proud might shall come down; from Migdol to Syene they shall fall within her by the sword, declares the Lord GOD. And they shall be desolated in the midst of desolated countries, and their cities shall be in the midst of cities that are laid waste. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have set fire to Egypt, and all her helpers are broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt will not fall alone: every nation that supports it will fall with it.

Those who support Egypt shall fall. Egypt’s allies and hired soldiers, from Cush, Put, Lud, Arabia and Libya, will fall with it, and “all her helpers are broken” (v. 8), from one end of the land to the other (see the note on 29:8–10). Egypt was the great helper others looked to; now its own helpers will be broken with it. And behind the invader’s torch is God’s hand: “I have set fire to Egypt.”

The land that is in league. When you tie yourself to a falling power, you fall with it. The only alliance that cannot fall is the covenant God makes with a people he has made his own.

Uncertain wording. “The people of the land that is in league” is literally “the sons of the land of the covenant” (ESV note): perhaps Egypt’s treaty allies, perhaps foreign troops serving under treaty; some suggest the Jews who had settled in Egypt (Jeremiah 44:1). “All Arabia” may mean “all the mixed peoples”, Egypt’s foreign troops, since the two words differ only in their vowels (compare Jeremiah 25:20). Put is probably in Libya, and Lud perhaps the Lydians of Asia Minor, who served Pharaoh as mercenaries; “Libya” translates a name found nowhere else in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: "On that day messengers shall go out from me in ships to terrify the unsuspecting people of Cush, and anguish shall come upon them on the day of Egypt's doom; for, behold, it comes!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The news of Egypt’s fall will reach even distant, careless Cush and shatter its false security.

Messengers shall go out from me in ships. Isaiah had pictured Cush sending its envoys “by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters” (Isaiah 18:2); now God’s messengers sail the other way, up the Nile, with news of doom.

To terrify the unsuspecting people of Cush. Cush, living carelessly and sure the trouble was someone else’s, will hear and tremble. “Behold, it comes!” The day of the LORD always arrives on people who thought they were safe, and Paul warns that the last day will come the same way: “the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself will dismantle everything Egypt trusted, with Nebuchadnezzar as his hand. The king of Babylon and “the most ruthless of nations” will fill the land with the slain (vv. 10–11). God will dry up the Nile, Egypt’s lifeline, and sell the land into the hand of foreigners (v. 12). He will destroy the idols of Memphis and leave Egypt without a prince of its own (v. 13). Then the oracle marches through the country city by city, the old capitals, the delta towns and the border fortresses: Pathros, Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium, On, Pi-beseth and Tehaphnehes, until Egypt’s proud might ends under a cloud (vv. 14–18). So all will know that the LORD has judged (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: No city, idol or river can shelter a nation from the LORD's judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: "I will put an end to the wealth of Egypt, by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He and his people with him, the most ruthless of nations, shall be brought in to destroy the land, and they shall draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain. And I will dry up the Nile and will sell the land into the hand of evildoers; I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it, by the hand of foreigners; I am the LORD; I have spoken. "Thus says the Lord GOD: "I will destroy the idols and put an end to the images in Memphis; there shall no longer be a prince from the land of Egypt; so I will put fear in the land of Egypt. I will make Pathros a desolation and will set fire to Zoan and will execute judgments on Thebes. And I will pour out my wrath on Pelusium, the stronghold of Egypt, and cut off the multitude of Thebes. And I will set fire to Egypt; Pelusium shall be in great agony; Thebes shall be breached, and Memphis shall face enemies by day. The young men of On and of Pi-beseth shall fall by the sword, and the women shall go into captivity. At Tehaphnehes the day shall be dark, when I break there the yoke bars of Egypt, and her proud might shall come to an end in her; she shall be covered by a cloud, and her daughters shall go into captivity. Thus I will execute judgments on Egypt. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will strip Egypt of everything it trusted, its wealth, its river, its gods and its cities, with Nebuchadnezzar as his hand.

By the hand of Nebuchadnezzar. The instrument is named, Nebuchadnezzar, but the one acting is God: “I will put an end to the wealth of Egypt.”

I will dry up the Nile. The river Pharaoh claimed to have made (29:3) is in God’s hand. The thing a nation depends on most can be dried up by the word of God.

I will destroy the idols. Jeremiah said the same: “I am bringing punishment upon Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods” (Jeremiah 46:25). So it was at the exodus, when God judged “all the gods of Egypt” (Exodus 12:12). “There shall no longer be a prince from the land of Egypt”: after the Persian conquest, foreigners ruled Egypt for most of the centuries that followed.

Through the whole land. The list marches through the whole country, south and north: the capitals (Memphis, Thebes), the delta towns (Zoan, On, Pi-beseth) and the border fortresses (Pelusium, and Tehaphnehes, where Judean refugees fled against God’s word, Jeremiah 43:7). Not one place is safe. The Hebrew spells On, city of the sun god, as Aven, “wickedness”, probably a deliberate pun, like Hosea’s “Beth-aven” for Bethel (Hosea 4:15).

The refuge they chose. For Judeans who ran to Egypt, this was a direct warning: the refuge chosen instead of God is under judgment too. The refuge God offers is himself, for those who come back to him: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1).
verseByVerse.note: Memphis, Thebes and Pelusium were among Egypt’s great cities.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The strength of nations is God’s to give and to take away. In April 587 BC, during the siege of Jerusalem, God announces that he has already broken Pharaoh’s arm, and no one has bound it up so that it can wield a sword again (vv. 20–21). He will break both arms, the strong one and the broken one, and scatter the Egyptians among the nations (vv. 22–23). At the same time he will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put “my sword” in his hand, while Pharaoh groans before him like a dying man (vv. 24–25). When the scattering comes, the nations will know that the LORD has done it (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: God breaks the human strength that people trust and strengthens whom he will.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eleventh year, in the first month, on the seventh day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and behold, it has not been bound up, to heal it by binding it with a bandage, so that it may become strong to wield the sword. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt and will break his arms, both the strong arm and the one that was broken, and I will make the sword fall from his hand. I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them through the countries. And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put my sword in his hand, but I will break the arms of Pharaoh, and he will groan before him like a man mortally wounded. I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, but the arms of Pharaoh shall fall. Then they shall know that I am the LORD, when I put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon and he stretches it out against the land of Egypt. And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them throughout the countries. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has broken Pharaoh’s arm and will put his own sword in Babylon’s hand, because the strength of nations is his to give and to take away.

I have broken the arm of Pharaoh. This oracle is dated about April 587 BC, during the siege of Jerusalem. It probably looks back to the time when Pharaoh’s army marched out to relieve Jerusalem and then withdrew (Jeremiah 37:5–7). The arm that held the sword is already broken, and no bandage will set it.

Put my sword in his hand. Two kings, four arms. God breaks Pharaoh’s and strengthens Nebuchadnezzar’s, and the sword in Babylon’s hand is “my sword”. Military power belongs to God: he gives it and he takes it away. That did not make Babylon righteous; its own judgment would follow in turn (Jeremiah 25:12).

An arm of flesh. Judah trusted Pharaoh’s arm. Hezekiah had once said of an invading king, “With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God” (2 Chronicles 32:8), and Jeremiah warned, “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength” (Jeremiah 17:5).

The arm of the LORD. The Bible’s answer to every broken human arm is the arm of the LORD. Isaiah asked, “to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1, words John applies to Jesus in John 12:38), and then described the suffering Servant. God’s mighty arm was revealed not in a Pharaoh or a Nebuchadnezzar but in a Saviour pierced for our transgressions. That arm does not break, and those who lean on it are held, not because their trust is strong, but because he is.

30.title: The Day of Egypt
30.overview:
Where we are. Here come the third and fourth of the seven oracles against Egypt (chapters 29–32). The second (vv. 1–19) carries no date of its own; the third (vv. 20–26) is dated April 587 BC, while Jerusalem was under siege.

The message. The day of the LORD that has fallen on Jerusalem is coming for Egypt and for everyone who leans on it. God himself will act, by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, against Egypt’s wealth, its river, its idols and every city in the land. He has already broken Pharaoh’s arm, and he will put his own sword in Babylon’s hand. Strength belongs to God, to give and to take away, and no alliance with a falling power can save.

Why it was said. Judah’s last earthly hope during the siege was Pharaoh’s army, which had marched out and then withdrawn (Jeremiah 37:5–8), and after the fall many Judeans would flee to Egypt against God’s word (Jeremiah 43:7). The exiles needed to hear that Egypt could not save Jerusalem and itself stood under judgment (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with a cry of alarm: the day of the LORD is near, a sword for Egypt and for its allies (vv. 1–5). All who support Egypt will fall with it from one end of the land to the other, and messengers will carry terror up the Nile to Cush (vv. 6–9). Then the agent is named, Nebuchadnezzar, and God strikes everything Egypt trusted: its river, its idols, and city after city from Memphis to Thebes (vv. 10–19). Last comes the dated word: Pharaoh’s arm is broken and will not heal; God will break both his arms and strengthen Babylon’s, putting his own sword in its hand (vv. 20–26).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by the character of God it reveals. The day of the LORD shows a God who judges pride and false trust, and Pharaoh’s broken arm exposes the weakness of every arm of flesh. The Bible’s answer is “the arm of the LORD” (Isaiah 53:1), revealed not in an army but in the suffering Servant, whom John identifies with Jesus (John 12:38). At the cross the judgment of that day fell on him, so that those who shelter in him need not dread it.

For us. Nations, economies and alliances that look strong can break in a day, and so can the strength we trust in ourselves. Ask what you would run to if the worst came. The safe place on the day of the LORD is not beside the powerful but in Christ, whose arm does not break.
30.theology:
The day of the LORD falls on the proud nations and on all who ally themselves with them (vv. 2-8; Zeph 1:14-15). God judges the gods of the nations along with the nations (v. 13; Jer 46:25), and no refuge chosen instead of him is safe (vv. 14-18).

God breaks the strength of one ruler and gives strength to another as he wills; the sword in any ruler's hand is his (vv. 21-25; 2 Chr 32:8; Jer 17:5). The arm of the LORD that never breaks is revealed in the suffering Servant, Christ (Isa 53:1).
30.examples:
The chapter opens with a cry, "Alas for the day!", and allies fall one after another like dominoes. A river is dried up by a word, and in the refugee city of Tehaphnehes the lights go out.

Pharaoh's broken arm cannot be bandaged, while God's own sword is placed in a pagan king's hand.

keyVerse.quote: Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have set fire to Egypt, and all her helpers are broken.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s point in a sentence: when the great helper of the nations and all who lean on it are broken, the world learns who is truly the LORD. Every false refuge that fails is a sign pointing to the one refuge that cannot.

30.reflection:
“The day of the LORD is near” (v. 3). Why do people, like “the unsuspecting people of Cush” (v. 9), so easily assume that judgment is for someone else? How does the gospel let a Christian face that day without dread?

Egypt’s allies fell with it (vv. 5–8). What powers, groups or causes are we tempted to tie our hopes to? What would happen to our hope if they fell?

God calls the sword in Nebuchadnezzar’s hand “my sword” (v. 25), yet Babylon was later judged too. How does God’s rule over the powers of the world both humble us and comfort us?

Hezekiah said, “With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God” (2 Chronicles 32:8). Where do you need to stop relying on an arm of flesh this week and lean on the arm of the LORD revealed in Jesus (Isaiah 53:1)?

31.text: <sup>1</sup>In the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude: "Whom are you like in your greatness?<sup>3</sup>Behold, Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches and forest shade, and of towering height, its top among the clouds.<sup>4</sup>The waters nourished it; the deep made it grow tall, making its rivers flow around the place of its planting, sending forth its streams to all the trees of the field.<sup>5</sup>So it towered high above all the trees of the field; its boughs grew large and its branches long from abundant water in its shoots.<sup>6</sup>All the birds of the heavens made their nests in its boughs; under its branches all the beasts of the field gave birth to their young, and under its shadow lived all great nations.<sup>7</sup>It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its branches; for its roots went down to abundant waters.<sup>8</sup>The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it, nor the fir trees equal its boughs; neither were the plane trees like its branches; no tree in the garden of God was its equal in beauty.<sup>9</sup>I made it beautiful in the mass of its branches, and all the trees of Eden envied it, that were in the garden of God.<sup>10</sup>"Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because it towered high and set its top among the clouds, and its heart was proud of its height,<sup>11</sup>I will give it into the hand of a mighty one of the nations. He shall surely deal with it as its wickedness deserves. I have cast it out.<sup>12</sup>Foreigners, the most ruthless of nations, have cut it down and left it. On the mountains and in all the valleys its branches have fallen, and its boughs have been broken in all the ravines of the land, and all the peoples of the earth have gone away from its shadow and left it.<sup>13</sup>On its fallen trunk dwell all the birds of the heavens, and on its branches are all the beasts of the field.<sup>14</sup>All this is in order that no trees by the waters may grow to towering height or set their tops among the clouds, and that no trees that drink water may reach up to them in height. For they are all given over to death, to the world below, among the children of man, with those who go down to the pit.<sup>15</sup>"Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day the cedar went down to Sheol I caused mourning; I closed the deep over it, and restrained its rivers, and many waters were stopped. I clothed Lebanon in gloom for it, and all the trees of the field fainted because of it.<sup>16</sup>I made the nations quake at the sound of its fall, when I cast it down to Sheol with those who go down to the pit. And all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, were comforted in the world below.<sup>17</sup>They also went down to Sheol with it, to those who are slain by the sword; yes, those who were its arm, who lived under its shadow among the nations.<sup>18</sup>"Whom are you thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? You shall be brought down with the trees of Eden to the world below. You shall lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword. "This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Greatness is God’s gift, and Assyria had more of it than any power before it. God asks Pharaoh and his multitude, “Whom are you like in your greatness?” (vv. 1–2), and answers with a parable. Assyria was a cedar of Lebanon with its top among the clouds, fed by the deep, its streams flowing out to the trees around it (vv. 3–5). Birds nested in its boughs, beasts gave birth under its branches, and great nations lived in its shade, for its roots went down to abundant waters (vv. 6–7). No tree in the garden of God could rival it, and the trees of Eden envied it; yet its beauty was God’s doing: “I made it beautiful” (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest earthly power is a tree God planted and watered.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude: "Whom are you like in your greatness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before announcing Pharaoh’s fate, God holds up a mirror and invites him to learn from the fall of a greater power.

Whom are you like in your greatness? The date is about June 587 BC, with Jerusalem under siege and Judah still hoping that Egypt would save it. The word is addressed to Pharaoh and to his multitude, his people and army with him. It is the fifth of seven oracles against Egypt (chapters 29–32), and it opens with a question rather than a threat: who do you compare yourself to? Then God tells him a story about someone greater, so that he can learn from how it ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches and forest shade, and of towering height, its top among the clouds. The waters nourished it; the deep made it grow tall, making its rivers flow around the place of its planting, sending forth its streams to all the trees of the field. So it towered high above all the trees of the field; its boughs grew large and its branches long from abundant water in its shoots.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Assyria, the superpower before Babylon, was like the greatest cedar in Lebanon, and its greatness came from waters far below it.

Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon. Assyria had dominated the ancient world for generations; it destroyed Samaria and carried the northern kingdom of Israel into exile (2 Kings 17:6). It is pictured as the most magnificent of the cedars of Lebanon, the grandest trees the Israelites knew, with its top “among the clouds”.

The waters nourished it; the deep made it grow tall. “The deep” is the great store of water beneath the earth (Genesis 7:11; 49:25). The tree’s greatness came from sources far below it, as Assyria’s did from the Tigris and the Euphrates. And its streams flowed out “to all the trees of the field”: lesser nations drew their life from it. So “it towered high above all the trees of the field” (v. 5).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for a kind of cypress differs from “Assyria” by a single letter, and some scholars read “a cypress” here, so that the whole tree would be Egypt itself. The ESV keeps “Assyria”, and either way verse 18 says the tree’s story is Pharaoh’s own. For “among the clouds” in verse 3 the ESV notes a possible “through the thick boughs”.

verseByVerse.quote: All the birds of the heavens made their nests in its boughs; under its branches all the beasts of the field gave birth to their young, and under its shadow lived all great nations. It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its branches; for its roots went down to abundant waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great tree sheltered all who came to it, and the secret of its greatness lay out of sight, in its roots.

Under its shadow lived all great nations. The tree was a blessing to many, and great empires do bring order and protection. Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of himself as just such a tree: “a tree in the midst of the earth, and its height was great” (Daniel 4:10).

For its roots went down to abundant waters. A tree is only as great as what it draws on. That will matter in verse 14, where the trees that “drink water” are reminded that they too are mortal.

verseByVerse.quote: The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it, nor the fir trees equal its boughs; neither were the plane trees like its branches; no tree in the garden of God was its equal in beauty. I made it beautiful in the mass of its branches, and all the trees of Eden envied it, that were in the garden of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Assyria’s beauty surpassed even the trees of Eden, but every bit of it was God’s gift: “I made it beautiful.”

The trees of Eden envied it. This is poetry, picturing the tree so high that God’s own garden envied it, to show how high it rose and how far it would fall.

I made it beautiful. Its height, its water and its beauty were all gifts from God; its roots went down to waters it did not create. Every great power stands on what God provides, and so does every life. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride in God-given greatness brings even the greatest down to death, and Pharaoh is next. Because the cedar “towered high… and its heart was proud of its height”, God handed it to a mighty nation who cut it down and left it; its branches lie in the ravines, and the peoples have walked away from its shade (vv. 10–13). This is a warning to every tree, for all are “given over to death” (v. 14). When it went down to Sheol, God closed the deep over it, darkened Lebanon and made the nations quake, while the fallen trees below took comfort (vv. 15–17). Then comes the mirror: “This is Pharaoh and all his multitude” (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride in one’s own greatness ends in the grave; learn from the fall of those who were greater than you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because it towered high and set its top among the clouds, and its heart was proud of its height, I will give it into the hand of a mighty one of the nations. He shall surely deal with it as its wickedness deserves. I have cast it out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the tree grew proud of the height God had given it, God handed it over to be felled, as its wickedness deserved.

Its heart was proud of its height. Here is the turn. The tree forgot who made it beautiful and took pride in its own greatness. It is Nebuchadnezzar’s boast in another form: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power” (Daniel 4:30).

A mighty one of the nations. Assyria fell to Babylon: Nineveh was destroyed by the Babylonians and the Medes in 612 BC, and the last Assyrian forces were broken a few years later. “He shall surely deal with it as its wickedness deserves”: the fall was not bad luck but just judgment, and the one who says “I have cast it out” is God.

Uncertain wording. In verse 10 the Hebrew reads “you” where the ESV has “it” (ESV note), as if the words slip from Assyria to Pharaoh himself, the one the parable is really about.

verseByVerse.quote: Foreigners, the most ruthless of nations, have cut it down and left it. On the mountains and in all the valleys its branches have fallen, and its boughs have been broken in all the ravines of the land, and all the peoples of the earth have gone away from its shadow and left it. On its fallen trunk dwell all the birds of the heavens, and on its branches are all the beasts of the field. All this is in order that no trees by the waters may grow to towering height or set their tops among the clouds, and that no trees that drink water may reach up to them in height. For they are all given over to death, to the world below, among the children of man, with those who go down to the pit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The felled cedar lies abandoned, a warning to every proud power that all, however tall, are given over to death.

All the peoples of the earth have gone away. The great cedar is felled, its branches scattered over mountains and valleys, and the nations who sheltered in its shade simply walk away. The world’s loyalty lasts as long as your power does. God’s faithfulness to his own does not end when their strength does (Isaiah 46:4).

On its fallen trunk. The birds and beasts that once nested in its living branches (v. 6) now settle on its remains, as lesser powers pick over a fallen empire.

In order that no trees by the waters may grow to towering height. God gives the reason for the felling: a warning to every other tree not to “set their tops among the clouds”. The fall of one proud power is a sermon to all the others.

They are all given over to death. Here is the lesson for everyone. However tall the tree, it goes down to the pit “among the children of man” (the ESV notes, perhaps “of Adam”). Death makes the great and the small alike: “For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him” (Psalm 49:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day the cedar went down to Sheol I caused mourning; I closed the deep over it, and restrained its rivers, and many waters were stopped. I clothed Lebanon in gloom for it, and all the trees of the field fainted because of it. I made the nations quake at the sound of its fall, when I cast it down to Sheol with those who go down to the pit. And all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, were comforted in the world below. They also went down to Sheol with it, to those who are slain by the sword; yes, those who were its arm, who lived under its shadow among the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fall of the great tree shakes the world above and brings a grim comfort to the fallen powers below.

On the day the cedar went down to Sheol. Sheol is the Old Testament’s name for the realm of the dead (see the note on 32:17–32). When the tree goes down, creation itself mourns: the waters stop and Lebanon is clothed in gloom (v. 15). And in the world below, the other fallen trees, the great powers that fell before, are “comforted”, a grim comfort: at least mighty Assyria has come down to join them.

Those who were its arm. The allies who had been Assyria’s strength, “who lived under its shadow among the nations”, went down to Sheol with it. A great power does not fall alone; those who lean on it fall too, as Egypt’s helpers would (30:6–8).

verseByVerse.quote: "Whom are you thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? You shall be brought down with the trees of Eden to the world below. You shall lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword. "This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable is Pharaoh’s own story: he is as great as the cedar, and he will fall as it did.

This is Pharaoh and all his multitude. The question comes back to Pharaoh: “Whom are you thus like”? He thinks he is like the great cedar, and he is right. He will fall like it.

You shall lie among the uncircumcised. For Egypt, which practised circumcision, this meant a dishonoured grave among peoples it despised (see the note on 32:17–32).

The tree God plants. The answer to pride in our own greatness is not merely to fear the fall. It is to find the one tree God himself plants. Ezekiel has already heard of it: a tender sprig planted by God on a high mountain, in whose shade “birds of every sort will nest” (17:23). Jesus said his kingdom is like that: a small seed that becomes a tree where the birds nest (Mark 4:32). The empires of pride fall. The kingdom of the humble King grows, and it grows by grace, sheltering those who come to it with nothing of their own. “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

31.title: The Fall of the Great Cedar
31.overview:
Where we are. This is the fifth of the seven oracles against Egypt (chapters 29–32), dated June 587 BC, while Jerusalem still held out under siege. Instead of a river monster, Ezekiel now tells a parable of a tree.

The message. Greatness is God’s gift, and pride in it is fatal. God holds up Assyria, once the greatest power on earth, as a cedar of unrivalled beauty, watered by the deep and sheltering all nations: “I made it beautiful.” But because its heart grew proud of its height, God cut it down and sent it to the realm of the dead. Pharaoh, who imagines himself beyond compare, is that tree: “This is Pharaoh and all his multitude.”

Why it was said. Judah and the exiles still hoped that Egypt would break the siege (see the introduction). Assyria’s fall was within living memory: Nineveh had been destroyed in 612 BC, only twenty-five years before. If the mightiest empire of their fathers’ day could be felled, so could Egypt, and so could any power they trusted in place of God.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with a question to Pharaoh: whom are you like? (vv. 1–2). The answer is a parable. Assyria was a cedar towering to the clouds, fed by the deep, sheltering birds, beasts and nations, envied by the trees of Eden, and made beautiful by God (vv. 3–9). Because it grew proud, God gave it to a ruthless nation who felled it, and the peoples walked away from its shade (vv. 10–13), a warning to every tree, for all go down to death (v. 14). Its descent to Sheol shook the nations and comforted the fallen trees below (vv. 15–17). Then the mirror turns: this is Pharaoh (v. 18).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The tree of pride falls, but Ezekiel has already heard of a tree God himself plants, a tender sprig on a high mountain in whose shade “birds of every sort will nest” (17:23). Jesus pictured his kingdom the same way, as a seed that grows until the birds nest in its shade (Mark 4:32). And the pattern of pride brought low is reversed in Christ himself: he who was truly highest humbled himself to death on a cross, and “therefore God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9).

For us. Everything you are and have, your gifts, your influence, the people who shelter under you, has grown from waters you did not make. Pride forgets that, and pride falls. The safe way is the way of Christ: to humble yourself under God’s hand and to find shelter in the kingdom of the humble King.
31.theology:
All the greatness of earthly powers is God's gift; he makes them beautiful and waters their roots (vv. 4, 9). Pride in one’s own greatness is certain to end in a fall (vv. 10-12; Dan 4:30-32; Luke 14:11), and death levels every great power and person (v. 14; Ps 49:16-17). God teaches the proud through the fall of those greater than they (vv. 2, 18).

The empires of pride fall, but the kingdom God plants in humility grows to shelter the nations (17:22-24; Mark 4:32).
31.examples:
God's question to Pharaoh still searches every proud heart: Whom are you like in your greatness? The answer is a cedar so tall that the trees of Eden envied it, with nations sheltering in its shade.

Then the nations walk away from the fallen trunk, and birds perch on a log. "This is Pharaoh," God says, and he says it to every life that forgets who made it beautiful.

keyVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because it towered high and set its top among the clouds, and its heart was proud of its height, I will give it into the hand of a mighty one of the nations. He shall surely deal with it as its wickedness deserves. I have cast it out.
keyVerse.note: These verses are the hinge of the parable. Everything before them describes a greatness God gave; everything after describes the fall that pride brought. The sin is not height but a heart proud of its height, and the one who casts the proud down is God himself.

31.reflection:
God says of the great tree, “I made it beautiful” (v. 9). What gifts, positions or achievements are you most tempted to treat as your own? How does Paul’s question, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7), speak to that?

The tree sheltered nations, yet “its heart was proud of its height” (v. 10). How can a person or a church do a great deal of good and still be ruined by pride? What are the warning signs?

When the cedar fell, the peoples “have gone away from its shadow and left it” (v. 12). What does this teach about the loyalty the world gives to the powerful, compared with God’s faithfulness to his people?

Jesus humbled himself to the point of death, “therefore God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9). How does his path, and his kingdom that grows like a small seed (Mark 4:32), reshape your idea of greatness?

and her company is all around her grave, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who spread terror in the land of the living.<sup>24</sup>"Elam is there, and all her multitude around her grave; all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who went down uncircumcised into the world below, who spread their terror in the land of the living; for they spread their terror in the land of the living.<sup>27</sup>And they do not lie with the mighty, the fallen from among the uncircumcised, who went down to Sheol with their weapons of war, whose swords were laid under their heads, and whose iniquities are upon their bones; and he shall be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharaoh’s picture of himself as the lion of the nations is false, and God will expose it before the world. In March 585 BC Ezekiel raises a funeral song: Pharaoh thinks himself “a lion of the nations”, but he is “like a dragon in the seas”, thrashing and fouling the rivers (vv. 1–2). God will throw his net over him with a host of peoples, haul him onto dry land, and feed the birds and beasts with his carcass until the hills and ravines are full of him (vv. 3–6). At his end God will darken the sun, moon and stars (vv. 7–8), and kings far away will shudder, each fearing for his own life (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: The proud ruler who troubles the nations will be hauled out by God, and heaven itself darkens at his fall.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, raise a lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt and say to him: "You consider yourself a lion of the nations, but you are like a dragon in the seas; you burst forth in your rivers, trouble the waters with your feet, and foul their rivers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh sees himself as a noble lion, but God sees a thrashing monster that fouls every river it moves in.

A lion of the nations. This lament is dated about March 585 BC, after the news of Jerusalem’s fall had reached the exiles (33:21). Pharaoh sees himself as “a lion of the nations”: noble, majestic, king of beasts. God sees “a dragon in the seas”, a water monster that muddies every river it moves in. What Pharaoh called leadership, God calls fouling the waters for everyone else.

You burst forth in your rivers. The picture is of a crocodile thrashing in the Nile channels and churning them to mud. Egypt’s ventures into Judah’s affairs did just that: Pharaoh’s army, probably under Hophra (Jeremiah 44:30), marched out in 588 BC, the Babylonians briefly lifted the siege of Jerusalem, and then Egypt withdrew and left Judah to its fate (Jeremiah 37:5–8). He stirred the waters and helped no one.

Uncertain wording. “You consider yourself” is literally “you are likened”, whether by Pharaoh himself or by others. A verb spelled the same way means “to be destroyed”, and some hear a play on both: the “lion” is already undone.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: I will throw my net over you with a host of many peoples, and they will haul you up in my dragnet. And I will cast you on the ground; on the open field I will fling you, and will cause all the birds of the heavens to settle on you, and I will gorge the beasts of the whole earth with you. I will strew your flesh upon the mountains and fill the valleys with your carcass. I will drench the land even to the mountains with your flowing blood, and the ravines will be full of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will haul the monster out in his net and leave its carcass unburied for the birds and beasts, the deepest disgrace for a king of Egypt.

They will haul you up in my dragnet. As in chapter 29, the monster is caught, this time in “my dragnet”, cast “with a host of many peoples”: the nations God gathers are the hands that haul it out. The imagery is grisly because the fall of a violent empire is grisly. The carcass is left in the open field for birds and beasts, filling the valleys and ravines. To lie unburied was the deepest disgrace in the ancient world, and none felt it more than Egypt, whose kings spent their lives preparing their tombs.

verseByVerse.quote: When I blot you out, I will cover the heavens and make their stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of heaven will I make dark over you, and put darkness on your land, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s fall will be like the lights of heaven going out: a day of the LORD in which a whole world order collapses.

I will cover the heavens. Sun, moon and stars go dark. This is the prophets’ language for the day of the LORD, not a forecast of an eclipse: when a world order collapses under God’s judgment, it is as if the lights of heaven go out. Isaiah used it for the fall of Babylon: “the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light” (Isaiah 13:10). Jesus used it for the end of the age: “the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light” (Matthew 24:29). Every such judgment in history is a preview of the last judgment, and at the cross, when darkness covered the land (Mark 15:33), that judgment fell on God’s innocent Son in the place of sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will trouble the hearts of many peoples, when I bring your destruction among the nations, into the countries that you have not known. I will make many peoples appalled at you, and the hair of their kings shall bristle with horror because of you, when I brandish my sword before them. They shall tremble every moment, every one for his own life, on the day of your downfall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt’s fall will send a shudder through kings far away, each one fearing for his own life.

I will trouble the hearts of many peoples. The news travels into “countries that you have not known”, far beyond Egypt’s borders. The kings who see God “brandish” his sword over Pharaoh shudder, as the coastlands did over Tyre (27:35), and tremble “every one for his own life”: if so great a power can fall, none is safe.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names the instrument and the target: Babylon’s sword against Egypt’s pride. “The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you” (v. 11), and the most ruthless of nations will bring Egypt’s pride and multitude to ruin (v. 12). With man and beast gone from its waters, no one will churn them to mud any more; God will make them clear and make the rivers run smooth as oil (vv. 13–14). When the land is emptied, Egypt will know that he is the LORD (v. 15). This is a lament for the daughters of the nations to chant over Egypt and all her multitude (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: When God brings down the proud, the world they troubled has peace again.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you. I will cause your multitude to fall by the swords of mighty ones, all of them most ruthless of nations. "They shall bring to ruin the pride of Egypt, and all its multitude shall perish. I will destroy all its beasts from beside many waters; and no foot of man shall trouble them anymore, nor shall the hoofs of beasts trouble them. Then I will make their waters clear, and cause their rivers to run like oil, declares the Lord GOD. When I make the land of Egypt desolate, and when the land is desolate of all that fills it, when I strike down all who dwell in it, then they will know that I am the LORD. This is a lamentation that shall be chanted; the daughters of the nations shall chant it; over Egypt, and over all her multitude, shall they chant it, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The picture becomes plain history: Babylon’s sword will ruin Egypt’s pride, and the waters Pharaoh fouled will run clear.

The sword of the king of Babylon. The dragon gives way to plain fact, and the target is named: “the pride of Egypt”. God’s judgment aims at pride.

I will make their waters clear. The dragon had fouled the rivers (v. 2). Once it is gone, God makes their waters clear, and the rivers run smooth “like oil”. When a violent power is removed, the world it troubled has peace.

The daughters of the nations shall chant it. The women of the nations, who led the mourning at funerals, will sing this dirge. Egypt, which caused so much weeping, will be wept over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–32 — With Those Who Go Down to the Pit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In death the terrors of the earth lie helpless and ashamed, and God alone is to be feared. Two weeks after the first lament Ezekiel is told to wail over Egypt and send her down to the world below (vv. 17–18): “Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be laid to rest with the uncircumcised” (vv. 19–21). There already lie Assyria, Elam, Meshech-Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north and the Sidonians, all slain, all of whom once spread “terror in the land of the living”, all now bearing their shame (vv. 22–30). Pharaoh will find grim comfort in their company and lie among them, for in the end it is God who spreads terror (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology: Every power that spread terror on earth ends in the same shameful grave, unless it finds the one who holds the keys of death.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, wail over the multitude of Egypt, and send them down, her and the daughters of majestic nations, to the world below, to those who have gone down to the pit: 'Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be laid to rest with the uncircumcised.' They shall fall amid those who are slain by the sword. Egypt is delivered to the sword; drag her away, and all her multitudes. The mighty chiefs shall speak of them, with their helpers, out of the midst of Sheol: 'They have come down, they lie still, the uncircumcised, slain by the sword.' "Assyria is there, and all her company, its graves all around it, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, whose graves are set in the uttermost parts of the pit; and her company is all around her grave, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who spread terror in the land of the living. "Elam is there, and all her multitude around her grave; all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who went down uncircumcised into the world below, who spread their terror in the land of the living; and they bear their shame with those who go down to the pit. They have made her a bed among the slain with all her multitude, her graves all around it, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for terror of them was spread in the land of the living, and they bear their shame with those who go down to the pit; they are placed among the slain. "Meshech-Tubal is there, and all her multitude, her graves all around it, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for they spread their terror in the land of the living. And they do not lie with the mighty, the fallen from among the uncircumcised, who went down to Sheol with their weapons of war, whose swords were laid under their heads, and whose iniquities are upon their bones; for the terror of the mighty men was in the land of the living. But as for you, you shall be broken and lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword. "Edom is there, her kings and all her princes, who for all their might are laid with those who are killed by the sword; they lie with the uncircumcised, with those who go down to the pit. "The princes of the north are there, all of them, and all the Sidonians, who have gone down in shame with the slain, for all the terror that they caused by their might; they lie uncircumcised with those who are slain by the sword, and bear their shame with those who go down to the pit. "When Pharaoh sees them, he will be comforted for all his multitude, Pharaoh and all his army, slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD. For I spread terror in the land of the living; and he shall be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezekiel escorts Egypt down to the grave, where the empires that once terrified the world lie helpless and ashamed, and God alone is to be feared.

Wail over the multitude of Egypt. Two weeks later comes the last and most haunting oracle against Egypt. Ezekiel is to escort Egypt, in words, down into the grave, and show her who is already there.

Whom do you surpass in beauty? In death nobody surpasses anybody; all beauty and rank are left at the door. To be laid “with the uncircumcised” was a special humiliation for Egypt, which itself practised circumcision (Jeremiah 9:25–26): Pharaoh would lie among the peoples he despised.

Out of the midst of Sheol. The dead rulers greet the new arrivals, as Isaiah pictured the kings of the underworld rising to greet the fallen king of Babylon: “You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!” (Isaiah 14:10).

Assyria is there. Then comes a roll call of the fallen. Assyria is there (vv. 22–23), the empire whose fall chapter 31 described. Elam, east of Babylon, once a feared power, is there (vv. 24–25). Meshech-Tubal, peoples of Asia Minor (27:13), is there (vv. 26–27). Edom is there, with her kings and princes (v. 29). The princes of the north are there, probably the rulers of Syria and Phoenicia, with all the Sidonians (v. 30).

Who spread terror in the land of the living. The refrain comes for each: every one of these powers terrified the world, and every one now bears “their shame with those who go down to the pit”. The terror they spread on earth becomes the shame they carry below.

Whose swords were laid under their heads. Verse 27 adds a detail about fallen warriors, “whose swords were laid under their heads, and whose iniquities are upon their bones”. They were buried with their weapons as heroes, but what lies on their bones is not glory; it is iniquity.

He will be comforted. Pharaoh’s only comfort is the bleak comfort of company: he is not the only one. And the last word goes to God: “For I spread terror in the land of the living.” The nations thought they were the terror of the earth. God is the one whose judgment is to be feared.

The keys of Death and Hades. But the Bible does not leave the pit with the last word. One went down into death who had spread no terror, only mercy, and he came back. The risen Christ says, “I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). Because of him Paul can taunt the grave: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?… thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:55, 57).

Elamites at Pentecost. The nations in the pit are not beyond the gospel’s call. On the day of Pentecost, among those who heard the mighty works of God in their own tongues were Elamites and visitors from Egypt (Acts 2:9–10). The empires went down; their peoples were invited up.

Facing the grave. This chapter confronts everyone with the grave: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). Power, beauty and fame do not go down after us (Psalm 49:17). The time to settle where we stand with God is now.

What is Sheol, and are the dead conscious here? The scene of the dead nations lying in the pit is poetry, a dirge over Egypt, not a map of the afterlife. Scripture does teach that the dead are conscious (Luke 16:22–24; Revelation 6:9–10), but this passage is not a description of hell. The “uncircumcised” are those outside God’s covenant, dishonoured in death; warriors were buried with their swords under their heads, but these lie in shame.

Uncertain wording. Verse 17 names no month (the ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks “in the twelfth month”), so the ESV assumes the month of verse 1, two weeks later. In verse 27 many scholars read “shields” for “iniquities”, a change of one Hebrew letter that fits the warriors’ burial with their weapons; the ESV keeps the Hebrew, and the shame stands either way.
verseByVerse.note: The nations are pictured lying in Sheol, the realm of the dead.

32.title: Down to the Pit
32.overview:
Where we are. The last two of the seven oracles against Egypt close the long section on the nations (chapters 25–32). They are dated March 585 BC, a few weeks after the news of Jerusalem’s fall reached the exiles (33:21). Both are funeral songs sung over a king still alive.

The message. Every power that terrifies the earth goes down to the grave, and God alone is finally to be feared. Pharaoh, who fancies himself a lion, is a river monster that God will haul out in his net; at his fall the lights of heaven go dark and the nations tremble. Then Ezekiel escorts Egypt down to the realm of the dead, where the empires that once spread terror already lie in shame. The last word belongs to God: “I spread terror in the land of the living.”

Why it was said. Jerusalem had fallen, and Egypt had done nothing to save it. Yet some still looked to Egypt as the power of the future (see the introduction). God tells them that Egypt is not the future: it is going where every proud empire goes.

How the chapter makes its case. The first lament exposes Pharaoh, a lion in his own eyes, a monster fouling the rivers in God’s (vv. 1–2), whom God will net and fling to the birds (vv. 3–6) while the heavens darken and far-off kings tremble (vv. 7–10). Then plainly: Babylon’s sword will ruin Egypt’s pride, its waters will run clear, and the nations will chant its dirge (vv. 11–16). The second lament sends Egypt down to the pit (vv. 17–21), where the empires that spread terror already lie in shame (vv. 22–30). Pharaoh will find only grim comfort among them (vv. 31–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by promise. It leaves every reader at the edge of the grave with no way out from below. The way out came from above. The Son of God went down into death, though he had spread no terror, only mercy, and he rose. He shared our flesh “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14), and now says, “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). Even the darkened heavens of verse 7 find an echo at the cross, where darkness covered the land as God’s judgment fell, not on a proud tyrant, but on his innocent Son, for us (Mark 15:33).

For us. Power, beauty and fame do not go down after us. This chapter asks each of us to face the grave honestly now, while the gospel’s invitation stands. Those who belong to Christ need not fear the pit, because he has been there and come back with the keys.
32.theology:
God sees the true effect of proud power: not a noble lion but a dragon fouling the waters (v. 2). He aims his judgment at pride (v. 12), and the darkening of sun, moon and stars is the prophets’ way of picturing that judgment on world powers, a foretaste of the last day (vv. 7-8; Isa 13:10; Matt 24:29).

Death levels all powers; those who spread terror on earth bear shame in the grave (vv. 18-32; Isa 14:9-11; Heb 9:27; Ps 49:17). But Christ holds the keys of death and gives victory over the grave, and the gospel calls the peoples of the fallen empires (Rev 1:18; 1 Cor 15:54-57; Acts 2:9-10).
32.examples:
A self-styled lion turns out to be a monster muddying the river, and when he is gone the waters run clear. Over the fallen empire the lights of heaven go out.

Below, a roll call of empires lies in the grave, swords under their heads and iniquity on their bones, with nothing to offer one another but the bleak comfort of company. Only one has ever gone down there and come back holding the keys.

keyVerse.quote: For I spread terror in the land of the living; and he shall be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD.
keyVerse.note: The last word of the oracles against Egypt, and of the whole section on the nations. The empires thought they were the terror of the earth, but they all lie in the pit; God alone is to be feared. That is the truth that drives us to the one who holds the keys of death.

32.reflection:
Pharaoh thought himself “a lion of the nations”, but God saw “a dragon in the seas” fouling the rivers (v. 2). How might the way we see ourselves differ from the way God sees us? Where might we be troubling the waters for others?

Again and again the fallen powers are those who “spread terror in the land of the living” and now “bear their shame” (vv. 23–30). Why is it a comfort to people who have suffered under cruelty that God will judge tyrants and abusers?

“Whom do you surpass in beauty?” (v. 19). Death levels everyone. How should facing our own death honestly shape the way we live this week (Hebrews 9:27)?

The risen Christ says, “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). How does that change the way a Christian thinks about the grave, and about loved ones who have died in Christ?
