verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God renews Ezekiel’s commission as a watchman, because the change from warning to comfort does not end the need to warn. The picture is plain: when the watchman sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet, anyone who ignores it is responsible for his own death, and if he had listened he would have lived (vv. 2–5). If the watchman stays silent, the people still die in their sin, but their blood is on his hands (v. 6). Then God applies it: “So you, son of man, I have made a watchman for the house of Israel” (v. 7). Whether the wicked turn or not, Ezekiel must warn them (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The messenger must warn, and the hearer must heed.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, speak to your people and say to them, If I bring the sword upon a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and make him their watchman, and if he sees the sword coming upon the land and blows the trumpet and warns the people, then if anyone who hears the sound of the trumpet does not take warning, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood shall be upon his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take warning; his blood shall be upon himself. But if he had taken warning, he would have saved his life. But if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, so that the people are not warned, and the sword comes and takes any one of them, that person is taken away in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the people responsible to heed the watchman, and the watchman responsible to warn them. Chapter 33 opens the second half of Ezekiel’s ministry, as chapters 1 to 32 come to an end and the news of Jerusalem’s fall is about to arrive (v. 21), by renewing the call God gave at the beginning (3:16–21).

If I bring the sword upon a land. A watchman on the wall blew the ram’s horn when an army appeared, and everyone knew how it worked: if he blew and you stayed in bed, your death was your own fault.

He heard the sound of the trumpet. This time the picture starts with the hearers. “He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take warning”; then the tragic line, “But if he had taken warning, he would have saved his life.” The warning was the offer of life, and ignoring it was choosing death.

His blood I will require. And the other side: a silent watchman is guilty. Both the preacher and the hearer carry responsibility, and the New Testament says the same of the greater warning that comes through Christ: “See that you do not refuse him who is speaking” (Hebrews 12:25).

verseByVerse.quote: "So you, son of man, I have made a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me. If I say to the wicked, O wicked one, you shall surely die, and you do not speak to warn the wicked to turn from his way, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the wicked to turn from his way, and he does not turn from his way, that person shall die in his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God repeats Ezekiel’s commission because even a message of hope must keep calling people to turn. These verses repeat almost word for word what God said at the start (3:17–19).

So you, son of man, I have made a watchman. Why repeat it? After the fall of Jerusalem Ezekiel’s message will change from warning to hope, and it would be easy to think the watchman’s job was over. It is not. Grace that never calls anyone to repent is not the grace of the Bible.

The watchman who stood under the sword. Jesus warned as no watchman ever did, weeping over the city that would not listen (Luke 19:41–44). But he did more than blow the trumpet. The sword he warned of fell on him, so that all who heed the warning and run to him find it has already been borne.

For those who warn. The trumpet is not only bad news. It sounds so that people can be saved.

Is every Christian a watchman with blood on his hands? Ezekiel’s office was unique, given by God to warn Israel. Its principle applies most directly to pastors who keep watch over souls (Hebrews 13:17; Acts 20:26–27). Every Christian is called to bear witness to Christ (1 Peter 3:15; Matthew 28:19), out of love, not fear of guilt; salvation and judgment are God’s, and our part is faithfulness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — How Then Can We Live?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s answer to a people crushed by guilt is an oath that he wants them to live. The exiles now say, “Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?” (v. 10). God replies, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (v. 11). The past does not settle the future: a good record will not save someone who turns to sin, and a bad record will not condemn someone who turns back and puts things right; none of his sins will be remembered (vv. 12–16). Those who call this unjust are the unjust ones, for God judges each by his ways (vv. 17–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Despair over sin is answered by God's plea to turn and live, and by the promise that the repentant sinner's sins are not remembered.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, say to the house of Israel, Thus have you said: 'Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?' Say to them, As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
To people crushed by their sins God swears that he wants them to live, and calls them to turn back to him.

How then can we live? For years the exiles denied their guilt, blaming their fathers (18:2) or God (18:25). Now they have swung to the opposite extreme: “our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them.”

Two opposite errors. From denial to despair is a common path. First we insist we are not that bad; then, when the truth sinks in, we conclude it is hopeless: “my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me” (Psalm 38:4). Both keep a person away from God.

Turn back, turn back. God’s answer to despair is the same as his answer to denial. On oath, “As I live”, he declares that he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death: he wants them to live. The proof came later and cost him more than words: he “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

If your sins weigh on you. That weight is not meant to drive you away from God but to him. “If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness” (Psalm 130:3–4). Jesus says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The question “How then can we live?” has an answer: by turning to the God who does not want you to die.

Where Christians differ: if God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, how can he choose some and not others? Arminian Christians answer that God gives all the same grace and leaves the choice to them. Reformed Christians distinguish what God commands and delights in from what he decrees: he sincerely calls all to turn and live, and the death of the wicked is no pleasure to him, yet he has not chosen to give the new heart (36:26) to all, for reasons he has not revealed (Deuteronomy 29:29; Romans 9:18–23). This commentary’s view: the second view does justice to both truths Scripture states. The call to repent is sincere, and no one who turns to God is turned away (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, say to your people, The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him when he transgresses, and as for the wickedness of the wicked, he shall not fall by it when he turns from his wickedness, and the righteous shall not be able to live by his righteousness when he sins. Though I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, yet if he trusts in his righteousness and does injustice, none of his righteous deeds shall be remembered, but in his injustice that he has done he shall die. Again, though I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' yet if he turns from his sin and does what is just and right, if the wicked restores the pledge, gives back what he has taken by robbery, and walks in the statutes of life, not doing injustice, he shall surely live; he shall not die. None of the sins that he has committed shall be remembered against him. He has done what is just and right; he shall surely live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither a good past nor a bad past decides a person’s future; what matters is which way he is now going. The principle of chapter 18 is restated: a good record is no insurance for someone who turns away, and a bad record is no prison for someone who turns back.

If he trusts in his righteousness. The key phrase. The danger is not only turning to sin but trusting in one’s own goodness as if it gave permission to sin. The person who thinks, “I have served faithfully for years, so this small compromise hardly counts”, has already stopped trusting God. (The ESV notes that “by his righteousness” in v. 12 is literally “by it”.)

The good record that gives permission. Psychologists call this moral licensing: in a number of studies, people who had just done something virtuous felt freer afterwards to cut corners, as though goodness were a bank balance they had earned the right to spend. The religious moralist does it in church and the decent secular person at work, and both are quietly being their own saviour. The gospel cuts the root. A Christian’s righteousness is not a balance he has built up but a gift he has received, “the righteousness from God that depends on faith” (Philippians 3:9). You cannot spend what was never yours to bank. And a heart that knows it lives on grace finds sin not more permissible but less attractive, because the debt it was spared was paid in blood.

If the wicked restores the pledge. Real repentance is practical. It returns what was taken as security for a loan, and “gives back what he has taken by robbery”. When Zacchaeus met Jesus, he said, “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). Turning to God includes making things right with people wherever that can be done.

The statutes of life. God’s commands are not a cage but the path that leads to life.

None of the sins that he has committed shall be remembered. That is the answer to “our sins are upon us” (v. 10): the sins that were crushing them can be lifted and forgotten by God.

Is Ezekiel saying that giving back stolen goods earns forgiveness? No. Restitution is the fruit of a heart that has truly turned, not the price of pardon. How a just God can forget real sins is answered at the cross. The new covenant promise, “I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12; Jeremiah 31:34), rests on the one sacrifice of Christ, who “himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). God does not pretend the sins never happened; he remembers them no more because his Son has carried them away.

Where Christians differ: can a truly righteous person fall away and be lost? Arminian Christians read such warnings as showing that a true believer can lose salvation. This commentary’s view: Ezekiel speaks of a righteous man who turns from his righteousness and persists in evil, and Scripture shows that such a person was never truly made new, since those God has given a new heart (36:26) are kept by him (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and “if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which God keeps his own from falling.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet your people say, 'The way of the Lord is not just,' when it is their own way that is not just. When the righteous turns from his righteousness and does injustice, he shall die for it. And when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does what is just and right, he shall live by this. Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' O house of Israel, I will judge each of you according to his ways."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s way is perfectly just: he judges each person by the way he is actually going.

The way of the Lord is not just. The complaint of chapter 18 is still around (18:25, 29). People object that it is unfair for God to forgive a wicked person who turns, or to condemn someone who had lived well and then turned away.

I will judge each of you according to his ways. God looks at where a person is heading and whom he is trusting. That is perfectly just; what would be unjust is a God who condemned the repentant or excused the rebellious. Those who complain are usually those who do not want to repent. The same complaint met Jesus when he welcomed sinners, and he answered it with the elder brother who would not come in to the feast (Luke 15:28–32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–22 — The City Has Been Struck Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word God spoke has come true, and now the prophet can speak again. In the twelfth year of the exile a survivor reaches Babylon with the news, “The city has been struck down” (v. 21). The evening before, the hand of the LORD came on Ezekiel and opened his mouth, “and I was no longer mute” (v. 22). The silence that began at his call (3:26) ends, and from here his message turns from judgment to hope.
verseByVerse.theology: When God's word is fulfilled, his messenger's mouth is opened to speak hope.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year of our exile, in the tenth month, on the fifth day of the month, a fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and said, "The city has been struck down." Now the hand of the LORD had been upon me the evening before the fugitive came; and he had opened my mouth by the time the man came to me in the morning, so my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem has fallen, just as God said, and at that very moment God gives his prophet back his voice.

The city has been struck down. The moment the first half of the book has been leading to: a survivor, worn out from the long journey, reaches the exiles with the news.

Fulfilled to the letter. The walls had been breached months before (Jeremiah 39:2), and the news has only now reached Babylon; a journey like that could take four months or more (Ezra 7:9). Everything Ezekiel had acted out in chapters 4, 5 and 12, the brick, the siege, the shaved hair, the baggage through the wall, had come true. The hopes of a quick return, the promises of the false prophets, the confidence that God would never let his temple fall: all collapsed in a single sentence.

I was no longer mute. At exactly that moment Ezekiel’s long silence ends (3:26–27; 24:27). God opened his mouth the night before the news arrived, so that when the people were ready to listen, the prophet was ready to speak.

From judgment to hope. What will he speak? Not more judgment on the city; that word has been fulfilled. From here on, his message turns to hope: a true shepherd (chapter 34), a new heart (chapter 36), dry bones living (chapter 37), a new temple (chapters 40 to 48). The prophet who was silent while the people were proud will speak comfort now that they are broken, the same pattern as Isaiah: after the judgment, “Comfort, comfort my people” (Isaiah 40:1). God often has to take away the false hopes before people will hear the true one.
verseByVerse.note: News of Jerusalem’s fall reached the exiles in Babylon, probably in January 585 BC, about five months after the city fell. A few ancient manuscripts read “eleventh year”, which would shorten the gap; most translations follow the standard Hebrew text.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Abraham Was Only One Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Claiming God’s promise while refusing God’s ways is not faith but presumption, and it will not stand. The survivors in the ruined land reason, “Abraham was only one man, yet he got possession of the land; but we are many” (v. 24). God lists their lives in reply: they eat blood, look to idols, shed blood, rely on the sword and defile their neighbours’ wives, and he asks twice, “shall you then possess the land?” (vv. 25–26). Sword, beasts and pestilence will find them wherever they hide, and the land will be desolate, so that they know that he is the LORD (vv. 27–29).
verseByVerse.theology: Claiming the promises of God while living in rebellion against him is presumption, not faith.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, the inhabitants of these waste places in the land of Israel keep saying, 'Abraham was only one man, yet he got possession of the land; but we are many; the land is surely given us to possess.' Therefore say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: You eat flesh with the blood and lift up your eyes to your idols and shed blood; shall you then possess the land? You rely on the sword, you commit abominations, and each of you defiles his neighbor's wife; shall you then possess the land?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The survivors claim Abraham’s promise while living in open rebellion, and God says they will not possess the land.

Abraham was only one man. Even after the catastrophe, those left in the ruins of Judah reason: if God gave the land to one man, surely he will give it to all of us. We are the heirs of the promise.

Presumption, not faith. It sounds like faith; it is presumption. They claim Abraham’s promise without Abraham’s faith. John the Baptist met the same attitude: “do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’” (Matthew 3:9), and Jesus said, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works Abraham did” (John 8:39).

Shall you then possess the land? Twice God asks it. They ate blood, worshipped idols, murdered, trusted violence and committed adultery, and still expected his blessing. That is always the danger of claiming God’s promises without living under his lordship. The true children of Abraham are “those of faith” (Galatians 3:7), and the promise comes “through the righteousness of faith” (Romans 4:13). Faith that is real shows itself in turning from sin.

Does the ban on eating blood still bind? It was given to Noah before Israel (Genesis 9:4), and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep it for the sake of fellowship with Jewish Christians (Acts 15:20, 29). But the New Testament declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19; 1 Timothy 4:4), and most Christians have concluded that the principle, reverence for the life God gives, remains, while eating meat that is not fully drained is not sin. The command concerns eating, not medicine; a blood transfusion gives life and does not break it.

verseByVerse.quote: Say this to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: As I live, surely those who are in the waste places shall fall by the sword, and whoever is in the open field I will give to the beasts to be devoured, and those who are in strongholds and in caves shall die by pestilence. And I will make the land a desolation and a waste, and her proud might shall come to an end, and the mountains of Israel shall be so desolate that none will pass through. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have made the land a desolation and a waste because of all their abominations that they have committed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wherever the presumptuous hide, God’s judgment will find them, and the land they claimed will lie empty.

In strongholds and in caves. In the ruins, in the open country, in caves and strongholds: the sword, the beasts and pestilence of 5:17 and 14:21 will reach them. The survivors who presumed on God’s promise will not inherit it.

Her proud might shall come to an end. The same words were used of Egypt (30:18); now they are used of Israel. God’s people who behave like the nations will be judged like the nations.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It is possible to enjoy God’s word and never obey it. Now that Ezekiel has been proved right, people talk about him in doorways and invite one another to come and hear “what the word is that comes from the LORD” (v. 30). They sit before him as God’s people, but they do not do what he says, for their hearts are set on gain (v. 31). To them he is like a fine singer with a beautiful voice: “they hear what you say, but they will not do it” (v. 32). When his words come true, they will know that a prophet has been among them (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: Enjoying the preaching of God's word without obeying it is a dangerous self-deception.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, your people who talk together about you by the walls and at the doors of the houses say to one another, each to his brother, 'Come, and hear what the word is that comes from the LORD.' And they come to you as people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear what you say but they will not do it; for with lustful talk in their mouths they act; their heart is set on their gain. And behold, you are to them like one who sings lustful songs with a beautiful voice and plays well on an instrument, for they hear what you say, but they will not do it. When this comes—and come it will!— then they will know that a prophet has been among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exiles flock to hear God’s word and enjoy it, but they will not obey it, and one day they will know it was not a song.

Come, and hear. Proved right, Ezekiel is now popular. People talk about him on their doorsteps: “Come, and hear what the word is that comes from the LORD.” It sounds like revival.

They will not do it. But God sees beneath the surface: they come, they sit, they hear, “but they will not do it”. Their mouths are full of warm, eager talk, but “their heart is set on their gain”. They come to hear God’s word, and leave unchanged.

Like one who sings lustful songs. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is literally “like the singing of lustful songs with a beautiful voice”. To the people Ezekiel is entertainment: they enjoy the sermon as they would a love song, admire the delivery, and go home and do nothing.

Herod and Felix. Herod was like that with John the Baptist: “When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly” (Mark 6:20), and still he had him killed. Felix listened to Paul speak about judgment, was alarmed, and said, “Go away for the present” (Acts 24:25).

Hearers only. It is possible to love good preaching and never obey it. “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1:22). “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?” (Luke 6:46). The question after every sermon is not “Did I enjoy that?” but “What must I do?”

The perfect hearer. We hear and do imperfectly at best. Christ was the one perfect hearer and doer, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19); his Spirit, now in us, turns hearing into doing (36:27), and when we fail, the way back is confession and his promised mercy (1 John 1:9).

A prophet has been among them. The chapter closes with the words of Ezekiel’s first commission (2:5). When his words come to pass, they will realise too late that it was not a song. It was the word of God.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “lustful talk” (v. 31) and “lustful songs” (v. 32) is rare. It comes from a root used of sexual desire, as of the two sisters’ lusting after their lovers in chapter 23, so the ESV reads “lustful”; others take it more broadly as words or songs of love, so that the people speak warmly of their devotion while their hearts chase gain, as several modern versions translate it. Either way the point is the same: what they say and enjoy is not what they do.

33.title: Hearers but Not Doers
33.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 33 is the hinge of the book. Twenty-four chapters have warned that Jerusalem would fall, and eight have judged the nations that gloated over it (25 to 32); now a fugitive arrives with the news that it has fallen (v. 21), and the prophet who was struck dumb at the start (3:26) is given back his voice.

The message. God means every warning he gives, and he gives them because he wants people to live. After the disaster he does not stop calling; he calls more tenderly: “turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die?” (v. 11). But the right response to his word is not despair, nor presumption, nor enjoyment of the preacher. It is to turn and obey.

Why it was said. The exiles had swung from denying their guilt (18:2) to drowning in it: “we rot away because of them. How then can we live?” (v. 10). Back in the ruined land, the survivors were claiming Abraham’s promise while living as though God had never spoken. And in Babylon, now that Ezekiel had been proved right, crowds came to hear him and went home unchanged (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God renews Ezekiel’s commission as a watchman: the trumpet makes the hearer responsible for his own life, and silence makes the watchman responsible for it (vv. 1–9). He answers the exiles’ despair with an oath that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and shows that the past, good or bad, does not decide anyone’s future; he judges each by the way he is going (vv. 10–20). Then the news comes, and Ezekiel’s mouth is opened (vv. 21–22). Two kinds of false hearer close the chapter: the survivors who say “Abraham was only one man… but we are many” (vv. 23–29), and the exiles who listen to the prophet as to a beautiful singer and do nothing (vv. 30–33).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the character of God it reveals. The God who swears “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” wept over Jerusalem in Jesus (Luke 19:41–42) and gave his Son so that the wicked need not die. Ezekiel is also a pattern of Christ, the faithful watchman who warned of the coming sword and then stood under it himself for those he warned. And the chapter’s last picture, hearers who admire and do not obey, is the one Jesus used to close the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7:24–27).

For us. If your sins feel too heavy, God’s word to you is not “too late” but “turn back”. If you are sure you are safe because of your family, your church or your past, the same word sounds as a warning. And if you love good preaching, ask after every sermon not whether you enjoyed it but what you must now do, and lean on the Spirit Christ gives to make you a doer.
33.theology:
The messenger is responsible to warn and the hearer to heed; even a message of hope must call people to turn (vv. 1-9; Heb 12:25). Both denial of sin and despair over sin keep people from God, and his answer to both is to turn and live (vv. 10-11; Ps 130:3-4; Matt 11:28).

Real repentance is practical and includes restitution, and God does not remember the sins of the repentant (vv. 14-16; Luke 19:8). He judges each person justly by the direction of his life (vv. 17-20), and he opens his servant's mouth to speak hope at the right time (vv. 21-22; 3:26-27; 24:27).

Claiming God's promises while living in rebellion is presumption; Abraham's true children share his faith (vv. 24-26; Matt 3:9; John 8:39; Gal 3:7). Enjoying preaching without obeying it is self-deception (vv. 30-32; Jas 1:22-25; Luke 6:46; Mark 6:20).
33.examples:
A trumpet sounds and a man stays in bed. A people swing from "we're not that bad" to "there's no hope", and a thief quietly gives back what he stole.

A fugitive arrives with six words, The city has been struck down, to find the prophet's mouth already opened the night before. Survivors call themselves Abraham's heirs with idols in their hands, and a congregation loves the preacher's voice and goes home unchanged.

keyVerse.quote: As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?
keyVerse.note: This is God’s answer to the despairing question of v. 10, given on oath at the very moment Jerusalem falls. It shows the heart behind every warning in the chapter: the watchman sounds the trumpet, and the righteous Judge judges each by his ways, because God wants people to live. It is the plea that Christ himself made, and made good, when he went to the cross.

33.reflection:
God says the watchman who keeps silent is responsible, but so is the hearer who ignores the trumpet (vv. 1–9). Who has been a watchman in your life? Is there anyone you have been reluctant to warn, and what holds you back?

The exiles swung from denying their guilt to despairing over it: “How then can we live?” (v. 10). Which of the two comes more naturally to you, and how does God’s oath in v. 11 answer both?

The survivors said, “Abraham was only one man… but we are many” (v. 24). In what ways might people today claim God’s promises while ignoring his ways?

Ezekiel’s hearers enjoyed him like a fine singer and did nothing (vv. 30–32). What helps you move from enjoying a sermon to obeying it, and how could your group help one another with that this week?

Should not shepherds feed the sheep?<sup>3</sup>You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep.<sup>4</sup>The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them.<sup>5</sup>So they were scattered, because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the wild beasts. I will feed them in justice.<sup>17</sup>"As for you, my flock, thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and male goats.<sup>18</sup>Is it not enough for you to feed on the good pasture, that you must tread down with your feet the rest of your pasture; and to drink of clear water, that you must muddy the rest of the water with your feet?<sup>19</sup>And must my sheep eat what you have trodden with your feet, and drink what you have muddied with your feet?<sup>20</sup>"Therefore, thus says the Lord GOD to them: Behold, I, I myself will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep.<sup>21</sup>Because you push with side and shoulder, and thrust at all the weak with your horns, till you have scattered them abroad,<sup>22</sup>I will rescue my flock; they shall no longer be a prey. And I will judge between sheep and sheep.<sup>23</sup>And I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them: he shall feed them and be their shepherd.<sup>24</sup>And I, the LORD, will be their God, and my servant David shall be prince among them. And they shall know that I am the LORD, when I break the bars of their yoke, and deliver them from the hand of those who enslaved them.<sup>28</sup>They shall no more be a prey to the nations, nor shall the beasts of the land devour them. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God holds the leaders of his people to account for using the flock instead of feeding it. His charge is a single question: “Should not shepherds feed the sheep?” (v. 2). They took the fat and the wool, and neglected the weak, the sick, the injured, the strayed and the lost, ruling them “with force and harshness” (vv. 3–4). So the sheep scattered over the face of the earth and became prey, with no one to look for them (vv. 5–6). With an oath God declares, “Behold, I am against the shepherds” (v. 10): he will hold them to account and rescue his sheep from their mouths (vv. 7–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who lead God's people exist to serve the flock, and God holds them to account for how they use it.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel; prophesy, and say to them, even to the shepherds, Thus says the Lord GOD: Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves! Should not shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders of God’s people had turned the flock into something that existed for them, and God calls them to account. The message of hope begins by answering the question: why did the flock end up scattered? Because of its shepherds.

Should not shepherds feed the sheep? In the ancient world kings and leaders were commonly called shepherds, and Israel’s kings, officials, priests and prophets were meant to be shepherds of God’s people. The charge against them is one simple, devastating question. They had it backwards.

You clothe yourselves with the wool. Picture a shepherd who shears the sheep for his own coat, eats the best lambs for his dinner, and never leads the flock to pasture. That was Judah’s leadership: taxes, privileges, comfort and power, and no care for the people.

For pastors and elders. The temptation to use the flock is always there: for income, for status, for the pleasure of being needed and admired. Peter wrote to elders: “shepherd the flock of God that is among you… not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2–3). Shepherds can do this only as sheep of the Good Shepherd themselves, fed by him and given his Spirit; and when they fail, as every shepherd does, his life laid down for the sheep covers them too.

verseByVerse.quote: The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The false shepherds failed every kind of sheep that needed care, and ruled the rest by force.

The weak you have not strengthened. Five kinds of sheep needed care, and there were five failures: the weak, without strength to keep up; the sick; the injured, whose wounds needed binding; the strayed, who had wandered off; and the lost, gone altogether.

Every congregation’s needs. Read the list slowly and you have any congregation: the weak in faith, the sick in body and mind, those wounded by life and by other people, the drifting, and the completely lost. A good shepherd notices each kind and goes to each one.

With force and harshness. Instead these shepherds drove the sheep instead of leading them, governing by pressure instead of love. Paul gives the opposite pattern: “admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). And the pattern for every Christian leader is Christ, who said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and of whom it was said, “a bruised reed he will not break” (Matthew 12:20).

verseByVerse.quote: So they were scattered, because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the wild beasts. My sheep were scattered; they wandered over all the mountains and on every high hill. My sheep were scattered over all the face of the earth, with none to search or seek for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no true shepherd, God’s sheep were scattered, preyed on and left unsought, and God still calls them “my sheep”.

Because there was no shepherd. The shepherds existed, but they did not shepherd. The result was a scattered flock, wandering on the mountains, falling prey to wild beasts, with nobody looking for them. That was the exile: God’s people scattered “over all the face of the earth”.

My sheep were scattered. God keeps repeating “my sheep”. The flock never belonged to the shepherds; it belonged to God. Whenever leaders forget that the people they lead are God’s, not theirs, abuse follows.

Like sheep without a shepherd. Jesus looked at the crowds of his day and saw the same thing: “he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). His response was not to condemn the sheep but to care for them: “he began to teach them many things” (Mark 6:34).

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD: As I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely because my sheep have become a prey, and my sheep have become food for all the wild beasts, since there was no shepherd, and because my shepherds have not searched for my sheep, but the shepherds have fed themselves, and have not fed my sheep, therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep at their hand and put a stop to their feeding the sheep. No longer shall the shepherds feed themselves. I will rescue my sheep from their mouths, that they may not be food for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God swears that he is against the shepherds who preyed on his flock, and that he will rescue his sheep from their mouths. He repeats the charge with an oath, as if he cannot let it go, and “my sheep” comes again and again: a Shepherd-God angry on behalf of his flock.

I will require my sheep at their hand. Every leader will give an account for every soul in his care (Hebrews 13:17). And “I will rescue my sheep from their mouths”: the shepherds had become predators, and God will pull the sheep out of their teeth.

For the hurt. This is great comfort for anyone hurt by a leader who should have protected them, in a church, a family or a nation. God sees. He is against those shepherds, and he rescues the sheep.

If you are being harmed. Abuse is never to be tolerated or covered up in God’s name. Seek safety at once, and tell someone who can act, whether faithful church leaders or the civil authorities God has appointed to protect the weak (Romans 13:3–4). Speaking up is not disloyalty to the flock; it is siding with the Shepherd.

Why trust anyone in charge? Many have concluded that you cannot, and they have reasons: the abusive pastor, the cover-up. A whole style of modern thought teaches us to ask of every claim to authority not whether it is true but whose interests it serves. Ezekiel would not call that suspicion paranoid; he made the charge first, with God himself as prosecutor: “the shepherds have fed themselves, and have not fed my sheep” (v. 8). But God does not leave the sheep free and alone on the mountains, which is where the modern answer leaves us: each person the only authority he trusts, and the loneliest one. He promises a different kind of shepherd. The only authority it is safe to give your whole life to is one who has used his power to give his life for you, and that is exactly the claim Jesus makes: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Those hurt by false shepherds do not have to choose between blind trust and no trust. They can come to the Shepherd who bled for the flock, and measure every other leader by him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — I Myself Will Be the Shepherd
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where the shepherds failed, God himself will shepherd his flock. “Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out” (v. 11). He will rescue them from wherever they were scattered on the dark day of Jerusalem’s fall, bring them home and feed them on good pasture on the mountains of Israel (vv. 12–14). “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I myself will make them lie down” (v. 15). Point by point he reverses the false shepherds’ failures: he will seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind up the injured and strengthen the weak, and feed them in justice (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Where human shepherds failed, God himself comes to seek, heal and feed his people.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock when he is among his sheep that have been scattered, so will I seek out my sheep, and I will rescue them from all places where they have been scattered on a day of clouds and thick darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will not wait for better shepherds: he himself will search for his scattered sheep and rescue them.

I, I myself will search for my sheep. Here is the turning point. The shepherds “have not searched” (v. 8); God says, I will do it myself. The doubled “I” is emphatic.

A day of clouds and thick darkness. The day of Jerusalem’s fall. God knows exactly where each sheep went in the darkness, and he will go there to get it.

Until he finds it. The New Testament shows how literally God kept this promise. Jesus told of a shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to “go after the one that is lost, until he finds it”, and “lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing” (Luke 15:4–5). And he said of himself, “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). In Jesus the God of Ezekiel 34 came in person to search for his sheep.

If you have wandered. If you feel you have wandered far, into a dark place, this is God’s word to you: he knows where you are, and he is the kind of shepherd who comes looking.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will bring them out from the peoples and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land. And I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, by the ravines, and in all the inhabited places of the country. I will feed them with good pasture, and on the mountain heights of Israel shall be their grazing land. There they shall lie down in good grazing land, and on rich pasture they shall feed on the mountains of Israel. I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I myself will make them lie down, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will gather his scattered flock home and feed it himself, giving it rich pasture and rest.

I will bring them out from the peoples. The scattered flock will be gathered from the nations into its own land, and the mountains once cursed for their idolatry (chapter 6) will become pastures.

I will feed them with good pasture. The selfish shepherds fed themselves and starved the flock; God feeds the flock. Sheep lie down only when they are full and feel safe.

I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep. It is impossible to read this without hearing Psalm 23: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul” (Psalm 23:1–3). Ezekiel 34 is Psalm 23 for a whole scattered nation.

Rest for the weary. The Shepherd does not only rescue; he gives rest and food. Jesus says that whoever enters by him “will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture” (John 10:9).

Where Christians differ: how is this return fulfilled? The return from Babylon was its first fulfilment. Dispensationalists (who see God’s purposes for Israel and for the church as running on separate tracks) look for a future regathering of ethnic Israel to the land, and some see it in the modern state of Israel. This commentary’s view: the promises reach beyond any return to territory: a new heart, a Davidic King, the nations gathered. They are fulfilled in Christ, who gathers his scattered people from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), including, on the most natural reading of Paul, a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26), and they will be complete in the new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak, and the fat and the strong I will destroy. I will feed them in justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Point by point, God will do for his sheep everything the false shepherds failed to do, and he will judge those who fattened themselves on the weak.

I will seek the lost. Compare this verse with v. 4. They did not seek the lost; “I will seek the lost”. They did not bring back the strayed, bind up the injured or strengthen the weak; God will do every one.

Those the world overlooks. That is the heart of God toward his people. The lost, the drifting, the wounded and the weak, the people the world overlooks, are exactly the ones he goes after first.

The fat and the strong I will destroy. As the Hebrew stands, the fat and strong are the sheep who, as the next verses show, have grown fat by pushing others aside. “I will feed them in justice”: God’s care for the weak includes justice against those who abuse them.

Textual note. The ESV notes that the Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate read “I will watch over” instead of “I will destroy”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God judges not only bad shepherds but bullies within the flock. “Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep” (v. 17). Some sheep eat the good pasture and trample the rest, drink the clear water and muddy what is left for others (vv. 18–19). They shove the weak with side and shoulder and thrust at them with their horns until they scatter (vv. 20–21). God takes the side of the lean sheep: “I will rescue my flock; they shall no longer be a prey” (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: God defends the weak members of his flock against the strong who abuse them.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, my flock, thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and male goats. Is it not enough for you to feed on the good pasture, that you must tread down with your feet the rest of your pasture; and to drink of clear water, that you must muddy the rest of the water with your feet? And must my sheep eat what you have trodden with your feet, and drink what you have muddied with your feet?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God judges within his own flock too, against the strong who take the best and spoil what is left for others.

I judge between sheep and sheep. Now God turns from the shepherds to the flock itself. Not all the trouble came from the leaders; some sheep harmed others. Jesus used this very picture for the last judgment: “he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25:32). Belonging to the flock outwardly exempts no one from judgment.

You must muddy the rest of the water. Picture strong sheep that eat the best grass and then trample what is left, drink the clear water and then stir up the mud with their hooves. The others get trampled grass and dirty water.

In the church too. The powerful among God’s own people take the best for themselves and spoil what is left for others: the wealthy honoured and the poor pushed aside. James rebuked exactly this: “if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, ‘You sit here in a good place,’ while you say to the poor man, ‘You stand over there’… have you not then made distinctions among yourselves” (James 2:3–4)?

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, thus says the Lord GOD to them: Behold, I, I myself will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep. Because you push with side and shoulder, and thrust at all the weak with your horns, till you have scattered them abroad, I will rescue my flock; they shall no longer be a prey. And I will judge between sheep and sheep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes the side of the weak sheep against the bullies, and will rescue them himself.

The fat sheep and the lean sheep. Again, “I, I myself”. God steps between them.

You push with side and shoulder. Shoving with the shoulder, barging with the side, jabbing with horns, until the weak are driven off: this is bullying in the flock.

The strong and the weak. Believers are called to the opposite: “We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Romans 15:1). The reason is Christ’s own example, “For Christ did not please himself” (Romans 15:3), and the measure of a healthy church is how it treats its weakest members.

I will rescue my flock. The weak will not be left at the mercy of the strong. (The ESV notes that “rescue” could be translated “save”.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–24 — One Shepherd, My Servant David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will give his flock one shepherd, a new David, and in him God himself will be with his people. “I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them” (v. 23). David had been dead for centuries, so this is the promised King of David’s line, who will unite the scattered flock. The LORD will be their God, and his servant David “prince among them” (v. 24). The two promises of the chapter, God the Shepherd and David the shepherd, stand side by side, waiting to meet in one person.
verseByVerse.theology: The promised Shepherd-King from David's line is Jesus, in whom God himself shepherds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them: he shall feed them and be their shepherd. And I, the LORD, will be their God, and my servant David shall be prince among them. I am the LORD; I have spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises one shepherd from David’s line to feed his people, and the promise is fulfilled in Jesus, in whom God the Shepherd and David’s Son are one.

I will set up over them one shepherd. Here is the high point of the chapter. God says “I myself will be the shepherd” (v. 15), and also “I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David”. How can both be true?

My servant David. King David had been dead for nearly four hundred years. So “my servant David” is not David come back to life but the promised King of David’s line, a new David. Jeremiah spoke of him the same way: “David their king, whom I will raise up for them” (Jeremiah 30:9). He will be “one shepherd”, uniting the scattered and divided people (37:24).

God and David in one. Here the two promises meet in one person. God himself will shepherd his people, and a son of David will shepherd them, because the Son of David is God come in the flesh. Jesus said: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). He is from David’s line (John 7:42), and he is “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25).

He shall feed them. See what makes him different from the shepherds of v. 2. They fed on the sheep; he lays down his life for them. They scattered the flock; he says, “there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16). Zechariah foresaw the price: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered”, words Jesus applied to himself on the night of his arrest (Matthew 26:31). The Good Shepherd was struck so that the flock could be gathered.

Prince among them. Not a distant tyrant, but a ruler who lives among his people: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). And “I am the LORD; I have spoken”: the promise is signed and sealed.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish interpreters agree that “my servant David” is not David raised from the dead but the King Messiah of his line; rabbinic tradition can even say that the Messiah’s name will be David. Here the two readings stand very close. Where they part is in how the two shepherds relate: Jewish readers take the LORD as shepherding his flock through a human king, as he once did through David, while this commentary sees God the Shepherd and David’s Son meeting in one person, Jesus, the good shepherd (John 10:11), who is God come in the flesh (John 1:14).
verseByVerse.note: “My servant David” is the coming Messiah from David’s line.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under the shepherd King, God’s flock will live in his peace and safety. He will make “a covenant of peace”, banish the wild beasts so the sheep can sleep even in the woods, and send “showers of blessing” on fruitful land (vv. 25–27). He will break their yoke; they will no longer be prey to the nations, “and none shall make them afraid”, nor will they suffer hunger or shame (vv. 27–29). Above all, they will know that the LORD is with them and that they are his people: “you are my sheep, human sheep of my pasture, and I am your God” (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: The Shepherd's covenant brings security, provision and the joy of belonging to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will make with them a covenant of peace and banish wild beasts from the land, so that they may dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods. And I will make them and the places all around my hill a blessing, and I will send down the showers in their season; they shall be showers of blessing. And the trees of the field shall yield their fruit, and the earth shall yield its increase, and they shall be secure in their land. And they shall know that I am the LORD, when I break the bars of their yoke, and deliver them from the hand of those who enslaved them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God binds himself by covenant to give his flock peace: safety, plenty and freedom.

A covenant of peace. Peace in the Bible is more than the absence of war. It is wholeness, safety, everything as it should be, and God binds himself to give it (37:26). The wild beasts that devoured the scattered sheep (v. 5) will be gone, and the flock can sleep safely “in the woods”, the most dangerous place for sheep. For Christians this peace has a name: “he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14).

Showers of blessing. Rain at the right time was life in a dry land. The blessings promised in Leviticus to a people keeping God’s covenant return: “I will give you your rains in their season” (Leviticus 26:4). And God’s people become “a blessing” to the places around “my hill”, Zion, as Abraham was promised (Genesis 12:2).

When I break the bars of their yoke. The Shepherd is also a Deliverer. For the exiles it meant freedom from Babylon; for all God’s people it points to a deeper freedom: “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

verseByVerse.quote: They shall no more be a prey to the nations, nor shall the beasts of the land devour them. They shall dwell securely, and none shall make them afraid. And I will provide for them a renowned place for planting so that they shall no more be consumed with hunger in the land, and no longer suffer the reproach of the nations. And they shall know that I am the LORD their God with them, and that they, the house of Israel, are my people, declares the Lord GOD. And you are my sheep, human sheep of my pasture, and I am your God, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s flock will live without fear, honoured and fed, because the LORD is their God and is with them.

None shall make them afraid. Micah pictured the same: “they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid” (Micah 4:4). Fear of enemies, of hunger and of loss will be gone. Jesus says of his sheep: “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). That is the ultimate security of the flock.

No longer suffer the reproach of the nations. No more hunger, no more shame before the nations: the flock that was mocked will be honoured.

The LORD their God with them. That is the heart of the covenant. The name given to Jesus at his birth says exactly this: “Immanuel” (which means, God with us) (Matthew 1:23).

Human sheep of my pasture. The chapter ends by saying plainly what the picture means. God is not talking about animals but about people, about you: “we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture” (Psalm 100:3).

The Lamb as shepherd. The Bible’s final picture is the same: “the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 7:17). The Shepherd who was struck becomes the Lamb who shepherds, and the flock he gathers will never be scattered again.

Uncertain wording. The phrase “a renowned place for planting” (v. 29) is literally “a planting for a name”. Most take it, as the ESV does, as land famous for its crops, which fits the promise of no more hunger; others read it as a renowned plant, the King James Version’s “plant of renown”, and many older Christian interpreters saw in it the Messiah, the righteous Branch. The context of food and fruitful land favours the first.

34.title: The Good Shepherd
34.overview:
Where we are. Jerusalem has fallen and Ezekiel’s mouth has been opened (33:21–22). The message now turns to hope, and the first word of hope is about shepherds: why the flock was scattered, and who will gather it.

The message. The leaders of God’s people used the flock instead of caring for it, and so God himself will be its shepherd. He will search for the lost, bring back the strayed, bind up the injured and strengthen the weak; he will judge the strong who bully the weak; and he will set over his people one shepherd, “my servant David”, under a covenant of peace. God is not finished with a scattered, wounded people. He comes looking for them.

Why it was said. In the ancient world kings were called shepherds, and Judah’s kings, officials, priests and prophets had fed themselves while the people starved, ending in a nation scattered across the earth (see the introduction). The exiles needed to know why it had happened, and whether anyone would ever care for them again.

How the chapter makes its case. God indicts the shepherds who took the wool and the meat and ruled “with force and harshness”, so that the sheep scattered and became prey, and he declares himself against them (vv. 1–10). Then the turn: “I, I myself will search for my sheep”, gather them home, feed them on good pasture, and do point by point all that the false shepherds failed to do (vv. 11–16). He will also judge within the flock, between the fat sheep that trample the pasture and the lean ones they push aside (vv. 17–22). He will set over them one shepherd, his servant David (vv. 23–24), and make with them a covenant of peace: safety, showers of blessing, broken yokes, and God with his people (vv. 25–31).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise. The chapter makes two promises that seem to compete: God himself will shepherd his flock (v. 15), and he will set over them a son of David to shepherd them (v. 23). They meet in Jesus, who is both: the Lord who came “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10) and David’s son, the good shepherd who “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Unlike the shepherds who fed on the flock, he fed the flock with himself.

For us. If you have wandered, or been wounded by those who should have cared for you, the Shepherd knows where you are and comes looking. If you lead others, in a church, a home or a workplace, this chapter asks whether they exist for you or you for them. And it calls every believer to stop pushing the weak aside and to follow the Shepherd who carries them.
34.theology:
Leaders of God's people are shepherds who exist to serve the flock, and God will require his sheep at their hand (vv. 2-10; 1 Pet 5:2-3; Acts 20:28; Heb 13:17). Faithful shepherding cares for the weak, sick, injured, straying and lost, and rules with gentleness, not force (vv. 4, 16; 1 Thess 5:14; Matt 12:20).

Where human shepherds fail, God himself comes to seek and save his people (vv. 11-16; Ps 23:1-3; Luke 15:4-7; 19:10). He judges within the flock and defends the weak against the strong (vv. 17-22; Matt 25:31-33; Jas 2:1-6; Rom 15:1).

The promised Shepherd, God's servant David, is Jesus, God in the flesh from David's line, who lays down his life for the sheep and gathers one flock (vv. 23-24; Jer 30:9; John 10:11-16; Matt 26:31). His covenant of peace brings security, provision, freedom and the presence of God (vv. 25-31; Eph 2:14; John 10:28; Rev 7:17).
34.examples:
Picture a shepherd in a warm coat made from his flock's wool while the sheep go hungry, and the five kinds of sheep he never noticed: the weak, the sick, the injured, the straying and the lost. Picture strong sheep muddying the water after they have drunk their fill.

Then hear God say, Behold, I, I myself will search, and see a shepherd carrying a lost sheep home on his shoulders, a shepherd who lays down his life, and a flock sleeping safely in the woods. You are my sheep, human sheep of my pasture: he means us.

keyVerse.quote: For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the chapter. The shepherds had not searched for the lost, so God says he will come and do it himself. Taken with v. 23, where God sets over his flock one shepherd from David’s line, it points to Jesus, the Lord who came in person to seek and to save the lost.

34.reflection:
God’s charge against the shepherds is, “Should not shepherds feed the sheep?” (v. 2). Think of the places where you have responsibility for others: home, church, work. What would it look like there to feed the sheep rather than yourself?

Look at the five kinds of sheep in v. 4: the weak, the sick, the injured, the strayed and the lost. Which describes you at the moment? Who in your church fits each one, and how might your group care for them?

God promises, “I, I myself will search for my sheep” (v. 11), and Jesus told of the shepherd who goes after the one that is lost (Luke 15:4–5). How does it change your picture of God to know that he comes looking?

God judges “between sheep and sheep” (v. 17), against those who push the weak aside. Where might the strong be trampling the pasture or muddying the water for others in our churches today?

35.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, set your face against Mount Seir, and prophesy against it,<sup>3</sup>and say to it, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir, and I will stretch out my hand against you, and I will make you a desolation and a waste.<sup>4</sup>I will lay your cities waste, and you shall become a desolation, and you shall know that I am the LORD.<sup>5</sup>Because you cherished perpetual enmity and gave over the people of Israel to the power of the sword at the time of their calamity, at the time of their final punishment,<sup>6</sup>therefore, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will prepare you for blood, and blood shall pursue you; because you did not hate bloodshed, therefore blood shall pursue you.<sup>7</sup>I will make Mount Seir a waste and a desolation, and I will cut off from it all who come and go.<sup>8</sup>And I will fill its mountains with the slain. On your hills and in your valleys and in all your ravines those slain with the sword shall fall.<sup>9</sup>I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities shall not be inhabited. Then you will know that I am the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"Because you said, 'These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will take possession of them'—although the LORD was there—<sup>11</sup>therefore, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will deal with you according to the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred against them. And I will make myself known among them, when I judge you.<sup>12</sup>And you shall know that I am the LORD. "I have heard all the revilings that you uttered against the mountains of Israel, saying, 'They are laid desolate; they are given us to devour.'<sup>13</sup>And you magnified yourselves against me with your mouth, and multiplied your words against me; I heard it.<sup>14</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD: While the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate.<sup>15</sup>As you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so I will deal with you; you shall be desolate, Mount Seir, and all Edom, all of it. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets himself against Edom because it nursed an ancient hatred and joined in the slaughter when Israel fell. “Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir” (v. 3): Edom’s mountain homeland will be made a desolation and a waste (vv. 1–4). The charge is that Edom “cherished perpetual enmity” and handed Israel to the sword “at the time of their calamity” (v. 5). Because it did not hate bloodshed, blood will pursue it; its mountains will be filled with the slain, and the endless enmity will be answered by “a perpetual desolation” (vv. 6–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Hatred nursed for generations reaps what it sows.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face against Mount Seir, and prophesy against it, and say to it, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, Mount Seir, and I will stretch out my hand against you, and I will make you a desolation and a waste. I will lay your cities waste, and you shall become a desolation, and you shall know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets himself against Edom’s mountains, which will be made desolate just as Israel’s mountains are about to be made fruitful.

Why another oracle against Edom? Chapter 25 has already judged Edom (25:12–14); this oracle is here because of where it stands. Chapter 35 speaks to “Mount Seir”, Edom’s mountains; chapter 36 speaks to “the mountains of Israel”. Edom’s mountains will be made desolate, Israel’s fruitful again. The enemy who wanted Israel’s land will lose its own.

A desolation and a waste. The word desolation comes again and again in this chapter. Edom rejoiced when Israel was desolate; it will learn what desolation is.
verseByVerse.note: Mount Seir, the hill country south-east of the Dead Sea, is Edom: Esau's descendants settled there (Gen 36:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Because you cherished perpetual enmity and gave over the people of Israel to the power of the sword at the time of their calamity, at the time of their final punishment, therefore, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will prepare you for blood, and blood shall pursue you; because you did not hate bloodshed, therefore blood shall pursue you. I will make Mount Seir a waste and a desolation, and I will cut off from it all who come and go. And I will fill its mountains with the slain. On your hills and in your valleys and in all your ravines those slain with the sword shall fall. I will make you a perpetual desolation, and your cities shall not be inhabited. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom nursed its hatred for centuries and joined in Israel’s slaughter, so the bloodshed it did not hate will pursue it.

You cherished perpetual enmity. Edom’s hatred of Israel went back to the brothers Esau and Jacob: “Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing”, and said, “I will kill my brother Jacob” (Genesis 27:41). Centuries later Amos said Edom “pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity, and his anger tore perpetually” (Amos 1:11). The word “cherished” matters: Edom did not just feel hatred; it nursed it, kept it alive and handed it down.

At the time of their calamity. When Israel was at its lowest, Edom joined in, handing fugitives over to the sword (Obadiah 14). The psalmist remembered their cry: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!” (Psalm 137:7).

The grudge that becomes who we are. After enough generations the grievance was no longer something Edom had but something Edom was. Communities, movements and families can build their whole identity around an injury, and some injuries are real and terrible. A grievance explains my troubles, makes me the innocent party and binds me to everyone who shares my enemy, which is why letting it go feels like losing myself. But a self built on an enemy needs the enemy to stay guilty for ever, and so it can never heal. And a grudge cherished long enough becomes cruelty, in nations, families and individuals alike: what we refuse to forgive, we eventually act on.

A deeper identity than the injury. The gospel does not ask the wronged to pretend the wrong was small. It gives them something deeper to be. Esau’s hatred began over a blessing; in Christ the blessing goes to people who were themselves God’s enemies, “reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). Someone who knows himself as a forgiven enemy no longer needs an enemy of his own, and there the long feud can finally end: “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).

You did not hate bloodshed. Edom was comfortable with violence, so “blood shall pursue you”. Jesus stated the principle simply: “all who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). And “perpetual enmity” is answered by “a perpetual desolation” (v. 9).

Uncertain wording. The middle of v. 6 is compressed Hebrew, built like an oath (literally “if you did not hate blood”), and its exact force is debated; most versions read it, as the ESV does, “because you did not hate bloodshed”, and the sense is clear. There is also a play on words: “blood” is dam, which echoes the name Edom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — Although the LORD Was There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom thought the ruined land of Israel was empty and its for the taking, but the LORD was there, and he heard every word. Edom said the two nations, Israel and Judah, would be its own, “although the LORD was there” (v. 10). God will repay its anger and envy and make himself known in judging it (v. 11). He heard all its revilings against the mountains of Israel, and counts them as words against himself: “I heard it” (vv. 12–13). As Edom rejoiced over Israel’s desolation, so it will be desolate, and all will know that he is the LORD (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who attack God's people attack God, and he hears every word.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because you said, 'These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will take possession of them'—although the LORD was there— therefore, as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will deal with you according to the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred against them. And I will make myself known among them, when I judge you. And you shall know that I am the LORD. "I have heard all the revilings that you uttered against the mountains of Israel, saying, 'They are laid desolate; they are given us to devour.' And you magnified yourselves against me with your mouth, and multiplied your words against me; I heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom saw empty land to seize, but the LORD was there, and he took every insult against his people as an insult against himself.

Although the LORD was there. With Israel and Judah both destroyed, Edom thought their land was up for grabs. Edom saw vacant property; God says, I was there. The temple was burned and the people gone, but the LORD had not left his land. What looks abandoned to the enemy still belongs to God, and the book will end with a city whose name is “The LORD Is There” (48:35).

Anger and envy. Envy of his brother’s blessing was the root of Esau’s hatred from the start, and God will deal with Edom in the measure of its own anger and envy (v. 11).

You magnified yourselves against me. Edom insulted Israel’s mountains, and God says it was against him. To mock God’s people is to mock God. When Saul persecuted the church, the risen Jesus asked, “why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

I heard it. Three short words. Every word spoken against God’s people is heard: “on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak” (Matthew 12:36).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: While the whole earth rejoices, I will make you desolate. As you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so I will deal with you; you shall be desolate, Mount Seir, and all Edom, all of it. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom’s judgment mirrors its sin: as it rejoiced over Israel’s desolation, so it will be desolate.

As you rejoiced. Edom rejoiced at Israel’s ruin; the whole earth will rejoice at Edom’s. Obadiah said the same: “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (Obadiah 15).

Did the prophecy come true? Edom was weakened by Babylon in the 500s BC, and its homeland passed to Arab peoples, the Nabataeans of Petra. Edomites who moved west into southern Judah became the Idumeans, who vanish from history after the Roman wars of the first century.

Esau in the New Testament. Esau is remembered as the one “who sold his birthright for a single meal” and later “found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears” (Hebrews 12:16–17). And when the Messiah, Jacob’s greatest descendant, was born in Bethlehem, the king who tried to kill him was Herod (Matthew 2:16), who, ancient historians tell us, was an Idumean, of Edomite descent. Many Christians have seen in this the ancient enmity reaching out against the Messiah himself.

Grace for Edom. But God’s King was not destroyed by Edom’s hatred, and the gospel that went out from him reaches every people. Amos had promised that David’s fallen house would be rebuilt and would possess even “the remnant of Edom” (Amos 9:11–12), and at the Jerusalem council James quoted that promise in its Greek form, which speaks of the Gentiles seeking the Lord, to show that their coming to Christ had been foretold (Acts 15:16–17). Mount Seir is judged, yet the door of Christ’s kingdom stands open to Esau’s children too, and to the heirs of every old enmity.

What it does not mean. Not that any people today is Edom, or that Christians may treat any nation as cursed. Edom was judged for what it did.

35.title: Against Mount Seir
35.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 34 promised God’s scattered flock a true shepherd and a covenant of peace. Before chapter 36 promises new life to “the mountains of Israel”, Ezekiel turns to Mount Seir, the mountains of Edom, Israel’s oldest neighbour and enemy, which wanted those empty mountains for itself.

The message. God’s people and God’s land are never ownerless, however ruined they look, because the LORD is there. Those who nurse hatred against his people, rejoice in their fall and help it along, are in the end fighting God, and he hears every word. The measure they use will be measured back to them.

Why it was said. When Jerusalem fell, Edom gloated, cut off fugitives and moved into Judah’s empty land (Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7). The exiles, watching their old rival take their inheritance, needed to know that God had seen it, and that the land was still his (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God sets himself against Mount Seir to make it a desolation (vv. 1–4). The reason is a hatred cherished for centuries, from Esau’s grudge against Jacob onwards, which came out at the worst moment, when Edom handed Israel to the sword; because Edom did not hate bloodshed, blood will pursue it, and its desolation will be as lasting as its enmity (vv. 5–9). Edom said Israel and Judah would be its own, “although the LORD was there” (v. 10); God heard every boast against his mountains as a boast against himself, and as Edom rejoiced over Israel’s desolation, so it will be desolate (vv. 10–15).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed and by a pattern that runs through Scripture. The God who was “there” in the empty land came to be with his people in Jesus, Immanuel, and the Edomite enmity reached for him too, when Herod, of Edomite descent, tried to kill the child born in Bethlehem. Yet the judgment on Edom is not the last word: Amos promised that David’s house would possess even “the remnant of Edom” (Amos 9:12), and James saw that promise fulfilled as Gentiles came to Christ (Acts 15:16–17). The Son of Jacob died for his enemies, Esau’s children among them.

For us. Do not cherish a grudge: what is nursed long enough becomes cruelty, and the way out is the forgiveness we have received in Christ. Do not rejoice when others fall, and remember that every word against God’s people is heard. And when your life looks like an abandoned ruin that others are ready to claim, the LORD is there.
35.theology:
Hatred cherished over generations becomes cruelty and reaps judgment (vv. 5-6; Gen 27:41; Amos 1:11; Matt 26:52; Gal 6:7).

God has not abandoned what is his, even when it lies desolate (v. 10).

To attack or mock God's people is to attack God; he hears every word (vv. 12-13; Acts 9:4; Matt 12:36-37).

God's judgment often mirrors the sin it punishes (vv. 6, 15; Obad 15).
35.examples:
A family feud passed down from grandparents to grandchildren, until no one remembers how it began but everyone knows whom to hate, is Edom's sin on a small scale. The gospel breaks such chains: the one who has been forgiven much can begin to forgive.

A believer whose church has dwindled, whose building stands half empty, may feel that God has left. Edom thought the same of Israel's land. But the LORD was there, and he has not abandoned what is his.

keyVerse.quote: As you rejoiced over the inheritance of the house of Israel, because it was desolate, so I will deal with you; you shall be desolate, Mount Seir, and all Edom, all of it. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers up the chapter: Edom rejoiced over Israel’s ruin and claimed its inheritance, and God answers it measure for measure. The inheritance of God’s people is never ownerless, because the LORD is there, and he will make himself known by defending it. The same God, in Christ, opens his inheritance even to the heirs of old enemies who come to him.

35.reflection:
Edom “cherished perpetual enmity” (v. 5), a grudge handed down for centuries. Where do you see grudges being kept alive today, in nations, churches, families or your own heart? What would it cost you to let one go?

Edom saw Israel’s ruined land as empty and up for grabs, “although the LORD was there” (v. 10). When has something in your life looked abandoned or lost? How does knowing that the LORD is there change how you see it?

God says of Edom’s words against his people, “you magnified yourselves against me… I heard it” (v. 13). How should this comfort Christians who are mocked, and how should it shape the way we speak about others?

Edom’s hatred reached all the way to Herod, yet James saw even Edom’s remnant gathered into Christ’s kingdom (Acts 15:16–17). How does the gospel make it possible for old enemies to become family?
