verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land that the nations mocked and seized still belongs to God, and he will not let its enemies have the last word. Ezekiel prophesies to the mountains of Israel (v. 1). Their enemies said “Aha!” and claimed the ancient heights; the land was crushed, plundered and made “the talk and evil gossip of the people” (vv. 2–4). In his hot jealousy God has spoken against the nations and Edom, who seized his land “with wholehearted joy and utter contempt” (vv. 5–6). Now he swears that the nations around will themselves suffer the reproach they heaped on Israel (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: God is jealous for his land and his people, and the mockers will be mocked.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, prophesy to the mountains of Israel, and say, O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the LORD. Thus says the Lord GOD: Because the enemy said of you, 'Aha!' and, 'The ancient heights have become our possession,' therefore prophesy, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: Precisely because they made you desolate and crushed you from all sides, so that you became the possession of the rest of the nations, and you became the talk and evil gossip of the people, therefore, O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD: Thus says the Lord GOD to the mountains and the hills, the ravines and the valleys, the desolate wastes and the deserted cities, which have become a prey and derision to the rest of the nations all around, therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Surely I have spoken in my hot jealousy against the rest of the nations and against all Edom, who gave my land to themselves as a possession with wholehearted joy and utter contempt, that they might make its pasturelands a prey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land the nations mocked and seized is God’s own land, and he speaks in hot jealousy against those who treated it with contempt.

O mountains of Israel. In chapter 6 Ezekiel prophesied against the mountains of Israel, where the idol shrines stood, and in chapter 35 against Mount Seir. Now he turns to Israel’s mountains again, and this time the message is hope.

The talk and evil gossip of the people. The land itself is pictured as a victim: crushed, seized and talked about with contempt. Yet God addresses every part of the landscape, down to the ravines and the deserted cities. Not one corner is forgotten.

My land. The nations thought they were taking empty territory; God calls it his (v. 5). He speaks “in my hot jealousy”, the jealousy of an owner and a husband who will not let what is his be treated “with wholehearted joy and utter contempt”.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore prophesy concerning the land of Israel, and say to the mountains and hills, to the ravines and valleys, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I have spoken in my jealous wrath, because you have suffered the reproach of the nations. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: I swear that the nations that are all around you shall themselves suffer reproach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God swears that the nations who mocked his people will bear the reproach themselves. He was the one who judged Israel, but he will not let their enemies have the last laugh.

I swear. Literally “I lift up my hand”, the gesture of an oath. God binds himself on behalf of his people: the mockers will be mocked.

For the ridiculed. For believers ridiculed for their faith, or who have watched the church become an object of contempt, this is steadying. God’s discipline of his people does not mean he has handed them to their enemies for ever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God turns to the ruined land with a promise of new life: “For behold, I am for you” (v. 9). The mountains of Israel will put out branches and fruit for his people, “for they will soon come home” (v. 8). The land will be tilled and sown, filled with people and animals, its cities rebuilt, and God “will do more good to you than ever before” (vv. 9–11). His people will walk on it again as their inheritance (v. 12). The land slandered as one that devours its people will no longer bereave them of children, nor bear the reproach of the nations (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who was against his sinful people declares himself for them, and does more good than before.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you, O mountains of Israel, shall shoot forth your branches and yield your fruit to my people Israel, for they will soon come home. For behold, I am for you, and I will turn to you, and you shall be tilled and sown. And I will multiply people on you, the whole house of Israel, all of it. The cities shall be inhabited and the waste places rebuilt. And I will multiply on you man and beast, and they shall multiply and be fruitful. And I will cause you to be inhabited as in your former times, and will do more good to you than ever before. Then you will know that I am the LORD. I will let people walk on you, even my people Israel. And they shall possess you, and you shall be their inheritance, and you shall no longer bereave them of children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who had been against his people, is now for them, and promises to bring them home to a land restored beyond its former glory.

But you, O mountains of Israel. After all the desolation, God speaks to the land as if it were a garden waiting for its people. The trees will put out branches and fruit for Israel, “for they will soon come home”. The land is told to get ready.

I am for you. Throughout the book God has said, “I am against you” (5:8; 13:8; 21:3; 26:3; 29:3). Now: “I am for you”. Paul draws the same conclusion for everyone in Christ: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

The whole house of Israel, all of it. Not only Judah, but the northern tribes lost long before. The divided people will be one again, as the next chapter shows: “they shall be no longer two nations, and no longer divided into two kingdoms” (37:22). God’s restoration reaches further than anyone dared hope.

Will do more good to you than ever before. God’s restoration does not merely put things back as they were; it is better than before. That is how God works: after the cross comes not just a return to life but resurrection life; after Eden was lost comes not merely Eden restored but the new creation.

You shall be their inheritance. The land is given back as a family inheritance, a gift passed from God to his children. The New Testament widens the horizon: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). The promise to Israel’s mountains is a foretaste of a whole renewed earth given to God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: Because they say to you, 'You devour people, and you bereave your nation of children,' therefore you shall no longer devour people and no longer bereave your nation of children, declares the Lord GOD. And I will not let you hear anymore the reproach of the nations, and you shall no longer bear the disgrace of the peoples and no longer cause your nation to stumble, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land slandered as a devourer of its people will be a place of life and honour again.

You devour people. The nations said the land of Israel was cursed. It was the slander the spies spread in the wilderness, calling Canaan “a land that devours its inhabitants” (Numbers 13:32), and famine, war and exile had made it seem true.

You shall no longer bear the disgrace. No more lost children, no more mockery, no more stumbling. When God restores, he removes not only the suffering but the shame that went with it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — For the Sake of My Holy Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will act to save his people because his own name is at stake, not because they deserve it. Israel defiled the land with blood and idols, so God justly scattered them (vv. 16–19). But wherever they went they profaned his holy name, for people said, “These are the people of the LORD, and yet they had to go out of his land” (v. 20). God had concern for his name (v. 21): “It is not for your sake, O house of Israel, that I am about to act, but for the sake of my holy name” (v. 22). Through the very people who dishonoured it, he will show the nations that his name is holy (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: God saves his people not because they deserve it but to vindicate the holiness of his own name.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, when the house of Israel lived in their own land, they defiled it by their ways and their deeds. Their ways before me were like the uncleanness of a woman in her menstrual impurity. So I poured out my wrath upon them for the blood that they had shed in the land, for the idols with which they had defiled it. I scattered them among the nations, and they were dispersed through the countries. In accordance with their ways and their deeds I judged them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel was scattered justly, because it defiled God’s land with violence and idols. Before God explains why he will restore them, he reminds them bluntly why they were scattered.

They defiled it by their ways. The comparison is with the uncleanness that, under the law, kept a person away from the sanctuary (Leviticus 15:19). That is how God saw their lives: unclean, making the land unfit for his presence. It is a comparison about ritual uncleanness, not a judgment on women or on the body God made.

In accordance with their ways and their deeds. Blood and idols, violence and false worship, are the two charges that run through the whole book. The exile was just, and God does not pretend they deserved restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they came to the nations, wherever they came, they profaned my holy name, in that people said of them, 'These are the people of the LORD, and yet they had to go out of his land.' But I had concern for my holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations to which they came.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s exile made the nations think little of Israel’s God, and God cares about his holy name.

They profaned my holy name. Scattering Israel brought a new dishonour on God. People looked at the refugees and said, “These are the people of the LORD, and yet they had to go out of his land”: what kind of God cannot keep his own people in his own land? Either he is weak, or he does not care.

Judged by his people. That is still how the world often judges God: by the condition of his people. When the church is weak, divided or disgraced, people conclude that its God is not real or not powerful. Paul quoted the same charge: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2:24).

I had concern for my holy name. God cares about his reputation, not out of vanity, but because his name is his true character, and the world’s salvation depends on knowing it truly.

Hallowed be your name. This is what Jesus taught us to pray first: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9). Before our needs, we ask God to do what Ezekiel 36 promises, to make his name known as holy in the world, knowing that our own lives have often done the opposite.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: It is not for your sake, O house of Israel, that I am about to act, but for the sake of my holy name, which you have profaned among the nations to which you came. And I will vindicate the holiness of my great name, which has been profaned among the nations, and which you have profaned among them. And the nations will know that I am the LORD, declares the Lord GOD, when through you I vindicate my holiness before their eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will save his people for the sake of his own name, and that is what makes the promise certain.

It is not for your sake. This is the foundation of everything that follows. At first it may sound cold; in fact it is the most secure ground of salvation there could be. If God saved Israel because Israel deserved it, the promise would be worthless, because Israel did not. If God saves for the sake of his own name, the promise is as certain as God himself. Moses had told Israel the same long before: “Not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart” (Deuteronomy 9:5). It humbles us and it steadies us: “Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 115:1); “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing” (Ephesians 2:8).

Not because you’re worth it. For decades a cosmetics firm has sold its hair colour with the slogan “Because you’re worth it”, and it caught the spirit of the age. We want to be loved for our worth, so “not for your sake” sounds like an insult. But love that rests on worth has to be kept up, like a membership, and underneath every relationship runs the anxious question whether you are still worth it today. If Israel’s rescue had depended on Israel’s value, Israel had no hope, and neither do we on our worst days. God grounds his love in something that cannot rise and fall: his own name, character and promise. Moses told Israel that God did not choose them for their size or strength, “but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers” (Deuteronomy 7:8). That is the only kind of love you cannot lose. At the cross it becomes plain: Christ did not die for people who had proved their worth. The love that was never earned by our worth is the very thing that gives us worth, and no bad day can take it back.

Through you I vindicate my holiness before their eyes. The very people who dishonoured God’s name will become the proof of his holiness, not by trying harder but by being transformed by God. Peter gives the same calling to Christians scattered among the nations: “Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God” (1 Peter 2:12). A people changed by God’s Spirit is the best answer to a world that doubts God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–32 — A New Heart and a New Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises to make his people new from the inside, by his own Spirit. He will gather them from the nations (v. 24), sprinkle clean water on them and cleanse them from all their idols (v. 25). “I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (v. 26): the heart of stone will be replaced by a heart of flesh. He will put his own Spirit within them and cause them to walk in his ways (v. 27). They will be his people in a fruitful land, never again shamed by famine (vv. 28–30). Then they will remember their ways and loathe themselves, knowing it was not for their sake (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology: God promises to cleanse his people, replace their hearts and put his own Spirit within them, so that they obey him from within.

verseByVerse.quote: I will take you from the nations and gather you from all the countries and bring you into your own land. I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses, and from all your idols I will cleanse you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will gather his scattered people and wash them clean himself, from every stain and every idol.

I will take you from the nations. First, a new exodus: as God once brought Israel out of Egypt, he will gather them from every nation and bring them home. And the gathering does not stop at Israel’s borders. Jesus would die “not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52).

I will sprinkle clean water on you. Second, cleansing. The people were unclean (v. 17), and God does not tell them to wash themselves. Sprinkling is the language of the priests’ purification rites, where water was sprinkled to make the unclean clean (Numbers 19:17–19). “From all your uncleannesses… from all your idols”: nothing is left out.

Washed in Christ. The New Testament speaks of this cleansing in Christ: “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). We draw near to God “with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22). If you feel stained by your past, this is God’s promise: he does not ask you to scrub yourself clean before you come. He does the cleansing.

From all your idols I will cleanse you. God’s cleansing reaches the idols of the heart (14:3), not only the stains of conduct. The Thessalonians were a picture of it: they “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

Where Christians differ: is this gathering the modern return of Jews to the land? Dispensationalists think so, and faithful Christians differ here. This commentary’s view: in this chapter the gathering is bound to cleansing, a new heart and God’s own Spirit (vv. 25–27), so its fulfilment is read first in the return from Babylon, then in Christ, who gathers his people from every nation (John 11:52), with a great turning of Jewish people to him still looked for (Romans 11:26), and finally in the new creation.

Where Christians differ: is the clean water baptism? Christians who see baptism as a means by which God gives new birth read Jesus’ words “born of water and the Spirit” (John 3:5) as baptism, and they are brothers to be heard with respect. This commentary’s view: this verse speaks of the cleansing God himself gives, with the new heart and Spirit (vv. 26–27), and Jesus’ words most likely echo it: one spiritual birth, the cleansing and renewing work of the Spirit. Baptism is the sign of that cleansing, not the means of it; the water that saves is what God sprinkles on the heart, and no outward rite can guarantee it.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to do what no law or leader could: take out his people’s hard hearts and give them living ones. Here is the centre of the chapter, and of the Old Testament’s hope.

I will give you a new heart. Israel’s problem was never merely that it lacked good laws or good leaders. It was their hearts. A heart of stone is cold, hard, unresponsive to God however many prophets he sends, and no reform can fix it. You cannot soften a stone by lecturing it.

I will remove the heart of stone. So God promises something only he can do: not repair, but replacement. A heart of flesh is living and responsive, able to love, grieve, repent and rejoice: a whole new inner life.

What he requires, he provides. Earlier God commanded, “make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit!” (18:31). Now he promises to give it. That is the gospel in the Old Testament. Moses had foreseen it: “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart… so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6). David prayed for it: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10). Jesus called it being born again. God is the surgeon who cannot fail, and he operates on people who could not even ask rightly to be healed.

What the Bible means by the heart. We think of the heart as feelings. In Scripture it is the centre of the whole person, where we think, choose, trust and love: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Timothy Keller often pointed out that this is why the Bible goes beneath behaviour: whatever your heart most trusts and loves will quietly steer your thinking, your feelings and your choices. So a heart of stone is not a bad mood. It is a whole life set hard on something other than God, which is why trying harder cannot fix it. God does not hand us a stricter rule; he gives us new loves. And what melts stone is being loved: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8), and by the Spirit that love “has been poured into our hearts” (Romans 5:5). In practice, when the same sin keeps coming back, do not ask only “What did I do?” Ask “What was my heart trusting just then?”, and bring that to the One who promised to change it. See also New Birth in the Theological Dictionary.

Textual note. One early Greek manuscript (a papyrus) lacks the second half of verse 23 through verse 38. Scholars debate why, whether a lost page, a copying slip or a shorter early edition, but the passage stands in every Hebrew manuscript, including an older scroll of these chapters found at Masada, and in the rest of the Greek tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes and be careful to obey my rules.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will put his own Spirit within his people, so that obeying him becomes the desire of their new hearts.

I will put my Spirit within you. Not only a new spirit, but “my Spirit”: God himself living inside his people. Ezekiel had watched the glory of the LORD leave the temple (10:18; 11:23). Now God promises a dwelling he will never leave: the hearts of his own people.

Cause you to walk in my statutes. The old covenant gave the law on stone and left the people to obey it with hearts of stone. The new covenant writes the law on hearts of flesh (Jeremiah 31:33) and puts God’s Spirit inside to move them to obey. Obedience is no longer a weight pressing from outside but a desire rising from within: “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16; “the flesh” is our old sinful nature). (The ESV notes that “my rules” could be translated “my just decrees”.)

Jesus and Nicodemus. When Nicodemus, a leading teacher of Israel, came to Jesus by night, Jesus told him, “unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God”, and then rebuked him: “Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?” (John 3:5, 10). Water and Spirit, a new birth from God: a teacher of Israel should have recognised the promise of Ezekiel 36.

The Spirit in every believer. Every true Christian has received this: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). The evidence is a changed life: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). If you long to obey God and find yourself unable, the answer is not merely to try harder but to depend on the Spirit he has put within you: “it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). And where we still fall short, as we all do, Christ’s perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), and the way back is confession.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers, and you shall be my people, and I will be your God. And I will deliver you from all your uncleannesses. And I will summon the grain and make it abundant and lay no famine upon you. I will make the fruit of the tree and the increase of the field abundant, that you may never again suffer the disgrace of famine among the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant promise comes true at last: God’s renewed people will be his, in a land he blesses.

You shall be my people. The words at the heart of the covenant come again, and now they are secure. What was always God’s goal becomes real in their lives through a new heart and the Spirit living in them.

I will deliver you from all your uncleannesses. The promise comes again after the promise of a new heart. Cleansing is not a single moment only; God keeps cleansing the people he has made new. “If we walk in the light… the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

I will summon the grain. God speaks to the harvest as a master calls a servant. Inner renewal is followed by outward blessing, and the land shares in the renewal of its people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will remember your evil ways, and your deeds that were not good, and you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and your abominations. It is not for your sake that I will act, declares the Lord GOD; let that be known to you. Be ashamed and confounded for your ways, O house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace that renews God’s people makes them hate their sin, and leaves them no room to boast.

Then you will remember your evil ways. Mark when this deep repentance happens: “Then”, after God has cleansed them, given them a new heart and blessed them. Grace does not make people careless about sin; it makes them hate it. The more clearly a person sees God’s kindness, the more clearly he sees how ugly his rebellion was.

Grief without despair. That is a mark of genuine conversion. The forgiven do not shrug at their past. They grieve over it, not with despair, but with a humbled, grateful heart.

It is not for your sake. For the second time (v. 22). God will not let his people take any credit for their salvation: “let that be known to you”. The only boasting left is boasting in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–38 — Like the Garden of Eden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A cleansed people will see a ruined land become like Eden, and God will invite them to pray for what he has promised. On the day God cleanses them, the cities will be inhabited and the waste land tilled (vv. 33–34), until passers-by say, “This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden” (v. 35). The nations will know that the LORD has rebuilt and replanted: “I have spoken, and I will do it” (v. 36). And God will let Israel ask him to multiply them, filling the empty cities with people like the flocks crowding Jerusalem at the feasts (vv. 37–38).
verseByVerse.theology: God's cleansing leads to a restored creation, and his promises invite his people's prayers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day that I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will cause the cities to be inhabited, and the waste places shall be rebuilt. And the land that was desolate shall be tilled, instead of being the desolation that it was in the sight of all who passed by. And they will say, 'This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden, and the waste and desolate and ruined cities are now fortified and inhabited.' Then the nations that are left all around you shall know that I am the LORD; I have rebuilt the ruined places and replanted that which was desolate. I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God cleanses his people, he rebuilds their ruins into a garden, and what he has promised he will do.

On the day that I cleanse you. The rebuilding of the land flows from the cleansing of the people. Renewal always begins with forgiveness.

Like the garden of Eden. The passers-by who once mocked the ruins will marvel. Isaiah promised the same: the LORD “makes her wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden of the LORD” (Isaiah 51:3). The Bible’s story moves from Eden lost to Eden restored and surpassed: “the river of the water of life”, “the tree of life”, and leaves that “were for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:1–2).

I have spoken, and I will do it. God put these same words under his threats of judgment (22:14); now he puts them under his promises. What God said about ruin came true. What he says about renewal will come true.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: This also I will let the house of Israel ask me to do for them: to increase their people like a flock. Like the flock for sacrifices, like the flock at Jerusalem during her appointed feasts, so shall the waste cities be filled with flocks of people. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who once refused to be inquired of, now invites his people to ask him for the blessing he has promised.

This also I will let the house of Israel ask me. In chapters 14 and 20 God refused to be inquired of by the elders. Now the door of prayer, closed by their sin, is opened again by his grace.

Promises and prayer. God has just promised to do this, yet he invites them to ask for it. His promises do not make prayer unnecessary; they make it confident. “How much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:11). “You do not have, because you do not ask” (James 4:2).

Like the flock for sacrifices. Picture Jerusalem at Passover, the streets crowded with flocks brought for sacrifice (the ESV notes, literally “flock of holy things”). That is how full the empty cities will become: full of people, and full of people set apart to God.

The church gathered. A holy people, cleansed, given new hearts, filled with God’s Spirit, crowding into God’s presence: that is the church of Jesus Christ gathered from every nation, and it is the future of God’s people in the new creation.

36.title: A New Heart and a New Spirit
36.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 35 doomed the mountains of Edom, which had gloated over Israel’s ruin and claimed its land. Chapter 36 turns to “the mountains of Israel”, mocked, plundered and empty, and becomes one of the great chapters of the Old Testament.

The message. God will save his people not because they deserve it but for the sake of his own holy name, and he will do it from the inside. He will wash them clean, take away their heart of stone, give them a heart of flesh and put his own Spirit within them, so that at last they walk in his ways. The salvation is certain because it rests on who God is, and it is complete because God does what his people could never do for themselves.

Why it was said. The exiles had lost their land, their temple and their good name; the nations said of them, “These are the people of the LORD, and yet they had to go out of his land” (v. 20). Ezekiel had told them to make themselves a new heart (18:31), and their history showed they could not (see the introduction). They needed to hear whether God had any future for people like them.

How the chapter makes its case. God speaks to the mountains of Israel: the nations who seized and mocked them will bear reproach (vv. 1–7), and the land will bloom again, “for behold, I am for you”, filled with people and freed from its shame (vv. 8–15). Then he goes to the root. Israel defiled the land with blood and idols and was justly scattered, and even in exile profaned his name; so he will act “for the sake of my holy name” (vv. 16–23). He will gather them, sprinkle clean water on them, give them a new heart and his Spirit, and be their God (vv. 24–30). Then they will loathe their old ways, knowing it was not for their sake (vv. 31–32). The cleansed people will rebuild a land like Eden, and God will invite them to ask him to multiply them like the flocks at the feasts (vv. 33–38).

Where it leads. To Christ by direct promise. This is the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 told from the inside, and Jesus said it was made “in my blood” (Luke 22:20). He told Nicodemus that no one enters God’s kingdom unless he is “born of water and the Spirit”, and rebuked the teacher of Israel for not knowing it (John 3:5, 10). Christ came to glorify his Father’s name (John 12:28), died to gather God’s scattered children from every nation (John 11:52), and poured out the promised Spirit at Pentecost. Every heart of stone that becomes flesh is this chapter coming true in him.

For us. No one is too hard for God to change, and no one can change himself; so stop scrubbing and come to the one who washes. If you belong to Christ, your salvation rests not on your worth but on his name, which means it cannot be lost on a bad day. And the Spirit he has put within you is the power to walk in his ways, so ask boldly for what he has promised.
36.theology:
God is jealous for his people and his land, and does not let their enemies have the last word (vv. 5-7).

The God who was against his sinful people declares that he is for them, and his restoration exceeds what was lost (vv. 9, 11; Rom 8:31).

God's people profane his name when they fall, and he acts to vindicate his holiness (vv. 20-23; Rom 2:24).

Salvation rests not on what God’s people deserve but on the glory of God’s name, which makes it certain (vv. 22, 32; Deut 9:4-6; Ps 115:1; Eph 2:8-9).

God cleanses his people, replaces their heart of stone with a heart of flesh, and puts his own Spirit within them to move them to obey: the new birth fulfilled in Christ (vv. 25-27; Deut 30:6; Jer 31:33; John 3:3-10; 1 Cor 6:11; Titus 3:5; Heb 10:22).

The Spirit living in God’s people produces obedience from within (v. 27; Rom 8:9; Gal 5:16, 22-23; Phil 2:13).

Grace does not make sin easier to excuse; it deepens repentance (v. 31).

Cleansing leads to a restored creation like Eden (vv. 33-36; Isa 51:3; Rev 22:1-2).

God's promises invite confident prayer (v. 37; Matt 7:11; Jas 4:2).
36.examples:
A heart transplant is the nearest picture we have: the surgeon does not repair the failing heart but replaces it, and the patient contributes nothing but need. So God takes away the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh.

A Christian who has been mocked at work for her faith, or who watches her church become a joke in the local paper, can hear verse 7 as a promise: the mockery will not have the last word.

Someone who doubts that God could want him, because of what he has done, should notice where God rests his salvation: not for your sake, but for his own name. That is why it is certain.

keyVerse.quote: And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.
keyVerse.note: This is the centre of the chapter and one of the great promises of the Old Testament. Israel’s deepest problem was not its circumstances but its hard heart, and God promises to do what no law, leader or exile could do: replace it. Jesus called this being born again, and every believer is living proof that God keeps his word.

36.reflection:
The nations judged Israel’s God by the state of his people (v. 20). In what ways does the world judge God by the church today? How does it help to know that God acts “for the sake of my holy name” (v. 22) and not because we deserve it?

God promises to sprinkle clean water on his people and cleanse them from all their idols (v. 25). What idols of the heart are hardest to give up in our culture, and what does it mean that God himself does the cleansing?

Read vv. 26–27 slowly. How have you seen God turn a heart of stone into a heart of flesh, in yourself or someone else? Where do you still need to depend on his Spirit rather than simply try harder?

God has promised to bless, and yet he says, “This also I will let the house of Israel ask me to do for them” (v. 37). How should God’s promises shape the way we pray, for ourselves and for our church?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God can raise the hopelessly dead, and he does it through his word and his Spirit. The Spirit sets Ezekiel in a valley of bones, very many and very dry: death at its most final (vv. 1–2). Asked, “Son of man, can these bones live?”, he puts the impossible back into God’s hands: “O Lord GOD, you know” (v. 3). Told to preach to the bones, he obeys, and they rattle together and are clothed with sinews, flesh and skin, yet still have no breath (vv. 4–8). Only when he prophesies to the breath do they live and stand up, “an exceedingly great army” (vv. 9–10). Word and Spirit together make a second creation.
verseByVerse.theology: God gives life to the dead through his word and his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: The hand of the LORD was upon me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of the LORD and set me down in the middle of the valley; it was full of bones. And he led me around among them, and behold, there were very many on the surface of the valley, and behold, they were very dry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes Ezekiel look long and hard at death in its most final form, so that what happens next can only be his work.

It was full of bones. Ezekiel is set down “in the Spirit of the LORD” in a valley (or “plain”, as the ESV notes) full of bones: an old battlefield where no one ever buried the dead (v. 9 calls them “these slain”).

He led me around among them. God does not let him glance and look away. Two things strike him: “very many”, and “very dry”. This is not a sick patient who might recover; it is death at its most final, and whatever happens next cannot be explained as natural recovery.
verseByVerse.note: The vision of the valley of dry bones: Israel in exile, as good as dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, can these bones live?" And I answered, "O Lord GOD, you know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith does not pretend the dead can raise themselves; it hands the impossible to the God who can. Ezekiel’s “O Lord GOD, you know” is neither a confident yes nor a hopeless no.

Can these bones live? Every human answer is no. Ezekiel does not say yes, because he cannot see how; he does not say no, because he knows who is asking.

Optimism looks at the bones. Our culture runs on optimism, the belief that with enough effort and good will things will turn out well. It has nothing to say in a valley like this, because it must find some potential in the bones, and these have none. The Marxist literary critic Terry Eagleton argued in Hope Without Optimism that the two are not the same, and that real hope can look the worst squarely in the face. Ezekiel does not pretend the bones are only resting; he looks at them, and then looks up at the one who asked. Optimism is confidence in the material; hope is confidence in the Maker. That is why Christian hope is strongest exactly where optimism dies, at a graveside: its whole foundation is a tomb that held no potential at all, and a Father who called his Son out of it.

Our own valleys. A marriage that seems dead, a child who has walked away from God, a church where nothing spiritual seems to happen, a nation far from God, a heart gone completely dry. The honest answer to “Can this live?” is often: not by any power I have. The faithful answer is Ezekiel’s, the faith of Abraham, who believed in the God “who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17). Whatever valley you stand in, the question is not what the bones can do, but who is asking.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to me, "Prophesy over these bones, and say to them, O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD. Thus says the Lord GOD to these bones: Behold, I will cause breath to enter you, and you shall live. And I will lay sinews upon you, and will cause flesh to come upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you shall live, and you shall know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Ezekiel to preach to skeletons, because his word carries the power to do what it says. Every verb of life belongs to God: the prophet speaks, and God acts.

O dry bones, hear the word of the LORD. Dead bones cannot hear. But that is the situation of every preacher of the gospel, since we were all “dead in the trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1). Preaching to the spiritually dead makes sense only if God’s word carries God’s power, and it does: “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17), and we have been born again “through the living and abiding word of God” (1 Peter 1:23).

I will lay sinews upon you. In every line God is the one who acts: “I will cause breath to enter you… I will lay sinews upon you, and will cause flesh to come upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you.” And “breath” may also be rendered “spirit” (ESV note), here and all through the passage: hold on to that, for it is the key to the vision (v. 14).

The voice that wakes the dead. Jesus claimed this power for his own voice: “the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25). Wherever the gospel is preached, it is still his voice that the dead hear.

verseByVerse.quote: So I prophesied as I was commanded. And as I prophesied, there was a sound, and behold, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to its bone. And I looked, and behold, there were sinews on them, and flesh had come upon them, and skin had covered them. But there was no breath in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word works at once and visibly, yet bodies without breath are still dead: outward order is not yet life.

So I prophesied as I was commanded. While Ezekiel is still speaking there is a sound, a rattling (or “an earthquake”, as the ESV notes), across the valley as thousands of bones scrape and slide toward each other, “bone to its bone”, each to its right place. God’s word does not merely inform; it does things.

There was no breath in them. Yet when sinews, flesh and skin have come, the valley holds only well-formed corpses. As in Eden, the body is shaped first and the breath comes after (Genesis 2:7).

Structure without life. A person, or a church, can have all the right structure, doctrine, organisation, activity and respectability, and no breath. Order is not life; only God’s Spirit gives that (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to me, "Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and say to the breath, Thus says the Lord GOD: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live." So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only the breath of God, his Spirit, turns bodies into living people: this is a second creation.

Prophesy to the breath. Now Ezekiel prophesies not to the bones but to the breath (again perhaps “spirit”), calling it “from the four winds” (see the note). The picture goes back to creation, when God “formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature” (Genesis 2:7).

They lived and stood on their feet. The valley of death becomes “an exceedingly great army”. What no surgeon or prophet could do, the breath of God does in a moment.

He breathed on them. On the evening of his resurrection Jesus stood among his frightened disciples, “breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20:22). The breath that raised the bones is the Spirit whom the risen Christ gives.

The preacher and the Spirit. Word and Spirit belong together: words without the Spirit leave corpses, and the Spirit ordinarily works through the word. At Pentecost Peter preached, the Spirit moved, and “there were added that day about three thousand souls” (Acts 2:41). A valley of bones stood up.
verseByVerse.note: “Breath,” “wind” and “Spirit” are the same Hebrew word (ruach) throughout this chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — I Will Open Your Graves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers his people’s despair with a promise of resurrection by his Spirit. The bones are “the whole house of Israel”, exiles who say, “Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are indeed cut off” (v. 11). God does not rebuke them. He promises to open their graves, raise them as “my people” and bring them home (vv. 12–13), and he names the breath of the vision: “I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live” (v. 14). The first fulfilment was the return from exile; the fuller one is new birth in Christ and the resurrection of the body at the last day.
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to hopelessness is resurrection by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to me, "Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, 'Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost; we are indeed cut off.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bones are God’s people in exile, who have given up hope, and God answers their despair instead of rebuking it.

Our hope is lost. With temple, king and land gone, the exiles felt as dead as bleached bones, “cut off” from God and from any future. They speak like the darkest of the psalms: “like the slain that lie in the grave… cut off from your hand” (Psalm 88:5).

When we feel the same. Many feel exactly this after a devastating loss, a moral collapse, or years of prayer that seem unanswered. God does not rebuke the exiles for saying it; he answers it. If hopelessness has turned into thoughts of ending your life, tell someone you trust and get help today.

Is the vision of the dry bones the founding of the State of Israel in 1948? Some dispensationalists read it so. But the vision describes a people brought to life by God’s Spirit (v. 14) and restored with a new heart under David their king (v. 24), not a secular state formed by war and diplomacy. Its first fulfilment was the return from exile; its fullness is the Spirit giving life in Christ, and the resurrection at the last day. Christians may rightly marvel at Jewish survival, and many who disagree on the details share the hope that Jewish people in great numbers will one day turn to their Messiah (Romans 11:26). But the bones live only when God’s Spirit enters them.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore prophesy, and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will open your graves and raise you from your graves, O my people. And I will bring you into the land of Israel. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves, and raise you from your graves, O my people. And I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land. Then you shall know that I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to open his people’s graves, bring them home and put his own Spirit within them, so that they live and know him.

I will open your graves. The picture shifts to graves, and the promise becomes plain: God will bring the “dead” nation back to life and back to its land. Twice comes the tender phrase “O my people”. They thought they were cut off; God calls them his.

I will put my Spirit within you. The breath of the vision is “my Spirit”: the promise of 36:27 again. National restoration and spiritual rebirth are both the Spirit’s work, and both are sure: “I have spoken, and I will do it.”

Its fuller meaning. The first meaning is Israel’s return from exile, but Scripture shows more. It pictures the new birth: “you, who were dead in your trespasses… God made alive together with him” (Colossians 2:13). And it points to the resurrection of the body. Isaiah had said, “Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise” (Isaiah 26:19); Jesus said, “an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29); and Paul wrote, “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit” (Romans 8:11).

The resurrection and the life. At the heart of it all is the one who said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live” (John 11:25). He went down into a grave himself, and on the third day God opened it; so every believer’s grave will be opened too. No valley is too dry for him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will heal the oldest wound among his people and make them one, holy and his own. Ezekiel writes “For Judah” on one stick and “For Joseph” on another, and holds them together as one in his hand (vv. 15–17). When the people ask what he means (v. 18), God explains: he will join the northern and southern kingdoms, divided for more than three centuries, into one in his own hand (vv. 19–20), gather them from the nations and make them one nation under one king (vv. 21–22). It will be a cleansed unity, free of the idols that divided them: “they shall be my people, and I will be their God” (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: God heals the divisions of his people and makes them one under one King.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, take a stick and write on it, 'For Judah, and the people of Israel associated with him'; then take another stick and write on it, 'For Joseph (the stick of Ephraim) and all the house of Israel associated with him.' And join them one to another into one stick, that they may become one in your hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a simple sign, Ezekiel joins two sticks named for the two divided kingdoms into one in his hand.

Take a stick and write on it. On one stick (or piece of wood, as the ESV notes) Ezekiel writes “For Judah”, the southern kingdom; on the other “For Joseph (the stick of Ephraim)”, the northern kingdom, named after its leading tribe (see the note). Then he holds them end to end so that they look like one, “that they may become one in your hand”.

A people split in two. For more than three centuries God’s people had been divided. It began when the northern tribes rejected David’s grandson Rehoboam: “What portion do we have in David?… To your tents, O Israel!” (1 Kings 12:16). Two kingdoms, two kings, the rival shrines of Jeroboam, and often war between brothers. The north had been scattered by Assyria over a century before Ezekiel, and now Judah was in exile too.

Are the two sticks the Bible and the Book of Mormon, as Latter-day Saints teach? No. Ezekiel explains them himself: they are the two kingdoms, Judah and Israel, made one people under one king (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.note: The northern kingdom is called Joseph or Ephraim because Ephraim, Joseph's son, was its leading tribe and the tribe of its first king, Jeroboam (1 Kgs 11:26).

verseByVerse.quote: And when your people say to you, 'Will you not tell us what you mean by these?' say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am about to take the stick of Joseph (that is in the hand of Ephraim) and the tribes of Israel associated with him. And I will join with it the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, that they may be one in my hand. When the sticks on which you write are in your hand before their eyes, then say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will take the people of Israel from the nations among which they have gone, and will gather them from all around, and bring them to their own land. And I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel. And one king shall be king over them all, and they shall be no longer two nations, and no longer divided into two kingdoms. They shall not defile themselves anymore with their idols and their detestable things, or with any of their transgressions. But I will save them from all the backslidings in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only God can make his divided people one, and he will do it by gathering them, giving them one King and cleansing them from the idols that split them.

One in my hand. When the people ask what the sign means, God explains that Ezekiel’s hand pictures his own: “that they may be one in my hand” (v. 19). The resurrection of the bones leads to the reunion of the tribes: one nation, one king, “no longer two nations” (v. 22).

I will save them from all the backslidings. And the unity is holy. The idols that divided them, beginning with Jeroboam’s golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–29), will be gone; God will rescue them from their backslidings and cleanse them, and the covenant promise will come true at last: “they shall be my people, and I will be their God” (v. 23). True unity is not agreeing to overlook sin together; it is being cleansed together and belonging to God together.

One new man in place of the two. Jesus prayed for this unity in his church, “that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you” (John 17:21). And at the cross he did something greater than joining Judah and Ephraim: he joined Jew and Gentile, “that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace” (Ephesians 2:15). “You are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

For divided churches. Churches divided by pride, personalities and old grudges should hear this sign. The unity God gives is real, and it comes from being held together in his one hand; our part is to be “eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of v. 19 is compressed: “I will join with it the stick of Judah” is literally “and I will place them on it, the stick of Judah” (ESV note). The sense is not in doubt: God takes the northern stick, lays the southern one with it and makes them one.

Textual note. In v. 23 the ESV notes that other manuscripts read “dwellings” instead of “backslidings”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–28 — My Dwelling Place with Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The goal of everything God does is to live among his people for ever under his King. The one king is “my servant David”, the one shepherd of a people who now walk in God’s ways (v. 24), living in the land for ever with David as their prince for ever (v. 25). God will make a covenant of peace, an everlasting covenant, and set his sanctuary among them “forevermore” (v. 26). Then comes the heart of every covenant promise: “My dwelling place shall be with them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (v. 27). And the nations will see that it is the LORD who makes his people holy (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The goal of all God's work is his everlasting presence with a people united under his King.

verseByVerse.quote: "My servant David shall be king over them, and they shall all have one shepherd. They shall walk in my rules and be careful to obey my statutes. They shall dwell in the land that I gave to my servant Jacob, where your fathers lived. They and their children and their children's children shall dwell there forever, and David my servant shall be their prince forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one King who will unite God’s people is “my servant David”, a shepherd-king who reigns for ever, and that can only be Christ.

My servant David shall be king over them. The one king of v. 22 is David’s promised son, whom we met in 34:23–24: one shepherd for one flock. David had been dead some four hundred years, so this is the greater David whom God swore to raise from his line (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Jesus said, “So there will be one flock, one shepherd” (John 10:16).

They shall walk in my rules. Under this King God’s people “shall walk in my rules and be careful to obey my statutes”. Unity and obedience both come from having one King, and from the new heart of 36:26–27.

Their prince forever. “Forever” rings out again and again (vv. 25, 26, 28): the land, the generations, David’s reign. No mortal king could be “prince forever”, only the one of whom the angel said, “he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

How can they dwell in the land “forever”? The promise reaches beyond Canaan to the inheritance Christ gives, the renewed earth (Matthew 5:5; Romans 4:13), where God’s people will dwell with him for ever (Revelation 21:3).

verseByVerse.quote: I will make a covenant of peace with them. It shall be an everlasting covenant with them. And I will set them in their land and multiply them, and will set my sanctuary in their midst forevermore. My dwelling place shall be with them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Then the nations will know that I am the LORD who sanctifies Israel, when my sanctuary is in their midst forevermore."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will bind himself to his people in an everlasting covenant of peace and live among them for ever, and his presence will make them holy. This is the goal of the whole book, and of the whole Bible.

A covenant of peace. The covenant of peace of 34:25 and the everlasting covenant of 16:60 are one. It will never be broken, because it rests on God, not on Israel’s faithfulness: it is the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31–34, which Jesus sealed with his blood (Luke 22:20).

My sanctuary in their midst forevermore. Ezekiel watched the glory leave the sanctuary (chapters 10–11); the book now moves toward its return (43:1–5). The point of restoration is not land or prosperity, but God among his people again.

My dwelling place shall be with them. Paul applies this promise to the church: “we are the temple of the living God; as God said, ‘I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people’” (2 Corinthians 6:16). And John heard it announced from the throne at the end of all things: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

God’s dwelling came in a person. Between Ezekiel and Revelation stands Jesus: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), literally “pitched his tent” among us. God’s dwelling with his people came in a person before it came in a city.

From bones to sanctuary. God’s presence makes his people holy, and the nations will see it (v. 28). The valley of dry bones ends in a sanctuary: death gives way to life, division to unity, exile to home, and God’s absence to his presence. That is the story of the gospel, and the destination of every believer.

Uncertain wording. In v. 26 “I will set them in their land” is literally “I will give them”: the Hebrew lacks “in their land” (ESV note), which the ESV supplies; it may mean “I will establish them”. Either way, God will settle and multiply his people.

37.title: Can These Bones Live?
37.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 36 promised a new heart and God’s own Spirit within his people (36:26–27); chapter 37 shows what that promise means, first in a vision and then in a sign. Jerusalem has fallen (33:21), and the exiles feel as dead as their nation.

The message. God gives life to what is beyond all hope, and he does it by his word and his Spirit. A people who say “our hope is lost” will be raised from their graves, made one nation under one King, cleansed, and given God’s own presence among them for ever. No death is too final, and no division too old, for the God who says, “I have spoken, and I will do it” (v. 14).

Why it was said. After the city fell the exiles stopped hoping: temple, king and land were gone, and they said, “we are indeed cut off” (v. 11; see the introduction). Their despair was the honest end of their false hopes, and God met it not with a rebuke but with a resurrection.

How the chapter makes its case. In the vision (vv. 1–10) Ezekiel is led among bones very many and very dry, asked whether they can live, and told to preach to them; at the word they come together and are clothed with flesh, but only when he prophesies to the breath do they stand up, a great army. God explains it (vv. 11–14): the bones are Israel, their graves will be opened, and the breath is his own Spirit. Then a sign (vv. 15–23): two sticks, Judah and Joseph, joined as one in the prophet’s hand, for God will reunite the kingdoms divided since Solomon’s death and cleanse them from their idols. Last (vv. 24–28), the reunited people will have one shepherd, “my servant David”, an everlasting covenant of peace, and God’s sanctuary in their midst for evermore.

Where it leads. Christ fulfils the chapter by promise. The return from exile was its first answer, but the larger things it promised, the Spirit breathed into the dead, one flock under one shepherd, a David who reigns for ever, God dwelling among his people, all arrive in Jesus. He breathed on his disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22); he is the good shepherd who makes “one flock” (John 10:16); he is the Word who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14); and he is “the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25), whose opened grave guarantees the opening of every believer’s.

For us. Whatever valley you stand in, a hardened heart, a wayward child, a cold church, a graveside, the question is not what the bones can do but who is asking. Keep speaking his word, pray for his Spirit, and expect from the God who raised Jesus what no optimism could promise.
37.theology:
God can give life where every human hope is gone; faith answers the impossible with O Lord GOD, you know (vv. 1-3; Rom 4:17).

God gives life through his word and his Spirit together; outward form without the Spirit is still death (vv. 4-10; Gen 2:7; Rom 10:17; 1 Pet 1:23; John 20:22; Acts 2:41).

God answers his people's despair with the promise of resurrection by his Spirit (vv. 11-14).

The vision's promise reaches to the new birth and to the bodily resurrection, secured by Christ, the resurrection and the life (Col 2:13; John 5:28-29; 11:25; Rom 8:11; Isa 26:19).

God heals the divisions of his people and makes them one under one King, in holiness (vv. 15-23; John 17:21; Eph 2:15-16; Gal 3:28).

The promised David is Christ, the one shepherd who reigns forever (vv. 24-25; 34:23-24; John 10:16; Luke 1:32-33).

The goal of redemption is God's everlasting dwelling with his people, fulfilled in Christ, the church and the new creation (vv. 26-28; John 1:14; 2 Cor 6:16; Rev 21:3).
37.examples:
A mother who has prayed for twenty years for a son who wants nothing to do with God can stand where Ezekiel stood. She cannot say yes; she will not say no. She can say, O Lord GOD, you know, and keep speaking the word.

A church can have a full calendar, sound statements and a well-kept building, and still be bodies with no breath. The remedy is not more organisation but prayer for the Spirit and faithful preaching of the word.

At a Christian funeral, verse 12 is the last word: I will open your graves. Death is still an enemy, and grief is right, but the grave is not the end for those who belong to Christ.

keyVerse.quote: And I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land. Then you shall know that I am the LORD; I have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD.
keyVerse.note: Here the vision explains itself: the breath that raised the bones is God’s own Spirit, and the life he gives is certain because he has spoken it. The verse joins the new heart of 36:26–27 to the opening of graves, and Christ fulfils both, giving his Spirit to the spiritually dead now and raising the bodies of his people at the last day.

37.reflection:
When God asked, “Can these bones live?”, Ezekiel answered, “O Lord GOD, you know” (v. 3). What valley in your life or church tempts you to answer no? What would it look like to answer as Ezekiel did, and keep speaking God’s word?

The bones came together and were covered with flesh, but “there was no breath in them” (v. 8). How can a person or a church look alive and still lack the Spirit? Why does God give life through his word and his Spirit together (vv. 4–10)?

The exiles said, “our hope is lost” (v. 11), and God answered with a promise, not a rebuke. How should this shape the way we bring our despair to God, and the way we speak to others who feel the same?

The chapter ends with one people under one King and God’s dwelling place among them (vv. 22–28). How does Jesus fulfil this, and which divisions among the believers you know most need the unity he gives?
