Then they will know that I am the LORD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the greatest enemy of God’s people is on God’s leash. Ezekiel is to set his face against “Gog, of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal” (v. 2), a mysterious ruler from the far north. God will turn him about, put hooks into his jaws and lead him out with a vast, well-armed host drawn from every direction: Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer and Beth-togarmah (vv. 3–6). Let him prepare as he likes (v. 7). “In the latter years” he will sweep like a storm against a land restored from war, whose people now live securely (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the most fearsome enemy of God's people moves only by God's hook in its jaw.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward Gog, of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and prophesy against him and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. And I will turn you about and put hooks into your jaws, and I will bring you out, and all your army, horses and horsemen, all of them clothed in full armor, a great host, all of them with buckler and shield, wielding swords. Persia, Cush, and Put are with them, all of them with shield and helmet; Gomer and all his hordes; Beth-togarmah from the uttermost parts of the north with all his hordes— many peoples are with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God declares himself against Gog, the last great enemy, and leads him and his world-wide army out like a beast with hooks in its jaws.

Set your face toward Gog. After the promises of chapters 34–37, a new Shepherd, a new heart, dry bones living, God dwelling with his people, comes a final enemy, “Gog, of the land of Magog”, to answer the exiles’ fear that once home they would be crushed by the next empire. The first words settle it: “Behold, I am against you, O Gog.”

Who is Gog? No historical king of this name is known with certainty. Magog, Meshech, Tubal and Gomer appear in Genesis as descendants of Japheth (Genesis 10:2), peoples on the far northern edges of Israel’s known world; Meshech and Tubal lay in what is now Turkey (see the note). The name Gog may echo Gyges, a king of Lydia in the 600s BC, but no one knows. Gog is better understood as a symbol than as a ruler we can name: the enemy behind every enemy, gathered for the last time.

Put hooks into your jaws. The same picture was used of Pharaoh (29:4). Gog thinks the attack is his own idea; in fact God is leading him out like an animal on a hook.

Many peoples are with you. The coalition comes from every direction: Persia in the east, Cush (the upper Nile) and Put (probably Libya) in the south, Gomer and Beth-togarmah in the far north. It is the whole world gathering against God’s people.

Where Christians differ: who is Gog, and when does he come? Some read these chapters as a literal future invasion of a restored nation of Israel: dispensationalists place it before or around a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth, and historic premillennialists, following Revelation 20, after the thousand years. Others read them as a picture of the final assault of evil on God’s people at the end of history, since Revelation takes up the names “Gog and Magog” for the nations gathered against “the camp of the saints and the beloved city” just before the end (Revelation 20:8–9). This commentary’s view: the second reading, within the amillennial view that the thousand years of Revelation 20 are the present age of Christ’s reign. That is how the New Testament uses these chapters: Revelation draws on Ezekiel 38–39 twice, for the feast of the birds (19:17–21) and for Gog and Magog (20:8), which suggests one last battle seen from two angles rather than two battles a thousand years apart. Those who hold the other views love Scripture too, and none should be despised for it. On every reading the main message is shared: however great the last enemy, God will destroy it and protect his people.

Uncertain wording. “The chief prince of Meshech and Tubal” may also be rendered “the prince of Rosh, Meshech, and Tubal” (ESV note). Rosh is the ordinary Hebrew word for head or chief, and no people called Rosh is clearly known in Ezekiel’s day, so “chief prince” is the more likely meaning. Some have linked Rosh with Russia, but the name Russia comes from the Rus, a people who appear more than a thousand years after Ezekiel, and the text itself makes no such link.
verseByVerse.note: Meshech and Tubal were peoples of eastern Asia Minor, in what is now Turkey, known from Assyrian records as Mushku and Tabal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Be ready and keep ready, you and all your hosts that are assembled about you, and be a guard for them. After many days you will be mustered. In the latter years you will go against the land that is restored from war, the land whose people were gathered from many peoples upon the mountains of Israel, which had been a continual waste. Its people were brought out from the peoples and now dwell securely, all of them. You will advance, coming on like a storm. You will be like a cloud covering the land, you and all your hordes, and many peoples with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gog may muster every army he has, but “in the latter years” he will come against a people God has already restored and made secure.

Be ready and keep ready. The command is ironic: let Gog muster all his armies; it will make no difference. The attack comes after the restoration of chapters 34–37. God’s people are gathered, the land is rebuilt from “a continual waste”, and they “dwell securely, all of them”. It is when they are at peace that the final enemy strikes.

Like a cloud covering the land. The New Testament does not promise that the world will grow friendlier before the end. Jesus said, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

Is this modern Israel, so that Gog’s invasion is coming now? Some dispensationalists read it so. But Revelation places Gog, the last great enemy, at the close of the thousand years, that is, at the end of this present age (Revelation 20:8). The chapter describes the final assault of the world on God’s people, not a map of current events, and many confident identifications of Gog with the empire of the day have come and gone. No one can set the date: “concerning that day and hour no one knows” (Matthew 24:36). Jesus calls his people to be ready, not to calculate.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gog’s greed is his own, yet God uses it to show his holiness. Thoughts rise in Gog’s mind, and he devises an evil scheme: to plunder a quiet people living in unwalled villages, with no bars or gates (vv. 10–12). The merchants of Sheba, Dedan and Tarshish see through him and ask whether he has come for spoil (v. 13). But behind Gog’s plan stands God’s. He brings Gog against his land “that the nations may know me, when through you, O Gog, I vindicate my holiness before their eyes” (vv. 14–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The enemy's schemes against God's people serve God's purpose to reveal his holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: On that day, thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme and say, 'I will go up against the land of unwalled villages. I will fall upon the quiet people who dwell securely, all of them dwelling without walls, and having no bars or gates,' to seize spoil and carry off plunder, to turn your hand against the waste places that are now inhabited, and the people who were gathered from the nations, who have acquired livestock and goods, who dwell at the center of the earth. Sheba and Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish and all its leaders will say to you, 'Have you come to seize spoil? Have you assembled your hosts to carry off plunder, to carry away silver and gold, to take away livestock and goods, to seize great spoil?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gog’s attack is his own greedy scheme, and he is guilty for it, even though God is the one who brings him.

You will devise an evil scheme. God has hooked Gog’s jaw, yet Gog’s own mind devises the evil: God is sovereign over the attack, and Gog is guilty for his wicked intent. It is the pattern of the cross, where Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” and killed “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23).

The land of unwalled villages. Gog’s target is a people with no walls, bars or gates. They look defenceless, but they have something better than walls: God himself (compare Zechariah 2:4–5). “The gates of hell shall not prevail” against Christ’s church (Matthew 16:18).

Who dwell at the center of the earth. Literally “the navel of the earth”: the land where God dwells is the true centre of the world (compare 5:5).

Have you come to seize spoil? Gog’s motive is greed. The traders of Sheba and Dedan in Arabia, and of far-off Tarshish in the west, watch and ask the obvious question: are you here for plunder? Hostility to God’s people is often mixed with plain greed.

Uncertain wording. “All its leaders” is literally “all its young lions” (ESV note). It most likely means the leading men or warrior chiefs of these trading peoples; the sense of the verse is not affected.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, son of man, prophesy, and say to Gog, Thus says the Lord GOD: On that day when my people Israel are dwelling securely, will you not know it? You will come from your place out of the uttermost parts of the north, you and many peoples with you, all of them riding on horses, a great host, a mighty army. You will come up against my people Israel, like a cloud covering the land. In the latter days I will bring you against my land, that the nations may know me, when through you, O Gog, I vindicate my holiness before their eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind Gog’s plan stands God’s: he brings the enemy against his own land so that the nations may see his holiness.

My people Israel. Gog comes from the far north, the direction from which Israel’s invaders had always come (Jeremiah 1:14). But notice “my people” and “my land”: the attack is on what belongs to God.

That the nations may know me. Here is the purpose of the whole invasion: “that the nations may know me, when through you, O Gog, I vindicate my holiness before their eyes.” In 36:23 God vindicated his holiness by restoring Israel; here he does it by destroying Israel’s last enemy.

Even opposition serves God. The fiercest opposition to God’s people ends by displaying his glory. “Why do the nations rage…? He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:1, 4). The first Christians prayed that psalm when rulers had gathered against Jesus, and saw that they had done only what God’s hand and plan had decided beforehand (Acts 4:25–28).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the last enemy comes, God himself fights, and the whole world learns who he is. God asks whether Gog is the one the earlier prophets spoke of (v. 17). On that day his wrath will be roused: a great earthquake will make every creature tremble at his presence and bring down mountains, cliffs and walls (vv. 18–20). The invaders will turn their swords on one another, and God will judge them with pestilence, blood, hail, fire and sulfur (vv. 21–22). The battle is God’s alone, and its end is his glory: “I will show my greatness and my holiness and make myself known in the eyes of many nations” (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: At the climax of evil's assault, God himself fights for his people and makes himself known to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: Are you he of whom I spoke in former days by my servants the prophets of Israel, who in those days prophesied for years that I would bring you against them? But on that day, the day that Gog shall come against the land of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, my wrath will be roused in my anger. For in my jealousy and in my blazing wrath I declare, On that day there shall be a great earthquake in the land of Israel. The fish of the sea and the birds of the heavens and the beasts of the field and all creeping things that creep on the ground, and all the people who are on the face of the earth, shall quake at my presence. And the mountains shall be thrown down, and the cliffs shall fall, and every wall shall tumble to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gog is the final enemy the earlier prophets foresaw, and when he comes God’s holy anger will shake the whole creation.

Of whom I spoke in former days. No earlier prophet names Gog, so God points to what they said of the last gathering of the nations against his people. Zephaniah heard God’s decision “to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out upon them my indignation” (Zephaniah 3:8). Zechariah saw “all the nations against Jerusalem”, and then “the LORD will go out and fight against those nations” (Zechariah 14:2–3).

There shall be a great earthquake. God’s “jealousy” is not envy but a husband’s burning zeal for his own bride. When he rises to defend his people, all creation “shall quake at my presence”, and mountains, cliffs and walls fall. It is the language of the final shaking of the world, which Hebrews takes up: “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens”, so that “the things that cannot be shaken may remain” (Hebrews 12:26–27). Everything that is not God’s will fall; his people, “receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28), will stand.

verseByVerse.quote: I will summon a sword against Gog on all my mountains, declares the Lord GOD. Every man's sword will be against his brother. With pestilence and bloodshed I will enter into judgment with him, and I will rain upon him and his hordes and the many peoples who are with him torrential rains and hailstones, fire and sulfur. So I will show my greatness and my holiness and make myself known in the eyes of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God destroys the last enemy by his own hand, with no help from his people, so that every nation will know that he is the LORD.

Every man’s sword will be against his brother. The invading army turns on itself (the ESV notes, literally “against him”). God had done this before, in Jehoshaphat’s day, when the invading armies “all helped to destroy one another” and Judah did not have to fight (2 Chronicles 20:23).

Hailstones, fire and sulfur. These are the weapons of heaven, recalling Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and the plagues of Egypt. God’s people do not win this battle; God does. At the end, Revelation says of Gog and Magog, “fire came down from heaven and consumed them” (Revelation 20:9).

The battle already won. The decisive battle against evil was not fought by God’s people either. At the cross Christ, alone, “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). The last battle only completes what Calvary won: at his appearing the Lord Jesus will destroy his enemy “with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

Make myself known in the eyes of many nations. All history is heading toward that day: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).

An assurance. This chapter is not a code for predicting headlines. However powerful the forces that gather against Christ’s people, in any age and at the end, they move only on God’s hook, and they will fall. “He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4).

38.title: Gog of the Land of Magog
38.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 38 and 39 belong together. God has just promised to restore his people, raise them from their graves and dwell among them for ever (chapters 34–37). Now, before the vision of the new temple (chapters 40–48), comes one last enemy, Gog of the land of Magog, gathering the nations against them.

The message. The last and greatest enemy of God’s people moves only on God’s hook, and God will destroy him. A restored people living without walls look defenceless, and the whole world may gather against them, but God himself fights for them and shows his holiness to the nations. What God has restored, no enemy can undo.

Why it was said. The exiles had just heard promises of home, a new heart and God’s presence. The obvious fear was that, once home, they would simply be crushed by the next empire, as they had been before (see the introduction). God answers that fear in advance: even the greatest enemy imaginable, gathered from the ends of the earth, cannot undo what he has done.

How the chapter makes its case. God summons Gog and a vast coalition from every direction, leading him out like an animal with hooks in its jaws (vv. 1–9). Gog thinks the plan is his own: he plots to plunder a quiet, unwalled people, while the world’s traders ask whether he has come for loot (vv. 10–13). But God has brought him for his own purpose, to show his holiness to the nations through him (vv. 14–16). Then God rises in anger: a great earthquake shakes all creation, the invaders turn their swords on one another, and fire and hail fall from heaven, so that many nations know he is the LORD (vv. 17–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. Revelation takes up Gog and Magog for the nations gathered against “the camp of the saints and the beloved city” at the end of this age, when “fire came down from heaven and consumed them” (Revelation 20:8–9). The battle is won not by God’s people but by God, and that is the shape of the cross, where the rulers gathered against the Lord’s Anointed did only what God’s hand had planned (Acts 4:26–28), and where Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15). He who won that battle alone will finish the last one at his coming.

For us. This chapter is not a code for reading headlines but an assurance for anxious believers. However powerful the forces that gather against Christ’s church, in any age and at the end, they move only on God’s hook, and they will fall. So live without fear, ready rather than calculating, because “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4).
38.theology:
The fiercest enemies of God's people move only as God allows, yet remain guilty for their evil schemes (vv. 4, 10; Acts 2:23).

God's people may face their greatest assault even after restoration, but they are not defenceless (vv. 8-12; John 16:33; Matt 16:18).

God turns the rage of the nations into an occasion to vindicate his holiness and make himself known (vv. 16, 23; Ps 2:1-6).

God himself fights for his people at the climax of history, shaking all creation so that only what cannot be shaken remains (vv. 18-22; Zech 14:2-3; Heb 12:26-28; Rev 20:7-10).

The purpose of these chapters is assurance, not speculation: he who is in believers is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).
38.examples:
A believer in a country where the church is small, poor and watched by the authorities may feel like an unwalled village. Verse 11 is a comfort: the people without walls have the LORD as their defence.

Every generation has had its candidates for Gog, from the Scythians to the Soviet Union, and the confident charts have gone out of date. The faithful response to frightening headlines is not to calculate but to trust and be ready (Matt 24:36).

keyVerse.quote: So I will show my greatness and my holiness and make myself known in the eyes of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This is why Gog comes and why he falls. The whole terrifying invasion, from the hooks in his jaws to the fire from heaven, serves one end: that the nations should know the LORD. The last enemy of God’s people becomes, against his will, a witness to God’s glory, as every enemy of Christ will be.

38.reflection:
God puts “hooks into” Gog’s jaws and leads him out (v. 4), yet Gog devises his own “evil scheme” (v. 10). How can God rule over an attack and Gog still be guilty for it? Where else does Scripture show both, above all at the cross (Acts 2:23)?

Gog sees a people “dwelling without walls, and having no bars or gates” (v. 11) and thinks them an easy prize. What “walls” are we tempted to trust instead of God, and what does it look like for a church to rest in God’s protection?

Some read these chapters as a timetable of coming events; this commentary reads them as a picture of the last assault on God’s people (Revelation 20:8–9). Whatever view you hold, how should the chapter shape the way Christians respond to frightening news?

God fights this battle alone (vv. 19–22). How does Christ’s victory over evil at the cross (Colossians 2:15) give you courage in the battles you face now?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Gog Falls on the Mountains of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself will disarm and destroy the last enemy, so that his holy name is never dishonoured again. He is against Gog: he will turn him about and drive him to the mountains of Israel (vv. 1–2), strike the bow from one hand and the arrows from the other (v. 3), and leave him and his hordes fallen in the open field for birds and beasts (vv. 4–5). Fire will reach his homeland and the distant coastlands that felt secure (v. 6). The point is God’s name: “my holy name I will make known in the midst of my people Israel, and I will not let my holy name be profaned anymore” (v. 7). And it is certain: “Behold, it is coming and it will be brought about” (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God will end every assault on his people and never again let his name be profaned.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, prophesy against Gog and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, O Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal. And I will turn you about and drive you forward, and bring you up from the uttermost parts of the north, and lead you against the mountains of Israel. Then I will strike your bow from your left hand, and will make your arrows drop out of your right hand. You shall fall on the mountains of Israel, you and all your hordes and the peoples who are with you. I will give you to birds of prey of every sort and to the beasts of the field to be devoured. You shall fall in the open field, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. I will send fire on Magog and on those who dwell securely in the coastlands, and they shall know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God draws Gog to the mountains of Israel only to disarm him before a single arrow flies, and his judgment reaches even the far-off lands that felt secure.

I am against you, O Gog. Chapter 39 zooms in on the battlefield of chapter 38. (Once more the ESV notes the alternative “prince of Rosh, Meshech”; see on 38:1–6.)

I will strike your bow from your left hand. The archer raises his bow, and it is struck from his hand; his arrows fall to the ground. God disarms the enemy before a single arrow flies: “he breaks the bow and shatters the spear” (Psalm 46:9).

You shall fall on the mountains of Israel. The invader who came to plunder the mountains of Israel falls on them.

I will send fire on Magog. Judgment reaches back to Gog’s own homeland and to “those who dwell securely in the coastlands”, the distant nations who thought themselves safe. Their security was false; Israel’s, resting on God, was real (38:8).

Uncertain wording. “Drive you forward” translates a rare Hebrew verb; the ESV notes it may mean “drag you along”. Either way, Gog comes because God brings him, into a trap God has set.

verseByVerse.quote: "And my holy name I will make known in the midst of my people Israel, and I will not let my holy name be profaned anymore. And the nations shall know that I am the LORD, the Holy One in Israel. Behold, it is coming and it will be brought about, declares the Lord GOD. That is the day of which I have spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole point of Gog’s fall is God’s holy name: he will make it known among his people and the nations, and never let it be dishonoured again.

My holy name I will make known. Here is the heart of the chapter: “I will not let my holy name be profaned anymore.” Israel’s sin had dragged God’s name through the dirt among the nations (36:20); a successful attack on his restored people would do so again. God will not allow it. His name will be known as holy both “in the midst of my people Israel” and among the nations, who will know him as “the Holy One in Israel”.

Hallowed be your name. Jesus taught his disciples to pray first, “hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9), which is exactly what God promises here. And he lived for it, praying as the cross drew near, “Father, glorify your name” (John 12:28). Every answer to that prayer, from the spread of the gospel to the last judgment, is God keeping this promise.

It is coming and it will be brought about. God’s final victory is not uncertain: it is “the day of which I have spoken”. However long the conflict with evil seems, its outcome is settled.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Burning the Weapons, Burying the Dead
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s victory is so complete that nothing of the enemy is left to threaten or defile his people. Israel will gather the invaders’ weapons and burn them as fuel for seven years, needing no wood from the forests, and will plunder those who came to plunder (vv. 9–10). Gog will receive the only piece of the land he ever gains, a grave, in a valley named for “the multitude of Gog” (v. 11). For seven months all the people will bury the dead to cleanse the land, and men will be appointed to search it, marking every human bone until the buriers come (vv. 12–16). Not a trace of death is left.
verseByVerse.theology: God's victory is so complete that the weapons of war become firewood and the land is cleansed of every trace of death.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then those who dwell in the cities of Israel will go out and make fires of the weapons and burn them, shields and bucklers, bow and arrows, clubs and spears; and they will make fires of them for seven years, so that they will not need to take wood out of the field or cut down any out of the forests, for they will make their fires of the weapons. They will seize the spoil of those who despoiled them, and plunder those who plundered them, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The victory is so complete that the enemy’s whole arsenal becomes firewood, and the plunderers are plundered.

Make fires of the weapons. Israel collects the enemy’s weapons, shields, bows, arrows, clubs and spears (or “javelins”, as the ESV notes), and burns them for fuel, so many that no one needs to cut wood for seven years.

For seven years. Seven often suggests completeness in Scripture. This is the end of war that Isaiah foresaw, when “they shall beat their swords into plowshares” (Isaiah 2:4), and that the psalmist sang of: “he burns the chariots with fire” (Psalm 46:9). It is the peace that the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6) will bring in full.

Plunder those who plundered them. The would-be plunderers of 38:12 are plundered. “No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed” (Isaiah 54:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "On that day I will give to Gog a place for burial in Israel, the Valley of the Travelers, east of the sea. It will block the travelers, for there Gog and all his multitude will be buried. It will be called the Valley of Hamon-gog. For seven months the house of Israel will be burying them, in order to cleanse the land. All the people of the land will bury them, and it will bring them renown on the day that I show my glory, declares the Lord GOD. They will set apart men to travel through the land regularly and bury those travelers remaining on the face of the land, so as to cleanse it. At the end of seven months they will make their search. And when these travel through the land and anyone sees a human bone, then he shall set up a sign by it, till the buriers have buried it in the Valley of Hamon-gog. (Hamonah is also the name of the city.) Thus shall they cleanse the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gog gets the only piece of the land he will ever own, a grave, and God’s people search out every last bone until the land is clean.

A place for burial in Israel. Gog, who wanted to possess the land, gets a piece of it after all: a grave, in a valley named Hamon-gog, “the multitude of Gog” (ESV note), and even a town will carry the name (v. 16; see the note).

In order to cleanse the land. Under the law anyone who touched “a human bone or a grave” became unclean (Numbers 19:16), so a land strewn with corpses could not be a holy land. God’s victory must be followed by thorough cleansing, and the whole people share in the work, to their honour (v. 13).

He shall set up a sign by it. Men search the whole land; anyone who sees even a single bone marks it, and the buriers come.

Every last bone. Here is God’s thoroughness in purifying his people’s world. The new creation will hold no trace of death or defilement: “No longer will there be anything accursed” (Revelation 22:3). And it speaks to the Christian life too: God is not content to win the battle over sin; he cleans up every last bone of it, until Christ presents his church “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

Uncertain wording. Verse 11 is obscure. “The Valley of the Travelers” may be a place name, perhaps linked with the Abarim mountains east of the Dead Sea (Numbers 27:12), and “east of the sea” most likely means east of the Dead Sea. “It will block the travelers” is unclear: perhaps the mass grave blocks the road. In v. 14 “at the end” may be rendered “until” (see the note).
verseByVerse.note: The city named in verse 16, Hamonah, means “multitude” (ESV note): even a town's name will remember Gog's horde. In verse 14 At the end may be rendered “Until”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The proud who came to devour God’s people will themselves be devoured, in a terrible reversal of a feast. God invites the birds and beasts to “a great sacrificial feast on the mountains of Israel” (v. 17). The mighty men and princes of the earth are the sacrifice, pictured as rams, lambs, goats and fat bulls of Bashan (v. 18), and the animals are the guests, eating and drinking until they are full (v. 19): “And you shall be filled at my table with horses and charioteers, with mighty men and all kinds of warriors” (v. 20). Revelation takes up this feast for the end of the age (Revelation 19:17–21).
verseByVerse.theology: The proud powers that sought to devour God's people become a feast in God's judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, thus says the Lord GOD: Speak to the birds of every sort and to all beasts of the field: 'Assemble and come, gather from all around to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you, a great sacrificial feast on the mountains of Israel, and you shall eat flesh and drink blood. You shall eat the flesh of the mighty, and drink the blood of the princes of the earth—of rams, of lambs, and of he-goats, of bulls, all of them fat beasts of Bashan. And you shall eat fat till you are filled, and drink blood till you are drunk, at the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you. And you shall be filled at my table with horses and charioteers, with mighty men and all kinds of warriors,' declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proud warriors who came to devour God’s people become the sacrifice, and the birds and beasts are God’s guests: a terrible picture of final justice.

A great sacrificial feast. Normally people offered animals in sacrifice and shared the meal; here the mighty men and princes are the sacrificial animals, rams, lambs, goats and fat bulls of Bashan, the rich pasture land east of the Jordan, and the animals are the guests. Isaiah used the same shocking image: “For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom” (Isaiah 34:6).

The great supper of God. John saw this very scene at the return of Christ: an angel “called to all the birds… ‘Come, gather for the great supper of God, to eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of captains, the flesh of mighty men, the flesh of horses and their riders’” (Revelation 19:17–18).

Two suppers. The Bible holds out two suppers. One is “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9), to which God’s people are invited as guests. The other is “the great supper of God”, where God’s proud enemies are the meal. Everyone will be at one of them, and the invitation to the first is open now.

How can a loving God speak like this? The picture is deliberately shocking, in the vivid language of ancient battle, because it shows final justice on those who set themselves to destroy God’s people and would not turn. It gives no licence for human vengeance: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). And the Lamb who invites guests to his supper first bore God’s judgment himself, so that enemies could become guests (Romans 5:10).

In Revelation. Revelation uses this feast at Christ’s return (19:17–21) and names Gog and Magog in 20:8: on this commentary’s reading (see on 38:1–6), the same last battle, seen twice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — I Will Not Hide My Face Anymore
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The exile was God’s judgment, not his defeat, and his last word to his people is mercy and an unhidden face. God will set his glory among the nations, and Israel will know him from that day on (vv. 21–22). The nations will understand that Israel went into exile for its own treachery, when God hid his face from them (vv. 23–24). “Now I will restore the fortunes of Jacob and have mercy on the whole house of Israel” (v. 25): they will live securely and lose their shame, every one gathered home (vv. 26–28). And the climax: “I will not hide my face anymore from them, when I pour out my Spirit upon the house of Israel” (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The exile had a cause, and its end has a greater cause: God's mercy and the outpouring of his Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will set my glory among the nations, and all the nations shall see my judgment that I have executed, and my hand that I have laid on them. The house of Israel shall know that I am the LORD their God, from that day forward. And the nations shall know that the house of Israel went into captivity for their iniquity, because they dealt so treacherously with me that I hid my face from them and gave them into the hand of their adversaries, and they all fell by the sword. I dealt with them according to their uncleanness and their transgressions, and hid my face from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the nations see God’s judgment, they will understand that Israel’s exile was never God’s defeat: he hid his face from a people who had betrayed him.

I will set my glory among the nations. The chapter steps back and draws together the story of the whole book. God’s glory will be seen by all nations, and Israel will know him “from that day forward”: no more wavering, no more idols.

Into captivity for their iniquity. The nations assumed Israel’s God had been too weak to protect his people (36:20). Now they will understand that the exile came “for their iniquity”: Israel “dealt so treacherously” with God that he hid his face from them. It was not weakness but judgment.

When God hides his face. That is true when God’s people pass through his discipline today. When he hides his face, he has not gone away and he has not been defeated; he disciplines us “for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). Not every hardship is punishment for a particular sin (John 9:3), but every one is in the hands of a Father who has not lost control.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Now I will restore the fortunes of Jacob and have mercy on the whole house of Israel, and I will be jealous for my holy name. They shall forget their shame and all the treachery they have practiced against me, when they dwell securely in their land with none to make them afraid, when I have brought them back from the peoples and gathered them from their enemies' lands, and through them have vindicated my holiness in the sight of many nations. Then they shall know that I am the LORD their God, because I sent them into exile among the nations and then assembled them into their own land. I will leave none of them remaining among the nations anymore. And I will not hide my face anymore from them, when I pour out my Spirit upon the house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s last word to his people is mercy: he will bring every one of them home, lift their shame and never hide his face from them again, because he will pour out his Spirit on them.

Now I will restore the fortunes of Jacob. “Now” turns the page. The exile had a cause, their sin; the restoration has a cause too: “have mercy”, and “I will be jealous for my holy name”. These two reasons run through chapters 20 and 36.

They shall forget their shame. In 16:63 and 36:31 God said they would remember and be ashamed. Both are true in their time: grace first brings honest shame over sin, and then, in the security of God’s love, lifts the shame away. God’s forgiven people do not live for ever under the weight of what they were.

I will leave none of them remaining. Not one of God’s people will be left behind in exile. The Shepherd who seeks the lost (34:16) does not stop until every one is home (John 6:39).

I will not hide my face anymore. The hidden face was the heart of the exile’s pain (vv. 23–24); now it will never be hidden again, “when I pour out my Spirit upon the house of Israel”. Not a few drops, but a pouring out, as Joel foresaw: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28). On the day of Pentecost Peter declared that it was happening: “in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Acts 2:17), and “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts 2:21).

What God’s face means. In the Old Testament God’s face stands for his personal attention and favour: not only that he is there, but that he is turned towards you. Think of a small child in a crowded room looking for one face: if her father is smiling at her, she is safe; if he will not look at her, nothing makes up for it. We all live for some face, a parent’s approval, a boss’s nod, the crowd’s applause, and those faces turn away. That is why Israel’s great blessing was “the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:25), and the psalmist’s worst cry was “How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1).

God’s face is no longer hidden. On the cross the Son endured the forsaking that sin deserves (Mark 15:34), so that for everyone who belongs to him God’s face is no longer hidden. God “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), and the Spirit poured out on the church is the pledge that he will never turn away from his people again. Watch how Jesus looked at Peter just after his denial, “the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61), and you see how God looks at his own. So when you pray this week, especially after failing, do not come expecting a turned back. Come to the Father who, for Christ’s sake, will not hide his face anymore.

Is this the future of ethnic Israel or the church? Dispensationalists see a national restoration still to come, and faithful Christians differ here. The promise of the Spirit poured out (v. 29) points to the new covenant, fulfilled in Christ for Israel and the nations, as Peter declared at Pentecost; and Paul, on the most natural reading, looks for a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:26).

Uncertain wording. “They shall forget their shame” (v. 26) depends on how one Hebrew word is read; it can also be taken as “they shall bear their shame”, as some older translations have it. On that reading the verse matches 16:63 and 36:31: even when they live securely, they will feel the shame of their past, now as a forgiven people.

39.title: I Will Not Hide My Face Anymore
39.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 39 retells the fall of Gog from chapter 38 in close-up, then draws the threads of the whole book together before the closing vision of the new temple (chapters 40–48).

The message. God will finish the last enemy so completely that its weapons become firewood and its dead are buried bone by bone until the land is clean, and he will do it to make his holy name known. Then comes the deepest promise of all. The exile happened because of Israel’s sin, not God’s weakness; but now, in mercy, he will bring them home, lift their shame and never hide his face from them again, for he will pour out his Spirit on them.

Why it was said. The exiles needed to know two things: that no future enemy could undo their restoration (chapter 38), and that the disaster they had lived through was God’s judgment, not his defeat (vv. 23–24; see the introduction). A God who had been beaten could not save them; a God who had disciplined them could also restore them.

How the chapter makes its case. God disarms Gog on the mountains of Israel and sends fire on his homeland (vv. 1–6), so that his holy name is never profaned again (vv. 7–8). The victory is total: Israel burns the enemy’s weapons for seven years and buries his dead for seven months, until not one bone defiles the land (vv. 9–16). Birds and beasts are summoned to a grim sacrificial feast on the proud (vv. 17–20). Then the chapter steps back. The nations will see that Israel went into exile for its sin, when God hid his face (vv. 21–24), and that God has now had mercy, gathered every one of them home and poured out his Spirit, never to hide his face again (vv. 25–29).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. John saw Ezekiel’s feast of birds at Christ’s return, “the great supper of God” (Revelation 19:17), set against “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9), whose guests are former enemies reconciled by his death. The hidden face of God fell on Christ at the cross, when he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), so that it need never be hidden from his people; and the Spirit poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2:17) is the promise of v. 29 kept.

For us. Every enemy of Christ and his people will be finished, down to the last bone, so believers need not fear. And for anyone who has known God’s discipline and feels that his face is turned away, the promise stands: in Christ, and by the Spirit he has given, the Father will not hide his face anymore.
39.theology:
God disarms and destroys the final enemies of his people, and the outcome is certain (vv. 1-8; Ps 46:9; Isa 54:17).

God will never again allow his holy name to be profaned (v. 7).

God's victory is followed by thorough cleansing; nothing defiled will remain (vv. 11-16; Num 19:16; Rev 22:3).

The proud enemies of God become the feast of his judgment, while his people are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (vv. 17-20; Rev 19:17-18).

The exile was God's just judgment, not his weakness; the restoration is his mercy and zeal for his name (vv. 23-25).

Grace first brings honest shame over sin and then lifts it away (v. 26).

God pours out his Spirit and will never hide his face from his people again, fulfilled at Pentecost and in the church (v. 29; Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17, 21).
39.examples:
Someone who has known a long season when God seemed far away, when prayer felt like speaking into an empty room, can hold on to verse 29. God had hidden his face, but he had never gone away, and for those in Christ the hiding is not his last word.

A Christian struggling with an old sin she thought was defeated can take heart from the search party of verses 14-15. God does not stop at winning the battle; he keeps cleaning until no bone is left.

keyVerse.quote: And I will not hide my face anymore from them, when I pour out my Spirit upon the house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD.
keyVerse.note: The hidden face of God was the heart of the exile (vv. 23–24), and this verse undoes it for ever. The guarantee is the Spirit poured out, which happened at Pentecost because Christ bore the forsaking on the cross. For all who belong to him, God’s face is turned towards them and will never be turned away.

39.reflection:
God says the whole purpose of Gog’s fall is that “I will not let my holy name be profaned anymore” (v. 7). How does praying “hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9) change when we see that God is this zealous for his own name?

The people search the land until every human bone is buried and the land is clean (vv. 14–16). What does God’s thoroughness here teach us about how he deals with sin in his people, and in the world to come?

The nations will learn that Israel went into exile not because God was weak but because “I hid my face from them” (v. 23). How can we tell the difference between God’s discipline and his absence? What comfort does Hebrews 12:10 give in hard times?

“I will not hide my face anymore from them” (v. 29). How does Christ’s cry of forsakenness on the cross (Mark 15:34) make this promise sure for believers? How should it shape the way you come to God after you have failed?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — On a Very High Mountain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives his people, at their lowest point, a vision of his dwelling restored, and calls the prophet to take it to heart. Fourteen years after Jerusalem fell, the hand of the LORD brings Ezekiel “in visions of God” to a very high mountain in the land of Israel, where there is something like a city (vv. 1–2). A man whose appearance is like bronze, holding a linen cord and a measuring reed, stands in the gateway (v. 3). He tells Ezekiel to “look with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you”, and to declare it all to the house of Israel (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: After the ruin, God gives his people a vision of his dwelling restored in perfect order.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was struck down, on that very day, the hand of the LORD was upon me, and he brought me to the city. In visions of God he brought me to the land of Israel, and set me down on a very high mountain, on which was a structure like a city to the south. When he brought me there, behold, there was a man whose appearance was like bronze, with a linen cord and a measuring reed in his hand. And he was standing in the gateway. And the man said to me, "Son of man, look with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you, for you were brought here in order that I might show it to you. Declare all that you see to the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fourteen years after the temple burned, God shows Ezekiel a new one and tells him to take it to heart and declare it to Israel: God’s dwelling with his people has a future.

In visions of God. Fourteen years after Jerusalem was destroyed (see the note for the date), God shows Ezekiel a new temple, a restored land and a holy city. The book that began with the glory of God in Babylon ends with that glory coming home.

A perfect temple. These chapters are full of measurements and rarely read, but they matter. Ezekiel was a priest who had watched the glory leave a defiled temple (chapters 8–11); now God shows him a perfect one. If “the thirtieth year” of 1:1 was Ezekiel’s age (see the note there), he was now about fifty, the age at which a priest’s service ended (Numbers 4:3): the priest who never served at the altar is shown the perfect house of God.

A very high mountain. Isaiah had foreseen that “the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains” (Isaiah 2:2). And John was carried “in the Spirit to a great, high mountain” and shown “the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God” (Revelation 21:10).

A measuring reed in his hand. A heavenly guide, gleaming like bronze, with a linen cord and a measuring reed. In the Bible, measuring something often means claiming it, protecting it and setting it apart for God. Zechariah saw “a man with a measuring line in his hand” measuring Jerusalem, and God said, “I will be to her a wall of fire all around… and I will be the glory in her midst” (Zechariah 2:1, 5). John was told, “Rise and measure the temple of God” (Revelation 11:1).

Set your heart upon all that I shall show you. Three commands: look, hear, set your heart. This is not dry architecture but something to take to heart, and to pass on: “Declare all that you see to the house of Israel.” Exiles who had lost everything needed to see that God’s dwelling with them had a future, and that future has a name: Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21).

Where Christians differ: how should chapters 40–48 be read? Some believe they describe a literal temple still to be built; many dispensationalists take it as the temple of a future thousand-year reign, out of a desire to honour every detail God gave, and they deserve a respectful hearing. Others think the chapters gave a plan for the returning exiles that was never carried out. Many, especially in the Reformed tradition, read them as a symbolic vision of God dwelling in perfect holiness with a purified people, told in the language of temple and priesthood that Ezekiel knew. They see it fulfilled in Christ, who called his body “the temple” (John 2:21), in the church, “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22), and finally in the new creation, where John saw a city measured by an angel, with a river of life flowing from the throne (Revelation 21–22). This commentary’s view: the last reading is the most likely. Ezekiel says he saw it “in visions of God” (v. 2). The vision goes beyond ordinary geography: a river that heals the Dead Sea (47:8–9) and tribal lands laid out in equal strips (chapter 48). The exiles who returned did not build to this plan, and no prophet blamed them for it. A future temple with sin offerings (43:19–21) would sit uneasily with Hebrews, which says “there is no longer any offering for sin” (Hebrews 10:18), and John saw no temple in the city, “for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). And the New Testament takes up the vision’s images for Christ’s body (John 2:21), the Spirit he gives (John 7:38–39) and the city to come (Revelation 21–22). On every reading, the heart of the vision is the same: a holy God living among his people for ever. The chapters that follow are read in this light, and where the question presses again (the sacrifices of 40:38–43 and 43:18–27, the prince of chapters 45–46, the river of chapter 47) they point back here.
verseByVerse.note: The vision is dated to about 573 BC, in the twenty-fifth year of the exile that began in 597 BC. The measurements use the “long cubit” of about 21 inches (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is set apart and guarded, and its main gate faces the direction of the returning glory. Around the whole temple area runs a wall, one reed thick and one reed high, about ten feet each way, marking a clear boundary between the holy and the common (v. 5). The guide then measures the gateway facing east: its steps and thresholds, its three guardrooms on either side, its jambs and vestibule, and its windows and carved palm trees (vv. 6–16). It is a massive, fortress-like gate, yet its palm trees recall the garden where God first walked with people.
verseByVerse.theology: The way into God's presence is guarded, ordered and beautiful.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, there was a wall all around the outside of the temple area, and the length of the measuring reed in the man's hand was six long cubits, each being a cubit and a handbreadth in length. So he measured the thickness of the wall, one reed; and the height, one reed. Then he went into the gateway facing east, going up its steps, and measured the threshold of the gate, one reed deep. And the side rooms, one reed long and one reed broad; and the space between the side rooms, five cubits; and the threshold of the gate by the vestibule of the gate at the inner end, one reed. Then he measured the vestibule of the gateway, on the inside, one reed. Then he measured the vestibule of the gateway, eight cubits; and its jambs, two cubits; and the vestibule of the gate was at the inner end. And there were three side rooms on either side of the east gate. The three were of the same size, and the jambs on either side were of the same size. Then he measured the width of the opening of the gateway, ten cubits; and the length of the gateway, thirteen cubits. There was a barrier before the side rooms, one cubit on either side. And the side rooms were six cubits on either side. Then he measured the gate from the ceiling of the one side room to the ceiling of the other, a breadth of twenty-five cubits; the openings faced each other. He measured also the vestibule, sixty cubits. And around the vestibule of the gateway was the court. From the front of the gate at the entrance to the front of the inner vestibule of the gate was fifty cubits. And the gateway had windows all around, narrowing inwards toward the side rooms and toward their jambs, and likewise the vestibule had windows all around inside, and on the jambs were palm trees.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s house is walled off and entered through a massive, guarded gate facing east: his holiness is to be taken seriously, yet the way in leads to a garden.

A wall all around the outside. The first thing Ezekiel sees is a wall. An ordinary cubit was about eighteen inches and a handbreadth about three; the long cubit used here is the two together, about twenty-one inches (some 52 centimetres), so the reed of six long cubits was roughly ten feet (just over three metres). The wall is as thick as it is high.

Why start with a wall? Because the old temple had lost the separation between the holy and the ordinary. Idols stood at the altar gate and men worshipped the sun in the inner court (chapter 8). This wall marks a clear boundary (compare 42:20): God’s holiness is not to be treated casually.

The gateway facing east. The east gate is measured first because it faces the rising sun and the Mount of Olives, the direction in which the glory left (11:23) and from which it will return (43:1–2). With three guardrooms on each side it is a fortress gate: no one wanders casually into God’s presence.

On the jambs were palm trees. Palm trees were carved in Solomon’s temple too, with cherubim and flowers (1 Kings 6:29). They recall a garden: God’s house is decorated like Eden, the first place where God walked with people. The way into God’s presence is guarded, but it leads into paradise, and Christ, who opened it, could promise a dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Uncertain wording. Many of the architectural terms in vv. 6–16 are rare, and some measurements are hard to fit together (such as the sixty cubits of v. 14, or the windows “narrowing inwards” of v. 16), so drawings of the gate differ. The overall plan is clear: a long, massive gateway with three guardrooms on each side, a vestibule at the inner end, and windows and palm trees throughout.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — The Outer Court and Its Gates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is ordered and open, with matching gates for his people on every side. Through the east gate lies the outer court, with a pavement and thirty chambers around it, perhaps for the worshippers’ meals (vv. 17–18). The guide measures a hundred cubits from the outer gate to the inner one (v. 19). Then he measures the north gate and the south gate, each matching the east gate exactly, each reached by seven steps, and each facing a gate into the inner court (vv. 20–27). Nothing in God’s house is random, and no side is closed to those who come.
verseByVerse.theology: God's house is built with perfect symmetry, open on every side yet entered with care.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me into the outer court. And behold, there were chambers and a pavement, all around the court. Thirty chambers faced the pavement. And the pavement ran along the side of the gates, corresponding to the length of the gates. This was the lower pavement. Then he measured the distance from the inner front of the lower gate to the outer front of the inner court, a hundred cubits on the east side and on the north side. As for the gate that faced toward the north, belonging to the outer court, he measured its length and its breadth. Its side rooms, three on either side, and its jambs and its vestibule were of the same size as those of the first gate. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. And its windows, its vestibule, and its palm trees were of the same size as those of the gate that faced toward the east. And by seven steps people would go up to it, and find its vestibule before them. And opposite the gate on the north, as on the east, was a gate to the inner court. And he measured from gate to gate, a hundred cubits. And he led me toward the south, and behold, there was a gate on the south. And he measured its jambs and its vestibule; they had the same size as the others. Both it and its vestibule had windows all around, like the windows of the others. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. And there were seven steps leading up to it, and its vestibule was before them, and it had palm trees on its jambs, one on either side. And there was a gate on the south of the inner court. And he measured from gate to gate toward the south, a hundred cubits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The outer court is perfectly ordered, and its gates, all exactly alike, open to God’s people from every side.

Then he brought me into the outer court. Inside the wall is the outer court, with a paved area and thirty rooms around it, perhaps where worshippers gathered to eat their sacrificial meals (compare 46:21–24).

The same size as the others. The repetition is deliberate: every gate is identical. The chaos and corruption of the old temple give way to perfect proportion, order and balance, for “God is not a God of confusion but of peace” (1 Corinthians 14:33).

Gates on every side. There are gates on every side except the west, behind the temple, where the large building of 41:12 stands. God’s people come from every direction. John saw the same in the new Jerusalem, “on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates” (Revelation 21:13), and Jesus said that people “will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God” (Luke 13:29).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nearer to God, the higher the way. The guide brings Ezekiel into the inner court through its south gate and measures it, and then the east and north gates of the inner court (vv. 28–37). Each matches the outer gates in size, with side rooms, windows and palm trees, but its vestibule faces the outer court, and it is reached by eight more steps (vv. 31, 34, 37). The whole complex rises in levels, seven steps, then eight, then ten to the temple itself (v. 49), so that every worshipper climbing toward the altar meets the question of who may ascend to God.
verseByVerse.theology: Drawing nearer to God means going higher, step by step.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me to the inner court through the south gate, and he measured the south gate. It was of the same size as the others. Its side rooms, its jambs, and its vestibule were of the same size as the others, and both it and its vestibule had windows all around. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. And there were vestibules all around, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits broad. Its vestibule faced the outer court, and palm trees were on its jambs, and its stairway had eight steps. Then he brought me to the inner court on the east side, and he measured the gate. It was of the same size as the others. Its side rooms, its jambs, and its vestibule were of the same size as the others, and both it and its vestibule had windows all around. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. Its vestibule faced the outer court, and it had palm trees on its jambs, on either side, and its stairway had eight steps. Then he brought me to the north gate, and he measured it. It had the same size as the others. Its side rooms, its jambs, and its vestibule were of the same size as the others, and it had windows all around. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. Its vestibule faced the outer court, and it had palm trees on its jambs, on either side, and its stairway had eight steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The inner gates match the outer ones but stand higher, so that every step toward the altar is a climb: to come nearer to God is to go higher.

Its stairway had eight steps. Count the steps: seven up to the outer gates (vv. 22, 26), eight more to the inner gates, and ten to the temple itself (v. 49). The whole complex rises in levels, and the inner gates mirror the outer ones, their vestibules facing the outer court (v. 31).

Who may ascend? Worshippers have always felt this: “Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:3–4). The question those steps raise is who can climb them. No one, by his own purity. Only one has clean hands and a pure heart, and he takes his people with him: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–49 — Tables for Sacrifice, Rooms for Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The way to God passes the place of sacrifice, and it is served by faithful priests. In the vestibule of the inner gate are a room for washing the burnt offering and eight tables for slaughtering burnt, sin and guilt offerings, with hooks and instruments (vv. 38–43). Two chambers in the inner court belong to the priests who keep the temple and the altar, “the sons of Zadok, who alone among the sons of Levi may come near to the LORD to minister to him” (vv. 44–46). The inner court is a perfect square with the altar before the temple, whose vestibule rises up ten steps between two pillars (vv. 47–49).
verseByVerse.theology: Access to God is by sacrifice and through appointed priests, a pattern fulfilled in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a chamber with its door in the vestibule of the gate, where the burnt offering was to be washed. And in the vestibule of the gate were two tables on either side, on which the burnt offering and the sin offering and the guilt offering were to be slaughtered. And off to the side, on the outside as one goes up to the entrance of the north gate, were two tables; and off to the other side of the vestibule of the gate were two tables. Four tables were on either side of the gate, eight tables, on which to slaughter. And there were four tables of hewn stone for the burnt offering, a cubit and a half long, and a cubit and a half broad, and one cubit high, on which the instruments were to be laid with which the burnt offerings and the sacrifices were slaughtered. And hooks, a handbreadth long, were fastened all around within. And on the tables the flesh of the offering was to be laid. On the outside of the inner gateway there were two chambers in the inner court, one at the side of the north gate facing south, the other at the side of the south gate facing north. And he said to me, "This chamber that faces south is for the priests who have charge of the temple, and the chamber that faces north is for the priests who have charge of the altar. These are the sons of Zadok, who alone among the sons of Levi may come near to the LORD to minister to him." And he measured the court, a hundred cubits long and a hundred cubits broad, a square. And the altar was in front of the temple. Then he brought me to the vestibule of the temple and measured the jambs of the vestibule, five cubits on either side. And the breadth of the gate was fourteen cubits, and the sidewalls of the gate were three cubits on either side. The length of the vestibule was twenty cubits, and the breadth twelve cubits, and people would go up to it by ten steps. And there were pillars beside the jambs, one on either side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way to the altar runs past the place of sacrifice, kept by faithful priests, and the whole court is ordered around the altar before God’s house.

Where the burnt offering was to be washed. At the inner gate are a room for washing the sacrifices and stone tables for slaughtering them, burnt offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings, with hooks and a place for the instruments (vv. 38–43). The way to the altar goes past the place of sacrifice.

The sons of Zadok. Beside the inner gates are rooms for the priests who keep the temple and the altar. Of all the priests and Levites, a special place belongs to “the sons of Zadok”, the priestly family Solomon installed (1 Kings 2:35), which stayed faithful when others went astray; chapter 44 will explain (44:15). Faithfulness matters to God, and he remembers it.

The altar was in front of the temple. The inner court is a perfect square, a hundred cubits each way, and in it, just in front of the house of God, stands the altar. Everything in the vision is ordered around it. The temple’s vestibule rises up ten steps between two pillars, as Solomon’s had its two pillars, Jachin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:21).

The one sacrifice. The tables of Ezekiel 40 point to the one sacrifice that makes all others unnecessary: “when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). The priest of the altar now is Christ himself, who “has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily” (Hebrews 7:27), because he offered himself once for all.

What the measurements said. For exiles with the real temple a burnt ruin, every measurement said that God had not finished with his dwelling place. For Christians it says more: “something greater than the temple is here” (Matthew 12:6). Christ is the true temple, and his people are being built into God’s house.

Where Christians differ: why does the vision include sacrifices? Those who expect a literal future temple often understand them as memorials looking back to the cross, or as rites that make the temple ceremonially clean, fit for worship, without taking away anyone’s guilt. Those who read the vision symbolically understand Ezekiel to be describing true worship in the only terms he and his hearers knew, terms the New Testament shows are fulfilled in Christ. This commentary’s view: the second (see on vv. 1–4). On any reading Hebrews is clear: “Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin” (Hebrews 10:18).

Textual note. In v. 44 the ESV follows the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation; the Hebrew reads “chambers for singers”.

40.title: The Measured Temple
40.overview:
Where we are. The last nine chapters of Ezekiel (40–48) are one great vision. Fourteen years after Jerusalem fell, God shows the priest-prophet a new temple, a renewed land and a holy city. The book that began with God’s glory beside a canal in Babylon is about to end with that glory coming home (43:1–5).

The message. God has not finished with his dwelling among his people. The temple lies in ashes, but in this vision he measures out a new house: perfectly ordered, guarded in its holiness, open on every side, and centred on the altar. Chapter 40 says that the way into God’s presence is real, but it is holy, it rises step by step, and it passes the place of sacrifice.

Why it was said. The exiles had lost the temple, the centre of their faith and the sign that God lived among them (see the introduction). Many must have wondered whether God’s house and God’s presence were gone for ever. This vision, to be declared “to the house of Israel” (v. 4), told them that God’s dwelling with them had a future, and showed them the holiness the old temple had lost.

How the chapter makes its case. On a very high mountain a guide like bronze, holding a measuring reed, tells Ezekiel to look, listen and set his heart on all he sees (vv. 1–4). He measures the outer wall and the great east gate, with its guardrooms and palm trees (vv. 5–16), then the outer court and its matching north and south gates (vv. 17–27), then the gates of the inner court, higher still (vv. 28–37). At the inner gate stand tables for sacrifice and rooms for the priests who keep the temple and the altar, and the altar stands before the house (vv. 38–49). Every measurement says that God’s house is ordered, holy and secure.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by promise. The temple was where God lived among his people, and Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21): in him God dwells with us. The rising steps ask, “Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD?” (Psalm 24:3), and he is the one with clean hands who brings his people in. The tables of sacrifice point to his single offering for sins (Hebrews 10:12), and the measured house finds its completion in the city whose “temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22).

For us. God’s presence is not cheap, but it is open. Christians do not wait for a building to be raised: in Christ we have already come near, and are being built together into “a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). So come to God through Christ’s sacrifice, take his holiness seriously, and set your heart on the city where he will live among his people for ever.
40.theology:
After judgment God gives his people a vision of his dwelling restored in perfect holiness and order (vv. 1-4).

Measuring marks God's ownership and protection of what is his (vv. 3, 5; Zech 2:1-5; Rev 11:1; 21:15-17).

God’s holiness requires a clear boundary between what is holy and what is ordinary (v. 5).

Coming near to God is pictured as a climb, open only to those with clean hands and a pure heart, and Christ alone gives these (vv. 22, 31, 49; Ps 24:3-4; John 10:9).

The sacrifices of the vision point to the single sacrifice of Christ, after which no offering for sin remains (vv. 38-43; Heb 10:11-14, 18).

The temple vision finds its fulfilment in Christ the true temple, the church as God's dwelling, and the new creation (John 2:19-21; Eph 2:19-22; Rev 21:10-22).
40.examples:
A family who have lost their home in a fire may be shown the architect's plans for the new house before a single brick is laid. The plans are a promise. So were these measurements to a priest whose temple was ashes.

The steps of the vision (seven, then eight, then ten) are a picture every worshipper understands: no one climbs to God by his own purity, but Christ, who alone has clean hands and a pure heart, brings his people up with him.

keyVerse.quote: And the man said to me, “Son of man, look with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you, for you were brought here in order that I might show it to you. Declare all that you see to the house of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: This verse tells us how to read the whole temple vision: not as dry architecture but as something to look at closely, listen to and take to heart. It was given for a people who had lost everything, to show them that God’s dwelling among them had a future. That future has a name: Christ, the true temple, in whom God lives with his people.

40.reflection:
Ezekiel is told to “look with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you” (v. 4). Why do you think God gave exiles with a burned temple such a detailed vision? What does it look like to set your heart on God’s promises when what you can see is in ruins?

The vision begins with a wall that separates the holy from the common (v. 5; 42:20). In what ways do Christians today treat God’s holiness casually, and how does the gospel both welcome us in and call us to reverence?

The steps rise from seven to eight to ten as the worshipper comes nearer to God (vv. 22, 31, 49). How does Psalm 24:3–4 answer the question these steps raise, and how does Christ make it possible for us to “draw near” (Hebrews 10:22)?

The whole vision is ordered around the altar and the house of God (v. 47). How do Jesus’ words “something greater than the temple is here” (Matthew 12:6) change the way we read chapters like this one?
