verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — This Is the Most Holy Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the heart of God’s house is a room God alone fills, and Ezekiel is not taken into it. The guide measures the entrance and the nave, forty cubits by twenty (vv. 1–2). Then he goes alone into the inner room and measures it, twenty cubits square, the same as the inner sanctuary of Solomon’s temple, and names it: “This is the Most Holy Place” (vv. 3–4). The prophet is a priest, but not the high priest, so he watches from the doorway. The exiles are being told that God will again have a dwelling at the centre of his people’s life, and that he will be as holy there as he ever was.
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of God's house is the place of his holy presence, where no one may come casually.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me to the nave and measured the jambs. On each side six cubits was the breadth of the jambs. And the breadth of the entrance was ten cubits, and the sidewalls of the entrance were five cubits on either side. And he measured the length of the nave, forty cubits, and its breadth, twenty cubits. Then he went into the inner room and measured the jambs of the entrance, two cubits; and the entrance, six cubits; and the sidewalls on either side of the entrance, seven cubits. And he measured the length of the room, twenty cubits, and its breadth, twenty cubits, across the nave. And he said to me, "This is the Most Holy Place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guide alone enters the Most Holy Place, a perfect square at the heart of the house, while Ezekiel watches from outside.

He went into the inner room. The guide goes in; Ezekiel, a priest but not the high priest, is not said to follow. This was the room no ordinary priest could enter: “into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year” (Hebrews 9:7).

This is the Most Holy Place. Twenty cubits by twenty, the same size as the inner sanctuary of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:20): a perfect square at the heart of the vision, the place of God’s own presence. For the exiles, it promised that God would again be at the centre of his people’s life.

The curtain torn. For Christians it speaks of something greater. When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). Now “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20). The room that Ezekiel could only watch being measured from its doorway is open to every believer in Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The nave, the main hall, is forty cubits by twenty (v. 2), the same as in Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 6:2, 17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is built to last and set apart from everything around it. The temple wall is six cubits thick, and around it rise side chambers in three storeys, thirty to a storey, resting on ledges so that they do not lean on the temple wall itself and widening as they go up (vv. 5–7). The whole building stands on a raised platform, with open space around it and doors on the north and south (vv. 8–11). To the west stands a large building facing a separate yard (v. 12). Nothing here is temporary or makeshift. The God who returns to dwell with his people intends to stay.
verseByVerse.theology: God's house is solid, spacious and set apart.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he measured the wall of the temple, six cubits thick, and the breadth of the side chambers, four cubits, all around the temple. And the side chambers were in three stories, one over another, thirty in each story. There were offsets all around the wall of the temple to serve as supports for the side chambers, so that they should not be supported by the wall of the temple. And it became broader as it wound upward to the side chambers, because the temple was enclosed upward all around the temple. Thus the temple had a broad area upward, and so one went up from the lowest story to the top story through the middle story. I saw also that the temple had a raised platform all around; the foundations of the side chambers measured a full reed of six long cubits. The thickness of the outer wall of the side chambers was five cubits. The free space between the side chambers of the temple and the other chambers was a breadth of twenty cubits all around the temple on every side. And the doors of the side chambers opened on the free space, one door toward the north, and another door toward the south. And the breadth of the free space was five cubits all around. The building that was facing the separate yard on the west side was seventy cubits broad, and the wall of the building was five cubits thick all around, and its length ninety cubits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple is wrapped in solid walls and side chambers and set on a raised platform with open space around it: God’s house is permanent, secure and set apart.

The side chambers were in three stories. Much like those around Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:5–6), they probably stored offerings and temple equipment.

What do all these details say? That God’s house is solid, well built and orderly: not a flimsy tent pitched in a hurry, but permanent. And it is surrounded by space, separated from everything around it. God’s presence among his people is both secure and holy.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 7 is compressed and hard to follow. The likely sense is the ESV’s: the temple wall stepped inward at each storey, so each level of chambers was a little wider than the one below.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house is perfectly proportioned, and its walls are carved like a garden. The guide measures the temple, the yard behind it and the eastern front: a hundred cubits each way (vv. 13–15). Inside, the walls are panelled with wood from floor to windows, and on every wall, inside and out, is a carved pattern: “cherubim and palm trees, a palm tree between cherub and cherub”, each cherub with a human face turned to one palm and a lion’s face to the other (vv. 16–20). Cherubim and trees recall Eden, the garden where God walked with man. The house where God will dwell is the garden given back.
verseByVerse.theology: The temple is a picture of Eden, where God dwells with his people again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he measured the temple, a hundred cubits long; and the yard and the building with its walls, a hundred cubits long; also the breadth of the east front of the temple and the yard, a hundred cubits. Then he measured the length of the building facing the yard that was at the back and its galleries on either side, a hundred cubits. The inside of the nave and the vestibules of the court, the thresholds and the narrow windows and the galleries all around the three of them, opposite the threshold, were paneled with wood all around, from the floor up to the windows (now the windows were covered), to the space above the door, even to the inner room, and on the outside. And on all the walls all around, inside and outside, was a measured pattern. It was carved of cherubim and palm trees, a palm tree between cherub and cherub. Every cherub had two faces: a human face toward the palm tree on the one side, and the face of a young lion toward the palm tree on the other side. They were carved on the whole temple all around. From the floor to above the door, cherubim and palm trees were carved; similarly the wall of the nave.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole house is perfectly proportioned, and every wall is carved with cherubim and palm trees: the house where God dwells is Eden given back.

A hundred cubits long. A hundred cubits each way (vv. 13–15). Again and again the vision uses round, balanced numbers and squares, and nothing is out of proportion. The old temple had been corrupted by idols and disorder; this one is perfectly ordered.

A palm tree between cherub and cherub. Every wall bears the same design: cherub, palm tree, cherub, palm tree. Each cherub has two faces, one human and one like a young lion, looking toward the trees on either side. (The living creatures of Ezekiel’s first vision had four faces, 1:10, but a flat carving can show only two.)

Back to Eden. Cherubim and trees take us back to the beginning. After Adam and Eve sinned, God “placed the cherubim and a flaming sword” to guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24). Israel’s sanctuaries were decorated to recall Eden, the garden where God walked with people, and in Ezekiel’s vision cherubim and palms cover every wall of the house where God will live among his people. What was lost in Eden is being given back.

The Bible’s last garden. The Bible ends in that garden restored: “No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face” (Revelation 22:3–4).

Uncertain wording. Some building terms in verses 15–17, such as the “galleries” and parts of the panelling, are rare words of uncertain meaning (ESV notes). The main point, a house panelled and carved throughout, is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–26 — The Table Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the Holy Place stands a table, and the doors of the house are made to open. The guide notes something like a wooden altar, three cubits high and two square, and explains it: “This is the table that is before the LORD” (vv. 21–22). It is the only object in the building he interprets, and it speaks of fellowship with God in his presence. The nave and the Holy Place each have double doors with swinging leaves, carved with cherubim and palm trees like the walls, and windows and palm carvings line the vestibule (vv. 23–26). Holiness stands at the centre of God’s house, and beside it a table and an open door.
verseByVerse.theology: God sets a table in his presence for fellowship with his people.

verseByVerse.quote: The doorposts of the nave were squared, and in front of the Holy Place was something resembling an altar of wood, three cubits high, two cubits long, and two cubits broad. Its corners, its base, and its walls were of wood. He said to me, "This is the table that is before the LORD." The nave and the Holy Place had each a double door. The double doors had two leaves apiece, two swinging leaves for each door. And on the doors of the nave were carved cherubim and palm trees, such as were carved on the walls. And there was a canopy of wood in front of the vestibule outside. And there were narrow windows and palm trees on either side, on the sidewalls of the vestibule, the side chambers of the temple, and the canopies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one object the guide explains is a table before the LORD: God’s holy house is also a place of fellowship, with doors made to open.

This is the table that is before the LORD. It recalls the table in the tabernacle, where the priests set “the bread of the Presence on the table before me regularly” (Exodus 25:30), twelve loaves set out afresh every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–8).

A place of fellowship. It is the only furniture the guide explains, and it is a table. God’s house is not only a place of awe but a place of fellowship: the God before whom priests bowed also sets a table in his presence.

The living bread that came down from heaven. That table points to Christ: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:51). And the risen Lord still says to his people, “If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20).

The double doors had two leaves apiece. The doors are carved with the same cherubim and palms. Doors are made to open. The house of God is not a fortress sealed shut, but a house whose doors swing wide for those whom God welcomes.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of the word translated “canopy” (v. 25) is uncertain (ESV note). And the “altar of wood” that the guide calls a “table” (vv. 21–22) is usually taken as the table for the bread of the Presence, though its square, tall shape is closer to the incense altar that also stood before the inner room (Exodus 30:1–6). The guide’s own word, “table”, is the safest guide.

41.title: The Most Holy Place
41.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 40–48 are Ezekiel’s last vision, given in 573 BC, fourteen years after Jerusalem fell (40:1). A guide with a measuring reed has led him through the gates and courts of a new temple (chapter 40); now he brings him into the building itself.

The message. At the centre of God’s house is the room where God himself dwells, and before it a table set in his presence. God is telling exiles whose temple lay in ashes that he will again live among his people: as holy as ever, so that the inner room is entered only by his appointment, and as generous as ever, spreading a table before himself. The walls carved with cherubim and palm trees add that what was lost in Eden is being given back.

Why it was said. The temple had been burned and its glory had departed (see the introduction), and the exiles could easily believe that God’s presence among them was finished for ever. A house measured to the cubit answers that fear. God’s plan is not a vague hope but exact and settled; in Scripture, to measure something is to claim it and protect it (compare Revelation 11:1).

How the chapter makes its case. The guide measures the nave and then goes alone into the inner room, twenty cubits square: “This is the Most Holy Place” (vv. 1–4). Thick walls, three storeys of side chambers, a raised platform and open space all around show a house that is permanent and set apart (vv. 5–12). The whole complex is a hundred cubits each way, and its panelled walls are carved throughout with cherubim and palm trees, a garden in wood (vv. 13–20). Before the Holy Place stands the one object the guide names, “the table that is before the LORD”, and carved double doors that open (vv. 21–26).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The inner room that Ezekiel only watched being measured is the room Christ has opened: when he died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51), and now we enter “by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). The table before the LORD finds its meaning in him who is “the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51), and the carved garden points to the city where God’s servants “will see his face” (Revelation 22:4).

For us. Ezekiel stood at the doorway; in Christ, believers are welcomed inside. Do not treat that access lightly, for the room is still the Most Holy Place, but do not stand back from it either. Come near in prayer with confidence, and take your place at the table God sets for his children.
41.theology:
At the centre of God's dwelling is the Most Holy Place, where no one may enter casually (vv. 3-4; Heb 9:7-8).

In Christ the way into God's holy presence has been opened to all believers (Matt 27:51; Heb 10:19-22).

God's house is solid, ordered and set apart (vv. 5-17).

The cherubim and palm trees picture Eden restored, where God dwells with his people and nothing accursed remains (vv. 18-20; Gen 3:24; Rev 22:3-4).

God sets a table before him for fellowship, fulfilled in Christ the bread of life (v. 22; Exod 25:30; John 6:48-51; Rev 3:20).
41.examples:
A believer who feels unworthy to pray may think of the inner room that Ezekiel could only watch from the door. Because Christ gave his body to death for us, that door stands open, and the weakest Christian may come in with confidence.

At the Lord's Supper, Christians gather at a table in God's house. The table Ezekiel saw, before the LORD, says that God's holiness and his welcome belong together.

keyVerse.quote: And he said to me, “This is the Most Holy Place.”
keyVerse.note: Every measurement in the chapter leads to this room. At the centre of the house God promised to his exiled people is the place of his own presence, holy and entered only by his appointment. In Christ the curtain has been torn and the way into that presence opened to all who trust him (Hebrews 10:19–20).

41.reflection:
The guide goes into the Most Holy Place, while Ezekiel apparently stays at the doorway (vv. 3–4). How does Hebrews 10:19–22 change where a believer stands? What does “confidence” before God look like in your prayers?

The walls are carved with cherubim and palm trees, recalling Eden (vv. 18–20; Genesis 3:24). What does it tell us about God’s purpose that his house is pictured as a garden given back?

The only object the guide explains is “the table that is before the LORD” (v. 22). Why might God want his house to be a place of fellowship as well as awe, and how do we keep both together in our worship?

God’s house is solid, measured and permanent (vv. 5–15). Where do you need the assurance that God’s purposes for his people are settled and not makeshift?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the side rooms of God’s house are planned with care, because they are for holy use. The guide leads Ezekiel into the outer court and shows him a long block of chambers on the north side of the temple, a hundred cubits by fifty, three storeys high, with a passage in front (vv. 1–4). The upper chambers are set back and narrower than the lower ones, since they have no pillars (vv. 5–6). A wall runs in front of them, and an entrance on the east leads in from the outer court (vv. 7–9). A matching block stands on the south side, with the same measurements and doors (vv. 10–12). What these rooms are for comes in the next verses.
verseByVerse.theology: God's house provides a place for those who serve him to live out their holy calling.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he led me out into the outer court, toward the north, and he brought me to the chambers that were opposite the separate yard and opposite the building on the north. The length of the building whose door faced north was a hundred cubits, and the breadth fifty cubits. Facing the twenty cubits that belonged to the inner court, and facing the pavement that belonged to the outer court, was gallery against gallery in three stories. And before the chambers was a passage inward, ten cubits wide and a hundred cubits long, and their doors were on the north. Now the upper chambers were narrower, for the galleries took more away from them than from the lower and middle chambers of the building. For they were in three stories, and they had no pillars like the pillars of the courts. Thus the upper chambers were set back from the ground more than the lower and the middle ones. And there was a wall outside parallel to the chambers, toward the outer court, opposite the chambers, fifty cubits long. For the chambers on the outer court were fifty cubits long, while those opposite the nave were a hundred cubits long. Below these chambers was an entrance on the east side, as one enters them from the outer court. In the thickness of the wall of the court, on the south also, opposite the yard and opposite the building, there were chambers with a passage in front of them. They were similar to the chambers on the north, of the same length and breadth, with the same exits and arrangements and doors, as were the entrances of the chambers on the south. There was an entrance at the beginning of the passage, the passage before the corresponding wall on the east as one enters them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two matching blocks of rooms stand north and south of the temple, and the care taken over them prepares for their purpose: they are holy rooms for holy use.

Then he led me out into the outer court. Why so much detail about two blocks of rooms? The next verses give the answer: these are not storerooms but holy chambers (v. 13).

Why the detail matters. The long descriptions remind us that God cares about the whole of his house, not only its dramatic centre. The side rooms, the passages and the doors all belong to him.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of some words in these verses, and of verse 12 as a whole, is uncertain. The exact layout cannot be recovered with confidence, but the general picture, two matching blocks of rooms with passages and entrances, is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–14 — Holy Food and Holy Garments
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What is given to God must be handled as his. The guide explains the chambers: they are “the holy chambers”, where the priests who approach the LORD eat the most holy offerings and store them, the grain, sin and guilt offerings, “for the place is holy” (v. 13). And when the priests leave the Holy Place, they must lay aside the garments in which they ministered and put on others before they go out to the people (v. 14). Holy food is eaten in a holy place, and holy clothes are not worn into ordinary life. The line between God’s presence and common life is real, and it is kept.
verseByVerse.theology: What belongs to God must be treated as holy, and his servants must honour the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to me, "The north chambers and the south chambers opposite the yard are the holy chambers, where the priests who approach the LORD shall eat the most holy offerings. There they shall put the most holy offerings— the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering—for the place is holy. When the priests enter the Holy Place, they shall not go out of it into the outer court without laying there the garments in which they minister, for these are holy. They shall put on other garments before they go near to that which is for the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are holy rooms where the priests eat the most holy offerings and leave their holy garments: what is given to God is handled as his, and holiness is not a costume to wear anywhere.

The most holy offerings. The priests eat their portion of the “most holy offerings” here, as the law required: “The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. In a holy place it shall be eaten” (Leviticus 6:26). Things given to God were not to be handled casually or eaten just anywhere.

The garments in which they minister. The priests must also leave their holy garments in the chambers before going out among the people. On the Day of Atonement Aaron did the same: he was to “take off the linen garments that he put on when he went into the Holy Place and shall leave them there” (Leviticus 16:23). Holiness is not a costume to wear casually wherever you go. It marks a real difference between God’s presence and ordinary life.

Clothed by God. The gospel speaks of garments too. Zechariah saw the high priest standing in filthy clothes, and God said, “Remove the filthy garments from him … Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments” (Zechariah 3:4). Believers are those who “have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 7:14). Once the holy garments stayed in the holy rooms; in Christ, they go with us into ordinary life: “Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience” (Colossians 3:12).

What is given to God. The rules seem remote, but the principle is not. We were “bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20), so the time, money and gifts we dedicate to him are not ours to treat as ordinary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–20 — A Separation Between the Holy and the Common
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The purpose of the whole temple vision so far is a wall around holiness. The guide leads Ezekiel out by the east gate and measures the temple area from outside: east, north, south and west, five hundred cubits each, a perfect square (vv. 15–19). It has a wall around it, “to make a separation between the holy and the common” (v. 20). That was exactly the line Jerusalem’s priests had erased (22:26), and its loss had filled the old temple with idols. Now it is built into the plan. And the wall has a gate on the east, through which God himself will come (43:1–5).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole temple vision teaches that God is holy and must be approached as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he had finished measuring the interior of the temple area, he led me out by the gate that faced east, and measured the temple area all around. He measured the east side with the measuring reed, 500 cubits by the measuring reed all around. He measured the north side, 500 cubits by the measuring reed all around. He measured the south side, 500 cubits by the measuring reed. Then he turned to the west side and measured, 500 cubits by the measuring reed. He measured it on the four sides. It had a wall around it, 500 cubits long and 500 cubits broad, to make a separation between the holy and the common.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole temple area is a perfect square walled off “to make a separation between the holy and the common”: the line Jerusalem erased is built again in stone, so that the holy God can dwell among his people.

He measured it on the four sides. Five hundred cubits each side is about 875 feet. John saw the new Jerusalem the same way: “The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width” (Revelation 21:16).

A separation between the holy and the common. Here, at the end of three chapters of measurement, is the purpose of it all, and it explains everything that went wrong before. God had told Aaron’s sons from the start, “You are to distinguish between the holy and the common” (Leviticus 10:10). Ezekiel had charged Jerusalem’s priests: “They have made no distinction between the holy and the common” (22:26). Idolatry crept into God’s house because the line had been erased. In the new temple, the line is built in stone.

A gate in the wall. Yet the wall has a gate on the east, and in the next chapter the glory of God comes through it (43:4). Holiness is not meant to keep God away from his people; it is what makes it possible for him to live among them. And in Christ the Holy One did not stay behind the wall. He came out to the common and the unclean, to make them holy.

Nobody lives without holy ground. To many modern people a line between the holy and the common sounds like religious fussiness. Yet watch how people actually live. The historian of religion Mircea Eliade observed that even thoroughly secular people keep privileged places of their own: a birthplace, the scene of a first love, a grave they go back to. We lower our voices at a war memorial, fans call a stadium hallowed turf, and nations have flags that must not touch the ground. We all set something apart and treat it as untouchable. The question is never whether we have holy things, but which ones, and whether they deserve it. Ezekiel’s wall puts the line where it belongs, around the living God.

Holy in all your conduct. Christians do not worship in a walled temple, but the principle stands: “as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, ‘You shall be holy, for I am holy’” (1 Peter 1:15–16). The separation is no longer a wall of stone but a holy way of life: “go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you” (2 Corinthians 6:17). That holiness rests on what God has done: he called us and gives us his Holy Spirit (1 Thessalonians 4:7–8), and where we fall short, Christ himself is our holiness (1 Corinthians 1:30).

Does being separate mean Christians should withdraw from unbelievers? No. Paul says that would mean leaving the world altogether (1 Corinthians 5:9–10), and Jesus prayed not that his people be taken out of the world but kept from the evil one (John 17:15). The separation is from sin and false worship, not from people. Jesus shows what holiness does now: when he touched a leper, the leper did not make him unclean; Jesus made the leper clean (Mark 1:41–42).

Textual note. The King James Version reads “five hundred reeds”, six times longer; the ESV follows the Greek translation, which matches 45:2.

42.title: Between the Holy and the Common
42.overview:
Where we are. The tour of the new temple is ending. Having seen the Most Holy Place at the heart of the house (chapter 41), Ezekiel is led out to the priests’ rooms beside it, and then outside the whole complex to watch its outer wall measured. Chapter 43 will bring the climax: the glory of God returning through the east gate.

The message. God’s house is walled off “to make a separation between the holy and the common” (v. 20). The line that Jerusalem had rubbed out is drawn again, in stone. Holiness is not religious fussiness: it is what makes it possible for a holy God to live among his people, and so what belongs to him is to be treated as his, from the priests’ food to their clothes.

Why it was said. Ezekiel had charged Jerusalem’s priests: “They have made no distinction between the holy and the common” (22:26), and he had seen the result, idols worshipped inside the temple itself (chapter 8) and the glory departing (see the introduction). The exiles needed to understand that their disaster began when that line was erased, and that God’s new beginning would put it back.

How the chapter makes its case. The guide shows Ezekiel two long, three-storey blocks of chambers north and south of the temple (vv. 1–12). Then he explains them: these are “the holy chambers”, where the priests eat the most holy offerings and leave their holy garments before going out to the people (vv. 13–14). Finally he measures the whole temple area from outside, five hundred cubits on every side, a perfect square with a wall around it, and the chapter’s last words give the purpose of three chapters of measuring: “to make a separation between the holy and the common” (vv. 15–20).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by showing what God is like. The wall says God is holy; the gospel shows the Holy One coming out to the common and unclean to make them holy. When Jesus touched a leper, the leper did not make him unclean; Jesus made the leper clean (Mark 1:41–42). He clothes sinners in clean garments (Zechariah 3:4; Revelation 7:14) and is himself our “sanctification” (1 Corinthians 1:30), and the square wall points to the city that “lies foursquare” (Revelation 21:16), where God and his people live together.

For us. Everyone treats something as holy; the question is whether the line is drawn around the living God. Christians do not need walls of stone, but we are called to be “holy in all your conduct” (1 Peter 1:15): not to withdraw from people, but to refuse sin and false worship, gladly, because Christ has made us his own.
42.theology:
What is given to God is holy and must not be treated as ordinary (v. 13; Lev 6:26).

Holiness marks a real difference between God's presence and common life (v. 14; Lev 16:23-24).

In Christ believers are given clean garments and called to put on holiness in all of life (Zech 3:3-5; Rev 7:14; Col 3:12).

The purpose of the temple vision is to separate the holy from the common, reversing the failure that brought judgment (v. 20; 22:26; Lev 10:10).

God's people are called to be holy as he is holy, and holiness is what allows God to dwell among them (1 Pet 1:15-16; 2 Cor 6:17).
42.examples: A Christian who gives a regular gift to God's work and then quietly takes it back when money is tight has blurred the line Ezekiel saw in stone. What has been given to God is his.

keyVerse.quote: He measured it on the four sides. It had a wall around it, 500 cubits long and 500 cubits broad, to make a separation between the holy and the common.
keyVerse.note: The last words of the chapter give the purpose of three chapters of measuring. The line between holy and common that Jerusalem’s priests had erased (22:26) is built into God’s new house, so that he can dwell among his people. In Christ that holiness no longer keeps sinners out; it comes out to make them clean.

42.reflection:
Why do you think God spent three chapters measuring a house, ending with a wall “to make a separation between the holy and the common” (v. 20)? What had happened in Jerusalem when that line was erased (22:26)?

The priests had to leave their holy garments before going out to the people (v. 14), but Paul tells believers to “put on” compassion, kindness and humility every day (Colossians 3:12). What has changed in Christ, and what does it look like to wear those garments at work or at home?

Everyone treats something as untouchable: a place, a flag, a person, a cause. What are the “holy things” of the people around you, and of your own heart? Do they deserve that place?

Holiness in the New Testament means separation from sin, not from sinners (1 Corinthians 5:9–10; Mark 1:41–42). How can a church be clearly holy and still warmly open to outsiders?

And I fell on my face.<sup>4</sup>As the glory of the LORD entered the temple by the gate facing east,<sup>5</sup>the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple.<sup>6</sup>While the man was standing beside me, I heard one speaking to me out of the temple,<sup>7</sup>and he said to me, "Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever. Behold, this is the law of the temple.<sup>13</sup>"These are the measurements of the altar by cubits (the cubit being a cubit and a handbreadth): its base shall be one cubit high and one cubit broad, with a rim of one span around its edge. And this shall be the height of the altar:<sup>14</sup>from the base on the ground to the lower ledge, two cubits, with a breadth of one cubit; and from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge, four cubits, with a breadth of one cubit;<sup>15</sup>and the altar hearth, four cubits; and from the altar hearth projecting upward, four horns.<sup>16</sup>The altar hearth shall be square, twelve cubits long by twelve broad.<sup>17</sup>The ledge also shall be square, fourteen cubits long by fourteen broad, with a rim around it half a cubit broad, and its base one cubit all around. The steps of the altar shall face east."<sup>18</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, thus says the Lord GOD: These are the ordinances for the altar: On the day when it is erected for offering burnt offerings upon it and for throwing blood against it,<sup>19</sup>you shall give to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok, who draw near to me to minister to me, declares the Lord GOD, a bull from the herd for a sin offering.<sup>20</sup>And you shall take some of its blood and put it on the four horns of the altar and on the four corners of the ledge and upon the rim all around. Thus you shall purify the altar and make atonement for it.<sup>21</sup>You shall also take the bull of the sin offering, and it shall be burned in the appointed place belonging to the temple, outside the sacred area.<sup>22</sup>And on the second day you shall offer a male goat without blemish for a sin offering; and the altar shall be purified, as it was purified with the bull.<sup>23</sup>When you have finished purifying it, you shall offer a bull from the herd without blemish and a ram from the flock without blemish.<sup>24</sup>You shall present them before the LORD, and the priests shall sprinkle salt on them and offer them up as a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>25</sup>For seven days you shall provide daily a male goat for a sin offering; also, a bull from the herd and a ram from the flock, without blemish, shall be provided.<sup>26</sup>Seven days shall they make atonement for the altar and cleanse it, and so consecrate it.<sup>27</sup>And when they have completed these days, then from the eighth day onward the priests shall offer on the altar your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, and I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Glory of the LORD Filled the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The glory that left Jerusalem comes home. Ezekiel is brought to the east gate, the very gate by which the glory departed (10:19; 11:23), and “behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east”, with a sound like many waters, and the earth shone with it (vv. 1–2). It is the same glory he saw by the Chebar canal and when God came to destroy the city, and again he falls on his face (v. 3). The glory enters by the east gate, the Spirit lifts Ezekiel into the inner court, “and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple” (vv. 4–5). God has not abandoned his people.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who left his defiled house in judgment comes back to dwell with his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he led me to the gate, the gate facing east. And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east. And the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory. And the vision I saw was just like the vision that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and just like the vision that I had seen by the Chebar canal. And I fell on my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of God, which Ezekiel saw leave the temple years before, comes back from the east: the same holy God who judged now returns to dwell.

The glory of the God of Israel. This is the moment the whole book has been waiting for. Nineteen years earlier Ezekiel had watched the glory of God leave the temple. It rose from the cherubim, paused at “the entrance of the east gate” (10:19), and then “stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city” (11:23). Then it was gone, and God abandoned his defiled house to the Babylonians.

Like the sound of many waters. Now Ezekiel stands at that same east gate, and the glory is coming back from the direction it left. The sound is “like the sound of many waters”, the thunder of a great river or the sea; when John saw the risen Christ, “his voice was like the roar of many waters” (Revelation 1:15). “The earth shone with his glory”: not a private light in one building, but a glory that lights up the whole land.

Just like the vision that I had seen. Ezekiel makes sure we connect the three visions. The glory by the Chebar canal (chapter 1) came to call him; the glory in chapters 8–11 came “to destroy the city”; now the same glory comes to dwell. It is one and the same God, holy in judgment and holy in mercy. And Ezekiel responds exactly as before: “I fell on my face”. When God returns in grace, he is no less awesome.
verseByVerse.note: The east gate by which the glory enters will afterwards be shut for good (44:1-2): the LORD who has come home will not leave again.

verseByVerse.quote: As the glory of the LORD entered the temple by the gate facing east, the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory fills the temple as it once filled the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple: God has not left his people for good.

The glory of the LORD filled the temple. The words echo the great days of Israel’s worship. When Moses finished the tabernacle, “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). When Solomon dedicated the temple, “the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:11). Now, after the disaster of the exile, it happens again. For the exiles in Babylon, this answered their deepest fear, that God had left them for good. He had not. He would come back.

Glory as of the only Son. And he did, in a way beyond Ezekiel’s sight: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Jesus pointed to his own body and called it “this temple” (John 2:19–21). The glory that filled Ezekiel’s temple came to live among us in a person.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Place of My Throne
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The returning King claims his throne and sets its terms. God speaks from inside the house: “this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever” (v. 7). Israel and its kings had defiled his name with idols and by building their palaces right up against his house, “with only a wall between me and them” (vv. 7–8); now they must put those things away (v. 9). Ezekiel is to describe the temple so that the people will be ashamed of their sins and keep its laws (vv. 10–11). And the law of the temple is that the whole mountaintop is most holy (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's presence among his people is forever, and it makes everything around it holy.

verseByVerse.quote: While the man was standing beside me, I heard one speaking to me out of the temple, and he said to me, "Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever. And the house of Israel shall no more defile my holy name, neither they, nor their kings, by their whoring and by the dead bodies of their kings at their high places, by setting their threshold by my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, with only a wall between me and them. They have defiled my holy name by their abominations that they have committed, so I have consumed them in my anger. Now let them put away their whoring and the dead bodies of their kings far from me, and I will dwell in their midst forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God claims the temple as his throne for ever, and names what drove him out before: idols, and kings who treated his house as an annex to their own.

The place of my throne. Now God himself speaks from inside the house: “this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet”. The temple is where the King of heaven sets his feet on earth. And the promise is not for a season: “I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever”. The Bible ends with that promise kept: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Revelation 21:3).

What went wrong before? God names two things. First, idolatry: “their whoring”, the book’s blunt word for spiritual unfaithfulness. Second, the kings. Whatever the precise practice behind “the dead bodies of their kings” (see below), the kings had treated God’s house as an annex to their own. Solomon’s palace stood right beside the temple (1 Kings 7:1–8), “with only a wall between me and them”, and Manasseh even “built altars in the house of the LORD” to other gods (2 Kings 21:4–5).

Now let them put away their whoring. God calls them to put away their idols after he has already come back to his house. It is not a price they must pay before he will come; it is simply that his presence and idolatry cannot live in the same place. Paul applies the same truth to the church: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16).

With only a wall between me and them. The danger is not only open idolatry but crowding God: building our own house right up against his and treating him as a neighbour whose property we can use. God will not share his throne.

When God becomes the palace chaplain. The kings of Judah did not abolish the temple. They kept it next door: useful, impressive and under their management. Every Christian culture knows the temptation. A nation, a party or a movement finds it convenient to have God on its side: his name on the coins, his blessing on the cause, his house a wall away from the seat of power. It feels like faithfulness, but it turns God into the chaplain of our project, called in for ceremonies and kept out of decisions. Sceptics see this clearly and are repelled by it, and they are right to be; God is more offended than they are, for this is how “they have defiled my holy name” (v. 8). The answer is not a church that withdraws from public life, but one that remembers who is on the throne. When a crowd tried to make Jesus king on its own terms, he withdrew (John 6:15). A people who belong to that King can serve their nation gladly without lending it God’s name, because the throne is already taken.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “dead bodies” may mean “monuments”, and that “at their high places” (hilltop shrines) may be read “at their deaths”. The Hebrew can refer either to royal burials near the temple or to memorial pillars set up for dead kings, and no one can be sure which. Either way, the kings had brought what was theirs, and what was unclean, up against God’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, describe to the house of Israel the temple, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities; and they shall measure the plan. And if they are ashamed of all that they have done, make known to them the design of the temple, its arrangement, its exits and its entrances, that is, its whole design; and make known to them as well all its statutes and its whole design and all its laws, and write it down in their sight, so that they may observe all its laws and all its statutes and carry them out. This is the law of the temple: the whole territory on the top of the mountain all around shall be most holy. Behold, this is the law of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God shows his people the house he will give them so that his goodness will shame them into repentance, and holiness now covers the whole mountain.

That they may be ashamed of their iniquities. Why did God show Ezekiel all those measurements in chapters 40–42? Here is the answer. When the exiles saw the beauty and holiness of the house God intended, they would see how far they had fallen.

Shamed by goodness. This is how grace works on the heart. God does not first demand that his people become worthy and then show them his plans. He shows them what he is going to do, and the sight of his goodness makes them ashamed. Ezekiel had said the same of God’s covenant love: “that you may remember and be confounded, and never open your mouth again because of your shame, when I atone for you for all that you have done” (16:63).

That they may observe all its laws. Shame leads to instruction: once they are ashamed, Ezekiel is to teach them the temple’s laws (v. 11). And instruction leads to obedience. The one who is truly sorry for sin wants to know how to live: “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

This is the law of the temple. The phrase is stated twice, like a frame around one sentence. Before, only the inner room was “most holy”. Now “the whole territory on the top of the mountain all around” is most holy. Holiness spreads outward from God’s presence. Revelation shows where this ends: a city shaped like the Most Holy Place, whose “length and width and height are equal” (Revelation 21:16; compare 1 Kings 6:20), where nothing unclean will ever enter (Revelation 21:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the centre of the restored worship stands an altar, because a holy God dwells among sinners only through sacrifice. The measurements use the long cubit, a cubit and a handbreadth (v. 13). The altar rises in stages like a stepped tower: a base with a rim, a lower ledge and a larger ledge, and on top a square hearth twelve cubits each way, with four horns projecting from its corners (vv. 13–16). The ledge is fourteen cubits square, and the steps face east (v. 17), so that the priest who climbs them faces the temple and the presence of God. Right after the glory returns, the place of atonement is set in order.
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of the court stands the altar: the way to God is by sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: "These are the measurements of the altar by cubits (the cubit being a cubit and a handbreadth): its base shall be one cubit high and one cubit broad, with a rim of one span around its edge. And this shall be the height of the altar: from the base on the ground to the lower ledge, two cubits, with a breadth of one cubit; and from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge, four cubits, with a breadth of one cubit; and the altar hearth, four cubits; and from the altar hearth projecting upward, four horns. The altar hearth shall be square, twelve cubits long by twelve broad. The ledge also shall be square, fourteen cubits long by fourteen broad, with a rim around it half a cubit broad, and its base one cubit all around. The steps of the altar shall face east."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the glory comes the altar: a holy God can dwell among sinful people only on the basis of atonement.

The measurements of the altar. The altar is placed in front of the temple in the inner court (40:47). The ESV notes give the measures: a cubit about eighteen inches, a handbreadth about three inches, a span about nine inches. It rises in stages like a stepped tower (base, lower ledge, upper ledge, hearth), with “four horns” at the top corners, where blood was applied for atonement (Leviticus 4:25).

The steps of the altar shall face east. A square hearth, a square ledge, steps on the east side. The priest climbing them would face west, toward the temple and the presence of God.

Why does the altar get so much attention right after the glory returns? Because a holy God can dwell among sinful people only on the basis of atonement. The glory fills the house; the altar stands before the house. Access to God has always come by the blood of sacrifice, and it comes now through the one sacrifice to which every altar pointed. “We have an altar”, says Hebrews (Hebrews 13:10): the cross where Christ offered himself.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the line about the base (v. 13) may instead read “its gutter shall be one cubit deep”. The Hebrew word can mean either the base of the altar or a trench around it, and several building terms in these verses are rare. The overall shape, a stepped altar with a square hearth and four horns, is clear.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the altar must be cleansed before it can be used, and then God will accept his people. On the first day a bull is offered as a sin offering, its blood put on the horns, corners and rim of the altar, and its body burned outside the sacred area (vv. 18–21). On the second day a goat without blemish is offered, and then a bull and a ram as burnt offerings, salted and wholly given to God (vv. 22–24). So it continues for seven days, until the altar is consecrated (vv. 25–26). From the eighth day the priests offer the people’s offerings, and God promises, “I will accept you” (v. 27). Every step points to the one sacrifice that makes sinners acceptable.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides the atonement by which he can accept his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, thus says the Lord GOD: These are the ordinances for the altar: On the day when it is erected for offering burnt offerings upon it and for throwing blood against it, you shall give to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok, who draw near to me to minister to me, declares the Lord GOD, a bull from the herd for a sin offering. And you shall take some of its blood and put it on the four horns of the altar and on the four corners of the ledge and upon the rim all around. Thus you shall purify the altar and make atonement for it. You shall also take the bull of the sin offering, and it shall be burned in the appointed place belonging to the temple, outside the sacred area.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar itself must be purified with blood, and the sin offering burned outside the sacred area: a picture fulfilled in Jesus, who suffered outside the gate.

Thus you shall purify the altar. Even the instrument of atonement must be made clean. Ezekiel is given a part to play, like Moses at the first altar (Exodus 29:36–37), and the ministry is given to “the family of Zadok”, the priestly line that had stayed faithful (44:15).

Put it on the four horns of the altar. Blood on every horn, every corner, the whole rim. Nothing in the service of God is clean by nature; everything must be purified by blood. “Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (Hebrews 9:22).

Outside the sacred area. The body of the sin offering, carrying the uncleanness, is taken out and burned. Hebrews sees Christ in exactly this detail: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:11–12). Our Lord was led out of the city to die, bearing the uncleanness of his people, so that we could be brought in.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the second day you shall offer a male goat without blemish for a sin offering; and the altar shall be purified, as it was purified with the bull. When you have finished purifying it, you shall offer a bull from the herd without blemish and a ram from the flock without blemish. You shall present them before the LORD, and the priests shall sprinkle salt on them and offer them up as a burnt offering to the LORD. For seven days you shall provide daily a male goat for a sin offering; also, a bull from the herd and a ram from the flock, without blemish, shall be provided. Seven days shall they make atonement for the altar and cleanse it, and so consecrate it. And when they have completed these days, then from the eighth day onward the priests shall offer on the altar your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, and I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After seven days of cleansing with perfect offerings, the altar is ready and God gives the verdict all of it serves: “I will accept you.”

A male goat without blemish. Day after day the cleansing continues: first a bull, then a goat “without blemish”. God requires a perfect offering, because only the perfect can atone for the imperfect. That requirement is met in “the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).

Offer them up as a burnt offering. After the sin offering come burnt offerings, the offering of complete dedication, wholly consumed on the altar. First sin is dealt with; then the worshipper gives himself entirely to God. The salt follows the old law: “with all your offerings you shall offer salt” (Leviticus 2:13), which that verse calls “the salt of the covenant with your God”, a sign of a lasting bond.

Seven days shall they make atonement. Seven days, as at the first consecration of the altar under Moses (Exodus 29:37). The ESV notes that the Hebrew behind “consecrate it” is “fill its hand”, the phrase used for installing a priest in his work. The altar is set apart completely for God.

I will accept you. Here is the goal of all the blood and all the days. Everything in the temple vision moves toward that sentence: a holy God receives a sinful people.

What it means to be accepted. Most of us spend our lives auditioning. We long to be accepted by a parent, a team, the people whose approval would finally tell us we are enough, and so we perform, and the performance never quite ends. “I will accept you” can sound like the result of a successful audition. But look at what comes before it: not Israel’s achievements, but seven days of blood on an altar God himself designed. That verdict was won by someone else. Every altar pointed to Christ, who offered himself once for all, and God now receives sinners for his sake, the way a father welcomes a child home, not the way an examiner grades a candidate. God has “blessed us in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6): we are welcomed because we are in his Son. So when you fail, or when someone’s disapproval lands hard, you do not have to start auditioning again. Confess the failure, stand on the verdict already given, and pass it on: “welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you” (Romans 15:7). The accepted people respond with their own offering: “present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1).

Where Christians differ: how should these sacrifices be read? Believers who expect a literal future temple often take them as memorials of the cross, or as rites of ritual cleansing that do not take away guilt. Others read the vision symbolically, as true worship pictured in the terms Ezekiel knew and fulfilled in Christ. This commentary’s view: the second (see 40:1–4), because Hebrews treats every animal sacrifice as a shadow that has given way to the reality (Hebrews 10:1). On any reading, the New Testament is clear that “where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin” (Hebrews 10:18). God’s acceptance now rests on Christ’s one sacrifice.

43.title: The Glory Comes Home
43.overview:
Where we are. This is the turning point of the whole book. In chapters 10–11 Ezekiel watched the glory of the LORD leave the defiled temple by the east gate and depart over the Mount of Olives. Since chapter 40 he has toured a new, measured house standing empty. Now, in the vision, the glory comes back.

The message. The God who left his defiled house returns to live among his people for ever, and he comes on the ground of atonement. He comes in grace, but he is no less holy: the idols and the kings who crowded his house must go, and the altar must be cleansed with blood. Then comes the sentence the whole vision has been moving toward: “I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD” (v. 27).

Why it was said. The exiles’ deepest fear was that God had gone for good, abandoning them with his burned house (see the introduction). This chapter answers it: he will come back, by his own choice and from the same direction he left. It also corrects their old false comfort: God’s presence is a gift, kept only where idolatry is put away and sin is atoned for.

How the chapter makes its case. The glory comes from the east with a sound like many waters and fills the temple (vv. 1–5). God speaks from the house: this is his throne, where he will dwell for ever, and Israel and its kings will no longer defile his name with idols or by building up against his house (vv. 6–9). Ezekiel must show them the plan so that they will be ashamed and obey, for the whole mountain is now most holy (vv. 10–12). The altar is measured (vv. 13–17) and consecrated by seven days of sin offerings and burnt offerings, after which God will accept his people’s worship (vv. 18–27).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The glory that returned to Ezekiel’s temple came to live among us in a person: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The altar that had to be purified with blood, and the sin offering burned outside the sacred area, point to the cross: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). Because of that one sacrifice God says to sinners in Christ what he said here: I will accept you.

For us. Our acceptance with God does not rest on our performance but on a sacrifice God himself provided. That frees us to stop auditioning for his approval, and it calls us to put away whatever idols crowd his place in our lives, because the Holy One has come to live with us.
43.theology:
The God who departed from his defiled house in judgment returns in glory to dwell with his people (vv. 1-5; 10:18-19; 11:22-23).

God's glory came to dwell among us in Jesus Christ, the true temple (John 1:14; 2:19-21).

God's presence among his people is forever, and it cannot coexist with idolatry (vv. 7-9; 2 Cor 6:16; Rev 21:3).

The sight of God's gracious purposes produces godly shame and a desire to obey (vv. 10-11; 16:63; 2 Cor 7:10).

Holiness spreads outward from God's presence until the whole mountain is most holy (v. 12; Rev 21:16, 27).

A holy God dwells with sinners only on the basis of atoning blood (vv. 13-26; Heb 9:22).

The sin offering burned outside the sacred area points to Christ, who suffered outside the gate (v. 21; Heb 13:11-12).

God's aim is acceptance: "I will accept you", now grounded in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, to which believers respond with their lives (v. 27; Heb 10:18; Rom 12:1).
43.examples:
Someone who has drifted from God for years may fear that he has left for good. The exiles feared the same. The glory came back through the very gate by which it had left.

It is easy to build our own lives right up against God's house, with only a wall between: a Sunday faith next to a weekday life that has no room for him. Verses 8-9 call us to put that away, and verse 27 tells us how we are received when we do: I will accept you.

keyVerse.quote: Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever.
keyVerse.note: The glory that left in judgment has come home, and God declares that he will never leave again. Everything else in the chapter, the call to put away idols and the altar cleansed with blood, serves this promise of God living among his people. It is kept in Christ, the Word made flesh, and completed when “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

43.reflection:
Ezekiel fell on his face when the glory returned in mercy, just as he had when it came in judgment (v. 3). Why is God no less awesome when he comes in grace? How should that shape the way we come to worship?

God calls his people to put away their idols after he has come back to his house (v. 9). Why does that order matter? What “idols” crowd God’s place in our lives, our churches or our nation (vv. 7–8)?

God shows the exiles the beauty of his house “that they may be ashamed of their iniquities” (v. 10). How does seeing God’s goodness lead to true repentance in a way that threats alone cannot?

The chapter ends, “I will accept you” (v. 27), after seven days of sacrifice. Where are you still “auditioning” for approval, from God or from others, and how does Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (Hebrews 10:18) set you free?

And it was shut.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to me, "This gate shall remain shut; it shall not be opened, and no one shall enter by it, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it. Therefore it shall remain shut.<sup>3</sup>Only the prince may sit in it to eat bread before the LORD. He shall enter by way of the vestibule of the gate, and shall go out by the same way."<sup>4</sup>Then he brought me by way of the north gate to the front of the temple, and I looked, and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple of the LORD. You have broken my covenant, in addition to all your abominations.<sup>8</sup>And you have not kept charge of my holy things, but you have set others to keep my charge for you in my sanctuary.<sup>9</sup>"Thus says the Lord GOD: No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and flesh, of all the foreigners who are among the people of Israel, shall enter my sanctuary.<sup>10</sup>But the Levites who went far from me, going astray from me after their idols when Israel went astray, shall bear their punishment.<sup>11</sup>They shall be ministers in my sanctuary, having oversight at the gates of the temple and ministering in the temple. They shall slaughter the burnt offering and the sacrifice for the people, and they shall stand before the people, to minister to them.<sup>12</sup>Because they ministered to them before their idols and became a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel, therefore I have sworn concerning them, declares the Lord GOD, and they shall bear their punishment.<sup>13</sup>They shall not come near to me, to serve me as priest, nor come near any of my holy things and the things that are most holy, but they shall bear their shame and the abominations that they have committed.<sup>14</sup>Yet I will appoint them to keep charge of the temple, to do all its service and all that is to be done in it.<sup>15</sup>"But the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept the charge of my sanctuary when the people of Israel went astray from me, shall come near to me to minister to me. And they shall stand before me to offer me the fat and the blood, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>16</sup>They shall enter my sanctuary, and they shall approach my table, to minister to me, and they shall keep my charge.<sup>17</sup>When they enter the gates of the inner court, they shall wear linen garments. They shall have nothing of wool on them, while they minister at the gates of the inner court, and within.<sup>18</sup>They shall have linen turbans on their heads, and linen undergarments around their waists. They shall keep my laws and my statutes in all my appointed feasts, and they shall keep my Sabbaths holy.<sup>25</sup>They shall not defile themselves by going near to a dead person.
