You shall also give to the priests the first of your dough, that a blessing may rest on your house.<sup>31</sup>The priests shall not eat of anything, whether bird or beast, that has died of itself or is torn by wild animals.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The gate the LORD entered is shut, because he has come to stay. The guide brings Ezekiel back to the outer east gate, and it is closed (v. 1). God explains: “This gate shall remain shut; it shall not be opened, and no one shall enter by it, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it” (v. 2). The way the King has walked is his alone, and the gate through which the glory once departed (10:19; 11:23) will never see it leave again. One exception is made: the prince, Israel’s ruler in the vision, may sit in the gateway to eat bread before the LORD, coming and going by the vestibule (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The way the LORD has come in is honoured as his alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me back to the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faces east. And it was shut. And the LORD said to me, "This gate shall remain shut; it shall not be opened, and no one shall enter by it, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it. Therefore it shall remain shut. Only the prince may sit in it to eat bread before the LORD. He shall enter by way of the vestibule of the gate, and shall go out by the same way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The east gate is shut for ever because the LORD has entered by it: the way the King came is his alone, and his glory will never leave his house again.

This gate shall remain shut. In chapter 43 the glory of God came in through the east gate. Now that gate is shut, and it is to stay shut, “for the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it”.

The LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it. Two things are being said. First, honour: the way the King has walked is his alone, and no one else will tread where the glory went. Second, permanence: the glory once went out through the east gate (10:19; 11:23). The shut gate says it will never leave that way again: “I will dwell in their midst forever” (43:9).

Only the prince may sit in it. One exception: “the prince” may sit inside the gateway to eat a sacred meal “before the LORD”, coming in and going out through the vestibule, not the shut doors. He is Israel’s ruler in the vision, the leader of God’s restored people, honoured with a place near God’s way. But he is clearly a man: later he provides a sin offering “for himself” (45:22), and he has sons (46:16).

Pointing to the Messiah. So the prince is not the Messiah himself, but he reminds us of the Messiah’s greater glory. Ezekiel’s prince eats in the gateway the LORD has passed through; Jesus is the LORD who came through it. And unlike every earthly ruler and priest, “He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27).

Does the shut east gate refer to Mary’s perpetual virginity, as some Catholic and Orthodox writers have taught? Nothing in the text points to Mary. The gate is shut because the LORD’s glory entered by it (43:4), and no one else may use it: a sign of his holiness. And Scripture speaks of Jesus’ brothers and sisters (Mark 6:3).

Is it the sealed Golden Gate in Jerusalem’s wall today? That gate was walled up many centuries after Christ, for reasons historians debate, and it belongs to a later city wall, not to the temple of Ezekiel’s vision. Visitors are often told it fulfils this verse, but the vision’s gate is shut for a different reason: the LORD has entered by it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who failed in God’s service lose the right to come near, yet they are not cast out. Ezekiel is brought to the front of the temple, sees the glory filling it and falls on his face (v. 4). God tells him to mark well the laws of his house (v. 5). Israel had brought foreigners “uncircumcised in heart and flesh” into the sanctuary and handed them the charge of holy things; no such person will enter now (vv. 6–9). The Levites who went astray after idols and became a stumbling block to Israel will bear their punishment: “They shall not come near to me, to serve me as priest” (vv. 10–13). “Yet I will appoint them to keep charge of the temple” (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: God takes unfaithfulness in his service seriously, yet still gives the fallen a place to serve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me by way of the north gate to the front of the temple, and I looked, and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple of the LORD. And I fell on my face. And the LORD said to me, "Son of man, mark well, see with your eyes, and hear with your ears all that I shall tell you concerning all the statutes of the temple of the LORD and all its laws. And mark well the entrance to the temple and all the exits from the sanctuary. And say to the rebellious house, to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: O house of Israel, enough of all your abominations, in admitting foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and flesh, to be in my sanctuary, profaning my temple, when you offer to me my food, the fat and the blood. You have broken my covenant, in addition to all your abominations. And you have not kept charge of my holy things, but you have set others to keep my charge for you in my sanctuary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the light of God’s glory, Israel is rebuked for letting people with no heart for God handle his holy things: they wanted the privilege of his house without its responsibility.

The glory of the LORD filled the temple. Ezekiel sees the glory again, and again he falls on his face. Everything that follows is spoken in the light of that glory: who may serve such a God? For the exiles, who knew that the glory had left the old temple because of the idolatry practised inside it (8:5–18), these rules were God’s promise that his new house would never be profaned in the same way.

Enough of all your abominations. God names a specific sin of the old temple: Israel had brought into the sanctuary “foreigners, uncircumcised in heart and flesh” and let them handle holy things. Ezekiel does not say who they were; probably foreign temple servants and guards, such as the Carites who once kept watch in the temple (2 Kings 11:4–8).

Uncircumcised in heart and flesh. The words matter. The problem was not nationality as such, for the law had always welcomed the foreigner who joined himself to the LORD. Isaiah promised that God would bring such people “to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer” (Isaiah 56:7). The problem was people with no heart for God and no part in his covenant doing the work of worship. And Israel itself could be “uncircumcised in heart” (Jeremiah 9:26).

You have set others to keep my charge for you. Here is the root of the sin. God’s people, above all those charged with the sanctuary, had handed their work to others, wanting the privilege without the responsibility. The warning reaches every church that lets the unconverted lead its worship, and every believer who leaves to others what God has given him to guard.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and flesh, of all the foreigners who are among the people of Israel, shall enter my sanctuary. But the Levites who went far from me, going astray from me after their idols when Israel went astray, shall bear their punishment. They shall be ministers in my sanctuary, having oversight at the gates of the temple and ministering in the temple. They shall slaughter the burnt offering and the sacrifice for the people, and they shall stand before the people, to minister to them. Because they ministered to them before their idols and became a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel, therefore I have sworn concerning them, declares the Lord GOD, and they shall bear their punishment. They shall not come near to me, to serve me as priest, nor come near any of my holy things and the things that are most holy, but they shall bear their shame and the abominations that they have committed. Yet I will appoint them to keep charge of the temple, to do all its service and all that is to be done in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The uncircumcised heart is shut out, and the Levites who led Israel into idolatry lose their priesthood, yet in mercy keep humbler work in God’s house.

No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and flesh. The door is closed to the uncircumcised heart. In the new covenant this line runs not between nations but between those who have been born again and those who have not: “For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit” (Romans 2:28–29). Through Christ, Gentiles once “strangers to the covenants of promise” are now “fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:12, 19).

The Levites who went far from me. Many of the Levites, the tribe that served the temple, had followed Israel into idolatry, and they “shall bear their punishment” (the ESV notes this may be “iniquity”: the Hebrew word covers both the sin and its penalty). Ezekiel probably has in mind those who had served at the high places, the local shrines where the LORD was worshipped alongside idols. When King Josiah closed those shrines, their priests were brought to Jerusalem but did not serve at the altar (2 Kings 23:8–9), and Ezekiel’s rule makes that demotion permanent.

A stumbling block of iniquity. Those who led the people into sin lose the privilege of drawing near as priests, and the fact that they misled others makes it more serious. Jesus spoke with the same gravity: “whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened around his neck” (Matthew 18:6).

Yet I will appoint them to keep charge of the temple. And yet, surprisingly, they are not thrown out. They still guard gates, slaughter sacrifices and serve the people. This is mercy, though mercy with consequences. Forgiveness does not always remove every consequence of sin; David was forgiven, yet the sword did not depart from his house (2 Samuel 12:10, 13). But God still gives the fallen a place and a task. There is humble, useful work in God’s house for those who have failed him. That is no small grace, and it rests on the faithful Priest who served perfectly where every other servant failed, whose obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–27 — The Faithful Sons of Zadok
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The faithful are rewarded with nearness, and nearness calls for holiness in every part of life. The sons of Zadok, who kept God’s charge when Israel went astray, will come near to minister and approach his table (vv. 15–16). They will wear linen in the inner court and change before going out to the people (vv. 17–19). Their hair, their drinking and their marriages are regulated (vv. 20–22). “They shall teach my people the difference between the holy and the common”, judge disputes by God’s judgments and keep his Sabbaths holy (vv. 23–24). They keep away from the dead except their closest family, and after defilement they offer a sin offering before serving again (vv. 25–27).
verseByVerse.theology: Faithfulness is honoured with nearness to God, and those who come near must be holy and must teach holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept the charge of my sanctuary when the people of Israel went astray from me, shall come near to me to minister to me. And they shall stand before me to offer me the fat and the blood, declares the Lord GOD. They shall enter my sanctuary, and they shall approach my table, to minister to me, and they shall keep my charge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of Zadok, who stayed faithful when others wandered, are rewarded with nearness to God and a place at his table.

The sons of Zadok. In contrast, the sons of Zadok kept faith when everyone else wandered. Zadok had stayed loyal to David and Solomon and was made priest in place of Abiathar (1 Kings 1:8; 2:35). Long before, God had promised, “I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind” (1 Samuel 2:35).

Shall come near to me. Their reward is nearness: they “shall come near to me to minister to me”. The highest reward of faithfulness is not position or wealth. It is God himself.

They shall approach my table. This is the table measured in 41:22: the faithful are brought to God’s table. The faithful priest God promised is found finally in Christ, “a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 2:17). To make propitiation is to turn God’s just anger away by a sacrifice. And through him all believers are made “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), invited to draw near.
verseByVerse.note: Zadok’s descendants held the high priesthood from Solomon’s day until the second century BC.

verseByVerse.quote: When they enter the gates of the inner court, they shall wear linen garments. They shall have nothing of wool on them, while they minister at the gates of the inner court, and within. They shall have linen turbans on their heads, and linen undergarments around their waists. They shall not bind themselves with anything that causes sweat. And when they go out into the outer court to the people, they shall put off the garments in which they have been ministering and lay them in the holy chambers. And they shall put on other garments, lest they transmit holiness to the people with their garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests serve in clean linen and leave their holy garments behind: worship is not sweating labour to earn God’s favour.

They shall wear linen garments. The priests must wear linen, as the law had required (Exodus 28:39–42): clean, light, white, with “nothing of wool”.

Anything that causes sweat. The rule is partly practical: linen keeps the body cool and clean. Some have seen here an echo of the curse, “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread” (Genesis 3:19), as if in God’s presence the toil of the fall is left behind. Either way, worship is not the sweating labour of people trying to earn God’s favour. It is service offered in clean garments God provides.

Lest they transmit holiness to the people. The rule of 42:14 is repeated: the holy garments stay in the holy chambers. Holiness is not to be carried out and spread carelessly, as if it were something people could catch without meeting God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not shave their heads or let their locks grow long; they shall surely trim the hair of their heads. No priest shall drink wine when he enters the inner court. They shall not marry a widow or a divorced woman, but only virgins of the offspring of the house of Israel, or a widow who is the widow of a priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests’ appearance, sobriety and marriages must reflect their holy calling, at home as well as at the altar.

They shall not shave their heads. No shaved heads, no long unkempt hair: neither the marks of pagan mourning nor neglect. The priest is to look orderly and self-controlled. God’s servants do not draw attention to themselves by extremes.

No priest shall drink wine. This is the rule God gave Aaron after Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire: “Drink no wine or strong drink … when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die” (Leviticus 10:9). Those who handle holy things need clear minds: “Be sober-minded; be watchful” (1 Peter 5:8).

Only virgins of the offspring of the house of Israel. Marriage laws for priests follow Leviticus, but every priest must now marry a virgin of Israel, the stricter rule once given only to the high priest (Leviticus 21:7, 13–14), with one exception, the widow of a priest. The priest’s home, not only his work, was to reflect the holiness of his calling. The New Testament asks the same of church leaders: an overseer “must manage his own household well” (1 Timothy 3:4).

verseByVerse.quote: They shall teach my people the difference between the holy and the common, and show them how to distinguish between the unclean and the clean. In a dispute, they shall act as judges, and they shall judge it according to my judgments. They shall keep my laws and my statutes in all my appointed feasts, and they shall keep my Sabbaths holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The faithful priests must teach the difference between the holy and the common that Jerusalem’s priests had erased, judge by God’s judgments and keep his law themselves.

The difference between the holy and the common. Here is the priest’s great task, and the reversal of the old failure. Of the priests of Jerusalem God had said: “They have made no distinction between the holy and the common, neither have they taught the difference between the unclean and the clean” (22:26). Now the faithful priests will do what the unfaithful refused.

They shall teach my people. Teaching is at the heart of ministry: “For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Malachi 2:7). A church whose leaders no longer teach the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean, has already begun to drift where Jerusalem went.

According to my judgments. The priests also judge disputes, not by their own opinions but by God’s judgments, and they must keep his feasts and Sabbaths themselves. Those who teach God’s law must first obey it.

Where Christians differ: what of the Sabbath? Ezekiel describes the worship of God’s restored people in the forms of his own day, with Sabbaths and feasts. Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold the Lord’s Day to be the Christian Sabbath, and they are to be honoured as brothers. This commentary’s view: the Sabbaths and feasts were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and no day or feast binds the Christian conscience. The Lord’s Day is a gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy rather than as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience on it (Romans 14:5).

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not defile themselves by going near to a dead person. However, for father or mother, for son or daughter, for brother or unmarried sister they may defile themselves. After he has become clean, they shall count seven days for him. And on the day that he goes into the Holy Place, into the inner court, to minister in the Holy Place, he shall offer his sin offering, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests keep away from the dead, except their closest family, and even after cleansing offer a sin offering: God’s servants never outgrow their need of atonement.

They shall not defile themselves. Contact with a corpse made a person ceremonially unclean. Death is the fruit of sin, and the priests of the living God were to keep away from it, except for their closest family (Leviticus 21:1–3). God does not ask his servants to stop being sons, fathers and brothers. He allows them to grieve.

He shall offer his sin offering. Even after the normal time of cleansing, the priest (the ESV notes that “he” is a priest) waits another seven days, then offers “his sin offering” before ministering again. The servant of God is never above needing atonement himself.

Christ and death. Christ has changed our relation to death. It is still an enemy, the last to be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26), and Christians still weep at gravesides. But he entered death and came out of it, so that for believers death no longer defiles and has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55–57).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests own no land, because God himself is their inheritance. “This shall be their inheritance: I am their inheritance: and you shall give them no possession in Israel; I am their possession” (v. 28). They will live from what the people give to God: the grain, sin and guilt offerings, every devoted thing, the first of the firstfruits and every offering (vv. 29–30). The people are to give the first of their dough, “that a blessing may rest on your house” (v. 30). And the priests must not eat anything that has died of itself or been torn by animals (v. 31). Those who live from God’s table are content with him and keep themselves clean.
verseByVerse.theology: The best inheritance is God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "This shall be their inheritance: I am their inheritance: and you shall give them no possession in Israel; I am their possession. They shall eat the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering, and every devoted thing in Israel shall be theirs. And the first of all the firstfruits of all kinds, and every offering of all kinds from all your offerings, shall belong to the priests. You shall also give to the priests the first of your dough, that a blessing may rest on your house. The priests shall not eat of anything, whether bird or beast, that has died of itself or is torn by wild animals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests receive no land because God himself is their inheritance, and they live from what his people give: the richest portion is the LORD.

I am their inheritance. Here is the heart of the chapter’s promise. When the land is divided, the priests are given “a place for their houses” (45:4), but no farm, no estate to pass down. Instead: “I am their inheritance … I am their possession”.

An old promise. God had said the same to Aaron: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel” (Numbers 18:20). And David took it on his lips: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot” (Psalm 16:5).

What would you rather have: an estate, or God? The world counts the priests poor; God counts them rich. And every believer, as part of “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), is invited to say the same: “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26).

Living from the offerings. God provides for those who have no land. They live from what the people give to God. So also “the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).

The first of your dough. A small, daily gift: the first of the dough, before the family ate (Numbers 15:20–21), with a promise attached, “that a blessing may rest on your house”. Giving the first to God is not a loss, nor a payment that buys his favour; it is a household’s trust in the Father who already provides for it. “Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce; then your barns will be filled with plenty” (Proverbs 3:9–10).

That has died of itself or is torn by wild animals. A last rule of holiness, from Leviticus 22:8: the priests may not eat what has died on its own or been killed by animals. Ezekiel himself had kept this all his life (4:14). Those who live from God’s table must not feed on what is unclean.

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

44.title: I Am Their Inheritance
44.overview:
Where we are. The glory of the LORD has come home and filled the temple (chapter 43). Now the vision turns from the building to the people who serve in it.

The message. Nearness to the holy God is a gift: faithfulness is honoured with it, and unfaithfulness forfeits it, yet even the fallen are given a place. The gate the LORD entered is shut for ever, because he has come to stay. Those who let the uncircumcised in heart handle holy things, and the Levites who led Israel into idolatry, lose the right to come near, though not their place in God’s house. The faithful sons of Zadok come near to his table, and their reward is the best of all: “I am their inheritance” (v. 28).

Why it was said. The service of the old temple had been corrupted from the inside: outsiders with no heart for God guarding the sanctuary, and Levites ministering before idols (see the introduction). The exiles, Ezekiel the priest among them, needed to know whether there would ever again be a faithful priesthood, and on what terms.

How the chapter makes its case. The outer east gate is shut, for the LORD has entered by it; only the prince may sit in it to eat before the LORD (vv. 1–3). Ezekiel sees the glory again and hears God rebuke Israel for admitting foreigners “uncircumcised in heart and flesh” into his sanctuary (vv. 4–9). The Levites who went astray will bear their punishment: they will guard and serve, but not come near as priests (vv. 10–14). The sons of Zadok, who stayed faithful, will draw near to minister, their whole lives ordered by his holiness (vv. 15–27). They will own no land, because the LORD is their possession, and they will live from the people’s offerings (vv. 28–31).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. God had promised, “I will raise up for myself a faithful priest” (1 Samuel 2:35), and the sons of Zadok were only a partial answer, for each still needed “his sin offering” (v. 27). The answer is Christ, “a merciful and faithful high priest” (Hebrews 2:17), who has no need to offer sacrifices “first for his own sins” (Hebrews 7:27). Through him every believer becomes part of “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), brought near to God’s table with God himself as our inheritance.

For us. Those who lead God’s people carry a weightier responsibility, because they can make others stumble. Yet God has humble work even for those who have failed him. And the deepest reward of following Christ is not position or possessions but God himself: “God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26).
44.theology:
The way by which the LORD has come in is honoured as his alone, and his glory will never depart again (vv. 1-2; 43:9).

Israel's prince is a human ruler who needs atonement; Christ is the sinless Priest-King who offered himself once for all (v. 3; 45:22; Heb 7:26-27).

Worship led by the uncircumcised in heart profanes God's house; in the new covenant, circumcision is of the heart by the Spirit, and Gentiles in Christ are members of God's household (vv. 6-9; Rom 2:28-29; Eph 2:12-19).

Unfaithfulness in God's service has consequences, especially for those who lead others astray, yet God still gives the fallen humble work in his house (vv. 10-14; Matt 18:6; 2 Sam 12:10, 13).

Faithfulness is rewarded with nearness to God, fulfilled in Christ the faithful high priest and shared with his royal priesthood (vv. 15-16; 1 Sam 2:35; Heb 2:17; 1 Pet 2:9).

Those who serve God must be holy in dress, habits and home, and must teach God's people to distinguish holy from common (vv. 17-24; 22:26; Mal 2:7).

God himself is the inheritance of those who serve him (v. 28; Num 18:20; Ps 16:5; 73:26).

God provides for his servants through the gifts of his people, and giving the first to God brings blessing (vv. 29-30; 1 Cor 9:14; Prov 3:9-10).
44.examples:
A church leader who has fallen and been removed from office may think there is no place left for him. The Levites of verses 10-14 lost the altar but were given the gates to keep. Restoration to fellowship and humble service is real grace, even where some consequences remain.

A minister on a modest stipend, or a missionary living on gifts, may feel poor beside friends with houses and pensions. Verse 28 is their wealth: I am their inheritance.

keyVerse.quote: This shall be their inheritance: I am their inheritance: and you shall give them no possession in Israel; I am their possession.
keyVerse.note: The faithful priests are given no land, because they are given God. The verse turns the whole chapter’s talk of nearness into a promise: the reward of faithful service is the Lord himself. In Christ every believer is made part of a royal priesthood and can say, “God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26).

44.reflection:
The east gate is shut “for the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered by it” (v. 2). What does that say about God’s intention to stay with his people? How does the promise of Christ’s presence (Matthew 28:20) steady you when God feels far away?

Israel “set others to keep my charge for you” (v. 8). In what ways are we tempted to want the privileges of belonging to God’s people while leaving the responsibilities to others?

The Levites who led others astray lost their priesthood but were still given work in God’s house (vv. 10–14). What does this teach about both the seriousness of leading others into sin and the mercy God shows to those who have failed?

The priests had no land because God was their inheritance (v. 28). If God himself is your portion, how might that change the way you think about money, possessions and ambition this week?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A Holy District at the Centre
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the land is shared out again, God’s portion comes first and sits at the centre. Before any tribe receives its land, a holy district is set apart for the LORD (v. 1). At its heart stands the sanctuary in its square of 500 cubits, with land around it for the priests who serve there (vv. 2–4) and a strip beside it for the Levites (v. 5). Next comes land for the city, which belongs to the whole house of Israel, not to any one tribe (v. 6). The prince receives a generous estate on either side, and the reason is given plainly: “my princes shall no more oppress my people” (vv. 7–8). The map itself is a lesson in justice.
verseByVerse.theology: God's portion stands at the centre of the land, and rulers are given enough so that they need not steal.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you allot the land as an inheritance, you shall set apart for the LORD a portion of the land as a holy district, 25,000 cubits long and 20,000 cubits broad. It shall be holy throughout its whole extent. Of this a square plot of 500 by 500 cubits shall be for the sanctuary, with fifty cubits for an open space around it. And from this measured district you shall measure off a section 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 broad, in which shall be the sanctuary, the Most Holy Place. It shall be the holy portion of the land. It shall be for the priests, who minister in the sanctuary and approach the LORD to minister to him, and it shall be a place for their houses and a holy place for the sanctuary. Another section, 25,000 cubits long and 10,000 cubits broad, shall be for the Levites who minister at the temple, as their possession for cities to live in. "Alongside the portion set apart as the holy district you shall assign for the property of the city an area 5,000 cubits broad and 25,000 cubits long. It shall belong to the whole house of Israel. "And to the prince shall belong the land on both sides of the holy district and the property of the city, alongside the holy district and the property of the city, on the west and on the east, corresponding in length to one of the tribal portions, and extending from the western to the eastern boundary of the land. It is to be his property in Israel. And my princes shall no more oppress my people, but they shall let the house of Israel have the land according to their tribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s portion is set apart first, at the centre, and the prince is given enough land that he need never take the people’s.

When you allot the land as an inheritance. For exiles who had lost every field they owned, these words were themselves a promise: there would be land to share again. With the long cubit of about twenty-one inches (ESV notes), the holy district is roughly eight miles long and more than six wide. Within it lie the sanctuary’s 500-cubit square (42:20), the priests’ and Levites’ land, and the city’s, which belongs “to the whole house of Israel” (v. 6); chapter 48 sets it on the map.

Set apart for the LORD. God is not given what is left after everyone else is satisfied; he is given the centre, first. “But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33).

My princes shall no more oppress my people. The prince is given a generous estate so that he will not do what Israel’s kings did, taking their subjects’ fields (see the note on v. 9). Now the ruler has land of his own and no excuse to take anyone else’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Justice, Honest Weights and Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people gathered around God’s holiness must deal justly. The vision suddenly becomes a sermon to Israel’s rulers: “Enough, O princes of Israel!” They must stop their violence and their evictions, and do justice and righteousness (v. 9). Every measure of grain, oil and silver must be honest, fixed by God and not by the powerful (vv. 10–12). Then the people bring small, fixed offerings to the prince, and he in turn must supply the sacrifices for the feasts, new moons and Sabbaths, “to make atonement on behalf of the house of Israel” (vv. 13–17). The ruler receives in order to serve the worship of God’s people.
verseByVerse.theology: True worship and honest dealing belong together, and the ruler is to serve the worship of God's people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: Enough, O princes of Israel! Put away violence and oppression, and execute justice and righteousness. Cease your evictions of my people, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God breaks into the vision to command Israel’s rulers to stop seizing land and to do what is just and right.

Enough, O princes of Israel! Suddenly the vision becomes a sermon to Ezekiel’s own day. God names the rulers’ conduct, “violence and oppression”, and calls them to what Jeremiah had demanded of Judah’s kings: “Do justice and righteousness” (Jeremiah 22:3).

Cease your evictions of my people. The word means driving people out of their holdings. In Israel the land was each family’s inheritance from God, not the king’s to hand out (Leviticus 25:23). Kings took it all the same. Samuel had warned that a king “will take the best of your fields and vineyards” (1 Samuel 8:14); Ahab had Naboth killed to take his vineyard (1 Kings 21); and Ezekiel had condemned the shepherds who ruled “with force and harshness” (34:4). The rule returns in 46:18.

Power under God. God cares how power is used. Everyone with authority, in government, business, church or home, answers to him for those under them. The King who holds all authority used it to give his life (Mark 10:45), and he is the measure of every lesser ruler.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall have just balances, a just ephah, and a just bath. The ephah and the bath shall be of the same measure, the bath containing one tenth of a homer, and the ephah one tenth of a homer; the homer shall be the standard measure. The shekel shall be twenty gerahs; twenty shekels plus twenty-five shekels plus fifteen shekels shall be your mina.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself fixes honest measures, so that no ruler or merchant can quietly shift them.

Just balances, a just ephah, and a just bath. An ephah was a dry measure and a bath a liquid measure, each about twenty-two litres (so the ESV notes). Cheating with scales was an old sin, and the law had forbidden it (Leviticus 19:35–36): “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1).

The homer shall be the standard measure. A homer (probably a donkey’s load) held ten ephahs or ten baths. One standard for dry and liquid goods alike, and a shekel of twenty gerahs as the law had fixed it (Exodus 30:13), left no room for the trick Amos condemned: to “make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances” (Amos 8:5).

Worship and honest business. This rule stands between the sanctuary and the sacrifices: the God worshipped at the altar watches the scales. “He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). Micah said this to a people already redeemed (Micah 6:4): it is not a way of earning favour. Where we have not dealt justly, Christ the perfectly just King obeyed in our place, so we come back to God by confessing our sin, not by despairing.

Uncertain wording. Twenty plus twenty-five plus fifteen shekels makes a mina of sixty, the standard also used in Babylon. Why the sum is written in three parts is not known; the total, and the point, are clear.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the offering that you shall make: one sixth of an ephah from each homer of wheat, and one sixth of an ephah from each homer of barley, and as the fixed portion of oil, measured in baths, one tenth of a bath from each cor (the cor, like the homer, contains ten baths). And one sheep from every flock of two hundred, from the watering places of Israel for grain offering, burnt offering, and peace offerings, to make atonement for them, declares the Lord GOD. All the people of the land shall be obliged to give this offering to the prince in Israel. It shall be the prince's duty to furnish the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings, at the feasts, the new moons, and the Sabbaths, all the appointed feasts of the house of Israel: he shall provide the sin offerings, grain offerings, burnt offerings, and peace offerings, to make atonement on behalf of the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people give small, fixed offerings to the prince, and he uses them to supply the nation’s sacrifices: he receives in order to serve.

This is the offering that you shall make. The rates are small: a sixtieth of the wheat and barley (a sixth of an ephah from each homer of ten ephahs), a hundredth of the oil, one sheep in two hundred. “The watering places of Israel” probably means well-watered pastures.

It shall be the prince’s duty. The gift goes “to the prince in Israel” (v. 16), not to enrich him, but to supply the burnt, grain and drink offerings for the feasts, the new moons and the Sabbaths, “to make atonement on behalf of the house of Israel” (v. 17). The ruler exists to serve the worship of God’s people.

A priest on his throne. Here is good leadership, and a pointer to the King who did not merely provide offerings but became the offering. Zechariah foresaw one who would “sit and rule on his throne. And there shall be a priest on his throne” (Zechariah 6:13).

How can there be sin offerings after Christ? The vision uses the forms its hearers knew to picture God dwelling with a cleansed people (see the notes on 40:1–4 and 43:18–27). Christ’s sacrifice was offered once for all (Hebrews 10:12, 18); the offerings in the vision point to it, they do not return after it. Ezekiel’s calendar also differs from Moses’, with no Day of Atonement and different amounts for the offerings, because it is a new picture, not a revision of the law. The differences troubled Jewish teachers too; an old tradition says some wanted to withdraw the book from public reading until a scholar showed how it could be squared with Moses. Read as a vision of worship made new, they are part of its message, not mistakes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even in the renewed temple, the year begins with atonement. On the first day of the first month a bull is offered, and its blood is put on the doorposts of the temple, the altar and the inner gate; the rite is repeated on the seventh day for those who have sinned without knowing it (vv. 18–20). At Passover the prince provides a sin offering “for himself and all the people of the land”, and burnt offerings on every day of the feast (vv. 21–24). The autumn feast of the seventh month receives the same (v. 25). The calendar of God’s people is built on cleansing, redemption and rejoicing.
verseByVerse.theology: God's people keep his calendar of cleansing and celebration, fulfilled in Christ our Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: In the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall take a bull from the herd without blemish, and purify the sanctuary. The priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering and put it on the doorposts of the temple, the four corners of the ledge of the altar, and the posts of the gate of the inner court. You shall do the same on the seventh day of the month for anyone who has sinned through error or ignorance; so you shall make atonement for the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The year begins with the sanctuary cleansed by blood, because even here the worshippers are sinners, and a holy God meets them only through atonement.

Purify the sanctuary. On the first day of the year a bull’s blood is put where worship passes: the temple doorposts, the altar ledge, the inner gate. The doorposts recall the first Passover, when blood on Israel’s doorposts turned judgment away (Exodus 12:7, 13), in the month God had made “the beginning of months” (Exodus 12:2). Ezekiel calls it making “atonement for the temple” (v. 20): the place where a holy God meets sinful people must be covered by blood.

Through error or ignorance. God provides even for the sins people do not know they have committed (Leviticus 4:2), and how many of ours are like that. In Christ we have a high priest who is not “unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15), and whose blood “cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7), noticed or not.

verseByVerse.quote: "In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall celebrate the Feast of the Passover, and for seven days unleavened bread shall be eaten. On that day the prince shall provide for himself and all the people of the land a young bull for a sin offering. And on the seven days of the festival he shall provide as a burnt offering to the LORD seven young bulls and seven rams without blemish, on each of the seven days; and a male goat daily for a sin offering. And he shall provide as a grain offering an ephah for each bull, an ephah for each ram, and a hin of oil to each ephah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Passover the prince gives lavishly, but his sin offering is for himself too: the best human ruler still needs atonement.

The Feast of the Passover. Passover remembered the night God passed over the houses marked with blood, and the seven days of unleavened bread followed. On its first day the prince provides a sin offering “for himself and all the people of the land” (v. 22): he too needs atonement.

Seven young bulls and seven rams. On each of the seven days the prince provides seven bulls, seven rams and a goat for a sin offering, with an ephah of grain for every bull and ram and a hin of oil (about four quarts, the ESV notes) to each ephah. That is far more than Moses required for the same week: two bulls, one ram and seven lambs a day (Numbers 28:19–24). The picture is of richer worship and a ruler who gives freely.

Christ our Passover. For Christians, Passover finds its meaning in one person: “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Ezekiel’s prince offers for himself; our King “has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins” (Hebrews 7:27). He needed no offering, and gave himself for us.

Where Christians differ: who is the prince? Some take him to be the Messiah, the coming David called “their prince forever” (37:25). Many dispensationalists see a human ruler governing under Christ in a future millennium. Others see in him a picture of godly rule among God’s renewed people. This commentary’s view: the prince of these chapters is a man, not the Messiah, for he offers a sin offering for himself (v. 22) and has sons (46:16) (see the note on 44:1–3). He pictures rule set right, and so points, by likeness and by contrast, to the true Prince who needed no offering.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month and for the seven days of the feast, he shall make the same provision for sin offerings, burnt offerings, and grain offerings, and for the oil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The autumn feast receives the same offerings as Passover: the whole year, redemption and harvest joy alike, rests on atonement.

In the seventh month. The fifteenth day of the seventh month is the date of the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:34). So the year turns on two feasts, one remembering redemption from Egypt, the other God’s care in the wilderness: a calendar of grace.

He shall make the same provision. The autumn feast receives exactly what Passover received. Booths was the feast of rejoicing at the end of harvest (“you shall rejoice before the LORD your God seven days”, Leviticus 23:40), yet it too begins with sin offerings: even joy before God rests on atonement. Ezekiel names only these two feasts; the Feast of Weeks is not mentioned (on how this calendar differs from Moses’, see the note on vv. 13–17).

At the feast of Booths. It was at this feast, on its last and greatest day, that Jesus stood in the temple and offered “rivers of living water” to all who are thirsty (John 7:37–39; see the note on 47:8–9). The sacrifice and the river meet in him.

45.title: Enough, O Princes of Israel
45.overview:
Where we are. The temple has been measured (chapters 40–42), the glory of God has come home to it (chapter 43), and the priests have been set in order (chapter 44). Now the vision widens from the house to the land around it and to the man who rules there.

The message. When God lives among his people, everything is arranged around him: his portion at the centre, then the priests, the Levites, the city and the prince. And a people with God at the centre must be a just people. Rulers must stop seizing land, every measure must be honest, and the prince must serve his people’s worship instead of profiting from it.

Why it was said. Israel’s kings had treated the land and the people as theirs to take, from Ahab’s seizure of Naboth’s vineyard to the shepherds who ruled “with force and harshness” (34:4) (see the introduction). Exiles who owned nothing needed to hear that there would be land to share again, and that it would never again lie at the mercy of greedy rulers.

How the chapter makes its case. First a holy district is set apart at the centre of the land, with the sanctuary at its heart and the prince’s estate on either side, so that “my princes shall no more oppress my people” (vv. 1–8). Then the vision breaks into a sermon: “Enough, O princes of Israel!” Violence and evictions must end, and every measure must be just (vv. 9–12). The people bring small, fixed offerings to the prince, who must supply the sacrifices for all the feasts (vv. 13–17). The year begins with the sanctuary cleansed by blood (vv. 18–20), and at Passover and the autumn feast the prince provides sin offerings for himself and all the people (vv. 21–25).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by contrast, and by the need it exposes. The prince is a better ruler than Israel’s kings: he has enough, takes nothing, and provides for his people’s worship. Yet he is only a man, who must bring a sin offering for himself (v. 22). The longing for a just ruler who serves his people before God is met in the King who needed no offering for himself, “since he did this once for all when he offered up himself” (Hebrews 7:27): Christ our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

For us. God still watches the scales. Whatever power we hold, at work, in church or at home, is his, to be used for others and not taken from them. And where we have taken, Christ the just King has already given himself for us, so we come back to him by honest confession, not by despair.
45.theology:
God's portion comes first and stands at the centre of his people's life (vv. 1-6; Matt 6:33).

God condemns rulers who use power to oppress and dispossess, and calls all in authority to justice and righteousness (vv. 8-9; 1 Sam 8:14; 34:4; Jer 22:3).

Honest dealing belongs with true worship; God delights in a just weight (vv. 10-12; Lev 19:35-36; Prov 11:1; Mic 6:8).

The ruler is to serve the worship of God's people, pointing to Christ, the priest-king who gave himself (vv. 16-17; Zech 6:13).

God provides atonement even for sins committed in error or ignorance (v. 20; Lev 4:2; Heb 4:15).

The Passover is fulfilled in Christ, our Passover lamb (vv. 21-22; 1 Cor 5:7).
45.examples:
A shopkeeper who rounds the weight up, a tradesman who pads an invoice, a manager who quietly squeezes his staff: verses 9-12 deal with these in the middle of a vision about worship. The God we worship on Sunday watches the scales on Monday.

A believer troubled by sins she cannot even name can rest in verse 20. God provided for sins of error or ignorance, and Christ's sacrifice covers what we never knew to confess.

keyVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: Enough, O princes of Israel! Put away violence and oppression, and execute justice and righteousness. Cease your evictions of my people, declares the Lord GOD.
keyVerse.note: Here the vision breaks into a sermon, and the verse explains why the land is mapped as it is: with God at the centre, there must be justice at every edge. Rulers are to stop taking and start doing right, a demand that exposes every human ruler and is fully met only in the King who used his power to give himself.

45.reflection:
Before any tribe receives its land, God’s portion is set apart at the centre (vv. 1–4). What would it look like for God to have the centre, and not the leftovers, of your time, money and plans?

“Enough, O princes of Israel!” (v. 9). Where do you hold some power over others, at work, in church or at home? How might you be tempted to take instead of give, and what would justice look like there?

The rule about honest weights stands in the middle of a vision of worship (vv. 10–12). Why does God join worship and business so closely? Where are the “scales” in your own working life?

Even the prince must bring a sin offering for himself (v. 22). What does that teach about every human leader, and how does it deepen your gratitude for Christ, who needed no offering and offered himself?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Prince and People at Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship sets the rhythm of life in God’s house, and the ruler worships as one of the people. The inner east gate is shut on working days but opened on Sabbaths and new moons; the prince worships at its threshold while the priests offer his sacrifices, and the people bow at its entrance (vv. 1–3). His offerings are set out, with grain “as much as he is able” (vv. 4–8). At the great feasts the crowds pass straight through the courts, and the prince goes in and out with them (vv. 9–10). A freewill offering opens the east gate for him (vv. 11–12), and beneath every special day lies the daily lamb, offered “morning by morning” for ever (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Ruler and people worship God together, and worship rests on a daily offering that never stops.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: The gate of the inner court that faces east shall be shut on the six working days, but on the Sabbath day it shall be opened, and on the day of the new moon it shall be opened. The prince shall enter by the vestibule of the gate from outside, and shall take his stand by the post of the gate. The priests shall offer his burnt offering and his peace offerings, and he shall worship at the threshold of the gate. Then he shall go out, but the gate shall not be shut until evening. The people of the land shall bow down at the entrance of that gate before the LORD on the Sabbaths and on the new moons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On Sabbaths and new moons the inner gate is opened, and prince and people worship together, he at its threshold and they at its entrance: even the ruler is a worshipper, not a priest.

On the Sabbath day it shall be opened. On the six working days the inner east gate stays closed; on the Sabbath and the new moon it opens. Time itself is marked out for God.

He shall worship at the threshold of the gate. The prince stands in the gateway, closer than anyone except the priests, but he goes no further: “The priests shall offer his burnt offering and his peace offerings” (v. 2). He is a worshipper, not a priest. Israel’s kings had not always kept that line: King Uzziah burned incense in the temple and was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). And the people bow at the same gate behind him: leader and people facing the same Lord.

The gate shall not be shut until evening. The gate stays open all day, and through it the people bowing at the entrance (v. 3) could look across to the altar. On God’s appointed days the way stands open, and even those who may not go in can see the sacrifice offered for them.

Must Christians keep Sabbath and new-moon worship? These are shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and no day binds the conscience; worship on the Lord’s Day is a gift to keep gladly. Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession, hold the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath, and they are honoured brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: The burnt offering that the prince offers to the LORD on the Sabbath day shall be six lambs without blemish and a ram without blemish. And the grain offering with the ram shall be an ephah, and the grain offering with the lambs shall be as much as he is able, together with a hin of oil to each ephah. On the day of the new moon he shall offer a bull from the herd without blemish, and six lambs and a ram, which shall be without blemish. As a grain offering he shall provide an ephah with the bull and an ephah with the ram, and with the lambs as much as he is able, together with a hin of oil to each ephah. When the prince enters, he shall enter by the vestibule of the gate, and he shall go out by the same way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prince’s offerings for Sabbath and new moon are set out, generous yet never beyond what the worshipper has.

Six lambs without blemish and a ram without blemish. The Sabbath offering is larger than the two lambs Moses asked (Numbers 28:9); at the new moon Moses had required two bulls, a ram and seven lambs (Numbers 28:11), and Ezekiel’s figure is slightly smaller. These are not corrections of Moses but part of a new picture of worship (see the note on 45:13–17).

As much as he is able. The ram and the bull each have a fixed grain offering, an ephah, but with the lambs it is “as much as he is able” (v. 5). God does not demand what his servants do not have: “For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12).

He shall go out by the same way. Since the prince goes no further than the threshold (v. 2), he leaves the way he came; the people’s route at the feasts is different (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: "When the people of the land come before the LORD at the appointed feasts, he who enters by the north gate to worship shall go out by the south gate, and he who enters by the south gate shall go out by the north gate: no one shall return by way of the gate by which he entered, but each shall go out straight ahead. When they enter, the prince shall enter with them, and when they go out, he shall go out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the great feasts the crowds pass straight through the courts, and the prince goes in and out among them: the leader belongs with those he leads.

Each shall go out straight ahead. The crowds are large, so there is a one-way system: in by the north gate and out by the south, or the reverse. It is also a picture: the worshipper does not go out the way he came in. Meeting God moves us forward.

The prince shall enter with them. On feast days the prince has no private entrance. He goes in with the people and out with the people. Our Lord is like that: “he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, ‘I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise’” (Hebrews 2:11–12).

verseByVerse.quote: "At the feasts and the appointed festivals, the grain offering with a young bull shall be an ephah, and with a ram an ephah, and with the lambs as much as one is able to give, together with a hin of oil to an ephah. When the prince provides a freewill offering, either a burnt offering or peace offerings as a freewill offering to the LORD, the gate facing east shall be opened for him. And he shall offer his burnt offering or his peace offerings as he does on the Sabbath day. Then he shall go out, and after he has gone out the gate shall be shut.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grain offerings at the feasts follow the Sabbath pattern, and a freewill offering opens the east gate for the prince, but only while the offering is made.

At the feasts and the appointed festivals. The grain offering follows the Sabbath pattern (v. 5): a fixed ephah with each bull and each ram, and with the lambs whatever the worshipper can give.

A freewill offering. When the prince brings a freewill offering, a gift beyond what is required, the east gate is opened for him (v. 12). God welcomes the worship that is not demanded but freely given (Psalm 54:6).

After he has gone out the gate shall be shut. A freewill offering could be brought on any day, so the east gate might open even on a working day; but it opens for the offering and is shut again as soon as the prince leaves. The gate through which the glory of God came back (43:1–5; 44:1–2) is never treated as an ordinary door.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall provide a lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering to the LORD daily; morning by morning you shall provide it. And you shall provide a grain offering with it morning by morning, one sixth of an ephah, and one third of a hin of oil to moisten the flour, as a grain offering to the LORD. This is a perpetual statute. Thus the lamb and the meal offering and the oil shall be provided, morning by morning, for a regular burnt offering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beneath every special day lies an ordinary morning and its lamb: the worship of God’s people rests on a sacrifice provided day after day.

A lamb a year old without blemish. Every morning a lamb is offered, with flour and oil (v. 14), as “a perpetual statute”. Under Moses there was a lamb in the morning and another at twilight (Exodus 29:38–39); here Ezekiel mentions only the morning. Every day begins with an offering.

This is a perpetual statute. The daily offering was the heartbeat of Israel’s worship, and losing it was a mark of disaster: in Daniel’s vision an enemy takes away “the regular burnt offering” (Daniel 8:11). In Ezekiel’s vision it is restored and never stops.

Morning by morning. Those daily lambs could never finish the work of taking sin away: “every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins” (Hebrews 10:11). But they pointed to the one of whom John said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Because his offering is complete, every morning the believer wakes to mercy already provided: “his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — The Prince Must Not Take
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prince must give from his own and never take what belongs to the people. If he gives land to one of his sons, it stays in the family; if he gives it to a servant, it returns to him in the year of liberty (vv. 16–17). Above all, “The prince shall not take any of the inheritance of the people, thrusting them out of their property” (v. 18). The reason is God’s care for his flock: “so that none of my people shall be scattered from his property”. The evictions condemned in 45:9 are ruled out for good.
verseByVerse.theology: God's King gives to his people; he does not take from them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: If the prince makes a gift to any of his sons as his inheritance, it shall belong to his sons. It is their property by inheritance. But if he makes a gift out of his inheritance to one of his servants, it shall be his to the year of liberty. Then it shall revert to the prince; surely it is his inheritance—it shall belong to his sons. The prince shall not take any of the inheritance of the people, thrusting them out of their property. He shall give his sons their inheritance out of his own property, so that none of my people shall be scattered from his property."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prince may give land to his family from his own estate, but he must never take the people’s inheritance, so that none of God’s flock is scattered.

The year of liberty. This is the Jubilee, every fiftieth year, when “each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan” (Leviticus 25:10). A gift to a servant lasts until then; land was never to be lost for good from the family God gave it to.

The prince shall not take any of the inheritance of the people. He must reward his family from what is his, not take what is theirs. The old shepherds had scattered the flock: “My sheep were scattered” (34:6). The new ruler must never scatter them from their inheritance.

The good shepherd. How different is the true King. “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:10–11). He does not take our inheritance; he gives us his (Romans 8:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — The Kitchens of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tour of the temple ends, surprisingly, in the kitchens. Ezekiel is shown a place beside the priests’ chambers where the most holy offerings are boiled and baked, so that their holiness is not carried out among the people (vv. 19–20). Then, in the four corners of the outer court, he sees small courts lined with hearths: “These are the kitchens where those who minister at the temple shall boil the sacrifices of the people” (vv. 21–24). The holy God who keeps his things apart also prepares a meal for his people to share in his presence.
verseByVerse.theology: In God's house there is a place to eat with joy before him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me through the entrance, which was at the side of the gate, to the north row of the holy chambers for the priests, and behold, a place was there at the extreme western end of them. And he said to me, "This is the place where the priests shall boil the guilt offering and the sin offering, and where they shall bake the grain offering, in order not to bring them out into the outer court and so transmit holiness to the people." Then he brought me out to the outer court and led me around to the four corners of the court. And behold, in each corner of the court there was another court— in the four corners of the court were small courts, forty cubits long and thirty broad; the four were of the same size. On the inside, around each of the four courts was a row of masonry, with hearths made at the bottom of the rows all around. Then he said to me, "These are the kitchens where those who minister at the temple shall boil the sacrifices of the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tour ends in the kitchens: the most holy offerings are kept apart, but the people’s sacrifices are cooked for a shared meal before the LORD.

Where the priests shall boil the guilt offering. The priests’ kitchen keeps the most holy portions apart (compare 42:13; 44:19), so as not to “transmit holiness to the people” (v. 20). In the four corner courts the people’s peace offerings are cooked, so that worshippers and their families can eat together in God’s house. Moses had said, “And there you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households” (Deuteronomy 12:7).

These are the kitchens. So the tour that began at the gates ends among cooking pots. The God of the Most Holy Place is also the God of the shared meal. Zechariah foresaw a day when “every pot in Jerusalem and Judah shall be holy to the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 14:21). And all history is heading toward a feast: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). Even now the Lord’s Supper gives a taste of it, a meal at which Christ himself is host.

Uncertain wording. The word that describes the four corner courts in v. 22, translated “small” in the ESV, is uncertain in Hebrew (so the ESV notes). Their size and purpose are clear: four equal courts with hearths for cooking.

46.title: Morning by Morning
46.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 45 set out the prince’s land and duties; chapter 46 completes the rules for worship in the new temple before the river of chapter 47. It also ends the tour of the temple in an unexpected place: the kitchens.

The message. In God’s renewed house the whole of life keeps time with worship: the week, the month, the feasts and every single morning. Leader and people worship the same Lord together, the ruler at their head but not above them, giving and never taking. And worship ends at a shared meal, because the holy God wants his people to eat and rejoice in his presence.

Why it was said. Israel’s kings had treated the temple as their own chapel and the land as their own estate (43:7–9; 45:9), and when the temple burned, the daily offerings stopped (see the introduction). To exiles who had lost both the house and the rhythm of its worship, the vision promised that both would be restored, and set right.

How the chapter makes its case. The inner east gate opens on Sabbaths and new moons; the prince worships at its threshold while the people bow at its entrance (vv. 1–8). At the great feasts the crowds pass straight through the courts, and the prince goes in and out among them (vv. 9–10). Grain offerings and freewill offerings are regulated (vv. 11–12), and beneath every special day lies a lamb offered “morning by morning” (vv. 13–15). The prince may give land to his sons from his own estate, but must never take the people’s inheritance (vv. 16–18). Finally Ezekiel is shown the kitchens where the offerings are cooked for priests and people (vv. 19–24).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The daily lamb points to “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), whose single offering finished what the morning sacrifices could only repeat (Hebrews 10:11–12). The prince who enters with his people points to the Son who “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11), and the ruler forbidden to take points, by contrast, to the good shepherd who gives his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The kitchens look ahead to “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

For us. Christians do not keep Ezekiel’s calendar, but we still need its rhythm: worship that shapes every week and every morning, offered not to earn mercy but because mercy has been provided. So come to God gladly, together with his people, and expect to be fed.
46.theology:
God sets apart holy time for worship (vv. 1, 3).

The ruler is a worshipper among God's people, not a priest, and goes in and out with them, as Christ is not ashamed to call his people brothers (vv. 2, 10; 2 Chr 26:16-21; Heb 2:11-12).

God accepts offerings according to what a person has, and welcomes freewill worship (vv. 5, 7, 11-12; 2 Cor 8:12).

The daily lamb points to Christ, the Lamb of God, whose once-for-all sacrifice means mercy new every morning (vv. 13-15; Heb 10:11-12; John 1:29; Lam 3:22-23).

God's king must give to his people, not take from them, fulfilled in the good shepherd who lays down his life (vv. 16-18; Lev 25:10; 34:6; John 10:10-11).

Worship includes joyful fellowship at the table in God's presence, heading toward the marriage supper of the Lamb (vv. 19-24; Deut 12:7; Zech 14:20-21; Rev 19:9).
46.examples:
A widow on a small pension who is embarrassed by how little she can put in the offering may take heart from verse 5: as much as he is able. God measures the gift by the heart and the means, not by the amount.

A church meal after the morning service, with families eating together, is closer to Ezekiel's temple kitchens than it might seem. Fellowship at table is part of worship, and a foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb.

keyVerse.quote: When they enter, the prince shall enter with them, and when they go out, he shall go out.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter about the rhythm of worship, this small rule shows its spirit: the ruler has no private way into God’s presence but worships among his people. It answers the kings who had treated the temple as their own, and it points to the Son who “is not ashamed to call them brothers” and sings God’s praise in the midst of the congregation (Hebrews 2:11–12).

46.reflection:
Worship in this chapter keeps time with the week, the month and every morning (vv. 1–15). What rhythms of worship shape your own life? Which of them have slipped, and what would help you recover them?

The prince stands at the threshold but goes no further, and at the feasts he goes in and out with the people (vv. 2, 10). What does that teach about leaders in the church, and about how Christ relates to his people?

The daily lamb could never take sin away, but it pointed to the Lamb who did (vv. 13–15; Hebrews 10:11–12). How does knowing that his offering is complete change the way you begin each day?

The tour of God’s house ends in the kitchens, with families eating together before the LORD (vv. 19–24). How can your church’s shared meals, and the Lord’s Supper, express the joy of belonging to God’s household?

Then he led me back to the bank of the river.<sup>7</sup>As I went back, I saw on the bank of the river very many trees on the one side and on the other.<sup>8</sup>And he said to me, "This water flows toward the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah, and enters the sea; when the water flows into the sea, the water will become fresh.<sup>9</sup>And wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live, and there will be very many fish. For this water goes there, that the waters of the sea may become fresh; so everything will live where the river goes.<sup>10</sup>Fishermen will stand beside the sea. From Engedi to Eneglaim it will be a place for the spreading of nets. Its fish will be of very many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea.<sup>11</sup>But its swamps and marshes will not become fresh; they are to be left for salt.<sup>12</sup>And on the banks, on both sides of the river, there will grow all kinds of trees for food. Their leaves will not wither, nor their fruit fail, but they will bear fresh fruit every month, because the water for them flows from the sanctuary. Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing."<sup>13</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD: "This is the boundary by which you shall divide the land for inheritance among the twelve tribes of Israel. Joseph shall have two portions.<sup>14</sup>And you shall divide equally what I swore to give to your fathers. This land shall fall to you as your inheritance.<sup>15</sup>"This shall be the boundary of the land: On the north side, from the Great Sea by way of Hethlon to Lebo-hamath, and on to Zedad,<sup>16</sup>Berothah, Sibraim (which lies on the border between Damascus and Hamath), as far as Hazer-hatticon, which is on the border of Hauran.<sup>17</sup>So the boundary shall run from the sea to Hazar-enan, which is on the northern border of Damascus, with the border of Hamath to the north. This shall be the north side.<sup>18</sup>"On the east side, the boundary shall run between Hauran and Damascus; along the Jordan between Gilead and the land of Israel; to the eastern sea and as far as Tamar.
