With you they shall be allotted an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.<sup>23</sup>In whatever tribe the sojourner resides, there you shall assign him his inheritance, declares the Lord GOD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Life flows from God’s presence, and it grows from nothing into more than anyone can cross. Water comes out from under the temple threshold, toward the east and past the south side of the altar, and Ezekiel finds it trickling outside the shut east gate (vv. 1–2). The guide measures a thousand cubits at a time, and the water rises from ankle-deep to knee-deep to waist-deep, until it is “a river that I could not pass through” (vv. 3–5). No other stream feeds it. On the way back Ezekiel sees very many trees on both banks (vv. 6–7). The temple has become a new Eden.
verseByVerse.theology: The life that flows from God's presence grows from a trickle into a river too deep to cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me back to the door of the temple, and behold, water was issuing from below the threshold of the temple toward the east (for the temple faced east). The water was flowing down from below the south end of the threshold of the temple, south of the altar. Then he brought me out by way of the north gate and led me around on the outside to the outer gate that faces toward the east; and behold, the water was trickling out on the south side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Water flows out from under the temple threshold, beside the altar, and appears outside the shut east gate as a trickle: life for the world comes from God’s presence and the place of sacrifice, and it begins small.

Water was issuing from below the threshold. After chapters of measurements and rules, the vision suddenly comes alive: “and behold, water”. It flows east, the direction from which the glory came (43:2). In the Bible’s dry lands water meant life, and water flowing from God’s dwelling runs through Scripture. “A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden” (Genesis 2:10). “There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High” (Psalm 46:4). Joel promised that “a fountain shall come forth from the house of the LORD” (Joel 3:18). The temple is pictured again as Eden, and from God’s presence flows life for the world.

South of the altar. The river of life flows out beside the place of sacrifice: life for the world does not come without atonement. Some readers have also thought of the moment when a soldier pierced Jesus’ side, “and at once there came out blood and water” (John 19:34), from the body he had called the temple (John 2:19–21).

The water was trickling out. The east gate is shut (44:2), so Ezekiel is led out by the north gate and round to the outside of it, and there the water is only trickling. Not a flood: a trickle.

The day of small things. That is how God’s work so often begins: a baby in a manger, twelve ordinary men, a small group praying in an upper room. “For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice” (Zechariah 4:10). Jesus said the kingdom is like a mustard seed: “It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree” (Matthew 13:32). Never despise a trickle that comes from the sanctuary.
verseByVerse.note: From Jerusalem the river would run east through the Judean wilderness and drop about 1,200 metres to the Dead Sea, the lowest place on the earth's surface.

verseByVerse.quote: Going on eastward with a measuring line in his hand, the man measured a thousand cubits, and then led me through the water, and it was ankle-deep. Again he measured a thousand, and led me through the water, and it was knee-deep. Again he measured a thousand, and led me through the water, and it was waist-deep. Again he measured a thousand, and it was a river that I could not pass through, for the water had risen. It was deep enough to swim in, a river that could not be passed through.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The river deepens with no stream feeding it, from ankle-deep to deep enough to swim: its source is God, and the life he gives rises until it carries us.

The man measured a thousand cubits. The man who measured the temple now measures the river. Rivers grow deeper because streams flow into them, but no other stream is mentioned. This water grows by itself as it goes. Its source is inexhaustible because its source is God.

A river that I could not pass through. Ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, then out of his depth. At ankle depth a man is in control; he walks where he likes. At swimming depth, the river carries him.

Deeper into grace. Many people are content with ankle-deep faith: enough to say they have been in the water, not so much that it decides where they go. But God’s grace is not meant to stay at the ankles. It rises until we are carried by it, and its depth can never be fully measured: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). Paul prayed that believers would “comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:18–19).
verseByVerse.note: A thousand long cubits is about 580 yards, roughly a third of a mile.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, have you seen this?" Then he led me back to the bank of the river. As I went back, I saw on the bank of the river very many trees on the one side and on the other.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guide makes Ezekiel stop and take in what he has seen, and on the way back he finds the banks lined with trees: where the river flows, things grow.

Have you seen this? The guide stops Ezekiel as if to say: do not rush past this. Take in what you have just walked through.

Rivers of exile. The exiles in Babylon lived beside rivers: “By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept” (Psalm 137:1). Ezekiel himself had received his first vision by the Chebar canal (1:1). But those were rivers of exile. This is a river flowing from God’s house.

Very many trees. Going back, Ezekiel sees what he had not noticed going in: the banks are lined with trees, “very many”, on both sides. The land along this river is a garden, like Eden with its trees “pleasant to the sight and good for food” (Genesis 2:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — Everything Will Live Where the River Goes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The river heals the deadest place in the land. It flows down through the Arabah into the Dead Sea and makes its water fresh: “so everything will live where the river goes” (vv. 8–9). Fishermen spread their nets along the shore from Engedi to Eneglaim, and the fish are as many and varied as those of the Mediterranean (v. 10). Only the swamps and marshes are left for salt (v. 11). The trees on the banks never wither and bear fruit every month, “because the water for them flows from the sanctuary”, their fruit for food and their leaves for healing (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's presence brings life and healing to what was dead, fulfilled in the Spirit Christ gives and in the river of life in the new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "This water flows toward the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah, and enters the sea; when the water flows into the sea, the water will become fresh. And wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live, and there will be very many fish. For this water goes there, that the waters of the sea may become fresh; so everything will live where the river goes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The river flows into the Dead Sea and heals it, so that everything lives where the river goes: God’s life does not avoid the dead places but flows straight into them.

The water will become fresh. The Arabah is the deep valley in which the Jordan and the Dead Sea lie, and “the sea” is the Dead Sea, the lowest, deadest place in the land. Its water is nearly ten times saltier than the open sea, so no fish can live in it, and fish carried down by the Jordan die when they reach it. There the river works a miracle: the water “will become fresh”, or, as the ESV notes, it “will be healed”. God’s river does not avoid the dead places. It flows straight into them and heals them.

So everything will live where the river goes. Here is the heart of the chapter: life follows the river. And no one is too far gone for it. The Dead Sea is not asked to make itself fresh first; the river comes to it.

Rivers of living water. On the last day of a feast Jesus stood in the temple courts and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’ Now this he said about the Spirit” (John 7:37–39). No single Old Testament verse says those exact words, so Jesus was probably gathering up several promises. Ezekiel 47 is one. Another is Zechariah’s promise of living waters flowing from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8), in a passage about the Feast of Booths (Zechariah 14:16), the very feast at which Jesus was speaking. Whether the rivers flow from the believer’s heart or from Christ’s own (the Greek can be punctuated either way), their source is Christ. The river Ezekiel saw is given through Christ by the Holy Spirit, and it still flows into dead places, dead hearts, dead families, dead cities. Where it goes, things live.

Can people really change? Many thoughtful people quietly doubt it. We are told that temperament is largely inherited, that the patterns of childhood run deep, and that the best most of us can hope for is to manage ourselves a little better. There is honesty in that modesty, and it is gentler than the old advice simply to pull yourself together. But both views assume that whatever change comes must come from inside the sea. Ezekiel’s picture overturns that. The Dead Sea does not reform itself; nothing in it could. Fresh water arrives from somewhere else, and keeps arriving, until what was dead is full of fish. That is the New Testament’s account of change too: not self-improvement but new life given. “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). It is often slow, like a river rising a thousand cubits at a time, and the marshes (v. 11) remind us that it is not finished in this life. But the deadest places in a person are exactly where the river is heading.

Where Christians differ: is the river literal? Some, especially dispensationalists, expect a real river to flow from a rebuilt temple and heal the Dead Sea in a future millennium. This commentary’s view: it is a picture of the life God gives, flowing from his presence and healing all it reaches, as the New Testament reads it: Revelation takes it up for the river of life in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:1–2), and Jesus for the Spirit flowing from those who believe (John 7:38–39). This is how this commentary reads the whole temple vision (see the note on 40:1–4).
verseByVerse.note: The Dead Sea is nearly ten times saltier than the ocean, far too salty for fish.

verseByVerse.quote: Fishermen will stand beside the sea. From Engedi to Eneglaim it will be a place for the spreading of nets. Its fish will be of very many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fishermen spread their nets along the healed sea, and its fish are as many and varied as the Mediterranean’s: the dead place has become a place of plenty.

Fishermen will stand beside the sea. Picture it: fishermen on the shore of the Dead Sea, their nets spread out to dry. Engedi was an oasis on its western shore. Where there had never been a single fish there is now a fishing trade, and the healed sea is as full of life as the Great Sea itself.

Fishers of men. It is hard to read this without thinking of Jesus calling fishermen by the Sea of Galilee: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19). And of his parable: “the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind” (Matthew 13:47). Where the river of God’s Spirit flows, people of every kind are gathered in.
verseByVerse.note: En-gedi and En-eglaim lay along the Dead Sea; “the Great Sea” is the Mediterranean (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: But its swamps and marshes will not become fresh; they are to be left for salt. And on the banks, on both sides of the river, there will grow all kinds of trees for food. Their leaves will not wither, nor their fruit fail, but they will bear fresh fruit every month, because the water for them flows from the sanctuary. Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The marshes are left salt, but the trees on the banks bear fruit every month and their leaves heal, because their water flows from the sanctuary.

Its swamps and marshes will not become fresh. One exception: the swamps and marshes around the sea stay salty (again the Hebrew says they will not be “healed”, the ESV notes). Some see a practical provision: salt was valuable, needed even for the offerings (43:24), so God leaves a supply. Others see a sober note: the places the river does not enter remain as they were. Both are true to Scripture. God’s river brings life wherever it goes, and there is no life apart from it.

Because the water for them flows from the sanctuary. The trees bear “every month”, with no barren season, and the reason is given. They are not fruitful because they are strong trees, but because of where they are planted. That is the whole secret of a fruitful life: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither” (Psalm 1:3). Jesus put it simply: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing. The fruit is not for the tree; it is for others. A life planted beside God’s river becomes a source of nourishment and healing for others.

The Bible’s last chapter. The Bible’s last chapter returns to this very scene: “Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb through the middle of the street of the city; also, on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:1–2). What Ezekiel saw from afar, John saw in the new creation. The river flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb: the one who was sacrificed is the source of life for ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — The Boundaries of the Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his oath to the fathers by sharing out the land among his whole people. The land is to be divided among the twelve tribes, with two portions for Joseph, “And you shall divide equally what I swore to give to your fathers” (vv. 13–14). The borders are traced much as Moses traced them: on the north from the Great Sea to beyond Damascus (vv. 15–17), on the east down the Jordan to the Dead Sea (v. 18), on the south from Tamar to the Brook of Egypt (v. 19), and on the west along the Great Sea (v. 20). To exiles who owned nothing, a map this exact meant they would go home.
verseByVerse.theology: God keeps the promise he swore to Abraham, and gives his people an inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD: "This is the boundary by which you shall divide the land for inheritance among the twelve tribes of Israel. Joseph shall have two portions. And you shall divide equally what I swore to give to your fathers. This land shall fall to you as your inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God divides the land equally among all twelve tribes, because he swore to give it to their fathers: the exile has not cancelled his oath.

The twelve tribes of Israel. The land is to be divided among “the twelve tribes”, the whole people of God, north and south together again (37:22).

Joseph shall have two portions. That is, one for each of his sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as Jacob had promised: “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are” (Genesis 48:5). The tribe of Levi receives no ordinary territory, because God is their inheritance (44:28), so Joseph’s two portions keep the number at twelve.

Divide equally. In the old days some tribes had large lands and others small; here no tribe is more favoured in God’s gift.

What I swore to give to your fathers. The basis of it all is an oath. Centuries earlier God had said to Abraham, “To your offspring I will give this land” (Genesis 12:7). The exile seemed to cancel that promise. It did not. God keeps what he swears.

Uncertain wording. “This is the boundary” (v. 13) is a probable reading of the Hebrew, the ESV notes. The sense is not in doubt: the verses that follow trace the boundary.

verseByVerse.quote: "This shall be the boundary of the land: On the north side, from the Great Sea by way of Hethlon to Lebo-hamath, and on to Zedad, Berothah, Sibraim (which lies on the border between Damascus and Hamath), as far as Hazer-hatticon, which is on the border of Hauran. So the boundary shall run from the sea to Hazar-enan, which is on the northern border of Damascus, with the border of Hamath to the north. This shall be the north side. "On the east side, the boundary shall run between Hauran and Damascus; along the Jordan between Gilead and the land of Israel; to the eastern sea and as far as Tamar. This shall be the east side. "On the south side, it shall run from Tamar as far as the waters of Meribah-kadesh, from there along the Brook of Egypt to the Great Sea. This shall be the south side. "On the west side, the Great Sea shall be the boundary to a point opposite Lebo-hamath. This shall be the west side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The borders are traced much as Moses traced them, from the Great Sea to the Jordan: a map this exact told exiles that they would go home.

The boundary of the land. The borders follow those Moses had traced (Numbers 34:1–12).

Along the Jordan. The east boundary is the Jordan, so the lands east of it, where Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh once settled, are not included. The whole people will live together in the land first promised to Abraham’s children, west of the Jordan.

The waters of Meribah-kadesh. The south reaches to Meribah-kadesh, where Israel had quarrelled with God (Numbers 20:13). Even the place of old rebellion lies within the inheritance. For the exiles, a list of borders as exact as this said: you will go home. For Christians, it is a pledge that God will give his people their whole inheritance.

Where Christians differ: do these borders still promise the land to the Jewish people, and to the modern state of Israel? Dispensationalists hold that they do: God’s promise to Abraham’s physical descendants remains literal, with its borders, and awaits fulfilment. This commentary’s view: Joshua says that “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed” (Joshua 21:45), and the New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs looked for “a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16). The tribal allotments in equal strips, with the sanctuary at the centre, read best as a picture of a people perfectly ordered around God, not a map for a modern state. The land is fulfilled in Christ and the new creation his people will inherit (Matthew 5:5). Faithful Christians differ here, and many on both sides share the hope of a great turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:26).

Uncertain wording. Part of verse 17 is uncertain in Hebrew (ESV notes), and many of the places named cannot now be located with certainty. The general line is clear: from the Mediterranean north and east to the region of Damascus, then down the Jordan.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–23 — An Inheritance for the Sojourner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land is shared with outsiders too. Israel is to divide it by tribes, but also to give an inheritance to the sojourners, foreigners who have settled among them and raised children there (vv. 21–22). “They shall be to you as native-born children of Israel”, allotted land among the tribes, and wherever a sojourner lives, there he receives his inheritance (vv. 22–23). The law had always told Israel to love the stranger; now the stranger is written into the family inheritance, a picture of the gospel that would bring the nations into God’s people.
verseByVerse.theology: Outsiders who join God's people share fully in the inheritance, as Gentiles do in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "So you shall divide this land among you according to the tribes of Israel. You shall allot it as an inheritance for yourselves and for the sojourners who reside among you and have had children among you. They shall be to you as native-born children of Israel. With you they shall be allotted an inheritance among the tribes of Israel. In whatever tribe the sojourner resides, there you shall assign him his inheritance, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Foreigners who have settled among God’s people receive an inheritance like the native-born: the outsider is written into the family.

The sojourners who reside among you. Then comes a surprise. The sojourners, foreigners who have settled in Israel and raised children there, are to receive land: not charity, not a corner, but an inheritance.

Love for the stranger. The law had always told Israel to love the stranger: “You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself” (Leviticus 19:34). But under the old arrangement the land stayed within the tribes. Here the outsider is written into the family inheritance.

In whatever tribe the sojourner resides. Wherever he lives, he belongs. This is the gospel shown beforehand in an Old Testament picture. Isaiah had heard God say, “Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, ‘The LORD will surely separate me from his people’” (Isaiah 56:3). And Paul tells Gentile believers: “So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). “And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29).

If you are in Christ. If you are in Christ, you are not a guest in God’s family, tolerated at the edges. You have an inheritance with his people.

47.title: The River of Life
47.overview:
Where we are. The glory has come home to the temple (chapter 43), and the priests, the prince and the worship have been set in order (chapters 44–46). Now the measured house comes alive: water flows out of it. After the river, the land is shared out (47:13–48:29), and the book ends with the city’s new name.

The message. Where God dwells, life flows out, and it grows with no other source until no one can wade across it. It runs into the deadest place in the land and heals it, so that “everything will live where the river goes” (v. 9). And the land it waters is shared, by God’s oath, among all his people, including the outsiders who have come to live among them.

Why it was said. The exiles sat by the rivers of Babylon, far from a ruined temple and a land they had lost (see the introduction). They needed to know that God’s presence would not merely return but overflow, and that his promise to their fathers still stood.

How the chapter makes its case. Water trickles from under the temple threshold, south of the altar (vv. 1–2), and grows, measured a thousand cubits at a time, until it is a river too deep to cross (vv. 3–5), lined with trees (vv. 6–7). It flows down into the Dead Sea and makes it fresh, so that fishermen spread their nets where nothing lived (vv. 8–10); the marshes are left for salt, but the trees bear fruit every month, with leaves for healing (vv. 11–12). Then God sets the boundaries of the land he swore to the fathers, to be shared equally by the twelve tribes (vv. 13–20), and gives the sojourners settled among them an inheritance as though they were born in Israel (vv. 21–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. On the last day of the Feast of Booths Jesus offered “rivers of living water”, and “this he said about the Spirit” (John 7:38–39). The river flows out beside the altar, as the Spirit’s life comes to us through Christ’s sacrifice, and John saw it at the end of the Bible, flowing “from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1). The sojourners’ inheritance is the gospel shown beforehand: in Christ, outsiders become “fellow citizens with the saints” (Ephesians 2:19).

For us. No one is too far gone for this river; the Dead Sea is not asked to make itself fresh first. So do not stay at ankle depth: plant your life where the water flows, and it will bear fruit for others. And if you once stood outside God’s people, in Christ you have a full inheritance among them.
47.theology:
Life flows from God's presence, as in Eden and the city of God, and it flows past the altar (vv. 1-2; Gen 2:10; Ps 46:4; Joel 3:18).

God's work often begins small and grows beyond all measuring (vv. 2-5; Zech 4:10; Matt 13:31-32; Rom 11:33; Eph 3:18-19).

The river pictures the life-giving Spirit whom Christ gives to those who believe (vv. 8-9; John 7:37-39).

God's life reaches into the deadest places and heals them; everything lives where the river goes (vv. 8-9).

Where God's life flows, people of every kind are gathered in (v. 10; Matt 4:19; 13:47).

Fruitfulness comes from being planted by the water that flows from God's presence, and its fruit is for the nourishment and healing of others (v. 12; Ps 1:3; John 15:5).

The vision is completed in the new creation, where the river of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb (v. 12; Rev 22:1-2).

God keeps the promise he swore to Abraham and gives his whole people an equal inheritance (vv. 13-20; Gen 12:7; 48:5; Rom 4:13; Heb 11:16).

Outsiders who join God's people share fully in the inheritance, as Gentiles do in Christ (vv. 22-23; Lev 19:34; Isa 56:3; Eph 2:19; Gal 3:29).
47.examples:
A small Bible study of four people in a flat, or a tiny church plant meeting in a school hall, may look like a trickle. The river of Ezekiel 47 began that way, and it was still God's river.

Someone who thinks his life is a Dead Sea, too bitter and too far gone for anything to grow, should notice that the sea did not make itself fresh. The river came to it.

A refugee family who join a church may wonder whether they will always be guests. Verses 22-23 answer: in God's family the sojourner receives an inheritance.

keyVerse.quote: And wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live, and there will be very many fish. For this water goes there, that the waters of the sea may become fresh; so everything will live where the river goes.
keyVerse.note: Its last words sum up the chapter: life follows the river that flows from God’s presence, and it flows into the deadest place in the land and heals it. Jesus offered this river to the thirsty as the Holy Spirit (John 7:37–39), and it still reaches places and people that seem beyond change.

47.reflection:
The river begins as a trickle and grows with no other stream feeding it (vv. 1–5). Where have you seen God’s work begin small? Why are we tempted to despise “the day of small things” (Zechariah 4:10)?

Ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, then deep enough to swim (vv. 3–5). How deep would you say you are in God’s grace at the moment? What keeps people at the depth where they still choose where they walk?

“Everything will live where the river goes” (v. 9). What “dead seas” in your life, family or town seem beyond change? How do Jesus’ words about rivers of living water (John 7:37–39) give hope for them?

Settled foreigners receive an inheritance as though they were native-born (vv. 22–23). What does this show about God’s heart for outsiders, and how should it shape the way your church welcomes people who feel they do not belong?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Seven Tribes to the North
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every tribe receives its place, beginning from the far north. The land is divided into strips running from east to west. Dan comes first, at the northern border, then Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Reuben and Judah, each with “one portion” (vv. 1–7). The order is not the order of Joshua’s day: the sons of Jacob’s servant wives lie toward the northern edge, and Judah lies next to the holy centre. But the words repeated for every tribe say what matters most. Near or far, every tribe receives a full share, even Dan, whose history had been one of wandering and idolatry.
verseByVerse.theology: Every tribe receives its place in the land God promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "These are the names of the tribes: Beginning at the northern extreme, beside the way of Hethlon to Lebo-hamath, as far as Hazar-enan (which is on the northern border of Damascus over against Hamath), and extending from the east side to the west, Dan, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Dan, from the east side to the west, Asher, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Asher, from the east side to the west, Naphtali, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Naphtali, from the east side to the west, Manasseh, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Manasseh, from the east side to the west, Ephraim, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Ephraim, from the east side to the west, Reuben, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Reuben, from the east side to the west, Judah, one portion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each tribe receives “one portion” in strips from north to south: in God’s kingdom every member of the family has a place, and none is written off.

One portion. The last chapter of Ezekiel reads like a map, and “one portion” is repeated for every tribe: each has its place. Dan, which had once wandered north and fallen into idolatry (Judges 18:30), is not written off. Reuben, whose tribe had settled east of the Jordan, now has land west of it.

A new arrangement. The order is not the order of Joshua’s day. Dan and Naphtali, sons of Rachel’s servant Bilhah (Genesis 30:5–8), and Asher, son of Leah’s servant Zilpah (Genesis 30:12–13), lie toward the northern edge, farthest from the sanctuary, while Judah lies next to the holy centre. But every tribe, near or far, receives a full portion. In God’s kingdom there are no second-class members of the family.

Where Christians differ: how should this map be read? Dispensational Christians, reading the promises to Israel’s tribes at face value, expect a literal future division of the land. Many others read it as a picture, in the terms of Israel’s inheritance, of God’s whole people settled securely around his presence, fulfilled in Christ and completed in the new creation. This commentary’s view: the second, as for the whole temple vision (see the note on 40:1–4), because the New Testament applies Ezekiel’s closing vision to the church and the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:10–22:2), with Christ himself as the temple (John 2:19–21). Faithful believers differ here, and on either reading the promise is the same: God will give each of his people a place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–22 — The Holy Portion at the Centre
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the centre of the land lies the portion set apart for the LORD, “with the sanctuary in the midst of it” (v. 8). The faithful priests, the sons of Zadok, live nearest to it, on land called “a most holy place” (vv. 9–12). The Levites have the next strip, which may never be sold, “for it is holy to the LORD” (vv. 13–14). The city’s land is worked by people “from all the tribes of Israel” (vv. 15–20), and the prince’s land lies on either side, between Judah and Benjamin (vv. 21–22). God’s presence stands at the centre and holds the whole people together.
verseByVerse.theology: God's presence stands at the centre of his people's life, uniting them around himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Adjoining the territory of Judah, from the east side to the west, shall be the portion which you shall set apart, 25,000 cubits in breadth, and in length equal to one of the tribal portions, from the east side to the west, with the sanctuary in the midst of it. The portion that you shall set apart for the LORD shall be 25,000 cubits in length, and 20,000 in breadth. These shall be the allotments of the holy portion: the priests shall have an allotment measuring 25,000 cubits on the northern side, 10,000 cubits in breadth on the western side, 10,000 in breadth on the eastern side, and 25,000 in length on the southern side, with the sanctuary of the LORD in the midst of it. This shall be for the consecrated priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept my charge, who did not go astray when the people of Israel went astray, as the Levites did. And it shall belong to them as a special portion from the holy portion of the land, a most holy place, adjoining the territory of the Levites. And alongside the territory of the priests, the Levites shall have an allotment 25,000 cubits in length and 10,000 in breadth. The whole length shall be 25,000 cubits and the breadth 20,000. They shall not sell or exchange any of it. They shall not alienate this choice portion of the land, for it is holy to the LORD. "The remainder, 5,000 cubits in breadth and 25,000 in length, shall be for common use for the city, for dwellings and for open country. In the midst of it shall be the city, and these shall be its measurements: the north side 4,500 cubits, the south side 4,500, the east side 4,500, and the west side 4,500. And the city shall have open land: on the north 250 cubits, on the south 250, on the east 250, and on the west 250. The remainder of the length alongside the holy portion shall be 10,000 cubits to the east, and 10,000 to the west, and it shall be alongside the holy portion. Its produce shall be food for the workers of the city. And the workers of the city, from all the tribes of Israel, shall till it. The whole portion that you shall set apart shall be 25,000 cubits square, that is, the holy portion together with the property of the city. "What remains on both sides of the holy portion and of the property of the city shall belong to the prince. Extending from the 25,000 cubits of the holy portion to the east border, and westward from the 25,000 cubits to the west border, parallel to the tribal portions, it shall belong to the prince. The holy portion with the sanctuary of the temple shall be in its midst. It shall be separate from the property of the Levites and the property of the city, which are in the midst of that which belongs to the prince. The portion of the prince shall lie between the territory of Judah and the territory of Benjamin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the centre of the land lies the holy portion with the sanctuary in its midst, and around it priests, Levites, city and prince: the whole nation is gathered around one centre.

The portion which you shall set apart. Chapter 45 described this area (45:1–8); here it is placed on the map, next to Judah.

The consecrated priests, the sons of Zadok. The priests who stayed faithful live closest to the sanctuary, on land called “a most holy place” (vv. 11–12). Faithfulness is remembered. Next to them are the Levites (v. 13).

They shall not sell or exchange any of it. This land cannot be sold or traded away, “for it is holy to the LORD” (v. 14). The whole land had always belonged to God (“for the land is mine”, Leviticus 25:23), but this portion is especially his. What is given to God is not ours to bargain with.

The workers of the city, from all the tribes of Israel. The city’s workers come from every tribe (v. 19). It belongs to no single tribe. It is a place where the whole people of God live and labour side by side.

Between the territory of Judah and the territory of Benjamin. Judah and Benjamin were the two tribes that stayed with David’s house when the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:21). Now they lie on either side of God’s dwelling, and around them the whole nation, once two kingdoms (37:22), is gathered around one centre.

Held together by his presence. God is not only at the centre of his people’s life; his presence is what holds them together. In Christ, “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one” (Ephesians 2:13–14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Five Tribes to the South
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Five more tribes lie south of the holy portion: Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun and Gad, down to the southern border that runs from Tamar to the Brook of Egypt and the Great Sea (vv. 23–28). The list ends with a summary and a signature: “This is the land that you shall allot as an inheritance among the tribes of Israel, and these are their portions, declares the Lord GOD” (v. 29). A promise drawn on a map, given to people who owned nothing, carries the full weight of God’s word.
verseByVerse.theology: God's promise is kept in full; no tribe is forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the rest of the tribes: from the east side to the west, Benjamin, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Benjamin, from the east side to the west, Simeon, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Simeon, from the east side to the west, Issachar, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Issachar, from the east side to the west, Zebulun, one portion. Adjoining the territory of Zebulun, from the east side to the west, Gad, one portion. And adjoining the territory of Gad to the south, the boundary shall run from Tamar to the waters of Meribah-kadesh, from there along the Brook of Egypt to the Great Sea. This is the land that you shall allot as an inheritance among the tribes of Israel, and these are their portions, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five tribes lie to the south, and the allotment ends with God’s own signature: a promise so certain that it can be drawn on a map.

Declares the Lord GOD. Gad, son of Zilpah (Genesis 30:10–11), lies at the southern edge; “the Great Sea” is the Mediterranean (ESV notes). The list ends with God’s own signature: “declares the Lord GOD”. It was spoken to exiles who owned nothing: no land, no temple, no city. God tells them exactly where each family will live. The promise is so certain that it can be drawn on a map.

A place prepared. So too for the Christian: “In my Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?” (John 14:2). The place is prepared by the one who does not forget his own.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends with a city and its name. Each of its four sides is 4,500 cubits long, with three gates named for the sons of Jacob, so that every tribe has its own way in (vv. 30–34). Its circumference is 18,000 cubits. But what matters most is not its walls or its measurements: “And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There” (v. 35). The glory that Ezekiel watched leave Jerusalem has come home for good, and at the end of the Bible John sees the same city.
verseByVerse.theology: The final word of the book is the presence of God with his people forever.

verseByVerse.quote: "These shall be the exits of the city: On the north side, which is to be 4,500 cubits by measure, three gates, the gate of Reuben, the gate of Judah, and the gate of Levi, the gates of the city being named after the tribes of Israel. On the east side, which is to be 4,500 cubits, three gates, the gate of Joseph, the gate of Benjamin, and the gate of Dan. On the south side, which is to be 4,500 cubits by measure, three gates, the gate of Simeon, the gate of Issachar, and the gate of Zebulun. On the west side, which is to be 4,500 cubits, three gates, the gate of Gad, the gate of Asher, and the gate of Naphtali. The circumference of the city shall be 18,000 cubits. And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city has twelve gates, one for every son of Jacob, and a new name, “The LORD Is There”: the book ends with God living among his people for good.

The gates of the city being named after the tribes. Levi, who had no territory, has a gate, and Joseph has one gate rather than two. When the land was divided, Joseph’s two sons Ephraim and Manasseh each counted as a tribe and Levi was left out; the gates go back to Jacob’s own twelve sons. Every son of Israel has a way into the city. No one is left without a door.

John saw the same city. “It had a great, high wall, with twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and on the gates the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel were inscribed” (Revelation 21:12). And the wall had twelve foundations bearing “the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb” (Revelation 21:14). The people of God from both covenants dwell in one city.

The LORD Is There. So the book ends, not with walls, gates or measurements, but with a name. Think of the journey Ezekiel has taken. He began as an exile by the Chebar canal, and there the glory of God appeared to him (1:1, 28). He watched that glory leave Jerusalem, pausing at the threshold and the east gate before it went (10:4, 18–19; 11:22–23). He preached the fall of the city, and the city fell. He saw the glory return (43:1–5). Now the last words of the book give the city a new name. Whatever it had been called before, the city of David, “the bloody city” (24:6), the ruined city, it will be called “The LORD Is There”.

God with us. Not wealth, not safety, not fame: the blessing of this city is God himself present in it. And the presence the exiles longed for came nearer than Ezekiel could have pictured: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The glory that left the temple in chapter 10 returned in a person, whose name is Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), and who promised, “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). John’s vision of the new Jerusalem ends where Ezekiel’s does: “And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

The last word. For the exiles, the last word of their prophet was not a threat but a promise: God will be with you. For believers today it is the same. Wherever we are called to live, however far from home we feel, the God who says “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5) is there. And one day we will live in the city whose name says it all.

The ache for home. Modern people move more than any generation before us: new cities, new jobs, new circles of friends, often a new self to go with them. The sociologists Peter Berger, Brigitte Berger and Hansfried Kellner called their study of modern consciousness The Homeless Mind (1973), arguing that modern life leaves many people with a lasting sense of belonging nowhere. We try to cure it with a place: the right house, the town we grew up in, the country as it used to be. But a place cannot be home by itself. Every house is emptied in the end, and the exiles knew better than anyone that a city can be lost. What makes Ezekiel’s city home is not its walls or its map but its name: someone is there. That is why a Christian can be at home anywhere and yet not fully at home anywhere yet. Home turns out to be a person, and he has promised to bring us to it: “I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also” (John 14:3).
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew the name is Yahweh-shammah. Some hear in its sound an echo of the Hebrew name Jerusalem; either way the city is defined not by its past but by who lives in it.

48.title: The LORD Is There
48.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of the book and of the great temple vision (chapters 40–48). The river has flowed and the borders have been drawn (chapter 47); now the land is shared out tribe by tribe, and the book ends with a city and its name.

The message. God will give every one of his people a place, and at the centre of it all will be God himself. Each tribe receives “one portion”, the holy portion with the sanctuary lies in the middle, and the city that belongs to all the tribes receives a new name: “The LORD Is There” (v. 35). The prophet who watched the glory leave Jerusalem ends with God dwelling among his people for good.

Why it was said. The exiles owned nothing: no land, no temple, no city, and some of their tribes had been scattered for generations (see the introduction). To them God drew a map with every tribe on it, and named the city for the one thing they had lost above all: his presence.

How the chapter makes its case. Seven tribes receive equal strips of land from the northern border southwards (vv. 1–7). Next to Judah lies the holy portion: the sanctuary in its midst, land for the faithful priests and for the Levites, the city’s land worked by people from every tribe, and the prince’s land on either side (vv. 8–22). Five tribes lie to the south (vv. 23–29). The city has twelve gates, three on each side, named for the sons of Jacob, and its name is “The LORD Is There” (vv. 30–35).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The presence that the name promises came nearer than Ezekiel could have pictured: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and his name is Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23). John saw the same city, with twelve gates named for the tribes and foundations named for the apostles, and “no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22).

For us. Every Christian has a place prepared, as certain as a tribe’s portion on Ezekiel’s map (John 14:2). What makes it home is not the place but the one who is there. So take comfort that wherever you are, he is with you now, and live as people whose home is with him.
48.theology:
God gives every member of his people a place; no tribe is second-class or forgotten (vv. 1-7, 23-29).

God's presence stands at the centre of his people's life and unites those who were divided (vv. 8, 21-22; 37:22; Eph 2:13-14).

Faithfulness is remembered, and what is holy to the LORD may not be bargained away (vv. 11-14; Lev 25:23).

The city of God belongs to all his people together (v. 19).

God's promise of an inheritance is so certain it can be mapped, fulfilled in the place Christ prepares for his people (v. 29; John 14:2).

The twelve gates of the city are fulfilled in the new Jerusalem, where the people of God from both covenants dwell together (vv. 30-34; Rev 21:12-14).

The goal of the whole book, and of all God's purposes, is his presence with his people: The LORD Is There, fulfilled in Immanuel and in the new creation (v. 35; Matt 1:23; 28:20; Rev 21:3, 22).
48.examples:
A Christian who feels on the edge of the church, never asked, never noticed, may think of Dan and Asher at the far edge of the map. They received the same full portion as Judah. In God's family no one is second-class.

Someone moving yet again for work, or living in a care home far from where she grew up, can take the last words of Ezekiel with her. Wherever God's people are, the deepest truth about the place is The LORD Is There.

keyVerse.quote: The circumference of the city shall be 18,000 cubits. And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There.
keyVerse.note: The last words of the book are its whole message in a name. The prophet who watched the glory of God leave a defiled temple ends with a city defined by who lives in it. That promise is kept in Immanuel, God with us, and completed in the new Jerusalem, whose temple is the Lord God and the Lamb.

48.reflection:
Every tribe, even Dan with its history of idolatry, receives “one portion” (vv. 1–7). What does that say to someone who feels written off by God or by the church?

The holy portion lies at the centre, and the city is worked by people from every tribe (vv. 8–22). What does it look like for God’s presence to be the centre that holds a church together, instead of a shared background, class or culture?

Ezekiel’s book moves from the glory leaving (chapters 10–11) to “The LORD Is There” (v. 35). How has Christ, Immanuel, fulfilled this promise already, and what are you still waiting for?

“Home turns out to be a person.” Where do you look for a sense of home and belonging? How does Jesus’ promise in John 14:2–3 change the way you live where you are now?
